The auction will be conducted on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (E-Kuber) system on November 17, 2026 (Tuesday). The Government Stock up to ten per cent of the notified amount of the sale of each stock will be allotted to eligible individuals and institutions, subject to a maximum limit of one per cent of its notified amount for a single bid per stock as per the 'Scheme for Non-competitive Bidding Facility'. Individual investors can also place bids as per the non-competitive scheme through the Retail Direct portal (https://rbiretaildirect.org.in).
Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (E-Kuber) system on November 17, 2026 (Tuesday). The competitive bids should be submitted between 10:30 A.M. and 11:30 A.M. and non-competitive bids should be submitted between 10:30 A.M. and 11:00 A.M.
In case of technical difficulties, Core Banking Operations Team may be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-69870466, 022-69870415).
For other auction related difficulties, IDMD Auction Team can be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-22702431, 022-22705125).
Only in the event of system failure, physical bids would be accepted. Such physical bids should be submitted to the Public Debt Office (email; Phone no: 022-22603456, 022-22603457, 022-22603190) in the prescribed form obtainable from RBI website (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewForms.aspx) before the auction timing ends.
The yield per cent per annum or the price as the case may be, expected by the bidder should be expressed up to two decimal points. An investor can submit more than one competitive bid at same/different rates of yield or prices in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (E-Kuber) system. However, the aggregate amount of bids submitted by a bidder should not exceed the notified amount for each State.
The Reserve Bank of India will determine the maximum yield / minimum price at which bids will be accepted. Stock will be issued for a minimum nominal amount of ₹10,000.00 and in multiples of ₹10,000.00 thereafter.
The results of the auction will be announced on November 17, 2026 (Tuesday) and payment by successful bidders will be made during banking hours on November 18, 2026 (Wednesday) at Mumbai and at respective Regional Offices of RBI.
The new State Government Stocks will bear interest at the rates determined by RBI at the auctions. For the new stock, interest will be paid half yearly on May 18 and November 18 of each year till maturity. For the re-issued Government Stock, interest will be paid at the rate as determined on the date of original issue of Government Stock and will be paid on half yearly basis till maturity. The Stocks will be governed by the provisions of the Government Securities Act, 2006 and the Government Securities Regulations, 2007.
The investment in State Government Stocks will be reckoned as an eligible investment in Government Securities by banks for the purpose of Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The stocks will qualify for the ready forward facility.
Ajit Prasad          
Deputy General Manager
(Communications)

items.content:
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 06, 2026, imposed a monetary penalty of ₹9.00 lakh (Rupees Nine Lakh only) on One Mobikwik Systems Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of the directions issued by RBI on ‘Prepaid Payment lnstruments (PPIs)’ and ‘Fraud reporting’. This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under the provisions of section 30(1) read with section 26(6) of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its operations for the period from June 2025 to March 2026. Based on supervisory findings of non-compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be imposed on it for its failure to comply with the said RBI directions.
After considering the company’s reply to the notice, additional submissions made by it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary penalty:
the company had allowed fund transfer by certain PPI holders to non-pre-registered beneficiaries beyond the prescribed limit.
the company failed to report certain frauds within the prescribed timeline.
The action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the company with its customers. Further, imposition of monetary penalty is without prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company.
(Brij Raj)           
Chief General Manager
Press Release: 2026-2027/1496

items.content:
I came looking for ancient soldiers and left thinking about Nigeria’s tourism potential. One thing I was particularly looking forward to during my visit to China was seeing the famous Terracotta Warriors in Xi’an. I had read about them, seen pictures, and of course, watched films inspired by the mysteries of ancient China. But nothing quite prepared me for the experience of standing in front of thousands of life-sized soldiers who have been buried underground for more than 2,000 years. And what an experience it was!
If you have watched Hollywood’s The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor, you may remember the mysterious army of clay soldiers that comes alive. Well, I finally got to see the real thing. Thankfully, none of them came alive while I was there. But standing in those enormous exhibition halls, surrounded by thousands of soldiers, horses and chariots arranged in military formation, I couldn’t help wondering what must have gone through the minds of the people who created this extraordinary army.
The story takes us back to 221 BC when Qin Shi Huang became the first emperor to unify China. Like many powerful rulers of his time, he was obsessed with immortality and the idea of continuing his reign beyond death. His solution was to build an entire underground army to protect him in the afterlife. Think about that.
While some people prepared for retirement, this emperor was preparing for eternity, complete with his own military formation. The scale of the project is difficult to comprehend. Thousands of life-sized clay soldiers, horses and chariots were painstakingly created.
Above the excavation pit in Xi’an, I stood where visitors have looked down on the Terracotta Army for decades: thousands of figures, each made by hand, and still not fully unearthed.
What makes the discovery even more fascinating is that the soldiers are not identical. They have different facial features, hairstyles, uniforms and expressions. They look like real individuals, each with a distinct identity and military rank.
Then comes another remarkable twist. For over 2,000 years, this enormous army remained hidden beneath the earth until 1974 when some local farmers digging a well stumbled upon fragments of what would become one of the greatest archaeological discoveries in modern history. Imagine going out to dig a well and discovering an entire army. I wonder what the conversation was like that evening when they returned home.
Today, the site is recognised globally as one of the greatest archaeological treasures in the world, and is popularly described as the Eighth Wonder of the World. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) designated the Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor a World Heritage Site in 1987.
But beyond the fascinating history, what struck me most was what China has done with this discovery. This is where the story becomes particularly interesting for Nigeria. China has not simply uncovered an ancient treasure and left it to gather dust; it has invested in archaeological research, conservation, restoration, museum infrastructure, visitor facilities and tourism development.
The preservation work itself is remarkable. Some of the warriors originally had brightly painted surfaces, but exposure to the atmosphere caused much of the colour to deteriorate. This is why conservation experts have to work carefully to protect what remains. In other words, these people understand that preserving history requires knowledge, patience, investment and a long-term commitment.
And they have turned that commitment into an extraordinary tourism opportunity. The Terracotta Warriors Museum attracted more than 10 million visitors in 2025. Think about the economic activities generated by that number of visitors: flights, hotels, restaurants, taxis, tour operators, souvenirs, local businesses and employment opportunities.
The benefits do not end at the museum gates. Xi’an has built a thriving tourism economy around its ancient city walls, historical sites, museums, cultural performances, traditional architecture and cuisine.
The city reported tourism revenue of about 376 billion Chinese yuan in 2024. Of course that figure represents the wider city’s tourism economy, not the earnings of the Terracotta Warriors Museum alone. But it demonstrates the enormous economic possibilities that can emerge when a city deliberately invests in its history and culture.
Now, let us bring the conversation home. Nigeria is not lacking in history. If anything, we are sitting on a goldmine of historical and cultural treasures that we have not fully explored. Think about the ancient Nok civilisation and its remarkable terracotta sculptures. Think about the Benin Kingdom and its extraordinary bronze and brass works. Think about the ancient Kano city walls, the Zaria city walls, the Sukur Cultural Landscape, the Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove and the many historical settlements and monuments scattered across the country.
These are not just old buildings, sculptures or objects; they are the evidence of sophisticated societies, remarkable craftsmanship, political organisation, trade, religion and cultural achievements that existed long before modern Nigeria.
How much of this history have we properly preserved? How many of these sites have we developed into attractive, world-class tourism destinations? How many Nigerians, let alone international visitors, know the stories behind these remarkable places? This is where I think we have a lot to learn from China.
Restored warriors stand beside the rubble of those yet to be pieced together. Fragments of broken figures and vessels still litter the pit behind them.
Imagine what could happen if we invested seriously in restoring and developing some of our historical sites. Imagine a world-class Nok civilisation museum in Kaduna telling the story of one of Africa’s earliest known sculptural traditions, supported by archaeological research and carefully curated exhibitions. Imagine the Benin historical heritage properly preserved and presented to the world, with the history of the ancient kingdom told through its art, architecture, craftsmanship and institutions.
Imagine the Kano city walls becoming a major heritage tourism attraction with guided historical tours, cultural performances, museums, traditional markets and businesses benefitting from visitors.
Imagine the Sukur Cultural Landscape receiving the investment, accessibility and international promotion it deserves.
These are not unrealistic dreams; they are opportunities waiting for deliberate planning and investment. The government has a major role to play, but it should not be left to her alone. Private investors, universities, historians, architects, tourism operators, filmmakers and local communities all have something to contribute.
There is also a huge opportunity for Nigeria’s media and creative industries. We can tell these stories through documentaries, films, television programmes, digital exhibitions and educational content. We can make our history interesting to young Nigerians and attractive to international audiences. But we must get the fundamentals right. Restoration must be guided by professional archaeologists and conservation experts. We must protect the authenticity of our heritage and involve the communities that own and live with these historical treasures.
Tourism development should preserve these places, not commercialise them at the expense of their cultural value.
There is another lesson worth mentioning: national pride. The Terracotta Warriors are more than thousands of clay soldiers. They tell a story about China’s ancient civilisation, its craftsmanship, organisation and history.
They give visitors an opportunity to understand a part of China’s identity. Nigeria has equally compelling stories to tell. We have civilisations and cultural achievements that deserve global recognition. But we cannot expect the world to appreciate what we have not taken the trouble to preserve, interpret and present properly.
As I walked out of the exhibition halls, I found myself wondering how many other remarkable discoveries might still be buried beneath Nigerian soil, waiting to be found, studied and given the attention they deserve.
Perhaps the greatest lesson from this visit is that a country does not need to invent an extraordinary past to attract the world. Sometimes, it simply needs to recognise, preserve and invest in what its ancestors have left behind. China has turned an emperor’s underground army into a global attraction. Nigeria has its own treasures. We need to give them the attention, investment and storytelling they deserve.
On a lighter note, after seeing thousands of soldiers standing guard for more than 2,000 years, I have concluded that Emperor Qin Shi Huang took his security arrangements very seriously. Even in the afterlife, he wasn’t taking chances.
It is also worth acknowledging that this experience has been made possible through an exciting media exchange programme organised by People’s Daily of China under the Belt and Road Initiative’s Media Cooperation framework.
I am in China as part of a delegation of media professionals from different countries, with the opportunity to explore the country’s history, culture, development and media landscape. Beyond the official engagements, experiences like this are a reminder of how much we can learn from one another when countries create opportunities for meaningful exchange and understanding. What a fascinating experience. History really does come alive when you get the opportunity to stand right in front of it. Until the next China Diaries series!

items.content:
The Lagos University Teaching Hospital (LUTH), located at the Idi-Araba area of Lagos State, a full-fledged medical school and tertiary hospital, was established in July 1962. The federal medical institution was established to provide advanced medical services, train medical and other health care professionals and conduct research aimed at improving health care delivery in Nigeria
At a point, LUTH was regarded the pride of Africa as people all over the continent came there to seek medical treatment.
In 2022, the federal medical facility clocked 60. The then Chief Medical Director (CMD), Professor Chris Bode, had disclosed that the hospital had grown from a little above 300 beds to a 1000-bed medical facility and served over 25million patients.
Bode said the hospital had pioneered small incision cataract excision surgery in Nigeria and trained over 40 doctors from all over the country in the procedure in the past years.
He added that LUTH had also commenced laparoscopic general and gynaecologic surgery, which according to him, had dramatically reduced the duration of hospitalisation after surgery.
“Since 1962, the Lagos University Teaching Hospital has contributed in no small way in the training of medical and paramedical personnel; and our products are found across all hospitals and health care facilities, both within and outside the shore of Nigeria.
“As an institution, LUTH has grown from a 500-bedded hospital to 760-bed, and then to over 1000-bedded hospital serving over 25million Lagosians and its neighbouring states.
“LUTH has pioneered small incision cataract excision surgery in Nigeria and has trained over 40 doctors from all over the country in the procedure in the past years. The hospital has also commenced laparoscopic general and gynaecologic surgery, which has dramatically reduced the duration of hospitalisation after surgery.
“LUTH also boasts of a comprehensive diagnostic centre and VIP clinic, state of the art laboratories, radiodiagnosis, radiotherapy and renal dialysis facilities. From a humble beginning of 330 beds, LUTH today is the largest teaching hospital in Nigeria with over 1,000 beds. The College of Medicine of the University of Lagos is involved in the training of hundreds of medical, dental, pharmacy and other allied health science students,” Bode said.
Over the years, like many other things in Nigeria, LUTH has been abandoned by successive governments. Industry experts identified funding as being epileptic, amid increasing number of patients in a country where poverty is dealing a deadly blow on a huge percentage of the populace.
While physical structures are still at the same place, maintenance has been a huge headache.
 
LUTH grapples staff shortage, amid brain drain
The facility has been grappling with shortage of personnel following the emigration of medical doctors from the country in the past years.
In November 2023, the House of Representatives Committee on Health hinted that the challenge of workforce was already leading to shutdown of wards at LUTH. The shutdown was attributed to a severe shortage of health workers, particularly nurses and doctors, highlighting the escalating brain drain crisis affecting the renowned institution.
After an oversight visit to LUTH, the chairman of the committee, Dr Amos Magaji, expressed concern over the threat posed by the massive migration of health professionals in search of better opportunities abroad.
Magaji lamented that the operational wards had to be shuttered due to the absence of health workers, leaving the hospital struggling to meet the health care needs of its numerous daily patients.
He outlined a multifaceted approach to tackle the brain drain crisis, including interventions from university enrollment to the residency programme. While acknowledging that the issue won’t be resolved overnight, he assured that the committee is committed to implementing both short-term and long-term strategies to mitigate the impact.
The committee chairman underscored the need to examine funding, infrastructure and working conditions for health professionals in Nigeria. He recognised the sacrifices made by health workers and pledged the committee’s dedication to ensuring affordable and accessible health care for Nigerians.
“The government has spent a lot on infrastructure, and it is visible. LUTH today is not what it was four or five years ago. It is an irony. We have modernised wards, we can’t fully operate because we lack personnel,” the Chief Medical Director of LUTH, Prof Wasiu Adeyemo reportedly said during another round of visit by the committee in 2025.
According to him, many health workers now prefer to take jobs in Lagos State-owned hospitals or travel abroad for better remuneration and opportunities, saying the state’s staff salary can be up to N120,000 higher than federal institutions like LUTH.
Adeyemo said that during a recent recruitment exercise, only 50 per cent of the approved nurses actually reported for duty.
“We are losing both to internal migration and international opportunities,” he alleged.
 
‘Poor accommodation, salary delay’
In July this year, resident doctors at the LUTH went on an indefinite strike over poor residential accommodation, delayed salary payment for newly employed doctors and the withdrawal of call duty meals.
The president of the Association of Resident Doctors, LUTH chapter, Dr Omogbolahan Adenuga, said industrial action began after efforts to resolve the issues failed.
The ARD president stated that the doctors were demanding the immediate completion of the renovation of the hospital’s doctors’ residential quarters, payment of salaries owed to newly employed doctors due to delay in their enrolment on the Integrated Personnel and Payroll Information System, and the restoration of call duty meals.
Adenuga said resident doctors had been forced to sleep in their cars and hospital lounges because the residential quarters undergoing renovation remained inaccessible for 18 months.
He noted that the prolonged delay in completing the project had worsened the welfare of doctors, many of whom travel long distances to work.
“Doctors are sleeping in their cars and in hospital lounges while treating patients. We need the federal government to release funds so that the Chief Medical Director can complete the renovation immediately.
“The building has been locked for almost 18 months. It has not been completed because of lack of funding. We need the government to intervene urgently and give us a timeline for the completion of the project,” he said.
The ARD president added that doctors commuted daily from locations as far as Badagry and Ikorodu to the centre, making it difficult to resume early and remain productive during demanding clinical duties.
In May 2019, the ARD in LUTH embarked on a two-day warning strike over doctors’ shortage, unpaid salaries and victimisation of medical doctors.
 
Inside LUTH
Our correspondent who visited the facility observed some challenges impeding quality health care delivery at the over six decades old medical centre.
A new emergency patient who passes through Mushin en route to Idi-Araba, where the Lagos University Teaching Hospital (LUTH) is located, will have to overcome the hurdles of dotted potholes, as the decrepit Agege Motor Road is becoming uncomfortable for both motorists and commuters, limiting the flow of easy traffic.
While dotted potholes might inhibit traffic, the clustered adjoining streets, jam-packed with shops, might teach the patient patience before getting to the destination.
The entrance of the hospital, painted cream and bearing the inscription ‘Lagos University Teaching and College of Medicine, University of Lagos’ boldly written, signals the building in the sprawling, high-traffic street of Akintan, relieving the patient of the stress of locating the hospital.
The identification of the hospital will usher in a glimpse of hope for treatment. However, gaining entry welcomes the patient into the litany of hassles involved in securing the right attention.
Our correspondent who visited the hospital observed that entry through the gate coming from Mushin marks a step into one of the foremost tertiary hospitals in Nigeria, established in 1962, shortly after independence in 1960.
The left turn is the path to the hospital, while a right turn leads to the College of Medicine, indicating the co-existence of the twin institutions on the premises.
The left turn is replete with structures that appear to have been abandoned for a long time. A few steps further reveal a building housing equipment that has been overgrown with grass. A further walk reveals an abandoned building where laundry takes place. The building looks neglected, and its paint has faded, a reflection of non-use.
The cylinder store building looks faded, and some of the power-transmitting sets have been overgrown with grass.
Not far from the cylinder store is a road that leads to the Department of Ear. The road is dotted with faulty bed spaces and other equipment.
Among the buildings, the accident and emergency building calls for an ‘emergency’ as its paint is fading away and parts of its windows are battling for space with grass. The entrance of the building is always filled with patients either going in or exiting, as well as those waiting for their relatives and guardians to return to their respective homes.
Inside the building, one becomes aware of the surge for medical attention as patients wait patiently in turns. Our correspondent observed that the emergency unit is never silent as it is a beehive of activity involving people seeking medical attention.
The steel chairs provided for waiting patients to sit on are wobbly, while part of the white ceiling covering the room is open.
While some are inside the building, the entrance has a small space for those waiting for patients, leaving them to either stay inside their cars or find a spot somewhere around to sit.
In interviews with relatives of patients, they expressed concerns and grievances over the high cost of medical services, prolonged waiting periods for treatment and alleged poor treatment by some hospital personnel.
They appealed to the federal government and relevant authorities to urgently address the challenges confronting people seeking medical care at the public health facility.
One of the issues highlighted was the financial burden associated with accessing treatment, particularly for patients requiring surgery.
A relative of a patient, Kola Edmund, whose head and hands were resting on the rail close to the modular theatre, lamented the cost of a procedure, saying his patient was advised to budget N1.2 million.
He also expressed concern over the lengthy process involved in securing a surgery date, explaining that some patients could wait several months before undergoing surgery.
Asked how long the process had taken in one case, he said it depended on the situation, adding that it could take up to eight months.
“Why not subsidise health? Why not subsidise education? Why not subsidise agriculture?” he queried, while expressing concern that patients in public hospitals
continued to bear significant financial responsibilities.
 
‘My 11-day-old baby neglected’
In a separate account, a father identified as Aliu Babatunde accused nurses of allegedly mishandling the treatment of his baby, claiming that the family had experienced repeated delays and distress since last year.
Babatunde said that despite several visits to the hospital, the family had continued to receive instructions to return without what he considered adequate attention to the baby’s condition.
He said the baby’s neck had become swollen and alleged that hospital personnel had been unkind to the family whenever they raised concerns about the treatment.
“Last year (2025), up to date, they are telling me to go and come back. They didn’t even care whether the baby would survive,” he said.
He alleged that the family had been threatened with a refusal of treatment when they complained about the baby’s condition.
“They will be chasing us as if we were dogs,” he alleged.
Appealing to the federal government to intervene, he said: “Please, the federal government, help us and get into this matter. We are tired of this group of narcissists.”
He disclosed that he had spent close to N500,000 on the baby’s treatment since last year, including payments for injections and prescribed medications.
Asked whether he had experienced difficulties securing a hospital bed, he said he had been provided with one but was required to pay N10,000 daily for the space.
 
Family recounts ICU experience, alleges negligence
Esther Ilebani recounted an experience involving her mother’s illness, describing the difficulties the family encountered while trying to secure intensive care treatment at a public health facility.
According to Esther, her family was told that they had to wait for another patient to die before an ICU bed could become available.
She also alleged that family members had to constantly remind hospital personnel to change the oxygen supply and alert them whenever the oxygen ran out.
“When my mum was sick and they needed an ICU, they told us to wait for one person to die. We were the ones telling them to change the oxygen when it finished,” she said.
Expressing frustration over what she described as inadequate public health care infrastructure, she questioned the state of facilities in government-owned hospitals.
“There are not enough adequate public facilities in these health centres, so why are they existing when they are killing more than saving lives?” she queried.
She also criticised the cost of treatment and the attitude allegedly displayed towards patients, claiming that some general hospitals charged increasingly high fees while patients were treated as though their concerns did not matter.
“You have to remind them of everything. The amount of negligence these doctors and nurses are showing towards patients is too sad,” she alleged.
 
We are a hospital because of patients- CMD
In an interview with Weekend Trust, the Chief Medical Director, LUTH, Professor Wasiu Adeyemo, reacted to the complaints of patients over the unwelcome attitude ofstaff , describing the complaints as human beings’ reaction to what they perceived as wrong to them.
He added that the hospital records attendance of over 2000 out-patients daily in facility with 1050 bed space and over 5000 staff.
“Complaints are normal. The moment humans don’t complain, the man is dead. We see over 2,000 patients per day. So, if somebody is complaining, you don’t take that as a representation of the hospital. He is not being fair, even in terms of data collection, analysis .People always complain,” he said.
He added that the hospital has established measures to curb patients through complaints by creating online forms for them to channel their complaints and train the hospital staff.
“We also spend a lot of resources training our staff. From the view of the attitude of the staff, the management cannot be everywhere and we have also noticed some of the attitude of our employees.
“Our responsibility is that we have employed them already. What we need to do is to train them and we are doing that,” he said.
He added that the hospital has zero tolerance for rudeness, emphasising on its social responsibility to administer healthcare to the public.
“We discourage rudeness because really, if we do not have patients, if patients don’t come here, this facility can be called any other name, not a hospital.
“We are a hospital because of patients and patients can be anybody. In the clinic, some of our staff are there.
“But you know, human beings are very complex. Also, the patient also, and their relation also complex,” he said.
On Infrastructure development, he rnoted that the federal government has invested close to N40 billion since he assumed office as the CMD in 2023.
“Since I became the CM, the government has pumped something close to N40 billion in terms of infrastructure because essentially, we have so many problems, but there are two major problems.
Reacting to the fading paint on the wall of the Accident and Emergency (A&E) ward, he disclosed that there are ongoing construction works of another outpatient facility outside the hospital premises, saying once it’s completed, the facility would be available for use.
“The government has given us money in the last 3 years to renovate many of those inpatient wards.
“However, in our outpatient we see 2,000 a day.
“We pushed from many past administrations to this administration for the government to give us money to build a new outpatient facility, and that is what the government is doing.
“We have 256 consortiums. There is nowhere in Nigeria where you have that,” he said.
Reacting to the shortage of staff, he said the government has increased staff salaries since February.
The government is putting a lot of money on infrastructure but people are leaving. So, the government must also make sure that that salaries are paid and the government just started that in early February.
“Many of them are still leaving, and we told government that we still need to increase it because the question is why people are moving abroad.
“Primarily, people may not look at that perspective. There’s one major reason why people move abroad. It’s not because Nigeria is bad. It is because there is a space there. Spaces for them.
“If there is no space, everybody will stay here. That’s the truth.
“There’s nothing like welfare. The only thing that is welfare is money, salary. Doctors that are leaving, it’s not because they are building houses there. No, they pay people enough for them to sort out their welfare.” He noted.

items.content:
For some members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC), the monthly N77,000 allowance, popularly called “allawee”, is barely enough to cover basic needs, leaving them struggling to afford accommodation, feed and travel home to see their families.
Some corps members serving away from their states of residence told Weekend Trust that the cost of rent, food, transportation and other necessities often consumes their monthly allowance before the end of the month.
For those posted far from home, the cost of travelling to visit family members has become an additional burden, forcing some to cancel planned trips, rely on phone calls to maintain family relationships or wait months before returning home.
The experiences vary, depending on the cost of living in their service locations, the support they receive from their places of primary assignment (PPAs) and whether they can earn additional income.
Precious Yohanna, a resident of the Federal Capital Territory serving in Nasarawa State, said living in a rented apartment some distance from her PPA had increased her transportation expenses.
“Well, I have been surviving. I stay alone in a rented apartment, although it is quite a distance from my PPA, which automatically increases the cost of transportation; but somehow, I still manage to feed,” she said.
Yohanna said her monthly expenses included N7,700 for tithe, about N20,000 for foodstuff, electricity bills, transportation, Community Development Service (CDS) contributions and other necessities.
She said she sometimes had to cut back on expenses when her allowance was insufficient and occasionally relied on family support to meet her needs.
Her PPA provides a monthly stipend of N7,500 and allows her a day off apart from scheduled CDS activities. However, she said living closer to her place of assignment would reduce transportation cost and ease the pressure on her finances.
Yohanna said the distance between her service location and home also made family visits expensive. The journey takes about four hours, while a return trip costs approximately N20,000.
She said she usually visited home once every two or three months and had cancelled a trip in the past because she could not afford the fare. Her last visit was in August.
Although she said the limited visits had not significantly affected her family relationships because she remained in regular contact with them, the cost of travelling continued to influence how often she could see them.
For another corps member serving in Gombe State who is from Benue State, accommodation and feeding consume much of the monthly allowance.
The corps member, who requested anonymity, said the PPA did not provide accommodation, forcing an individual to share a rented apartment with two other corps members.
The respondent said feeding cost between N1,500 and N3,000 per meal, while daily transportation to the PPA cost about N400.
The corps member estimated monthly expenses at N20,000 for accommodation, between N30,000 and N35,000 for feeding, N12,000 to N15,000 for transportation, N5,000 for data and airtime, and another N5,000 for toiletries and cleaning supplies.
“The N77,000 finishes before month ends. Most months, nothing remains. If I have emergency or sickness, I go negative,” the corps member said.
The respondent said the journey from Gombe to Benue took between 10 and 11 hours, with return transport costing between N45,000 and N55,000.
The corps member said there had been no visit home since arriving in Gombe despite the desire to return every two months.
An Easter visit was cancelled after transport fares increased, coinciding with the deadline for paying rent.
“I haven’t physically seen my family for about 10 months,” the respondent said, adding that video calls had become the main way of maintaining contact.
“It has affected me emotionally, I feel homesick and sometimes isolated, and my parents worry a lot because I am far and they can’t support me much financially,” he said.
To cope, he said the shared apartment helped reduce accommodation cost, while bulk cooking made feeding more affordable. He also does sewing work, earning between N5,000 and N10,000, and occasionally receives small financial support from family members.
The corps member acknowledged receiving a monthly N7,500 stipend from the PPA but said it was insufficient to meet the range of expenses.
He called for an increase in the allowance to reflect differences in living costs across states, suggesting N100,000 as a possible monthly amount. The corps member also urged the NYSC and host institutions to provide accommodation, transport assistance and support for corps members posted to rural areas.
Another corps member serving in Lafia, Nasarawa State, said the allowance had been insufficient to meet daily needs, and that the financial strain had made travelling home difficult.
“It has not been easy as each day comes with different challenges. Some days, there’s little or nothing at all in all the areas listed in the questions,” he said.
He said transportation cost about N20,000 monthly for four working days and CDS activities, while another N10,000 was set aside for health-related necessities.
A return trip to the respondent’s hometown costs between N30,000 and N35,000. The corps member said there had been no visit home since arriving in Lafia and that two planned trips had been cancelled because of financial constraints.
He said there was uncertainty about whether a visit would be possible during Christmas, which is fast approaching.
Without any family support available because of circumstances at home, the corps member said the main option was to manage whatever was available. He also said the PPA did not permit other ways of earning money to supplement the allowance.
He called for government’s assistance with transportation and other essential expenses to ease the burden on members serving away from home.
Esther Mike, who is serving in Abuja and a resident of Kogi State, also identified accommodation and transportation as major challenges.
She said transportation expenses in Abuja could consume a substantial share of the allowance, while data subscriptions added to her monthly costs.
“Accommodation is chaotic, feeding is bearable, but transport is very bad, especially in Abuja. Up to 70 per cent of my ‘allowee’ without external assistance goes to transport,” she noted.
Esther said she had managed to save about 20 per cent of her allowance, although she did not consider the amount sufficient to meet significant needs. She said transportation and data remained among her major expenses.
A journey from her current residence in Kogi State to Abuja costs about N16,000, while travelling to her hometown in Edo State costs approximately N30,000.
According to her, when she was ill, she travelled home twice to receive support. She added that she had also relied on loans to meet her needs since the beginning of her service year.
Esther urged the NYSC to provide corps members with more accurate information before deployment, particularly about accommodation, transportation cost, the availability of suitable PPAs, and whether assignments align with their fields of study.
She also raised concerns about the treatment some corps members receive in host communities, saying insufficient information and difficult service conditions could leave members feeling unfulfilled and emotionally distressed.
But not all corps members interviewed reported the same level of financial pressure. One respondent said a higher payment from the host organisation had made it possible to live comfortably and save the NYSC allowance.
The corps member said that life at the current place of assignment had been manageable because the PPA paid more than the monthly N77,000 allowance.
“Presently, I have not been touching the allowance because I am saving. I am currently using the money I am being paid at my PPA since it is higher than my NYSC allowance,” the respondent said.
He said his hometown was close enough for a return trip to cost about N5,000, allowing monthly visits to family members.
He, however, said a planned visit had once been postponed because of financial discipline while saving money.
“I have had to postpone because of lack of fund since I was saving, I didn’t want to break it, so had to discipline myself,” the corps member said, adding that the distance had not affected family relationships.
he corps member said additional income from personal clients and small jobs also helped cover expenses, while the host organisation provided care, opportunities and development.
He said the hope was to secure permanent employment with the organisation after the service year.
The contrasting experiences highlight how PPA payments, access to extra work and proximity to home can influence whether corps members struggle to meet basic needs or manage to save part of their income.
The accounts come amid continuing pressure from the cost of basic necessities, even as Nigeria’s inflation rate has eased from its level a year earlier.
Figures provided by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) show that headline inflation stood at 14.63 per cent in September 2026, down from 15.39 per cent in August and 20.98 per cent in September 2025.
The year-on-year rate was 6.35 percentage points lower than the September 2025 figure. On a month-on-month basis, headline inflation slowed to 0.06 per cent in September from 0.71 per cent in August.
Food inflation also declined to 19.59 per cent year-on-year in September 2026, compared with 20.16 per cent in September 2025. On a month-on-month basis, food inflation stood at -1.55 per cent in September, compared with 1.02 per cent in August.
The figures indicate that the pace of price increases slowed, while average food prices fell, compared with the preceding month. However, lower inflation does not mean that prices have returned to earlier levels or that essential goods and services have become affordable for everyone.
For corps members receiving a fixed monthly allowance, the cost of food, rent and transportation must still be met at prevailing prices. Those posted far from their homes also face additional travel expenses that can take a significant share of their income.
Transport fare data from the NBS also illustrate the pressure. The average intra-city bus fare rose to N1,431.25 per trip in May 2026 from N1,397.27 in April, an increase of 2.43 per cent. Compared with May 2025, the fare was 38.63 per cent higher than the average of N1,032.46.
The average intercity bus fare increased to N9,699.55 in May 2026 from N9,607.41 in April, representing a 0.96 per cent rise. Year-on-year, the fare was 21.89 per cent higher than the N7,957.41 recorded in May 2025.
For corps members travelling longer distances to visit their families, these costs can make occasional trips difficult to afford, particularly when rent and other bills fall due in the same period.
Food costs also highlight the gap between the allowance and basic living expenses. The NBS’s latest reported average cost of a healthy meal was N1,589 per meal. At that rate, three meals a day would cost N4,767 or N143,010 over 30 days.
For some, a monthly food cost is N66,010, more than the N77,000 allowance, before accommodation, transportation, electricity, health care, data and other expenses are considered. Actual spending varies by location, food choices and access to affordable meals, but the estimate shows how quickly feeding alone can strain a limited income.
The pressure extends beyond daily survival. It affects the corps members ability to respond to emergencies and save for unexpected expenses.
For those posted far from home, the challenge is not only completing the service year but also finding a way to meet basic needs without losing the opportunity to maintain close contact with their families.
 
‘Increase tied to minimum wage’
Reacting to the concerns raised by corps members, the Director of Press and Public Relations of the NYSC, Mrs Caroline Embu, said “any increase in the monthly allowance was tied to an increment in the national minimum wage.”
However, the Country Director of Accountability Lab Nigeria, Friday Odeh, said the NYSC should press for an increase in the monthly allowance, noting that rising costs of accommodation, transportation, food and other essentials had significantly eroded its purchasing power.
Odeh said that a uniform increase in the federal allowance would not adequately address the financial difficulties faced by corps members because living costs vary across states and locations.
He said a corps member serving in Abuja or Lagos faced different financial realities from one posted to a rural community in Benue or Ebonyi State.
He advocated a shift from a uniform allowance to a cost-of-posting model that reflects the actual living conditions of corps members in their respective locations.
According to him, a sustainable approach should combine a federal base allowance indexed to inflation with location-adjusted support from state governments and mandatory welfare provisions by PPAs.
Odeh also called for an upward review of the federal allowance, transparent cost-of-living supplements for corps members in expensive urban centres, enforceable accommodation and transportation provisions or payments in lieu, as well as guaranteed timely disbursement.
He said the demand should go beyond increasing the amount paid to ensuring that corps members could meet basic living costs wherever they were deployed.
“National service should not impose security and financial hardship because of the location or institution to which a corps member is deployed,” he said.

items.author: David Ngobua
items.content:
Even as it has not lived up to its full potential, the Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL) has made notable strides in recent seasons – from improved broadcast visibility to heightened competitiveness among clubs. Yet, like a stubborn stain on a freshly pressed jersey, the recurring menace of poor officiating continues to undermine the league’s credibility.
The recent indefinite suspension handed to a centre referee, Abdulrasheed Jimoh from the Bauchi State Referees Council, and an assistant referee, Adamu Zakari from Jigawa, by the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) Refereeing Development Committee following their controversial decision to disallow a valid goal by Kwara United against Rangers International, has once again thrust match officials into the spotlight for all the wrong reasons. The unprofessional behaviour of the suspended referees has reinforced the opinion of some observers that the majority of arbiters are determined to remain the black sheep of the beautiful game.
While the swiftness of the NFF’s disciplinary action deserves commendation, the incident serves as a stark reminder that officiating errors remain one of the greatest existential threats to domestic football in Nigeria. When a referee blows the whistle wrongly, the consequences ripple far beyond the 90 minutes on the pitch.
Truth be told, in the NPFL, poor officiating inflicts damage across multiple fronts. Since football thrives on fairness, poor officiating erodes sporting integrity. When outcomes are decided by fabricated off-sides, dubious penalties or wrongly disallowed goals, the entire competitive balance of the league is distorted.
Clubs invest millions of naira in player recruitment, travel and logistics, only to see their efforts undone by a single lapse in judgement, or worse, compromised officiating. For no fault of theirs, Kwara United lost three points against Enugu Rangers, and no amount of punishment for the offending match officials will reverse the final result.
Poor officiating also breeds fan apathy and stadium violence. Nigerian football fans are deeply passionate, and perceived injustice on the pitch is often the spark that ignites stadium unrest. When supporters feel that their team has been robbed, frustration can quickly boil over into crowd trouble, leading to heavy fines and stadium bans for clubs. Conversely, repeated controversies drive genuine fans away from match venues, leaving stadiums empty and robbing the league of its vibrant atmosphere.
Apart from driving fans away from match venues, referees who make dubious calls scare away corporate sponsors. Corporate Nigeria wants to associate with credible, well-managed brands. Continuous headlines about suspended referees and disputed match results create a toxic perception around the NPFL. Potential sponsors and broadcast partners become hesitant to commit funds to a product plagued by integrity questions.
Furthermore, the endless embarrassment of Nigerian clubs in competitions like the CAF Champions League and Confederation Cup can be traced to compromised referees who are often “recruited” by clubs desperate to secure continental tickets. This is perhaps the most telling impact of sheltered officiating. It is now an open secret that teams accustomed to winning home matches through questionable officiating often struggle in continental tournaments, where neutral referees enforce the laws of the game strictly.
In addition, referees indulging in dubious officiating also dig their own graves. They may fail to realise the full extent of the reputational damage they inflict upon themselves, but the persistent absence of Nigerian referees at major international tournaments like the FIFA World Cup and the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) speaks volumes about how global bodies view the standard of domestic officiating.
Suspending erring officials after the damage has been done is merely treating the symptom rather than the disease. To permanently tame the menace of poor officiating in the NPFL, football authorities must adopt a holistic and structural approach in line with modern trends. Therefore, football authorities in Nigeria should immediately consider the introduction of Video Assistant Referee (VAR) technology. While full-scale VAR may currently be capital-intensive for all league venues, the NPFL and NFF can begin with a phased rollout. Introducing VAR-lite or goal-line technology for high-stakes matches and televised fixtures would immediately eliminate glaring errors like the disallowed goal in Awka.
There is also an urgent need for improved welfare and prompt remuneration for match officials. It is unfortunate that referees in the NPFL are often left at the mercy of clubs that exploit their financial vulnerabilities, creating a major breeding ground for corruption. Referees must be paid competitive indemnities, and their allowances—including travel and accommodation—must be settled promptly before matches. When officials are financially secure and independent of host clubs for logistics, their susceptibility to external inducements drops drastically.
Nevertheless, even as some referees deliberately set out to carry out hatchet jobs, we must acknowledge that some mistakes are unintentional. Because modern football is faster and more tactical than ever, referees should be supported with regular workshops on the evolving Laws of the Game, fitness drills, and psychological training to handle the intense pressure of hostile away grounds without buckling.
Meanwhile, reforms alone will fail if there is no deterrence. For far too long, a culture of impunity has allowed compromised or grossly incompetent officials to return to the pitch after brief, quiet stints on the sidelines. The NFF must draw a firm line in the sand. Suspensions must be accompanied by total delisting for repeat offenders or those found culpable of match-fixing. Stepping a referee down indefinitely, as seen in the cases of Jimoh, Zakari and earlier this season with Yakubu Aliyu, is a step in the right direction—provided “indefinite” truly means permanent removal from the top flight for egregious errors.
The NFF Refereeing Development Committee is also encouraged to publicly publish the findings of its investigations into controversial matches. Naming and shaming compromised officials—and any club administrators found guilty of attempting to bribe or intimidate referees—will serve as a powerful deterrent.
In conclusion, criminal prosecution should be pursued where clear evidence of match manipulation exists. Match-fixing is economic sabotage against clubs, players and sponsors. Treating it as a criminal offence rather than a mere internal sports infraction will send an unmistakable message that the era of business as usual is finally over.

items.author: David Ngobua
items.content:
On Saturday, November 7, Nigeria’s Flamingos edged out Asian giants Japan 2-1 in Rabat, Morocco, to lift the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. They became the first African nation to claim the global title and placed Nigeria alongside France as the only countries to win both the men’s and women’s U-17 World Cups. The Flamingos’ male counterparts, the Golden Eaglets—with five titles—remain the most successful team in the world at that level.
The victorious Flamingos returned to Nigeria on Monday, November 9, to a rousing welcome. Yet amid the national celebrations, federal cash rewards, and Senate commendations, a familiar anxiety lingers over the future of the young players.
For decades, Nigeria has dominated youth tournaments, only to watch many of its brightest teenage sensations fade into obscurity. While stars like Victor Osimhen and Asisat Oshoala successfully transitioned to the global stage, countless others, hampered by poor management, unhealed injuries, or structural neglect, abandoned football altogether before their prime.
Indeed, the history of Nigerian football is replete with stories of teenage sensations who sparkled at dawn with youth national teams only to fade into obscurity before noon. Thus, in spite of Nigeria’s dominance at the U-17 level, the country is yet to taste global victory at the U-20 level. The Flying Eagles, the team meant to harness the best talent from victorious U-17 squads, have managed to claim only two silver medals and one bronze since their first appearance in 1983.
Similarly, only a handful of players have successfully transitioned from the U-17 to the U-20 and senior Super Eagles squads. Nduka Ugbade, Jonathan Akpoborie, Celestine Babayaro, Mikel Obi, Chinedu Obasi, Lukman Haruna, Ramon Azeez, Isaac Success and Taiwo Awoniyi are among the few who completed the full international pathway.
Nigerias’ Flamingos U17 celebrating their World Cup win
To ensure the 2026 Flamingos squad, and the next generation of young Nigerian athletes, don’t become cautionary tales, Nigerian football administrators must shift their focus from one-off tournament celebrations to sustainable career architecture.
One of the biggest leaks in Nigerian football happens immediately after a youth tournament ends. Without a centralised database, young players return to disorganised local setups and vanish from national team radars. It is, therefore, a step in the right direction that the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) has promised to preserve the core of the victorious Flamingos, with 11 players still eligible for the next U-17 competition. Meanwhile, the federation stated that others would be groomed for the U-20 national team, the Falconets, and eventually the Super Falcons.
To achieve this objective, the NFF and the National Sports Commission (NSC) must maintain a strict digital registry for every youth international. Standout U-17 players should be systematically integrated into the U-20 Falconets and invited to understudy senior Super Falcons camps, ensuring a seamless developmental bridge rather than leaving their progress to chance.
Furthermore, early exposure to humongous cash rewards has historically served as a major distraction for upcoming players. Sudden wealth without financial guidance easily erodes the discipline required for long-term growth. Acting on lessons from the past, the Federal Government decided to invest the Flamingos’ reward of N100 million each in government bonds to protect the teenage footballers from the pitfalls of sudden wealth and ensure their long-term financial security.
According to the Chairman of the National Sports Commission (NSC), Mallam Shehu Dikko, the five-year investment is expected to yield annual returns of approximately 12 to 14 per cent while preserving the N100 million principal until maturity. He noted that the arrangement would enable the young players to support their education, training, and other legitimate needs without jeopardising their professional development.
“What the President has done today (Wednesday, November 11) is unprecedented because these are young kids under 17. There is no need to flood them with money that can distort their careers.
“We are giving the (Flamingos) what we call an FG savings bond for about five years. That savings bond comes with about 12 to 14 per cent interest annually, meaning each of them will be earning the equivalent of over N1.1 million monthly for the next five years.
“That is enough to look after their education, their training and other needs. By the time the money matures, they will already be adults and can make clear decisions about what to do with their money,” said Dikko.
Moreover, when youth stars return home without immediate European offers, playing in an underfunded domestic league with poor pitches and irregular salaries often stalls their momentum. Therefore, the NFF must strengthen the Nigeria Women Football League (NWFL) and the Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL). By enforcing club licensing standards,requiring proper training facilities, medical insurance, and guaranteed minimum wages, domestic clubs can serve as reliable springboards where teenagers play competitive minutes regularly before moving abroad.
For most football stakeholders, it is a welcome development that the government has taken proactive steps to protect the Flamingos from the ordeal faced by many of their predecessors, who squandered the money accrued from continental and global victories without giving a second thought to tomorrow. However, while guiding the youngsters to make informed financial decisions and stay on their current trajectory, the menace of fake football agents must also be addressed.
Sudden fame and financial windfalls often attract predatory agents who push teenagers into unsuitable foreign clubs purely for quick transfer commissions. Therefore, the NFF should vet and certify player intermediaries, offering mandatory legal and contract advisory services to youth internationals and their parents.
Nigerian footballers like Sunday Mba, Macauley Chrisantus, and Kelechi Nwakali had their promising careers derailed by exploitative club deals, disputed transfers, and fraudulent foreign contracts. This has been the fate of both established youth internationals trapped in toxic professional contracts and immensely talented grassroots players lured abroad under false pretences.
The Flamingos’ 2026 World Cup triumph proved once again that Nigeria has no shortage of world-class raw talent. However, trophies at age 17 are merely the starting line. By replacing ad-hoc rewards with structured mentorship, medical protection, credible management, and a strong domestic league, Nigeria can finally turn its youth champions into enduring global legends.

Investor concerns intensified after India's retail inflation rose to 6.09% in October, crossing the RBI's 6% upper tolerance limit for the first time in two years.Read more: 12 bluechip stocks within 5% of their 52-week highs; should you chase them now?"The market's risk environment has become more complicated towards the end of the week with October retail inflation rose to 6.09%, moving above the RBI's upper tolerance band, while food inflation accelerated to 8.94%, raising concerns about the interest-rate outlook and household consumption," said Gaurav Garg, head -research, Lemonn. items.content: Mumbai: Has Indian IT turned the corner?After surging more than 17% in October, the Nifty IT index appears to have lost momentum, declining nearly 2% so far in November, although the Sensex and Nifty harnessed new-found enthusiasm from foreign funds to climb more than 10% in the run-up to Diwali and its immediate aftermath.Legacy IT stocks have stagnated despite a precipitous plunge in AI-heavy bets across Asia, putting a question mark over whether earnings concerns at outsourcing firms would continue to keep prices - and valuation multiples - in restraint despite obvious opportunities arising from a sectoral churn.135820397Since the beginning of October, South Korea's Kospi and Taiwan's stock index have fallen around 20% and 13%, respectively. Japan's Nikkei has declined 10%, while the Nasdaq Composite has lost 6%. The Shanghai Composite and Hang Seng have fallen 4.4% and 2.4%, respectively, reflecting the correction in global AI-related stocks.The September-quarter earnings of Indian IT companies, meanwhile, point to an uneven recovery, with mid-tier players outperforming larger peers while underlying demand conditions remain largely unchanged. Choice Institutional Equities said companies under its coverage reported average sequential revenue growth of around 5.4% for tier-2 players, compared with nearly 1.1% for tier-1 companies.Read more: BSE launches 14 new sector indices, expands BSE 500-based suite to 20 benchmarksCoforge led the mid-tier pack with 10.9% growth, followed by Persistent Systems at 7.8%, while Tech Mahindra and HCLTech led among larger companies.However, healthy deal bookings have yet to translate into commensurate revenue growth. Phased transitions, staggered project ramp-ups and longer client decision-making cycles continue to delay revenue conversion.Shorter-cycle AI engagements, typically lasting one to two quarters, are also limiting the visibility traditionally associated with large, multi-year deals, Choice said.A key concern for the sector is the changing economics of technology services as clients increasingly use AI to improve productivity and reduce costs. While AI is creating new business opportunities, these gains are yet to fully offset pricing pressure in traditional services.Kotak Institutional Equities estimates gross deflation of around 7% and net deflation of 3.5% for companies as clients seek a greater share of productivity savings through contract renewals.Read more: 12 bluechip stocks within 5% of their 52-week highs; should you chase them now?Sandeep Gogia, MD and co-head, Investment Banking, Equirus Capital, said pressure on enterprise clients to improve returns on AI-related investments, alongside concerns around safety, security and token-cost optimisation, could create fresh opportunities for IT services providers. "Integration of systems of records and data systems with systems of intelligence and AI models is not plug and play," Gogia said, pointing to opportunities in data engineering, application modernisation, cloud migration and cybersecurity as enterprises move towards large-scale AI implementation.On profitability, Choice said operational efficiency and cost discipline had partly offset wage and delivery-related pressures, although margin performance remained mixed. Kotak expects margins at large IT companies to remain largely stable, with rupee depreciation providing some support. However, pricing pressure and AI-related investments could weigh on profitability.The earnings outlook also remains uneven. Kotak expects Infosys to lower its FY27 revenue growth guidance to 1.5-2.5%.

items.title: 2027: Aaro Meta urges Kwara South APC to back Danladi
items.summary:
By Demola Akinyemi, Ilorin
A political pressure group in Kwara South, Aaro Meta, has urged aggrieved members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the district to set aside their grievances and support the party’s governorship candidate, Speaker of the Kwara State House of Assembly, Rt. By Demola Akinyemi, Ilorin
A political pressure group in Kwara South, Aaro Meta, has urged aggrieved members of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the district to set aside their grievances and support the party’s governorship candidate, Speaker of the Kwara State House of Assembly, Rt. Hon. Yakubu Salihu Danladi, ahead of the 2027 general elections.
The group also backed the emergence of a governorship candidate from Kwara North, arguing that equity, fairness and political balance informed the need for a shift in power to the district.
The group’s Coordinator, Engr. Adebayo S. Daramola, made the appeal on Friday while addressing journalists at the News Keg organised by the Correspondents’ Chapel of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) in Ilorin.
Aaro Meta said it played an active role in the 2018 O to Ge movement, which contributed to the emergence of the APC-led government in the state in 2019, adding that its position was informed by the need to sustain the party’s political fortunes and promote fairness among the three senatorial districts.
The group recalled that during the 2019 governorship election, it supported the emergence of an APC candidate from Kwara Central, despite its base in Kwara South, in consideration of the prevailing political circumstances.
That decision, it noted, resulted in the emergence of Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, who won the 2019 election and secured a second term in 2023.
It urged APC members in Kwara South to demonstrate a similar spirit of political accommodation by supporting Danladi, who hails from Kwara North.
“Why can’t we also have a free mind like we did in 2019 to rally support for any candidate that emerged from the Kwara North Senatorial District, rather than having a preferred candidate?” the group queried.
Aaro Meta acknowledged that Kwara South had aspired to produce the APC governorship candidate but maintained that political power should be distributed fairly among the three senatorial districts.
It argued that since 1999, Kwara South had produced a governor for eight years, while Kwara Central would have accounted for 20 years in office by the time AbdulRazaq completes his tenure in May 2027.
The group said supporting a candidate from Kwara North would provide the district an opportunity to produce the state’s next governor.
It particularly appealed to aggrieved APC members in Kwara South and members of the G-15 political bloc to embrace reconciliation and work for the success of Danladi and other party candidates in the 2027 elections.
“We cannot afford to be a party to the destruction of the house and family we have all toiled to build and nurture all these years, but to always learn to forgive one another when we offend ourselves,” it said.
The group warned that internal divisions could give opposition parties an opportunity to gain political advantage, urging APC members not to abandon the party because their preferred aspirants failed to secure its tickets.
On security, Aaro Meta commended President Bola Tinubu and Governor AbdulRazaq for efforts to address banditry and kidnapping in Kwara South, particularly in Ifelodun Local Government Area.
It said insecurity had reduced considerably in the region but identified the Oro Forest corridor, stretching from Oro-Ago and Oreke Road towards Egbe, Okoloke and Lade, as a major security concern.
The group also commended the establishment of military bases in Oro-Ago and Babanla, as well as the recent establishment of the 184 Battalion in Omu-Aran, describing the military presence as strategic to tackling banditry and kidnapping.
It urged APC members to prioritise reconciliation, forgiveness and collective responsibility, maintaining that party unity was important to its electoral prospects in 2027.

items.content:
—Restricts use of document in ongoing criminal trial
By Henry Ojelu
The Lagos State Special Offences Court, Ikeja, on Friday admitted a Supreme Court judgment tendered by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, in the ongoing trial of former Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, Godwin Emefiele, over the forfeiture of properties allegedly linked to him.
However, the trial judge, Justice Rahman Oshodi, ruled that although the judgment was admissible, it could not be used for or against any of the parties in the criminal proceedings.
Ruling on objections raised by the defence, led by Olalekan Ojo, SAN, and submissions by the prosecution, led by the Federal Director of Public Prosecutions, Rotimi Oyedepo, SAN, Justice Oshodi held that the document was a public document and a certified true copy of a Supreme Court decision.
The judge consequently admitted it as Exhibit A but restricted its use in the trial.
He said: “The judgment is a public document, and it is a certified true copy of the Supreme Court decision. It would be accepted as an exhibit (in rem), but cannot be used in the case either for or against any party.”
Justice Oshodi explained that the document satisfied the legal requirements for admissibility under the Evidence Act.
On the defence’s objection that the prosecution tendered only the lead judgment without the separate judgments of other Supreme Court justices, the judge relied on the Court of Appeal decision in Matthias Sikiri and Others v. Nketchukwu Onyema and Others (2021) LPELR-56552(CA).
He also cited Avacha and Others v. Fawole, where the Supreme Court held that the lead judgment represents the decision of the court.
Addressing concerns over the use of a judgment arising from civil forfeiture proceedings in a criminal trial, Justice Oshodi said the restriction on its use had adequately addressed the issue.
Citing David Itauma v. Friday Jasi, the judge said previous judgments tendered in subsequent proceedings were intended to establish what was decided in the earlier cases and not to prove the guilt or innocence of parties in the subsequent proceedings.
He consequently overruled the defence objection and admitted the document.
Earlier, Ojo had opposed its admission, arguing that the judgment was irrelevant to the charges against his client, incomplete without the other justices’ opinions and arose from non-conviction-based civil forfeiture proceedings.
Counsel to the second defendant, A.M. Kotoye, SAN, aligned himself with the objection and urged the court to reject the document.
However, Oyedepo argued that the judgment was admissible as a certified true copy of a Supreme Court decision, adding that the prosecution had complied with Sections 103 and 104 of the Evidence Act.
He maintained that the fact that only the lead judgment was tendered did not affect its admissibility, while the civil nature of the forfeiture proceedings did not make the document inadmissible.
Emefiele is standing trial alongside Henry Omoile on a 19-count charge bordering on alleged abuse of office, receiving gratification, accepting gifts through agents, corruption and fraudulent property transactions involving about $4.5 billion and N2.8 billion.
Omoile is also facing a separate three-count charge over allegations of receiving unlawful gifts in connection with transactions involving the CBN.
Both defendants have pleaded not guilty.
The court adjourned further hearing to December 17, 18, 2026 and January 11, 2027.

Party credits Tinubu, Fashola, Ambode, Sanwo-Olu administrations
By Olasunkanmi Akoni
The Lagos State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) has welcomed the proposed commencement of construction of the Epe International Airport in 2027, describing the project as a major step towards transforming the Lekki-Epe corridor into an economic hub.
The party said the project reflected years of planning and infrastructure development across successive administrations in Lagos State.
The Lagos APC spokesman, Seye Oladejo, stated this in a statement on Friday, following Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu’s announcement at the Lagos East APC governorship election campaign flag-off in Epe on Thursday.
According to Oladejo, the Deputy Governor and APC governorship candidate, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, also confirmed that the current administration had advanced the necessary groundwork and documentation for the proposed aviation project.
The party said the airport initiative was the outcome of strategic planning and continuity in governance rather than the achievement of a single administration.
Tracing the project’s background, the APC credited President Bola Tinubu, who governed Lagos State before becoming president, with laying the initial development blueprint for the eastern axis, including the framework for the Lekki Free Trade Zone and land allocation for the Dangote Refinery.
It also recognised former Governor Babatunde Fashola for expanding infrastructure and connectivity in the region, while former Governor Akinwunmi Ambode was credited with advancing preparatory initiatives and integrating the proposed airport into the broader Epe development master plan.
Oladejo said Sanwo-Olu’s administration had built on those foundations through major infrastructure projects, including the Lekki Deep Sea Port and the Lagos Coastal Road.
He described the proposed airport as a key component of an interconnected industrial, maritime and logistics network expected to support international trade, tourism and job creation.
The party said the assurances by Sanwo-Olu and Hamzat at the Epe rally reinforced the importance of continuity in governance and the determination to move the project from planning to implementation.
“For President Tinubu, it would undoubtedly be a moment of immense personal satisfaction to witness the completion and commissioning of an economic vision whose foundations were laid under his leadership as Governor of Lagos State,” the statement said.
The APC also suggested that naming the airport after Tinubu would be an enduring tribute to his contributions to Lagos State’s development.
It said the proposed airport represented an opportunity to open a new economic chapter for Epe Division, noting that the area was gradually emerging as a destination for industrial investment, international commerce, logistics, aviation and tourism.
The party, however, said government must ensure that the investments translated into tangible benefits for host communities through employment, improved infrastructure, business opportunities, skills development and inclusive economic growth.
It added that the development of Epe and the wider Lagos East axis would feature prominently in public discussions about governance and the state’s future as the 2027 elections approach.
The APC said successive administrations had demonstrated the importance of institutional continuity, arguing that meaningful development required governments to build on existing foundations rather than abandon previous initiatives.
It commended Tinubu for the original vision, Fashola and Ambode for their contributions, and Sanwo-Olu for advancing the development agenda and providing renewed assurances on the proposed airport.
The party also acknowledged Hamzat’s commitment to sustaining the development trajectory.
“The story of Epe is ultimately a story of vision, continuity and transformation. From Tinubu’s original blueprint through Fashola’s and Ambode’s contributions to Sanwo-Olu’s ongoing interventions, a new economic future is taking shape,” the statement added.

The Commissioner of Police in Jigawa State, CP Tijjani Murtala, has warned newly promoted senior officers against abusing their positions, urging them to uphold discipline, integrity and professionalism in the discharge of their duties.

The commissioner, who spoke on behalf of the Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Rilwan Disu, described the promotions as recognition of the officers’ dedication, competence and contributions to the Nigeria Police Force.

Murtala urged the beneficiaries to see their promotions not merely as symbols of authority but as renewed commitments to service, leadership and sacrifice.
He charged them to lead by example, respect the fundamental rights of citizens and maintain high standards of discipline, integrity and professionalism.
The commissioner also urged the officers to mentor junior personnel, promote teamwork and discharge their responsibilities with fairness, humility and accountability.
According to him, the Inspector-General expects the newly promoted officers to justify the confidence reposed in them by strengthening efforts to protect lives and property, maintain law and order and improve public confidence in the police.
Speaking on behalf of the beneficiaries, DCP Adebayo expressed appreciation to the Inspector-General, the commissioner and the Command’s management team for their support.
She assured that the promoted officers would reciprocate the confidence placed in them through renewed dedication, loyalty, discipline and commitment to effective service delivery.
