items.author: Akshit Pushkarna
items.content:
The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has introduced a new scheme to expand UPI acceptance among small merchants. Under the new initiative, the payments body will offer incentives to banks for deploying QR codes and soundboxes to further drive transaction growth.
The scheme will be funded through a portion of the merchant discount rate (MDR) earned by banks and other UPI ecosystem participants.
In a circular dated November 11, NPCI announced the launch of the ‘UPI Vyapaar Saksham Scheme’, which aims to address the limited availability of digital payment acceptance infrastructure among small merchants, particularly in smaller cities and towns.
The scheme will run for a period of three years from the implementation of UPI MDR, which is yet to be notified.
The initiative will focus on merchants in Tier III to Tier VI cities, northeastern states, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. Small merchants covered under notified central government schemes, including PM SVANidhi and PM Vishwakarma, will also be eligible.
NPCI defines small merchants as businesses with an annual turnover of up to ₹40 Lakh in the preceding financial year.
The fund will be created from MDR collections rather than a separate government allocation. Each issuing bank, acquiring bank, payer payment service provider (PSP) and UPI application provider participating in UPI will contribute 5% of its MDR share to the fund.
The contribution will exclude MDR earned from categories that are not eligible for the scheme.
The fund will be divided into three components, with the largest allocation going towards increasing transaction volumes among existing merchants.
Under the first component, which accounts for 30% of the fund, acquiring banks will receive ₹300 for every physical QR code and ₹750 for every soundbox deployed at an eligible new small merchant. To qualify, a merchant will have to record at least 25 eligible transactions in any two months of a quarter, with a minimum transaction value of ₹5,000 per month.
For context, the scheme defines eligible transactions as successfully settled UPI payments of up to ₹2,000 at small merchants. It excludes transactions that are subsequently reversed, refunded or cancelled, as well as artificial transactions created by splitting payments to remain below the ₹2,000 threshold.
The second component will receive 50% of the fund and reward acquiring banks for growing UPI transaction volumes among existing and newly onboarded small merchants.
Banks will need to demonstrate at least 5% QoQ growth in eligible transaction volumes to qualify for incentives. They will receive 0.03% of the aggregate value of eligible transactions, with merchants in the targeted geographies receiving an additional 50% incentive.
The remaining 20% will be allocated towards incremental growth in targeted geographies. Under this component, acquiring banks will receive an incentive of 0.2% of the incremental value of eligible transactions compared with the previous quarter, over and above the incentive under the second component.
NPCI has also set out ambitious deployment targets. The scheme is expected to facilitate 6 Lakh to 1 Cr new physical QR code deployments and 5 Lakh to 10 Lakh new soundbox installations annually. It also aims to drive 30% to 50% annual growth in transaction volumes among existing small merchants.
UPI’s MDR Transition
This comes as the Centre is all set to re-introduce MDR on select “high-value” UPI transactions after nearly six years of a zero-MDR regime.
In September 2026, the government notified amendments to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, paving the way for MDR on select merchant transactions. Subsequently, NPCI introduced a framework under which person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000 would attract an MDR of 0.4%, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above.
Transactions of up to ₹2,000 and peer-to-peer (P2P) payments have been kept outside the MDR framework. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh per month through UPI QR codes under the P2M-to-P2P merchant (P2PM) category were also exempted from MDR.
The government said the move was intended to create a sustainable revenue stream for banks and payment companies while supporting the infrastructure required to operate UPI at scale. The MDR collected is distributed among ecosystem participants rather than retained by the government.
The proposed MDR framework faced pushback from retailers, with a possible deferment of its rollout to January next year. Later, the imposition was pushed beyond Diwali. Four days after Diwali, NPCI is yet to come out with a date for the implementation for this.
Whenever MDR comes into place, the new NPCI scheme would effectively channel a portion of the MDR revenue back into expanding UPI acceptance among this merchant segment.
That said, NPCI will administer the fund, validate incentive claims and oversee settlements. Acquiring banks will submit claims quarterly, with NPCI required to process incentive payments within 30 days of claim submission, subject to validation.
The scheme also mandates that acquiring banks report merchant locations, unique merchant identifiers and details of deployed QR codes and soundboxes to enable transaction-level monitoring.
The underlying policy shift is significant: while the MDR framework creates a revenue stream for UPI ecosystem participants, the new scheme attempts to use a portion of that revenue to address the infrastructure gap that has kept digital payment acceptance concentrated among larger merchants and in urban markets.

items.title: Setback for Google as EU Court adviser backs $1.7b antitrust fine
items.summary:
Google suffered a setback on Thursday ‌as an adviser to Europe's top court faulted a lower tribunal's decision to scrap a €1.49 billion ($1.7 billion) fine levied against the US ​tech giant seven years ago for anti-competitive practices related ​to online advertising.
The General Court rejected the EU decision in ⁠2024, prompting the Commission to appeal to the Luxembourg-based ​Court of Justice of the European Union.
The European Commission, the ​EU's competition watchdog, in its 2019 finding said Google used restrictive clauses in contracts with publishers that prevented rivals from placing search ​advertisements on the publishers' websites, reinforcing Google's dominance in ​online search advertising.
Read More: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic hit with lawsuit seeking halt to frontier AI development
It said the practices ran from 2006 to 2016. Google, ‌whose ⁠AdSense platform provides search advertising, removed the contested clauses from publisher agreements in 2016.

The ⁠court, which usually follows the majority of such recommendations, will rule next year.

items.author: Muhammad Bilal
items.content:
The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) has encouraged businesses to obtain fire and property insurance to protect their assets against unexpected damage and financial losses.
The regulator organized an awareness session in collaboration with the Rawalpindi Chamber of Commerce and Industry (RCCI) at the chamber’s premises.
The event brought together business owners, traders, and industrialists to discuss the financial risks associated with fire incidents and the importance of insurance coverage.
Fire Risks Can Disrupt Business Operations
Discussions highlighted that fire incidents can cause losses beyond physical property damage, including business interruptions, lost income, and disruptions to livelihoods. Participants were encouraged to adopt effective fire prevention measures and secure adequate insurance coverage for their businesses.
The session also highlighted the importance of protecting commercial properties, machinery, equipment, and inventory against unforeseen losses.
Representatives from the insurance industry explained different fire and property insurance products, key policy considerations, available coverage options, and the claims settlement process.
Participants were also briefed on Takaful, a Shariah compliant alternative to conventional insurance. The discussion highlighted business interruption coverage and its role in helping companies recover financially after insured losses.
An interactive question and answer session allowed participants to seek clarification about insurance and Takaful products, coverage options, and claims related matters.
SECP Targets Greater Insurance Awareness Among Businesses
The session forms part of SECP’s efforts to increase awareness and encourage the adoption of fire and property insurance among businesses, particularly small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs).
The initiative aims to promote financial preparedness and encourage businesses to protect their assets against potential risks while strengthening their ability to maintain operations following unexpected losses.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) Central Secretary General Salman Akram Raja on Thursday said that party founder Imran Khan has directed its leadership to remain steadfast in its ideology and principles, stressing that the party should not compromise on its stance for political gains.
Lawyers representing the PTI met Imran on November 11, a day after the Islamabad High Court (IHC) ordered authorities to facilitate the meeting. The permission for the meeting was granted after Barrister Salman Safdar and Latif Khosa had argued that they could not proceed with arguments in the ongoing appeals in the £190 million case without first meeting their clients.
Speaking to a local television programme, Capital Talk, Raja said Imran had conveyed his message to party leaders through Safdar, urging them to stand firm on the party’s ideology.
Raja acknowledged that a small group within the PTI was unhappy with him, believing that he was too ideological and placed excessive emphasis on principles.
“There is a section or a small group in the party that is unhappy with me. It believes I am too ideological and talk about principles more than necessary. They think we should seize the opportunities available to us at this time, whether it concerns the 28th Amendment or something else, and find a way forward,” he said.
However, Raja said Imran's message was the opposite.
“His message to me is entirely different. We have to find room for ourselves based on principles and move forward. We are a political party, but we must not compromise on our principles,” he said.
Quoting Imran, Raja said the PTI founder had described Allama Nasir and Pakhtunkhwa Milli Awami Party (PkMAP) chief Mahmood Khan Achakzai as people who would neither bow down nor be bought.
Read: Naqvi makes surprise dash to Nawabshah with ‘important message’ for Zardari
“Imran Khan said he had appointed them after careful consideration and that the positions assigned to them reflected their wisdom and judgement,” Raja said.
He added that he, too, had received instructions to remain steadfast in the party’s ideology.
“Whatever the nature of the matter, we have to act on Khan sahib’s instructions. He has also given directions regarding discussions on provinces, both after yesterday’s meeting and before it,” he said.
Raja said Imran was unwilling to abandon his principles, commitment to democracy or vision of public welfare under any circumstances, adding that the wishes of people in Sindh, Balochistan, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Jammu and Kashmir mattered to him.
“For Imran Khan, the sovereignty of the people comes first. His personal comfort is of no importance to him,” Raja said, adding that the founder’s fundamental message was that the party must not bow down.
Health concerns
Speaking about concerns over Imran’s health, Raja said party members were deeply worried as his blood pressure remained uncontrolled and had reached 193 on Saturday.
Asked whether Safdar’s delivery of a political message could lead to restrictions on future meetings with the PTI founder, Raja said the conversation involving Safdar and senior lawyer Latif Khosa had not been held secretly.
“The discussion was not concealed. There were microphones there, and the entire proceedings were being recorded,” he said.
Raja said the three-hour conversation had taken place without interruption and covered several matters. He added that Khosa had made several statements after the meeting, which were available on social media.
He said some remarks made by Safdar differed from those made by Khosa, prompting the former to clarify matters through a conversation after Khosa's statements.
New provinces
On the debate over the creation of new provinces, Raja said Imran had always supported the establishment of additional administrative units.
However, he said the PTI founder wanted clarity on the background to the proposal, the process through which new provinces would be created and how public opinion in the areas concerned would be obtained transparently.
Raja expressed reservations about holding a referendum, saying the term had acquired negative connotations because of past referendums held by military rulers Ziaul Haq and Pervez Musharraf.
He said those concerns would have to be addressed before the party could support such an exercise.
“We will not rush into becoming part of a process that distorts history and for which history may hold us responsible,” he said.

items.author: Gina Yauri
items.content:
Students are demanding a just future for all
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot of X video of the October 10, 2026 protest in Quito, Ecuador. Video by X user Elena Rodríguez. Fair Use.
This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.
In Quito, in defiance of the Jóvenes en Acción (Youth in Action) strategy with which Daniel Noboa’s government has attempted to boost employment for young people, thousands of students have been staging marches and sit-ins in streets and squares, demanding medicines, security, and a budget for education.
Their protests show a clear departure from the traditional approach to collective mobilization in Ecuador. Previously, these types of events have been led by the Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE); trade union groups such as the Ecuador Confederation of Free Trade Union Organizations (CEOSL), the United Workers’ Front (FUT), and the National Union of Educators (UNE); as well as feminist, anti-mining, and environmentalist movements.
However, on the afternoon of Saturday, October 10, 2026, the Ecuadorian capital witnessed a massive mobilization led by high school and university students, who gathered outside the Central University to march to Quito’s Historic Center. The call was made by the Autonomous Resistance Front (FARO), which comprises several youth collectives:
Lo que pasa en Quito es impresionante:
Quienes encabezaban la marcha anunciaron su finalización y llamaron a dispersarse. Sin embargo, la multitud continúa avanzando por las calles de Quito, desafiando el asedio policial y haciendo resonar consignas contra el Gobierno de Daniel Noboa.
@teleSURtv
— Elena Rodríguez Yánez (@ElenaDeQuito) October 10, 2026
What is happening in Quito is striking:
Those leading the march announced its conclusion and called for the crowd to disperse. Nevertheless, the throng continues to move through the streets of Quito, defying a police blockade and chanting slogans against the government of Daniel Noboa.
With their presence in the streets, the young people of Quito denounced the deterioration of public services, including the lack of medical supplies and medicines in hospitals, cuts to the public education budget, low youth employment, a persistent increase in insecurity, and forced disappearances at the hands of state agents. Their slogans also spoke out against the genocide in Palestine and the United States’ interventionism in Latin America.
Structural failures driving youth mobilization
According to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), 40 percent of unemployed people in Ecuador are between 15 and 24 years old. Labor precariousness, a dearth of opportunities, and the high cost of living are just some of the factors affecting the country’s youth.
Meanwhile, on October 30, the Noboa administration launched its third edition of “Youth in Action,” an initiative aimed at the 18-29 demographic, who are promised temporary, two-month jobs with a salary of USD 400 per month. The measure has faced harsh criticism from various academics and civic sector representatives, who maintain that the absence of a comprehensive, long-term vision proves its inefficiency in tackling youth unemployment.
In November 2025, Ecuador’s National Assembly approved the country’s 2026 budget proposal, which hit public universities, polytechnic schools, co-financed institutions, and postgraduate programs with an allocated budget reduction of approximately USD 99 million. The decrease was reflected in the absence of student scholarships, non-existent investment in research, and a reduction in available slots to access free public higher education, which is established as a fundamental right in Article 26 of Ecuador’s Constitution.
Slogans as the language of youth resistance
During the peaceful youth march, participants chanted slogans like “Out Noboa, out,” “If the people have no peace, the government won’t either,” and “Noboa, fascist,” expressing indignation against a government they believe has failed to solve social problems that affect not only young people, but the majority of the population.
Direct rejection of deficient public administration, coupled with excessive state violence against citizens, motivated the students to protest. Many videos posted on social media captured police aggression against peaceful demonstrators, as well as physical assaults on journalists as they reported on the protests.
teleSUR reporter Elena Rodríguez Yánez shared her experience on X:
Estoy harta de tener que narrar, una y otra vez, las agresiones policiales contra la prensa. Hoy, mientras intentaba documentar la violencia con la que los agentes golpeaban a jóvenes manifestantes, recibí por la espalda un toletazo en la cabeza. Me di la vuelta, mostré mi micrófono de teleSUR para identificarme como periodista y la respuesta fue otro toletazo que terminó partiéndolo.
Los periodistas no queremos ser noticia. Yo no quiero ser protagonista de nada. Estoy en las calles para contar lo que ocurre, para documentar aquello que el poder muchas veces preferiría que nadie viera.
Y si creen que a punta de golpes van a conseguir que deje de registrar la brutalidad policial, que aparte mi micrófono o que me repliegue varias cuadras para ejercer el periodismo desde donde no incomode, se equivocan.
No somos los periodistas quienes debemos alejarnos de los hechos. Son los policías quienes deben dejar de agredir. El derecho a informar no se negocia a punta de tolete.
— Elena Rodríguez Yánez (@ElenaDeQuito) October 11, 2026
I am fed up with having to recount, time and again, police assaults against the press. Today, while attempting to document the violence with which officers were beating young protesters, I was struck on the back of the head with a baton. I turned around and held up my teleSUR microphone to identify myself as a journalist; the response was another blow from a baton, which ended up shattering it.
We journalists do not want to be the news. I have no desire to be the protagonist of anything. I am out on the streets to report on what is happening — to document things that those in power would often prefer no one to see.
And if they think that by using force — by raining down blows — they can make me stop recording police brutality, force me to put away my microphone, or push me back several blocks so that I might practice journalism from a place where I won’t cause any ‘inconvenience,’ they are sorely mistaken.
It is not the journalists who should step away from the events; it is the police who must stop the assaults. The right to report cannot be negotiated at the end of a baton.
Hatari Ulcuango, President of the Federation of Students of the Catholic University of Ecuador, warned in one of his speeches that these mobilizations were “just the beginning.”
On October 10, as young people occupied the streets with their marches and sit-ins, they also used art to make their voices heard, singing songs, playing musical instruments, wearing masks, and dressing up in costumes. In doing so, they demonstrated that together, they can be very strong and that violence is not needed to speak one’s mind.
The government responded by sending the authorities to quell the protests and repress the demonstrators. Denunciations of the outcomes of state violence — dozens of students suffocated, injured, and detained — quickly spread across social media. These young people promised, however, that as long as they go unheard and continue to be treated with the blunt coercion of the state, they will return to the streets and not falter.
The leading role of youth in the streets of Ecuador, pitted against the state’s capacity for violent repression, evidence not only the crisis of the social state and the consolidation of an exclusionary state, but also the historical role of young people as agents of political change.
The glass generation — the one society has tried to shield — is experiencing the contradictions of an economic and political system that excludes them, making their future increasingly uncertain, and they are doing something about it.
Written by Gina Yauri

items.title: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic hit with lawsuit seeking halt to frontier AI development
items.summary:
A group of ​nonprofits sued OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX's (SPCX.O), AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google on Thursday, seeking to block the ‌further development of the most advanced AI models over concerns, voiced by the companies' own leaders, that the technology could pose a threat to humanity.
The nonprofits, which focus on tech accountability and include the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and Heat Initiative, sued in San Francisco, saying California’s laws against ​unfair business practices provide the grounds for a court order barring the companies from further development of products like ​ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude.
The lawsuit cites comments from company leaders, like Dario Amodei, chief executive of ⁠Anthropic, and Elon Musk, SpaceX's chief executive, about AI's potential to cause the destruction of civilization. It also describes recent incidents where models ​have escaped testing environments and autonomously attacked government websites.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
A group of ​nonprofits sued OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX's (SPCX.O), AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet's Google on Thursday, seeking to block the ‌further development of the most advanced AI models over concerns, voiced by the companies' own leaders, that the technology could pose a threat to humanity.
The nonprofits, which focus on tech accountability and include the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and Heat Initiative, sued in San Francisco, saying California’s laws against ​unfair business practices provide the grounds for a court order barring the companies from further development of products like ​ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude.
The lawsuit cites comments from company leaders, like Dario Amodei, chief executive of ⁠Anthropic, and Elon Musk, SpaceX's chief executive, about AI's potential to cause the destruction of civilization. It also describes recent incidents where models ​have escaped testing environments and autonomously attacked government websites.
“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ​ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the lawsuit says. “Nor is any industry granted the right to self-regulate the development of such dangerous products.”
The lawsuit accuses the companies of engaging in business practices that create a public nuisance, or harm to public health and enjoyment, pointing to both past incidents ​and the potential for future harm.
A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. Representatives of the other companies did not immediately respond ​to requests for comment.
Other lawsuits seek to bar development
While the Trump administration has so far declined to pursue large-scale AI regulation over fears it could ‌harm ⁠the country’s ability to compete with China, states and private entities have sought to use lawsuits to force the companies to make changes.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in June, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, saying it has harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users. In September, Florida asked the ​judge overseeing the lawsuit to bar ​OpenAI from developing new artificial ⁠intelligence models without outside oversight. That motion remains pending, according to court records.
Read More: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down in big blow to AI boom
After Florida's filing, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had paused training its most capable models and would not ​resume until they have additional safeguards in place.
"Governments have an important role to play in setting ​robust safety standards ⁠for AI, and we’re committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company," Pusateri said.
Separately, a group of eight states sued OpenAI last month in courts across the country alleging ChatGPT ⁠has coached ​its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others. OpenAI did not respond ​to requests for comment after the filing.
The states' lawsuits seek financial penalties, as well as an order barring the company from developing self-improving AI models unless it ​can ensure those models are aligned with human values.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah on Thursday rejected “conspiracy theories” suggesting that the permission granted to Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder Imran Khan to meet his lawyers was linked to "discussion" on the proposed 28th Amendment.
Lawyers representing the PTI met Imran on November 11, a day after the Islamabad High Court (IHC) ordered authorities to facilitate the meeting. The permission for the meeting was granted after Barrister Salman Safdar and Latif Khosa had argued that they could not proceed with arguments in the ongoing appeals in the £190 million case without first meeting their clients.
Speaking on a private television programme, Capital Talk, Sanaullah said: “Conspiracy theories are circulating that these meetings with Imran have happened and things are now moving towards the passage of the 28th Amendment. I want to say that this was a simple meeting of the lawyers who had committed to the IHC that they would proceed with the appeal and make their arguments if they were allowed to meet with Imran."
Read: IHC orders one-hour jail meeting for Imran Khan, Bushra Bibi with lawyers
He underlined that after the meeting, the IHC would be able to proceed with the legal case and pass judgment on the matter.
Responding to a question about whether a “message” was being sent to the federal government through these meetings, Sanaullah stated that the decision of the IHC would come in the “next few days” and then a more “informed discussion” could take place on this matter.
He further elaborated that the court would decide the matter on "merit", adding that speculation linking the PTI founder’s meeting with his lawyers to discussions on the 28th Amendment would die down subsequently.
“It is not true that this meeting has been allowed to take place because discussion on the 28th Amendment was on the agenda,” Sanaullah asserted.
Asked whether Imran could be moved to a private hospital, Sanaullah replied that if the panel gave the medical opinion that Imran could not be treated in a government hospital and needed to be taken to another hospital, then the “court and the government can make the decision”.
He added: “If the medical facilities are available in the government hospital, then the law dictates that the convict cannot be treated in a private hospital.”
The IHC has allowed Imran to meet twice a week with his family, lawyers and other associates. Despite this, access to Imran and Bushra Bibi at Adiala Jail has remained restricted, with meetings between the PTI founder and his lawyers becoming increasingly infrequent. Authorities have denied weekly meetings between Imran and his family and legal team since December 2025.
Read More: Long wait ends as lawyer meets jailed Imran, Bushra
In April 2026, Barrister Safdar met Imran for a 60-minute legal consultation on the IHC’s orders, but Bushra was not brought in to join the meeting. Safdar said Imran and Bushra were being kept in solitary confinement for almost 24 hours a day, with no access to books, television, family or lawyers.
The courts subsequently intervened to facilitate access. In June, the IHC directed authorities to arrange a meeting between Imran, Bushra and their legal counsel within seven days to complete legal formalities and pursue their appeals.
The Supreme Court also ordered weekly meetings between Imran and his family in August. Imran’s sister Noreen Niazi met him at Adiala Jail on August 18 after about nine months, and the meeting lasted about 15 minutes. However, Safdar was not allowed to meet both his clients again until November 2, when jail authorities facilitated a 40-minute meeting with Imran and Bushra.

items.content:
The Board of Peace said on Thursday that US President Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan must be implemented "immediately without further delay" after a deadly Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, while not criticising Israel.
The board said the "tragic loss of life" underscored why the plan must move forward.
"Otherwise, we will continue to see tragedies in which Hamas alleges deliberate Israeli attacks on hospitals, Israel maintains that Hamas exploits these facilities for terrorist operations, and innocent Gazans ultimately pay the price," it said in a statement on X.
pic.twitter.com/8Uuv7GN7mm
— Board of Peace (@BoardOfPeace) November 12, 2026
The board said it "deplores the death of any civilians" and denounced Hamas, but refrained from condemning the Israeli attack.
It urged all parties to "honour their commitments" under the plan, and said it had established a strategic framework to ensure Gazans "can live safely and access essential medical care in secure, demilitarised facilities".
"All parties must cede the necessary authority and operational space to the Board of Peace to implement this framework without further obstruction or delay," it said.
Read More: Israeli strike on southern Gaza hospital kills six, Gaza civil defence says
An Israeli airstrike hit the second floor of the Al-Yasin building at Nasser Medical Complex in western Khan Younis, killing six and injuring more than 20 others, Gaza’s Civil Defence said today.
The hospital director said the strike caused extensive damage to the intensive care and surgical wards.
Israeli Army Radio described the attack as an “assassination operation” but provided no further details.
Those killed included medical staff, patients and their companions, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
The UN expressed deep alarm.
"The special coordinator ad interim is deeply alarmed by the Israeli airstrike on Nasser Hospital in Gaza last night, which killed six people, injured 27 others, and caused extensive damage to the facility," said deputy spokesman Farhan Haq.
UN Special Coordinator for Middle East Peace Process ad interim Ramiz Alakbarov said that the ongoing violence and recent increase in military operations exacerbated the immense human suffering in Gaza and jeopardised the increasingly fragile ceasefire, Haq added.
"The special coordinator reiterates his call for rapid, safe, and unimpeded access for humanitarian assistance, including the entry of durable shelter materials and winterisation items to ease the suffering of the population as the coldest months approach," he said.
The attacks came amid continued Israeli violations of the ceasefire agreement that took effect on October 10, 2025. The violations have killed 1,622 Palestinians and wounded 5,878.
Since October 2023, Israel’s war on Gaza has killed more than 74,600 Palestinians and wounded nearly 176,000. Most of those killed or wounded were women and children. The war has also destroyed 90% of the territory’s infrastructure.

items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
Sports retail startup PlayBlue has onboarded cricketer KL Rahul as an investor and brand ambassador days ahead of launching its flagship store in Bengaluru. PlayBlue is set to open a 20,000 sq ft flagship store on 80 Feet Road in Bengaluru and launch its mobile app this Saturday (November 14).
The flagship store will be spread across three retail floors, a café level and a rooftop terrace. Its product portfolio will span sports apparel, footwear, equipment, accessories, recovery products and sports nutrition, catering to both amateur and professional athletes.
Beyond conventional retail, PlayBlue is positioning itself around specialised product discovery and in-store experiences. The store will offer gait analysis, treadmill-based footwear testing and cricket bat sensors to help customers assess products before making purchases.
It will also provide services such as racquet stringing, cricket bat knocking and bicycle servicing.
The rooftop space, called The Playground, will have a pickleball court, one-on-one futsal turf and a cricket net equipped with a bowling machine. The company also plans to host community classes, recovery sessions and sports club events at the venue.
The startup aims to expand to over 100 stores across 25 Indian cities over the next five years.
Founded in 2025 by former GMR Sports’ CEO Satyam Trivedi and former Cult.fit’s executive Jayam Vora, PlayBlue sells an assortment of athleisure, footwear, gear, fitness equipment, recovery products and nutrition through its retail stores and ecommerce platform.
“We’re building the store we wanted to walk into ourselves. Having KL Rahul on board as both an investor and our ambassador gives us a partner who knows what the right gear means to someone who plays,” Vora said.
The development comes months after PlayBlue secured $2.7 Mn (₹25.7 Cr) in a seed funding round in July, co-led by Centre Court Capital and MIXI Global, with participation from WEH Ventures.
To note, KL Rahul has backed numerous brands in the Indian startup ecosystem, including Boldfit, Flam, XYXX and Metaman.
With the Indian sports market projected to more than double to $130 Bn by FY30, investors’ interest remains lukewarm in backing startups in this space.
For instance, fitness and sportswear brand Boldfit raised around ₹400 Cr (about $41.8 Mn) from Bharat Value Fund as part of its Series B funding round in October, for its nationwide retail expansion, product innovation, and manufacturing.
Earlier in April, sportstech startup SportVot raised ₹32.7 Cr (about $3.8 Mn) in a fresh funding round led by IAN Alpha Fund, to expand its international presence and strengthen its AI-powered production and analytics capabilities.

items.author: ismail.domki
items.content:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi made an unscheduled visit to Nawabshah on Thursday night and held a nearly hour-long meeting with President Asif Ali Zardari at Zardari House, amid speculation over discussions on key political developments.
According to sources, the meeting focused on proposals for the creation of new provinces, the possibility of holding a referendum on the issue and potential action against the Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F).
Sources claimed that Naqvi had travelled to Nawabshah on an urgent basis carrying an important message from a senior national figure and sought to take the president into confidence over the matters discussed.
Read: Bilawal and I 'almost' on same page over 'system reset': Naqvi
Naqvi arrived at Nawabshah airport from Islamabad aboard a special aircraft, where he was received by Sindh Home Minister Zia Ul Hassan Lanjar, Minister for Works and Services and Prisons Haji Ali Hassan Zardari, Deputy Commissioner Abdul Samad Nizamani and SSP Dr Sameer Noor Channa.
He was escorted to Zardari House under tight security. The meeting reportedly lasted around 59 minutes, after which the interior minister departed for Islamabad aboard his special aircraft.
The visit has drawn attention in political circles given the reported agenda and the involvement of senior political figures. However, no official statement has yet been issued regarding the meeting or the alleged message.
The meeting came hours after Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said he and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari were largely on the same page regarding a reset of the system, referring to the latter’s remarks a day earlier.
On Wednesday, Bilawal said there was indeed a need to “reset” the system, but argued that the country should be run by the people “instead of traders and businessmen” and through greater unity.
He reiterated that Pakistan, like the rest of the world, was facing an economic crisis and that the country’s politics needed to be reset to address the challenge.
Also Read: Bilawal calls for ‘system reset’ through unity
Addressing a press conference at the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) earlier on Thursday, Naqvi said Bilawal had spoken about resetting the “political system”, whereas his own proposal concerned an “overall reset”.
The interior minister maintained that “no decision would be taken without the consent of the parties concerned”. He also dismissed suggestions circulating on social media that differences could emerge among coalition partners.
On the question of creating new provinces, Naqvi urged political parties to seek public opinion through a referendum.
Recent reports have suggested that a proposal to reorganise Pakistan into 12 provinces was under consideration, with a nationwide referendum envisaged ahead of a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment.
Debate over new provinces
The debate over creating new provinces as part of a broader restructuring of the system gained momentum on July 31, when Naqvi called for additional administrative units or provinces to overhaul what he described as the country's outdated governance system.
Addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 in Islamabad, he argued that the existing governance model had effectively “collapsed” after decades of failing to deliver. He said decentralisation was essential to improving public services, ensuring timely justice and creating opportunities for young people.
His remarks drew a mixed response, with several PML-N leaders criticising him and describing him as one of the beneficiaries of the existing system.
Among them was PML-N leader and Prime Minister's aide Rana Sanaullah, who questioned how Naqvi could criticise the political system after rising to the office of interior minister through the same system in just three and a half years.
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, however, differed with his party colleague, saying he largely agreed with the interior minister's assessment.
Also Read: PML-N's Asif backs twelve new provinces
On September 4, the Sindh Assembly passed a resolution rejecting attempts to divide the province or create new administrative units. Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah declared that “there will be no compromise on Sindh's geographical unity”.
Two days later, Naqvi renewed his call for a “reset” of the country's governance system, stressing the need to restructure its administrative framework.
The proposal has also drawn interest from Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) leader Mustafa Kamal, who heads the federal health ministry and has repeatedly advocated carving out new provinces from Sindh.
Even before Naqvi's July 31 remarks, Kamal had floated the idea of dividing Sindh, drawing strong opposition. He remains a prominent advocate of the demand.
However, the creation of new provinces would require a demanding constitutional process. Legal experts cited by The Express Tribune have pointed out that a public vote alone cannot lead to the creation of a new province. Any change to provincial boundaries must follow the constitutional amendment procedure, including approval by the relevant provincial assembly.
A referendum could potentially provide democratic legitimacy to such a move, but would not replace the constitutional requirements.
The debate over new provinces, therefore, extends beyond administrative restructuring to questions about the distribution of powers between the federation, provinces and local governments, as well as the role of citizens in decisions affecting governance and public service delivery.

items.author: John Kennedy Philip
items.content:
Every year, development organisations and social enterprises invest in programmes and products designed to help people build more secure lives. Women receive vocational training, young people learn new skills, entrepreneurs receive business support, and low-income households gain access to assets, finance, products and services. At the end of a programme, organisations can report clear results: people trained, businesses started, assets distributed, customers reached and incomes increased.
But these numbers do not always tell us whether the change will last.
I have experienced this reality through my work as the Coordinator of the ECO Wheels Project at Shishu Mandir, a non-profit organisation in Bengaluru, India, founded by German doctor Hella Mundhra. It runs a free English-medium school for children from economically disadvantaged families, and operates a registered adoption centre and children’s home, childcare centres, a vocational training centre for young people, and higher education and community welfare programmes.
Eco Wheels is one of the organisation’s major livelihood programmes. It trains underprivileged women to drive both cars and electric auto-rickshaws (e-autos) and helps them access e-autos so they can become entrepreneurs and earn their own livelihoods. Today, 266 e-autos are operating in Bengaluru through the initiative. But the training and the vehicle are not the end of the intervention. In many ways, they are the beginning. Once a woman receives an e-auto and starts working, she has to deal with the realities of running a business to earn her livelihood, and this is where continued support becomes important.
My experience with the programme has made me question whether we sometimes measure social impact too early.
 
The Gap Between Delivery and Lasting Change
Development organisations have become good at designing programmes with clear targets and measurable outputs. Donors need evidence that resources are being used well. Governments need measurable results. Organisations need targets to manage their work. So measurement is essential. The problem begins when what is easiest to measure becomes what we value most. We can count how many people completed training. It is harder to know how many are still using those skills a year later. We can count businesses started, but it takes more time to understand how many remain active and profitable. We can record the number of assets distributed, but the more important question is whether those assets helped people build more stable incomes.
The same issue exists for enterprises serving low-income customers. A business can measure how many products it sold, customers it acquired or services it delivered. But adoption or sales alone do not necessarily tell us whether the customer actually used the product and benefited from it.
As a result, there’s a key question that must be asked after delivery, which is relevant to both development programmes and market-based enterprises: What happens next?
People’s lives do not follow project timelines. A six-month training programme may end, but establishing a livelihood may take much longer. A new entrepreneur may discover that the market is different from what she expected. A woman entering paid work may face resistance from her family, or experience an unexpected financial crisis that can undo months of progress. These challenges do not necessarily mean that an intervention failed: They simply show that it is only one part of a much longer journey.
 
Balancing the Tension Between Support and Scale
We already know that support needs to go beyond one intervention — the development sector has recognised this for years. The Graduation Approach, developed by BRAC and adapted by organisations working in different countries, aims to address this reality by combining several forms of support, including livelihood assets, savings, financial services, training and coaching. The approach recognises that people experiencing poverty may face several constraints at the same time, and may need different forms of support in sequence. Coaching can be particularly important because it provides support while people are trying to turn an opportunity into a livelihood.
But there is an important tension here: The more individual and intensive the support, the more difficult and expensive it can become to deliver at scale.
I do not think the answer is to choose between scale and care. Nor am I arguing that every development organisation or social enterprise should replicate a full Graduation programme or provide intensive support for years. The more practical lesson is to think about the right level of support at the right stage. A person may need intensive support when starting out, practical guidance while building a livelihood, and much lighter contact once she becomes more confident. So the organisation’s role should change as the person’s capacity grows. The objective should not be to simply make every programme longer. Instead, organisations should strive to provide support that is responsive to what people actually need to achieve the intended outcome.
 
The Concept of Deep Care
I use the term “Deep Care” to describe this way of thinking. I do not claim that providing ongoing follow-up is an entirely new idea, as development practitioners have incorporated accompaniment, mentoring, coaching and community support into their programming for many years. What I am trying to highlight through the concept of Deep Care is a simple question: Are we designing programmes around the life of the project, or around the journey of the person?
Conventional programmes tend to follow a similar pattern: Recognise a need, address it through a service, establish and achieve a certain target, then exit. Deep Care asks organisations to think about what happens between the moment a person first receives an intervention and the moment they reach the point where they no longer need it.
The organisation can bring beneficiaries to this point by building trust, providing appropriate support, helping people respond to setbacks, connecting them with opportunities and gradually reducing direct assistance as their capacity grows. The purpose of this continued support should ultimately be to make continued support less necessary.
My experience with the Eco Wheels Project and Shishu Mandir has reinforced this idea for me. When a woman is trained to drive and receives an e-auto, it is tempting to see the completion of the training and the transfer of the asset as the measurable end of the programme. But from her perspective, that is the point at which another journey begins.
She now has an asset that can generate income, but she also has the responsibility of turning that asset into a sustainable livelihood. She has to operate in a real market, deal with customers and expenses, manage income, and respond to problems that cannot be anticipated in a training room. Our role is therefore not simply to provide the vehicle and walk away. Instead, we continue to handhold the women as they establish themselves as entrepreneurs. As their confidence and experience grow, the nature and intensity of the support we provide can be reduced. This is the distinction that’s important to acknowledge when we talk about long-term support: Care should not mean dependency — it should build independence.
 
The Relevance of Deep Care for Businesses
The Deep Care principle also has relevance beyond nonprofit programmes. Businesses serving low-income and emerging market customers often operate in environments where adoption can be difficult. A customer may purchase a product but lack the knowledge, confidence, finance, market access or support needed to use it successfully.
However, for an enterprise, thinking beyond the transaction does not necessarily mean providing open-ended assistance. It can mean designing better customer journeys. For instance, a financial services company might ask whether customers are successfully using an account rather than simply opening one. A company selling agricultural products might look beyond the sale to determine whether farmers are actually able to use the product to improve productivity. A training enterprise might measure not only completion of a course, but whether trainees find and retain employment afterwards.
These questions can also have a business rationale. Customers who successfully adopt and benefit from a product are more likely to continue using it, recommend it, and engage with additional products or services from the same company. In this sense, customer success and social impact do not have to be competing objectives. For enterprises serving emerging markets, creating lasting value for the customer can also create lasting value for the business.
 
The Implications of Deep Care for Measurement
This longer-term mentality changes the questions we ask after an intervention or transaction. If a woman receives an asset to start a business, we should not stop at recording the value of the asset and reporting that the business has started. We should ask: Is she finding customers? Can she manage her income? Can she deal with an unexpected expense? Does she know where to obtain additional finance? Is her family supporting her work? What happens if the business does not perform as expected?
The same questions can be adapted for enterprises and other development interventions. Is the customer still using the product? Is the service improving their economic position? Are they able to overcome the initial barriers to adoption? Are they returning because the product creates genuine value?
These questions require a continuing relationship, but that relationship does not have to look the same in every programme or business. For some people, it may mean providing intensive early coaching. For others, it may mean offering periodic check-ins, facilitating access to peer networks or other programmes or institutions, or providing support with digital communication or market linkages. The important thing is to design the relationship around the outcome rather than around the organisational calendar.
This has an important implication for measurement. We should continue measuring outputs like how many people were trained, how many businesses were started, or how many products were distributed. But we should also measure what happens afterwards. Are people still using the skills they learned after 12 months? Are the businesses they launched still operating? Has their income become more stable? Have customers continued using the product or service?
These measures require time and resources. But they tell us whether an intervention or product created lasting value. That also means follow-up cannot always be treated as an optional activity added when funding permits. If long-term outcomes matter, then the resources required to understand those outcomes should be built into the budget when the programme or business model is designed.
 
Rethinking What a Successful Exit Means
Deep Care ultimately asks us to rethink what constitutes a successful exit. For a development organisation, a successful exit should not simply mean that the organisation has completed its activities. It should mean that people have developed enough skills, confidence, resources and connections to continue moving forward with less direct support. For an enterprise, success should not necessarily end with a completed transaction. It should also include understanding whether the product or service has created sustained value for the customer.
This does not mean that organisations must maintain intensive relationships forever. Follow-up can become lighter. Peer networks can take over some functions. Former participants can become mentors. Local institutions can provide services. Technology can maintain lower-cost forms of contact. Businesses can build customer-support and engagement systems that are appropriate to their market. The aim is not to extend every programme indefinitely, but rather to recognise that the period after delivery is part of the outcome.
Ultimately, we need to recognise that people rarely build secure livelihoods through one intervention or one transaction. A project can open a door. Training can provide a skill. Finance can create an opportunity. An asset can help someone get started. And a business can provide a product that solves a real problem. But what happens after that opportunity is created may determine whether the change lasts.
 
John Kennedy Philip is the Coordinator of the ECO Wheels Project at Shishu Mandir.

items.author: Akshit Pushkarna
items.content:
Insurtech company Turtlemint managed to cut its consolidated net loss for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) by 67% to ₹25.8 Cr from ₹78.5 Cr in the year-ago period. On a sequential basis, the company’s loss declined 32% from ₹37.8 Cr.
Operating revenue for the quarter surged 35% YoY and 16% QoQ to ₹342.2 Cr. Including other income of ₹9.5 Cr, total income for the quarter surged to ₹351.7 Cr.
Meanwhile, total expenses for the quarter also zoomed by 25% to ₹375.2 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹299.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. The company also incurred an additional tax expense of ₹2.3 Cr in Q2 FY27.
In its investor presentation, Turtlemint said that its EBITDA loss stood at ₹17 Cr in Q2 FY27, which the management called the lowest ever during the quarterly earnings call. In contrast, the company reported an EBITDA loss of ₹40 Cr in Q2 FY26.
“Q2 FY27 has been another quarter of consistent delivery. Platform premium grew 55% You and revenue from operations rose 35%, underlining the depth of the distribution network we have built over the years. Our service EBITDA grew 47% YoY this quarter,which shows that every incremental Rupee of business is becoming more efficient to serve,” said Turtlemint cofounder and CEO Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and cofounder and COO Anand Prabhudesai in a joint statement.
On the operational front, Turtlemint noted that it processed platform premiums worth ₹1,214 Cr in the quarter under review, up 55% YoY. For context, platform premiums refers to the total value of insurance premiums on policies sold through Turtlemint’s platform during the period.
The company also claims to have added 37,000 new digital partners in the quarter under review, taking its total quarterly active digital partner base to 93,000.
Responding to a question about the impact of IRDAI’s new insurance reforms, the management, during the earnings call, estimated that the income of point-of-sales-persons (POSPs) could fall by about ₹1,000 a month compared to its agents. The company believes that this decline could be offset by selling one or two additional policies.
The management, however, declined to share FY28 stress-case numbers, saying it will do so once the final IRDAI rules are out. But it expects service EBITDA to hold flat in absolute terms next year.
Founded in 2015 by Prabhudesai and Mahyavanshi, Turtlemint operates an insurance distribution platform, connecting consumers with insurers through a network of financial advisors for car, bike, health, and term life insurance.
Operationally, the company claims to be active in 19,186 pincodes with 83 physical branches.
Shares of Turtlemint closed 1.5% higher at ₹61.38 apiece on the BSE today.

items.author: Zaigham Naqvi
items.content:
The federal government on Thursday reduced the prices of petrol and high-speed diesel by Rs3 and Rs4 per litre, respectively, for November 13.
The new petrol price is Rs332 while that of HSD is Rs360, according to a press release from the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority.
On November 2, the government announced that oil refineries would bear a burden of Rs15 billion per month, which would allow petrol to be sold Rs15 cheaper than it was in the global market amid the US-Israeli war on Iran.
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
International students are turning away from the United States and Britain in favour of universities in Asia and continental Europe, a global university survey showed ​on Thursday, as tighter visa rules redraw the global map of higher ‌education.
International students typically pay far higher fees than domestic ones and are a major source of revenue, helping offset their host countries' teaching and research costs.
Britain and the US recorded the steepest drops in international undergraduate ​numbers, down 19% and 13%, respectively, in the October-August period compared with the ​same period a year earlier, the survey of 437 universities in 63 countries ⁠conducted by Studyportals, NAFSA and Oxford Test of English showed.
Canada and Australia also saw ​weaker demand, while universities in Asia and Europe reported stronger international enrolment growth, they said. Studyportals ​is a Netherlands-based student recruitment platform, NAFSA is a US-based nonprofit that advocates for international education, and the Oxford Test of English is run by Oxford University Press.
US institutions were the most pessimistic about the outlook, ​with more than a third expecting enrolments to decline further in the coming years.
Read More: Visa scam exposed at Islamabad airport
The survey ​found that visa restrictions and government policies were the biggest barriers to recruitment, with processing delays, tougher ‌screening and ⁠changes to post-study work rules prompting students to defer or abandon plans to enrol.
The decline in interest in US universities comes after President Donald Trump tightened scrutiny of international students, expanding social media checks, revoking thousands of visas and imposing tougher rules on how long they can ​stay in the country. ​The survey was conducted ⁠before the November 3 midterm elections in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, although the president retains executive authority over ​visa rules.
Meanwhile, Britain has tightened its student visa rules as successive ​governments seek to ⁠reduce immigration, restricting most international students from bringing dependants and planning to shorten the period graduates can remain in the country to work or seek employment.
"These survey results affirm what we've observed ⁠before: ​national policies matter to international students making major decisions about ​where to study, conduct research, or start a career," Dr Fanta Aw, the executive director and CEO of NAFSA, ​said.

items.author: Debarghya Sil
items.content:
Online pharmacy startup PlatinumRx is in talks to raise around $32 Mn (over ₹300 Cr) in a funding round led by Belgium-based investment giant Sofina Ventures, as per sources familiar with the discussion. The proposed transaction is expected to value the Bengaluru-based startup somewhere in the range of $150-200 Mn (₹1,400-1,878 Cr).
The proposed investment comes around a year after the startup raised $6 Mn in its Series A round. Stellaris Venture Partners and India Quotient backed the startup in its Series A round. The startup had previously raised around $800K in a seed round in April 2024, also led by India Quotient.
Inc42 has reached out to the aforementioned investors to understand whether they will participate in the round.
The September 2025 round had helped the startup strengthen its supply chain, expand fulfilment capabilities and build its product and technology teams. It had also outlined plans to add five fulfilment centres and improve sourcing efficiencies to make affordable substitute medicines more accessible.
The discussions are understood to be ongoing, and the final terms of the transaction, including the valuation and investor participation, could change. Questions sent to PlatinumRx and Sofina Ventures didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story.
If concluded, the funding round would mark a significant jump in PlatinumRx’s valuation and provide it with the fresh capital required to strengthen its presence in India’s online pharmacy market.
Founded in 2023 by Ashutosh Pandey and Piyush Kumar, PlatinumRx operates an online pharmacy platform focused on helping consumers find affordable alternatives to prescribed medicines.
The platform recommends substitute medicines with the same composition, allowing customers to access lower-cost options, particularly for recurring and chronic medication requirements. These medicines are sourced directly from pharmaceutical companies and offer alternatives with the same composition, addressing the price difference between branded medicines and their substitutes.
It claims to have served over 10 Lakh customers till date.
The proposed funding comes amid continued investor interest in specialised healthcare and pharmacy platforms. While quick commerce platforms are expanding into medicine delivery, online pharmacy startups are also attempting to build differentiated models around affordability, assortment and access.
Broadly, the online pharmacy segment has continued to attract sizable investments. Quick medicine delivery startup Plazza raised $15 Mn in a Series A funding round in July 2026, co-led by Accel, Elevation Capital and Nexus Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors All In Capital and Better Capital.
The Bengaluru-based startup operates a pharmacy-first quick commerce model focused on 15-30 minute medicine deliveries. On the other hand, last year, Truemeds had raised $85 Mn in funding to scale generic medicine delivery.

items.author: Pop Culture & Art
items.content:
Netflix is facing criticism for keeping Russell Brand’s stand-up special, Russell Brand: Re, in its catalogue following the comedian’s conviction for rape and sexual assault.
The streaming service has reportedly stopped recommending the 2018 special to subscribers, while its title page remains publicly available.
LBC and NME also reported that the programme has been hidden from Netflix’s search results, making it less visible to viewers.
Filmed at London’s Hackney Empire and released in December 2018, the hour-long performance features Brand discussing changes in his life after becoming a father. Netflix classifies the special as TV-MA.
A source at the streaming company told The Telegraph that the decision to retain the programme was based on giving subscribers control over what they watch.
The move has prompted mixed reactions. Some have called for Netflix to remove the special, with one questioning why the company had previously dropped Kevin Spacey from the final season of House of Cards.
Netflix resumed production without Spacey after sexual misconduct allegations emerged in 2017 and shelved his film Gore, which was awaiting release.
Others questioned whether Brand continues to receive payments from the special, while some criticised Netflix’s decision to keep it available.
Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison at Southwark Crown Court on November 9.
He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women, for offences committed between 2004 and 2009. He denied the charges and was acquitted of three other counts.

items.author: Abbas Naqvi
items.content:
The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) has removed Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui’s name as the convener of Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) from its official website, leaving the party among 13 political parties without a recognised head in the commission's records.
The commission removed Maqbool over MQM-P's inability to hold an intra-party election.
The list also includes Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), Tehreek-e-Labbaik Pakistan (TLP), Pakhtunkhwa Milli Awami Party (PkMAP) and Pakistan Sunni Tehreek. The remaining eight are relatively lesser-known political organisations with no representation in the national or provincial assemblies.
Read: ECP delists two political parties over violations
The development has brought into focus the status of political party leadership under the ECP’s regulatory framework, with several parties, including those represented in parliament, currently lacking officially recognised heads.
PTI lost its recognised leadership status following a dispute over its intra-party elections and related electoral matters involving party founder Imran Khan.
TLP is also listed without a recognised head. Its former chief, Saad Rizvi, has remained out of public view since a state crackdown following the party’s violent long march last year. Concerns have persisted over his whereabouts, with speculation that he may be in government custody. However, his detention has not been officially confirmed.
Similarly, PKMAP chief Mahmood Khan Achakzai no longer appears as the party’s recognised head in the ECP records. Achakzai was elected as the party’s sole member of the National Assembly, while PKMAP has no representation in any provincial assembly.
Pakistan Sunni Tehreek is also among the parties without a recognised head on the commission's list.
Meanwhile, the ECP has issued a show-cause notice to MQM-P over its failure to hold intra-party elections. The party has submitted its response to the commission.
MQM-P last held intra-party elections on October 15, 2021. Since then, the ECP has issued several notices to the party, which secured extensions totalling one year at different stages to fulfil the requirement.
Also Read: MQM-P calls for new administrative units to address urban Sindh’s woes
The latest extension expired on October 15, 2026.
Under the relevant legal and regulatory requirements, political parties are required to hold intra-party elections at intervals not exceeding five years.
The removal of Siddiqui's name from the ECP website comes amid the party’s failure to hold fresh intra-party elections within the prescribed timeframe, raising questions about its leadership status in the commission's official records.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has taken legal action against Chinese automaker BYD over concerns that the company may have used protected design or technical features of the Land Rover Defender while developing its Ti7 plug-in hybrid SUV. However, a recent court ruling in the Netherlands has dealt a setback to JLR by overturning an earlier order allowing the seizure of evidence from BYD’s offices.
The District Court of The Hague ordered JLR to end the evidence seizure and destroy the collected data under specified conditions. The ruling follows a legal dispute that became public in August 2026, when court-appointed bailiffs visited BYD offices in Schiedam and Hoofddorp. They collected digital records under an order obtained by JLR.
JLR Takes BYD to Court Over Alleged Land Rover Defender Copying
The British automaker reportedly suspected that BYD had dismantled and examined a Land Rover Defender to gather information for developing its Ti7 SUV. However, the specific design features or technical details allegedly copied have not been publicly identified.
BYD challenged the evidence collection, arguing that JLR was conducting an unnecessary search for information without a clearly defined purpose. The company described the operation as a “fishing expedition” and claimed that it involved collecting excessive amounts of data.
The Dutch court’s latest decision also stopped enforcement measures linked to the evidence seizure. However, the ruling does not determine whether BYD violated JLR’s intellectual property rights. The main legal dispute over the alleged use of protected designs and technology remains unresolved.
BYD Ti7’s Design and Specifications
BYD introduced the Fangchengbao Tai 7 in China in September 2025. The SUV has a boxy exterior, squared wheel arches and an upright rear design, which have drawn comparisons with the Land Rover Defender.
The UK version of the vehicle offers three rows of seats and can accommodate seven passengers. It measures 5,146 mm in length, 1,995 mm in width and 1,865 mm in height.
The Ti7 uses BYD’s DM-p plug-in hybrid system, which combines a 1.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine with two electric motors. The setup produces more than 400 horsepower and comes with all-wheel drive.
The SUV also features a 35.6 kWh Blade Battery. According to BYD, it can cover up to 119 km on electric power under the WLTP testing cycle. The vehicle can accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in 4.8 seconds.
BYD Ti7 Costs Less Than the Defender
Price is another major difference between the two SUVs. BYD has set the starting price of the Ti7 in the UK at £47,995, while the seven-seat Land Rover Defender 110 starts at £68,465.
BYD plans to bring the Ti7 to UK showrooms in November 2026, with customer deliveries expected to begin in January 2027.
The legal dispute comes shortly before the SUV’s UK launch. However, the latest Dutch court decision does not impose any restriction on its sales.
This is not the first time JLR has challenged a Chinese automaker over vehicle design similarities. In 2019, the British company won a legal case involving the Landwind X7, a Chinese SUV that attracted criticism for its resemblance to the Range Rover Evoque.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) government has linked its e-Registry system with the Land Record Management System and the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) to make land registration and mutation processes faster, more transparent and efficient.
KP Chief Secretary Dr Muhammad Fakhre Alam Irfan and Adviser on Finance and Revenue Tariq Mehmood Pasha formally inaugurated the integrated digital system on Wednesday.
KP Integrates E-Registry with Land Record System and FBR
During the inauguration ceremony, officials explained that the integration would automate the process from property registration to mutation. The new system is expected to reduce delays, improve record management and minimise the chances of irregularities in land-related transactions.
Under the new arrangement, several steps, including mutation preparation, biometric verification, and the entry of mutation numbers, will take place automatically. This will reduce manual work and make the overall process more efficient.
See Also: FBR Introduces New Rules for Electronic Scrutiny of Tax Returns
FBR Taxes to Be Paid and Verified Online
The integration of the Land Record Management System with the FBR will also allow citizens to pay federal taxes on property mutations online.
The FBR will directly verify these tax payments through the integrated system. A record of the relevant tax payment will also be attached to each mutation, helping maintain a transparent record of property transactions.
The digital arrangement is also expected to reduce the need for citizens to visit government offices repeatedly or wait for lengthy procedures to complete their land registration and mutation requests.
Senior Member Board of Revenue, relevant government secretaries, the Managing Director of the Information Technology Board and other Revenue Board officials also attended the inauguration ceremony.
The initiative marks another step towards digitising land administration in KP. By connecting different government systems, the provincial government aims to simplify property-related procedures, improve transparency and make public services more accessible to citizens.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Nigerian fintech startup Raenest has completed the acquisition of Remitise, a UK-based payments company, for an undisclosed amount to expand its regulatory footprint and gain greater control over its global payments infrastructure.
Founded in 2022 by Victor Alade, Sodruldeen Mustapha, and Richard Oyome, Raenest initially operated as an Employer of Record (EOR) before evolving into a platform that redefines global banking for Africans, helping businesses and freelancers receive international payments, convert between currencies, operate a multi-currency wallet, while managing transactions seamlessly.
The platform also enables customers to open global bank accounts in their names, access physical and virtual dollar cards, and manage payments in USD, EUR, and GBP. To date, the company has amassed over one million individual customers across more than 50 countries, processed over US$2 billion in payments, and served over 300 businesses. It also offers a consumer-focused product, Geegpay, which provides Africa’s gig economy with efficient payment solutions.
Raenest raised US$11 million in Series A funding in February 2025 to expand its reach in existing and new markets, and its acquisition of Remitise is linked to that ambition.
“Acquiring Remitise is part of our long-term strategy to build a global financial company. We want to own more of the infrastructure behind our products, deepen our relationships with financial institutions and create a stronger foundation for the customers and businesses we serve,” said Victor Alade, Raenest’s CEO.
The acquisition builds on Raenest’s regulatory footprint and includes a money services business (MSB) and payment service provider (PSP) licence in Canada, as well as an international money transfer operator licence in Nigeria.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has introduced new rules for the electronic scrutiny of income tax returns for tax year 2026. The system will use automated technology to identify errors and discrepancies in tax returns while allowing taxpayers to explain or correct them before the authorities initiate legal or penalty proceedings.
The FBR has issued SRO 2098(I)/2026 to amend the Income Tax Rules, 2002, by adding a new Rule 38B. The provision, titled “Procedure for Electronic Scrutiny and Intimation of Issues Detected by the Automated System,” outlines how the electronic review process will work.
FBR Introduces New Rules for Electronic Scrutiny of Tax Returns
Under the new rules, the FBR will use an automated Computerised Risk Management (CRM) system to examine income tax returns submitted under Section 120(2A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.
The system will analyse tax returns and identify possible factual or legal errors, inconsistencies and other discrepancies. It may then send online notifications or advance intimations to taxpayers through the IRIS portal, explaining the issues that require attention.
Taxpayers to Get Seven Days to Respond
The new mechanism will allow taxpayers to clarify discrepancies, correct mistakes or take other necessary steps before the FBR considers legal or penal action.
Taxpayers will receive at least seven days to respond to an electronic notification. If they fail to reply within the given period, the automated system will issue a reminder, providing another response period of at least seven days.
The rules also allow the relevant Officer of Inland Revenue to issue advance notifications directly to taxpayers if discrepancies are identified during the scrutiny process.
FBR to Maintain Digital Records of Responses
The FBR will maintain records of all discrepancies identified by the automated system, notifications sent to taxpayers, and responses received from them.
These details will also be shared with the Officer of Inland Revenue responsible for the taxpayer’s case. A dedicated dashboard will record notifications, taxpayer responses and any subsequent action taken by the authorities.
The new rules further provide for the use of a Change Request Form (CRF) to implement automated scrutiny, data analysis, cross-matching and electronic communication with taxpayers.
After reviewing a taxpayer’s response, or the failure to provide one, the concerned Inland Revenue officer will decide whether further action is necessary under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, and its relevant rules.
The new system aims to make tax return scrutiny more organised and transparent while giving taxpayers an opportunity to address potential issues before the FBR takes further action.
