items.author: NITDA
items.content:
By Oluwole Alao
The Director General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa, CCIE, has reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to building a resilient, inclusive and competitive digital economy through strategic partnerships with international technology companies, emphasising that the country’s digital policies are designed to attract investment, strengthen local capacity and secure its digital future.
The DG stated this while receiving a delegation from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, led by the President of the U.S.-Africa Business Centre, Kendra Gaither, during a visit to NITDA to explore opportunities for deeper collaboration between Nigeria and the United States in digital transformation, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, data governance and technology investment.
Inuwa explained that Nigeria’s digital transformation agenda is anchored on two fundamental objectives: ensuring citizens have reliable access to essential digital services and positioning them to participate meaningfully in value creation within the digital economy.
“Our policy intent is just about two things. First, to make sure our citizens have basic access, no matter what. What I mean by no matter what means we should have a capacity for digital self-determination,” he said.
He explained that the Agency’s sovereign cloud initiative is intended to strengthen national control over critical digital infrastructure, enhance resilience against disruptions, mitigate risks and provide flexibility in the adoption of technology solutions.
According to him, digital sovereignty should not be interpreted as an attempt to exclude international technology companies, but rather as an opportunity to encourage them to invest in Nigeria’s digital infrastructure and collaborate with local businesses to deliver sustainable solutions.
“It’s not about politics. It’s not about locking our doors against anybody, but it’s about inviting you to come and build with us,” the DG noted.
Inuwa further highlighted the importance of developing local infrastructure and capacity to ensure that Nigeria derives greater economic value from its growing digital market. He asserted that investments in domestic data centres and cloud infrastructure would create opportunities for local businesses, support innovation and strengthen the country’s position as a technology hub for West and Central Africa.
He disclosed that the Federal Government had invested more than ₦4.5 trillion in information technology between June 2023 and June 2026, noting that appropriate infrastructure and policy frameworks could help channel relevant government technology services towards locally hosted sovereign cloud solutions.
The NITDA boss also addressed concerns surrounding data localisation and regulatory compliance, particularly in the financial technology ecosystem. He said that the Agency was working with relevant regulators, including the Central Bank of Nigeria, to develop an assurance framework that would provide clarity on technical requirements, support compliance and encourage investment in local infrastructure.
Emphasising the importance of resilience and flexibility, he said, “We need that portability. If Google has better services, I should be able to move my services from Microsoft to Google or AWS.”
He added that policies must create an environment where technology providers can compete fairly while government and businesses retain the flexibility to adopt solutions that best meet their needs.
Inuwa also underscored the importance of collaboration in developing effective digital policies, noting that NITDA had previously worked with major technology companies, local providers and other stakeholders in shaping Nigeria’s cloud-first policy. He encouraged members of the delegation to sustain engagement with the Agency and explore practical ways of aligning their investments and solutions with the country’s digital priorities.
Responding to a proposal by Kavista Holdings for collaboration in digital transformation, workforce development and employment-oriented skills programmes, the DG invited the company to formally submit its proposal for assessment by the relevant NITDA team.
Earlier in her remarks, Kendra Gaither reaffirmed the American business community’s interest in deepening commercial engagement with Nigeria, identifying digital transformation, regulatory clarity and investment predictability as critical to expanding bilateral economic cooperation.
She described Nigeria as an important player in Africa’s information technology and digital economy landscape, noting that the country’s policy direction has significant implications for businesses operating across West Africa and the wider continent.
Gaither further noted that the delegation was seeking constructive dialogue with NITDA to better understand Nigeria’s evolving digital regulatory environment and identify practical ways to support shared economic and innovation objectives.
She stressed that a secure, competitive and predictable regulatory environment would benefit Nigerian businesses, U.S. companies and other international investors by providing clearer expectations for compliance and long-term investment decisions. She highlighted concerns around overlapping regulatory responsibilities and areas requiring greater clarity, particularly in cloud computing, data governance and financial services, while emphasising that companies wanted to comply with Nigeria’s requirements and continue expanding their operations.
Gaither also acknowledged Nigeria’s growing leadership in digital policy and trade discussions across the continent, expressing the Chamber’s readiness to draw on international experience and facilitate further engagement between NITDA and its member companies. She maintained that sustained dialogue would help address uncertainties, strengthen confidence and create opportunities for partnerships that advance Nigeria’s digital transformation while supporting the commercial interests of U.S. businesses.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce delegation included representatives of technology, financial services and investment organisations, including Microsoft and Citi, alongside members of the American Business Council and the U.S. Embassy.

items.summary:
By Oluwole Alao
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening Nigeria’s digital sovereignty and protecting the nation’s critical digital infrastructure through its partnership with the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) to advance the implementation of the National Sovereign Cloud Initiative and data localisation.
NITDA Director General, Kashifu Inuwa, CCIE, made this known at the Executive Regulatory Dialogue, organised by NITDA in partnership with the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), which brought together stakeholders across the financial services, telecommunications, data centre, and technology sectors to discuss strategies for strengthening Nigeria’s control over the digital infrastructure that underpins its economy.
During his welcome and context-setting address, Inuwa emphasised that digital sovereignty has become a critical national priority as Nigeria’s economy increasingly relies on digital platforms and infrastructure

items.content:
By Oluwole Alao
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) has reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening Nigeria’s digital sovereignty and protecting the nation’s critical digital infrastructure through its partnership with the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) to advance the implementation of the National Sovereign Cloud Initiative and data localisation.
NITDA Director General, Kashifu Inuwa, CCIE, made this known at the Executive Regulatory Dialogue, organised by NITDA in partnership with the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), which brought together stakeholders across the financial services, telecommunications, data centre, and technology sectors to discuss strategies for strengthening Nigeria’s control over the digital infrastructure that underpins its economy.
During his welcome and context-setting address, Inuwa emphasised that digital sovereignty has become a critical national priority as Nigeria’s economy increasingly relies on digital platforms and infrastructure to deliver essential services, particularly in the financial sector.
While highlighting the potential implications of external disruptions to essential digital services, Inuwa questioned, “Imagine what will happen to our economy if tomorrow a major disruption or geopolitical crisis prevents our banks from accessing critical digital infrastructure hosted outside our country. Can our citizens still transfer money? Can businesses still receive payments? Can our banks keep processing transactions? Can our economy continue functioning?”
He explained that such concerns extend beyond technology to issues of national economic security, financial stability and the country’s ability to maintain control over its digital future.
According to the NITDA DG, digital sovereignty should not be interpreted as technological isolation or an attempt to develop every technology locally. Rather, it involves building the national capacity required to make informed decisions about the technologies, infrastructure and standards on which the country depends.
“Digital sovereignty is not about politics. It is not about isolation. It is not about building everything ourselves, but it is about building our digital capacity to compete in the world we are today,” Inuwa stated.
 
He noted that Nigeria’s financial sector provides a compelling example of how deliberate policy decisions can stimulate digital transformation and local innovation. Recalling the introduction of the CBN’s cashless policy years ago, he explained that the policy’s push for financial institutions to upgrade their technology infrastructure helped create opportunities for fintech companies to develop innovative solutions, contributing to Nigeria’s emergence as a leading fintech ecosystem.
He commended the CBN for taking further steps to strengthen the country’s control over the infrastructure supporting financial services, expressing confidence that the sector could once again lead the way in advancing Nigeria’s digital transformation.
“Through this partnership, NITDA and CBN are working together to make sure the financial sector is the first sector to comply with our National Sovereign Cloud Initiative,” he stated.
Inuwa further explained that NITDA’s role is to provide the standards and overarching policy framework that sector-specific regulators can leverage to advance digital transformation within their respective industries. He stressed that achieving digital sovereignty requires a collaborative ecosystem involving financial institutions, telecommunications operators, data centre providers, system integrators, technology companies and global cloud service providers.
He assured stakeholders that the Nigerian technology ecosystem has the capacity to support the initiative, noting that the country is building on existing capabilities and international experience rather than starting from scratch.
“We have done it before, and we are going to do it now. So this is not something you can doubt; it is something that already exists,” he said, urging stakeholders to work collectively towards implementing the initiative.
The NITDA boss further disclosed that an assurance framework would guide implementation, with the Agency seeking to leverage existing international certification standards while ensuring compliance with Nigeria’s national sovereign architecture requirements. He added that the development of national certification options was also being explored to provide greater flexibility and choice.
He identified control, independence, resilience, risk management and freedom of choice as fundamental principles of digital sovereignty. According to him, Nigeria must develop the capacity to maintain essential services despite external disruptions, reduce exposure to geopolitical and technology-related risks, and avoid excessive dependence on individual vendors or jurisdictions.
 
While underscoring the need for resilient digital infrastructure capable of sustaining critical financial operations during disruptions, Inuwa averred, “Submarine cable disruption cannot automatically affect our payment system.”
He added that the initiative would help prevent vendor lock-in and strengthen Nigeria’s ability to determine the technologies and infrastructure best suited to its national interests.
In his keynote address, the Deputy Governor, Financial System Stability, CBN, Mr Lamido Abubakar Yuguda, reaffirmed the Bank’s commitment to strengthening Nigeria’s financial stability, cybersecurity and protection of critical financial data through the implementation of the National Sovereign Cloud Initiative (NSCI) and data localisation.
Yuguda commended NITDA for its leadership in advancing Nigeria’s digital transformation agenda, noting that the growing adoption of digital payments, fintech, mobile money and digital banking has increased the financial sector’s dependence on digital infrastructure.
He stressed that financial institutions must strengthen cybersecurity, business continuity, disaster recovery and risk management arrangements, while ensuring compliance with applicable data localisation requirements and the January 1, 2027, implementation timeline for critical payment transaction data.
The CBN Deputy Governor emphasised that the initiative should promote innovation rather than isolate Nigeria from global technological developments, calling for stronger collaboration among regulators, financial institutions and technology providers.
“Our collective objective should be clear: to build a digital financial ecosystem that is innovative without compromising security, sovereign without becoming isolated and resilient enough to sustain public confidence,” he stated.
In his presentation on the pre-event survey findings, the Special Assistant to the NITDA DG on Policy, Dr Muhammad Aminu Lawal, disclosed that the survey has identified regulatory clarity, migration timelines and local infrastructure capacity as critical issues requiring urgent attention ahead of the January 1, 2027, deadline.
He, however, highlighted that on the supply side, the survey indicated that Nigeria has existing capacity to support early adopters, with 79 per cent of the 42 digital infrastructure and service providers surveyed reporting readiness to accommodate additional financial-sector workloads, while 74 per cent said they could onboard new financial customers within three months.
Dr Lawal stated that much of the planned infrastructure expansion is expected in 2027, with financing costs, power supply and foreign exchange identified as major constraints.
The findings therefore called for clear written regulatory guidance, phased or risk-based implementation milestones, a defined exceptions process and verifiable information on assured local infrastructure providers.
He concluded that the survey underscores the need for coordinated action by NITDA, CBN and industry stakeholders to address implementation uncertainties, strengthen local digital infrastructure and support a smooth transition to Nigeria-based data hosting and management.

items.content:
By Oluwole Alao
 
In alignment with the presidential agenda of Reforming the Economy for Sustained Inclusive Growth, the Director General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa, CCIE, has called for a fundamental shift in Nigeria’s education system from an economy that places primary emphasis on academic certificates to one that prioritises practical capabilities, innovation, and the ability to translate knowledge into solutions that drive national development.
The DG, who was represented by the agency’s Director of the Special Duties Department, Dr Aristotle Onumo, made this call while delivering the keynote address at the 3rd International Biennial Conference of the College of Physical Sciences (COLPHYS 2026) at the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta (FUNAAB), Ogun State.
Speaking on the theme, “From Scientific Discovery to National Prosperity: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence and Convergent Innovation to Transform Nigeria,” he emphasised the need for universities to move beyond the traditional boundaries of academic disciplines and embrace collaborative research, emerging technologies, and practical problem-solving.
Addressing the university community, researchers, scientists, entrepreneurs, and students, Inuwa noted that Nigeria’s development would depend not merely on the volume of research produced or the number of academic publications generated, but on the country’s ability to convert scientific knowledge into productive enterprises, innovative solutions, improved public services, and better livelihoods.
“The future of our country will not be determined simply by how much research we produce. It will be determined by how effectively we convert research into productivity, innovation, enterprise and national prosperity,” he stated.
He explained that Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly enabling convergence across disciplines such as agriculture, healthcare, environmental science, mathematics, engineering, and data science, creating opportunities to address complex national challenges through multidisciplinary collaboration.
According to him, AI should complement human expertise and strengthen scientific discovery rather than replace researchers or diminish the importance of human judgment.
While stressing that the real value of technological advancement lies in its practical application to improve human lives, the DG said, “AI does not replace science. It amplifies science.”
Using agriculture as an example, he illustrated how integrating agricultural science, satellite imagery, climate modelling, Internet of Things sensors, and AI could help farmers improve planting decisions, detect crop diseases, optimise irrigation, reduce input waste, and access better market information.
He, however, cautioned that innovations must be designed around Nigeria’s realities, including local languages, affordability, limited connectivity, and the specific needs of the people expected to use them.
He similarly highlighted opportunities for AI-enabled solutions in healthcare and climate resilience, including improved disease surveillance, clinical decision support, flood-risk prediction, and early-warning systems. He maintained that such technologies must be responsibly deployed, with appropriate safeguards for data privacy, accountability, fairness, and public trust.
Inuwa reaffirmed NITDA’s commitment to strengthening Nigeria’s digital transformation ecosystem through digital literacy, talent development, digital infrastructure, innovation, and responsible technology adoption. He referenced the Agency’s Strategic Roadmap and Action Plan (SRAP 2.0), the National Digital Literacy Framework (NDLF), the Digital Literacy for All initiative (DL4ALL), and the 3 Million Technical Talent (3MTT) programme as key efforts supporting the development of the skills and capabilities required for a technology-driven economy.
He also highlighted the importance of expanding access to reliable connectivity and research infrastructure, noting that scientific institutions need suitable computing resources, quality datasets, secure cloud environments, and dependable electricity to compete effectively and develop locally relevant innovations. He called for stronger partnerships among government, academia, industry, investors, and entrepreneurs to create pathways through which promising research can be validated, commercialised, and deployed at scale.
Turning specifically to higher education institutions, the NITDA DG urged universities to redefine how they measure academic and institutional success by placing greater emphasis on research impact, collaborative problem-solving, entrepreneurship, and the development of graduates capable of creating opportunities rather than merely seeking existing jobs.
“The university of the future cannot remain merely a place where knowledge is transmitted, and certificates are awarded. It must become a place where problems are investigated, solutions are developed, enterprises are created, and society is transformed,” he said.
He encouraged universities to strengthen technology transfer mechanisms, establish more effective research-industry partnerships, expand entrepreneurship education, and connect innovation hubs to real market and community needs. He further challenged researchers to consider how their discoveries could progress from academic publications to working prototypes, field-tested solutions, and sustainable products or services that address pressing national challenges.
Speaking directly to students, Inuwa emphasised that academic qualifications remain important but must be complemented by relevant competencies, including digital and AI literacy, critical thinking, communication, teamwork, ethical judgment, and the capacity to solve practical problems.
“Your certificate may open the door, but your capability will determine how far you go,” he remarked, urging students to use emerging technologies not merely to reproduce existing knowledge but to investigate difficult questions, discover new possibilities, and develop solutions to problems affecting their communities.
As part of his challenge to FUNAAB and its partners, the DG proposed a practical 12-month innovation agenda aimed at translating conference deliberations into measurable outcomes. He urged the College of Physical Sciences to identify a select number of high-impact national challenges within the first 90 days, establish collaborative research teams and begin developing prototypes within six months, test promising solutions with relevant communities and industry partners within nine months, and organise a research-to-impact showcase within 12 months.
He stressed that the proposed agenda should be assessed through tangible outcomes, including validated prototypes, effective partnerships, commercialisation opportunities, and measurable benefits to society, rather than speeches and presentations alone. He also encouraged the conference organisers to build on the technical sessions and proposal-writing workshop to develop fundable, collaborative research projects.
Inuwa expressed NITDA’s openness to exploring structured, mandate-aligned collaboration with academic and research institutions, particularly in areas that advance digital skills, responsible AI, indigenous innovation, and practical applications of emerging technologies. He maintained, however, that successful partnerships must begin with clearly defined problems and credible implementation plans.
He challenged researchers, university leaders, and students to reflect on the problems their research would solve, the lives their innovations would improve, and the benefits Nigeria would derive from translating knowledge into action.
“Let this conference be remembered not merely as another gathering of brilliant minds, but as a turning point where we resolved to convert the power of science into the prosperity of our nation,” he concluded.
 
Earlier in his welcome address, the Vice-Chancellor of FUNAAB, Professor Olusola Babatunde, who was represented at the event by the Dean of the College of Environmental Resources Management (COLERM), Professor Olusegun Oguntoke, applauded NITDA for its remarkable contribution to the advancement of digital transformation in the country and appealed for the establishment of an Information Technology (IT) Hub at the university.
He emphasised the importance of such a facility in strengthening the institution’s digital capacity, supporting research and innovation, and providing an enabling environment for students and researchers to develop practical technology-driven solutions.

LAGOS, October 30, 2026 — The Director-General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, CCIE, has challenged African innovators, investors and policymakers to transform the continent from a major consumer of digital technologies into a globally competitive creator of innovative solutions, intellectual property and sustainable technology enterprises.
In his keynote address prepared for Moonshot 2026, organised by TechCabal at the National Theatre, Lagos, from October 28–29, under the theme “Courage & Conviction — Building for a New World,” the NITDA boss emphasised that Africa’s technological future must be defined by innovation, entrepreneurship, collaboration and measurable economic impact.
“Africa’s next chapter will not be written by the technologies we consume. It will be written by the value we have the courage to create,” he declared.
Abdullahi observed that Africa possesses exceptional technological talent but continues to face significant gaps in access to infrastructure, financing, mentorship and markets. He stressed that bridging these gaps requires stronger collaboration among government, universities, investors, technology companies and innovation hubs.
Highlighting NITDA’s evolving role as an ecosystem orchestrator, he explained that the Agency’s Strategic Roadmap and Action Plan (SRAP 2.0) prioritises connecting digital talent to opportunities, research to commercialisation, startups to capital, innovation to markets and technological advancement to public trust.
He challenged Nigeria’s technology ecosystem to move beyond celebrating hackathons, pitch competitions and funding announcements towards building commercially viable enterprises that create jobs, solve real problems and compete internationally.
“The true measure of an innovation ecosystem is not how many startups it celebrates. It is how many sustainable enterprises it helps create,” he stated.
As part of this transformation, the Director-General highlighted the forthcoming Builders’ Festival at the Digital Nigeria International Conference and Exhibition, scheduled for November 10–12, 2026, in Abuja. The initiative aims to connect indigenous startups developing solutions to real industry challenges with corporate organisations, investors and potential customers, targeting a ₦3 billion investment pipeline for promising entrepreneurs. He clarified that the figure represents a mobilisation target rather than funding already secured.
On artificial intelligence, Abdullahi urged Nigeria to develop indigenous AI capabilities in agriculture, healthcare, education, manufacturing and local-language technologies rather than remain dependent on imported applications.
He called on investors to support promising indigenous enterprises, corporations to create opportunities for startup solutions, and government institutions to strengthen enabling policies, infrastructure and strategic partnerships.
Concluding, the NITDA boss maintained that Africa’s technological competitiveness would depend on three critical foundations: innovation, trust and disciplined execution.
“The future will not belong only to those who predict it. It will belong to those with the courage to build it, the conviction to sustain it, and the discipline to make it work,” he declared.
He urged African innovators to embrace global ambition while developing solutions that create lasting economic opportunities and prosperity across the continent.
“Let us stop asking whether Africa can build the future. Let us start demonstrating how Africa will build it.”

items.content:
By James Ishaku
The National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) has reaffirmed the importance of strategic partnerships and stakeholder collaboration in advancing Nigeria’s digital transformation agenda, calling for renewed commitment to the implementation of its strategic roadmap and action plan.
The Director General of NITDA, Kashifu Inuwa, who was represented by Dr Aristotle Onumo, Director, Special Duties Directorate made the statement during the SRAP 2.0 Stakeholders’ Engagement at Lagos Business School, Lagos State.
Inuwa commended the leadership of Lagos Business School for sustaining the partnership with the agency, noting that collaboration and collective intelligence remained critical to achieving meaningful progress in Nigeria’s digital ecosystem.
He stressed that the impact of the agency’s initiatives could be deepened through stronger partnerships, adding that inclusive stakeholder participation was essential to delivering sustainable results in the country’s digital transformation efforts.
According to him, the strategic roadmap and action plan were developed through extensive stakeholder consultations and collaborative engagements, rather than as an internal document produced without external input.
He noted that stakeholders, including members of Lagos Business School, actively participated in developing the document, making their continued involvement in reviewing its implementation necessary.
The DG explained that the engagement provided an opportunity to assess progress, determine whether existing priorities remained relevant, identify areas requiring modification and establish whether the initiatives were delivering their intended impact.
He emphasised that the review was also necessary to evaluate progress against commitments made to stakeholders and ensure that the agency’s programmes continued to respond to the evolving needs of Nigeria’s digital ecosystem.
The NITDA DG also acknowledged the contributions of colleagues at the agency, highlighting its gradual transition towards becoming an ecosystem platform for digital innovation.
He observed that the agency’s approach was increasingly embracing co-creation and collaboration, moving beyond the traditional model of issuing regulations, directives and guidelines to working with stakeholders in developing and delivering digital solutions.
According to him, this approach was essential to building an enabling environment where innovation could thrive and digital initiatives could achieve broader societal and economic impact.
Inuwa further noted that the agency had spent the past three years advancing the transition and was approaching the final phase of the process. He urged stakeholders to renew their commitment and sustain the momentum required to achieve the desired outcomes.
Reaffirming the agency’s vision, he said the goal remained to make Nigeria a digitally enabled nation, fostering inclusive economic development through technological innovation.
He explained that the eight strategic pillars underpinning the roadmap remained central to achieving this vision and would continue to guide the agency’s priorities and interventions.
The DG urged stakeholders to critically assess progress across these areas, particularly in digital skills development, regulatory effectiveness, digital infrastructure and services, entrepreneurship, innovation and the growth of Nigeria’s startup ecosystem.
He also highlighted the importance of examining progress in implementing the Startup Act and assessing its contribution to strengthening the startup community and promoting innovation-driven enterprise development.
On stakeholder engagement, he stressed the need to ensure that relevant players across the digital ecosystem were carried along, noting that effective collaboration remained essential to achieving the objectives of the national digital agenda.
He expressed confidence that sustained partnerships, collective commitment and constructive contributions from stakeholders would help the agency address emerging challenges, strengthen implementation and advance Nigeria’s digital development goals.
Inuwa concluded by urging stakeholders to embrace the partnership approach and work collectively towards building a digitally enabled Nigeria that could serve as a catalyst for digital transformation across Africa.

items.author: NITDA
items.content:
By James Ishaku
The Director-General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa, has emphasised the need for inclusive digital infrastructure, affordable connectivity and sustained investment in emerging technologies to accelerate Nigeria’s economic growth and ensure that no citizen is left behind in the digital economy.
Inuwa stated this while participating in a session titled “Inclusive Growth in the Digital Age” at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit (NES#32), organised by the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning while highlighting the importance of expanding telecommunications infrastructure, particularly to underserved and rural communities, noting that Africa’s telecommunications history demonstrates how innovation can overcome seemingly insurmountable barriers to development.
Reflecting on the growth of the telecommunications sector since 2000, he recalled that many investors were initially reluctant to commit resources to the industry because of doubts about Africans’ ability to afford mobile phones. However, innovative approaches to infrastructure development and service delivery helped transform the sector despite inadequate electricity, roads and other essential infrastructure.
According to him, innovation must focus on democratising access, reducing costs and extending connectivity to rural communities to ensure that every citizen can participate meaningfully in the digital economy.
He noted that connectivity has become fundamental to social and economic inclusion, particularly as artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes decision-making and service delivery worldwide.
“If you are not represented, if you are not digitally visible, AI will not see you or consider you when making decisions,” he said, stressing that the exclusion of communities from the digital ecosystem could also mean the underrepresentation of their cultures, values and languages in emerging technologies.
Inuwa said the Federal Government, under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s leadership, was committed to using technology to promote inclusivity and national prosperity.
He explained that the President of Nigeria had directed the Minister of communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Bosun Tijani to conceptualise two major initiatives aimed at expanding connectivity across the country: the Universal Service Provision Fund (USPF) project and Project BRIDGE.
According to him, the USPF initiative is designed to extend telecommunications coverage to underserved areas through the deployment of base stations, while Project BRIDGE aims to deploy approximately 95,000 kilometres of fibre-optic infrastructure nationwide.
He said the initiatives would promote open-access infrastructure, encourage private-sector participation and make broadband services more affordable for Nigerians.
The NITDA Director General also called for a broader understanding of infrastructure development, arguing that the digital economy requires investments beyond conventional infrastructure such as roads and railways.
“Today, we are in a digital era; therefore, we need to build digital highways for our data as well,” he said.
He added that as Nigeria advances its artificial intelligence ambitions, investments in data centres, computing capacity and AI factories would be essential to ensuring that the country can harness the technology’s economic potential.
Inuwa further highlighted the relationship between connectivity, productivity and affordability, describing it as a chicken-and-egg situation. He explained that while telecommunications operators are concerned about consumers’ ability to pay for services, improved connectivity can enhance productivity, expand business opportunities and increase incomes, thereby strengthening citizens’ capacity to afford digital services.
He stressed the need to connect underserved communities so that individuals and businesses could use technology to improve their livelihoods, access new markets and participate more effectively in economic activities.
Beyond economic benefits, Inuwa said expanded digital infrastructure would enable the government to improve public service delivery and reduce operational costs by making essential services more accessible online.
He explained that citizens interact with government institutions at different stages of their lives, from birth registration and healthcare to education, employment, business development, marriage and property ownership.
However, the traditional process often requires citizens to visit multiple government offices to access these services.
According to him, a well-developed digital infrastructure would enable citizens to access government services more conveniently, improve service delivery and reduce administrative overheads.
He maintained that bridging Nigeria’s digital divide requires coordinated action by government and the private sector, supported by sustained investment in connectivity and advanced digital infrastructure.
Inuwa reiterated that inclusive digital development remains essential to ensuring that all Nigerians can benefit from technological innovation, contribute to national productivity and participate in the country’s emerging digital economy.

Pakistan’s largest integrated telecom and ICT services provider, Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL) has signed a partnership agreement with myco, a Web3-enabled international video streaming and entertainment platform, to offer PTCL customers an exclusive 50% discount on monthly English Premier League (EPL) subscription for the entire duration of the League. myco holds the official and exclusive streaming rights to EPL in Pakistan for the 2026-27 season.
The partnership brings together PTCL’s extensive customer base and billing ecosystem with myco’s premium digital sports entertainment proposition to provide Pakistani football fans a convenient and affordable way to follow the English Premier League throughout the season.
The partnership furthers PTCL’s efforts to expand its consumer services and value-added services (VAS) ecosystem by bringing relevant digital experiences within its customers’ reach. The offer is available to all PTCL customers, regardless of their connection type. The subscription journey has also been digitalized to make the process seamless, while the payable amount is conveniently added to the customer’s monthly PTCL bill.
Commenting on the partnership, Amad Khan, Chief Marketing Officer, PTCL, said,
“PTCL has always focused on evolving the customer experience beyond connectivity by bringing together services that add meaningful utility and convenience for our customers. This strengthens our standing as a 360 degree digital lifestyle partner for our customers that goes beyond simply keeping customers connected to enriching the many ways they live, work and engage in the digital world.”
Umair Masoom Usmani, Founder & Group CEO, myco, said,
“At myCo, our focus has always been on making premium entertainment and sports more accessible, affordable, and convenient for audiences across Pakistan. Our partnership with PTCL is another step towards that vision. By offering PTCL customers 50% off on myCo subscriptions, along with the convenience of paying directly through their PTCL bills, we are simplifying the streaming experience and bringing greater value to households across the country.”
With the collaboration, PTCL continues to explore ways of integrating relevant third-party services into its customer experience, creating greater value through convenience, accessibility and a seamless digital journey. The 50% monthly discount will remain available to PTCL customers for the duration of the English Premier League through May 30, 2027. PTCL Customers can subscribe to the offer through UPTCL App: https://uptcl.ptclgroup.com/Mjc3 or by visiting the website: https://ptclflashfiber.com/Home/PTCLMyco

items.title: CCPA Fines Ola ₹10 Lakh For Advance Tipping Prompts
items.summary:
The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of ₹10 Lakh on ANI Technologies Pvt Ltd, parent of ride-hailing platform Ola, for misleading customers into paying extra to improve their chances of getting a ride.
In an order dated November 10, the consumer watchdog said Ola’s advance tipping feature is an unfair trade practice and an unfair contract under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
The CCPA also directed Ola to stop the practice immediately, pay the penalty within 15 days of receiving the order and submit a compliance report within the same period.
The proceedings followed a complaint received against this issue where the app prompted users to pay extra to get bookings faster.
“Adding a tip might help increase the chances of getting a ride faster,” a message read.
Customers were initially offered preset amounts ranging from ₹10 to ₹40. These later increased to as much as ₹140, while customers could also enter custom amounts of up to ₹499.

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of ₹10 Lakh on ANI Technologies Pvt Ltd, parent of ride-hailing platform Ola, for misleading customers into paying extra to improve their chances of getting a ride.
In an order dated November 10, the consumer watchdog said Ola’s advance tipping feature is an unfair trade practice and an unfair contract under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
The CCPA also directed Ola to stop the practice immediately, pay the penalty within 15 days of receiving the order and submit a compliance report within the same period.
The proceedings followed a complaint received against this issue where the app prompted users to pay extra to get bookings faster.
“Adding a tip might help increase the chances of getting a ride faster,” a message read.
Customers were initially offered preset amounts ranging from ₹10 to ₹40. These later increased to as much as ₹140, while customers could also enter custom amounts of up to ₹499.
Ola argued that the payment was voluntary and went directly to drivers. It said the feature encouraged drivers to accept rides that were less attractive to them, particularly those requiring longer distances to reach passengers. The company also said that tipping did not affect its ride allocation system or guarantee faster ride confirmation.
However, the CCPA found that Ola’s own data did not support its claims. Data for June 1-15, 2026, showed that in Delhi, drivers accepted 38% of ride requests with an add-on, compared with 62% of requests without one. In Bengaluru, the acceptance rates were 40% and 68%, respectively, while in Mumbai they stood at 39% and 68%.
The authority also noted that Ola changed the feature’s name from ‘tip’ to ‘add-on’ on May 22, 2025, but continued to show messages suggesting that additional payments could help customers get a ride faster. During a hearing in June 2026, Ola demonstrated that its app still displayed messages such as “Improve your chances of quicker ride confirmation!” alongside preset payment amounts. The CCPA said the change in wording did not alter how the feature worked.
The authority also examined Ola’s data for Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai for June 1-15, 2026. The platform received nearly 39.94 Lakh ride requests across the three cities, of which 3.93 Lakh, or around 9.8%, included an add-on. Drivers accepted 1.51 Lakh of these requests.
Based on the average add-on amounts reported by Ola, the CCPA estimated that customers paid around ₹56 Lakh over and above the disclosed fares for these accepted rides.
The share of customers opting for add-ons also increased between June 2025 and June 2026. In Delhi, it rose from 8.2% to 11.04%, while in Bengaluru it increased from 9.7% to 10.64%. In Mumbai, it went up from 7.9% to 8.37%.
The CCPA rejected Ola’s argument that only a small number of customers used the feature, noting that everyone booking a ride was shown the prompts while waiting for confirmation.
It also said the feature could particularly affect people booking rides from hospitals, railway stations, bus terminals and airports, where they may be in a hurry and more dependent on getting a ride quickly.
CCPA Flags Confirm Shaming Dark Pattern
The CCPA’s action comes after the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) directed ride-hailing aggregators, including Uber, Rapido and Ola, to remove tipping prompts displayed before or during a ride, citing violations of the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025.
In a directive dated August 11, the ministry flagged prompts such as “Advance Tip”, “Choose an Add-on” and “Improve your chances of quicker ride confirmation”. It also objected to messages suggesting that tipping could increase the chances of a driver accepting a ride.
Under Clause 14.15 of the guidelines, passengers can tip drivers only after completing a ride. Aggregators cannot offer tipping options during booking, before a ride starts or while it is in progress. The guidelines also stipulate that the entire tip must go to the driver, without any commission charged by the aggregator, and that tipping options must not be misleading or manipulative and must comply with the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
The CCPA rejected Ola’s argument that the additional payment was merely a voluntary tip, observing that tipping ordinarily represents appreciation for services already rendered, whereas Ola solicited payments before drivers accepted bookings.
It also highlighted a contradiction in Ola’s arguments. If the add-on did not influence ride acceptance, the representation that it improved booking chances was misleading. If it did, customers who did not pay were placed at a relative disadvantage.
The authority classified the interface as confirm shaming, a dark pattern prohibited under the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023. It noted that the prompts created apprehension among customers that declining to pay could result in delayed confirmation or no ride at all. The absence of an option to decline or close the prompt was also flagged.
The CCPA further rejected Ola’s contention that it did not derive any commercial benefit from the feature because the entire add-on amount went to drivers. It observed that the feature could improve the platform’s attractiveness to drivers and its ride fulfilment rates, thereby serving Ola’s commercial interests.
In September 2026, the CCPA had imposed a similar ₹10 Lakh penalty on ride-hailing platform Rapido over its advance tipping feature, citing misleading advertisements, unfair trade practices and dark patterns.
While determining Ola’s penalty, the authority considered the scale and duration of the practice, its impact on consumers and the company’s financial position. It noted that Ola operated across more than 200 cities in India and had over 40 Mn users.
The CCPA also noted that Ola reported standalone revenue from operations of around ₹1,060 Cr in FY25. It said the ₹10 Lakh penalty was less than 0.01% of the company’s revenue and was warranted to deter similar violations.

items.content:
By Mansour Aliyu Hassan.
Cybersecurity experts, lawmakers and international partners have called for stronger global cooperation to combat emerging cyber threats driven by artificial intelligence (AI), warning that the rapidly changing digital landscape requires countries to rethink how they protect citizens, institutions and economies.
The call was made on Tuesday at the opening ceremony of the International Cybersecurity Conference in Abuja, where stakeholders highlighted the growing sophistication of cyberattacks and the need to strengthen human awareness, institutional resilience and international collaboration.
The Director-General of the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), Kashifu Inuwa CCIE, said the increasing use of AI by cybercriminals had created a new dimension to cybersecurity, requiring organisations to deploy advanced technologies to anticipate, detect and counter attacks.
He explained that cybersecurity and cyber resilience were complementary but distinct, noting that while cybersecurity focused on preventing attacks, resilience involved the capacity to recover after an attack had occurred.
Inu said the growing sophistication of AI had made it necessary to expand cybersecurity strategies beyond the protection of computer systems and digital infrastructure to include the human mind.
According to him, cybercriminals increasingly exploit human weaknesses because manipulating people can be easier than breaching sophisticated technological systems.
He said the conference would therefore examine how individuals and institutions could strengthen their defences against both technological attacks and attempts to manipulate human behaviour.
In his remarks, the Chairman of the Senate Committee on ICT and Cybersecurity, Senator Shuaib Afolabi Salisu described the conference as an opportunity to advance technology diplomacy and strengthen Nigeria’s international partnerships in the digital sector.
He said the participation of legislators from other countries demonstrated growing international interest in Nigeria’s technology initiatives and reinforced the country’s potential as a destination for business and collaboration.
The Director-General’s position was reinforced by the Chairman of the House of Representatives Committee on ICT and Cybersecurity, Hon. Adedeji Stanley Olajide who described cybersecurity as a moving target that demanded continuous learning and adaptation.
He warned that strategies effective today might no longer be sufficient tomorrow, given the speed at which artificial intelligence was changing the methods and capabilities available to cybercriminals.
He called for stronger collaboration among cybersecurity practitioners, policymakers, diplomats, judges and heads of government agencies, stressing that cyber threats transcended national and continental boundaries.
The lawmaker said countries across the Americas, Europe, Asia, Africa and Latin America needed to recognise cybersecurity as a common challenge requiring coordinated international action.
Similarly, the Chair of the Council of Europe’s Cybercrime Convention Committee, Pedro Verdelho stressed the need to bridge the gap between the rapid adoption of digital technologies and public understanding of their associated risks.
He observed that artificial intelligence and other digital tools had become integral to everyday activities, including travel planning, online searches and commercial transactions, but awareness of the dangers accompanying their use remained inadequate.
He called for greater cybersecurity awareness among government institutions, private-sector organisations and ordinary citizens.
The European official also highlighted the importance of the Budapest Convention, an international treaty designed to facilitate cooperation against cybercrime and improve access to electronic evidence, welcoming the participation of countries in the region in the framework.
Meanwhile, the Swedish Ambassador to Nigeria, Anna Westerholm said cybersecurity was essential to building public confidence in digital transformation, warning that increased connectivity also created greater exposure to cyber risks.
The ambassador said Nigeria’s digital transformation offered significant opportunities for innovation, economic growth and inclusion, with Sweden and Swedish companies supporting the country’s journey.

items.author: Sandra Tuombouh
items.content:
The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empowering community members
Originally published on Global Voices
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre preparing the farm. Photo by Support Humanity Cameroon. Used with permission.
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year. Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September. Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.
Cameroon continues to face a decade-long humanitarian crisis, contributing to food insecurity in the Anglophone regions and Far North, while displacing thousands of families. Earlier this year, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported worsening hunger among nearly 6,000 Cameroonian households following an assessment. More than 3.3 million people were struggling to find enough food, while about 64 percent of households experienced severe food insecurity.
Children are among those affected. Nationwide, 29 percent of children under five experience chronic malnutrition. Beyond its nutritional consequences, food insecurity can also affect children’s ability to learn and participate in school activities.
According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), hunger can impair concentration and memory and affect classroom attendance. In February 2026, the organisation reported that only 2.8 percent of primary school pupils in Cameroon received a free hot meal at school, highlighting the limited reach of school lunch programmes.
Conflict, climate-related disasters, agricultural losses and rising staple food prices are among the main drivers of this crisis.
School gardens in action
To combat persistent food insecurity, educators and nonprofit organisations are partnering to teach children how to grow their own food.
In Bamenda, North West region of Cameroon, the Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) runs the ADAPT Programme, which engages 70 pupils from two nursery and primary schools. Created after a survey revealed that few schools had gardens or provided environmental education, the ADAPT Club has established gardens with five sections: nurseries, vegetables, fruit trees, composting and tubers.
Muluh Kelly Vughose, Programme coordinator for ADAPT, says pupils are involved in more than just planting. “Our volunteers, together with the teachers and pupils, designed each garden. Children are also involved in learning basic agricultural skills like plantain propagation and grafting of fruit trees.” The club holds two sessions each week, lasting about two hours.
In the same region, in Nkambe and neighbouring villages, pupils from six primary and two secondary schools are learning agricultural skills through the Smart School Gardens Project, launched by Youth Development Organisation – Yodo Cameroon. Schools have received wheelbarrows, watering cans and compost manure to support the project.
“During the two years of implementation, I have watched these pupils and students care for plants from seed germination until harvest,” says Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s Programme Coordinator. The gardens produce cabbage, huckleberry, carrots and Irish potatoes.
Meanwhile, SUHUCAM’s regenerative school garden programme in the Centre region combines fruit trees, including guava, soursop, orange and papaya, with plantains and produce such as huckleberry, cabbage and waterleaf. Through these activities, pupils are learning techniques such as composting, plant propagation and grafting.
Children are embracing the school gardens with enthusiasm, discovering the importance of food production and sustainability through practical experience. Queeninver Ngwangung, SUHUCAM’s Youth and Advocacy Lead, explains:
“Rather than simply teaching students about sustainable agriculture, food security or climate action, we give them opportunities to practice these concepts,” she said. “Through growing food, managing organic waste and caring for their gardens, we have observed that students have learnt that environmental solutions can begin with everyday actions within their own schools.”
For Amang Mael, a Form Three student, seeing vegetables grow on an abandoned plot behind his school has been particularly exciting. “Since we planted the vegetables, I have been so eager to harvest. We add organic manure to all our crops so they can be healthy.”
Another student, Kouba Princesse, believes the garden can contribute to the fight against hunger. “Now that I know how to grow my own vegetables, I will not have to depend on buying from the market all the time,” she says. Some kids have taken the practice home, where they maintain small gardens and use plastic bottles for drip irrigation during the dry season. Other students also say the experience has sparked an interest in pursuing careers in agriculture.
Supporting community nutrition
In 2025, the ADAPT Club produced approximately 45 kilogrammes of dry compost from biodegradable waste. At the end of each planting cycle, YACA organises a Mini School Garden Market Day, where parents and community members can buy the harvest. “Income gained is reinvested in the next planting cycle,” says Muluh Kelly.
At SUHUCAM, the harvests serve nutritional and educational purposes. Students eat fruits from the gardens, while vegetables are sold to purchase seeds and fund their continued management. Some students take extra produce home to establish household gardens.
After two years with two regenerative school garden cycles, SUHUCAM’s Climate Change and Innovation Club has benefitted thousands of households and planted over 400 trees.
In Nkambe, pupils involved in Yodo Cameroon’s project also sell their harvests to community members at affordable prices. The proceeds have helped schools purchase basic educational materials, including chalk and exercise books. Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s project manager says:
The gardens have become practical outdoor classrooms. Not only are the children learning new agricultural skills, but they are also gaining an appreciation for nature, responsible environmental practices and sustainable resource management.
The nutritional potential of school-based production is also evident in other initiatives. In 2025, an integrated school production programme supported by FAO in Cameroon’s East and South regions established 18 school gardens. The programme produced 236,859 kilogrammes of vegetables, alongside eggs and fish, helping provide weekly healthy meals to 10,833 students. Children, teachers and community members also received training in sustainable agriculture, hygiene and nutrition.
Nkimih Clinton, a researcher at the Institute of Agricultural Research for Development (IRAD), says regenerative practices, such as those deployed in the community gardens, can improve soil health and support sustainable agriculture. Composting, mulching, crop rotation and organic manure, he explains, “can contribute to maintaining the health of pieces of land” for crop production. However, he cautions against expecting small-scale school gardens to eliminate hunger entirely.
Although they may not provide all the food pupils need, they can improve dietary quality by supplying vegetables, legumes and fruits rich in essential vitamins and minerals. “School gardens can be used as a source of production of micro-nutrients to complement basic staples (cassava, maize, rice) provided by parents,” Clinton says.
Challenges to overcome
Despite their benefits, maintaining school gardens remains difficult. Programme coordinators say unpredictable rainfall makes it harder to plan planting activities and sustain crop production. Changing weather conditions can also contribute to pest outbreaks and seed shortages.
Maintaining the gardens during school holidays is another challenge, as pupils are less available to care for the crops. These difficulties can interrupt children’s opportunities to follow the entire production cycle, from planting to harvesting. Expanding the initiatives will therefore require coordinated support from government officials, agricultural research institutions and development partners.
Schools need funding, reliable water supply, farming tools, quality seeds and technical assistance to maintain productive gardens throughout the year.
Government and policy support
Cameroon has previously taken steps to promote environmental education in schools. In 2018, the Ministry of Secondary Education and the Israeli Ambassador to Cameroon launched a Green School campaign that planted 300 trees in 30 schools.
In May 2023, the country launched the second phase of the Classes Vertes project, a three-year initiative developed by FAO in partnership with the Special Council Support Fund for Mutual Assistance (FEICOM) and several government ministries. Targeting 80 schools across the Far North, North, Adamawa, East and South regions, the programme sought to promote vegetable production, fish farming and poultry farming to improve children’s access to nutritious food. It also included tree planting and initiatives to build school canteens, water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities, with an allocated budget of approximately FCFA 722 million (USD 1.2 million).
The government’s commitment to improving children’s access to nutritious food is also reflected in its National School Feeding Strategy for 2025–2030, which aims to expand school meals and strengthen links between schools and local food producers.
Officials hope the program will reach one million learners by 2030. In July 2026, the government, through the Ministry of Basic Education, signed a EUR 3.6 million (USD 4 million) agreement with the World Food Programme (WFP) to expand home-grown school feeding in the Adamawa, East and Far North regions. The 2026–2029 programme is expected to provide nutritious meals to nearly 11,000 children in ten public primary schools while creating market opportunities for 600 smallholder farmers.
Meanwhile, experts believe school gardens can be replicated across Cameroon but stress that their implementation must reflect the country’s different agro-ecological zones. Rather than adopting a uniform approach, schools need solutions suited to their agro-ecological zones.
While school gardens may not independently resolve Cameroon’s food insecurity challenges, they offer opportunities to strengthen children’s nutritional knowledge, promote sustainable agriculture and encourage household food production. Their long-term impact, however, will depend on sustained investment, technical support and policies that enable more schools to establish and maintain these initiatives.
Written by Sandra Tuombouh

Retailers have also flagged growing differences between online and offline prices, which they say are affecting traditional distribution channels.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
South African cross-border payments startup Lumepay has raised US$6 million in pre-seed funding, alongside US$10 million in capital float, as it builds institutional-grade payment infrastructure for African businesses.
Led by CEO Harry Huang, Lumepay provides cross-border payment solutions for SMEs, corporates and institutions. Its rail-agnostic platform combines traditional finance and stablecoins to enable fast, cost-effective and transparent B2B transfers within and across African jurisdictions.
The startup launched Lumetrade, its digital asset and stablecoin trading venue, in April, before rolling out its payments platform in June, and has now raised US$6 million in pre-seed funding. The round was backed by founder-led angels and South African fintech investors. The US$10 million capital float was secured to give clients access to deep, reliable liquidity.
“The future of cross-border payments isn’t traditional finance or stablecoins; it’s a combination of both, backed by the FX depth to make them work for real businesses,” said Huang. “Our integrated approach addresses the real drivers of friction: fragmentation, liquidity inefficiency and execution risk.”
Lumepay is now live in Nigeria, Ghana, Tanzania, Malawi, Mozambique and Kenya, as well as the West and Central African CFA franc zones, and is awaiting further regulatory approvals to expand its payment capabilities in these markets.
Last month, the startup received regulatory clearance from the Central Bank of Kenya, marking its entry into East Africa. Businesses in Kenya can now use Lumepay to pay international suppliers in currencies including Chinese yuan, US dollars and Indian rupees, and to move money across intra-African trade corridors.
“In the months since the raise, we’ve turned plans into working products: diversified and reliable liquidity; a platform that handles cross-border payments end to end; a growing network of partners and payment rails; and regulatory clearance in South Africa and Kenya,” said Luc Varejes, Lumepay’s COO.
In South Africa, Lumepay works with Nedbank as its Third-Party Payment Provider (TPPP) sponsoring bank, while sister business Lume Trade, an authorised financial services provider covering crypto asset intermediary services, banks with Standard Bank.
“Working with Nedbank and Standard Bank across our two businesses reflects the compliance standards we have built from day one,” said Tatenda Nhemachena, Lumepay’s chief legal and compliance officer.
The pre-seed funding has been used to build out Lumepay’s core infrastructure, including its payment rails, banking relationships, regulatory approvals and licensed partner network. The startup is now focused on expanding its regulatory footprint across Southern, West and Central Africa, with Malawi, Mozambique and the CFA franc regions key targets, as it lays the groundwork for a Series A round.

vivo appears to be preparing another battery-focused smartphone for the Pakistani market. The vivo Y600i, which debuted in China in September 2026, has appeared in local smartphone listings, revealing its expected price, specifications, and possible release timeline in Pakistan.
The biggest highlight of the handset is its massive 8,000mAh battery, which could make it an attractive option for consumers looking for longer battery life in the mid-range segment.
The smartphone features a 6.87-inch display with a 120 Hz refresh rate, offering a larger screen for video streaming, browsing, and everyday use.
Under the hood, the vivo Y600i is powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 2 chipset, which supports 5G connectivity and is designed to deliver power-efficient performance for affordable smartphones.
Local listings suggest that the handset could be available with 6GB RAM and 256GB internal storage, although additional memory configurations could be introduced depending on the market.
In terms of photography, the smartphone features a 50MP primary rear camera.
However, the battery remains the most interesting aspect of the device.
vivo has already introduced several smartphones with large batteries in Pakistan, including the vivo Y500, which features an 8,100mAh battery.
The Y600i could further strengthen the company’s battery-focused Y-series lineup, particularly among users who prioritize battery endurance over flagship-level camera and performance features.
The combination of a power-efficient Snapdragon chipset and an 8,000mAh battery could make the smartphone suitable for students, office workers and users who spend long hours away from charging facilities.
vivo Y600i Expected Price and Release Timeline in Pakistan
According to one unofficial Pakistani smartphone listing, the vivo Y600i is expected to cost around Rs. 83,999. Other listings quote different prices, so this figure should be treated as an early estimate rather than an official retail price.
The smartphone is listed with an expected release date of November 30, 2026, suggesting that it could arrive in Pakistan before the end of this month.
However, vivo Pakistan has not officially confirmed the device’s local launch date or retail price.
For comparison, the recently updated official vivo smartphone price list in Pakistan lists the vivo Y32 with 6GB RAM and 128GB storage at Rs. 82,999, while the vivo Y500 with 6GB RAM and 128GB storage costs Rs. 89,999.
Interestingly, the vivo Y32 also features an 8,000mAh battery, meaning the Y600i could face competition from vivo’s existing smartphones if it launches at the expected price.
However, the anticipated 256GB storage configuration and 5G connectivity could give the Y600i an advantage over some similarly priced alternatives.
With Pakistan’s ongoing 5G rollout, the availability of more affordable 5G-enabled smartphones could also help consumers access next-generation mobile services without purchasing expensive flagship devices.
The final local specifications, pricing, and availability of the vivo Y600i will be important in determining how it competes against existing smartphones in Pakistan’s increasingly competitive mid-range market.
For now, consumers interested in the handset should wait for an official announcement from vivo Pakistan, as the expected price and November release timeline remain unconfirmed.

According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, the company’s board is reportedly preparing to take action, although details about the possible departure and a successor remain unclear.
The latest development has raised questions about Nvidia’s leadership at a time when the company remains one of the biggest players in the global artificial intelligence industry. Huang’s future at the company is now uncertain as the board reportedly considers its next steps.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Could Be Ousted Following Second Affair Report
The controversy follows earlier reports linking Huang to an alleged relationship with a person accused of having connections to Chinese intelligence. The latest allegations involving a second affair have reportedly increased pressure on the company’s leadership.
Nvidia Faces Pressure Amid AI Market Uncertainty
The reported leadership crisis comes as the AI industry faces growing concerns about its long-term profitability. Investors have started questioning whether major technology companies can maintain their heavy investments in artificial intelligence and generate sufficient returns.
Nvidia has been particularly exposed to changes in the AI market because it supplies graphics processing units (GPUs) and other essential hardware used to develop and operate AI systems.
Market uncertainty has also affected the company’s valuation. Reports surrounding Huang’s personal life and leadership have added to investor concerns, with Nvidia reportedly losing more than $800 billion in market value in a single trading day following the controversy.
See Also: NVIDIA Shareholders Sue Jensen Huang Over Alleged Links to Chinese Spy
The company’s share price has remained under pressure as investors assess the potential impact of the situation.
Questions Remain About Nvidia’s Future
Despite the controversy, Nvidia continues to hold an important position in the global technology industry. Its GPUs and AI-related hardware remain essential to many companies developing advanced artificial intelligence systems.
However, a possible change in leadership could create further uncertainty for investors and the wider AI sector. The company’s board has yet to provide details about a potential replacement for Huang or how a leadership transition would take place.
It also remains unclear whether the reported developments will have a lasting impact on Nvidia’s business or contribute to broader concerns about the AI market.
For now, Huang’s position and the company’s next steps remain uncertain.

items.content:
Government of India (GoI) has announced the sale (re-issue) of one dated security for a notified amount of ₹34,000 crore as per the following details:
Sr No Security Date of Repayment Notified Amount
(₹ Crore) GoI specific Notification Auction Date Settlement Date
1 6.94% GS 2036 May 11, 2036 34,000 F.No.4(1)-B(W&M)/2026 dated
November 09, 2026 November 13, 2026
(Friday) November 16, 2026
(Monday)
  Total   34,000      
2. GoI will have the option to retain additional subscription up to ₹2,000 crore against the security mentioned above.
3. The security will be sold through Reserve Bank of India Mumbai Office, Fort, Mumbai – 400001. The sale will be subject to the terms and conditions spelt out in the ‘Specific Notification’ mentioned above and the General Notification F.No.4(2)–B(W&M)/2018, dated March 26, 2025.
4. The auction will be conducted using multiple price method. Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system) on November 13, 2026 (Friday). The non-competitive bids should be submitted between 10:30 a.m. and 11:00 a.m. and the competitive bids should be submitted between 10:30 a.m. and 11:30 a.m. The result will be announced on the same day and payment by successful bidders will have to be made on November 16, 2026 (Monday).
5. Bids for underwriting of the Additional Competitive Underwriting (ACU) portion can be submitted by ‘Primary Dealers’ from 09:00 a.m. up to 09:30 a.m. on November 13, 2026 (Friday) on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
6. The security will be eligible for “When Issued” trading for a period commencing from November 11, 2026 – November 13, 2026.
7. Operational guidelines for Government of India dated securities auction and other details are given in the Annex.
Ajit Prasad          
Deputy General Manager
(Communications)    
Press Release: 2026-2027/1474
ANNEX
Type of Auction
1. For multiple price-based auction, successful bids will get accepted at the respective quoted yield/price for the security. For uniform price-based auction, bids will get accepted at the cut off yield/price accepted in the auction.
2. The auction will be yield based for new security and price based for securities which are re-issued.
3. In case of a Floating Rate Bonds (FRB), the auction will be spread-based for new security and price based for securities which are reissued. At the time of placing bids for new FRB, the spread should be quoted in percentage terms.
Minimum Bid Size
4. The securities will be issued for a minimum amount of ₹10,000/- (nominal) and in multiples of ₹10,000/- thereafter.
Non-Competitive Segment
5. In all the auctions, Government security up to 5% of the notified amount for sale of individual security will be allotted to the eligible individuals and institutions under the Scheme for Non-competitive Bidding Facility in the Auctions of Government Securities. Individual investors can also place bids as per the non-competitive scheme through the Retail Direct portal (https://rbiretaildirect.org.in).
6. Each bank or Primary Dealer (PD) on the basis of firm orders received from their constituents will submit a single consolidated non-competitive bid for individual security on behalf of its constituents in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
7. Allotment under the non-competitive segment will be at the weighted average rate of yield/price of the successful bids that will emerge in the auction on the basis of the competitive bidding.
Submission of Bids
8. Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
9. Bids in physical form will not be accepted except in extraordinary circumstances.
Business Continuity Plan (BCP)-IT failure
10. Only in the event of system failure, physical bids will be accepted. Such physical bids should be submitted to the Public Debt Office, Mumbai through (email; Phone no: 022-22603456, 022-22603457, 022-22603190) in the prescribed form which can be obtained from RBI website (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewForms.aspx) before the auction timing ends.
11. In case of technical difficulties, Core Banking Operations Team should be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-69870466, 022-69870415).
12. For other auction related difficulties, IDMD auction team can be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-22702431, 022-22705125).
Multiple Bids
13. An investor can submit more than one competitive bid in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).
14. The aggregate amount of bids submitted by an investor in an auction should not exceed the notified amount of auction.
Decision Making Process
15. On the basis of bids received, the Reserve Bank will determine the minimum price/maximum yield up to which tenders for purchase of Government Security will be accepted at the auctions.
16. Bids quoted at rates lower than the minimum price/higher than the maximum yield determined by the Reserve Bank of India will be rejected.
17. Reserve Bank of India will have the full discretion to accept or reject any or all bids either wholly or partially without assigning any reason.
Issue of Securities
18. Issue of securities to the successful bidders will be by credit to Subsidiary General Ledger Account (SGL) or to Constituents’ Subsidiary General Ledger Account (CSGL), maintained with Reserve Bank of India.
Periodicity of Interest Payment
19. Interest on the Government Security will generally be paid half-yearly other than in case of securities with non-standard maturities. The exact periodicity of coupon payment is invariably mentioned in the specific notification for the issue of security.
Underwriting of the Government Securities
20. The underwriting of the Government Securities under auctions by the ‘Primary Dealers’ will be as per the “Revised Scheme of Underwriting Commitment and Liquidity Support” announced by the Reserve Bank vide circular RBI/2007-08/186 dated November 14, 2007 as amended from time to time.
Eligibility for Repurchase Transactions (Repo)
21. The securities will be eligible for Repurchase Transactions (Repo) as per the conditions mentioned in Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Repurchase Transactions (Repo)) Directions, 2025 as amended from time to time.
Eligibility for ‘When Issued’ Trading
22. The securities will be eligible for “When Issued” trading in accordance with the guidelines on ‘When Issued transactions in Central Government Securities’ issued by the Reserve Bank of India vide circular No. RBI/2018-19/25 dated July 24, 2018 as amended from time to time.
Investment by Non-Residents
23. Investments by Non-Residents are subject to the guidelines on ‘Fully Accessible Route’ for Investment by Non-residents in Government Securities and other related guidelines as issued by the Reserve Bank from time to time.
