items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
A password sent over WhatsApp usually stays in the chat for as long as the chat exists. WhatsApp view-once text messages, now reaching some Android beta testers, change that for text.
The feature appeared in WhatsApp beta for Android 2.26.45.6, available on the Google Play Store. A recipient can open the message once, and then it is gone from the conversation.
The rollout is gradual. Only some beta testers have it today, and more accounts should receive it over the coming weeks.
How to Send a View-Once Text on Android
Users who have the feature see a short tutorial toast at the bottom of the screen when they open a conversation. It tells them to press and hold the send button.
The steps are simple. Type the message in the chat bar, then press and hold send. A menu opens with two options: schedule the message or send it as view-once. Tapping “view once” sends the message immediately.
The menu offers both options, but they cannot be combined yet. A view-once text cannot be scheduled.
What the Recipient Sees
The message does not appear in the chat when the recipient opens the conversation. They have to tap it, and it opens on a separate screen.
Once they close that screen, they cannot open the message again. WhatsApp replaces it in the chat with an indicator that marks it as opened.
Senders who have read receipts turned on can see when the message was opened. After that, neither side can see the text.
What WhatsApp Blocks
WhatsApp blocks screenshots and screen recordings while the recipient reads the message. Long-pressing the message does nothing, so the usual actions are unavailable.
Action
Status on a view-once text
Screenshot or screen recording
Blocked while reading
Copy the text
Not available
Forward to another chat
Not available
Save the message
Not available
Reopen after closing
Not possible
Schedule the message
Not yet supported
Photos, videos and voice notes have had a view-once option for some time. Text was the obvious gap, since most of what people send on WhatsApp is text.
What to Watch Next
WhatsApp has not said when view-once texts will reach everyone. Beta features sometimes change before a stable release, so the details above may shift.
The practical test is behaviour. If people start using the option for codes and passwords by habit, it will matter. If it stays a novelty, it will not. The guarantee also depends on the recipient’s phone and the recipient’s honesty, which no setting can control.
Source: WABinfo

items.content: Nvidia Corp. shares sank in extended trading Wednesday as investors grappled with the possibility of the company without Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang at the helm.The stock fell as much as 10% in postmarket trading in New York. Shares began to drop following a New York Times report that the CEO had a relationship with one of his direct reports. Losses extended after the Wall Street Journal said Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust him. Huang admitted over the weekend that he had a separate affair with an alleged Chinese spy.Wall Street sentiment toward Nvidia Corp. is starting to crack. Bernstein was the latest firm to downgrade the stock, cutting its rating to market perform from outperform while lowering its price target to $200 from $400. Baird earlier downgraded the shares to neutral, while Morgan Stanley removed them as a top pick.If Nvidia’s postmarket losses hold, the stock is set to fall below $4 trillion in market capitalization when cash trading resumes.“We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip,” Bernstein analysts including Stacy Rasgon wrote in a note. “But our gut tells us that we probably haven’t yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here. We’ve had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines.”Other artificial intelligence-linked stocks followed shares of Nvidia lower in postmarket trading. CoreWeave Inc. slid more than 5%, Intel Corp. and Dell Technologies Inc. each fell 3% and Super Micro Computer Inc. declined more than 4%.Nvidia is scheduled to report its quarterly results on Nov. 17.“It is going to be a very challenging situation,” said Michael O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading. “Jensen had forecast 70% sales growth this year. With the vendor financing and the aggressive tactics, his successor will spend the next year putting out fires and cleaning up messes.” .Here’s what investors and strategists across Wall Street are saying:Matt Maley, chief market strategist at Miller Tabak + Co“This second shoe to drop is likely going to force the board’s hands. It looks like he’ll be lucky to survive the week after this disclosure.”“The issue that worries me the most is that Nvidia is such a large financier for the AI industry. Will these developments cause them to pull in their spending some what?”Haris Khurshid, CIO at Karobaar CapitalThis is starting to look less like a one-off personal scandal and more like a broader question around him, governance and key man risk. The China angle obviously makes it much more serious, and the additional reporting around other relationships adds another layer. Given how closely he’s associated with Nvidia’s strategy and relationships, I think the market is having to reprice more than just the headline scandal.”Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment ManagementYou could maybe see a path forward for him to be a part of the board, but not CEO, because his strategic vision is so important to what happens next in terms of innovation, research & development, and then honestly execution.He could be reprimanded and not remain CEO, but still be a strategic vision advisor, board member.David Meier, senior investment analyst at The Motley FoolFrankly, I am a little surprised how quickly these stories have come to light. And the board is going to have to act quickly now to do its investigation of the situations. Jensen is the key figure at Nvidia. He’s structured the company for him to be the main decision maker. If the risk he’s going to be terminated is rising, that’s material. And the board needs to communicate to shareholders about this right away.Joe Gilbert, portfolio manager at Integrity Asset ManagementThis is an unequivocal negative for Nvidia and the entire AI ecosystem. He is not only the face of AI but arguably the architect of the AI infrastructure. Now the company will need to get a new face of the company out there and that person will have to prove that they are competent. Even with this, it will be difficult if not impossible to replicate Jensen’s vision.Gary Tan, portfolio manager at Allspring GlobalNvidia’s latest developments could weigh on sentiment across the broader AI trade, but we see selective opportunities emerging among semiconductor companies that can offer credible second source alternatives for critical AI chips. Near term, however, investor reception to Anthropic’s IPO is likely to be a more important driver of AI sentiment.Any near term demand air pocket from Nvidia will be absorbed by competing AI chipmakers, while tight memory supply near term should continue to support pricing and earnings visibility.Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist of Saxo MarketsInvestors now have to put a higher probability on a leadership change at Nvidia. Some of the stock’s premium reflects confidence in Jensen Huang’s ability to set the direction of the AI industry. Uncertainty over who carries that vision forward, and what happens to Nvidia’s China strategy, could weigh on valuations even if earnings remain strong.While a recovery in the AI trade was just starting to brew, but this raises the bar for the AI rally to regain momentum. Strong demand signals are reassuring, but they cannot fully offset uncertainty at the company at the center of the buildout.

items.title: Gung-ho politics, gun-toting politicians and a democracy under siege
items.author: Abubakar Adam Ibrahim
items.content:
Elections are costly affairs; everyone knows this. In Nigeria, they seem far more expensive than in most places because, far too often, elections cost far too many lives. The elections have not even been held yet, and the campaign season only opened a few short months ago, but already, 27 Nigerians have been killed in election-related violence.
Between January and the end of October 2026, there have been 70 violent political incidents across 19 states. In Enugu, a supporter of the NDC was reportedly killed during a campaign flag-off; in Katsina, an APC campaign convoy reportedly came under attack; in Ado Ekiti, Omoyele Sowore, running for president under the banner of the AAC, was reportedly assaulted; and in Sokoto and Kebbi, there have been reports of attacks on the ADC’s campaign convoy.
The worst thing, though, is that 20 out of the 70 violent incidents have resulted in the loss of 27 lives. The loss of one life for the political ambition of any person should not even be an option; the loss of 27, with elections still months away, is a crisis warning.
A recent survey by the Abuja-based Yiaga Africa National Voting Intentions Survey 3.0, conducted this September, interviewed 2,470 Nigerians aged 18 and above across the 36 states and the FCT. The responses portend major impediments to our democracy. A majority, 61 per cent, of those surveyed expressed fear that violence could prevent them from voting, while another 82 per cent were concerned that insecurity could affect the elections.
While Nigerians have questioned the merits of our democracy, its culture and dividends, many are even more concerned with the risk of democratic participation. Any citizen who desires to vote but fears being attacked for exercising a civic right is not politically apathetic. That person is being denied the conditions necessary for meaningful participation in such an important process and civic duty.
Political violence is a form of voter suppression. Voter suppression, of which this country has a rich history, does not only manifest through obstructing access to polling stations or interfering with ballot papers. It can also occur through intimidation, threats, and the creation of an atmosphere of fear and terror around elections and democratic participation.
Through violence, candidates are kept from campaigning in certain communities, supporters are prevented from attending rallies or from travelling to polling stations to vote. These are all acts of depriving people of the chance of meaningful political participation. INEC might procedurally organise the most credible elections it conceivably can, but the elections can still fail the test of democratic participation if violence and fear are allowed to fester.
But that is not the only thing that could hamper democratic participation in the 2027 elections. The politics itself is as big a turn-off as the fear and violence. Across the board, political parties are making politics unappealing. We have a ruling party that is relaunching its second-term promises without accounting for its performance in the first term, and an opposition that is distracted by its own ambition.
First, the ruling party’s “Renewed Hope Agenda 2.0” is slammed on top of the Renewed Hope Promise of 2023, without taking stock of how that initial manifesto had fared. We all recognise that here, manifestos are mere documents waved around during campaigns, but no politicians feel beholden to the contract they enter with electorate during campaigns. Questions about these are often waved away during the seemingly more important dancing and aso-ebi parades that campaign rallies have been reduced to. If the APC argues that the first phase of the “Renewed Hope” was about making tough decisions and stabilising the economy, shouldn’t the question now be what exactly has been achieved for the ordinary Nigerian and what remains outstanding?
Take insecurity, for instance. The manifesto promises four additional army divisions and 28,000 additional military personnel, 50,000 additional police officers, body cameras and digital policing, and improved border surveillance. This all sounds good and promising. But the question is how the promises of three years ago have held up—the purported mass recruitment from where the infamous “agbado” meme arose, and the immediate end to insecurity within a short term. Every available record shows more deaths and displacements in the last three years, instead of less.
The issue has never been about the substantial commitments candidates make—although sometimes it really is—but mostly it should be about opportunities to ask questions about implementation. The same scrutiny can be applied to the economic commitments made prior, and the result would be the same. Campaigns should never make commitments they have no means or plans to see through. Grand-gesture statements must be backed up by a blueprint, not be followed by the DJ blasting music while candidates dance and artfully sidestep the issues. A manifesto, by its very nature, is a contract with voters, not a literary exercise in political optimism. As our history has amply demonstrated, that optimism has far too often been abused.
At the moment, the opposition parties are too distracted by themselves to even engage fully in policy debates with the ruling party. The opposition was supposed to provide a credible alternative and a strong democratic challenge. Supposed to. What they are providing now is peripheral drama.
The emergence of the ADC as a platform for opposition realignment initially generated some political interest. That coalition brought together prominent figures including Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi, Rabiu Kwankwaso, David Mark, Rauf Aregbesola and Rotimi Amaechi. Instead of creating a viable platform to challenge the APC in the 2027 elections, the group has devolved into disagreement over leadership, party control, zoning and irreconcilable presidential ambitions that have led to further fragmentation of an already weakened opposition.
The decision by the Federal High Court on November 6 to nullify the David Mark-led ADC National Working Committee and invalidate the decisions taken by that leadership, including the process that produced Atiku as the party’s candidate, demonstrates the extent of the chaos in the opposition camp.
What that decision means is that Atiku’s presidential candidacy has been thrown into legal uncertainty. Instead of focusing on campaigning for the elections, Atiku will now be investing time, energy and resources into appealing that decision. Instead of tussling against Tinubu, Atiku is being distracted by a tussle with one Nafiu Bala Gombe for the control of the party. And we are only three months from the election.
Beyond failing to answer the question of who actually leads the opposition, it has already proven that candidates with longstanding presidential ambition cannot sacrifice these ambitions for the greater good. It is now hard to see how this opposition can establish any sort of coherent national structure to challenge for power. The 2015 opposition alliance succeeded in ousting a sitting incumbent only by bringing together different political interests around a common objective. It would seem that lesson so recently learned has been so quickly forgotten already.
A weak opposition is a democratic problem, not just a political one. A fractured opposition weakens the democratic system. Political competition is not just about which party wins but about providing voters with meaningful alternatives and holding government accountable while ensuring that power remains contestable. None of these seems to apply in Nigeria’s current political layout.
All things considered, with 27 years of uninterrupted democracy behind us, it would seem our democracy today is weaker than it has ever been. With the violent antecedents we have already seen, which are only likely to increase in the weeks and months ahead, an almost indomitable ruling party that controls 34 of our 36 states, and an opposition entangled in a web of personal ambitions and litigation, we will be heading into elections without the robust and critical discussions about how exactly we can better our country.
Democracy is not just about periodic voting but requires an environment in which political choices can be freely expressed, and alternatives are allowed to compete and those seeking office are held accountable.
But with voters even terrified to attend rallies and insecurity threatening elections in most parts of the country, the quality of democratic participation in an already flawed system is further diminished.
Those who lead our democratic expedition today must realise that they are obliged to protect the system and the institutions that oversee the democratic process. Consequently, President Tinubu and the leadership of all parties must condemn and reject political violence and the use of thugs as instruments of political competition.
Security agencies must also be encouraged and allowed to investigate political violence, not aid and abet it, and their findings should be made public in a transparent way. Alongside INEC, they must establish clear arrangements for protecting candidates, supporters, electoral officials and voters.
Finally, while the ruling party must exhibit greater transparency, opposition leaders too must exercise greater responsibility. What is at stake here is the soul of our country, not petty personal ambitions.

items.title: GoKwik’s ESOP Twist, New CEO At Unacademy & More
items.summary:
GoKwik’s Golden Handcuffs
GoKwik has added a contentious twist to its ESOP policy. Under the new rules, current and former employees could forfeit their unvested and vested-but-unexercised options if they join any of GoKwik’s nine rivals. Can the startup use ESOPs to restrict where its talent goes next?
A New Kind Of Restriction: GoKwik’s amended ESOP Plan 2021 names Razorpay, Shiprocket, CRED, Cashfree Payments, BiteSpeed, Snapmint, WebEngage, Shopflo and Pine Labs as restricted companies. Employees cannot join, advise and invest in them without risking the loss of outstanding options. Crucially, the restriction applies retroactively to previously issued grants and extends for two full years after an employee’s departure.
Employees In Limbo: For GoKwik employees with significant ESOP holdings, the new policy has created a difficult choice between career mobility and potential wealth loss. Many are weighing offers from larger or better-known companies against the risk of forfeiting ESO
items.author: Team Inc42
items.content:
GoKwik’s Golden Handcuffs
GoKwik has added a contentious twist to its ESOP policy. Under the new rules, current and former employees could forfeit their unvested and vested-but-unexercised options if they join any of GoKwik’s nine rivals. Can the startup use ESOPs to restrict where its talent goes next?
A New Kind Of Restriction: GoKwik’s amended ESOP Plan 2021 names Razorpay, Shiprocket, CRED, Cashfree Payments, BiteSpeed, Snapmint, WebEngage, Shopflo and Pine Labs as restricted companies. Employees cannot join, advise and invest in them without risking the loss of outstanding options. Crucially, the restriction applies retroactively to previously issued grants and extends for two full years after an employee’s departure.
Employees In Limbo: For GoKwik employees with significant ESOP holdings, the new policy has created a difficult choice between career mobility and potential wealth loss. Many are weighing offers from larger or better-known companies against the risk of forfeiting ESOPS they have already earned the right to exercise.
The timing has added to concerns. GoKwik has seen several senior-level departures in the recent past, while the recent layoff, earlier this year, is further adding to the staff’s concerns.
A Legal Gray Area: Non-compete clauses are common in Indian employment agreements, but explicitly linking rivals to the forfeiture of vested options is unusual. Legal experts believe that GoKwik’s amendment could face legal scrutiny if it is used to penalise employees for joining a competitor.
The issue also raises governance concerns. By converting earned equity into an aggressive retention tactic, startups risk eroding the trust that underpins employee wealth creation. So, will GoKwik stand by its restrictive ESOP policy or roll back the controversial clause? Let’s find out…
From The Editor’s Desk
New CEO At Unacademy
Barely two months after upGrad completed the acquisition of the edtech platform, Gaurav Munjal is now stepping down as the CEO of Unacademy. He will now transition to the role of executive chairman at the startup and will “help” with upGrad’s IPO.
Meanwhile, Unacademy’s chief business officer Akhilendra Kumar will take over as the chief executive of the recently-acquired edtech platform.
The transition marks the end of Munjal’s tenure as the top executive of the once-high flying edtech platform. Unacademy raised billions of dollars at the peak of the pandemic, but ran into monetisation issues and ballooning losses as soon as schools reopened.
RentoMojo’s Mixed Q2
The recently-listed furniture rental company saw its profits tank 62.6% YoY to ₹18.2 Cr in Q2 FY27. This decline was largely due to a deferred tax expense of ₹6.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 and a deferred tax credit of ₹32.8 Cr in the year-ago quarter.
Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 52.8% YoY to ₹142.1 Cr in Q2 FY27, driven by growth in customer orders, live subscribers and rental inventory. Nevertheless, expenses continued to bite and rose 53.2% YoY to ₹119.8 Cr.
On the operational front, Rentomojo expanded its network to 96 stores at the end of September 2026. The platform’s live subscriber base also grew 43% YoY to 3.2 Lakh, while users ordered 3.8 Lakh gross items during the quarter under review, up 45% YoY.
Cult.fit’s Trademark Dispute
The Madras HC has directed the IPO-bound gym chain to file its response on a petition, which seeks the cancellation of the CULT trademark held by one of Cult.fit’s subsidiaries. The matter has been scheduled for next hearing on December 2.
The plea in the HC was filed by Deepak Poduval, who cofounded the CULT fitness business in 2015. He alleges that his signatures on a 2017 assignment deeds, which purportedly transferred the brand to Cult.fit, were forged.
If the challenge succeeds, the case could affect Cult.fit’s right to use the trademark. Additionally, the gym chain could also face SEBI scrutiny for previously acknowledging that its DRHP did not correctly describe the ownership of the CULT trademarks.
Govt Bans Black Mass Exports
The directorate general of foreign trade has issued directions to prohibit export of ‘black mass’, a mineral-rich product of recycled EV batteries. The order will be applicable immediately to all outbound shipments of the battery waste material.
Obtained from shredding end-of-life lithium-ion batteries, black mass is rich in metals like lithium, cobalt and nickel. These minerals can be recovered from the black mass and reused in new batteries, which could save costs and reduce foreign dependence.
While the restriction could retain critical raw materials within domestic borders, India still has limited capacity for black mass extraction and refining. As such, capabilities will have to be built up to capture the full economic value of black mass.
Dull Diwali For Retailers
Weak consumer demand and rising prices weighed heavily on the recently-concluded Diwali festive season. According to AIMRA, mobile phone retailers saw sales volumes decline by 18-20% over the four-day period between November 6 and November 9.
However, overall sales value remained broadly in line with last year’s festive season on the back of higher average selling prices. Nevertheless, AIMRA noted that the contraction in volumes squeezed margins and store profitability across retail channels.
The sub-₹20,000 segment was particularly impacted by a shortage of fresh, competitive 5G models from leading brands. On top of this, financing emerged as another constraint during the festive season as only 60-70% of the loan applications were approved.
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
Can Qucev Break Diesel’s Grip On The Indian Freight?
India’s EV revolution is gathering pace, but heavy-duty trucks remain difficult to electrify because of heavy payloads, long duty cycles and patchy charging infrastructure. Qucev is trying to fix this gap with its indigenously designed and manufactured electric commercial vehicles.
Electrifying India’s Logistics: Founded in 2022, Qucev sells delivery and refrigerated vans, heavy-duty trucks, electric tractors, and electric concrete mixers. The startup caters to sectors including logistics, manufacturing, construction and cold-chain operations. Besides, it also offers charging support, financing partnerships, fleet tracking and after-sales services.
The High-Mileage Ride: The Hyderabad-based startup operates two manufacturing facilities and operates a service network that spans 17 cities. Qucev claims that its vehicles, which have clocked over 1.3 Mn kms so far, cater to more than 20 enterprise customers, including DHL, Blue Dart, Mondelez and Godrej.
The Road Ahead: Backed by Singularity AMC, the startup now plans to scale manufacturing and develop new products. But the road ahead may not be easy. Competing against rivals like Tata Motors and Euler Motors, its next challenge will be proving that its purpose-built electric trucks can deliver dependable economics at scale. So, can Qucev make heavy-duty electrification India’s next EV success story?

A major highlight of the training was the practical demonstration of vehicle conversion to Compressed Natural Gas, which gave participants firsthand exposure to the technology and its operational processes.

items.author: Joshua Odeyemi
items.content:
The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Commission has launched the Resilient Rice Value Chain Development Project (REWARD), a programme estimated at $650 million,
The West African region will need $25 billion to meet the 2035 target of 35 million tonnes of rice sufficiency.
The Commission also inaugurated a regional steering committee to oversee its implementation from 2025 to 2035.
REWARD is backed by the African Development Bank (AfDB) and supported technically by AfricaRice.
It aims to strengthen rice production, improve processing and marketing, and make locally produced rice more competitive.
Speaking at the launch, the ECOWAS Commission’s Vice President, Anthony Ogunjimi, said the project followed a directive from the region’s leaders.
“Our heads of state of ECOWAS gave the ECOWAS Commission a mandate to raise funding to ensure availability and food sufficiency for the subregion,”
Ogunjimi, who was represented by the Commission’s Commissioner for Economic Affairs and Agriculture, Mr Dephue Zuo Dephue, said the overall rice investment portfolio is about $25 billion.
“From the financing conference we had in Accra, we were able to raise 1.5 billion dollars, which is going to be used for the time being to ensure that we have access to financing for farmers, for business value chains, for production in the subregion,” he said.
“We want to encourage all West African citizens, business partners, and individuals with the resources to join this initiative,” he said.
Dephue said food sovereignty in West Africa depends on the region producing more of what it eats.
“West Africa’s food sovereignty depends on our ability to produce more of the food we consume and reduce our vulnerability to external shocks,” he said.
“Rice is central to this ambition. Yet, increased production alone will not deliver self-sufficiency,” he said, adding that fertiliser, irrigation, quality inputs, processing, financing, market access and the policy environment must also be addressed.
He said the Regional Rice Roadmap 2025-2035, which builds on the 2004 Yamoussoukro Declaration, puts investment needs at $25.6 billion.
He said the Accra investment roundtable generated about $1.5 billion in commitments, expressions of interest and ongoing discussions.
“Our responsibility now is to translate this interest into finance projects and tangible results for farmers, processors, and consumers,” he said.
ECOWAS’ contribution to REWARD, he said, covers regional policy and regulatory reform, coordination, better regulation of agricultural inputs and digital monitoring through the ECOWAS Rice Observatory.
The steering committee will provide strategic oversight and decision-making, and help identify bottlenecks early so that implementation stays accountable.
A representative of AfricaRice, Dr Sali Atanga, said poor access to quality seeds, low productivity, climate variability, inadequate mechanisation, post-harvest losses and fragmented markets are among the challenges facing rice production in West Africa.
“Addressing these challenges will require more than isolated national investments and interventions,” he said.
AfricaRice, he said, will concentrate on rice seed systems, climate-resilient varieties, sustainable production technologies, mechanisation and post-harvest management.
The Coordinator, ECOWAS RiceAgenda and REWARD Programme, Dr Boladale Adebowale, said five countries in the subregion have keyed into the programme in the first phase, adding that more will join in the second phase next year.

items.title: UAE Announces New Work Permit Rules
items.summary:
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has scrapped all supporting document requirements for 13 types of work permits and cut the data needed on some application forms by up to 97 percent.
The Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation (MoHRE) announced the changes under the government’s Zero Bureaucracy initiative, Gulf News reported.
Required data fields for certain permits have been reduced by between 75 and 97 percent, and processing times have also been shortened.

items.author: Business Desk
items.content:
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has scrapped all supporting document requirements for 13 types of work permits and cut the data needed on some application forms by up to 97 percent.
The Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation (MoHRE) announced the changes under the government’s Zero Bureaucracy initiative, Gulf News reported.
Required data fields for certain permits have been reduced by between 75 and 97 percent, and processing times have also been shortened.
All 13 permit services are now available through MoHRE’s unified digital channels, so employers can apply entirely online.
What It Means for Workers
Fewer forms and no document uploads should mean faster hiring, quicker job transfers, and less hassle for employers bringing in staff from abroad. That matters for Pakistan, as the UAE is issuing about 30,000 visas to Pakistanis every month.
The ministry said the reforms aim to support private businesses, protect workers’ rights, and build a more efficient labour market.
It has also started a new phase of improvements focused on simpler procedures and wider digital services.
The 13 Work Permits Covered
Private tutoring work permit
Recruitment from outside the UAE (valid for two years)
Transfer work permit (valid for two years)
Work permit for residents sponsored by their families (valid for two years)
Temporary work permit
Mission work permit for short-term projects
Part-time work permit, allowing work for more than one employer (valid for two years)
Juvenile work permit for ages 15 to under 18
Student training or employment permit for ages 15 and above
Work permit for UAE nationals and GCC citizens (valid for two years)
Golden Residency work permit
National trainee work permit
Freelance work permit, allowing foreigners to work under their own residency sponsorship
The move follows earlier steps such as the new digital work permit for overseas hiring.

items.summary:

Russia’s Foreign Ministry announced his death on Wednesday but gave no details about the circumstances.
In a tribute, the ministry described Darchiev as an “outstanding diplomat, an experienced leader and a kind colleague”.
He was appointed ambassador to the United States in March 2025, shortly after President Donald Trump returned to power.
Before his appointment, Darchiev served as Russia’s ambassador to Canada from 2021 to 2024.
A specialist in Russia-US relations, he also headed the Foreign Ministry’s North America Department between 2014 and 2020.
His appointment to Washington came amid strained relations between Russia and Western countries over Moscow’s military offensive in Ukraine.
In 2022, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Darchiev described the military action as a “necessary measure”.
His death was announced by the Russian Foreign Ministry, which did not disclose further information.

items.content:
Last week, I started a discussion of General Yakubu Gowon’s multi-themed memoirs, My Life of Duty & Allegiance. My focus was on the book’s general tone, which I find unduly self-justificatory. In his attempts to defend his legacy, General Gowon presents himself as a saintly figure who did no wrong as a leader, whereas some introspection and nuanced reflection would have helped. That said, the book is a treasure trove of insightful details that enrich our historical narrative. This week, I will focus on one of such insights, namely, the quality of governance and public service ethos under General Gowon’s regime, with Chief Obafemi Awolowo singled out as the arrowhead of a remarkable governance approach that, if replicated today, would transform how Nigeria is governed and, thus, this country’s fortunes.
As a political economist and policy practitioner who spent nearly 20 years advising the UK government on diverse policy areas, in addition to teaching public policy, I have professional and intellectual interests in how government is run. Thus, I was enthralled by General Gowon’s fascinating accounts of how the affairs of state were conducted under his administration, with the triumvirate of politicians (as ministers), civil servants (as technocrats), and universities and think-tanks (as sounding boards) driving policy formulation and implementation and setting standards of good and effective governance. Sitting atop the triumvirate was Chief Awolowo, an extraordinarily transformative leader!
Indeed, if General Gowon’s memoirs can be said to have a hero, that hero is Chief Obafemi Awolowo, appointed by Gowon as the Vice Chairman of the Federal Executive Council, FEC, and Commissioner of Finance in his administration. In every reference to Chief Awolowo in the memoirs, General Gowon writes glowingly and superlatively about him. Gowon also gives credit to his colleagues in the Supreme Military Council, SMC, and the first-class mandarins who ran the civil service for his administration’s successes, especially its ability to prosecute a 30-month civil war “without endangering the national economy”. But he reserves his most generous praise for Chief Awolowo. Hear Gowon: “Chief Awolowo’s business acumen, political sagacity, economic wizardry and thorough man-management ability would later prove quite useful and helpful in ensuring that we kept our finances intact during and immediately after the civil war that broke out a few weeks after his appointment to the FEC.” He adds: “Without any argument, he made invaluable contributions.”
Of course, Chief Awolowo’s reputation preceded him. As the premier of the Western Region, he performed so superbly that Harold Wilson, then British prime minister, described him as a “world-class leader”, who would make an outstanding President of America or Prime Minister of Britain. General Gowon himself referenced Chief Awolowo’s pedigree, saying that he appointed him as the Commissioner of Finance with concurrent responsibility as Vice-Chairman of the FEC “because of his experience in politics and management of the economy of the old Western Region.” Indeed, General Gowon was so enamoured of Chief Awolowo that he admits in his memoirs that one of his administration’s flagship policies, the Universal Primary Education, UPE, was based on a policy introduced by Chief Awolowo as premier. “In scope and content,” Gowon writes, “UPE was not radically different from the model that was initiated by Chief Awolowo in the defunct Western Region while he was the Premier.”
Two lessons emerge from this narrative. First, good leaders get the brightest and best in their teams; they form what a British prime minister described as GOATs (“Government of All the Talents”). Second, good leaders embrace good ideas and best practices worldwide. Indeed, one of the universally recognised approaches to sound policymaking is international comparison, which allows a government to consider what works elsewhere. Sadly, neither lesson is embedded in governance in Nigeria today. For instance, today, a Nigerian leader would fill his cabinet with cronies and political jobbers rather than seasoned technocrats and brilliant administrators. There’s also the phenomenon of policy discontinuities. Virtually every government won’t complete projects started by its predecessor, let alone copy sensible policies elsewhere, resulting in widespread abandoned projects and policy failures.
But there’s another unlearned lesson. Chief Awolowo was never a yes-man in General Gowon’s government. Gowon himself cites two instances to prove this. In both instances, General Gowon eventually had his way, but Awolowo laid down the marker. In one case, General Gowon procured the services of a Lebanese contractor for the government. But Chief Awolowo refused to approve payment to the contractor, arguing that “the process of getting help from the Lebanese was not properly followed and documented and, as such, was an extra-budgetary expenditure.” Tell me, how many extra-budgetary expenditures are waived through without due process today? Can a finance minister challenge a president’s frivolous spending today? In another case, Chief Awolowo refused to approve a request for additional money for Gowon’s upkeep after the original budget was exhausted. He argued that the possibility of overshoots should have been considered before the budget was prepared and approved. This is how Gowon puts it in his memoirs: “Everyone knew how difficult it was to get anything out of Chief Awolowo without well-reasoned arguments.” What an extraordinary testimonial! But where are such principled and painstakingly meticulous ministers and public officers in Nigeria today? Sadly, none! 
To be sure, a tree does not make a forest, and Chief Awolowo did not act alone. As premier of the Western Region and later as Commissioner for Finance and Vice Chairman of the FEC, Chief Awolowo was surrounded by outstanding colleagues and civil servants. For instance, General Gowon mentions the sterling role of Professor Adebayo Adedeji, the world-renowned economist, who was the Commissioner for Economic Development. And talking about bureaucrats, who can forget the “Super Perm Secs” of the Gowon era? As the German sociologist and political economist Max Weber put it, “the state will not conduct its affairs without the bureaucracy.” Oxbridge-educated mandarins like Ahmed Joda, Allison Ayida and Philip Asiodu led what Gowon describes as “the deeply cerebral, committed and efficient technocrats in the civil service”, which he calls “the engine room” of his government. But where are today’s “super perm secs”? Where is today’s vibrant and technocratic civil service? Sadly, today, Nigeria has one of the worst civil services in the world, a subject I discuss in my book, In The National Interest, arguing that the collapse of the civil service and the public sector in general is at the heart of Nigeria’s acutely weak state capacity.
As a scholar-practitioner, I was also excited about General Gowon’s accounts of how his government worked closely with universities. He writes: “We made exceptionally effective use of the many eggheads that populated the various university campuses to shape the policy directions.” He adds: “Many of the dons at the university were our formal and informal sounding boards for policy formulations and analyses.” In the UK, the government works in tandem with universities and think-tanks to shape policies. Sadly, in Nigeria, the government is anti-intellectual, with academics and think-tanks ostracised and treated as pariahs, rarely engaged in policy development. General Gowon makes another profound point about the policy process, saying: “These policies were not unilateral decisions. We diligently thought through the policies, and we implemented them based on their overall benefits to the people.” Compare that with how President Tinubu impulsively removed the fuel subsidy after he was “possessed by courage”, with zero consideration of the impacts on the people!
Truth be told, General Gowon led an extremely effective government, with the prudent management of the economy during the civil war, without external borrowing, a genuine candidate for the Guinness Book of Records. Indeed, Nigeria managed its finances so well that the World Bank borrowed money from the country. Yet crude oil was selling for just $15 per barrel, while Nigeria was pumping just about 1.2m barrels per day. Today, in peacetime, with crude selling for nearly $100 per barrel and Nigeria pumping nearly 2mn barrels per day, the government is borrowing excessively. General Gowon hails Chief Awolowo’s “economic wizardry”. He’s right. But Awolowo didn’t just save Nigeria from economic collapse during and after the war; he also set world-class standards on how to run a country. Nigeria is eternally in his debt!
The post Gowon’s memoirs: Nigeria owes Awolowo an eternal debt, by Olu Fasan appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
By YVONNE-FAITH ELAIGWU
The history of payments is, in many ways, the history of making value easier to move. We started at barter and are now at electronic transfers, with stablecoins suggesting that the next evolution is here. New payment methods rarely make their predecessors useless. Cash did not immediately eliminate barter. Cards did not eliminate cheques. Account-to-account payments will not eliminate cards. But payments evolve. And one of the most interesting examples of that evolution can be found in an unlikely comparison: Nigeria and the United States. The United States built perhaps the world’s greatest card ecosystem. Nigeria just seems to have built past it. The American card system is extraordinary. Over decades, the U.S. built an ecosystem connecting consumers, merchants, issuing banks, acquiring banks, and card networks. Around it grew credit bureaus, credit scores, revolving credit, chargebacks, fraud protection, loyalty points, airline miles, and billions of dollars of rewards. Consequently, Americans have a compelling reason to use cards. And use them, they do.
Data from the Federal Reserve show that credit-card payments reached 67.1 billion transactions in 2024, while ACH processed an enormous $104.06 trillion in 2024. America, therefore, doesn’t lack account-to-account infrastructure. The difference is where A2A sits in everyday consumer behaviour. Walk into an American store, and the natural question is still: Which card am I using? In Nigeria, increasingly, a different question is asked: “What is your account number?” That difference is more significant than it appears. Nigeria took another road. Nigeria never developed America’s deep credit-card culture. Debit cards became widespread, but cards did not become as deeply embedded in the country’s economic architecture as they did in America. Instead, Nigeria increasingly solved digital payments at the bank-account level. At the centre of this transformation is the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System and its NIBSS Instant Payment platform, built to operate 24/7 with most transactions settling in under one second. This infrastructure changed behaviour. Any individual or company can pay another individual or merchant, and the transaction can be executed on a Friday evening or a Sunday morning. The expectation is still remarkably simple: the money should arrive now.
That expectation is one of Nigeria’s greatest payment achievements. America’s success may be part of its problem. This is where the comparison becomes fascinating. America isn’t stuck on cards because it cannot build something better. It may be stuck on cards partly because cards work so well. The merchant already has the terminal. The consumer already has the card. The bank earns card revenue. Visa and Mastercard provide enormous networks. Consumers receive points, miles, fraud protection, and access to credit. Everyone has something to lose from changing the system. Even the Federal Reserve has acknowledged the economic tension. The better yesterday’s infrastructure becomes, the harder tomorrow’s infrastructure can be to adopt. Nigeria had a different incentive. Nigeria faced different circumstances. Card payments existed, but the country had stronger incentives to develop alternative digital rails. Rather than building everything around the card, Nigeria created interoperable infrastructure allowing value to move directly between accounts. The result is not perfect. Instant payments introduce their own fraud problems. So, this is not an argument that cards are bad. Cheques aren’t bad either. They are simply technologies belonging to particular stages in the evolution of payments.
America is catching up. The United States has recognized the need for real-time payments. The Clearing House launched RTP in 2017, and in July 2023, the Federal Reserve launched FedNow, allowing participating financial institutions to transfer funds in near real time, 24/7/365. The rails now exist. The challenge is making instant A2A payments as culturally normal at the American checkout as tapping a credit card. Nigeria has already crossed much of that behavioural bridge. It has also established formal Open Banking guidelines. There is a broader lesson here: technological development isn’t always linear. Sometimes, developing countries do not follow developed countries through every generation of infrastructure. They skip one. America perfected the card. Nigeria had less reason to protect it. And that may have made it easier to build what comes after it.
*Elaigwu is an experienced operations leader with a background in financial services and corporate social responsibility. She is currently Head of Operations at OnePipe, where she drives customer experience and governance.
The post The US built world’s greatest card system appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri
With the 2027 general elections just 65 days away, all eyes are on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to conduct a smooth, free, fair, and credible poll.
Meanwhile, preparations for the aftermath are already under way.
A total of 375 judges have been nominated to serve on election petition tribunals, where they will adjudicate disputes brought by candidates and parties dissatisfied with the results.
The judges, drawn from courts across the federation, were inaugurated on Monday, November 9, at a ceremony held at the Body of Benchers Complex in Abuja.
Section 285(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, vests in the President of the Court of Appeal the responsibility for constituting election petition tribunals to adjudicate disputes arising from National and State Houses of Assembly and governorship elections.
Similarly, section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026, prescribes the timelines for constituting the tribunals and opening their registries.
The swearing-in, organised by the President of the Court of Appeal, Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem, marked the formal assumption of a responsibility with considerable constitutional, professional and public significance.
A three-day intensive workshop followed immediately.
It was designed to deepen the judges’ knowledge of the Electoral Act 2026, familiarise them with applicable practice directions and the evolving jurisprudence of the courts on election-related cases, and sharpen the practical skills needed for case management, evaluation of evidence, control of proceedings, and the delivery of clear, well-reasoned judgments within the prescribed timelines.
The CJN also used the occasion to launch the second edition of the Judicial Electoral Manual (JEM), which she said will help judicial officers locate relevant authorities, appreciate the development of the law and approach recurring issues with greater clarity.
According to the CJN, by bringing together the relevant constitutional provisions, the Electoral Act 2026, applicable practice directions and judicial decisions, the Manual provides a useful resource for judicial officers and other stakeholders in the electoral adjudicatory process.
She was quick to warn, however, that it should serve only as a guide and a reference tool.
It does not replace independent judicial reasoning or relieve any judicial officer of the duty to consider each case on its own facts, the arguments of counsel and the applicable law.
The Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, said the early swearing-in of the tribunal judges was a clear demonstration of the judiciary’s commitment to ensuring that electoral disputes are handled promptly, competently and in accordance with the law.
Fagbemi noted that election petition tribunals occupy a unique position in Nigeria’s democratic architecture, which is why the adjudication of electoral disputes continues to attract intense public attention and scrutiny.
By providing the constitutional mechanism through which electoral grievances are peacefully resolved, he said, the tribunals are indispensable to political stability and public trust in the electoral process.
The AGF drew attention to the far-reaching reforms introduced by the Electoral Act 2026, which he said aim to strengthen electoral transparency, promote internal party democracy, modernise electoral administration and redefine the framework for electoral disputes.
The Act restricts judicial intervention in internal party affairs.
Section 83(5) ousts the jurisdiction of the courts over disputes concerning the internal affairs of political parties, while Section 83(6) stipulates sanctions for intra-party litigation.
The Act restricts interim and interlocutory injunctions in prohibited intra-party proceedings, provides for accelerated hearings, and prescribes minimum costs of N10 million each against the litigant and counsel.
Likewise, Section 138(1) limits the grounds for election petitions.
The amended law confines election petitions to corrupt practices, substantial non-compliance with electoral law, and failure to secure a majority of lawful votes.
Significantly, it omits candidate disqualification as an express post-election ground, potentially shifting qualification disputes to pre-election proceedings.
The AGF argued that the innovations in the amended Act represent a significant recalibration of Nigeria’s electoral framework ahead of the general elections.
“Their ultimate transformative impact will depend on effective enforcement by INEC, compliance by political parties and judicial interpretation,” he added.
For the INEC Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, SAN, electoral litigation has become increasingly complex.
He observed that, beyond the familiar questions of voting, counting and collation, disputes now concern voter accreditation, electronic transmission of results, technological failures, the integrity of digital records, party primaries, candidate nominations and the conduct of election officials.
He said the Electoral Act 2026 has provided the legislative framework for the forthcoming general elections.
“Of particular relevance is Section 60(3), which addresses electronic transmission of polling-unit results and the legal implications of communication failures.
“Its interpretation, alongside other provisions of the new Act, may feature prominently in future petitions.
“The deployment of the BVAS and the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV) has brought greater technological sophistication to election administration and public access to electoral information.
“At the same time, these systems raise questions about the authenticity, admissibility and probative value of electronic records, their relationship with physical documents, and the consequences of technical disruptions.
“A clear distinction must be maintained between the generation of technological information, the statutory purpose it serves and the legal standard required to prove a case before a tribunal.
“The distinction between pre-election matters and post-election petitions must be carefully observed,” the INEC Chairman added.
Although INEC and the judiciary perform distinct but complementary constitutional functions, the credibility of the elections cannot be judged solely by the conduct of voting or the declaration of results.
It will also depend on public confidence that electoral disputes will be determined independently, fairly and in accordance with the law.
As the CJN pointed out, the 2027 elections will be a defining moment in the nation’s democratic journey.
She warned that the courtroom must not become an extension of the political arena, stressing that disputes must be resolved on the basis of the pleadings, evidence and applicable law.
Of the 375 judges nominated, 138 have previous tribunal experience, while 237 are new to such proceedings.
The workshop is expected to have equipped them with the skills and knowledge to navigate the murky waters of election litigation and arrive at legally sound decisions. By fairly determining any disputes arising from the 2027 elections, the judiciary stands to safeguard the people’s mandate, uphold constitutional supremacy and sustain public confidence in democratic governance.
The post 2027 Elections: Beyond INEC, 375 Judges’ integrity under trial appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
tags: Speaking and Writing with Ruth Oji
items.content:
Among the many communication challenges professionals encounter, few produce as much immediate anxiety as being asked an unexpected question in a public setting. The scenario is familiar to almost everyone: You are sitting in a department review, an academic seminar, an industry panel, or a client briefing. Without warning, the chairperson turns to you and says, “What are your thoughts on this proposal?” or “How should we handle this unexpected operational delay?” In that single second, your heart rate increases, adrenaline surges, and your mind races. You have relevant experience and informed opinions, but under the sudden spotlight of the room, your working memory feels temporarily paralyzed. Fearing that silence will make you look unprepared, you begin speaking immediately. You offer a few polite disclaimers, describe unrelated background context, and circle around three different ideas, hoping that a coherent conclusion will emerge along the way. By the time you finish two minutes later, you are out of breath, the room is slightly confused, and you realize you never directly answered the question. This common struggle is not a measure of intelligence, dedication, or professional competence. It is simply a structural problem. When put on the spot, you cannot rely on unstructured improvisation; you need a clear, dependable mental framework to organize your thoughts under pressure.
The Cognitive Dilemma of Spontaneous Speech
To understand why spontaneous speaking feels difficult, it helps to examine what happens to our thinking process under sudden stress. When you are asked an unexpected question in front of your peers or superiors, your brain experiences a mild threat response. Adrenaline floods your system, narrowing your focus and reducing your working memory capacity. In this heightened state, attempting to simultaneously decide what you want to say, how you want to sequence your arguments, and when you are going to stop speaking creates heavy cognitive overload. Without a roadmap, speakers instinctively resort to “verbal stall tactics”—rambling introductions, excessive throat-clearing, and endless qualifications—while their brains frantically search for a central point.
The solution to this dilemma is not to try harder or speak faster. The solution is to separate the structure of your answer from the content. When you have a simple, pre-learned structural template stored in your memory, you no longer need to invent an organizational method in real time. The template holds the shape of your ideas, freeing your mind to focus entirely on sharing your perspective clearly and calmly.
The Architecture of the PREP Method
One of the most effective and versatile mental models for impromptu speaking is the PREP Framework. Originally developed in classical rhetoric and refined in modern executive training, PREP stands for four clear, sequential stages: Point, Reason, Example, Point.
  [ Point ] – State your core recommendation or conclusion directly.
  [ Reason ] – Explain the primary logic or data supporting your point.
 [ Example ] – Provide a concrete illustration, past metric, or case study.
  [ Point ] – Restate your core recommendation with a clear call to action.
Let us examine each stage in practical terms:
Point: Lead with the Conclusion
The most critical habit in spontaneous communication is stating your main takeaway in the very first sentence. In formal writing, we often build up to our conclusion through pages of analysis. In spoken conversation, however, listeners need to know your destination immediately. When you open with a clear, direct statement—such as “I recommend we pause the maintenance schedule on Line 2 until Monday”—you give your listeners a mental hook. They now know exactly what you are proposing, making it easy for them to follow the supporting details that follow. Leading with your point also eliminates the nervous habit of opening with apologetic padding, such as “Well, I haven’t looked at all the latest reports yet, but maybe…” Directness is not arrogance; it is a courteous way to value the room’s time.
Reason: Provide the Core Logical Driver
Once your point is on the table, immediately explain the primary reason behind it. The reason answers the listener’s immediate question: “Why do you say that?” Keep your reason focused on a single, compelling argument rather than listing five secondary factors. For instance: “Because the weather forecast indicates high winds that exceed our safety operating limits for crane deployment.” By offering one clear, substantive reason, you provide solid logical backing without overwhelming your listeners with unnecessary detail.
Example: Anchor Your Logic in Concrete Reality
Abstract arguments are easy to forget; concrete examples are easy to understand and remember.
In the third stage of PREP, provide a brief piece of evidence, a specific past experience, or a concrete data point that proves your reason. For example: “Last October, when a team operated under similar wind conditions at the offshore terminal, equipment was damaged and operations were delayed by forty-eight hours.” Grounding your argument in a factual example moves the discussion from subjective opinion to objective reality. It gives your listeners a tangible reference point that reinforces your credibility.
Point: Close the Loop Cleanly
The final step is restating your original point in a decisive concluding sentence. Many professionals give an excellent explanation and share a great example, only to finish with an awkward fade: “…and, yeah, so, that’s basically what I was thinking.” A weak ending dilutes the impact of everything that came before. Instead, close the loop by restating your core recommendation: “Therefore, postponing the maintenance to Monday protects our personnel and ensures the work is completed safely.”
Restating your point signals clearly that you have finished speaking, leaving the room with a crisp, professional conclusion.
Applying the Model Across Industries
The strength of the PREP model lies in its universal adaptability. It functions equally well across varied professional and academic contexts:
In Technology:
Point: “We should implement automated testing for this billing module.”
Reason: “Because manual testing is taking two full engineering days per release cycle.”
Example: “During our last release, three minor edge-case errors slipped through and caused billing ticket spikes.”
Point: “Automating this test suite will shorten our release cycle and maintain software quality.”
In Energy and Operations:
Point: “We need to upgrade the pressure monitoring sensors at Station B.”
Reason: “The current analog sensors are reaching their end-of-life reliability limits.”
Example: “Over the past month, our field technicians had to perform three manual recalibrations during operating hours.”
Point: “Replacing these units during the scheduled shutdown will prevent unexpected downtime.”
In Higher Education and Research:
Point: “The study’s conclusion regarding student engagement needs qualification.”
Reason: “The underlying research methodology relies exclusively on self-reported surveys rather than behavioral metrics.”
Example: “In Section 3, over forty percent of participants acknowledged they completed the questionnaire in a single sitting without verifying their study hours.”
Point: “To make broader claims about academic habits, we need longitudinal tracking data.”
Structure as the Foundation of Confidence
There is a common misconception that having a structured approach restricts your personality, making you sound rigid or scripted. In practice, the opposite is true. When you do not have a reliable framework, nervous energy consumes your attention. You become preoccupied with managing your own uncertainty. But when you trust a reliable mental structure like PREP, the scaffolding handles the organization for you. Your cognitive energy is freed to focus on warmth, eye contact, and genuine connection with your colleagues. Confidence in communication is rarely a magical personality trait reserved for natural extroverts. It is the natural result of having dependable tools that function under pressure.
The next time an unexpected question is directed your way in a meeting, resist the urge to rush into speech or fill the silence with rambling disclaimers. Take a calm breath, identify your core point, support it with a clear reason and example, and close the loop decisively. By making structured thinking a daily habit, you will find that thinking on your feet becomes one of your greatest professional strengths.

items.content:
Following the November 5, ruling of Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, which nullified the Senator David Mark leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and invalidated all decisions taken under his watch, including the primary elections that produced the party’s candidates for the 2027 elections, Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, is behaving like the overfed little bird Nza in Igbo folklore that challenged his Chi (personal god) to a bout. Many Nigerians were aghast at the judge’s indiscretion and absolute lack of emotional intelligence when he voided not only the candidacy of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar but also every other ticket of the party simply because of the contrived grievance of one Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former official of the party. But Keyamo is over the moon with the consequential judgement, which import according to one of Gombe’s counsel, Luka Musa Haruna, a learned silk, is that, “As it stands today, the ADC has no candidate from the presidential level to the House of Assembly, governorship, Senate and all other elective positions for the 2027 election,” because apparently he sees in the defanging of the ADC even before the first ballot is cast the only pathway to the All Progressives Congress (APC) victory.
It didn’t bother Keyamo, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN) that the judgement was delivered only 72 days to the polls, a brazen and rascally act of judicial mischief by a judge whose actions were recently described by a three-member panel of the Court of Appeal led by Justice A. B. Mohammed as rendering him “unfit for the bench.” To every discerning observer of the unfolding political drama, the fact that the judgement ousting ADC, the main opposition party, from the 2027 ballot, was delivered barely 24 hours after Atiku, commenced his nation-wide campaigns with a hugely successful rally in Sokoto State, is telling both in reality and optics. It was a panic move by a ruling party afraid of competition. But Keyamo would rather gaslight Nigerians with his jejune “Heavens will not fall if a certain Atiku Abubakar is not on the ballot in 2027” rhetoric. Sheer orotundity borne out of fear. As a lawyer, Keyamo knows that the dictum “heavens will not fall,” derived from the Latin legal maxim Fiat justitia ruat caelum – Let justice be done, though the heavens fall – in principle attests to the inviolability of justice when the law is applied fairly, no matter the cost. In other words, it speaks to a strict moral and legal commitment to judicial integrity. So, heavens are not expected to fall when the courts and those in power do not bend the rules. But heavens definitely will fall in a situation where a judge recently lampooned by brother-judges on a superior bench as someone whose actions constitute the “gravest form of judicial misconduct” and “highest form of judicial impertinence” whimsically gives a ruling that flushes the candidacy of Atiku and his running mate, Rotimi Amaechi, 28 governorship hopefuls and their running mates, 346 House of Representatives and 108 senatorial candidates and thousands of House of Assembly contestants down APC’s invidious toilet of political mischief.   
Granted, because this is Nigeria, Lifu’s ruling could be upheld even by superior courts with the hope that nothing will happen. After all, what have we not seen? But if that is what gives Keyamo and his ilk the audacity to ride roughshod over fellow citizens, they are definitely not reading the tea leaves. Because if they are, they would have noticed that opposition political parties are no longer running away from state-sponsored thugs. They are increasingly confronting them. When the Sokoto State government denied the ADC venues for their campaigns, they took the rally to the streets and the entire state was shut down. Heavens fall when citizens have it up to their necks and insensitive leaders taunt them for their predicament as Senator Abdul’aziz Yari, Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, did this week in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, when he told poor Nigerians: “You are hungry because you are lazy. If you work hard, you will not be hungry.” Heavens fall when the inordinate ambition of men of power blights their sense of reasoning. Heavens fall when leaders become too arrogant to care about the consequences of their actions. Despite our legendary reputation for docility, the ramparts of ‘heaven’ as constructed by foolhardy and vainglorious politicians begin to crack when the people are pushed to the wall and urged to take a swim in a shark-infested lagoon if they grumble. And that is exactly what the APC is doing right now. That is why Keyamo’s “heavens will not fall” rhetoric is extremely dangerous. Anyone who supports the exclusion of Atiku and the entire ADC cast of candidates from the 2027 ballot at this late hour does not mean well for the country. This is neither about Atiku Abubakar nor ADC. It is about Nigeria and the inalienable right of citizens to choose their leaders without let or hindrance. It is about the peculiar circumstances of our fragile statehood.
It was for this same reason that the General Abdulsalami Abubakar-led junta registered the Alliance for Democracy (AD) in 1998 even when it didn’t meet the registration criteria. In his autobiography, Call of Duty, the former Head of State wrote: “We had to apply some wisdom and flexibility. As projected, the AD eventually didn’t meet the criteria for the registration of political parties. We tinkered with the rules and said any party that came third would be registered. That was how AD scaled through. We did not want to create a system in which the South-West would feel marginalised. Whatever decision we took was for the peace and progress of the country. If tinkering with the rule we made ourselves would give respite to Nigerians, why not? The rules were made by humans and for humans. The idea was to give peace a chance and to ensure that there was equity and justice.” It is imprudent for anyone to think that there will be no consequences for government’s bad behaviour, no matter how egregious because Nigeria is a captured state where citizens have been abused to submission. History does not validate such hypothesis. If only our leaders learn from history, they would know that no matter the vicious inclination of a country’s security forces, they are never a match to a people with their back against the wall. Last year, President Andry Rajoelina of Madagascar fled his Indian Ocean island nation following weeks of youth-led and Gen Z anti-government protests over severe power and water shortages, corruption, and economic hardships. In August 2024, Bangladesh’s longest-serving Prime Minister, Sheikh Hasina, was forced to resign and flee the country after waves of protests toppled her government. In July 2022, President Gotabaya Rajapaksa fled Sri Lanka after months of mass protests triggered by a crippling economic collapse, severe food and fuel shortages, and anger against the ruling family.
These are leaders who once believed like the current Nigerian leaders that they were invincible and the heavens will never fall because they had become the state writ large. In fact, in the case of Prime Minister Hasina, an estimated 1,400 people were killed by security forces who cracked down on the student-led protests that lasted for weeks. But she ultimately fled when she realised that rather than dampening their enthusiasm and weakening their resolve, the blood of their fallen compatriots emboldened the protesters and aggravated the protests. Those who relish lying to themselves could indulge their fantasy, but the truth staring us in the face is that Nigerian politicians are not planning for free, fair and credible elections in January. Weaponising the judiciary against the opposition as the APC is doing is an ill-wind. Using state governors to deny opposition parties level playing field is a recipe for chaos. Unleashing thugs on opposition leaders is a recipe for crisis. Using the judiciary to deny the opposition a foothold in the 2027 elections as Justice Lifu did with his ADC ruling is reckless. And boasting like Keyamo did that these shenanigans can endure without the heavens falling is crass ignorance and the height of foolhardiness. Time to pull back from the brink is now because the heavens can, indeed, fall when reason takes a flight.
The post What, if the heavens fall? By Ikechukwu Amaechi appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
By ROBERT UWEMEDIMO
When Debbi Fields observed that “there is no such thing as coincidence; people come into our lives for a reason,” she captured a truth I have come to know profoundly through my relationship with Mr. Gbenga Omotoso. As he turned 65 on November 11, 2026, I pause to reflect on the extraordinary journey of more than two decades I have been privileged to share with the man I call boss – one who has been to me a father, mentor, benefactor, teacher, and, above all, a blessing from God Almighty.
April 21, 2004, marked the beginning of a journey that would forever alter the course of my life. As I approached the wine-coloured plywood door on the second floor of a six-storey building at Ijora Causeway, Lagos – then the headquarters of The Comet newspaper – I opened it and found myself face to face with Mr. Omotoso, the Daily Editor, who needed someone to run errands for his office.
He asked my name. “Robert,” I replied. “When will you resume work?” he asked. I was stunned. Here stood a man offering me a job before I had even applied; no interview, no credentials to present, no long queue outside a human resources office. Just one simple question that would rewrite the course of my life. “Tomorrow, sir,” I answered.
That brief exchange marked the beginning of a relationship that shaped my life in ways I could never have imagined. I was a young boy who had lost his father at twelve. Little did I know that God was preparing another father figure for me in the person of Mr. Omotoso. When The Comet closed in 2006, a deep and overwhelming sense of uncertainty settled over us. Yet Mr. Omotoso looked me in the eye and assured me that wherever his career took him next, I would not be left behind. True to his word, when The Nation newspaper launched on July 31, 2006, I continued working with him as a 16-year-old boy. One quality that set him apart from the very beginning was his uncommon, almost instinctive generosity. I remember one particular week when he repeatedly asked whether I had eaten. Each time, he would give me some money for food. As time passed and his instinctive generosity continued, I grew uncomfortable and began answering, “Yes, sir, I have eaten,” not because I had suddenly become rich, but because I did not want him to think I was turning hunger into a business strategy. That is Mr. Omotoso. His kindness is never calculated; it flows naturally.
His generosity was never limited to me. I recall a difficult period when the newspaper’s salaries were delayed for months. The newsroom was dampened, heavy with frustration. Sensing and discerning the quiet despair of his colleagues, he reached into his own pocket and gave everyone money to ease the hardship. That single gesture taught me a lesson I have never forgotten: true leadership is not about occupying an office; it is about lifting others when life weighs them down.
Beyond feeding my body, Mr. Omotoso fed my dreams.
He encouraged me to keep studying while working and never once treated my academic ambitions as an inconvenience. During one management meeting, when questions were raised about my qualifications, he defended my potential and appealed for patience while I worked toward becoming a graduate. I was determined not to disappoint him. In 2014, I graduated from the then Lagos State Polytechnic with a Distinction. He celebrated the achievement, then immediately urged me to aim higher. With his continued support, I went on to Caleb University, Imota, Lagos, where I earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Computer Science in 2019, graduating with Second Class Upper honours and a CGPA of 4.36. For someone who had started as an errand boy, this was more than academic progress. It was living proof that when someone believes in your potential, your circumstances need not determine your destination. Mr. Omotoso’s fatherly role extended far beyond the professional and academic. When I married in 2018, he provided a Honda Pilot and a personal driver to take me around all day, ensuring the occasion was memorable.
On August 20, 2019, he was appointed Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy. Before leaving The Nation, he ensured my contributions were recognised with a promotion to Web Officer. A month into his new assignment, he invited me to join him at the Ministry of Information and Strategy. That invitation opened yet another significant chapter in my career. Since then, I have had the privilege of serving closely with him as his Personal Assistant and Programme Analyst within the Lagos State Government. His commitment to my progress did not end there. He played an instrumental role in my appointment to the Lagos State Civil Service on December 31, 2024, personally presenting my credentials to Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu for consideration and approval. How does one adequately thank a man who has consistently opened doors, sometimes long before one even knew those doors existed? Yet my story is only one among countless testimonies of his compassion.
Over the years, I have watched him discreetly pay hospital bills for people with whom he shares no family ties, sponsor the education of children whose parents could not afford school fees, and quietly rescue others from difficult circumstances.
He does not need a camera to demonstrate kindness, nor does he wait for applause before helping others. Behind his serious editorial background and the demands of public office is also a man blessed with a remarkable sense of humour. An accomplished journalist, columnist and writer, Mr. Omotoso has a gift for satire. His humorous observations can turn even tense moments into shared laughter. And then there is table tennis. Anyone who has faced him across the table knows that losing is not exactly his favourite pastime. He approaches every game with the intensity of an editor scrutinising a controversial front-page headline. Every point matters, every rally is a battle, and every defeat deserves a detailed explanation. At 65, I suspect his opponents will still need more than youthful energy to defeat him.
As I celebrate this remarkable man, I see far beyond the professional titles and accomplishments. I see a compassionate father figure, a bridge-builder, a generous leader, and a man whose quiet influence continues to transform lives. Sir, on your 65th birthday, I pray that Almighty God grants you long life, sound health, renewed strength, divine protection, and enduring peace. May the years ahead be filled with greater accomplishments, happiness, and the joy of seeing the many lives you have touched continue to flourish. May God reward every sacrifice you have made for others, replenish every resource you have so freely and generously shared, and surround you with love, honour and abundant blessings. May your pen never run dry, your wisdom never diminish, your laughter never cease, and may you continue winning your table tennis matches, even when your opponents believe they deserve a chance! For more than 22 years, I have experienced your kindness firsthand. I may never be able to repay all you have done for me, but I will forever remain grateful.
Happy 65th birthday, my boss, my mentor, my father figure, and my God-sent benefactor. The world may know you as Gbenga Omotoso, the accomplished journalist and Commissioner. I know you as the man God used to rewrite the story of a fatherless boy. And for that, I will remain eternally grateful.
•Uwemedimo is a Programme Analyst and Personal Assistant to the Lagos State Commissioner for Information and Strategy.
The post Gbenga Omotoso at 65: A rare gift of generosity and mentorship appeared first on Vanguard News.
