items.title: Chinese university bought Nvidia H200 chips despite US blacklist
items.summary:
A Chinese university with ​deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced ‌technology.
The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology. But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips can speed China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation.
Read: US tackles loopholes in curbs on AI chip exports to China
PLA-Linked Blacklisted Chinese University Bought NVIDIA AI Chips
Northweste
items.author: Reuters
items.content:
A Chinese university with ​deep ties to the People's Liberation Army bought Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a US export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington's efforts to curb China's access to advanced ‌technology.
The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation.
Huang has argued that continued US sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology. But some US lawmakers say access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips can speed China's development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernisation.
Read: US tackles loopholes in curbs on AI chip exports to China
PLA-Linked Blacklisted Chinese University Bought NVIDIA AI Chips
Northwestern Polytechnical University paid $123,000 for two NVIDIA H200 chips through a Chinese supplier and also signed five contracts to rent access to advanced NVIDIA processors.https://t.co/a1Nc3b4wRa
— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 11, 2026
Both Democrats and Republicans in Congress have urged stronger controls on China's access to advanced AI chips, such ​as chip-tracking requirements and greater congressional oversight of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on November 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.
Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips ​last month for 874,700 yuan ($123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website.
Northwestern is a member of the "Seven Sons of National Defence" group of Chinese universities under US sanctions and ⁠has a history of conducting defence-related research for Beijing.
The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows.
The H200 is among Nvidia's most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems ​and is subject to US export licence approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical.
Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, ​procurement records show.
Reuters is reporting the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology.
Trade blacklist
Based in the northwestern city of Xian, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites.
The US Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. It tightened the restrictions in ​2019, making licences for exports of controlled US technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances.
Read More: Nvidia chips pile up in Hong Kong as China withholds import approval
Northwestern Polytechnical's purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain US AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying ​chips outright or renting access to servers containing them.
A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying US-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close ‌links to China's ⁠defence industry or military research.
The universities named in the records did not respond to requests for comment.
Nvidia chips for military-linked research
US President Donald Trump's administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organisations such as Northwestern Polytechnical.
The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models.
In addition to the management school's outright purchase of the two H200 chips, procurement records show the university's cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each. The contracts, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, covered fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training.
It also ​rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight ​A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from ⁠export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical's procurement records.
In April, another university institute bought computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips in a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and fluid-dynamics simulations.
The awards went to several little-known Chinese technology suppliers. The records offered scant information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers ​operated.
Under Chinese law, public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers can fulfil orders before announcing winning bidders and signing contracts.
A wider market
The procurement records show a wider market for restricted ​Nvidia AI chips and computing services ⁠at Chinese universities.
Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the US, for 769,800 yuan in September. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips in a separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show.
Beihang University, another of the Seven Sons of National Defence universities, bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. Beihang has close ties to China's aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programmes.
Two government procurement announcements in ⁠July and September named ​suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips restricted from export to China to the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. One ​listed H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate January procurement award named a supplier of six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a Shenzhen-based public institution.
Reuters has previously reported that Chinese institutions acquired restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers made by Super Micro Computer, Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers. Reuters has also ​documented an underground market in China for restricted Nvidia chips sourced from overseas inventories and third-country intermediaries.
Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports.

items.title: Binance hack reveals crypto's uphill battle against hackers
items.summary:
An elite North Korean hacking group’s $6.3 billion theft from Binance is renewing scrutiny of a longstanding weakness in the cryptocurrency industry: hackers may need ​to compromise only one employee to get inside, while inconsistent security practices can allow them to turn that foothold into a massive theft.
The October 29 heist, described ‌by experts as the largest cryptocurrency theft ever, unfolded in a matter of minutes after months of planning and preparation, according to Binance’s investigation.
Cybersecurity experts said the attack raises questions not only about how exchanges defend employees against sophisticated social engineering, but also about whether they have adequate internal controls to limit what an attacker can do once an employee’s computer or credentials are compromised.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
An elite North Korean hacking group’s $6.3 billion theft from Binance is renewing scrutiny of a longstanding weakness in the cryptocurrency industry: hackers may need ​to compromise only one employee to get inside, while inconsistent security practices can allow them to turn that foothold into a massive theft.
The October 29 heist, described ‌by experts as the largest cryptocurrency theft ever, unfolded in a matter of minutes after months of planning and preparation, according to Binance’s investigation.
Cybersecurity experts said the attack raises questions not only about how exchanges defend employees against sophisticated social engineering, but also about whether they have adequate internal controls to limit what an attacker can do once an employee’s computer or credentials are compromised.
Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what analysts say is the biggest crypto hack ever, an attack that could prompt investors to rethink the risks of owning digital assets https://t.co/0oa56SQpJj pic.twitter.com/gWZiB7nivK
— Reuters (@Reuters) October 30, 2026
Read: Binance hackers used fake job interview in $6.3b attack
Social engineering is a well-understood threat in the industry, said Jonathan Alexander, chief ​technology officer of S&P Global’s OpenZeppelin, a blockchain security provider. The bigger question, he said, is why exchanges do not have stronger internal safeguards and circuit breakers to prevent ​an attacker who breaches an engineer’s computer — like what happened at Binance — from escalating access and moving assets.
Varying cybersecurity practices across the industry compound the ⁠problem, Alexander said, along with a longstanding aversion among some cryptocurrency advocates to controls they view as inconsistent with blockchain’s decentralised ethos that sometimes views things such as limits on transaction amounts and ​automatic reviews of patterns of spending as infringing on inherent privacy rights.
"I think that falsely, that has led some people to think that things like circuit breakers, things like more controls on the ​accounts, would be unacceptable or would be absolutely in conflict with that need to avoid censorship," Alexander said. "In my view, you can have security controls and have protections against that."
The Binance attack is the latest in a string of major cryptocurrency hacks that have resulted in more than $22.3 billion in stolen funds since 2021, according to blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis. The scale of the losses has intensified debate over whether exchanges need more consistent standards governing ​access, transaction controls and other defences.
“I do expect we’ll see more clarity and standardisation in the kind of cybersecurity expectations and, hopefully, requirements for investor protection and trust," Alexander said. “These things show ​why it has to change."
Highly visible, attractive targets
Cryptocurrency exchanges present unusually attractive targets because hackers can identify wallets holding enormous sums of readily transferable digital assets and, in some cases, the employees with access to the ‌systems controlling them.
That ⁠has made engineers and IT workers prime targets for elaborate social-engineering operations.
Alex Pruden, CEO of blockchain and digital-asset security firm Project Eleven, said defenders face a fundamental disadvantage against attackers who need to succeed only once.
“This is an extremely hard problem,” Pruden said. “The best practices in cybersecurity that we've had up to this point are just simply not up to the task of the world that we live in in terms of what the threat is.”
Cybersecurity workers in the industry, he added, “live in a world of constant warfare. We are under constant attack”.
Read More: North Korea's army of world-class hackers is secret weapon that took down Binance
Pruden expects the Binance theft to spur greater ​investment in cybersecurity, including safeguards around internal AI tools ​and agents that could themselves expand an ⁠attacker’s capabilities if compromised.
"We're at the beginning of the beginning of that story, but I just think as the Binance hack showed, those tools can be turned against you very, very quickly and they can be very hard to undo the damage once it's done."
Cryptocurrency exchanges have already begun ​moving to bolster defences and increase information sharing following the Binance hack, Reuters reported October 30.
Patchwork oversight, uneven defences
The uneven security practices identified by experts ​are mirrored by a ⁠fragmented US regulatory system.
Unlike banks, US cryptocurrency exchanges do not operate under a single federal cybersecurity regime. Instead, requirements vary depending on where companies operate and which state licenses they hold.
New York imposes some of the industry's toughest requirements. The state's Department of Financial Services requires licensed companies to maintain cybersecurity programs, use multi-factor authentication and designate a chief information security officer.
Elsewhere, crypto companies may be subject primarily to state money-transmitter ⁠rules. Those ​regimes generally require companies to provide regulators with information about their cybersecurity programs and undergo examinations, but often do not ​prescribe particular technical controls, such as encryption standards.
Many exchanges do not operate in the US and are not subject to those state oversight regimes, although they may operate under separate requirements wherever they do business.
Banks, by contrast, are subject ​to federal requirements covering areas including risk assessments, monitoring and incident response, while the largest institutions undergo continuing examinations by dedicated supervisors.

items.content:
Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah on Wednesday called for a "ceasefire" between the government and Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, saying that he should not, under any circumstances, stand on the other side in the war against terrorism.
Tensions between the JUI-F chief and the federal government have escalated sharply over constitutional disputes, security policies in K-P and new accountability inquiries targeting his inner circle.
Speaking on a private television programme, Capital Talk, Sanaullah acknowledged Maulana Fazl’s efforts and sacrifices in the fight against terrorism and said the JUI-F chief should not, under any circumstances, stand on the other side in this war.
“If, for some reason, Maulana stands on the other side, I believe it would be a loss for the country,” he said.
Sanaullah said he would discuss the matter with the prime minister and would also speak to Maulana Fazl, emphasising the need for a ceasefire between the two sides.
“Both sides have to make an effort. There should be a ceasefire in this matter,” he said.
Sanaullah expressed concern over the JUI-F chief’s recent speeches, saying he appeared to be attributing the mistakes and undemocratic actions of successive establishments over several decades to the current military leadership.
He said there was a need to engage Maulana Fazl in a dialogue and explain why such criticism was inappropriate.
“Maulana should be told that this kind of dialogue is not appropriate. The incumbent army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, has not only removed the liabilities accumulated by the army over 78 years but has also brought honour to the armed forces, the nation and Pakistan through Marka-e-Haq,” he said.
Asked about reports that efforts were being made to distance the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) from Maulana Fazl, Sanaullah questioned why the JUI-F chief should not be brought closer to the government. "Isn’t that much more appropriate?"
He stressed that all political differences should be set aside in the fight against terrorism, which he described as a threat to Pakistan’s existence.
Sanaullah added that, given Maulana Fazl’s standing and influence in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, he should support the armed forces in their fight against terrorism.
Following the imposition of the emergency and governor's rule in K-P, Fazl accused the government of backing out of negotiations with the PTI and the opposition despite initially agreeing to their demands.
He categorically rejected the imposition of governor's rule or an emergency in K-P, saying that if an emergency had to be imposed, it should be imposed on the federal government, which he described as illegitimate.
The criticism subsequently spilt over into the assembly, escalating the war of words between the government and the JUI-F chief. Fazl had accused the government of misusing the Constitution.
Federal ministers hit back, accusing the JUI-F chief of overlooking his own role in forming and toppling governments.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi criticised Fazl over his opposition to governor's rule in the province, suggesting that the religious-political leader was unhappy at not being offered a role in the new provincial setup.
Later, a delegation of the PTI and TTAP expressed full support for the JUI-F chief's speech in the National Assembly and condemned what it described as his character assassination by government ministers following his strong criticism of the government's actions.

items.title: Indian billionaire, doctors spar over $900 brain blood-flow tracker Temple
items.summary:
A tiny, $900 wearable device developed by an Indian billionaire entrepreneur and showcased by some of India's top sportspersons has drawn criticism from doctors who say its claims of tracking blood flow to the brain are exaggerated.
The Temple device is less than 1 inch (2.54 cm) wide and weighs under 2 grams (0.07 oz). It sticks to the side of the head between the forehead and the ear, or the temple area.
Promotional materials for the device, developed by Deepinder Goyal, say that its BrainFlow feature shows how well the brain ​is being supplied with blood in real time, and its Entropy feature can detect how hard the body works to shed ​heat.
Read: Smartphones are revolutionising medicine
It can also measure thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive and emotional readings that help to transform how a person ⁠regulates their health, they say.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
A tiny, $900 wearable device developed by an Indian billionaire entrepreneur and showcased by some of India's top sportspersons has drawn criticism from doctors who say its claims of tracking blood flow to the brain are exaggerated.
The Temple device is less than 1 inch (2.54 cm) wide and weighs under 2 grams (0.07 oz). It sticks to the side of the head between the forehead and the ear, or the temple area.
Promotional materials for the device, developed by Deepinder Goyal, say that its BrainFlow feature shows how well the brain ​is being supplied with blood in real time, and its Entropy feature can detect how hard the body works to shed ​heat.
Read: Smartphones are revolutionising medicine
It can also measure thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive and emotional readings that help to transform how a person ⁠regulates their health, they say.
Deepinder Goyal's Rs 85,000 wearable faces questions over scientific claims | Deepinder Goyal, co-founder of Zomato, has launched a wearable startup called Temple that has run into a public scientific credibility test. Doctors are questioning the evidence behind its ₹85,000… pic.twitter.com/cBGS89Y3Ft
— Economic Times (@EconomicTimes) November 9, 2026
Priced at 85,000 rupees ($907), the device comes in six colours. India's cricket captain Shubman Gill and Olympic medal-winning badminton ​player PV Sindhu have worn it.
Some well-known doctors in the country, however, are sceptical of the claims, saying peer-reviewed research does not back the device's capabilities. In prime-time shows and on social media, they are calling for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators.
Prominent Indian hepatologist Cyriac Philips, known as "TheLiverDoc", has been criticising the device on his X account with 328,000 followers, calling Temple "the biggest health scam".
The Liver Doc goes another round with Deepinder Goyal | Hepatologist and social media personality Cyriac Abby Philips, popularly known as ‘The Liver Doc,’ has again challenged Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal, alleging his wearable device Temple was nothing but a “beautiful scam.”… pic.twitter.com/8o0kCngdJ8
— Economic Times (@EconomicTimes) November 10, 2026
"People must be aware of wellness hacks such ​as wearables also, even though they are not marketed as health devices," he told Reuters.
On one prime-time TV discussion, paediatrician and nephrologist Sanjeev ​Bagai called Temple a "gimmick", saying it had "no formal approval or clearance".
Goyal has hit back at the criticism from doctors, saying Temple is a "fitness tracker and wellness ‌device", not ⁠a medical one.
Temple is an ambitious project. The team is delusional enough to think we can build this. And we will.
Here's what we are building. Join the ride. https://t.co/sZugOhdb2f pic.twitter.com/fPZSISAr6V
— Deepinder Goyal (@deepigoyal) November 6, 2026
Indian doctor Jason Philip wrote on X that assessing blood flow to the brain was not easy, and optical signals placed over the temple skin would only give data on the "superficial temporal artery" that supplies blood to the face and skin.
Temple's core pitch collapses under basic medical scrutiny. It is sold as an adhesive optical sensor placed over the temple of the head, that gives a measure of the blood flow of the brain. And a laughable gravity ageing hypothesis.
Blood flow to the brain is by the… pic.twitter.com/C5pfoWRTKT
— Dr Jason Philip. M.S., MCh (@Jasonphilip8) November 6, 2026
In a statement to Reuters, Temple said BrainFlow and Entropy were new metrics "with emerging science", and that more research would follow, adding that some metrics would eventually need regulatory ​approval.
India's health ministry did not respond ​to Reuters queries, and the ⁠government has so far not reacted to the public debate.
Scrutiny on wearables makers
The debate on Temple comes as wearable makers overseas also face questions on when a fitness feature becomes a medical one.
Read More: Your fitness tracker is 27% to 93% inaccurate: Stanford
Some Apple Watch ​features, such as hypertension notifications, have received US Food and Drug Administration clearance as software-based medical features. Last ​year, the US ⁠FDA warned Whoop, saying its wrist-worn fitness tracker's blood-pressure feature looked like a medical one — a view the company disputes.
Goyal is best known for co-founding Eternal, which houses India's biggest listed food-delivery company, Zomato and has a market value of about $35 billion. The 43-year-old stepped down as chief executive of Eternal ⁠this year ​to focus on Temple.
Temple, which has professors from the University of Ottawa and Harvard ​on its advisory board, raised $54 million in February at a valuation of about $190 million.
Goyal said Temple has received orders from more than 62 countries since November 1.
On its website, ​Temple says it is also working on detecting conditions including snoring and jaw clenching.

items.summary:
Karachi's water woes were set to deepen on November 13, with a scheduled power shutdown and subsequent maintenance at the Dhabeji pumping station expected to slash the city's daily water supply by around 130 million gallons, leaving residents across several neighbourhoods bracing for shortages.
According to a Water Corporation spokesperson, K-Electric announced a scheduled power suspension at the Dhabeji grid station from 10am to midnight on November 13 for its annual maintenance. The shutdown would render nine of the pumping station’s 21 pumps inoperative, reducing Karachi’s daily water supply from approximately 650 million gallons to 520 million gallons.
The disruption was likely to affect residents of Landhi, Korangi, Malir, Shah Faisal, Gulshan-e-Iqbal, Clifton, Saddar and Lyari, as well as parts of Jinnah, Chaneser, Nazimabad, Liaquatabad and North Karachi. Water supply to parts of Nazimabad and Gulberg Town would also be partially affected.

A 14-hour shutdown at Dhabeji Pumping Station on Nov 13, will result in an estimated 130 MGD shortfall in water supply.
During the period, KW&SC will supply around 520 MGD against the daily requirement of 650 MGD, as nine of the station’s 21 pumps remain non-operational.

The spokesperson said the Landhi and Sherpao hydrants would remain closed during the power shutdown.

The spokesperson said water distribution would be gradually restored once electricity supply resumed.

items.summary:

items.author: Garry Pierre-Pierre
items.content:
Last summer, as I drove along the backroads of Indiana, through the vast flatlands punctuated by cornfields, grain silos and the occasional farmhouse, I noticed something peculiar. The ubiquitous Trump flags and lawn signs were disappearing.
I had made this journey countless times during my years living in the Midwest. In previous summers, Trump signs were as much a part of the landscape as the corn itself. Some were enormous, mounted on barns or planted defiantly along highways. Others were modest declarations of allegiance on neatly manicured lawns.
But something had changed. The signs weren't simply fading. They were vanishing.
I wondered whether their disappearance signaled a political awakening, quiet disillusionment or merely exhaustion with the endless spectacle of Donald Trump. Perhaps people had simply grown tired of advertising their loyalties. I couldn't tell. But I suspected something was stirring beneath the surface.
On Tuesday, November 3 we got our first answer. I should have been ecstatic. Instead, I found myself somewhere between relief and suspicion.
Was this a repudiation of Trumpism, or had Americans simply grown weary of the carnival? Had they rejected the cruelty, the xenophobia, the casual contempt for democratic institutions? Or were they merely dissatisfied with the price of groceries, the economy and the chaos of a presidency that seems to manufacture a new crisis every morning?
The distinction matters enormously.
A war that never ended
On June 16, 2015, I remember how my jaw dropped as though I had been struck by a Mike Tyson left hook. Donald Trump, holding the hand of his wife, Melania, glided down the golden escalator at Trump Tower in Manhattan. It was a theatrical entrance befitting a reality television star. Then came the words that would change American politics.
“When Mexico sends its people, they're not sending their best,” he declared. “They're bringing drugs. They're bringing crime. They're rapists.”
I had witnessed plenty of ugliness in American politics, but this was different. Here was a man seeking the presidency casually dehumanizing millions of people. Surely, I thought, Americans would reject someone so crass, so cruel, so contemptuous of others. Surely his candidacy would backfire spectacularly.
A few months before the elections, speaking to university students in Karachi, Pakistan, I confidently predicted that Trump would lose. My reasoning wasn't based on polling. It was personal.
I had married into an Indiana family. I knew Republicans in the Midwest and South, decent, churchgoing people who worked hard, cared for their neighbors and believed in treating others with respect. My wife's relatives and friends were among them. I couldn't imagine them supporting someone whose behavior so thoroughly violated the values they professed.
But many did.
Trump lost the popular vote by nearly three million ballots but won the Electoral College. He transformed that narrow victory into a sweeping mandate, turning American politics upside down.
More troubling than his victory was what it revealed about the country I had embraced as my own.
Forty years earlier, as a sophomore at Florida A&M University, I was enjoying an afternoon with friends at a park near where the FAMU and Florida State campuses overlapped.
I’ve written before about how a white student near me waxed nostalgic about the Civil War. “The South should have won,” he said wistfully, as though mourning a missed opportunity rather than a moral catastrophe. “We beat you last time,” I shouted back, “and we'll do it again.”
But that exchange has stayed with me. What seemed like an isolated encounter with an unreconstructed Southerner was a glimpse into something deeper: a war that had never truly ended.
When Trump returned to the White House in 2025, I became convinced that America was entering the final battle of its unfinished Civil War. The guns fell silent in 1865, but the struggle over who belongs in this country, who holds power and whose humanity matters never truly ended.
This isn't simply a war between North and South, or even Republicans and Democrats. It is a struggle within white America itself. On one side are those willing to build a country where power is shared and history confronted. On the other are those clinging to a fantasy in which they remain the rightful heirs to the republic.
Trump didn't create this conflict. He exploited it brilliantly.
He recognized that economic insecurity and the fear of losing status could be transformed into a potent political weapon. Immigrants became invaders. Black Americans became undeserving beneficiaries of government largesse. LGBTQ people became threats to traditional values.
The message was unmistakable: America was being taken away from its rightful owners.
For generations, whiteness had functioned as an invisible currency, conferring advantages often taken for granted. As America grew more diverse, some interpreted equality as a loss of their own standing. Trump gave those fears a voice and built a political movement around them.
The mask comes off
There is something almost perversely useful about Trump's decade of political dominance.
He stripped away the politesse that had long concealed America's racial contradictions. His bigotry, contempt for democratic norms and willingness to demonize entire communities exposed wounds that many Americans preferred to believe had healed.
Remember the declarations of a post-racial America after Barack Obama's election? That comforting fiction didn't survive Trump.
But governing through grievance had consequences. Economic hardship persisted. Families struggled with housing, healthcare and the rising cost of living. Immigrants were vilified, yet the promised prosperity remained elusive.
Scapegoating could win elections. It couldn't pay the rent.
Then came November 3, 2026.
Voters delivered a stunning rebuke to Trump and the Republican Party, handing Democrats control of both chambers of Congress, flipping Senate seats in states Trump had carried and electing Democratic governors in traditionally Republican territory.
The magnitude of the victory was remarkable. But what struck me most was its geography.
This wasn't simply another Democratic triumph in familiar liberal strongholds. The repudiation extended into regions where Trumpism had once seemed invincible.
I thought about the people I knew in Indiana. I thought about the diminishing Trump signs I had noticed while traveling through the Midwest. And I wondered whether something fundamental was shifting beneath the surface.
For the first time in a decade, I began to believe that the final battle might be approaching a turning point.
Not because racism had disappeared, or because Americans had suddenly become immune to demagoguery. But because enough voters appeared unwilling to continue accepting cruelty and division as substitutes for competent government.
Perhaps people were finally recoiling from what they saw.
Winning isn't the same as governing
Across the world, from Brazil to Serbia, citizens are turning against political leaders with extraordinary intensity. Yet their anger conceals a troubling paradox: they are often united in what they reject but deeply divided over what should replace it.
Anger can remove a government. It cannot build a better one.
Democrats now face precisely that challenge.
Their victory is not necessarily an endorsement of a single ideology. Progressives, moderates, independents and disillusioned Republicans helped produce this outcome for different reasons.
Democrats would make a historic mistake if they interpreted the results as permission to return to business as usual. They must address the economic insecurity that made Trump's promises attractive, restore faith in public institutions and demonstrate that government can improve people's lives.
They must also pursue accountability. The corruption, abuses of power and cruelty inflicted on vulnerable communities cannot simply be swept aside in the name of national healing.
Reconciliation without accountability is an invitation to repeat the past.
Europe's choice
Europe should pay close attention to America's painful reckoning.
Across the continent, from France and Germany to Italy and the Netherlands, political movements are exploiting the same anxieties that fueled Trump's rise: fear of immigrants, nostalgia for an imagined past and the conviction that national identity belongs exclusively to those who can trace their ancestry back generations.
The language may differ, but the message is familiar. Someone is coming to take your country away. It is a seductive lie.
Nobody is replacing anybody. Generations come and go, as they always have. Nations are not museums preserving the identities of their founders in perpetuity. They are living societies, constantly reshaped by the people who inhabit them.
A Black boy born in Ghana who grows up in Rome can be every bit as Italian as someone whose ancestors have lived in Sicily for centuries. He may speak Italian with a Roman accent, cheer for the national football team and understand the country's customs as intimately as anyone else.
His skin color does not diminish his claim to belonging.
Acculturation is not instantaneous. It takes a generation, sometimes two, for newcomers and their descendants to weave themselves fully into the social fabric. The children of immigrants inhabit two worlds; their grandchildren often know only one.
The process can be uncomfortable, even contentious, but difference is not a threat to national identity. It is one of the ways national identity renews itself.
My advice to Europe is simple: don't follow America down the road of xenophobia and manufactured grievance. Follow instead the more difficult path we have struggled to forge through our contradictions, toward a multicultural democracy in which belonging is defined by shared citizenship rather than bloodlines.
America's journey has been rocky, often brutally so. But over time, what once seemed foreign becomes familiar, and what one generation resisted, the next embraces without a second thought.
The road doesn't smooth itself. It takes political courage, economic opportunity, strong institutions and a willingness to recognize one another as equals.
Europe can learn from our mistakes without repeating them.
Rebuilding the House
America is a house on fire, I wrote last year, its foundations weakened by slavery, exclusion and generations of unresolved injustice.
The midterms suggest that enough Americans may finally be reaching for the water.
As a Haitian immigrant, a Black boy with a French accent who later married a white woman from Indiana and raised biracial children, I have lived many of this country's contradictions.
Our family's very existence has sometimes challenged other people's assumptions about what America should look like.
I have never expected a perfect country. But I have always believed in the possibility of a better one.
America has spent generations learning, often painfully, that a nation cannot preserve its identity by excluding those who are helping to shape its future. We have not completed that journey, and perhaps we never will. But the road becomes less treacherous with every generation willing to travel it together.
We have shown what happens when fear becomes a political movement and grievance becomes a governing philosophy. The question is whether Europe will heed the warning—or wait until its own house is on fire.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan’s fixed broadband operators have failed to meet key quality-of-service benchmarks across several cities, with inadequate upload speeds, network latency, jitter, and packet loss emerging as major weaknesses, according to a Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) survey for the third quarter of 2026.
The survey, covering 12 broadband service providers in 15 cities between July 1 and September 30, found widespread shortcomings in service delivery, with Multinet Pakistan recording particularly poor performance in Rawalpindi, where it met only two out of eight prescribed quality indicators, translating into a compliance score of just 25 percent.
Cyber Internet Services also recorded weak results in Lahore, achieving a compliance score of 37.5 percent, while its Islamabad operations secured only 50 percent.
The PTA has asked operators to take corrective measures within specified timelines, including capacity enhancement, network optimisation, congestion management and improvements in routing and service quality. Follow-up testing will be conducted to verify compliance with the Fixed Broadband Quality of Service Regulations, 2022.
PTA Survey Finds Major Internet Quality Issues Across Pakistan
The survey assessed eight key performance indicators, including local and international network latency, jitter, packet loss, download and upload throughput, webpage loading time and voice quality.
Among the surveyed operators, Wide Band Communications in Peshawar was the only service provider to achieve full compliance, meeting all eight prescribed indicators. Multinet Pakistan in Rawalpindi recorded the lowest score, followed by Cyber Internet Services in Lahore.
Naya Tel in Multan, Connect Communications and PTCL in Karachi, SCO in Ghalapan and Gupis-Yasin, and Cyber Internet Services and Enigma Fiber in Abbottabad each achieved compliance scores of 87.5 percent.
The most significant concern identified by the regulator was upload throughput, with the survey reporting that most operators failed to meet the prescribed benchmarks.
Under PTA regulations, upload speeds must remain at least 25 percent of advertised package speeds for xDSL connections and above 50 percent for other technologies.
Download speeds are required to exceed 80 percent of advertised package speeds. However, Multinet, Cyber Internet, Connect Communications, Nexlinx Networks, PTCL, Naya Tel and Burak Tech were identified as falling short of the prescribed download-throughput requirements.
The regulator also identified elevated latency and jitter at several locations, potentially affecting real-time applications such as video conferencing and online gaming.
Multinet, NTC, Cyber Internet and PTCL recorded deficiencies in local network latency, while Multinet also failed the international terrestrial latency benchmark.
PTCL, NTC, Cyber Internet, Nexlinx and Multinet were identified for excessive jitter, which measures variations in network delay and can disrupt the smooth delivery of data packets.
See Also: PTA Survey Finds Broadband Quality Issues at Multiple ISPs in Pakistan
Packet loss was another area of concern. Cyber Internet, PTCL, Connect Communications, Naya Tel, Multinet and SCO recorded performance deficiencies against the prescribed threshold of a maximum one percent packet loss.
The survey also found that Cyber Internet and Nexlinx exceeded the four-second webpage loading benchmark in the locations examined.
Voice quality, measured through the Mean Opinion Score (MOS), was generally within regulatory limits, with PTCL in Peshawar recording a score of two against the required benchmark of above three. PTCL in Faisalabad also recorded a score of four, indicating compliance, according to the detailed results.
The PTA said its user-end surveys were conducted by its Enforcement Division in areas selected on the basis of high subscriber density to assess actual network performance and identify service delivery gaps.
The findings underline persistent quality challenges in Pakistan’s fixed broadband market despite the growing importance of reliable internet connectivity for businesses, households and digital services.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) has identified quality-of-service issues in fixed broadband networks operated by several internet service providers, with Pace Telecom failing prescribed network availability benchmarks and Falcon Broadband falling short of the jitter standard, according to the regulator’s third-quarter 2026 survey.
The survey, covering 23 unique operators across 21 major cities during July-September 2026, also found that bandwidth utilisation exceeded the prescribed threshold in some networks, potentially affecting internet speeds during peak traffic hours.
PTA Survey Finds Broadband Quality Issues at Multiple ISPs in Pakistan
According to the PTA’s Network-End Quality of Service (QoS) Survey, Pace Telecom and Broadcasting (Pvt) Ltd failed to meet the minimum requirements for both core and access network availability in Abbottabad. Its core network availability stood at 99.73 percent against the required 99.9 percent, while access network availability was recorded at 97.13 percent against the 99 percent benchmark.
The regulator also flagged Falcon Broadband in Vehari for failing to meet the prescribed jitter threshold of less than 15 milliseconds. Its jitter was recorded at 40.61 milliseconds, indicating potential disruptions in services requiring stable connections, including video conferencing and online gaming.
The findings highlight persistent quality challenges in parts of Pakistan’s fixed broadband infrastructure despite most surveyed operators meeting the regulator’s prescribed performance standards.
The PTA assessed operators against seven key performance indicators (KPIs), including bandwidth utilisation, core and access network availability, local and international latency, jitter and download and upload data throughput.
See Also: Pakistan’s Internet Speeds Increase 60% as 5G Users Reach 1.8 Million, Claims IT Minister
Under the regulatory framework, bandwidth utilisation must remain below 80 percent, core network availability above 99.9 percent and access network availability above 99 percent. The prescribed latency thresholds are below 40 milliseconds for local networks and below 110 milliseconds for the international terrestrial segment.
The report found that all surveyed operators complied with the prescribed local and international latency thresholds. Similarly, all operators met the minimum data throughput requirements of four megabits per second for downloads and two megabits per second for uploads.
However, the regulator noted that bandwidth utilisation exceeded the prescribed threshold in some broadband service providers’ networks, which could result in reduced internet speeds, particularly during peak traffic hours.
The operator-wise assessment showed that 16 of the 28 city-operator entries achieved full compliance across all seven KPIs, while the remaining entries recorded compliance scores of 85.71 percent or 57.14 percent.
Pace Telecom’s Abbottabad operation recorded the lowest compliance score of 57.14 percent, meeting only four of the seven assessed indicators. Its Swat operation, however, achieved 85.71 percent compliance.
See Also: PM Directs Task Force to Finalise Recommendations on Industrial Electricity Tariffs for Telecom Sector
Other operators with individual KPIs requiring improvement included Net-Cloud Telecom in Dadu, New Millennium Network in Haripur, TES Media and GH Wireless Internet Service in Islamabad, Gerry’s Information Technology in Karachi, Khyber Internet Services Provider in Mardan, Wateen WiMax in Quetta, Multinet Pakistan in Rawalpindi, D3 Advertising and Communications in Shaheed Benazirabad, Wavecomm in Usta Muhammad and Falcon Broadband in Vehari.
The survey was conducted by the PTA’s Enforcement Division through inspections at the network operation centres (NOCs) of broadband service providers. The assessment covered fixed broadband technologies, including DSL, copper and fibre-optic networks.
The regulator said the survey was intended to assess network reliability, service availability and compliance with the Fixed Broadband Quality of Service Regulations, 2022.
It concluded that non-compliant operators needed to undertake corrective measures, including capacity enhancement, improvements in network availability and jitter reduction, to ensure continued compliance with prescribed standards.

The federal government on Wednesday decreased the price of petrol by Rs3 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs7 per litre for November 12.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs335 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs364 per litre for Thursday.
The revision comes a day after the government slashed the price of petrol by Rs8 per litre and that of HSD by Rs7 per litre for November 11.
Read: Petrol drops by Rs8, diesel by Rs7 for Nov 11
On November 2, the government announced that oil refineries would bear a burden of Rs15 billion per month, which would allow petrol to be sold Rs15 cheaper than it was in the global market amid the US-Israeli war on Iran.
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.

items.title: Russia and Ukraine say some progress made at talks, US cites a lack of trust
items.summary:
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators reported some progress in two days of peace talks in Abu Dhabi that ​ended on Wednesday, but US mediators said there was a lack of trust between the warring sides and differences remained on issues including territory.
In their first peace talks ‌for nine months, Russia and Ukraine agreed to a major release of prisoners of war, but there was little else in the way of concrete announcements after the US-brokered meetings.
US envoy Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, said mediators were appealing to each side's interests to end Europe's biggest conflict since World War Two and that he was convinced they could find a pathway to peace.
Read: New round of US-brokered Russia-Ukraine peace talks starts in Abu Dhabi
Despite public optimism from Trump, there has been no sign of major compromises on the main ​issues after more than 4-1/2 years of war since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
With talks deadlocked on land - Ukrai
items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators reported some progress in two days of peace talks in Abu Dhabi that ​ended on Wednesday, but US mediators said there was a lack of trust between the warring sides and differences remained on issues including territory.
In their first peace talks ‌for nine months, Russia and Ukraine agreed to a major release of prisoners of war, but there was little else in the way of concrete announcements after the US-brokered meetings.
US envoy Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, said mediators were appealing to each side's interests to end Europe's biggest conflict since World War Two and that he was convinced they could find a pathway to peace.
Read: New round of US-brokered Russia-Ukraine peace talks starts in Abu Dhabi
Despite public optimism from Trump, there has been no sign of major compromises on the main ​issues after more than 4-1/2 years of war since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
With talks deadlocked on land - Ukraine has rejected Russian President Vladimir Putin's demands to surrender the whole of ​the eastern region of Donbas in return for peace - US mediators have tried to steer talks toward post-war security guarantees and reconstruction.
"The reality is there is ⁠no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this," Kushner said, adding that the talks in the capital of the United Arab Emirates had touched on ​territorial issues and that these would be the hardest to resolve.
"Some areas we see places where we can find compromises, other we need to have more discussions, but I think this was a very good ​step," he said.
Kushner said he and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff would travel to Moscow on Thursday for talks with Putin at which they would raise the question of broadening the talks to include European partners, who he said must be at the table.
He said security architecture in Europe could form the basis for an agreement, without providing details.
As the Trump administration has scaled back its direct support to Ukraine, Europe has become its leading provider of finance and military ​support.
After Thursday's meetings in Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff will fly for talks with Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy during a visit to Ireland.
Attacks continue
Each side said the other had launched attacks overnight, despite the peace talks ​being under way.
Russia struck six large electricity substations in central Ukraine, officials said, and an attack on a busy market in the Odesa region killed three people, the regional governor said. One person was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack ‌in Russia's Belgorod ⁠region, local authorities said.
Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said the talks had been tough, with Russia's delegation arriving with "strict directives", but they provided "good momentum" towards solving the end of the year. He gave no details.
Arakhamia said that future talks should be multilateral, not trilateral, and should include European officials. Although European officials and NATO representatives met US and Ukrainian envoys in Abu Dhabi, Russia's delegation declined to meet them.
Russia's chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, said understanding had been reached on some issues, but was cool on the prospects of European countries joining talks.
He told a press conference it was unclear what Moscow could discuss with ​the European Union because it had made no new ​proposals. Even so, Russian state news agency ⁠TASS cited the Kremlin as saying Putin was open to contacts with the EU.
There has been no sign publicly that Putin is willing to drop a demand that Ukraine surrender all the land in the Donbas region that it still holds before a peace deal can be struck.
Front line static
Russian forces control about ​a fifth of Ukraine, much of it captured before the 2022 invasion, and their progress on the battlefield has slowed this year.
With the front line largely ​static, Moscow has been pounding ⁠Ukrainian cities and energy sites, while Ukraine has stepped up attacks on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure.
Russian officials are increasingly calling for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before tackling the specifics of the war.
Before its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Russia demanded the withdrawal of NATO forces from countries that joined the alliance after 1997, which the alliance rejected.
Trump said last week the war was close to being ⁠settled in a "big ​beautiful agreement" that could include security guarantees for Europe. He has frequently predicted breakthroughs that have not materialised.
Trump has intensified ​pressure on Kyiv to reach a deal to end the war, or face "a very bad thing".
The new American peace drive has galvanized European officials into pushing for a place at the talks.
European officials say wider security talks should only come after a ceasefire, ​and Russia should not be allowed to influence Europe's security arrangements or rewarded for starting the war.

items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
Update | November 11, 17:18 IST
Months after Inc42 exclusively reported on Greenjoules’s fundraise, the cleantech startup announced the closure of its Series B round at ₹150 Cr ($16 Mn). The round was co-led by Amazon’s Smbhav Venture Fund and Climate Pledge Fund, with participation from Rainmatter and Singularity’s Strategic Autonomy Fund.
The startup said that the fresh funds will support its new plant at Pune’s Khed City with the capacity to produce 2 Lakh litres of biocrude a day from agricultural waste. The facility will be developed in phases from 2027, which is expected to be the largest of its kind in India.
Additionally, Greenjoules also secured a ₹100 Cr debt from Technology Development Board (TDB), under the Government of India’s Department of Science and Technology.
“Greenjoules was built without a map; every step forward meant first inventing the path. We took two things that looked irreconcilable — low-energy-density agricultural waste and specification-grade fuel — and spent more than six years proving they were one and the same. With the concept proven and partners such as TDB and our Series B investors behind us, we are ready to make a deep impact on the global energy market, and to carry that pioneering spirit into sustainable aviation fuel,green hydrogen and sustainable materials.” said Shweta Viraraghavan, cofounder and chief technology officer, Greenjoules.
Original | August 21, 18:58 IST
Pune-based green energy startup Greenjoules has raised about ₹62 Cr ($6.5 Mn) in what appears to be an ongoing Series B funding round.
While Amazon’s investment arm, Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings, is leading the funding round, Singularity AMC’s Singularity Strategic Autonomy Fund also participated in the round.
As per MCA filings accessed by Inc42, the startup’s board allotted 40,338 Series B1 compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) at ₹11,155.5 apiece for ₹45 Cr to Amazon.com NV Investment Holdings LLC.
Separately, it also allotted 15,238 Series B1 CCPS to a sum of about ₹17 Cr to Singularity Strategic Autonomy Fund.
Greenjoules declined to comment on Inc42’s queries regarding the total size of the round.
Founded in 2018 by S Viraraghavan, V Radhika, VS Shridhar and R Sethunath, Greenjoules converts farm residues into renewable fuels that can be used in existing diesel engines and industrial equipment, effectively substituting crude oil with agricultural waste.
The startup is developing green fuels that can cater to sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), green hydrogen and biomethane areas.
Prior to the ongoing round, the climatetech startup raised $4.5 Mn in a combination of equity and debt from Blue Ashva Capital in 2021, to set up commercial scale waste to energy plants and invest into new R&D initiatives.
The investor interest in the eight-year old startup aligns with India’s broader push to scale renewable fuel sources in a bid to attain the country’s net zero goals.
India aims to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by the year 2070. Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced this target during the COP26 climate summit in Glasgow, backed by a climate plan known as the “Panchamrita”.
The country’s long-term low-carbon development strategy rests on seven key transitions to low-carbon development pathways. These include low-carbon development of electricity systems, enhancing forest and vegetation cover consistent with socioeconomic, development of CO2 removal and related engineering solutions, among others.
Amid this push, India’s cleantech market is projected to become a $152.5 Bn market by 2030, creating a suitable market opportunity for new and emerging players as well as more established industrial players to leverage the opportunity.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Indonesia's Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has resigned, an aide said on Wednesday, a move that threatens ​to split a key political alliance and risks further political uncertainty in Southeast Asia's largest economy.
Gibran, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko ‌Widodo, has come under intense scrutiny from lawmakers following Constitutional Court and Supreme Court rulings last month that his education documents did not meet election requirements.
The aide, Budi Arie Setiadi, told Reuters that Gibran had tendered his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto earlier on Wednesday.
Indonesia's vice president resigns over high school certificate that was ruled invalid https://t.co/dxXfsuSTAa
— BBC News (World) (@BBCWorld) November 11, 2026
Separately, two sources at the parliamentary upper house, which will oversee the process of approving his resignation and selecting a replacement, said that ​he would submit his resignation letter to the upper house on Thursday morning.
Neither Gibran's office nor Prabowo's office immediately responded to a request for comment.
Late ​on Wednesday, Prabowo gave a long speech at a political party event. He did not mention Gibran's resignation.
The resignation comes amid growing ⁠signs of strain in the political alliance between Prabowo, a powerful former general, and Widodo, also known as Jokowi, a highly popular leader who twice defeated Prabowo for the ​presidency before giving him his support after facing term limits.
Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has reportedly resigned, with Projo Chairman Budi Arie Setiadi confirming the submission of his resignation letter to President Prabowo Subianto. The development comes amid growing political scrutiny over Gibran’s educational qualifications. pic.twitter.com/5M0gImaBPZ
— The Jakarta Globe (@thejakartaglobe) November 11, 2026
An open split could spark further instability for an administration hit by scandals over signature programmes, such as its free school ​meals policy, and doubts over its handling of the economy, political analysts say.
Investor sentiment has weakened towards Indonesia this year amid heightened scrutiny of the government's fiscal plans and its broader policy directions, as well as lingering downgrade risks for its stock market by global index provider MSCI.
Last week, Prabowo fired his chief of staff, widely seen as a Jokowi loyalist, after he was arrested ​on accusations of bugging the president, among other figures.
Read: Troops deployed in Indonesia as president sacks aide accused of wiretapping
Calls for impeachment
Gibran stated his intention to resign during a meeting with Prabowo on Tuesday.
The parliamentary upper house will have to convene ​a session to declare a vacancy following the submission of Gibran's resignation letter, while writing a letter to the president requesting that he submit two names for his replacement, said senior law ‌minister Yusril ⁠Ihza Mahendra.
After that, the upper house would hold an election within 60 days.
Earlier on Wednesday, some 120 Indonesian lawmakers from across the political spectrum submitted a petition demanding Gibran's impeachment, fuelling tensions around his political future.
Gibran "no longer meets the requirements as vice president as stipulated in Indonesia's constitution", said Mardani Ali Sera, one of the lawmakers who signed the petition.
Eligibility questions
Gibran faced complaints over whether his education credentials met legal requirements, and on Tuesday the Supreme Court said it was instructing the education ministry to withdraw Gibran's ​education equivalence certificate, which the court had ​annulled.
Gibran, who studied abroad, used the certificate ⁠to comply with education requirements and run in the 2024 election, which he won alongside Prabowo.
Indonesian election law requires vice-presidential candidates to have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education, but the court found that the certificate was issued based ​on evidence that did not actually prove Jokowi's eldest son had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a ​foreign diploma or certificate ⁠that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," the court said in the ruling.
The Supreme Court also took into account the Constitutional Court's ruling, which said Gibran's education documents did not meet election requirements.
Gibran's spot on the 2024 ticket was previously marred by ethics complaints after the Constitutional Court, headed at the time ⁠by his ​uncle, removed an age limit that would have prevented his candidacy.
Sana Jaffrey, a researcher at the Australian ​National University, said the crisis showed how the political fortunes of a small number of elites took precedence over the country’s need for effective and stable governance.
"Prolonged uncertainty at the highest levels of power will only ​deepen anxieties at home and abroad about where the country is headed," she said.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Recently listed furniture rental company Rentomojo reported a 62.6% year-on-year (YoY) decline in its profit after tax to ₹18.2 Cr in the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Q2 FY27) from ₹48.6 Cr in the year-ago quarter.
The decline was largely due to a deferred tax credit of ₹32.8 Cr recognised in the year-ago quarter, compared with a deferred tax expense of ₹6.2 Cr in Q2 FY27.
On a sequential basis, the company’s net consolidated profit zoomed 133% from ₹7.8 Cr in the previous quarter.
Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 52.8% YoY and 12% QoQ to ₹142.1 Cr in the quarter under review, driven by growth in customer orders, live subscribers and rental inventory. Including other income of ₹1.7 Cr, total income for the quarter stood at ₹143.8 Cr.
Total expenses increased 53.2% YoY to ₹119.8 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹78.2 Cr in the year-ago period. Employee benefit expenses rose 38.3% to ₹19.5 Cr, while finance costs increased 46.7% to ₹9 Cr.
The company said its normalised profit after tax, excluding exceptional items and deferred tax adjustments, increased 52.2% YoY to ₹24 Cr from ₹15.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. Normalised EBITDA also grew 52.7% to ₹58.8 Cr from ₹38.5 Cr a year earlier.
Subscriber Additions, Higher Utilisation Drive Growth
Rentomojo expanded its omnichannel network to 96 experience stores across 14 cities by the end of September, compared with 67 stores a year earlier.
Customers ordered 3.8 Lakh gross items during the quarter, up 45% higher than last year’s quarter. Besides, the company’s live subscriber base grew 42.5% to approximately 3.2 Lakh, while live item inventory increased 44% to 10.5 Lakh.
Average occupancy grew by 61 basis points to 85.9% while average revenue per item (ARPI) increased 4.6% YoY to ₹1,650.
The company also reported higher asset utilisation. Assets procured in the FY17 cycle generated cumulative revenue equivalent to 5.3X its original value, with around 54% of the cohort continuing to generate revenue. The FY18 cohort had generated 4.71X its original value, with 59.2% of its items still generating revenue.
For context, higher utilisation of its rental assets allows the company to generate repeat revenue from its asset base. Purchase displaced, which measures the estimated retail value of consumer purchases replaced by customers choosing to rent furniture, grew 61% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹446.9 Cr.
This was the company’s second quarterly results following its public market debut in September after it raised ₹1,255.6 Cr from an initial public offering.
The company said it had utilised ₹90 Cr, or 63.7%, of the ₹141.4 Cr net proceeds allocated to the IPO’s stated objectives as of September 30. This included the complete utilisation of ₹70 Cr earmarked for debt repayment, ₹8.1 Cr towards warehouse and experience store lease rentals, and ₹11.9 Cr for general corporate purposes.
Commenting on the performance, founder, chairperson, managing director and CEO Geetansh Bamania said the company would continue focusing on subscriber growth, better asset utilisation and technology while maintaining profitability, cash generation and returns on capital.
Shares of Rentomojo ended today’s trading session 3.30% higher at ₹610.9 apiece on the BSE.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan has recorded a 60 percent improvement in internet speeds over the past two and a half years, while the number of 5G subscribers has reached approximately 1.8 million, Federal Minister for Information Technology and Telecommunication Shaza Fatima Khawaja claimed during her address at the Margalla Dialogue.
Speaking about Pakistan’s digital transformation and the growing influence of artificial intelligence (AI), the minister highlighted improvements in the country’s telecom infrastructure, including expanded internet capacity, additional submarine cables, increased spectrum availability, and wider fiber-optic coverage.
According to Shaza Fatima, Pakistan’s internet data consumption has increased by approximately 2 terabits per second, while the country’s total live internet capacity currently stands at around 7 terabits per second.
She also revealed that two additional internet cables have been introduced to strengthen Pakistan’s international connectivity and support growing demand for digital services.
The minister highlighted the country’s recent 5G spectrum auction, describing it as the largest in Pakistan’s history.
During the auction, 480 MHz of spectrum was sold, increasing the total spectrum availability from approximately 274 MHz to more than 750 MHz, according to the minister.
The additional spectrum is expected to support the expansion of mobile broadband networks and improve connectivity as telecom operators continue deploying next-generation services.
Shaza Fatima also said that 5G services have been introduced in Pakistan, with approximately 1.8 million users already subscribing to the technology. Earlier reports have examined how far 5G coverage has expanded and whether consumers can access it.
Meanwhile, the government is accelerating the expansion of fiber-optic infrastructure to support faster and more reliable internet connectivity.
According to the minister, fiber-optic network reach has more than doubled, increasing from around 3 million to over 6 million during the period under discussion.
She maintained that Pakistan has made considerable progress in expanding its digital infrastructure over the past two years, with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif personally overseeing the Digital Nation Pakistan vision.
AI Could Become a $4.8 Trillion Global Economy by 2033
Apart from developments in Pakistan’s telecom sector, the IT minister also discussed the economic impact of artificial intelligence and the need for countries to prepare their workforces for technological change.
According to Shaza Fatima, the global AI economy could reach $4.8 trillion by 2033, while artificial intelligence is expected to affect approximately 40 percent of jobs worldwide.
However, she argued that AI would not necessarily eliminate employment opportunities. Instead, it would transform the nature of jobs and change the skills required in the workplace.
The minister emphasized that individuals who learn to use AI effectively could achieve significantly higher productivity than others with similar conventional skills.
She claimed that AI-assisted workers could potentially become up to 100 times more productive in certain circumstances, highlighting the importance of adopting emerging technologies.
Shaza Fatima stressed that acquiring new digital skills has become essential for future employment, particularly as AI continues to reshape industries and professional roles.
She also raised concerns about the concentration of influence over international AI governance.
According to the minister, most of the 118 countries she referenced are not part of major global AI governance initiatives, while decision-making remains heavily influenced by a small group of developed nations.
She claimed that seven advanced economies currently exercise considerable control over global AI policymaking, raising questions about the representation of developing countries in international technology governance.
Her remarks highlight two challenges facing Pakistan: expanding the digital infrastructure required to support modern technologies and ensuring that its workforce is equipped with the skills needed in an AI-driven economy.
While the reported improvements in internet speeds, spectrum availability, and fiber-optic coverage indicate progress, the next challenge will be translating these developments into more reliable connectivity, wider digital access and new economic opportunities for Pakistani consumers and businesses.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Operation Bluebird has launched a new website, Twitter.now, while its legal trademark battle with Elon Musk’s social media platform X over the former Twitter brand remains unresolved.
The launch follows Operation Bluebird’s efforts to claim trademark rights associated with the original Twitter identity. The organisation argues that X abandoned parts of the former Twitter branding after Musk renamed the platform in 2023.
Operation Bluebird Launches Twitter.now as Trademark Battle With Elon Musk’s X Continues
Operation Bluebird believes that the rebranding created an opportunity to reclaim the Twitter name and related trademarks. Its launch of Twitter.now marks a new development in that effort.
Legal Dispute Over Twitter Name and Branding
The trademark dispute centres on whether X still holds rights to the Twitter name, the term “tweet” and the platform’s well-known blue bird logo.
A federal judge has tentatively questioned X’s rights to some of these trademarks. However, the court has not issued a final ruling, and the case remains active in federal court.
Operation Bluebird argues that X abandoned parts of the original Twitter identity when it replaced the Twitter name and bird branding with X.
However, X disputes these claims and continues to contest the trademark challenge.
Twitter.now Launches as Case Remains Pending
With Twitter.now now launched, Operation Bluebird is moving forward while the trademark dispute continues.
The launch does not mean that Operation Bluebird has won the rights to the original Twitter trademarks. The court still needs to resolve the dispute, and no final decision has established who can legally use the contested branding.
The outcome could determine the future ownership and use of the Twitter name, the word “tweet” and the platform’s iconic bird logo.

items.title: JI to continue protests nationwide as it demands end to petroleum levy
items.summary:
Jamaat-e-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman said on Wednesday that the party would continue its nationwide protest campaign against the petroleum levy while holding talks with the government, as he announced a rally in Quetta on November 22 and a public gathering at Minar-e-Pakistan in Lahore on November 29.
Addressing a news conference at the party’s headquarters in Mansoora, Lahore, Rehman said JI had not withdrawn its demand for the complete abolition of the levy, stating that the party would continue its public campaign, with further rallies planned in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and Karachi.
He said the government had told JI that 15 million people were receiving relief, but argued that the support should cover more households and sectors, calling for extending the fuel relief scheme from vehicles with engines up to 800cc to those up to 1,300cc, saying middle-income and salaried families also used the latter.
