حافظ نعیم الرحمان امیر جماعت اسلامی پاکستان#لیوی_بھتہ_نامنظور #HafizNaeemUrRehman pic.twitter.com/hRCaPcJzvD
— Jamaat e Islami Pakistan (@JIPOfficial) November 11, 2026
Read: JI, govt agree on draft outlines for petroleum levy relief
The JI chief also pressed for tractors and public transport vehicles to be included, saying farmers and commuters needed relief from fuel costs.
Rehman stated that he also proposed raising import duties on vehicles with engine capacities above 1,800cc and shifting the petroleum levy towards owners of larger vehicles, adding that people who could afford such vehicles should bear more of the cost, rather than the public at large.
بڑی گاڑیوں کے لیے پیٹرول پر لیوی عائد کی جائے
ٹریکٹرز اور پبلک ٹرانسپورٹ کو ریلیف پیکج میں شامل کیا جائے
امیر جماعت اسلامی حافظ نعیم الرحمان #لیوی_بھتہ_نامنظور #HafizNaeemUrRehman pic.twitter.com/xvaex80FjP
— Jamaat e Islami Pakistan (@JIPOfficial) November 11, 2026
The JI chief added that he also called for restricting government officials’ use of vehicles above 1,300cc and reducing official privileges and spending to help fund relief.
He underlined that JI had presented proposals for ending the levy and had completed nine rounds of talks with the government, adding that the government had described the levy as an issue linked to the International Monetary Fund programme.
احتجاج سے دستبردار نہیں، ہمارا مطالبہ ہے لیوی ختم ہونی چاہئے، حافظ نعیم الرحمٰن
مزید پڑھیں:https://t.co/XtNCgTCiEt#HafizNaeemUrRehman #JamaatEIslami #PetroleumLevy #Latestnews #Expressnews pic.twitter.com/1Q7U4TPITH
— Express News (@ExpressNewsPK) November 11, 2026
Rehman said the government had previously indicated that petrol could reach Rs1,000 per litre, and credited JI’s campaign with helping bring prices down, stating that falling prices were not a reason for the party to stop its campaign.
اگر جماعت اسلامی کا دباؤ نہ ہوتا تو حکومت ریلیف نہ دیتی، ہم نے لیوی کے خاتمے کے لیے واضح تجاویز پیش کی ہیں
بڑی گاڑیوں کا امپورٹ ٹیکس بڑھائیں، لیوی ان پر عائد کریں اور ٹریکٹرز اور پبلک ٹرانسپورٹ کو ریلیف پیکیج میں لایا جائے
پاکستان میں آئل ریفائنریز، چینی، گیس، آٹا اور آئی پی… pic.twitter.com/9rSqtVTQ3O
— Jamaat e Islami Pakistan (@JIPOfficial) November 11, 2026
He noted that JI had also argued that the government’s relief offer was too limited compared with the scale of fuel costs, highlighting that the government collected around Rs150 billion a month through the petroleum levy but provided Rs26 billion to Rs30 billion in relief.
Read More: Govt, JI form committee to expand fuel relief scheme, phase out petroleum levy
Rehman also said that more than 25 million motorcycle users in Pakistan were not adequately covered in the relief offer.
The JI chief also criticised the Punjab government’s agriculture and education policies, stating that farmers in Punjab were not receiving the full price for wheat and alleging that the province’s agriculture had fallen behind.
پنجاب میں کسان کو گندم کا پورا معاوضہ نہیں ملتا
پنجاب کی زراعت پیچھے چلی گئی ہے
ملک میں غذائی تحفظ کا مسئلہ پیدا ہو گیا
حافظ نعیم الرحمان کی پنجاب حکومت کی زرعی و تعلیمی پالیسیوں پر کڑی تنقید#HafizNaeemUrRehman pic.twitter.com/VncclphrC5
— Jamaat e Islami Pakistan (@JIPOfficial) November 11, 2026
He further questioned the government over school examination results, asking why 52% of ninth-grade students had failed.
He also accused oil refineries, sugar, gas, flour and power producers of operating as a cartel that benefited at the public’s expense.
Background of JI protests
JI’s campaign against the petroleum levy intensified in August, when the party organised demonstrations and sit-ins across the country against rising fuel prices, inflation and what it described as an additional tax burden on consumers. On August 16, JI workers staged sit-ins outside governors’ houses in the provincial capitals, demanding the withdrawal of the levy and a reduction in petrol prices.
The party subsequently expanded its protests to other cities, including Karachi, where it established additional protest camps across Sindh. JI maintained that the government should abolish the levy rather than offer limited reductions in fuel prices.
On September 3, the government and JI agreed to establish technical committees to examine proposals for reducing the petroleum levy and fuel prices. During the first round of negotiations on September 7, the party submitted six proposals to the government, while insisting that its protests would continue until meaningful relief was provided.
However, the negotiations failed to resolve the dispute. On September 12, the JI chief announced a long march towards Islamabad for September 20, warning that the party would intensify its campaign if the government did not abolish the levy.
Also Read: JI launches third phase of protest campaign against petroleum levy
The march began on September 20, with participants travelling from Karachi by train. The caravan moved through Sukkur towards Multan, where Naeem addressed supporters. The march was subsequently suspended after PM Shehbaz telephoned the JI chief and requested that the party postpone its protest to allow further negotiations.
JI agreed to give the government an opportunity for talks but maintained that it had not abandoned its demand. The party’s position was that negotiations and protests could continue simultaneously, with any agreement required to address the complete abolition of the levy.
The JI chief then gave the government 10 days to abolish the petroleum levy and provide meaningful relief to the inflation-hit public, warning that his party would resume its long march towards Islamabad in mid-November if its demands were not met.

items.author: Guest Contributor
items.content:
The world cannot build prosperous economies, peaceful societies or resilient democracies while neglecting its people’s everyday justice needs.
Originally published on Global Voices
Image courtesy HiiL
This post by Jude Udo Ilo is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.
Imagine visiting a hospital with a serious illness, only to discover that every patient receives the same medication, regardless of their symptoms. We would rightly call this a failure of healthcare. Yet this is remarkably close to how justice is delivered in much of the world.
We have built justice systems around institutions rather than people, procedures rather than problems, and legal traditions rather than lived realities. We measure progress by the number of courts constructed, judges appointed and laws enacted, while paying insufficient attention to whether ordinary people can actually resolve the disputes disrupting their lives.
This institutional obsession reflects a deeper failure in how we understand development. Justice is not simply a legal service or a moral aspiration. It is essential for economic and social infrastructure. Our collective failure to treat it as such is undermining development, deepening inequality and threatening global stability. With the level of discontent across the world, distrust in institutions, poverty and inequality, and growing footprints of violent conflict, we need to refocus on what is necessary to heal our bleeding world.
The missing infrastructure of development
When governments and international financial institutions discuss infrastructure, the conversation invariably turns to roads, bridges, electricity and digital connectivity. These investments matter. But what happens when a highway project becomes trapped in unresolved land disputes; when a small business cannot recover payments from a supplier? When a woman cannot claim her inheritance, or communities cannot secure remedies for environmental destruction?
Physical infrastructure cannot deliver its promised benefits when the institutions and mechanisms for resolving grievances are inaccessible, ineffective or distrusted. Justice is the soft infrastructure that allows economies and societies to function.
For businesses, it provides the certainty necessary for investment, contract enforcement and growth. For individuals, it protects rights, livelihoods and opportunities. For communities, it creates peaceful pathways for addressing grievances before they escalate into confrontation.
Without functioning justice systems, economic development becomes fragile and social stability increasingly precarious. The World Justice Project estimates that the economic costs of legal problems, including lost income, health impacts and expenses of seeking resolution, average 1.7 percent of GDP across the countries studied.
The scale of the problem is staggering. The Justice for All report estimates that 5.2 billion people lack meaningful access to justice. HiiL's research demonstrates that everyday legal problems are widespread, while effective, satisfactory resolutions remain elusive. This is a crisis of development.
When injustice becomes insecurity
Across the world, unresolved grievances are quietly eroding the foundations of social cohesion.
In parts of Africa, disputes over land ownership, natural resources and community rights have contributed to recurring tensions. In fragile and conflict-affected societies, the absence of credible mechanisms for resolving grievances can deepen mistrust and reinforce cycles of violence.
But justice failures are hardly confined to developing countries. From housing disputes and discriminatory employment practices to unequal access to legal representation, even wealthy democracies struggle to ensure that justice works for everyone.
The consequences extend beyond those directly affected. When people repeatedly encounter institutions that cannot protect their rights or resolve their problems, confidence in public authority deteriorates. When people encounter injustice, they can easily become the enemy of the state. And where legitimate institutions fail, alternative systems of enforcement emerge. Sometimes these are constructive community mechanisms. At other times, they involve coercion, exploitation or violence. We cannot sustainably address insecurity while ignoring the injustices that help fuel it.
This should fundamentally change how governments approach peacebuilding and security. Military and policing investments may respond to immediate threats, but accessible justice can help address grievances before they become security crises.
Justice should therefore be understood as preventive infrastructure, not merely a mechanism for responding to wrongdoing after it occurs.
What the evidence tells us
Fortunately, evidence from across HiiL’s global operations demonstrates how people-centred approaches are transforming the design and delivery of justice services. Rather than relying solely on formal courtrooms or conventional approaches to conflict resolution, community-led initiatives and alternative justice pathways are meeting people where their disputes actually occur.
In Kenya, research informed the Judiciary’s Social Transformation through Access to Justice (STAJ) Blueprint. The Alternative Justice Systems (AJS) centres in Kenya are resolving family, land and other disputes locally, thereby preserving community cohesion. In Ethiopia, government-led community justice centers bridge formal laws and customary traditions to deliver rapid, reconciliation-focused resolution. In Nigeria, pilot community justice centers and domestic violence one-stop shops in Imo and Ogun States provide scalable, data-driven dispute resolution. In Tunisia, digital platforms co-developed for employment disputes directly connect workers, employers, and inspectors to resolve conflicts before they escalate.
Instead of assuming what institutions need, the question is: What justice problems do people actually experience, and what would help resolve them fairly?
Through Justice Needs and Satisfaction (JNS) surveys, we gather data on everyday legal experiences rather than institutional outputs. The data consistently reveal a significant disconnect between supply and demand. In Tunisia, we found that nearly one in three adults experiences a legal problem annually, yet only a fraction reach formal courts. Similarly, research in Nigeria highlights widespread justice needs alongside heavy reliance on community and informal mechanisms. These insights expose the core limitation of traditional justice reform: expanding court capacity alone cannot solve the problem. People facing family, land, employment, or commercial disputes rarely seek lengthy litigation. They need solutions that are fair, accessible, affordable, and timely.
Similar approaches are yielding results. In Bangladesh, a government-led initiative has strengthened village courts, enabling rural communities to resolve minor disputes locally, more quickly and affordably. These courts resolved over 82 percent of reported cases in an average of 25 days, at an average cost of just USD 2.70 to users. In Canada, the Indigenous Justice Program supports community-based initiatives that involve Indigenous communities in designing and delivering culturally appropriate justice services, reflecting their needs and traditions. In Colombia, Houses of Justice bring together formal and informal justice services, providing communities with access to legal information, mediation and dispute resolution through integrated service centres. These examples illustrate how justice services can be brought closer to people and organised around different pathways to better respond to their needs.
This does not make courts obsolete; rather, it underscores that formal courts are only one component of a healthy justice ecosystem. To truly serve society, functional justice infrastructure must integrate formal institutions with trusted community mechanisms, mediation, legal support, and innovative services.
From justice reform to justice investment
If justice is infrastructure, we must fundamentally rethink how we finance, govern and deliver it.
First, governments must stop treating justice as the Ministry of Justice's exclusive responsibility. Economic planners, finance ministries, development institutions, businesses and peacebuilding organisations all have a stake in effective dispute resolution.
Second, justice investments must be guided by evidence about people's needs and outcomes. HiiL's Delivering Justice, Rigorously framework emphasises data, evidence-based practices, scalable services, enabling environments, and accountability.
Third, we must move beyond endless small-scale pilots towards financing solutions that demonstrate results and can reach entire populations. The Justice Financing Framework developed under the Justice Action Coalition offers important proposals for making people-centred justice services financially sustainable.
Finally, justice must become integral to development financing. International financial institutions and development partners should recognize that investments in agriculture, infrastructure, entrepreneurship, gender equality and peacebuilding depend partly on people’s ability to resolve disputes fairly and the credibility of the entire justice system. This is not an argument for diverting resources from development priorities. It is an argument for making those investments more effective and sustainable.
The foundation we cannot afford to ignore
The world faces intersecting crises of inequality, economic uncertainty, democratic distrust and violent conflict. Governments are searching for ways to build more resilient societies, yet one of the most important foundations of resilience remains chronically neglected.
Justice cannot continue to be treated as an institutional afterthought.
A society is not resilient simply because it has strong borders, modern highways or growing financial markets. It is resilient when people trust that grievances can be addressed fairly, rights can be protected, and conflicts can be resolved without violence.
The question is no longer whether we can afford to invest in people-centred justice. It is whether we can afford the economic, social and political consequences of failing to do so. This spotlight provides the argument for the justice case, evidence of what is working and a roadmap of what we must do to make justice work for our societies.
Udo Jude Ilo is the CEO of the Hague Institute for Innovation of Law.
Written by Guest Contributor

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Axact and its founder, Shoaib Ahmed Shaikh, have been cleared of all fraud and fake degree allegations following a series of acquittals by Pakistani courts. The Supreme Court of Pakistan dismissed the State’s petitions against the acquittals on August 3, 2026, bringing an end to the legal proceedings that began in 2015.
The development follows 11 years of legal battles involving allegations that Axact operated a fake degree business. According to the company’s November 9 press release, the Sindh High Court, Islamabad High Court and a Special Court in Islamabad all acquitted Shaikh and other members of Axact’s management.
Axact Fake Degree Case Ends After 11 Years as Supreme Court Clears Founder
The Supreme Court dismissed the State’s petitions because they were filed beyond the prescribed time limit. It refused to accept the government’s request to condone the delay, making the earlier acquittals final.
Sindh High Court Finds No Evidence Against Axact
One of the major developments came on March 10, 2023, when the Sindh High Court acquitted Shaikh and other members of Axact’s management in the Karachi case.
The court observed that the State had failed to present evidence supporting the allegations. It also noted that investigators had not produced any victims, forged documents or other material proving that Axact sold fake degrees.
The State had initially listed 91 witnesses but later dropped 64 of them. According to the court’s findings, the prosecution failed to establish that anyone had been defrauded or that Axact had prepared forged educational documents.
The court also criticised the authorities for pursuing the case for eight years without gathering meaningful evidence. It described the proceedings as an ill-conceived action initiated by the State.
Islamabad High Court Overturns Earlier Conviction
The Islamabad case followed a separate legal path. A court initially acquitted Shaikh and other accused individuals on October 31, 2016. However, the State later challenged the acquittal over allegations that the judge had received a bribe.
A retrial in 2018 resulted in a conviction. However, the Islamabad High Court overturned that decision on November 22, 2023, and acquitted Shaikh and the other accused.
The High Court ruled that authorities could not prosecute someone twice on the same allegations after a court had acquitted or convicted them. It referred to the constitutional protection against double jeopardy under Article 13 of the Constitution of Pakistan.
Special Court Also Clears Shaikh in Bribery Case
A separate bribery case also ended in Shaikh’s favour.
On December 4, 2023, the Special Court (Central) in Islamabad acquitted him after the prosecutor and investigating officer informed the court that they had found no evidence against the accused.
The court concluded that the charges could not succeed without supporting evidence.
Supreme Court Dismisses State’s Petitions
The final development came on August 3, 2026, when the Supreme Court dismissed the State’s petitions challenging the Sindh High Court’s acquittal decisions.
The court ruled that the petitions were time-barred and that the government department had failed to provide sufficient grounds for the delay.
With the Supreme Court’s decision, the acquittals of Shaikh and Axact’s management attained finality.
Axact Case and Its Impact on Pakistan’s IT Industry
The allegations against Axact emerged in May 2015, just days before the planned launch of its media network, BOL.
Authorities closed Axact’s Islamabad offices within hours of the allegations and seized its Karachi offices as well. The legal action affected around 15,000 employees, according to Axact’s press release.
The company also highlighted the impact on Pakistan’s IT exports. It claimed that Axact generated $355 million out of Pakistan’s total IT exports of $432 million in 2014. Following the crackdown, national IT exports reportedly fell to $55.1 million.
The case also affected BOL’s planned launch and attracted extensive media attention across the country.
Axact Shifts Focus Towards Artificial Intelligence
Despite the legal challenges, Axact continued its business operations abroad and later moved its focus from traditional IT services towards artificial intelligence.
According to the company, it now develops AI-based software for businesses, including solutions for document management, customer service, sales, and customer support.
With the Supreme Court dismissing the State’s petitions, the company says all legal cases linked to the 2015 allegations have now concluded.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Update| Nov 11, 18:43 IST
Shares of Veefin ended today’s trading session 2% higher at ₹248.70 apiece on the BSE, while they closed 2.1% higher at ₹249 apiece on the NSE.
Original| Nov 11, 13:38 IST
BSE SME listed Veefin Solutions has migrated to the main board of the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and the BSE, more than three years after its SME IPO. Veefin’s shares opened for trade on the BSE mainboard at ₹249.75 (2.5% higher than previous close) and at ₹250.84 on the NSE.
Veefin’s market capitalisation as of 13:20 IST stood at ₹633.76 Cr ($67.61 Mn). Shares of Veefin were trading 1.2% higher at ₹249 apiece on the BSE and 1.2% higher at ₹246.65 apiece on the NSE around 13:30 IST.
Veefin listed on the BSE SME platform in July 2023 at ₹86.05, a near 5% premium from its IPO price. The company’s ₹46.73 Cr IPO comprised about 57 Lakh shares, with equal parts of fresh issue and offer for sale shares.
Its mainboard debut comes on the heels of the company solidifying its financial position over the recent quarter. Its operating revenue for the first half of the ongoing fiscal year (H1 FY27) doubled to ₹238.8 Cr while its consolidated net profit zoomed 127% YoY to ₹24.9 Cr.
Veefin reported a 127% year-on-year (YoY) increase in consolidated net profit to ₹24.9 Cr in H1 FY27 from ₹11 Cr in the corresponding period last year. Net profit was also up 9% from ₹22.8 Cr in H2 FY26.
In Q2 FY27, Veefin’s net profit rose 61% sequentially to ₹15.3 Cr from ₹9.5 Cr in the preceding quarter. Operating revenue increased 9% sequentially to ₹124.7 Cr from ₹114.2 Cr, while total income stood at ₹125.7 Cr.
The company also reported a deal pipeline of around ₹920 Cr alongside its half-year results. Around 84% of the pipeline comprises opportunities from banks and financial institutions outside India, with Southeast Asia emerging as a key market.
The mainboard listing is expected to widen access to Veefin’s shares among retail and institutional investors. Unlike the fixed trading lots on the SME platform, the main boards allow investors to buy and sell shares individually.
Veefin Bets On AI Employees
In a statement, the fintech SaaS company said that it will now look at expanding beyond fintech with an AI platform that enables businesses to deploy digital employees for defined roles. Alongside the listing, the company announced a rebranding from veefin.com to veefin.ai, reflecting the growing role of AI in its products and growth strategy.
Its next growth opportunity is through the Veefin AI Operating System (AIOS), a platform designed to help businesses create, deploy and supervise AI employees for defined roles.
Veefin has developed more than 1,000 reusable AI skills and has started deploying AIOS internally across three functions: customer implementation, customer support and software testing. The company is using these deployments to improve productivity and build experience before offering the platform to customers.
The company sees an opportunity to cross-sell the platform to its current customers and reach enterprises beyond the financial services sector.
“We listed on the SME platform three years ago as a supply chain finance technology company. We come to the main boards as a multi-product company whose revenue has more than doubled in the past year, and with many more investors able to take part in what we build next,” Gautam Udani, vice chairperson, cofounder and COO of Veefin Group, said.
Founded in 2020 by Udani and Raja Debnath, Mumbai-based Veefin develops lending, supply chain finance and transaction banking software for banks, NBFCs, fintech companies and enterprises.
The company began with supply chain finance and has since expanded into trade finance, cash and liquidity management, loan origination, loan management, collections, and corporate and retail digital banking. Its customers use its technology through complete applications, platforms or individual components integrated into their own systems.
Veefin has also expanded through acquisitions and strategic investments, including stakes in digital marketing firm White Rivers Media, generative AI startup Walnut AI and lending enablement platform EpikInDiFi.
The mainboard transition follows a similar move by E2E Networks, which made its BSE mainboard debut in June after being listed on the NSE since 2018. E2E took the direct listing route to list its shares on the BSE.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Nigerian fintech startup Rex Africa has launched what it says is the country’s first AI-native bank, built around an AI-powered financial agent that gives customers personalised guidance on saving, investing and borrowing.
Founded by Yinka Odeleye, Rex Africa has built its own banking infrastructure, RexCore, with AI integrated from the outset rather than added on later. At the heart of the offering is Rex Atlas, an agent that analyses users’ financial history and lets them interact with their bank conversationally, offering tailored recommendations on savings, investments, credit and risk management.
“We built Rex with AI at the heart of the banking experience, not as an additional feature,” said chief technology officer Opeyemi Emmanuel.
Alongside the agent, Rex offers a suite of products for individuals and businesses. Consumers can access flexible savings through RexSave, fixed-term savings via RexVault, credit through RexFlex, and payments with RexCard. For businesses, RexPOS enables payment acceptance, while RexCredit provides SME and corporate financing.
“Our founding conviction at Rex is that the next generation of banking will be defined by intelligence,” said Odeleye. “We believe banking should go beyond moving money to understanding customers and helping them manage, protect and grow their wealth.”
Rex is powered by Rex Microfinance Bank, which is licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), with eligible deposits insured by the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC).
Beyond its consumer app, the company’s ecosystem includes an established lending business and a live banking-as-a-service (BaaS) portal that supports customer accounts, collections and payouts.
Rex says it has already signed up thousands of individual users and hundreds of businesses since launching this month. Nigeria is the company’s immediate focus.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
The Enforcement Directorate (ED), Chennai, has provisionally attached movable and immovable assets worth approximately ₹14.2 Cr in connection with an alleged cryptocurrency investment fraud operated by Pan India Cryptocurrency, HashPe.
The attachment was made on October 30, 2026, under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002. The ED has also filed a prosecution complaint before the Special Court (PMLA), Puducherry.
According to the ED, Hashpay allegedly operated a fraudulent cryptocurrency-based ponzi investment scheme that lured investors with promises of daily returns of 1%, returns of up to 3X the invested amount, referral commissions and rewards such as luxury cars and foreign trips.
The agency said the attached assets include immovable properties in Tamil Nadu, Haryana and New Delhi, a BMW car and funds deposited in bank accounts.
The investigation was initiated based on an FIR registered by the Cyber Crime Police Station, Puducherry, under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, and the Information Technology Act, 2000.
How The Ponzi Scheme Worked
ED’s investigation found that HashPe operated through a website, hashpe.io, and a multi-level marketing network. Its promoters allegedly used cash payments, bank transfers and cryptocurrency transactions to mobilise investments from the public.
The scheme reportedly used USDT (Tether), a stablecoin, and Bitcoin to facilitate transactions. However, the agency found that the purported trading activities were not backed by actual cryptocurrency trading.
Instead, money collected from new investors was allegedly used to repay earlier investors and pay commissions to agents. Withdrawals were eventually stopped and the platform was frozen, leaving investors with financial losses.
The ED further found that the promoters allegedly created fictitious cryptocurrency tokens, including TCX and HashPe, at an almost zero acquisition cost and assigned artificial values to them. The platform displayed profits to investors despite the absence of genuine cryptocurrency trading activity to generate the promised returns.
To attract investors, the promoters used celebrity endorsements, promotional events featuring luxury cars and gold, and foreign cruises to build credibility. They also established a multi-level marketing network, with agents designated as ‘Leaders’ receiving commissions for bringing in new investors.
The ED said approximately ₹112.91 Cr was collected through the scheme, a portion of which was returned to investors. The remaining funds were transferred to bank accounts of ‘HIFY Circle’ and other related entities before being converted into cryptocurrency.
The proceeds were allegedly diverted towards personal expenses, loan repayments, hefty commissions and promotional activities, among other purposes.
The agency has identified approximately ₹49.54 Cr as proceeds of crime in the case.
The development comes after the ED conducted search operations at premises linked to HashPe, its promoters and associates on September 1.
Following the searches, four individuals namely Imran Basha, Hitesh Kumar, Syed Usman alias Babu, and Dharmendra were arrested under Section 19 of the PMLA, 2002. All four accused are currently in judicial custody while the investigation is ongoing.
The investigation revealed that Usman handled large cash investments and operated the HIFY Circle bank account, while Dhamodharan managed HashPe’s software, database and cryptocurrency operations, including its wallet functions.
Heightened Crypto Crackdowns
Branches of ED across the country have stepped up the heat on suspected illegal cryptocurrency activities in recent months. On November 7, the ED in Bengaluru conducted searches at premises linked to crypto exchanges CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India (DEI) over alleged unauthorised cross-border transactions involving crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks.
It had earlier conducted similar searches on October 29 at premises links to crypto platforms Mudrex and Saber.money, as well as decentralised finance (DeFi) protocol Instadapp and its associated platform Fluid, over alleged unauthorised cross-border fund transfers worth more than ₹4,940 Cr.
Prior to this in June this year, the ED had also searched six premises linked to five platforms, namely Transak, Carret, Xpat, Onramp.money and Onmeta, over alleged unauthorised cross-border crypto transfers.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Under its new global head Kunal Shah, WhatsApp is looking to expand beyond messaging. In a social media post, Shah said that the Meta-owned platform would focus on making services such as bill payments, financial transactions and international connectivity as seamless as sending a message.
Shah, who took charge of WhatsApp earlier this year, said the messaging platform would focus on three broad areas — making communication more expressive, simplifying everyday tasks and using AI to improve user experiences.
WhatsApp users could potentially complete tasks such as paying bills, borrowing money and staying connected while travelling without having to navigate multiple platforms or services.
“We’re working with financial services and telecom partners so that finishing something feels as easy as starting it,” he said.
Shah’s statement signals WhatsApp’s intent to deepen its push into financial services and commerce, building on its existing payments and business offerings.
In India, the platform has been expanding its payments capabilities through WhatsApp Pay, although its adoption has remained limited compared with established UPI players.
It also outlined plans to integrate AI more deeply into the messaging experience, with the technology expected to help users find relevant information, complete tasks and keep track of bookings and appointments.
“The best technology saves you time, so you can get back to the connections that matter,” he said.
However, Shah did not specify which AI capabilities the company plans to introduce or whether these would involve more advanced agentic features. It currently offers AI-powered features through Meta AI, including assistance with queries and content generation.
WhatsApp’s Three Priorities
On the communication front, WhatsApp wants to make features such as voice notes, groups, stickers and video simpler and more expressive. Shah said users send more than 10 Bn voice messages and 4 Bn stickers on the platform every day, highlighting how communication habits continue to evolve.
It also wants to reduce the number of steps involved in completing everyday activities that originate in conversations. This could involve deeper integrations with financial services and telecom partners, although Shah did not disclose specific partnerships or timelines.
The third priority is the use of AI to make the platform more efficient by helping users retrieve information and manage everyday tasks.
However, Shah emphasised that these changes would not come at the cost of user privacy. He reiterated that personal messages and calls on WhatsApp would remain end-to-end encrypted.
“Whatever we build, WhatsApp must remain simple, reliable and private. These principles we’ve had for years aren’t changing,” he said.
Shah’s remarks come nearly five months after he moved from CRED to Meta to take over as the global head of WhatsApp.
In June 2026, Shah announced that he would step down from day-to-day operations at CRED to join Meta. CRED cofounder Miten Sampat took over as interim CEO, while Shah retained his personal shareholding in the fintech startup.
His appointment also marked a leadership transition at WhatsApp, with former head Will Cathcart moving to a new role within Meta.
Shah’s move came alongside Meta’s investment in CRED as part of the fintech startup’s ₹8,550 Cr Series H funding round, which valued the company at ₹43,239 Cr post-money.
At WhatsApp, Shah now faces the challenge of expanding the platform’s utility beyond communication while maintaining its simplicity and privacy standards.
India, WhatsApp’s largest market globally, has an estimated 535 Mn to 550 Mn monthly active users, with some industry databases putting the figure as high as 853.8 Mn.
Globally, the platform has more than 3 Bn users. However, driving adoption of its payments, financial services and other offerings will remain a key challenge.

items.content:
Nigerian agri-tech startup Bridge Merchant is combining a network of rural agents, storage infrastructure and its own technology platform to link smallholder farmers more efficiently with processors, manufacturers and other institutional buyers.
Founded in 2020 by CEO Chinwendu Nweke, Bridge Merchant began as an agricultural trading and aggregation business before evolving into a tech-enabled supply chain company. It is now led by a four-person founding team, with six core employees and a network of more than 1,300 rural agents, around 65 per cent of whom are women.
“Bridge Merchant was established after I saw first-hand how much value farmers were losing, not necessarily because they could not produce, but because the infrastructure between production and the market was fragmented,” Nweke told Disrupt Africa.
The startup’s platform, Aladinn Agro, is used alongside its field network to onboard and verify farmers, map farms, aggregate produce, manage quality and traceability, and coordinate logistics. Bridge Merchant works mainly with staple commodities such as maize, soybeans, paddy rice, sorghum, millet and beans, as well as selected export and agricultural by-product value chains.
“We realised that Nigeria does not necessarily have a production problem alone; it also has a significant market-access and agricultural infrastructure problem,” said Nweke. “A farmer can produce successfully and still lose income because there is inadequate storage, fragmented demand, poor logistics, quality inconsistencies or no reliable buyer available at the right time.”
At the other end of the chain, processors and large buyers struggle to source consistent volumes of traceable, quality-controlled commodities from thousands of fragmented smallholders. Bridge Merchant aims to solve both problems at once.
Nweke said the startup faces competition from other agricultural marketplaces, aggregators, commodity traders and supply chain technology companies. It differentiates itself by integrating the digital and physical layers of the supply chain rather than solving only one part of the problem.
“The real challenge is building a system that works reliably in rural communities where connectivity, storage, logistics and trust remain major constraints,” Nweke said.
Bridge Merchant has engaged more than 10,000 farmers and aggregated more than 20,000 tonnes of agricultural commodities to date. It has access to around 3,000 tonnes of partner warehousing capacity and has deployed three solar-powered storage units in northern Nigeria.
“The strongest indication of uptake for us is repeat demand. Farmers and agents continue to work with us because we provide access to structured markets, while institutional buyers return because they need reliable aggregation, quality control and fulfilment at scale,” said Nweke.
The startup makes most of its money from commodity aggregation and trade, earning a margin between procurement and final sale on transactions where it acts as principal. On larger transactions it facilitates without taking ownership of the commodity, it earns commissions of between two and five per cent.
The startup has grown mainly through operating revenue, founder capital, grants and non-dilutive funding, and has received support from organisations including Acumen, Heifer International, Standard Chartered Foundation, Access Bank and Sahara Group Foundation. It is now progressing towards institutional debt financing to boost its working capital for commodity aggregation.
“Agricultural commodity transactions are capital intensive. A business can have farmers ready to supply and buyers ready to purchase but still be unable to execute the transaction because it does not have enough capital to bridge procurement and buyer payment,” Nweke said.
Bridge Merchant has built a presence across 16 Nigerian states over time, and is currently focusing its expansion on major production corridors in Kaduna, Niger, Benue and Nasarawa states. Nweke said the immediate priority is to deepen operations in Nigeria, but the model could eventually extend to other West African markets facing similar challenges.
“Our ambition is to build agricultural supply-chain infrastructure that can work across borders while remaining deeply connected to local farming communities,” Nweke said.

items.content:
Inside ShareChat’s Mixed FY26
ShareChat parent Mohalla Tech delivered some hits and some misses in FY26. While the homegrown social media giant crossed the ₹1,000 Cr revenue mark and found a new growth engine in microdramas, what played the spoilsport were losses and surging expenses.
Here is a quick look at Mohalla Tech’s FY26 numbers:
Operating revenue zoomed 40.4% YoY to ₹1,016.3 Cr
Net loss widened 78.5% YoY to ₹1,978.4 Cr
Total expenses surged 65.6% YoY to ₹3,083 Cr
Loss Widens: Mohalla Tech’s FY26 losses were largely driven by rising expenses. Employee benefit costs more than doubled YoY in the fiscal under review, while forex losses also surged following Rupee’s depreciation. Meanwhile, marketing and user acquisition spending also jumped nearly 8X YoY as Mohalla Tech invested aggressively in growth.
The Microdrama Pivot: The launch of QuickTV opened a crucial new revenue stream and generated nearly a third of Mohalla Tech’s total income in FY26. This pivot helped buffer against advertising headwinds in the aftermath of the ban on real-money gaming last year. But the unit economics of microdramas remained challenging, forcing the platform to rely heavily on ad-supported models to mint revenues.
The EBITDA Turnaround: Despite the widening losses, Mohalla Tech’s operating performance showed improvement. The startup halved its FY26 EBITDA loss YoY to ₹91 Cr, suggesting that its core business is inching closer to profitability. The management also claimed that the startup posted its first EBITDA-positive quarter in Q1 FY27 due to better monetisation across subscriptions, livestreaming and advertising.
The FY27 Test: Mohalla Tech is now targeting an EBITDA profit of ₹25 Cr in FY27, and claims to have already reported around ₹740 Cr in revenue in H1 FY27. The management now expects advertising to rebound strongly, with AVOD top line projected to cross ₹350 Cr in the ongoing fiscal. The startup remains little optimistic about subscriptions, believing most Indian users will not pay for microdramas and that paying users will remain below 100 Mn even as the market matures.
As ShareChat taps into microdramas to finally build a durable business, here is all about how parent Mohalla Tech fared on the financial front in FY26…
From The Editor’s Desk
MakeMyTrip All Set For IPO
The Nasdaq-listed online travel aggregator’s India arm has received SEBI’s approval to launch its IPO in the country. This comes four months after MMT filed its draft IPO papers with SEBI in July this year.
The issue is expected to consist entirely of an offer for sale component worth $1 Bn, with no fresh issue of shares. MMT India will continue to remain a subsidiary of the US-listed entity following the IPO.
MakeMyTrip listed on the Nasdaq in 2010 due to the maturity of the US tech ecosystem. However, since then, the Indian new-age tech landscape has grown to house over 70 listed startups, which have raised billions of dollars from their respective IPOs.
Casualties At Tata’s iPhone Factory
Three workers died of asphyxiation during maintenance work at Tata’s iPhone component manufacturing unit in Tamil Nadu’s Hosur. The incident took place inside a nano-filtration feed tank, operated by US-based Ecolab’s subsidiary Nalco Water.
While the preliminary probe suggests toxic smoke inhalation, sources added that there were no proper safety measures in place.
Tata Electronics is now expected to face an investigation by a joint team of officials from the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board and the state’s Directorate of Industrial Safety and Health.
InMobi’s New Marketing Move
The IPO-bound adtech unicorn has paid ₹65 Cr (excluding GST) to secure the naming rights for Bengaluru’s Ibbaluru metro station for a period of 30 years. With this, the station will now be called InMobi Ibbaluru Metro Station.
The sum will go towards Bengaluru Metro Rail Corporation Ltd’s non-fare revenue. The BMRCL also expects the partnership to encourage higher corporate participation in the city’s public transport ecosystem.
The deal comes as InMobi’s IPO continues to be in limbo. Last heard, the startup was eyeing a 2025 IPO at a valuation of around $10 Bn. While the unicorn has roped in four bankers to helm its public issue, InMobi is yet to file its DRHP.
Sarvam Ropes In Ex-Google Exec
The AI unicorn Sarvam has appointed former Google Cloud India MD Sashikumar Sreedharan as its new president and chief business officer. He will also join the startup’s board of directors.
With more than 35 years of experience under his belt, Sreedharan has previously worked at big tech giants like Google India, Microsoft India and IBM. He previously also served at Wipro, Happiest Mind Technologies, among others.
His appointment comes as Sarvam looks to build a larger enterprise AI business and strengthen its client roster. Founded in 2023, Sarvam develops foundational AI models, compute infrastructure and enterprise AI tools. It has raised $380 Mn to date.
Google Backs Froncort.AI
The healthtech startup has raised $2.3 Mn from the big tech giant’s philanthropic arm, Google.org, to scale its AI-powered disease surveillance and detection platform. The support also includes $200K in Google Cloud credits and technical expertise.
Founded in 2024, Froncort leverages AI, satellite imagery and health data to identify areas with higher prevalence of infectious diseases like tuberculosis. It also guides health workers with dedicated routes to enable targeted screenings.
The funding comes as the AI sector is attracting a growing share of investor capital, driven by novel solutions, enterprise AI use cases and a thriving local talent base. As per Inc42 data, AI funding in India grew 265% YoY to $438 Mn in Q3 2026.
Matrimony’s Q2 Show
The listed matchmaking platform’s consolidated net profit skyrocketed 165.4% YoY to ₹20.7 Cr in Q2 FY27. This came on the back of expanding margins, a tighter leash on expenses and operating revenue rising 17.6% YoY to ₹134.8 Cr.
On the operational front, Matrimony added 3.02 Lakh paid subscribers to its kitty in Q2 FY27, up 27% YoY. The matchmaking vertical also saw its reported billings jump nearly 11% YoY to ₹130 Cr in the quarter under review.
The listed company also said that its board approved the acquisition of an additional 50% stake in astrology-based matchmaking platform, Astro-Vision, for ₹8 Cr. Post the deal, Matrimony’s stake in the startup will rise to 76.9%.
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
Legacy Equipment Enters The Unmanned Era
Automation often means buying expensive new robots and redesigning operations around them. Hyderabad-based TensrAI is trying to flip this model by retrofitting existing industrial equipment with autonomous capabilities.
Built For Automation: Founded in 2022, TensrAI is building a unified autonomy platform for industrial and commercial robots, vehicles and machines. Its stack combines camera-first navigation, AI-based localisation, vision-language-model reasoning and autonomous mobility. It is also developing a mobile manipulator for handling materials and performing other tasks.
A Retrofit-First Stack: The startup’s AI stack is designed to help equipment perceive surroundings, interpret instructions, navigate changing spaces and perform work with limited human intervention. TensrAI initially plans to target factories, warehouses, airports, hospitals, malls and commercial campuses.
The Road Ahead: TensrAI’s retrofit approach is intended to reduce the cost and complexity of adopting robotics. But the startup will have to prove that its autonomy stack can work reliably across machines, environments and real-world tasks. With India’s robotics market projected to become a $4.6 Bn opportunity by 2030, can TensrAI make retrofitting autonomy easy for Indian factories?

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
…Good-spirited man begins rebuilding the house
By Chinedu Adonu
ENUGU – For 74-year-old Mr. Stephen Ogbo, the rainstorm that ripped through his residence at Ugbo Ezeji, D-Line, Abakpa Nike, Enugu metropolis, was a terrifying, unforgettable experience. The ugly incident left him soaked in water for hours, trapped in a shattered building and unable to find his way to safety because of his blindness.
As the storm raged, Ogbo could neither see the destruction around him nor find his way out. He remained helpless until an unidentified female tenant eventually came to his rescue.
Recounting his ordeal, Ogbo said the woman approached him after he had spent several hours soaked in water, unable to escape from the disaster.
“The female tenant came to me after several hours but couldn’t find any way to escape as a blind man. She said: “Daddy, we have been trapped by the windstorm,” he recalled.
According to him, the woman held him, led him out of the destroyed building, and searched for shelter where he could find safety. Although he could not identify his rescuer, he remembered that the voice belonged to a woman.
“I do not know the name of the woman who came to my rescue, but the voice was a woman’s voice,” he said.
A native of Nomeh Unateze in Nkanu East Local Government Area of Enugu State, Ogbo said he had lived in the compound for about eight years before the incident.
The rainstorm damaged the residential building housing 23 families, ripping off its roof and destroying property belonging to tenants. The incident left the occupants struggling to find shelter and salvage their belongings.
For the affected families, what began as an ordinary evening quickly turned into a nightmare, with the destruction leaving them with the difficult task of restoring their homes and livelihoods.
A cry for help
However, days after the incident, help has begun to come following an appeal by the victims for help.
Chief Kingsley Chizoba Nweke, the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) senatorial candidate for Enugu East Senatorial District, where the blind man hails from, has commenced the reconstruction of the damaged home after watching a video in which the victims appealed for assistance.
Nweke visited the affected residents at Ugbo Ezeji and said their plight moved him to intervene, and announced that building materials had been purchased and contractors mobilised to commence the reconstruction.
“It’s a pity, actually. If you look at the roof, it is damaged, and the place is messed up. I saw them interviewed two days ago and they cried out that they needed help.
“That touched me so much, so I said it was important that I come to their rescue. We have bought the materials, mobilized the contractors, and the work has already commenced,” he said.
He explained that the exercise would involve reinforcing the affected structures and replacing damaged roofs to enable the residents to return to their homes.
“My priority is to make sure they get back to their houses and keep living again,” he said.
Nweke said the intervention was humanitarian and not politically motivated, insisting that he would have assisted the victims irrespective of their political affiliations.
“This is not politically motivated. If they were wearing the caps of a different party and they said they needed help, I would still come. They just need help, not because of party,” he said.
He described the intervention as part of his broader humanitarian activities, which he said included supporting people who had lost their jobs and means of livelihood.
“I will do more than this. We have been doing more than this already. This is just a minor thing from what we have been doing,” he said.
He answered my cry.
Another resident and woman leader in the area, Mrs. Promise Ugochukwu, described the incident as devastating. She said the storm occurred between 9pm and 10pm, when strong winds ripped off the roof, and rainwater damaged household belongings.
Ugochukwu thanked Nweke for responding to the residents’ appeal, describing his intervention as an answer to their call for help.
“When I cried out to my father, Odaa Opuo (Nweke), the man whom I trusted, he answered me,” she said.
Ogbo also expressed gratitude to Nweke for the intervention and prayed for God’s guidance in his political career.
For the 23 families affected by the disaster, the immediate challenge is to restore their homes, replace damaged belongings, and regain the sense of security they lost when the storm struck.
But for Ogbo, the memory of that night will remain tied to the kindness of a woman whose name he may not know, but whose helping hands guided him out of danger.
In the aftermath of the destruction, her intervention stands as a reminder that even in moments of helplessness, an unexpected act of kindness can make the difference between despair and hope.

items.author: Debarghya Sil
items.content:
Employee stock options (ESOPs) have become a major talking point in India’s startup ecosystem this year, with questions around liquidity, employee wealth creation and the ability to monetise years of accumulated stock options taking centre stage. While Flipkart’s ESOP-related employee woes have been in the news all through this summer, digital commerce startup GoKwik has brought another dimension to the ESOP debate.
GoKwik, which is backed by the likes of Z47 Partners, Peak XV Partners, RTP Global and Think Investments, has amended its existing ESOP Plan 2021, through the insertion of a new non-compete clause, naming nine companies that employees are barred from joining or associating with, if they want to retain their ESOP rights.
The provision gives the startup the authority to revoke unvested and vested-but-unexercised employee stock options if employees (even those who have quit GoKwik) are found to have breached the restriction.
Inc42 has seen a copy of the internal document in question which has caused consternation among current and former employees. The mail was also sent to former GoKwik employees who continue to hold options.
The insertion of the clause has raised questions around employee mobility and the rights of existing ESOP holders, particularly as the new provision applies to options granted in the past as well as future stock options.
The clause was communicated to employees in the month of August, amid a spate of senior-level exits. The exits include vice president Sneha Rao, Sharad Gupta, the senior director of product management for the Checkout business, and Siddhartha Bahl, head of product, among others.
The policy lists Razorpay, Shiprocket, CRED, Cashfree Payments, BiteSpeed, Snapmint, WebEngage, Shopflo (acquired by Pine Labs), and Pine Labs as competing businesses.
Under the provision, employees cannot accept employment with, render services to, advise, invest in or otherwise associate with these companies. If the company determines that an employee has breached the restriction, it can forfeit their unvested options as well as vested options that have not yet been exercised.
The GoKwik ESOP Plan 2021 (“Plan”) allows GoKwik to cancel or forfeit both unvested and vested-but-unexercised options if the Board or Nomination and Remuneration Committee determines that an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach”.
While unvested options are stock options that employees are not yet entitled to exercise, vested-but-unexercised options are those that employees are entitled to exercise but have not yet converted into shares. The provision does not affect ESOPs that have already been exercised.
In effect, an employee joining a competing business could lose options that are yet to vest, as well as those that have already vested by have not been exercised. This means that even employees who completed the vesting period and earned the right to buy shares coils lose those options if the company determines that they have breached the competition restriction. However, options already exercised and converted into shares are not covered by this forfeiture provision.
Importantly, the restriction applies to all grants, whether issued before or after its effective date, and continues to bind former employees holding vested options even after their employment ends.
The restriction, however, is not indefinite. A special resolution passed by GoKwik shareholders at the company’s September, 2025 AGM provides that the competition related restriction will remain in force from the grant date until two years after an employee;s last date of employment or engagement with the company or its affiliates. In other words, the restriction applies throughout an employee’s tenure at GoKwik and continues for two years after their departure. During this period, joining or associating with a competing business could put their outstanding ESOPs at risk.
The policy appears to carve out passive investments in publicly traded securities. It also allows the GoKwik Board to approve exceptions in writing, with employees required to write to the company for such deviations.
The inclusion is significant because it directly links an employee’s association with named competitors to the potential loss of their stock options, including options that have already vested but remain unexercised.
Questions sent to GoKwik didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story even after Inc42 extended the deadline for responses upon the company’s request.
Instead, GoKwik issued a press release claiming former employees might get 9X average returns on their ESOPs and the startup has turned EBITDA positive in October 2026. But this press release does not mention any of the concerns that employees have brought up.
Employees In Limbo
“The sudden change in the ESOP policy was a shock. People who have quite a significant ESOP holding are all of a sudden in fear that they will lose it if they leave the company and try to join a better company. Now the names that they have mentioned are much superior companies that they would want to join as part of having a better career trajectory,” a former GoKwik employee told Inc42.
Employees with significant ESOP holdings, particularly those who may consider moving to other companies in the same sector, are stuck in limbo.
Sources in the company say they are weighing potential job opportunities against the potential loss from forfeiting their outstanding stock options. This is especially relevant for employees whose options have vested but have not been exercised, since the new clause explicitly includes vested-but-unexercised options within the scope of potential forfeiture.
The forfeiture, however, is not automatic. The Board or the Nomination and Remuneration Committee has the discretion to determine whether an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach” and decide whether to cancel or forfeit their unvested and/or vested-but-unexercised options.
Worryingly for employees, the provision is ambiguous about what kind of relationships are covered. For instance, it says that ESOPs may be revoked for employees who may “otherwise associate” with a competing business. This could cover relationships beyond direct employment, and the policy does not make the scope of this phrase immediately clear.
The timing of the amendment is also notable against the backdrop of GoKwik’s growth ambitions and recent senior-level departures as well as layoffs.
Founded in 2020 by Chirag Taneja, Vivek Bajpai, and Ankush Talwar, GoKwik is an ecommerce enablement startup that offers software tools to help online brands improve checkout, reduce order returns, automate customer engagement and increase sales. Earlier this year, Inc42 exclusively reported that GoKwik had laid off around 120 employees.
The startup has to date raised $68 Mn in funding and counts investors including Peak XV Partners, Z47 Partners, RTP Global, and Think Investments, among others.
In an interview with BW Disrupt, published in July 2025, cofounder and CEO Taneja said the company generated around ₹250 Cr in revenue in FY25. However, GoKwik Commerce Solutions Pvt Ltd’s financial disclosures show consolidated operating revenue of ₹146.2 Cr for FY25, and total consolidated revenue of approximately ₹163 Cr. GoKwik did not respond to questions about this discrepancy.
Among the nine companies named in the policy, GoKwik directly competes with the likes of Shiprocket’s Fastrr, Razorpay’s Magic Checkout, Shopflo, and Cashfree’s One Click Checkout, while the remaining companies operate in adjacent or overlapping segments of ecommerce enablement, fintech, and merchant services ecosystem.
Making Sense Of Non-Compete For ESOPs
Non-compete restrictions are commonly included in employment agreements in India, although their enforceability is difficult to establish.
However, explicitly naming competitors in an ESOP policy and linking an employee’s association with them to the cancellation of vested-but-unexercised options is unusual, according to Siddharth Manchanda, Partner at JSA Advocates & Solicitors. Manchanda further clarified that his comments reflected a general understanding of the law and should not be construed as an opinion on GoKwik.
He also said that a restriction on an ESOP policy is unusual but its substance is not entirely new. Most ESOP policies, in his view, contain provisions that allow options to lapse if an employee breaches their employment agreement.
Since employment agreements commonly include non-compete restrictions, companies may already have an indirect route to link an employee joining a competitor with the loss of ESOPs.
However, companies do not typically go after employees solely for joining a competitor, unless the situation also involves allegations of confidentiality breaches, data theft or misuse of proprietary information.
Under Rule 12(8)(f) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, unvested options ordinarily expire upon resignation or termination, while vested options can be exercised within the period specified by the ESOP scheme.
The more consequential question, according to Manchanda, is whether a company can introduce additional grounds for forfeiture after employees have already received their options. While employers have discretion to set the grounds for cancellation when drafting an ESOP policy, changing those terms later to employees’ disadvantage could be legally questionable.
In GoKwik’s case, the amendment applies to options that were already outstanding.
As per another lawyer Inc42 spoke to, this change could be challenged from a legal standpoint, as amendments that adversely affect employees’ existing ESOP rights raise questions around their validity. He added that the enforceability of non-compete restrictions and the cancellation of ESOPs on that basis remains an unsettled issue that could be tested in legal dispute.
ESOPs Turn Into A Governance Question
The clause also raises a governance question that goes beyond enforceability. Plus, some clauses in the changed policy are ambiguous at best.
Under the plan, it is the Board or its Nomination and Remuneration Committee that decides whether an employee has committed a “Competitive Breach”, a decision in which employees, and the former employees the clause continues to bind, have no part.
ESOPs are a critical lever when it comes to attracting employees to early stage startups. They stand in for salary. An early stage startup can’t match what IT services giants, multinationals or global capability centres (GCCs) pay.
Stock options fill the gap. The employee takes a lower monthly salary in exchange for a share of the upside in the future. At that stage the ESOP is part of the offer, not a perk.
ESOPs are also seen as a retention tactic. Options vest over time and it ties in employees to the success of the business in the long run. Leaving early means giving up the options that haven’t vested or even leaving money on the table.
And finally, ESOPs are one wealth creation instrument in the hands of employers. A total of 12 startups executed ESOP buybacks in 2025, paying ₹1,409 Cr ($158 Mn) to more than 9,200 employees. In 2024, 23 startups paid out ₹1,448 Cr to employees through buybacks.
Even a minor change in the ESOP policy can lead to employees having to sacrifice an amount that can be equivalent to years of salary.
GoKwik would not be the first startup to change ESOP terms after the options were granted. In December 2025, Unacademy cut the window its former employees had to exercise their vested options from 10 years to 30 days, while it was in M&A talks. Unacademy put the change on hold a month later, after a backlash from former employees.
GoKwik’s claim of 9X average returns for former employees tells us what the options may be worth, but do employees get to keep them?
GoKwik’s handling of the issue will be tested the first time an employee with vested options joins one of the nine companies it names, unless, like Unacademy, the ecommerce company decides to revisit this provision before then.
Until that happens, every employee holding ESOPs, current or former, is left with the question: does a vested option actually belong to them even if it has been allocated on paper, or is it only theirs for as long as they stay away from the companies that GoKwik bars?
Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam
Creatives: Varshita Srivastava

The Federal Government (FG) has proposed sweeping reforms in the agricultural sector, including digitalisation, mechanisation and improved coordination among government agencies in the sector, to boost food production, reduce food inflation and strengthen food security.
Senior Special Adviser on Agricultural Innovation to the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, Professor Ademola Adenle, disclosed this in an interview where he outlined plans to resolve long-standing challenges in the sector.
Adenle said digitalisation will help government identify genuine farmers, monitor production, ensure transparent distribution of inputs and expand farmers’ access to markets.
He said the National Agricultural Growth initiative had introduced a system where agro-dealers distribute inputs to verified farmers while monitoring their output. According to him, the intervention has increased production by 30%, with wheat output rising from 420,000 tonnes to 480,000 tonnes annually.
He, however, admitted that higher production alone would not bring down food prices unless institutional weaknesses and structural inefficiencies were addressed.
“Previous programmes focused mainly on production and input distribution without addressing institutional capacity, food security and agro-industrialisation,” he said.
Adenle called for an overhaul of the ministry’s administrative and legal structures, noting that bureaucratic bottlenecks had limited the impact of interventions.
He identified poor coordination among federal, state and local governments as a major challenge, and advocated harmonised agricultural policies across the three tiers.
He also proposed performance-based financing, annual key performance indicators, stronger monitoring and evaluation, data-driven decision-making, and legislation to promote accountability and transparency.
On rising food prices, Adenle blamed illegal movement of produce across Nigeria’s borders and hoarding of food commodities for creating artificial scarcity.
He said the Nigeria Customs Service and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission are working with security agencies to address the problem.

items.content:
… Says Nigeria’s 2060 net-zero ambition contradicts 3m barrels-per-day oil target
… Demands phase-down of fossil fuels, grants, protection of community land rights
By Chioma Obinna
Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) on Tuesday warned that African governments risk turning their climate commitments into instruments for expanding fossil fuel production and advancing corporate interests at the expense of vulnerable communities.
The organisation, alongside the Africa Make Big Polluters Pay Coalition (MBPP Africa), said Africa’s climate transition would amount to little more than rhetoric unless governments confronted the contradictions between their renewable energy commitments, continued investments in oil and gas, and growing dependence on foreign climate financing.
The warning came as the organisations unveiled two reports examining Nigeria’s Energy Transition Plan and the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) of five African countries at a media presentation in Lagos.
The reports, titled Four Years On: Examining Nigeria’s Just Transition Plan and Nationally Determined Contributions in Africa: A Five-Country Policy Analysis, assessed the climate commitments of Nigeria, Cameroon, South Africa, Togo and Uganda.
They identified fossil fuel expansion, uncertain climate financing, carbon markets and the growing influence of private corporations in climate policy development as major threats to achieving a genuinely just transition across the continent.
Speaking, the Executive Director of CAPPA, Akinbode Oluwafemi, said the central question was whether African climate policies were genuinely transforming economies and protecting people or creating fresh opportunities for corporate interests to profit while communities bear the consequences.
He said: “These reports emerge from a fundamental concern: Are Africa’s climate policies genuinely transforming our economies and protecting our people, or are they creating new opportunities for corporate interests to profit while communities bear the consequences?”
Oluwafemi said governments could not claim to be pursuing decarbonisation while simultaneously approving projects and infrastructure that entrenched dependence on fossil fuels.
He cited the contradictions in Uganda, where French multinational TotalEnergies promotes investments in renewable energy, including solar, while remaining a leading developer of the East African Crude Oil Pipeline, EACOP, and the Tilenga oil project.
He also referenced Cameroon’s award of five of nine oil blocks offered to fossil fuel operators, including Murphy Oil and Octavia Energy, despite its stated decarbonisation commitments.
In Nigeria, the report identified a major contradiction between the country’s ambition to achieve net-zero emissions by 2060 and its official target of producing three million barrels of crude oil daily by 2030.
It acknowledged progress in renewable energy deployment and policy development but argued that the country’s energy transition was being layered onto an economy still heavily dependent on oil and gas.
The report also questioned the promotion of natural gas as a clean transition fuel, warning that methane, its principal component, is a powerful greenhouse gas responsible, alongside methane emissions from other sources, for nearly 30 per cent of global warming since the Industrial Revolution.
According to the organisations, the challenge is not merely setting climate targets but establishing institutions, financing arrangements and enforceable social protections capable of delivering them.
They noted that Nigeria’s Energy Transition Plan lacked sufficiently enforceable guarantees for workers and communities affected by the transition, particularly in areas where livelihoods depend on oil and gas activities.
The report further highlighted the scale of Nigeria’s energy access challenge, citing World Bank figures showing that more than 80 million Nigerians lacked access to electricity as of March 2025.
It argued that a successful transition must deliver affordable and reliable electricity, secure livelihoods, environmental restoration and viable economic alternatives for communities in the Niger Delta and other extraction zones.
On climate financing, the reports raised concerns about the growing dependence of African countries on international funding, particularly loans that could deepen their debt burden.
Nigeria estimates that it requires $337 billion between 2026 and 2035 to implement its climate commitments, with 80 per cent expected from international funding.
Similarly, Togo has made 69.9 per cent of its financing requirements conditional on international support, while South Africa’s NDC indicates that approximately 80 per cent of international financial support recorded for 2021 and 2022 came in the form of loans.
Oluwafemi, in his opening remarks, warned against financing arrangements that could further impoverish countries already bearing the consequences of a climate crisis they contributed relatively little to creating.
He said: “Even worse, climate finance delivered as loans risks pushing African nations deeper into debt as they respond to a crisis they have contributed little to creating.”
He also criticised the outsourcing of climate policy development to foreign private companies, citing Togo’s engagement of Paris-based Cibola Partners to prepare key technical deliverables for its climate mitigation, adaptation and investment planning.
He said such arrangements raised questions about whose interests ultimately shaped national climate policies.
The reports also expressed concern over carbon markets and offsetting schemes, which allow polluters to compensate for emissions through projects elsewhere, including commercial plantations and forestry initiatives.
The organisations warned that such arrangements could shift responsibility from major polluters to communities whose lands and natural resources are used for carbon projects.
Uganda’s climate plan, for instance, assigns significantly greater projected emissions reductions to commercial plantations than to its two natural-forest restoration measures.
The report also cited documented forced evictions associated with a forestry and carbon-credit project in Kachung, Uganda, as an example of the dangers of climate interventions that fail to protect community rights.
Contributing partners from the five-country study also called for greater accountability and community participation.
Also, the Founder and Chief Executive of Yielding Intersectional Movements in South Africa, Ndivile Mokoena said: “The persistent gap between global climate commitments and local realities raises critical questions about political will and economic systems that continue to prioritise profit and growth over human well-being and ecological sustainability. This report underscores the urgent need to move beyond promises to tangible implementation, adequate climate financing, and meaningful support for developing countries.”
Also, the Executive Director of Nia Environment & Zero Carbon Alliance in Uganda Acola Amina said: “Achieving a rights-based, ecofeminist climate agenda that reflects Uganda’s realities and responds to the needs of affected communities requires inclusive participation and collective commitment.”
The Executive Director of Centre pour la Justice Environnementale in Togo, Kwami Kpondzo said: “Carbon markets and geoengineering are not solutions to the climate crisis. Rather, they are dangerous distractions that risk worsening the plight of vulnerable communities, threatening livelihoods, and undermining genuine climate action. We must put people and the planet before profit. Nature is not a commodity for sale, and we remain steadfast in our commitment to defending it.”
Oluwafemi further said: “The Nigeria Energy Transition Plan and the Five-Country NDCs Reports offer an opportunity to rethink how energy policies and climate commitments serve people and communities. These reports emphasise that equity, transparency and accountability must remain central in every plan, while ensuring that affected communities have a meaningful voice in decisions that shape their future.”
The organisations called on African delegates attending the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye, to reject carbon offsetting as a substitute for actual emissions reductions and oppose arrangements that allow continued fossil fuel pollution to be balanced against temporary carbon storage.
They also demanded a planned and funded phase-down of fossil fuel extraction, substantial public investment in decentralised renewable energy, affordable electricity and legally binding protections for workers and affected communities.
Other demands include grant-based climate financing from historically high-emitting countries, legal protection for communal land, transparent climate budgets and binding safeguards against corporate influence in national climate policy decisions.
The organisations insisted that Indigenous Peoples, smallholder farmers, rural women and frontline communities must have enforceable rights to reject projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and access to natural resources.
Their intervention comes amid growing concerns over the widening gap between global climate commitments and actual emissions reductions.
The United Nations Environment Programme’s latest Emissions Gap Report projects that current policies could lead to 2.8 degrees Celsius of warming this century, while full implementation of national climate pledges could still result in 2.6 degrees Celsius.
The post Climate plans: CAPPA warns against fossil fuel expansion, corporate capture appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.title: Agbazuere backs Otti’s second-term bid after U-turn
items.summary:

By Steve Oko

He said the allegation would not undermine Otti’s support base, particularly among the Ngwa people.
