items.content:
It would be naive to think that getting listed on quick commerce platforms is half the battle won. If anything, that’s where the real battle begins. Building sales velocity, keeping products in stock, managing sky-high platform costs, and, believe it or not, we have barely peered into the abyss.
Gramiyaa, a premium cold-pressed edible oil brand, learnt this the hard way when it boarded the quick commerce bandwagon through Blinkit in 2024.
The first hurdle was affordability. When Gramiyaa finally made it onto quick commerce platforms, it found itself paying nearly twice the commission its national competitors paid. For a small brand already operating on razor-thin margins, that was a steep price to pay just to get a foot in the door.
On top of that, the brand had to set aside a hefty advertising budget, only to burn through it while learning the ropes and figuring out how to make the channel work.
After weathering several battles, including pricing wars between platforms, Gramiyaa has managed to turn the tables. Today, quick commerce is its largest revenue contributor, accounting for 35% of its ₹5 Cr monthly recurring revenue (MRR).
So, how did Gramiyaa navigate these hurdles and turn quick commerce from a costly gamble into its biggest revenue driver?
In an exclusive conversation for The Quick Commerce Code by Inc42 and Nitro Commerce, Gramiyaa cofounder Mohamed Yaseen shed light on what worked for the brand, how it managed to bring down platform commissions, and the dos and don’ts for emerging D2C brands looking to crack quick commerce.
Why Gramiyaa Had To Look Beyond Its D2C Playbook
Founded by three friends, Mohamed Yaseen, Naveenrajamaran RL and Sibi Manivannan, Gramiyaa’s journey began in 2018 as a local offline business.
Manivannan’s grandfather ran an oil mill, and Manivannan wanted to breathe new life into the family business, which sold unbranded oil in PET bottles through five to six retail shops in Chennai.
While these shops brought in ₹15-20 Lakh a month, high rents and operating costs ate into the earnings. Besides, each store could only cater to customers in its immediate neighbourhood, leaving little room for growth.
“We had a very stable audience, but were not moving anywhere in terms of growth,” Yaseen told Inc42.
In 2022, Yaseen and Naveenrajamaran RL joined Manivannan, and the three decided to build a new company. Gramiyaa was born.
The founders initially took the D2C route, selling through their own website and setting up small warehouses across four metros to deliver orders within a day. They also looked beyond India, tapping distributors that catered to the Indian diaspora in the US, to take their products overseas. This gave the company a small but high-margin revenue stream.
“However, this was not enough, even though we were doing quite well from our website,” Yaseen said.
As a brand selling only cold-pressed oils, Gramiyaa could attract only so many customers to its own website. To reach a wider audience, the founders decided to list their products on Amazon in November 2022. But this came with an unexpected trade-off. Instead of bringing in only new customers, Amazon began eating into Gramiyaa’s existing D2C sales. Customers who previously bought from its website started ordering through the marketplace, where the brand earned less on every sale.
With its own website offering limited room for growth and Amazon eating into margins, the founders began looking for another avenue to scale, and quick commerce seemed like the obvious next step.
The High Cost Of Breaking Into Quick Commerce
The founders were convinced that quick commerce was a channel they could no longer afford to ignore. But wanting to get on board and actually making it happen were two different things.
For nearly a year, the Gramiyaa founders remained hesitant. The reason? Blinkit and Instamart’s steep commissions. With the brand operating on a razor-thin profit margin of just 2-3%, the cost of entering quick commerce was simply too much.
“This was one year of anxiety and worry. We wanted to do this but couldn’t,” Yaseen recalled.
According to him, if a national cooking oil brand paid a commission of X to a quick commerce channel, a premium oil from a national brand paid about 1.5X. And Gramiyaa, a small and unproven brand, had to pay twice as much.
However, Yaseen argues that quick commerce is not necessarily more expensive than other distribution channels. Consider a product selling for ₹400, where the brand needs to retain ₹300. The remaining ₹100 goes towards platform margins and advertising on quick commerce. In traditional retail, a similar amount could be absorbed by distributor margins, retailer commissions and the cost of maintaining a sales team.
The bigger challenge for smaller brands, therefore, is not just the cost of distribution, but having enough capital to absorb these expenses before the channel starts generating meaningful sales.
The advertising commitment made the decision even harder. According to Yaseen, brands entering quick commerce with three to four SKUs may be expected to spend ₹5–10 Lakh a month on advertising, even before they have established consistent demand. For a business like Gramiyaa, which was operating on margins of just 2–3% at the time, committing such capital without any assurance of sales was a significant risk.
The decision was eventually made, and the brand got listed on Blinkit in 2024. But after the listing, the channel remained loss-making for nearly six months. According to Yaseen, most brands that do reasonably well on quick commerce barely break even or lose money for six months to a year, and Gramiyaa was no exception.
“Brands without the capital to absorb this often pause or shut down their quick commerce operations. Thankfully, we had raised funding by the time we went in,” said Yaseen.
For Gramiyaa, the commissions came down once it proved that demand was pulling customers toward the platforms. When its sales grew from ₹5 Lakh a month to ₹10-15 Lakh and repeat purchases showed that some customers would switch apps, the platforms began treating it more like a large brand.
“Our margins eventually moved gradually closer to what national brands paid,” Yaseen said.
The One-City, One-SKU Strategy Behind Gramiyaa’s Growth
On ecommerce platforms like Amazon, Gramiyaa could ship products to customers anywhere in India from a central warehouse. How well a product ranked depended on how many people clicked on its listing and went on to buy it. Where those customers lived hardly mattered.
Quick commerce, however, is a different ball game altogether. Here, what matters is how quickly a product is sold in a particular neighbourhood.
The challenge becomes clearer at the dark-store level. A slow-moving product may get just one unit of inventory in a particular store. Once a customer buys it, the product can remain unavailable for the next 24–48 hours until it is replenished. Unless the product consistently sells in that locality, platforms have little reason to increase the inventory allocated to it.
This creates a difficult cycle for smaller brands. Limited inventory leads to frequent stockouts, but without sustained sales velocity, securing additional inventory becomes equally difficult.
Yaseen’s rule is that a brand with full confidence in a product in one city should launch there alone, rather than spread across four cities where it is only fairly sure. Within that city, the product has to sell quickly in at least half the dark stores before platforms begin stocking it more deeply.
“Velocity is everything,” Yaseen said, adding that it was the hardest shift for Gramiyaa’s team.
Its ecommerce managers were used to optimise listings and found it difficult to plan around availability in each locality. Yaseen took charge of the channel himself and pushed the team to learn how supermarkets and general trade distributors manage stock in each area.
“I believe supermarkets have more in common with running a kirana counter than with running an Amazon listing,” said Yaseen.
To understand where its products were selling and where they weren’t, Gramiyaa began tracking performance city by city. An intern manually checked pin codes to see where its products appeared in search results and whether they were in stock.
Today, the brand uses tools such as Nitro Commerce to track these metrics, with Yaseen checking the dashboard every morning.
The exercise revealed two trends:
In some areas, platforms weren’t stocking Gramiyaa’s products at all.
In other areas, demand was strong enough for products to sell out quickly
Armed with these data points, the brand began pushing platforms to stock more units wherever demand was high.
The same data-driven approach helped Gramiyaa optimise advertising spend. Yaseen realised that the company was sometimes paying to promote products that were already ranking well organically on quick commerce apps. By tracking organic and paid share of voice at the SKU and city level, the team began redirecting advertising budgets towards products and locations where additional visibility could make a difference.
This allowed Gramiyaa to make better use of its marketing budget rather than spending indiscriminately across products that were already generating sales.
Over time, product availability became one of Gramiyaa’s most important metrics. The brand now targets 90% on-shelf availability (OSA) and typically achieves 85-90%. According to Yaseen, even the category leader manages only 92-93% in its best month.
And this is where Yaseen sees an opportunity for smaller brands. “When a leading brand runs out of stock, customers often turn to alternatives. If Gramiyaa is available at that moment and its product meets their expectations, it has a chance to win over a new customer,” the cofounder said.
The Big Trade-Off: Pricing, Assortment And Availability
Gramiyaa’s best-selling product on quick commerce is groundnut oil, and its best-selling size is one litre. At one point, it also listed half-litre bottles, a size only a few brands bet on. Yaseen expected it to work as a cheaper trial pack.
At first, the half-litre pack made up 30% of groundnut oil sales. The team expected that share to fade, but it held. Today, the smaller half-litre packs account for about 15% of total sales volume, which is roughly 30% of its customers.
This revealed an insight that its young and conscious customers cook occasionally, and others plan their groceries monthly, buy large packs on Amazon, and only use quick commerce when they run out a few days early.
Adding smaller pack sizes seemed like a good way to attract more customers, but it came with a trade-off. Dark stores have limited shelf space and stock for each brand. If Gramiyaa stocked both half-litre and one-litre bottles, its inventory would be split between the two sizes. A competitor selling only one-litre bottles could stock more units of that size and stay available for longer.
Yaseen decided to prioritise the larger pack, even if it meant losing customers who preferred smaller quantities.
“If you’re the 20% of customers who won’t buy my brand without the half-litre, I will let go of you. But the 80% who buy my one-litre, I want it repeatedly available for them,” he said, advising new brands to start with a single SKU and choose a product category where larger brands have left a gap.
Not every product decision worked out for Gramiyaa. Of the four oil products the brand introduced on quick commerce, one failed to gain traction because it could not be priced competitively. Yaseen acknowledged that the company had pushed ahead with a product despite knowing it was overpriced and not particularly suited to its core customer base in southern India.
The experience reinforced that expanding an assortment does not necessarily translate into higher sales, especially when dark-store inventory is limited, and a poorly performing SKU can tie up resources better allocated to bestselling products.
Pricing was another headache for Gramiyaa. Yaseen shared that platforms were changing the selling price of their products to match competitors.
For example, if Instamart offered a discount on one of its SKUs, Blinkit was just going ahead to match that price for the next 20 days to recover its margins. At times, as Yaseen shared, platforms also asked Gramiyaa to cover the price difference.
“We get caught between two giants fighting to acquire customers,” Yaseen said.
These price fluctuations caused significant losses for Gramiyaa in its early months on quick commerce. It took the company nearly five to six months of negotiations to bring platform margins closer to each other and push back against pricing changes and penalties that were beyond its control.
The pressure was compounded by competition from much larger FMCG players. Yaseen credits Tata with helping popularise the cold-pressed oil category, but its aggressive push has also intensified price competition. For a smaller brand like Gramiyaa, competing on discounts against national players with deeper pockets was never going to be a sustainable strategy.
Yaseen believes that while a popular product such as groundnut oil can help a brand establish itself on quick commerce, its longer-term position will depend on building a presence in more differentiated categories. For Gramiyaa, this makes products such as coconut and sesame oil important, particularly in segments where larger FMCG companies may not be competing as aggressively.
Today, Yaseen shared, Gramiyaa does not need to rely heavily on discounts to drive sales. At ₹350-750, a single one-litre bottle is expensive enough to qualify for a platform’s free delivery threshold.
The purchasing behaviour also works in Gramiyaa’s favour. According to Yaseen, its customers typically reorder every 40–45 days and buy an average of 1.3-1.4 products per order, while ₹350 is an effective price point for the brand on quick commerce.
Unlike lower-ticket products that may depend on being added to a larger grocery basket, a single bottle of Gramiyaa’s oil can account for a substantial portion of the order value. Combined with repeat demand, this gives the brand an advantage in building consistent sales velocity.
Gramiyaa’s Next Quick Commerce Test
Gramiyaa reported ₹18 Cr in revenue in FY25, which grew 61.1% to ₹29 Cr in FY26, with quick commerce the largest channel at 35%, or about ₹10.15 Cr. But this growth has come at the expense of profit.
According to Yaseen, the brand was profitable in FY25. As of now, remaining profitable is the least of its concerns, as the company expects to burn for brand visibility and new channels.
Recently, Gramiyaa raised ₹21 Cr as part of its ongoing Series A fundraise led by Optiscape Network Holdings, Homegrown Ventures, Campus Fund and others. The funds would be used to fuel its expansion in Tier II markets.
For Gramiyaa, the next phase of quick commerce growth lies beyond India’s metros. Yaseen believes the channel’s appeal in Tier II cities is somewhat different from that in larger markets. Rather than simply promising delivery within minutes, quick-commerce platforms are increasingly offering consumers access to products that may not be readily available at their neighbourhood kirana stores.
For a premium cold-pressed oil brand with limited offline distribution in these markets, that creates an opportunity to reach customers who might otherwise struggle to find its products locally.
The company expects quick commerce to remain its largest revenue channel as it expands into these markets. However, Yaseen acknowledges that the next phase will depend on how successfully platforms penetrate smaller cities, particularly as growth in established metro markets begins to moderate.
However, when asked about platforms prioritising their own labels over D2C brands, Yaseen does not see much competition there, as the brand operates in the premium category, selling to customers who prefer quality over price.
But for founders considering the channel, Yaseen’s advice is to wait.
“Quick commerce should be built only after a brand has a core business on its website or an ecommerce platform like Amazon. They need to know their hero products, figure out pricing, and have strong liquidity from another channel or cash flow,” the cofounder stated, outlining the imperatives for newer brands stuck at the bottom of the pyramid.
Gramiyaa avoided this trap, but the harder test of holding its position in Tier II cities is yet to come. Can it sustain demand in markets where premium purchases often take a backseat to essential spending?
[Edited By Shishir Parasher]
The post Why Gramiyaa Had To Think Like A Supermarket To Win On Quick Commerce appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Take-Two Interactive has raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts as excitement builds around the upcoming launch of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI). The company expects the highly anticipated game to generate strong sales when it reaches players on November 19, 2026.
The updated outlook reflects growing confidence in the game’s commercial potential. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick said that pre-orders for GTA VI were performing well above the company’s initial expectations. However, the publisher has decided to keep its annual bookings forecast unchanged until the game officially launches.
Take-Two Raises Annual Revenue Forecast as GTA VI Launch Approaches
Take-Two shares gained around 4% in extended trading following the announcement.
GTA VI Pre-Orders Exceed Expectations
GTA VI is one of the most anticipated video games in recent years. Its release will come after several delays and approximately 13 years since the launch of its predecessor, GTA V.
According to data from Sensor Tower, the game had received around 7.71 million digital pre-orders worldwide by November 3. Take-Two started accepting pre-orders in June.
The game’s pricing also points to strong revenue potential. The standard edition costs $79.99, while the Ultimate Edition carries a $99.99 price tag. Sensor Tower data showed that nearly 90% of pre-orders by the end of August came from customers choosing the more expensive edition.
The company expects GTA VI to remain a major source of revenue over the coming quarters.
Take-Two Raises Fiscal 2027 Financial Outlook
Take-Two now expects total revenue of $7.98 billion to $8.18 billion for fiscal 2027. Its previous forecast ranged between $7.90 billion and $8.10 billion.
The company also increased the lower end of its earnings-per-share forecast by two cents. It now expects earnings of 57 cents to 75 cents per share.
However, Take-Two kept its annual net bookings forecast unchanged at $8 billion to $8.20 billion.
NBA 2K27 Faces Strong Competition
Take-Two also discussed the performance of NBA 2K27, the latest entry in its basketball gaming franchise. The game launched during the September quarter but faced weaker demand amid increased competition.
The company expects player engagement and bookings to improve during the remaining part of the year. Upcoming in-game content could help attract more players and encourage existing users to remain active.
Despite the weaker performance of NBA 2K27, Take-Two remains confident about its overall business outlook.
Quarterly Bookings Fall Short of Expectations
Take-Two reported total bookings of $1.60 billion for the second quarter ended September. This represented an 18% decline compared with the same period a year earlier and fell below analysts’ expectations of $1.67 billion.
The company is now looking towards GTA VI to strengthen its financial performance. With millions of digital pre-orders already recorded, the November 19 launch could become a major milestone for Take-Two and its gaming business.

Xiaomi has officially confirmed the global launch date of its Xiaomi 18 Pro series. The company will unveil the new smartphones at an event in Paris on November 17, 2026, marking an important step in bringing its Pro models to international markets.
The announcement follows an earlier teaser from Xiaomi Vice President and Chief Marketing Officer Xu Fei, who hinted at the launch date a few days ago. Xiaomi had previously confirmed that the series would arrive in November but had not shared the exact date or venue.
This year’s launch also marks a change in the company’s international release strategy. Last year, Xiaomi introduced only the standard Xiaomi 17 to global markets, while the Pro models remained exclusive to China. With the Xiaomi 18 Pro series, the company appears ready to expand its flagship lineup to more markets.
Xiaomi 18 Pro Series Global Launch Confirmed for November 17 in Paris
The launch event will begin at 14:00 GMT+1 on November 17. Xiaomi will also stream the event live through its official X and YouTube channels, allowing viewers worldwide to follow the announcement.
The company has confirmed three colour options for the series: White, Cosmic Blue, and Velvet Red. These colours will give buyers several choices when the smartphones reach international markets.
Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max Battery Details
Both the Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max have already appeared in global certification databases. However, early reports suggest that the international versions may feature smaller batteries than their Chinese counterparts.
According to leaked information, the global Xiaomi 18 Pro could come with a 6,000mAh battery, while the Pro Max may feature a 7,050mAh battery.
In comparison, the Chinese versions reportedly offer larger 7,000mAh and 8,500mAh batteries, respectively. This would represent a noticeable difference in battery capacity between the two versions.
However, Xiaomi has not officially confirmed these specifications. The reported capacities come from code strings discovered in an earlier leak, so the final specifications could change before launch.
Launch Plans Remain Unclear
Xiaomi has also hinted at bringing the Xiaomi 18 Pro to other countries. However, the company has not yet confirmed whether the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max will launch in Pakistan.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy have forced the chipmaker's board to confront more than ordinary executive misconduct, raising ​existential questions for the company and concerns about the board's ability to investigate its CEO independently.
Among corporate leaders, "There have definitely been ‌affair scandals and sexual-harassment scandals. But honey-pot scandals? No," said Ann Lipton, a University of Colorado law professor who follows boardroom issues.
She was using a term for an espionage ploy in which an operative entraps a target by feigning romantic interest. Historical examples include the Profumo Affair in the early 1960s and tend to involve diplomatic or political consequences.
US President Donald Trump ​said on Monday the FBI was probing Huang's relationship, a day after Nvidia's board launched an internal investigation "regarding the national security concerns raised in news ​reports, ," according to an email Huang sent to Nvidia employees and released by the company.
The company's advanced semiconductors are at the ⁠heart of a global race for AI superiority. China's Foreign Ministry said the spying claim was "a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear."
Nvidia co-founder Huang, 63, has ​no obvious successor and close ties to Trump. He owns 3.6% of its stock and has dozens of direct reports, suggesting a tight grip on the company.
Read More: Nvidia's shares slide after-hours as tech giant probes CEO Jensen Huang
Shares ​in Nvidia fell Monday as Huang's future came under scrutiny. But the stock later trimmed its decline to close 4% lower as some investors bet that the CEO could survive the crisis.
Board's credibility
Unusually among its peers, Nvidia operates without a board chair among its 11 directors. While the company considers all but Huang independent, three independent directors have served since the 1990s ​and a fourth, Mark Stevens, for most of that time. Only two have joined the board since 2021.
The clubby roster may not be so unusual ​by the standards of charismatic Silicon Valley company founders like Apple's Steve Jobs, who died in 2011.
But the US probe has heightened scrutiny of whether directors who have worked alongside ‌Huang for ⁠decades are sufficiently independent to investigate his conduct.
"If you have a figure like Steve Jobs, I think people on Wall Street as well as in Silicon Valley would say they're entitled to some leeway or deference," said Marc Goldstein, head of US research for proxy adviser Institutional Shareholder Services.
Such deference could now raise questions about whether the board provided sufficient oversight of a CEO whose own judgment has come under scrutiny.
Nvidia said on Sunday that while its board had no ​reason to believe that either US national ​security or Nvidia secrets were ⁠compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information. The board said it had confidence in the CEO and his leadership team.
Goldstein said board members running that investigation should be given the latitude to hire their own legal advisers to bolster their ​credibility.
The company also might consider keeping long-serving directors away from the probe, he added, to avoid legal challenges from ​shareholders claiming it wasn't ⁠sufficiently independent.
Political economy
Yale University management professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld said the company faces additional national-security questions because of the ties between Huang and Trump. Trump, who has praised Huang, said on Monday that he had spoken to the executive and thought he would "be in good shape."
Washington has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China since 2022. Last ⁠year the ​Trump administration allowed Nvidia to resume certain China shipments under arrangements in which the US ​government receives a cut of the company's China chip sales.
The deal makes any suggestion of foreign espionage more sensitive for both executives and US government officials, Sonnenfeld said. "That's why you don't want state ​capitalism arrangements. You don't want the US government to be so involved in private companies," he said.

items.title: Australia to mandate AI breach reporting, create regulator after OpenAI breach
items.summary:
Australia will require artificial intelligence companies to report breaches ‌and consider changes to criminal law to address "serious misconduct", Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday, after an OpenAI agent broke into a government website.
The OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the medical statistics portal ​of Medicare, Australia's universal health insurance programme, while conducting research on public medical ​spending, the government said in September. The breach triggered a rapid ⁠government review into the incident.
Albanese said his government had accepted all recommendations of the ​review.
"(The recommendations) include mandatory AI company reporting when it comes to misaligned behaviour or cyber ​incidents, and consideration of reforming criminal law in cases of serious misconduct," Albanese told reporters.
"The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases, make sure that it catches up with what is ​a very fast-changing world.
items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Australia will require artificial intelligence companies to report breaches ‌and consider changes to criminal law to address "serious misconduct", Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Tuesday, after an OpenAI agent broke into a government website.
The OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the medical statistics portal ​of Medicare, Australia's universal health insurance programme, while conducting research on public medical ​spending, the government said in September. The breach triggered a rapid ⁠government review into the incident.
Albanese said his government had accepted all recommendations of the ​review.
"(The recommendations) include mandatory AI company reporting when it comes to misaligned behaviour or cyber ​incidents, and consideration of reforming criminal law in cases of serious misconduct," Albanese told reporters.
"The law needs to get ahead of, and in some cases, make sure that it catches up with what is ​a very fast-changing world."
OpenAI has said it learned of the breach only in August ​and that the incident was unintentional. Its review found no evidence that patient records were accessed by ‌the ⁠agent.
Read More: Nvidia CEO becomes subject of memes as social media reacts to alleged affair with chinese spy
The breach has added to friction between Australia and US technology companies, after Canberra refused ChatGPT maker OpenAI and rival Anthropic exemptions from copyright laws for model training, instead requiring them to negotiate licensing agreements with Australian rights holders.
However, both companies told Australian parliament last ​month that they would welcome ​laws requiring them to ⁠report data breaches carried out by their AI agents, acknowledging the decision to notify was currently at their discretion.
Albanese said his centre-left ​Labor government would set up an AI regulator to oversee security ​controls throughout ⁠the development and deployment of AI systems, identify serious risks and conduct independent evaluations of AI models.
"The AI safety regulator will be able to enforce significant penalties for AI companies ⁠doing the ​wrong thing," he said.
The mandatory AI safety and ​security protections will form part of the government's proposed AI legislation, Albanese said, which it plans to introduce in ​Parliament next year.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series could bring limited camera improvements, according to a new leak that has revealed the expected camera sensors across all four models. While the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra may receive upgraded main cameras, the standard Galaxy S27 and S27 Plus could retain much of the camera hardware found in their predecessors.
The Galaxy S27 lineup is expected to arrive early next year. Although Samsung has yet to confirm any details, a report from SammyGuru has shared the alleged camera specifications of the entire series.
Samsung Galaxy S27 Series Camera Specs Leak Ahead of Launch
According to the leak, the Galaxy S27 and S27 Plus will feature a 50MP main camera using either the Sony IMX955 or Samsung S5KGNG sensor. These are reportedly the same sensors used in the Galaxy S26 and S26 Plus.
The two phones may also retain the 12MP Sony IMX564 ultrawide sensor, which Samsung has reportedly used since the Galaxy S23 series. For zoom photography, both models could continue using a 10MP telephoto camera with 3x optical zoom and the Samsung S5K3K1 sensor.
The selfie camera may also remain unchanged, with a 12MP sensor from either Samsung or Sony.
Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra Could Get 200MP Main Cameras
The Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra are expected to receive more noticeable camera upgrades. Both models could feature a 200MP Samsung ISOCELL HP6 main sensor.
The leak also suggests that Samsung will equip both phones with a 50MP ultrawide camera. The sensor could be either the Samsung ISOCELL JN3 or Sony IMX855.
However, the telephoto cameras could differ between the two models. The Galaxy S27 Pro will feature a 10MP 3x telephoto camera using the Samsung S5K3LD sensor, which also appears in the Galaxy S26 Ultra.
The Galaxy S27 Ultra, meanwhile, could feature a 50MP telephoto camera with 5x optical zoom. It may use either the Samsung ISOCELL JN3 or Sony IMX855 sensor.
For selfies, both Pro and Ultra models could offer a 16MP front camera powered by Samsung’s S5K2P5 sensor.
See Also: Samsung Galaxy A08 and A18 Launching Soon in Pakistan: Specs, Features and Expected Price
Samsung May Make Limited Improvements to Zoom Photography
One interesting detail is that the Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra may feature a new 200MP main camera derived from Samsung’s ISOCELL HPC technology. Earlier reports suggested that this sensor could use DeepPix technology to improve dynamic range in photos and videos.
However, the reported telephoto setup raises some questions. The Galaxy S27 Pro could retain a 10MP 3x zoom camera, which would offer little improvement over existing hardware.
The Galaxy S27 Ultra could also move to a single telephoto camera instead of the dual 3x and 5x zoom setup found in recent Ultra models. While its 50MP 5x camera could deliver better zoom quality, removing the dedicated 3x camera would reduce the available optical zoom options.
Overall, the latest leak suggests that Samsung may focus most of its camera upgrades on the main sensor of its higher-end Galaxy S27 models. The standard and Plus variants could see almost no hardware changes. However, these details remain unofficial, and Samsung could still make changes before the launch.

items.title: After 10,000mAh Y600, vivo Reportedly Readies a 12,000mAh Battery for a Future Phone
items.summary:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The vivo 12000mAh battery has moved from the test bench to the factory floor, according to a well-known Chinese tipster. Digital Chat Station says the cell is now in mass production, with a rated capacity of 11,970 mAh.
The claim comes from a post on Weibo. vivo has not confirmed it, and the tipster did not say which phone will carry the battery.
From a February leak to production
The same tipster first raised the project earlier this year. In February, he said vivo was testing a phone with a 4.53V single-cell silicon battery. That leak gave a rated capacity of 10,000 mAh and a typical capacity between 11,000 mAh and 12,000 mAh.
Nine months later, the update says the battery is being manufactured at scale. That is a real step forward, because a cell that passes lab tests can still fail to reach production.
Production of a battery is also not a phone launch. Phone makers often build up cell supply months before a device appears
items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The vivo 12000mAh battery has moved from the test bench to the factory floor, according to a well-known Chinese tipster. Digital Chat Station says the cell is now in mass production, with a rated capacity of 11,970 mAh.
The claim comes from a post on Weibo. vivo has not confirmed it, and the tipster did not say which phone will carry the battery.
From a February leak to production
The same tipster first raised the project earlier this year. In February, he said vivo was testing a phone with a 4.53V single-cell silicon battery. That leak gave a rated capacity of 10,000 mAh and a typical capacity between 11,000 mAh and 12,000 mAh.
Nine months later, the update says the battery is being manufactured at scale. That is a real step forward, because a cell that passes lab tests can still fail to reach production.
Production of a battery is also not a phone launch. Phone makers often build up cell supply months before a device appears, and DCS gave no release window.
Rated and typical capacity do not quite match
The numbers need a careful reading. In battery labelling, rated capacity is usually the guaranteed minimum, while typical capacity is the average a cell delivers. February’s leak had rated 10,000 mAh and typical at 11,000 mAh to 12,000 mAh.
The new post puts rated capacity at 11,970 mAh. That either reflects an improved cell or loose wording somewhere in the chain of reports. The post, as relayed, does not explain which, so treat the exact figure with caution until a product page appears.
Where vivo stands today
vivo already sells a large-battery phone. It recently launched the Y600 in China with a 10,000 mAh battery. The Y600 is a rebranded version of the S2 FE, which is also sold as the V80 Lite in select regions.
The tipster also claims vivo is testing batteries larger than 12,000 mAh for future phones with big displays. No details, devices or timelines came with that claim.

Capacity
Status
vivo Y600
10,000 mAh

Realme P4 Power
10,001 mAh
Launched in India
vivo’s next cell
11,970 mAh rated (per DCS)

Redmi Turbo 6 Max
12,000 mAh
Reported in testing (DCS, April)
The capacity race is now a matter of engineering
Silicon-carbon cells let makers fit more energy into the same volume than conventional graphite designs. That is what makes 10,000 mAh phones possible without turning them into bricks.
Each new step raises practical questions the leaks do not answer. How heavy will the phone be, and how thick? What charging speed will it support? How will the battery age after hundreds of cycles? Silicon expands as it charges, and makers have to control that to protect cell life.
What to watch
The next clues will be regulatory certifications and a device name. Look for a charging-speed figure and a weight, which will show what vivo traded away for capacity.
The more telling signal is how the race ends. With Realme at 10,001 mAh and Redmi reportedly testing 12,000 mAh, brands are now matching each other’s headline numbers. The company that pairs a big cell with a normal-sized body will have the real advantage, not the one with the biggest figure on the box.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Nigerian off-grid energy startup Okra Solar has secured a US$7 million debt facility from British International Investment (BII) to accelerate clean energy access.
Founded in 2016, Okra provides mesh-grid technology for off-grid communities, combining solar generation, battery storage and smart controls so that neighbouring homes and businesses can share electricity cost-efficiently. The model delivers more power than typical solar home systems while needing less infrastructure than conventional mini-grids.
Okra currently has more than 13,000 households connected and over 2.3MW of installed capacity. The US$7 million financing from BII, the UK’s development finance institution and impact investor, will allow it to procure equipment for roughly 150,000 new connections, a more than tenfold increase, with the potential to bring electricity to 750,000 people in rural Nigeria for the first time.
The facility tackles a key barrier to scaling distributed renewable energy – access to flexible working capital. By buying inputs upfront and in larger volumes, Okra expects to cut equipment costs and shorten delivery times to Nigeria from four months to about two.
“Every month a project is delayed is another month a community goes without power,” said Afnan Hannan, CEO of Okra Solar. “Until now we would only order components once a transaction had closed, in batches of a few thousand units. With BII’s facility we are procuring long lead time components, batteries, and solar PV equipment upfront and in volume, reducing costs and having stock ready when a developer signs.”
Faster delivery should also help Okra’s developer customers bring projects online sooner and access results-based grant payments earlier. Mesh-grids are eligible under Nigeria’s Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up (DARES) programme, which is run by the Rural Electrification Agency with World Bank support.
“For innovative energy companies such as Okra, access to the right type of finance can be just as important as the technology itself,” said Geoffrey Manley, director and head of infrastructure and climate debt for Africa and South Asia at BII. “We believe this will help demonstrate the commercial viability of mesh-grids and establish the model as an increasingly important part of Africa’s distributed renewable energy market.”

nubia has officially launched the nubia Air Pro 5G in Pakistan, bringing together an ultra-slim design, high-resolution photography and robust durability in a premium 5G smartphone. Positioned as the segment’s slimmest 108MP 5G smartphone, the new device carries the tagline “So Slim, So Strong” and is priced at PKR 109,999.
Designed to make a statement
The nubia Air Pro measures just 5.99mm in thickness and weighs approximately 172g, offering a remarkably slim and lightweight feel. Its high-strength aluminium alloy mid-frame adds structural resilience, bringing a balance of refined design and everyday practicality.
Photography is a key highlight
The smartphone features a 108MP main rear camera designed to capture detailed images, supported by a 32MP front camera for high-resolution selfies. Camera features include Quick Snap, Burst Mode, Slow Motion and underwater photography, giving users more ways to capture everyday moments and action.
The nubia Air Pro is also built for demanding everyday use
It carries IP68, IP69 and IP69K dust- and water-resistance ratings, offering protection against immersion and high-pressure, high-temperature water jets under the specified test standards. The device also features a 6.77-inch AMOLED display with a 144Hz refresh rate and up to 4,500 nits peak brightness.
Powering the experience
The phone is equipped with a MediaTek Dimensity 7100 5G processor and a 5,000mAh silicon-carbon battery. It supports 45W fast charging, 10W reverse charging and bypass charging. A dedicated one-tap Sports Mode provides quick access to fitness tools and real-time workout information, while AI-powered tools add convenience to everyday tasks.
With its combination of a remarkably slim profile, 108MP imaging, 5G connectivity and advanced durability
The nubia Air Pro brings a distinctive option to Pakistan’s smartphone market. The device is now officially launched in Pakistan at a retail price of PKR 109,999.

The Pakistan Software Houses Association (P@SHA) says NCCIA raids on IT firms are putting export contracts at risk. The industry body wants the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency to follow court-warrant procedures when it enters registered software companies.
The complaint comes as the agency pursues scam centres. P@SHA does not dispute the crackdown. Its argument is that the method is hitting the wrong doors.
What member companies are reporting
According to P@SHA, member firms have complained that NCCIA teams entered offices without showing warrants. Employees were allegedly questioned for long stretches, and laptops, servers and mobile phones were taken, including in cases where no illegal activity was established.
These are the association’s claims, relayed from its members. NCCIA’s side of the account was not part of the material available for this report.

The Pakistan Software Houses Association (P@SHA) says NCCIA raids on IT firms are putting export contracts at risk. The industry body wants the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency to follow court-warrant procedures when it enters registered software companies.
The complaint comes as the agency pursues scam centres. P@SHA does not dispute the crackdown. Its argument is that the method is hitting the wrong doors.
What member companies are reporting
According to P@SHA, member firms have complained that NCCIA teams entered offices without showing warrants. Employees were allegedly questioned for long stretches, and laptops, servers and mobile phones were taken, including in cases where no illegal activity was established.
These are the association’s claims, relayed from its members. NCCIA’s side of the account was not part of the material available for this report.
For a software house, a seized server is more than an inconvenience. It can hold client source code, project files and contractual data that the company is legally bound to protect.
Why clients may not wait
P@SHA Chairman Dr Shoab Ahmed Khan said the industry’s overseas business rests on client trust. A raid and an equipment seizure can shake that trust quickly, he said.
His warning was specific about where the work could go. Foreign clients, he said, might move contracts to competing markets such as India, the Philippines and Eastern Europe rather than wait for an investigation to end.
That is how outsourcing decisions tend to work. A buyer with a delivery deadline rarely has the patience to find out whether the raid was justified. A vendor in another country becomes the safer option, and winning the work back is slow.
The export target leaves little room for shocks
P@SHA put the industry’s growth at roughly 20 percent, with exports reaching $4.6 billion in FY2026. The government’s Uraan Pakistan initiative targets $10 billion by FY2029.
The arithmetic is worth laying out, because it shows how thin the margin is. These figures are PhoneWorld’s own calculation from the numbers above, not official projections.
Scenario
FY2026
FY2029
Growth continues at 20% a year
$4.6bn
about $7.9bn
Growth needed to hit target
$4.6bn
$10bn (about 30% a year)
Steady 20 percent growth would leave exports around $2 billion short of the goal. Hitting $10 billion requires growth near 30 percent a year, so the industry has to accelerate, not just hold its pace. Anything that makes foreign buyers hesitate works directly against that.
What P@SHA is asking for
The association wants raids on registered IT companies to proceed only under court warrants and set standard operating procedures. It asked that employees be treated respectfully, with particular mention of women staff.
It also wants the NCCIA to verify a company’s registration with the Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB) and P@SHA before acting.
On equipment, P@SHA proposed forensic imaging on site. Investigators would copy the data they need and leave the hardware. Devices unrelated to the case would be returned within seven days.
It further asked for safeguards against harassment and physical mistreatment of staff and against interference with CCTV systems or digital recordings during a raid.
Finally, it proposed a joint coordination and grievance committee. The NCCIA, P@SHA, the Ministry of IT and Telecom and PSEB would sit on it to review complaints, share intelligence on fraudulent operators and write procedures for raids on registered businesses.
The registration problem
P@SHA itself concedes that some scam operators register as IT businesses. That complicates its main safeguard.
If a PSEB or P@SHA registration can be obtained by a fraudulent outfit, checking it before a raid will not by itself separate honest firms from fake ones. The check only works if registration standards are tight enough that a certificate means something.
The proposed committee is the more useful idea for that reason. Shared intelligence on known bad actors would let enforcement target them without sweeping up the companies that file taxes, pay salaries and sign export contracts.
What to watch
The agency has not been heard on these allegations, and the warrant and equipment-seizure claims remain unverified. Whether the NCCIA accepts any form of joint oversight will show how seriously it treats the export argument.
Pakistan wants scam networks shut down and a bigger share of the global outsourcing market at the same time. Those goals are compatible, but only if enforcement can tell the two sectors apart before it kicks in a door.
The post P@SHA Says NCCIA Raids Without Warrants Are Putting Pakistan’s IT Export Contracts at Risk appeared first on PhoneWorld.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Honor has officially revealed its upcoming Honor 700 series in China, confirming three smartphones instead of the previously expected two. The lineup includes the Honor 700, Honor 700 Pro, and a new Honor 700S, with all three devices featuring a secondary display on the back.
The company has listed the smartphones on its official Chinese website, revealing their designs, color options, and memory configurations ahead of the scheduled November 13 launch.
Reservations have also opened in China, giving buyers an early look at what Honor is preparing for its next generation of smartphones.
The biggest design highlight is the small rear display integrated into the camera module. Unlike earlier expectations that this feature would be limited to higher-end models, all three Honor 700 smartphones feature the secondary screen.
The rear display is shown displaying information such as the time and notifications. It may also serve as a viewfinder for capturing selfies using the main cameras.
Earlier Honor 700 Pro leaks had already hinted at a similar design, but the latest listings indicate that the feature extends across the lineup.
Honor has also introduced four color options for the series: Blue Tone, Cold White, Pink Mist, and Clear Sky.
Another interesting detail is the variety of RAM and storage configurations.
The standard Honor 700 will offer the widest selection, with four variants: 12GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB, 16GB/256GB, and 16GB/512GB.
Meanwhile, the Honor 700 Pro will be available in three configurations: 12GB/256GB, 12GB/512GB, and 16GB/512GB.
The newly introduced Honor 700S will have two variants, offering 12GB RAM with either 256GB or 512GB internal storage.
While Honor has revealed the models and configurations, several important hardware details are still based on leaks.
The Honor 700 and Honor 700 Pro are rumored to feature 6.57-inch AMOLED displays, with a smaller secondary screen measuring approximately 1.72 inches on the back.
The Pro model is also tipped to feature a 200MP primary camera, a 50MP periscope telephoto camera, and a battery capacity of around 9,000mAh.
If accurate, the battery upgrade could make the device particularly interesting for users who prioritize longer battery life.
Another rumored feature is support for an external teleconverter lens accessory, potentially offering a focal length equivalent of around 200mm for long-distance photography.
Previous reports about the Honor 700 series teleconverter suggested that Honor is exploring more advanced smartphone photography accessories.
However, the company has not officially confirmed the final camera specifications, battery capacities, or accessory compatibility.
Details about the Honor 700S remain particularly limited, although its positioning suggests it could be the more affordable member of the series.
Honor 700 Series Expected Price and Release Timeline in Pakistan
Honor has scheduled the Chinese launch for November 13, 2026. However, Honor has not yet announced official pricing or global availability details.
For Pakistan, the situation remains uncertain, as Honor has not confirmed whether the three smartphones will receive an official local release.
Based on unofficial Pakistani smartphone listings, the standard Honor 700 could cost around Rs. 199,999.
The Honor 700 Pro could potentially be positioned around Rs. 300,000, although this is an early editorial estimate based on previous-generation pricing rather than a verified retailer listing.
There is currently insufficient reliable pricing information to provide a meaningful estimate for the Honor 700S.
For comparison, earlier Honor 600 and 600 Pro pricing reports suggested that the previous generation could reach approximately Rs. 200,000 and Rs. 300,000, respectively, before local taxes.
If Honor follows a broader international rollout after the Chinese launch, the Honor 700 series could reach additional markets in early 2027.
A possible Pakistani release during the first quarter of 2027 cannot be ruled out, but this remains speculative and should not be treated as a confirmed launch schedule.
The final Pakistani prices would also depend on exchange rates, taxes, official distribution arrangements, and the availability of individual models.
Honor has also reportedly been developing multiple phones with rear displays and large batteries, pointing to a wider push toward more distinctive hardware.
With secondary rear displays, generous RAM options and potentially major camera and battery upgrades, the Honor 700 series could become an interesting competitor in the premium smartphone segment.
However, the actual value of these devices will depend on their final specifications and pricing when Honor officially launches the series.
For Pakistani buyers, the biggest question remains whether Honor will introduce all three models locally or limit availability to selected variants.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
AI unicorn Sarvam has appointed former Google Cloud India managing director Sashikumar Sreedharan as its president and chief business officer (CBO), as it looks to strengthen its enterprise and government business and scale the commercial deployment of its AI technology.
In his new role, Sreedharan will lead Sarvam’s business across enterprises and government institutions while expanding its engagement with digital-native companies, developers and partners. He will also oversee marketing, finance, forward-deployed engineering, service delivery and commercial operations, the company said in a blog post.
Sreedharan will also join the company’s board of directors.
Before joining Sarvam, Sreedharan served as MD of Google Cloud India for over a year. Across a career spanning about 35 years, he has served across companies like Microsoft India, IBM, Wipro, Happiest Mind Technologies, among others.
His appointment comes as Sarvam looks to move beyond developing indigenous AI models and build a larger enterprise business around its technology.
The startup said it provides its full-stack AI offerings to over 100 enterprises and government institutions. “The next phase of Sarvam is about advancing our research, developing products loved by people around the world, and building a company that can operate at a much greater scale,” the startup said.
Sarvam AI’s Push To Build The India Stack
Founded in 2023 by Pratyush Kumar and Vivek Raghavan, Sarvam develops foundational AI models, computing infrastructure, and enterprise applications. Its offerings target businesses and government agencies seeking tools tailored to Indian languages, data-security requirements, and local use cases.
The new CBO appointment comes shortly after Sarvam expanded its AI portfolio with the launch of Prism. The “System One” decision model built on top of Sarvam AI’s Sarvam 105B foundation model. Rather than generating open-ended text token-by-token like a conventional LLM, it evaluates a given context, a question, and a predefined list of options in a single processing pass to return calibrated probabilities for each choice.
The startup has also released several other models in recent months, including Sarvam Vision 2.1, a vision-language model for processing documents and recognising text in Indian languages, and Saaras V4, its speech-to-text model. In October, it launched Bulbul V4 Flash, a text-to-speech model for generating natural speech across Indian languages.
Earlier this year, Sarvam raised $234 Mn in the first close of its $300 Mn Series B funding round, which valued the company at $1.5 Bn. The unicorn minting round saw participation from investors HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners.
It is now reportedly in talks with Nasdaq-listed IT services company Cognizant Technology Solutions to raise further funds for the round. It is looking to raise around $300 Mn at a valuation of around $3.5 Bn to $4 Bn.

OnePlus may introduce a major design change with its next numbered flagship smartphone. An early leak suggests that the upcoming OnePlus 17 could feature a wide-screen design instead of the traditional tall display used in most Android smartphones.
The information comes from Chinese tipster Smart Pikachu, who mentioned the OnePlus 17 in a recent Weibo post. According to the tipster, five high-performance wide-screen smartphones are expected to arrive next year, with their wider displays offering a better field of view for gaming.
OnePlus 17 Leak Hints at a New Wide-Screen Design
Although the tipster did not share detailed specifications, the post suggests that OnePlus could join this emerging smartphone design trend in 2027. The company has not confirmed the information, and details about the OnePlus 17 remain unknown.
The latest leak also follows an earlier report from Digital Chat Station in late October. The tipster suggested that OnePlus might skip the successor to its OnePlus 15T and introduce a wide-screen smartphone instead. However, that report did not specifically mention the OnePlus 17.
Wide-screen smartphones are becoming a new area of interest among Android manufacturers. Huawei introduced this design direction with its Pura X View, while Vivo is also reportedly preparing a compact wide-screen flagship for 2027.
Unlike book-style foldable smartphones, these devices feature a wider candybar-style body without a folding mechanism. Their wider displays could provide more screen space for gaming and other activities.
For comparison, the current OnePlus 16 features a 6.78-inch OLED display with a refresh rate of up to 185Hz for gaming. The phone also comes with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, a 200-megapixel triple-camera system, and a 9,000mAh battery.
See Also: OnePlus Turbo 7 to Launch With 200MP Camera, 185Hz Display and Next-Gen Snapdragon Chip
The OnePlus 16 launched in China in October with a starting price of 5,999 yuan, approximately $897. The company has not announced its global or Indian pricing.
OnePlus has yet to reveal the OnePlus 17’s specifications, display size, camera details, or launch timeline. A newer-generation processor and a large battery could be expected from the next flagship, but these details remain unconfirmed.
For now, the possibility of a wide-screen design is the main detail emerging from the early leak. If accurate, the change could give OnePlus a different approach to its flagship smartphone lineup in 2027.

items.title: Grants aren’t a consolation prize: rethinking non-dilutive capital for early-stage founders
items.summary:
Ask an African founder how they funded their first year and you will often hear a slightly apologetic answer: “We did some grants while we figured out the VC side”. The tone matters. It suggests grants are what you take when the real money says “no” – a holding pattern, a consolation prize for not yet being fundable.
That framing is out of date, and it is costing founders. With venture capital still selective after the funding correction of the last few years, a growing number of early-stage startups across the continent are being built on government grants, foundation programmes, fellowships, cloud credits and small cheques from Web3 ecosystem funds.
The founders who will come out ahead are not the ones who tolerate this capital until a seed round arrives. They are the ones who stack it on purpose.
The recovery didn’t reach the bottom of the funnel
On paper, African tech funding has bounced back. Total investment into the African tech startup ecosystem increased by almost 50 per cent
items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Ask an African founder how they funded their first year and you will often hear a slightly apologetic answer: “We did some grants while we figured out the VC side”. The tone matters. It suggests grants are what you take when the real money says “no” – a holding pattern, a consolation prize for not yet being fundable.
That framing is out of date, and it is costing founders. With venture capital still selective after the funding correction of the last few years, a growing number of early-stage startups across the continent are being built on government grants, foundation programmes, fellowships, cloud credits and small cheques from Web3 ecosystem funds.
The founders who will come out ahead are not the ones who tolerate this capital until a seed round arrives. They are the ones who stack it on purpose.
The recovery didn’t reach the bottom of the funnel
On paper, African tech funding has bounced back. Total investment into the African tech startup ecosystem increased by almost 50 per cent to US$1.64 billion in 2025. Q3 figures for 2026 were up 70 per cent on the corresponding period in 2025, suggesting 2026 will equal or surpass 2025 in terms of funding raised.
That is a healthy sign for scaled fintechs and energy businesses. It is far less comforting for a two-person team in Kigali or Lagos with a prototype and 10 paying customers. Investors are rewarding traction and clear paths to profit, which means the gap between “idea” and “venture-backable” has widened, not narrowed.
Founders have filled that gap with whatever capital doesn’t ask for equity: national innovation agency grants, foundation-backed programmes, fellowships with stipends, prize money from pitch competitions, hyper-scaler cloud credits, and – increasingly – grants and small cheques from blockchain ecosystem funds looking for builders in emerging markets. What began as survival has quietly become a funding layer of its own.
Why “consolation prize” is the wrong frame
The case for taking grants seriously starts with arithmetic. A founder who gives up 10 to 15 per cent of the company in a pre-seed round to buy 12 months of runway has paid for that time with the most expensive currency they own. A founder who buys the same 12 months with three grants and a credits package has paid in paperwork. That is not a lesser outcome. On a cap table, it is a better one.
The second argument is about control. Early VC money arrives with expectations about market size, speed and exit that can push a startup into a shape it isn’t ready for. Grant money gives founders room to do the slow, unglamorous work – regulatory approvals, pilots with public health systems, agri-tech field trials – that many African businesses need before they can scale at all. In sectors such as climate, health and agriculture, the patient capital is often the right capital.
Third, grants are increasingly a signal, not a stigma. Getting through a competitive government or foundation process means a third party has vetted the team, the problem and the budget. Smart investors read that as reduced risk. A startup that walks into a seed conversation with US$150,000 in non-dilutive funding, a pilot and a clean cap table is negotiating from strength, not asking for rescue.
How to stack it on purpose
The difference between a founder who “did some grants” and one who built a non-dilutive capital stack is intent. The second founder treats grants the way a CFO treats a funding plan: mapped, sequenced and tied to milestones. In practice, that looks like five habits.
Give every source a job. Cloud and software credits cover infrastructure. Research and innovation grants pay for product development and pilots. Fellowships buy founder time and networks. A Web3 ecosystem grant funds a specific integration or open-source component. When each pot has a defined purpose, they complement each other instead of overlapping.
Sequence from small to large. A US$5,000 competition win or an accelerator stipend is rarely life-changing, but it is evidence. Use the smaller, faster awards to build a track record that makes the larger, slower government or foundation grants easier to win.
Run it like a pipeline, not a lottery. Keep a calendar of deadlines, eligibility rules and reporting dates across the year. Many founders apply reactively to whatever lands in a WhatsApp group. The ones who win consistently plan 6-12 months ahead and reuse a core application they sharpen each time.
Tie grants to the milestones investors care about. Work backwards from the seed round you eventually want. If investors will ask for a regulatory licence, a paid pilot or a first 1,000 users, point grant money directly at those proofs. Non-dilutive capital is most powerful when it de-risks the next equity cheque.
Read the fine print as a stack, not one by one. Matching-fund requirements, IP clauses, exclusivity terms and restrictions on other funding sources can clash. Check how each new award interacts with the ones you already hold before you sign.
Free money isn’t free
None of this means grants are costless. The most common failure is the professional applicant: a startup that becomes very good at winning programmes and much less good at winning customers. African tech has had its fair share of these. If a founder spends more hours on application forms than on sales calls, the stack has become a crutch.
Reporting is the second hidden cost. Several concurrent grants can mean several sets of quarterly reports, audits and site visits, each in a different format. For a team of three, that overhead is real and should be budgeted for, in time and sometimes in a part-time grants manager.
Third is mission drift. Funders have their own priorities, from gender inclusion to climate impact to digital public goods. Those are often worthy, but a founder who bends the product to fit each new call ends up with a company built to satisfy funders rather than a market.
Web3 money deserves its own warning. Ecosystem grants can be generous and fast, but they may be paid in volatile tokens, tied to building on one chain, or come with expectations about promotion and community activity. Convert what you can, understand any lock-ups, and make sure the protocol’s fortunes are not quietly becoming your own.
Stop apologising for it
The ecosystem has a part to play too. Governments and foundations could make stacking easier by harmonising reporting templates and being explicit about which other funding they allow alongside their own. Investors could stop treating a grant-heavy history as a red flag and start asking the more useful question: what did this founder achieve with the money?
But the biggest shift has to come from founders themselves. Non-dilutive capital is not what you settle for when VCs say no. Used well, it is how you get to a VC conversation on your own terms – or, for some businesses, how you avoid needing one at all. Stack it deliberately, point it at real milestones, and stop apologising for it.
The post Grants aren’t a consolation prize: rethinking non-dilutive capital for early-stage founders appeared first on Disrupt Africa.

items.author: Bismah Malik
items.content:
Quick commerce has tilted the balance for India’s beauty and personal care (BPC) brands. So much so, that some brands are now entirely reliant on quick commerce for growth and reevaluating how much they should invest in horizontal marketplaces.
At roughly $1 Bn in annualised gross merchandise value (GMV), sales of beauty products on quick commerce is growing by about 90% a year, according to Redseer. Separately, Elara Securities estimates the channel will grow to 25-30% of online BPC sales by FY30.
Karan Taurani, executive vice president at Elara Capital, says that BPC as a category was a natural progression for quick commerce platforms after they had figured out the grocery supply chain. “Beauty has got a very premium gross margin, and higher EBITDA margin as compared to other categories.That is why quick commerce is also getting on this aggressively,” Taurani said.
But while the balance is shifting, the contest between quick commerce and ecommerce marketplaces is far from settled.
Marketplaces are still the biggest destinations for shoppers to compare, read reviews and discover new products, especially those with a premium price tag. But the likes of Nykaa, Myntra, Amazon and Flipkart are having to play the game started by Blinkit, Instamart and Zepto to catch up.
For D2C brands, this is the time to recalibrate and optimise for both channels. From sizing their SKUs and dividing their marketing budgets to rethinking how shoppers find them, the brands Inc42 spoke to, are adapting to what they call a “tectonic shift” in consumer behaviour.
And it all started after the sales on quick commerce channels zoomed over the last couple of years.
How Brands Are Recalibrating
It’s not that long ago that marketplaces ruled the market.
“A year ago, they (quick commerce as a channel) didn’t even exist for us. So it’s growing very fast. Our largest channel used to be marketplaces, but that’s not the number one any more,” skincare brand Asaya cofounder and CEO Neeraj Biyani.
Others are reporting a similar boost from quick commerce as consumers splurged during the festive season. At haircare brand Moxie Beauty, whose annualised revenue had crossed ₹100 Cr last December, quick commerce is now the largest channel accounting for more than 30% of sales, cofounder Nikita Khanna told us.
Renee Cosmetics, which reported ₹440 Cr in FY26 revenue, has seen quick commerce’s share of sales grow from about 3% to over 13% in two years.
Typsy Beauty, which raised ₹20 Cr in August to double down on quick commerce and offline retail, is also keeping up with the fast paced trend.
“The biggest change has been quick commerce. A year ago it was a single-digit share of our revenue. Today, it has grown about 5x in absolute terms, faster than any other channel,” Typsy cofounder and CEO Kairavi Bharat Ram said.
That growth has pushed brands to rethink how much they spend on marketplaces vs quick commerce, when it comes to ads as well as in product development.
Quick Commerce Gets The Ad Money
As sales on quick commerce rose, brands have followed up by allocating more budget for visibility. The likes of Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart have reimagined placement of ads in a bid to grow their average order value and this means brands have more real estate to get that all-important click.
“We are spending more on quick commerce since we are selling more on quick commerce. It’s not that we spend more on ads and therefore that channel grows, it’s that people are choosing to buy there. And so then you want to be easily found on the platform where they’re going to be buying their hair care,” added Moxie Beauty’s Khanna.
Social media spending is still the largest part of ad spends, but At Typsy Beauty founder Bharat Ram believes the share going to quick commerce ads has risen through the year, following the shift in sales.
The data also points to a change in how shoppers search. Volumes for 10 generic makeup keywords rose 236% on Blinkit between Q1 2025 and Q2 2026 and fell 76% on Amazon, though Amazon’s volume still appears larger, according to a report by 1DigitalStack (1DS), which was accessed by Inc42.
Quick commerce has not suddenly eliminated marketplace or social media ad costs, but it is becoming a dedicated channel by itself. Awareness is still built elsewhere.
“Most new customers still find us on Instagram, through creator content and reels far more than polished brand ads. A lot of that discovery then converts somewhere else: someone sees a creator video and later searches for us on Nykaa, Blinkit or our website,” says Bharat Ram.
Brands Rethink Pricing, Packaging
The second biggest learning for brands is to customise SKUs and pricing to suit the replenishment cycles and consumption patterns on quick commerce, which typically involves faster stockouts. These are somewhat interlinked because repricing is often forced by SKU resizing.
“We realised that the typical consumer habit on quick commerce apps was not to buy full packs. Our product was usually a last minute purchase. Hence, we had curated special packs for Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart. And that really hit the spot,” Renee Cosmetics cofounder Ashutosh Valani said.
Brands are also curating a combo of small and full size packs depending on the demand from each one of the quick commerce platforms even as some BPC startups say that it is too early a stage to go full throttle on producing small size SKUs across all quick commerce channels.
“Eventually if you find something that works for you, you will continue to purchase that and you will want your regular size. So it’s a very healthy mix,” according to Moxie Beauty’s cofounder.
Founders like Asaya’s Biyani or Bharat Ram of Typsy Beauty warn that the biggest risk for a beauty brand on quick commerce is stockouts. A few days where the product is out of stock from key dark stores costs more than the lost sales. It hurts rank, visibility and results in poor return on advertising.
“Replenishment cycles have gone from monthly to weekly and we had to move from warehouse-level planning to much more frequent, city and SKU-level planning for quick commerce. This requires tighter forecasting around platform sale events,” the Typsy founder said, indicating that brands have had to make changes in their own supply chain operations to meet the rush.
Pricing and discount math is also undergoing a change. Quick commerce should not be necessarily regarded as a cheaper shelf, but it is true that brands encounter more value-conscious shoppers there.
“We agree that value and entry price points gain on quick commerce. We see it less as people trading down and more as quick commerce being where a first try or a top-up happens,” according to Typsy Beauty’s Bharat Ram.
While the average order value may be smaller on quick commerce, the frequency of purchases makes up for that.
Why Ecommerce Marketplaces Still Matter
None of this has, however, made marketplaces optional. The majority of the founders we spoke to say that serious, intent-based shopping is still prevalent in ecommerce. Horizontal as well as vertical marketplaces enjoy a premiumisation moat which is not easy to displace.
PAC Cosmetics, the self-funded makeup brand that crossed ₹100 Cr in FY26 revenue, has stayed off quick commerce thus far.
“Consumers are evolving, and some of them choose convenience. But for an informed decision, many still prefer to see more in front of them: shades, swatches, reviews, and the full range. Staying off quick commerce is a conscious choice, because we’d rather present the brand with clarity than make it available quickly,” said founder and director Bonish Jain.
Elara Capital’s Taurani highlighted that one of the reasons that Nykaa will be tough to beat is the exclusive tie-ups with the niche and international brands, which complements the company’s private label and owned brands business.
Nykaa has also shifted to an inventory-led model, which allows the company more flexibility in negotiating procurement.
“Marketplaces do have their own value. It is not like they can be completely replaced by quick commerce. If you are just looking for what to try, you will go to an Amazon or a Nykaa where you get to see the user experience and reviews, whereas this is not possible on quick commerce,” Moxie Beauty’s cofounder says.
For the past two years, vertical and horizontal marketplaces have been gradually moving to the quick commerce lane, using the learnings of the industry to enable 10-minute deliveries.
Nykaa has hired former Swiggy Instamart COO Ankit Jain to run Nykaa Now, which went to operate from three cities to 13 in a year. Myntra’s M-Now, which runs in over 12 cities, now carries 596 beauty brands, while Flipkart says beauty on Flipkart Minutes grew 5X in a year.
Taurani reads Nykaa Now as defence. “A Nykaa customer doesn’t really want a quick delivery,” he said, indicating that it is more of a need for marketplaces.
Quick commerce, she said, lacks the depth of product content because it is a platform geared towards faster transactions and fulfilment. “The apps don’t want you to get lost in the discovery. They want you to go from home to checkout in 60 seconds or whatever. So that kind of slower discovery, cart building is not happening there. And hence marketplace channels are still quite strong in our category,” Khanna told us.
The early trends indicate that quick commerce and 10-minute delivery models have taken over the beauty aisle. But don’t write off the ‘plain jane’ ecommerce marketplace that may still have a trick or two up its sleeves.
THE STARTUP SPOTLIGHT | HOW FORMIAL LABS IS TAKING THE GUESSWORK OUT OF SKINCARE
Formial Labs aims to address the trial-and-error approach to skincare by offering customised formulations tailored to individual skin concerns, including acne, pigmentation and uneven skin texture.
The startup combines dermatological expertise with personalised treatment plans, seeking to simplify skincare decisions and deliver more targeted solutions.
As India’s beauty market becomes increasingly crowded, Formial is betting on personalisation and professional guidance to differentiate itself from conventional skincare brands and build long-term consumer relationships.
ECOMMERCE BUZZ
Nykaa’s Q2 Profit More Than Triples: Beauty and fashion ecommerce major Nykaa reported a more than threefold jump in its Q2 profit to ₹101 Cr, while revenue grew 28% YoY. The strong performance reflects the company’s growing scale as it continues to expand its beauty and fashion businesses.
Lenskart’s Q2 Profit Surges 125%: Eyewear major Lenskart reported a 125% YoY jump in Q2 profit to ₹233 Cr, while revenue climbed 36%. The numbers highlight the company’s improving profitability alongside its expanding eyewear business.
GIVA Bags ₹975 Cr Funding: Jewellery startup GIVA raised ₹975 Cr in a funding round led by Multiples PE as it doubles down on offline expansion. The company plans to open 160 new stores in FY27, signalling its ambitions to scale its omnichannel jewellery business.
Blue Ashva Exits iD Fresh In ₹50 Cr Deal: Early investor Blue Ashva Capital exited iD Fresh Food by selling its entire stake for ₹50 Cr in a secondary transaction. The deal, co-led by Upsurge India, Triumph Global Fund and White Whale Ventures, saw around 1% equity change hands as the ready-to-cook food brand continues its growth journey ahead of its IPO ambitions.
THE DEEP DIVE
THE OPERATOR QUESTION
How Should Premium Beauty Brands Choose Between Marketplaces And Quick Commerce Without Compromising Their Positioning?
Bonish Jain, founder and director at PAC Cosmetics which targets professional makeup artists and everyday consumers, says these are the five things that matter:
Understand Purchase Behaviour: Not every beauty purchase is driven by convenience. Consumers buying foundations, concealers or setting sprays often want to compare shades, explore swatches, read reviews and understand product performance. The channel should support this decision-making process.
Protect Positioning: Being available everywhere isn’t always the right strategy. Quick commerce screens offer limited room to showcase an extensive portfolio or communicate the brand story. For premium brands, how products are presented matters as much as where they are sold.
Look Beyond Transactions: Marketplaces are more than sales channels. They enable discovery, allowing consumers to explore different categories and products. Alongside influencers, makeup artists and tutorials, they help build brand presence, improve product visibility and strengthen consumer engagement.
Evaluate Channel Economics: Every additional platform requires investment, inventory planning, marketing support and operational bandwidth. Assess the overall contribution of each channel, including opportunities to improve assortment, understand consumer preferences and strengthen platform partnerships.
Prioritise Sustainable Growth: Focus on improving product discovery, online experiences and repeat engagement across existing channels. Evaluate new opportunities, including quick commerce, based on business potential, consumer needs and brand fit. Growth isn’t about being present everywhere, but choosing platforms that support long-term scalability.
[Edited by Nikhil Subramaniam]
