items.summary:
At least 16 people were killed and 13 others injured, including two seriously, in an explosion at a steel plant in western Turkiye on Monday, Turkiye President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said.
Speaking after a cabinet meeting at the Turkish presidential complex in Ankara, President Erdogan said judicial and administrative investigations had been launched to determine the cause of the explosion in Izmir's Aliaga district and identify those responsible.
"An investigation has been launched into the explosion, both judicially and administratively. The cause and circumstances of this tragic incident, which has deeply saddened our nation, as well as any negligence and those responsible, will be established," Erdogan said.
Bugün öğle saatlerinde İzmir Aliağa’dan çok üzücü bir haber aldık.
Bir demir çelik fabrikasında sıvı çelik dökümü yapıldığı esnada meydana gelen patlamada hayatını kaybeden işçi kardeşle
items.author: Anadolu Agency
items.content:
At least 16 people were killed and 13 others injured, including two seriously, in an explosion at a steel plant in western Turkiye on Monday, Turkiye President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said.
Speaking after a cabinet meeting at the Turkish presidential complex in Ankara, President Erdogan said judicial and administrative investigations had been launched to determine the cause of the explosion in Izmir's Aliaga district and identify those responsible.
"An investigation has been launched into the explosion, both judicially and administratively. The cause and circumstances of this tragic incident, which has deeply saddened our nation, as well as any negligence and those responsible, will be established," Erdogan said.
Bugün öğle saatlerinde İzmir Aliağa’dan çok üzücü bir haber aldık.
Bir demir çelik fabrikasında sıvı çelik dökümü yapıldığı esnada meydana gelen patlamada hayatını kaybeden işçi kardeşlerimize Cenab-ı Allah’tan rahmet niyaz ediyor, kederli ailelerine taziyelerimi sunuyorum.…
— Recep Tayyip Erdoğan (@RTErdogan) November 9, 2026
Izmir Governor Suleyman Elban said the explosion occurred at around 11.46am local time (0846GMT) at the HABAS Iron and Steel Plant during furnace replacement work.
Elban said a ceiling crane collapsed, causing materials to fall into an electric arc furnace and triggering an explosion after damaging a natural gas line.
The governor initially reported 10 fatalities and 15 injuries, including four workers in serious condition.
He said search and rescue operations were continuing, with four people believed to be trapped beneath the debris.
İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi:
📌"İzmir Aliağa'da demir çelik fabrikasında patlama meydana geldi, akabinde yangın çıktı."
📌"İlgili birimlerimiz koordineli şekilde sahada arama-kurtarma çalışmalarını sürdürüyor." https://t.co/O9TWRgpIaK
— TRT HABER (@trthaber) November 9, 2026
According to Elban, approximately 200 workers were at the facility during the maintenance operation, compared with more than 300 during regular production shifts. No arrests had been made, and judicial and administrative investigations were underway.
Turkiye Labour and Social Security Minister Vedat Isikhan and Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar were travelling to the region, while Health Minister Kemal Memisoglu was also expected to visit Izmir.

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
A truck carrying goods across India spends several days or even weeks on the road, but it’s not just the vehicle that needs to keep moving. In fact, the technology watching and powering India’s trucking industry never stops, regardless of how slow or fast the journey is, or indeed whether it is the slow sales months or the peak festive season.
It is this technology that has made life easier over the years, for those reliant on India’s trucking system for delivery of parcels and goods. The transformation seen in the past decade has lifted businesses and startups in retail, ecommerce and logistics sectors.
The problem was manifold before technology changed things: Operators have to find loads for their vehicles, negotiate freight rates, make toll payments, track fuel consumption, monitor fleets and arrange financing. For an industry as fragmented as India’s trucking market, these everyday tasks can add to the cost and complexity of running a fleet.
It was this problem that BlackBuck set out to address when it was founded in 2015. The company began as a marketplace connecting truck operators with businesses looking to transport goods. Over the years, it expanded beyond load discovery to build a wider digital platform for truck operators, bringing payments, fleet tracking, freight services and vehicle financing under one umbrella.
Today, its offerings span five business lines — payments, telematics, loads classifieds, superloads and vehicle financing. While payments and telematics form its core businesses, the other three are classified as growth businesses.
What The Q2 Numbers Show
The expansion has translated into higher revenue. In Q2 FY27, BlackBuck reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹235.33 Cr, up 55.7% YoY from ₹151.14 Cr. Its net profit rose 41.8% to ₹41.4 Cr from ₹29.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Total income, including other income, increased 51.4% to ₹253.15 Cr.
But the growth is not coming from its established businesses alone. Revenue from its core Payments and Telematics businesses grew 31% to ₹161.39 Cr, while its growth businesses grew 166% to ₹73.94 Cr.
However, faster growth has its own cost.
Total expenses rose 64% YoY to ₹210.3 Cr during the quarter, with management attributing the increase primarily to customer acquisition across core categories and stepped-up investments in SuperLoads. Meanwhile, EBITDA stood at ₹50.61 Cr and adjusted EBITDA at ₹55.04 Cr.
During the Q2 earnings call, CEO Rajesh Yabaji said upfront acquisition costs can weigh on EBITDA even as the company expects to recover them over the lifetime of a customer. The company’s adjusted EBITDA grew at a slower 29% to ₹55.04 Cr.
“Wherever we see opportunities, we are expanding and gaining more market share. So, as and when there are spurts in customer acquisition, EBITDA suppresses in that particular quarter,” Yabaji said.
Clearly, there is a balancing act at the centre of BlackBuck’s business model. Its established businesses continue to generate operating cash flows, but the company is using that headroom to scale newer offerings. The question is whether these newer businesses can build sustainable economics without diluting the profitability of the core platform. To understand that, first, let’s decode how BlackBuck makes money.
BlackBuck’s Core: Monetising Trucking
While Payments and Telematics form its core businesses, BlackBuck has other verticals that contribute to its topline, including Loads Classifieds, SuperLoads and Vehicle Finance. These make up its newer businesses that leverage the core, and will play a role in BlackBuck’s future growth. But for now, the core is what sustains the trucking company.
BlackBuck earns through commissions, subscriptions, service fees and interest income, depending on the service being offered. Its payments business is built around two major use cases — tolling and fuel purchases. Through its platform, truck operators can buy and manage FASTags, make toll payments and access fuel cards.
BlackBuck earns commissions from banks for distributing and managing FASTags and from oil marketing companies (OMCs) for fuel card distribution and management. It also collects service fees for FASTag issuance, replacement, activation and recharge transactions.
Meanwhile, the telematics segment takes the relationship beyond the toll booth. The business offers GPS-enabled vehicle tracking, fuel sensors and dashcams, with customers paying for devices and related services through subscriptions.
BlackBuck recognises this revenue over the contract period rather than booking the entire amount when a device is sold. This explains why strong device sales do not immediately translate into an equivalent jump in reported revenue.
Most of the revenue acceleration for Telematics device sales in the previous quarter came from state-level AIS mandates. Newer offerings such as fuel sensors and dashcams contributed a smaller share, with dashcams still being piloted.
On The Periphery
BlackBuck’s pitch is to become more than a platform that helps truck operators pay tolls. It wants to be part of several decisions they make while running their businesses.
It is built around getting a truck operator to return to the platform for more of the services needed to keep a truck running. The catch is that each additional service also brings its own costs, execution challenges, and pressure on the bottom line.
The aforementioned newer business segments take BlackBuck further into the freight and financing value chain.
Loads Classifieds is a subscription-led marketplace where shippers post freight requirements and truck operators discover available loads. SuperLoads goes beyond listing loads. It offers managed freight services, matching shippers with truck operators and facilitating truck placements.
BlackBuck earns service income from these transactions, while truck hiring charges add to the cost of running the business.
Lastly, vehicle finance rounds out the offering by helping truck operators access loans to buy used commercial vehicles or raise finance against vehicles they already own.
BlackBuck works mostly through lending partners, which managed around ₹600 Cr of assets on the platform at the time of its Q4 FY26 results, while its own book stood at roughly ₹60 Cr. It earns through fees and interest income.
It earns through fees and interest income associated with the financing activity. The lending business is claimed to be on track to achieve EBITDA break-even in FY27, supported by growth in assets under management on a relatively steady cost base.
The traction across these businesses is reflected in their combined performance. Revenue from BlackBuck’s growth businesses increased 266% to ₹126.51 Cr in FY26. In Q2 FY27, the combined revenue stood at ₹73.94 Cr, up 166% YoY.
What Goes Into Running The Truck Business
The expanding revenue portfolio also comes with a wider cost base. Running a payments platform and selling telematics subscriptions is one thing, but managing freight transactions and facilitating truck placements brings an additional layer of operational expenses.
The company has to spend on people, technology, customer acquisition and, in the case of SuperLoads, truck hiring as well.
Manpower services emerged as the largest named individual expense head at ₹153.3 Cr, compared with ₹118 Cr a year earlier. This was followed by truck hiring charges which is a new cost head for the company from FY26.
The distinction between manpower services and employee benefits is worth noting. Employee benefits expense of ₹160.2 Cr covers the cost of BlackBuck’s employees, including salaries, bonuses, provident fund contributions, ESOP expenses, gratuity and staff welfare.
Manpower services, reported separately under other expenses at ₹153.3 Cr, capture costs associated with outsourced and contract manpower.
Meanwhile, truck hiring charges are particularly interesting in the context of SuperLoads, one of the newer businesses the company has launched to bulk up its customer lifetime value. Unlike a classifieds platform that primarily monetises access to listings, a managed freight business has to coordinate truck availability and placements.
That creates a different cost equation. But BlackBuck does not disclose how much of the ₹74 Cr was specifically attributable to SuperLoads.
The pressure to invest to grow will continue till the end of FY27. During the Q2 earnings call, management said higher customer acquisition spending across core categories and stepped-up investments in SuperLoads contributed to the rise in expenses.
Management also pointed to improving productivity in SuperLoads’ older markets through AI-led matchmaking, which it believes can help improve unit economics as the business expands.
That is the bet BlackBuck is making: spend more to get truck operators and shippers onto the platform, then earn more from each customer through multiple services.
But customer acquisition only works as a growth lever if the additional transactions eventually generate enough revenue to cover the cost of acquiring and serving them. For now, the company is still building out that equation.
The Core Pays For The Growth
BlackBuck’s core businesses are still generating cash, but like many other listed tech companies these days, the company is choosing to reinvest a larger share of that headroom into customer acquisition and newer offerings. The idea is to boost the customer lifetime value and the engagement opportunities.
This is beginning to show up in its operating leverage. CEO Yabaji said the core business historically delivered operating leverage of 70-85%, and at times 100%. In Q2 FY27, this had moderated to around 50% as the company stepped up upfront spending on acquiring customers.
“The nature of the core business continues to be a strong operating cash flow machine for the company. We are giving its due investments wherever needed, and we are seeing in a lot of niches a strong uptick in customer acquisition and revenue growth,” he added.
The lower operating leverage suggests that a larger share of the business’s earnings is being absorbed by the cost of acquiring customers and scaling newer offerings, rather than flowing through as incremental profit.
While the core continues to generate cash, its growth drivers are shifting. Telematics is gaining traction, but the tolling business has not seen a corresponding improvement in monetisation. BlackBuck’s next phase of growth rests on Loads Classifieds, SuperLoads and Vehicle Finance. While all three address different parts of the trucking value chain, they also represent a move beyond the company’s relatively established payments and telematics operations.
However, BlackBuck does not disclose revenue or profitability separately for Loads Classifieds, SuperLoads and Vehicle Finance. This makes it difficult to assess which business is driving the growth, how much each is costing to scale, or whether one is closer to profitability than the others.
For now, the numbers establish that these offerings are gaining traction. But growth alone will not determine whether they strengthen BlackBuck’s business model. The real test will be whether they can generate sustainable returns without relying indefinitely on the core.

items.content:
Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) Deputy Chief Qari Iftikhar has allegedly been taken into custody by unidentified individuals, the party's spokesperson said on Monday.
JUI-F Spokesperson Aslam Ghauri said he and his colleagues were intercepted by men dressed in plain clothes near E-11 in Islamabad, adding that four to five individuals forced them into a vehicle.
He said they also confiscated his mobile phone and other identification documents.
"We were not told which institution these individuals belonged to or why we were being taken into custody," Ghauri highlighted.
جمیعت علماء اسلام پاکستان کے مرکزی ترجمان جناب محمد اسلم غوری صاحب کو تھوڑی دیر پہلے ان کے ساتھیوں سمیت سادہ کپڑوں میں ملبوس اہلکاروں نے گرفتار کر لیا تھا جناب اسلم غوری صاحب کے ساتھ جمیعت علماء اسلام پاکستان اسلام اباد کے نائب امیر جناب قاری افتخار صاحب اور خالد شریف صاحب بھی…
— Aslam Ghauri (@AslamGhauriJUI) November 9, 2026
Ghauri also stated that he and one of his colleagues were driven around the city for approximately an hour before being released. However, he alleged that the unidentified men took Qari Iftikhar away and did not provide any information about his whereabouts.
Iftikhar serves as the deputy chief of JUI-F and is also in charge of the party's Islamabad office.
There was no immediate official statement from the relevant authorities regarding the alleged incident.
The arrest comes amid growing tensions between the government and the JUI-F following the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa.
Following the imposition of the emergency and governor's rule, Fazl accused the government of backing out of negotiations with the PTI and the opposition despite initially agreeing to their demands.
He categorically rejected the imposition of governor's rule or an emergency in K-P, saying that if an emergency had to be imposed, it should be imposed on the federal government, which he described as illegitimate.
The criticism subsequently spilt over into the assembly, escalating the war of words between the government and the JUI-F chief. Fazl had accused the government of misusing the Constitution.
Federal ministers hit back, accusing the JUI-F chief of overlooking his own role in forming and toppling governments.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi criticised Fazl over his opposition to governor's rule in the province, suggesting that the religious-political leader was unhappy at not being offered a role in the new provincial setup.
Later, a delegation of the PTI and TTAP expressed full support for the JUI-F chief's speech in the National Assembly and condemned what it described as his character assassination by government ministers following his strong criticism of the government's actions.

items.author: AFP
items.content:
President Donald Trump's "Board of Peace" said Monday that Israel needed to act immediately to help war-battered Gaza cope with impending winter, saying measures ahead of deadly floods had been insufficient.
"The situation no longer represents simply a threat posed by the approaching winter, but an immediate humanitarian emergency," the Board of Peace said in a statement.
Heavy rain over the past two days has swept away tens of thousands of tents in the territory, where virtually the entire population has been displaced at least once, and killed at least five people, according to Hamas-led authorities in Gaza.
Statement by the Board of Peace on Recent Flooding and Urgent Winterization Needs in Gaza pic.twitter.com/lWxKhPxGeH
— Board of Peace (@BoardOfPeace) November 9, 2026
The Board of Peace, tasked with implementation of an October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire announced between Israel and Hamas, said it had been warning Israel, which controls all entry into the territory, of the need to prepare both for the winter and seasonal flooding.
Moments before the statement came out, the Israeli military said it had allowed more than 8,200 trucks to enter the Gaza Strip with supplies including 91,000 tents.
The Board of Peace acknowledged steps being taken by Israel but said that they remain "insufficient".
"We call on the leadership of the current Government of Israel to act immediately to authorise and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterisation and humanitarian supplies," it said.
Israel has taken a biting tone against Hamas over the floods, saying the militant group should have invested in infrastructure instead of weaponry.
"Hamas doesn't get to escape responsibility every time it rains," the Israeli foreign ministry posted Sunday on X.
Palestinian Hamas’s own videos show it digging up water pipes and turning them into rockets to attack Israel.
Infrastructure meant to serve Gazans is sacrificed to fuel Hamas’s war.
When the rains come and sewage floods Gaza’s streets, outrage should be directed at Hamas. pic.twitter.com/Ri11O4T2UO
— Israel Foreign Ministry (@IsraelMFA) November 9, 2026
The Board of Peace also called on Hamas to abide by commitments under the ceasefire.
Despite the truce, Israel has kept up nearly daily strikes in Gaza.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is fighting for his political survival following tight elections last month, has vowed to kill anyone involved in Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack, the deadliest day ever for Israel.

Trump to meet Iran war mediator Qatar, no imminent deal seen to end the war
items.summary:
US ​President Donald Trump will meet the prime minister of key mediator Qatar on Monday as efforts to end the Iran war ramp up following last week's ‌midterm elections, though senior US and Gulf officials cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.
More than eight months into the conflict he launched alongside Israel on February 28, Trump has played down the likelihood of major warfare restarting soon but remains unwilling to accept an existing Iranian truce plan.
Mutual attacks continue, with the US striking Iran's Qeshm island overnight, according to Iranian state media, and Iran attacking tankers in the Gulf and ​Strait of Hormuz this month while its Yemeni Houthi allies have hit Saudi Arabia.
Diplomatic moves
Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, who is both prime minister and foreign minister of ​Qatar, will meet Trump and Vice President JD Vance in Washington later on Monday after having visited Tehran last week.
Read: Israel, US negotiating new multiyear military aid
items.author: Reuters
items.content:
US ​President Donald Trump will meet the prime minister of key mediator Qatar on Monday as efforts to end the Iran war ramp up following last week's ‌midterm elections, though senior US and Gulf officials cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal.
More than eight months into the conflict he launched alongside Israel on February 28, Trump has played down the likelihood of major warfare restarting soon but remains unwilling to accept an existing Iranian truce plan.
Mutual attacks continue, with the US striking Iran's Qeshm island overnight, according to Iranian state media, and Iran attacking tankers in the Gulf and ​Strait of Hormuz this month while its Yemeni Houthi allies have hit Saudi Arabia.
Diplomatic moves
Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, who is both prime minister and foreign minister of ​Qatar, will meet Trump and Vice President JD Vance in Washington later on Monday after having visited Tehran last week.
Read: Israel, US negotiating new multiyear military aid agreement: report
Iran's proposal to end ⁠the war involves an end to the US blockade of its ports, the lifting of some sanctions and a halt to bombing in return for Tehran stopping its own blockade ​of the Strait of Hormuz, with talks on its nuclear programme and other sanctions to follow.
The US has repeatedly rejected that plan, which Iran has said could be condensed to a ​two-day timeframe, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio describing Tehran's conditions on Sunday as "outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic".
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei defended the plan on Monday as the most reasonable offer on the table.
Senior US Republicans, including Vance, have blamed their party's losses in last week's elections on the Iran war, but despite growing domestic political pressure to end the conflict, Rubio said he did not believe ​a diplomatic breakthrough was imminent.
Read more: Iran, China discuss Yemen crisis, future regional security arrangements
A senior United Arab Emirates official, Anwar Gargash, echoed that view on Monday, saying a comprehensive political settlement between the US and Iran appeared difficult.
"We should ... ​prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted," he said.
Vance, who led the negotiations for a short-lived truce in June, ‌will also ⁠meet Al-Thani, whose country has been a prime mediator since early in the war, conveying messages between the sides and proposing ways to bridge their differences.
Anxiety over the war has pervaded the region for months, and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said on Monday he had told Trump that Ankara did not want to see a new escalation.
"We emphasise at every opportunity that it is possible to resolve these issues through dialogue and diplomacy. Unfortunately, we see a negative shift once again. We are doing our utmost to prevent this," Erdogan told reporters.
Military action
Sunday ​night's strikes on Qeshm island did not impact ​vital infrastructure or services, a provincial ⁠official told Iran's semi-official Fars news agency on Monday. The US has not commented on the Iranian media reports.
A senior Iranian source told Reuters that US strikes were targeting Iranian radar systems serving both air defence and ship navigation, as well as bases for missile launchers ​and mine-laying systems.
Also Read: Iran open to negotiations to end ‘no war, no peace’ situation: Iranian president
Attacks on tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz ramped up sharply in October and have continued at the ​highest rate since the ⁠start of the war, figures from international maritime agencies showed last week.
Iran, which typically does not acknowledge striking vessels that report being hit by projectiles, said on Sunday a tanker had hit a mine east of the Strait of Hormuz.
A state television reporter said on Monday that 11 tankers had been "disabled" over the past 10 days.
The war has triggered a global energy shortage, prompted Iranian ⁠strikes on Gulf ​Arab countries, spilt over into a major Israeli offensive in Lebanon during the spring and summer and reignited ​Yemen's long-frozen civil war.
On Sunday, Yemen's Iran-allied Houthi group said it had struck an office building of Saudi state oil company Aramco in Riyadh. The attack blew out windows across several floors of a building in the city's financial district. The ​Energy Ministry acknowledged damage from an attempted attack on the building without assigning responsibility.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
The Tehreek Tahaffuz-e-Ain Pakistan (TTAP) on Monday condemned the alleged use of force by state authorities against unarmed civilians in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), describing the reported loss of life and suppression of public demands as unacceptable, and called for immediate negotiations with protesters to quell the unrest and end the violence.
The statement comes as Rawalakot is currently gripped by unrest amid alleged clashes between security forces and supporters of the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) rights group, with casualties reported.
In a statement issued on the situation in AJK, the alliance said the government had initially opted to negotiate with the JAAC but later chose to suppress the movement instead of making practical progress on its demands.
“Firing on unarmed civilians, the loss of human lives and the suppression of public voices are unacceptable under any circumstances,” the statement said.
“The state's responsibility is to protect its citizens, not to allow them to be killed at the hands of its own institutions,” it added.
ترجمان تحریک تحفظ آئین پاکستان کی جانب سے آزاد کشمیر کی صورتحال پر جاری کردہ بیان
آزاد کشمیر میں نہتے شہریوں پر ریاستی طاقت کا استعمال، انسانی جانوں کا ضیاع اور عوامی مطالبات کو جبر سے دبانے کی پالیسی ناقابلِ قبول ہے، فوری مذاکرات کیے جائیں: تحریک تحفظ آئین پاکستان
اسلام آباد:… pic.twitter.com/zKkmAFibzo
— Tehreek-e-Tahafuz-e-Ayin-e-Pakistan (@TTAP_OFFICIAL) November 9, 2026
The alliance said a high-level TTAP delegation travelling to AJK to meet protesters, express solidarity with them and assess the situation had been stopped at Kahuta and not allowed to proceed.
“This action not only restricts political and democratic activities and the right to freedom of movement but also raises concerns about the government's intentions and its attempt to keep political leadership and the public away from the ground realities,” the statement said.
“There is no justification for preventing a peaceful political delegation from reaching the protesters. The government must explain this decision, which it has yet to do,” it added.
The TTAP called for immediate and meaningful negotiations with the protesters and practical progress on their demands.
It demanded that the bodies of all those allegedly killed by state forces be handed over to their families without delay. It also called for transparent and impartial investigations into reported civilian deaths and the use of force to identify those responsible.
The alliance urged the authorities to provide immediate medical treatment to the injured and ensure that arrested individuals had access to justice in accordance with legal requirements. It also demanded compensation for damage to public and private property.
Read: PML-N's ex-AJK PM Raja Haider appeals to authorities to 'intervene before it's too late' in Rawalakot
The statement called for the TTAP delegation and other political and social representatives to be given unrestricted access to affected people and protesters in AJK.
“Using force to suppress public protests, making unnecessary arrests and taking measures that could lead to further bloodshed must stop immediately,” it said.
The alliance said using force instead of addressing public demands, withdrawing from negotiations and restricting the movement of political representatives would further aggravate the situation.
“The government must refrain from such actions and ensure the protection of citizens' lives and property,” it said.
The TTAP said the people of AJK were not alone and pledged to raise its voice at every constitutional and legal forum to protect their constitutional, democratic and fundamental rights.
“There can be no justification for suppressing the voice of public rights through state force or taking the lives of innocent citizens. Preventing further bloodshed, ensuring justice for those killed and resolving public demands through negotiations are the government's immediate responsibilities,” the statement said.
Sindh Rangers Naik succumbs to injuries sustained in Rawalakot firing
Meanwhile, a Naik of the Sindh Rangers who was injured in firing at an AJK police post in Rawalakot on Nov 5 died of his injuries on Sunday, the AJK Police spokesperson said in a statement.
The deceased, identified as Naik Bostan Khan, belonged to Kohat district and was serving with the Sindh Rangers. He had been deployed alongside AJK Police at the latter's request to assist in maintaining law and order in the region.
pic.twitter.com/0z3OrDBItB
— AJKPolice (@AJKPoliceCPO) November 9, 2026
Also Read: AJK orders registration of all weapon licences within 10 days
It said law enforcement personnel were making sacrifices while carrying out their responsibilities to protect people's lives and property and maintain law and order. Naik Bostan Khan's death was among those sacrifices, it added.
The AJK Police expressed grief over his death and extended condolences to his family.
“Such cowardly acts cannot undermine the morale of law enforcement agencies,” the statement said.
It added that the state remained committed to protecting the public, restoring law and order and ensuring the rule of law.
Those involved in attacks on law enforcement personnel would be brought to justice in accordance with the law, the statement said.
JAAC council calls for end to force, independent probe
The Advisory Council of the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKJAAC) has expressed grave concern over the tense situation in Rawalakot and surrounding areas, calling for an immediate end to firing, an independent investigation into the incidents and negotiations between the government and the committee.
In a statement, the council said peaceful assembly, freedom of expression and public participation were democratic rights, adding that alleged wrongdoing by individuals should not be used to justify collective force against an entire community or demonstrators.
It urged all parties to exercise restraint, avoid violence and refrain from actions or statements that could heighten tensions.
The JKJAAC Advisory Council calls for an immediate end to firing on civilians in Rawalakot. We urge the authorities to return the bodies of those killed to their families, ensure immediate treatment for the injured and restore mobile and internet services.
We call on the… pic.twitter.com/MGFFACDUJJ
— JKJAAC (@JKJAAC_) November 8, 2026
The council called for the immediate return of the bodies of those killed to their families, along with formal condolences and appropriate support. It also demanded safe and non-discriminatory medical treatment for the injured, restoration of mobile and internet services, and a verified list of detainees, including their places of detention and legal status.
It further called for safe access to peaceful assembly, media coverage, legal assistance and impartial human rights monitoring.
The advisory council urged the political leadership of Azad Jammu and Kashmir, the Bar Council, bar associations, civil society, media and human rights representatives to form an impartial, credible and unarmed joint delegation without delay.
It said it was ready to facilitate a national fact-finding and reconciliation delegation's visit to Rawalakot.
The proposed delegation would visit the sit-in and affected areas, hear from protesters, residents, injured people, bereaved families and relevant authorities, and preserve evidence relating to deaths, injuries, arrests, alleged use of weapons and damage to property.
The council proposed that the delegation issue a preliminary public report within 48 hours, outlining established facts, urgent recommendations and disputed matters. It should also help establish communication between the parties and facilitate negotiations.
The statement called for an independent, impartial, transparent and time-bound investigation into all deaths, injuries, arrests and allegations of unlawful force, armed activity or incitement. It said the investigation's terms, evidence-preservation arrangements and deadline for publication should be defined in writing, adding that no allegation should be treated as established without verifiable evidence.
For negotiations, the council proposed that the government and the Joint Awami Action Committee nominate authorised delegations and hold an initial meeting within 24 hours at a mutually acceptable neutral venue. The parties should agree on an agenda, record decisions in writing and set implementation deadlines.
It also urged political leaders to hear directly from affected residents and protest representatives rather than rely solely on closed-door briefings.
The advisory council said it did not support hatred, threats or retaliation against any person, party or institution.
“Our sole purpose is to protect life, uphold the rule of law, establish the facts impartially and secure a dignified political solution,” it said.
“A peaceful route remains available, and every party has a duty to take it before further loss of life occurs,” the statement added.
It urged all sides not to allow disagreements to turn into enmity or protests to escalate into confrontation, saying human life, civic dignity, the rule of law and collective peace must come first.
The unrest in AJK stems from a prolonged protest movement led by the JAAC for constitutional and governance reforms, including the abolition of 12 refugee-reserved seats in the AJK Legislative Assembly, an end to privileges for the political elite and changes to the quota system.
Tensions escalated after the AJK government proscribed the JAAC on June 6, ahead of a planned long march and protest on June 9. The government said 35 of the committee's 38 demands had been accepted or implemented, yet they allegedly resorted to a series of violent attacks on state-backed personnel and assets.
"The Government of AJ&K has reasonable grounds to believe that Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JK-JAAC), also known by the names Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and Awami Action Committee (AAC), is engaged in terrorism," the notification stated.
Read More: Tarar alleges JAAC behind AJK unrest, claims group backed by Indian funding
On June 11, the government reinstated 177 FIRs against JAAC members, withdrawing concessions previously granted under an October 4, 2025 agreement. Authorities accused the committee of violating the agreement by returning to street protests.
The situation further deteriorated in July, when clashes between protesters and law enforcement personnel in Rawalakot resulted in casualties. The HRCP subsequently called for an independent investigation as the two sides presented conflicting narratives.
In August, the PML-N formed a government in the region after securing a majority in the AJK elections, with Barrister Syed Iftikhar Ali Gilani elected as the prime minister.
However, tensions have persisted despite the formation of a new government, with protests and clashes reported in Rawalakot and Muzaffarabad. The Express Tribune could not independently verify the authenticity of the claims.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Samsung is preparing to introduce two more Galaxy A series smartphones in Pakistan. The Samsung Galaxy A08 and Galaxy A18 are expected to arrive soon, and specification sheets shared ahead of their local release give us a closer look at what buyers can expect.
Both phones are listed with 6.7-inch displays, 90Hz refresh rates, Android 17 with One UI 9, IP64 protection and six generations of OS updates. However, the two models target different buyers: the Galaxy A08 focuses on battery life and affordability, while the Galaxy A18 offers a Super AMOLED screen and a more versatile camera setup.
Samsung Galaxy A08: 6,000mAh Battery and Helio G99+
According to the supplied product sheet, the Galaxy A08 features a 6.7-inch HD+ PLS Infinity-U display with a resolution of 720 × 1600 pixels and a 90Hz refresh rate. It is powered by the MediaTek Helio G99+ chipset, listed as a 6nm octa-core processor clocked at up to 2.2GHz.
The device is expected in 4GB and 6GB RAM options with 64GB or 128GB storage, alongside microSD expansion of up to 2TB. For photography, the phone has a 50MP main camera, a 2MP depth sensor and an 8MP front camera.
Its standout feature is a 6,000mAh battery with 25W charging. Other listed features include a side-mounted fingerprint scanner, IP64 dust and water resistance, and Dark Blue, Silver and Green colour options. The phone weighs approximately 197g.
Samsung Galaxy A18: Super AMOLED Display and 50MP Camera
The Galaxy A18 moves a step higher with a 6.7-inch Full HD+ Super AMOLED Infinity-U display, offering a 2340 × 1080 resolution and 90Hz refresh rate. The specification sheet lists two possible chipsets—Exynos 1610 and MediaTek Helio G99+—but does not clarify which processor will be used in the Pakistan variant.
The Galaxy A18 is listed with 6GB or 8GB RAM and 128GB or 256GB storage, with microSD expansion up to 2TB. On the camera front, it features a 50MP main sensor, a 5MP ultrawide camera and a 2MP macro camera, while a 13MP front camera handles selfies and video calls.
Samsung is expected to equip the Galaxy A18 with a 5,000mAh battery and 25W charging. It also features IP64 protection, a side-mounted fingerprint reader and a weight of around 196g. Listed colour options are Black, Silver and Light Blue.

Samsung has not provided a confirmed Pakistan launch date or official local retail prices for the Galaxy A08 and Galaxy A18 in the information shared with us. Both are expected to join the company’s budget and affordable mid-range lineup soon.
For buyers, the choice could be straightforward. The Galaxy A08 looks more attractive for those who prioritise battery endurance, while the Galaxy A18 offers a sharper AMOLED display, higher-resolution selfie camera and an ultrawide lens. Their final value will depend on Samsung’s Pakistan pricing.

Which Samsung Phones Have Become More Expensive?
In the budget segment, the Galaxy A07 6GB/128GB now costs Rs 69,999, up from Rs 68,500. Its 4GB/128GB and 4GB/64GB versions have increased by Rs 2,000 each, reaching Rs 58,999 and Rs 47,999, respectively.
For the Galaxy A17 range, the 5G 8GB/256GB model has moved from Rs 99,999 to Rs 104,999. The standard Galaxy A17 8GB/256GB is now Rs 99,999, while the 6GB/128GB variant has risen to Rs 76,999.
Higher up the lineup, the Galaxy A27 8GB/256GB has received a Rs 7,501 increase, taking its price to Rs 127,500. The Galaxy A37 8GB/256GB is now priced at Rs 154,999 after a Rs 5,000 increase.
The Galaxy A57 lineup has also become costlier. The 8GB/256GB version now sells at an RRP of Rs 174,999, while the 12GB/256GB and 12GB/512GB variants are listed at Rs 194,999 and Rs 234,999, respectively.
What Does This Mean for Buyers?
The revisions affect both entry-level and mid-range buyers, with some variants crossing key price thresholds. For example, the Galaxy A17 5G 8GB/256GB now costs over Rs 100,000, while the Galaxy A57 12GB/512GB is priced at nearly Rs 235,000.
These figures are recommended retail prices; actual shop offers may vary. Buyers should confirm the latest price, official warranty and availability with their retailer before making a purchase. No reason for the latest revision was specified in the price list shared with PhoneWorld.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Nigerian solar-powered cooling startup Koolboks has secured a credit facility from TLG Capital, which it will use to fund inventory and expand its retail and appliance partnerships.
Launched in 2018 by Ayoola Dominic and Deborah Gaël, Koolboks sells solar-powered freezers and appliances to traders, small businesses and corporate customers in Nigeria and beyond. Its products combine solar panels, patented ice-battery technology and connected pay-as-you-go capabilities, allowing them to provide cooling day and night, including during power outages.
Koolboks has sold more than 15,000 units to date and has shipped to over 25 markets. It assembles its products in Lagos and employs around 400 people across Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda. Its Koolbuy platform extends its pay-as-you-go technology to household appliances from major brands.
The new facility combines TLG’s private credit with a guarantee from Cascador, a Nigeria-focused platform for growth-stage founders that recently invested in Koolboks, delivered in partnership with Morgan Stanley. It will give Koolboks the working capital needed to meet growing demand across African markets.
“TLG recognised what our product means for our customers, and found the right kind of financing to back it at the pace that we needed,” said Dominic, who serves as Koolboks’ CEO. “We have serious ambitions to address cold-chain infrastructure across Africa, and this facility gives us the capital and support to chase them.”
The deal takes TLG’s commitments to US$65 million across 16 Nigerian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) over the past two years. It is the second deal TLG and Cascador have completed together in the space of a few weeks, having provided a US$3 million credit facility to Nigeria’s Drive45 Mobility.
“Koolboks has built an incredibly innovative product that addresses critical challenges for individuals and SMEs. Its ability to scale in recent years is a testament to the ingenuity of its cold chain solution,” said Isha Doshi, co-founder and partner at TLG Capital.
Trish Thomas, chief executive officer of Cascador, said her organisation had partnered with Koolboks for several years.
“Their product clearly solves a real problem that exists across countless markets, and they are building at a scale we always believed was possible,” she said. “Cascador finds local champions, but the question is always around positioning them with the right type of financing. With two deals closed in a matter of weeks, TLG and Cascador have identified a scalable product that will allow us to reach the businesses, countries, and sectors that matter most.”

items.author: Nshua Cali-Dibang
items.content:
How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
Originally published on Global Voices
Illustration by Nshua Cali-Dibang. Used with permission.
This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.
Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user. Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant. Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.
As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, technology companies are finding new ways to use data to develop their products, personalize services and generate revenue. While these developments offer considerable benefits, they also raise a difficult question: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
The issue extends beyond privacy policies and user agreements. It concerns the growing power of technology companies to collect information, draw conclusions about individuals, and influence the digital environments in which people communicate, work, and access information.
The business of knowing more about us
In September 2024, the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published findings from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch.
The FTC reported that these companies collected extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users. The information included personal details, interests, online activities, and data obtained from other sources. The investigation also raised concerns about lengthy data retention, inadequate privacy protections, and the use of personal information in automated systems, including AI.
The report highlighted a fundamental imbalance: Companies can accumulate substantial information about individuals, while those individuals may have limited understanding of how their data is used or how to prevent certain uses.
AI adds another dimension to this problem. Data can help train models, improve recommendations, and power automated decisions. However, the greater the volume and variety of information companies can access, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on its collection and use.
The concern is not that every company collecting data is necessarily acting maliciously. Rather, it is that systems designed to maximize commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.
Inclusion at what cost?
For millions of people, AI offers opportunities that were previously difficult to access. Students can use AI tools to support learning, small businesses can improve their operations, and journalists can explore new approaches to research and production.
In countries such as Nigeria, where access to resources and professional services can be uneven, these tools could help narrow certain gaps. AI systems that support local languages and reflect diverse cultural experiences could also make digital services more accessible.
Yet inclusion should mean more than allowing people to use a technology. It should also mean ensuring that they understand the conditions under which they use it and retain meaningful rights over their information.
Many digital services are governed by lengthy terms and privacy policies that users may accept without fully understanding the implications. Some AI products also raise questions about whether information submitted through prompts, uploaded documents, or other interactions may be retained or used to improve models.
The precise practices differ between companies and products. Nevertheless, users need clear explanations of what information is collected, why it is needed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for purposes beyond the immediate service.
Without these safeguards, the benefits of AI inclusion risk coming with an invisible cost: reduced control over personal information.
When corporate power begins to resemble surveillance
The connection between big tech and authoritarianism requires careful examination. Authoritarianism is not simply the collection of data by private companies. It involves the concentration and exercise of power in ways that undermine accountability, rights, and freedoms.
However, extensive corporate data collection can create conditions that make surveillance easier. Detailed personal information can support profiling, targeted persuasion and the prediction of individual behavior. Depending on the circumstances, businesses, governments, or other actors may exploit these capabilities.
The risks become particularly serious when personal data can be accessed or shared without adequate safeguards, when automated systems make consequential decisions without meaningful oversight, or when people have little opportunity to challenge how their information is used.
Concentrated corporate power adds another concern. When a small number of companies control widely used digital platforms, AI services, and large pools of information, individuals may have few practical alternatives. Leaving a platform may mean losing access to professional networks, customers, communities, or essential services.
This does not mean that every AI system is a surveillance tool or that every technology company intends to restrict freedom. It means that the infrastructure of digital life deserves scrutiny because its capabilities can be used in ways that extend beyond their original commercial purpose.
Nigeria’s data protection challenge
Nigeria has a legal framework intended to protect individuals against the misuse of their personal information. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and provides a framework for the lawful, fair and accountable processing of personal data.
Legislation is an important step, but effective protection also depends on implementation, public awareness, and regulators’ ability to hold organizations accountable.
As Nigerians increasingly adopt AI-powered services, questions about data governance become more pressing. Users need to understand their rights, while organizations must take responsibility for explaining their practices and protecting the information they collect.
There is also a wider question of representation. If AI systems are developed using data that inadequately reflects Nigerian languages, cultures, and social realities, their benefits may be distributed unevenly. Responsible AI governance must therefore address both the protection of personal information and the inclusion of communities whose experiences are often underrepresented.
UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence emphasizes privacy, data protection, transparency, accountability, and fairness throughout the AI lifecycle. These principles provide a useful foundation for ensuring that technological progress respects human rights.
Innovation must not come at the expense of control
The challenge is not to reject AI or prevent companies from using data to develop useful technologies. It is to establish boundaries that allow innovation without making personal privacy an acceptable casualty.
Technology companies should minimize unnecessary data collection, communicate their policies clearly, provide meaningful choices, and strengthen protections against unauthorized access. Regulators must ensure that existing laws remain effective as AI capabilities evolve, while users need accessible information about the rights available to them.
Ultimately, digital inclusion cannot be measured solely by the number of people using AI. It must also consider whether those people can participate safely, understand the systems they rely on, and exercise meaningful control over their information.
As AI becomes more powerful, the question is no longer simply what technology can do with our data. It is who decides what can be done, who benefits from those decisions, and who has the power to challenge them.
The future of AI should not be defined only by what machines learn about us, but also by how much control we retain over ourselves.
Written by Nshua Cali-Dibang

items.author: Sangita Swechcha
items.content:
‘We no longer see Nepali literature as something confined by geographical boundaries.’
Originally published on Global Voices
Rishi Ram Adhikari delivering a speech at the Kitab Jatra Festival held in London in August 2026. Photo by Kushal Shrestha. Used with permission.
The Kitab Jatra Festival has quickly become one of the most vibrant platforms for celebrating Nepali literature, books and culture. The Festival is organised and hosted by the Kitab Yatra Foundation, a Nepal-based organisation promoting literature, reading, art and cultural exchange. Since its launch in 2018, the festival has grown from a local gathering into a dynamic international event, connecting readers and writers not only across Nepal but also in India, the UK, and the USA, with plans to expand to Dubai, Australia, Portugal, Belgium and Germany. Working in collaboration with various organisations and institutions, it has created a global stage where Nepali voices are shared, celebrated and amplified.
At the heart of this movement is Rishi Ram Adhikari, Founder and Chairman of the Kitab Yatra Foundation and the Kitab Yatra book distribution company. In his early 30s, he emerged as a cultural entrepreneur dedicated to promoting Nepali literature and fostering a reading culture. His initiatives have not only expanded literary festivals abroad but also established over 20 libraries across Nepal and introduced scholarship programs for students.
Recognising these remarkable contributions, Kitab Yatra and Rishi Ram were honoured with the 5th edition of the Tally MSME Honours 2025 and the Public Choice ICT Award in 2019 for their pioneering efforts in enriching the Nepali literary world. This accolade further highlights his role as one of the leading advocates for Nepali literature today.
Sangita Swechcha from Global Voices interviewed Adhikari via email.
Sangita Swechcha (SS): What inspired you to start the Kitab Yatra book distribution company and the Kitab Jatra Festival at such a young age?
Rishi Ram Adhikari (RRA): My inspiration came from a simple but important realisation: books can transform individuals, and individuals can transform society. However, for that transformation to happen, books must be accessible, reading must become a habit and literature must be connected to people’s everyday lives.
Through Kitab Yatra, we began working to make books more accessible to readers across Nepal. But I gradually realised that distributing books alone was not enough. We also needed to create excitement around reading, bring writers and readers together, and make literature a part of public conversation. That realisation led to the Kitab Jatra Festival.
In my childhood, I listened to the chanting of my father reciting some slogans [from the epics] Mahabharat and Ramayan. While studying as a Chartered Accountant (CA) in New Delhi, India, despite my accounting career, I realised the value of words rather than numbers, so I dropped CA and came back to Nepal with four sacks of books and started an online bookstore in Kathmandu, Nepal. I believe young people should not wait for opportunities to create meaningful change; they should take the initiative to build them. Our journey has been driven by that belief, along with the dedication of our team, authors, partners and readers.
Book Exhibition at the 7th Edition of Kitab Jatra Festival in Nepal, December 2025. Photo by Kitab Jatra. Used with permission.
SS: How has the festival evolved since its beginnings in Nepal in 2018 to now being hosted in countries like the UK, USA, India, Portugal, Belgium, and Germany?
RRA: Since its beginning in 2018, Kitab Jatra has grown from a relatively small literary gathering into a broader platform for literature, culture and meaningful dialogue. What began with a limited number of voices and a single stage has developed into a festival bringing together writers, artists, thinkers, policymakers, entrepreneurs and readers from different generations.
The most important evolution has been in our ambition. We no longer see Nepali literature as something confined by geographical boundaries. Our international journey, including our work and outreach connected with the UK and other European countries, is an effort to connect Nepali writers with the diaspora and wider literary communities.
However, international expansion is not simply about taking a festival to another country. It is about building meaningful local partnerships, understanding the audience and creating a sustainable platform. Our goal is to make Kitab Jatra a bridge between Nepal and the world while ensuring that Nepali language, literature and cultural identity remain at its heart.
SS: What challenges do you face in promoting Nepali literature internationally, and how do you overcome them?
RRA: One of the biggest challenges is the limited international visibility of Nepali literature. We have talented writers, powerful stories, rich literary traditions and diverse cultural experiences, but many of these works remain inaccessible to international readers because of language barriers, limited translation opportunities, distribution challenges and insufficient global promotion.
Another challenge is sustainability. Organizing a meaningful literary festival requires financial resources, institutional partnerships, professional coordination and long-term commitment.
We are addressing these challenges by building partnerships with literary organizations, publishers, universities, diaspora institutions and cultural communities. We also want to encourage translation, book exchanges and conversations that introduce Nepali writing to audiences unfamiliar with our language and culture.
I believe we must move beyond simply asking the world to notice Nepali literature. We must create professional platforms, produce quality literary experiences and build lasting relationships that make such recognition possible. Our approach is to turn individual opportunities into long-term cultural connections.
Kitab Jatra Festival, 5th Edition Inaugural Session, New Delhi, India in February 2026. Photo Credit: Kitab Jatra. Used with permission.
SS: How do you see the role of the diaspora community in keeping Nepali literature and reading culture alive abroad?
RRA: The Nepali diaspora has a vital role in preserving and promoting our language, literature and cultural identity. For Nepalese living abroad, books can become a connection to their roots, history, memories, and sense of belonging. For younger generations growing up outside Nepal, literature can help them understand their heritage while encouraging them to explore their identity in a changing world.
I see the diaspora not merely as an audience but as an active partner in this literary journey. They can support Nepali authors, establish reading communities, organize literary discussions, introduce Nepali books to local libraries and connect our writers with international institutions.
Through Kitab Jatra’s international initiatives, we want to create spaces where these stories can travel across borders and where the diaspora can contribute to a living, evolving Nepali literary culture.
SS: Kitab Yatra Foundation has also been active inside Nepal, establishing libraries and supporting students — how do you balance its work at home and abroad?
RRA: For us, the work inside Nepal and our international initiatives are two sides of the same mission. We cannot talk about taking Nepali literature to the world while ignoring the need to make books accessible to people in our own communities.
Through our work in book distribution, library initiatives and student support, we aim to bring books closer to people — particularly those who have fewer opportunities to access them. Establishing libraries is not just about providing shelves and books; it is about creating spaces where curiosity can grow, young people can discover their potential, and communities can develop a lasting relationship with reading.
Internationally, we work to create visibility and opportunities for Nepali literature. At home, we work to strengthen the foundation from which that literature emerges. Balancing these responsibilities requires teamwork, partnerships and a clear sense of purpose.
Ultimately, success is not measured only by the size of a festival or the number of countries we reach. It is also measured by the child who discovers a love of reading, the student who receives an opportunity and the community that gains access to a library.
Written by Sangita Swechcha

State Governments, Union Territories with legislature, eligible Provident Funds in India, designated Foreign Central Banks and any person or institution specified by the Bank in this regard can participate on non-competitive basis, the allocation for which will be outside the notified amount. The auction will be Price based using multiple price method. Bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India’s Core Banking Solution (E-Kuber system) on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, during the below given timings:
Category of Bids Timing
Competitive 10:30 am - 11:30 am
Non-Competitive 10:30 am - 11:00 am
Results will be announced on the day of the auction.
Payment by successful bidders will have to be made on Thursday, November 12, 2026.
Only in the event of system failure, physical bids would be accepted. Such physical bids should be submitted to the Public Debt Office (email; Phone no: 022-22603456, 022-22603457, 022-22603190), before the auction timing ends, in the prescribed form. The form can be downloaded from RBI website (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewForms.aspx). In case of technical difficulties, Core Banking Operations Team should be contacted at email; Phone no: 022-69870466, 022-69870415. items.content:
Today, the Reserve Bank released the provisional results of the 2025-261 round of the annual census on foreign liabilities and assets (FLA) covering cross-border liabilities and assets of the Indian entities [viz., companies, limited liability partnerships (LLPs), alternative investment funds (AIFs) and partnership firms] with inward/outward direct investment. The FLA census captures detailed information on foreign liabilities and assets in terms of direct investment, portfolio investment and other investments comprising of trade credit, loans, currency & deposits and other payables and receivables accounts, activity sector, sales, purchase, exports, and imports. The variations in outstanding foreign assets / liabilities between the beginning and end of a financial year would be different from flows recorded in India’s balance of payments (BoP) statistics during the year, as the former would also include valuation changes due to price and exchange rate movements.
Key highlights:
Of the total number of Indian entities reporting foreign direct investment (FDI) and/or overseas direct investment (ODI), around 97 per cent entities were unlisted as at end-March 2026, and also held a major share in total FDI equity capital (at face value) in India (Tables 1 and 2A).
Non-financial companies accounted for more than 90 per cent of the FDI equity at face value (Table 2B).
In terms of market value, listed and unlisted companies had almost equal share in total FDI equity capital as at end-March 2026, however, 96.6 per cent of the FDI debt is held by unlisted companies (Table 3A).
In rupee terms, the ratio of inward FDI to ODI moderated to 4.2 times as on end-March 2026 from 5.5 times a year ago (Table 3B).
Other investment liabilities [viz., trade credit, loans, currency and deposits, and other payables with unrelated (third party) non-resident entities] recorded a growth of 11.9 per cent (y-o-y) in rupee terms as on end-March 2026; other investment assets with unrelated non-residents also rose by 16.1 per cent during the same period (Table 4).
The United States of America (16.5 per cent) followed by Mauritius (14.5 per cent), Singapore (13.7 per cent) and the United Kingdom (10.8 per cent) were the top sources of outstanding FDI. In case of ODI, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and the United States of America were the top destinations together accounting for more than 50 per cent share (Tables 5 and 6).
Manufacturing sector accounted for the highest share in the total outstanding FDI equity capital at market value (50.1 per cent), while 45 per cent share was held by services sector (Tables 7 and 8).
(Brij Raj)           
Chief General Manager

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has said the province’s security policy will be decided in Islamabad, not Kabul, and ruled out talks with those who take up arms against the state.
Speaking at a security briefing in Peshawar on Sunday, Kundi backed intelligence-based operations to restore peace. He said the provincial government had sought Rs. 160 billion for security needs, with the federal government supporting the demand.
More Support for Police
Kundi said police would receive modern weapons and ammunition, along with better salaries and compensation for the families of personnel killed in the line of duty. The province has already announced higher police salaries and increased compensation for bereaved families.
He said development projects could only benefit people when their lives were secure, and called for stronger trust between police and citizens.
District-Level Security Plans
Proposed measures include extending the Counter Terrorism Department’s operational jurisdiction to all 34 districts, establishing District Nerve Centres and creating a Safe City Authority in 10 districts.
Officials also outlined plans for Smart Front Desks at 406 police stations in major cities. Artificial intelligence tools would be used to counter what officials described as false narratives on social media.
The meeting decided to establish Dispute Resolution Councils and Tribal Liaison Committees across all districts, alongside monthly open courts and regular jirgas.

By Rotimi Ojomoyela
ADO-EKITI — A chieftain of the All Progressives Congress (APC) and member of the President Bola Tinubu/APC 2027 Presidential Campaign Council, Engineer Atinuke Owolabi, has expressed concern over the low voter turnout in Aramoko-Ekiti during the 2023 presidential election, saying about 73 per cent of registered voters in the community did not participate.
Owolabi, who is also the convener of PBAT-MOB Aramoko Community Engagement, spoke during an APC voter education exercise and community engagement in Aramoko, Ekiti Central Senatorial District, over the weekend.
The programme, organised in support of the re-election bids of President Tinubu and Senate Leader, Senator Michael Opeyemi Bamidele, was held under the theme, “My Vote, My Voice”.
She also represents the South-West as a member of the North Central Development Commission.
Owolabi said voter education was essential to strengthening democracy, particularly in rural communities where inadequate information about electoral procedures could discourage participation or lead to invalid votes.
Presenting figures from the 2023 presidential election, she said Ekiti State had 988,923 registered voters, out of whom 315,058 were accredited, while 308,171 valid votes were recorded and 6,301 ballots were rejected.
She said available ward-level records for Aramoko I and Aramoko II showed a combined 17,426 registered voters, compared with 4,680 votes reportedly cast during the presidential election.
According to her, the figures indicated that approximately 12,746 registered voters did not participate, representing about 73 per cent of the electorate in the two wards.
She urged residents to improve their participation in future elections, stressing the need for the community to translate its voting strength into meaningful democratic engagement.
Owolabi said the exercise was designed to educate residents on voting procedures, encourage participation and reduce the number of rejected ballots.
The programme also featured the unveiling of a voter education handbook intended to guide residents on electoral processes, identification of polling units and the proper use of their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs).
She said: “I believe voter education is key. If we cannot completely eliminate rejected votes, we should at least be able to reduce them in Ekiti State, particularly in Aramoko, my community.
“We are here to sensitise our people on the correct way to vote. When they go to the polling units, they must ensure that they vote correctly.
“We have the population, and we have the voters. What is really lacking is adequate information. Our people need to understand the right way to vote.
“Today, we have unveiled a voter education handbook, which is a welcome development. Through this handbook, our people will be taught what elections are all about. They will understand how to identify their polling units and how to participate in the electoral process.”
She also urged residents to consider the 2023 election figures as a basis for improving participation in subsequent elections.
Meanwhile, the Regent of Aramoko-Ekiti, Princess Owolabi Adeyemi, acknowledged the efforts of President Tinubu and Bamidele in grassroots development.
She, however, appealed to the Federal Government to address the deplorable condition of roads in the community to ease the difficulties faced by residents and commuters.
The post 2027: APC chieftain laments 73% voter apathy in Aramoko appeared first on Vanguard News.

In a company-wide email, Huang admitted he was unfaithful to his wife, took full responsibility, and said he supports the board’s investigation and will cooperate fully.
What Huang Said
The email, titled “A message to our company,” opened with an apology to his family and employees.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote.
He also apologized to Nvidia colleagues, board, partners, and shareholders, saying they deserve better from him. “Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life,” he added.
Addressing the security angle, Huang said, “Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.”
He said he remains committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security, and asked for privacy for his family. “My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy,” he wrote.
What It Means
The probe puts Nvidia’s leadership under rare scrutiny at a time when the chipmaker sits at the center of the global AI race and of US-China tensions over advanced chips. Nvidia has already been losing AI chip market share in China, where rivals like Huawei are stepping up.
The outcome of the board’s investigation has not yet been announced.

At least half of this amount remains unhedged, according to treasury heads at six banks ET spoke with, leaving lenders with more than $4 billion in dollar exposure to manage annually."The interest on FCNR(B) deposits is not covered by the window. Banks have to buy those dollars forward themselves, year after year, in the open market," said Anindya Banerjee, head of currency research at Kotak Securities.Read more: Bonus, stock splits & dividends: Dabur India, HUL, ONGC among 76 companies turning ex-record date this week"A forward premium is simply the extra price one pays today to lock in dollars for delivery later. When the entire banking system is buying dollars forward for the same reason, and there are not enough natural sellers, that extra price goes up," Banerjee said.Adding to the pressure is the RBI's new reserve requirement on banks' derivative positions. Introduced on October 10, the foreign exchange risk reserve (FERR) requires banks to maintain a cash reserve equivalent to 20% of the rupee value of eligible foreign-exchange derivative contracts.FERR makes it more expensive for banks to offer certain forward-dollar hedges because they must lock away cash against the contracts. Banks may pass on part of this additional cost to customers, putting further pressure on forward premia. The one-month and one-year forward premia were 2.50% and 2.78%, respectively, in early August. They surged to 8.50% and 4.85% by mid-October before easing to 3.83% and 3.91% by November 6, reflecting near-term dollar demand.A treasury head from a private bank said most banks had not put a hedging strategy in place as they were still assessing how best to manage this exposure. FERR in October added another layer of cost, making banks more cautious about locking in dollar liabilities over longer tenures. He explained that for now, the exposure was managed as it accrued, using short-term contracts that could be rolled over rather than hedging the entire interest obligation upfront. The reliance on short-term, rollover, contracts means banks will repeatedly return to the forward market as their interest liabilities accrue, sustaining demand for dollars instead of eliminating the exposure through an upfront hedge.Read more: Market may deliver bumper returns by next Diwali as valuations and earnings align, says Raamdeo AgrawalForeign banks, however, appear more comfortable carrying unhedged positions because they receive a steady stream of dollars from clients.A treasury executive from a foreign bank said some banks might hedge in the coming days as the rupee appreciated.The rupee staged a sharp recovery during the week, appreciating nearly 1.2% to close at 93.90 per dollar on Friday, its strongest level in more than six months.Some midsize banks, meanwhile, hedged the bulk of their dollar exposure after costs fell within their internal thresholds.
