items.content:
By Godwin Oritse
The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) processed 9,195 Pre-Arrival Assessment Reports (PAARs) and 99,839 Single Goods Declarations (SGDs) between September and October 2026, generating a combined revenue of approximately ₦1.42 trillion.
The figures were disclosed during a joint security press briefing at the National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC), under the Office of the National Security Adviser, in Abuja.
Speaking at the briefing, the National Public Relations Officer of the NCS, Deputy Comptroller Abdullahi Aliyu Maiwada, said the performance reflected the Service’s commitment to facilitating legitimate trade, improving cargo clearance and strengthening revenue generation through digital interventions and collaboration with stakeholders.
A breakdown of the figures showed that the Service processed 2,102 PAARs in September and 7,093 in October, bringing the total to 9,195.
Similarly, 48,832 SGDs were processed in September, while 51,007 were recorded in October, giving a combined total of 99,839 declarations.
The Service collected ₦697.8 billion in revenue in September and ₦722.9 billion in October, amounting to ₦1.4207 trillion during the two-month period.
In a statement, Maiwada also disclosed that the Service recorded significant progress in export trade facilitation.
At the Lilypond Export Command, export activities in the third quarter of 2026 generated a total export value of $752.85 million, compared with $586.15 million recorded in the corresponding period of 2025.
The statement put the increase at approximately 28.44 per cent, reflecting the growing contribution of the export sector and the impact of measures aimed at facilitating non-oil exports.
On enforcement, the NCS said it seized prohibited and restricted items with a combined Duty Paid Value exceeding ₦8.1 billion during the period under review.
The interceptions covered various categories, including illicit drugs, pharmaceutical products, prohibited goods and petroleum products.
The Service said it continued to collaborate with relevant regulatory and security agencies to ensure the appropriate handling and disposition of seized items.
On its anti-money laundering and counter-financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) responsibilities, the NCS highlighted the ongoing World Customs Organisation (WCO) Mentoring Mission, inaugurated on October 19, 2026.
The four-week engagement, scheduled to run from October 18 to November 13, 2026, is designed to strengthen the capacity of the Service to identify, investigate and tackle trade-based money laundering and other illicit financial activities associated with cross-border trade.
As part of the exercise, the NCS engaged six relevant agencies between October 27 and 29, including the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), the Nigeria Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) and the National Counter Terrorism Centre.
The Service also disclosed that it had transitioned to an electronic currency declaration platform as part of efforts to improve transparency, strengthen monitoring and enhance the detection of illicit financial flows across the country’s borders.
In another development, the NCS said six live pangolins were rescued in separate operations in Ogun State during the period.
Three were rescued by the Ogun I Area Command, while another three were intercepted by the Federal Operations Unit, Zone A.
The animals were subsequently handed over to the Green Fingers Wildlife Conservation Initiative for care and rehabilitation in line with Nigeria’s obligations under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).

But the Police denied that corps members were part of the victims.
In a statement on Sunday by the Police Spokesperson, Oluseyi Babaseyi, the command said it secured the safe release of the passengers following what it called “sustained security pressure and intelligence-led efforts” to secure their freedom.

“The Command has intensified efforts to apprehend the fleeing suspects and urges members of the public to promptly report anyone sighted with suspicious gunshot wounds to the nearest police station or through established police channels,” the statement added.

items.content:
Wheeling its way between dining booths at a neon-lit restaurant in Karachi, a robot waitress drops off a fresh pizza to an awaiting family.
While global buzz is growing around agile humanoids made in the United States, China and elsewhere, robotic staff are a rare sight in the South Asian country.
"Welcome to Sicilian. My name is Robia," the waitress says in an electronic voice, looking down at diners through blinking red LED eyes.
Robia and her colleague Jojo are the DIY creations of Pakistani engineer Syed Osama Aziz, who is bringing a sci-fi reboot to Karachi's storied dining scene.
They have spherical white heads and dark visors, similar to a motorcycle helmet, and sport black shawls around their neck in the style of a dupatta.
Aziz, who also established The Sicilian restaurant, developed the machines using mostly locally manufactured parts, designing their circuit boards and programming them in his own lab.
"The equipment, the things needed to make robots, are not so easily available here, so we had to arrange them," he told AFP.
The duo were developed through his robotics company, Cobot, with help from friends and some electronic components imported from abroad.
In China and other East Asian countries especially, robots are an increasingly common sight, shuttling food to customers in chain restaurants and taking on other jobs from cleaning to greeting hotel guests.
But they remain a novelty in Pakistan, where Aziz's home-grown creations are attracting curious diners.
When they arrive at a table, the customers must either take the food off their serving tray themselves or wait for a human member of staff to assist them.
Excited customers
Aziz, whose workshop manufacturing the robots is located in Multan, hopes to make his creations more sophisticated in the future.
"Our plans are to add camera-based processing and image-processing features," he said.
"That means the robot will also recognise you by looking at you, and it will remember what you ordered last time, and accordingly it will be able to give you better suggestions."
For now, the robots are proving a hit with families, who flock to the restaurant to watch the machines in action.
"The best thing about it is that it introduces itself," excited customer Ahmer Zameer told AFP, explaining the robot also "tells you what things you can order".
Children reach out to touch the robots while their parents snap photographs and selfies.
Young customer Sonia Dilosker said she was impressed by the androids' appearance and preferred their approach to serving customers, "because it is a machine and without any emotions".
Restaurant staff say the novelty has brought a surge in customers - some travelling from across the sprawling port city to meet the robots.
"Our business has grown. People are coming from far away for this. They have seen a robot for the first time here," staff member Hellen told AFP.
"People are excited to see this."

items.title: After 11-year fight, Louisiana woman wins right to block neighbours from road
items.summary: Mona Matherne spent over a decade contesting neighbors' use of a private road beside her country home. In November 2026, state appeals judges upheld her property rights and confirmed previous court orders. Matherne successfully argued against her neighbors, who claimed the road was public. The court ruled that only the first 1,000 feet was public, protecting Matherne's privacy.

items.author: Shakeel Ahmad Ramay
items.content:
Since the dawn of the 21st century, the world has been facing three unprecedented challenges: artificial intelligence (AI), the pandemic, and climate change. Artificial intelligence has challenged the traditional way of thinking, planning, and living. The most shocking aspect of AI is that it has threatened human intelligence and is emerging as a competitor to humans. In the past, every technological innovation and development helped humans enhance efficiency but never challenged humans or human intelligence. However, AI has challenged humans and human intelligence and is emerging as a competitor.
The pandemic is another challenge that has shaken the whole world. Covid-19 jolted the world and introduced entirely new challenges to humanity. It was the first time in modern human history that mobility came to a standstill and markets closed. Much-celebrated connectivity and mobility were checked. Industry and supply chains were disrupted and came to their lowest level. Now the world is living under the threat of new pandemics.
However, climate change is a completely different challenge and more severe than AI and pandemics. AI and pandemics only threaten human life, with no threat to the planet. Climate change, however, threatens both human civilisation and the planet. Therefore, climate change requires an urgent, unified response based on common but differentiated responsibility. The common but differentiated responsibility principle holds that countries contribute according to their historical responsibility and level of development. Thus, the UNFCCC proposed a solution in which industrialised and developed countries lead the fight. They reduce GHG emissions and provide the financial resources needed for less developed and developing countries. Financial assistance is also needed because most least developed and developing countries lack the resources to combat climate change impacts.
In 2009, developed countries agreed to mobilise $100 billion annually to combat climate change. Unfortunately, that promise remains a distant dream. Developed countries are not fulfilling their commitment to mobilise financial resources. They have applied various tactics to delay the mobilisation. After a strong backlash from the Global South and insistence from the UNFCCC, they began mobilising resources. It took many years to reach $100 billion. Financing came with its own problems. First, they misquoted the pledged amount and the amount actually mobilised. Oxfam report indicated that in 2022, developed countries announced that they had mobilised $116 billion in climate finance. However, the data showed that the actual mobilisation was around $28-35 billion. It was a deliberate attempt to fudge the data.
Moreover, financial mobilisation was expected to be reversed in 2024 and 2025, as the OECD indicated that ODA shrank 9% in 2024 and 9-17% in 2025. ODA matters because many countries accounted for parts of ODA as climate financing. This is unfortunate, as the need for climate finance is rising. Also, developed countries, the private sector, and multilateral institutions turned climate financing into an opportunity to extract more benefits from the developing world. Data analysis showed that almost 65-70% of climate financing came through loans. Moreover, 40% of climate financing from multilateral development banks was in the form of loans. These loans were not concessional; they were market-rate loans and, at times, expensive. As a result, countries and institutions are earning large profits. For example, it was estimated that for every $5 loan, they are getting $7, as developing countries paid back $88 billion and received $65 billion in 2022. This adds to developing countries' total debt and worsens the debt crisis.
Meanwhile, climate finance focuses more on mitigation than adaptation. Oxfam 2025 reported that only $15-18 billion was allocated to adaptation, while the actual requirement was around $310-365 billion. The most shocking fact is that rich countries and big corporations are exploiting disasters in vulnerable countries. They treat disasters and destruction as an opportunity to invest and extract profit. As a result, they do not help countries fight back against climate disasters or address the impacts and destruction they cause.
The most recent example comes from Pakistan. The 2022 floods have shaken the country's economic, social, and environmental infrastructure. Rough estimates show that Pakistan suffered losses of $30 billion. Since then, the country has struggled to secure financial help, with little success. Despite major promises and pledges, it secured only a few million dollars. This has worsened the economic and social problems. For example, rebuilding disaster-affected infrastructure requires huge financial resources, but Pakistan lacks them. As a result, it had to borrow more money, which further complicated its debt, economic, and social crisis. Pakistan had to impose higher taxes, which are contributing to an increase in poverty. Lastly, the market value of disaster-related impacts is projected to reach $92 billion.
Loss and Damage Fund is another developing story on this front. The fund was created after a long struggle by developing and most vulnerable countries facing climate change, and Pakistan was one of the leading countries. Developed countries and financiers are hesitating to provide the required resources and are trying to turn it into another opportunity for extracting benefits.
The question is why the UNFCCC is failing to reach consensus and cannot compel countries to fulfil their commitments when the future of humanity and the planet is at stake. In my view, three culprits are responsible: states represented by governments, the private sector, and the donor-think tank nexus. States are well-known actors that steer negotiations and are entrusted to find consensus for a secure and prosperous future. Unfortunately, they are divided along geographical boundaries and lose sight of the humanity behind it. The private sector's greed for profit and its tendency to shirk responsibility for tackling climate change without a profit incentive make it another visible player. Its behind-the-scenes role in creating stumbling blocks to consensus hinders efforts to combat climate change.
However, the most damaging actor is the donor-think tank nexus, yet its role is often overlooked in discussions of the UNFCCC's failure to compel states to fulfil their commitments. The donor-think tank nexus operates in a sophisticated way to achieve its objectives. Donors provide financial assistance and international exposure, while think tanks deliver on the ground. Donors, mostly developed countries, multilateral institutions, or the private sector, use this nexus to divert attention from their responsibilities. They use think tanks' strengths to shape global discourse and influence decision-making bodies to achieve objectives of delay or responsibility-shifting. Lastly, donors also use the nexus to create direct influence on policymakers and implementers. For example, think tanks are tasked with hiring bureaucrats at lucrative consultancies.
Against this background, two actions are needed: one at the national level and the other at the UNFCCC level. At the national level, countries, especially developing countries, should develop mechanisms to hold think tanks and donors accountable to the public and require heads and employees to declare their assets before joining think tanks and every 10 years thereafter. Second, at the UNFCCC level, the UNFCCC must ban donor-funded think tanks from attending COPs. Only self- or national government-funded think tanks should be allowed to participate in COPs.
In conclusion, everyone needs to understand that the threat is complex and growing in severity. Disasters have become more frequent and more damaging in financial, environmental, and human terms. Vulnerability is expanding, and countries are falling into a vulnerability trap one after another, without distinction of development status or power. In a nutshell, humanity and planet Earth are on the verge of collapse. The situation urges us to cooperate, find solutions together, and act together.
THE WRITER IS A POLITICAL ECONOMIST AND A VISITING RESEARCH FELLOW AT HEBEI UNIVERSITY, CHINA

items.author: Aadil Nakhoda
items.content:
A recent debate between industry representatives and policymakers has erupted over the calculation and the implications of the tariffs presented in the National Tariff Policy (NTP) 2025-2030. Industry representatives state that the tariff rates for Pakistan reported in the World Trade Organisation (WTO) World Tariff Profiles 2025 are not only much lower than those reported in the NTP but are also consistent with the tariff rates applied by regional export powerhouses such as Vietnam, Thailand and Indonesia.
The simple average most favoured nation (MFN) tariff rate applied by Pakistan in 2024 was 10.3%, which is not an outlier given that the aforementioned countries applied 9.5%, 9.9% and 8% respectively. On the face of it, the comparison holds. The question that needs to be answered is whether the WTO figure measures what the debate is about.
It is important to note that the figures provided in the NTP 2025-2030 stack regulatory duties (RDs) and additional customs duties (ACDs) on top of the statutory customs duties. The WTO reports the latter only. The NTP has a baseline tariff rate of 20.2%, which includes RDs and ACDs. The WTO figures hide the para-tariffs applied by Pakistan. The information in the WTO tariff profile merits deeper analysis.
WTO tariff profiles report another crucial indicator, which is often overlooked, namely the tariff ceiling rate, or the bound rate. This matters because WTO members commit not to charge above it. The simple average bound tariff for Pakistan is 60.8%, with 63.5% of non-agricultural tariff lines bound between 50% and 100%. Vietnam's bound rate is 11.7% and China's is 10%. While the ceiling set by Pakistan is far above the tariff it applies, the ceilings set by Vietnam and China are close to the tariffs they apply. Both had to bind close to their applied rates as a condition of their entry into the WTO.
The founding members, such as Thailand and Indonesia, have average bound rates of about 27% and 37% respectively. The gap between bound and applied rates is often labelled "tariff overhang" or "water in the tariff" and is crucial for policymakers. Pakistan has a gap of 50.5 percentage points, while Thailand and Malaysia have a gap of less than 17 percentage points.
The first consequence of this gap is that the para-tariffs applied by Pakistan are largely WTO-legal. Pakistan can apply significantly large RDs and ACDs, unlike Vietnam and China, as doing so would breach their commitments to the WTO. Pakistan has repeatedly done so through statutory regulatory orders (SROs) and Finance Acts. This gap allows the actual tariffs applied by Pakistan to drift from the MFN rate it reports to the WTO. The large gap makes tariff policy unpredictable, and investors are unable to treat it as stable.
A firm planning to build supply chains and invest in a factory tied into global value chains will be wary of tariff unpredictability caused by the large gap. Further, tariff uncertainty undermines the payoff from every other reform, as a firm will not invest in meeting European Union (EU) standards if its input costs can change overnight through SROs. For instance, certain products in the auto sector may find a 100% tariff on their imports while the group average is 22.5%. The NTP 2025-2030 narrows the gap between what the WTO reports and what Pakistan actually applies on its imports by eliminating the web of RDs and ACDs and placing customs duties into simpler slabs.
However, it does not touch the bound rates set at the WTO. As applied tariffs fall, the overhang will widen, and each reduction can be reversed by the next Finance Act. Locking in the reform requires narrowing the tariff overhang. The biggest beneficiary of this reform will be the manufacturing sector itself.
A second problem with the comparison is that Southeast Asian countries pay MFN rates on a shrinking share of their imports, as most trade with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Japan, China and South Korea moves under reciprocal trade agreements. Yet, even on MFN rates, the gap is stark. Approximately 60% of non-agricultural imports into Vietnam and Thailand enter duty-free, compared with 40% for Pakistan. Approximately 35% of non-agricultural imports into Pakistan face duties above 10%. This drops to about 16% for Vietnam and less than 10% for Thailand. Their MFN schedules are tilted towards lower rates. Pakistan's is not.
There is significant evidence reported across the developing world that cheaper imported inputs raise plant productivity and have played an important role in increasing the introduction of new products by firms, which eventually boosts export capabilities. The tariff structure in Pakistan raises the costs of importing essential inputs deemed necessary for local production. Further, the quality of exports by firms is inversely related to the tariffs on inputs. In essence, imports carry technology, and its access is critical in enhancing the productive capacity of firms. Cheap and better access to inputs is critical to ensure a more productive manufacturing sector.
Further, several non-tariff measures such as customs procedures, technical barriers to trade (TBTs), sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) measures and others create hurdles and disincentives for increasing productive capacities. With the focus entirely on tariff measures, reforms on non-tariff measures that define trade are often neglected. Pakistan must undertake a holistic approach to ensure that it participates more intensely in regional and global value chains.
According to data extracted from the Regional Integration and Value Chain Analyser created by the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), Pakistan's exports are overwhelmingly home-made, with foreign value added in exports accounting for 8.5% of gross exports. In comparison, this figure is 37% in Vietnam, 34% in Cambodia and 29% in Thailand.
While half of Pakistan's export value is domestic content in final goods, other countries rely on their products crossing borders multiple times. Interestingly, the most export-oriented sector in Pakistan, textiles, reports foreign value-added content of less than 9%. The same indicator is more than 21% in Bangladesh. Localisation behind a tariff wall is a double-edged sword, as Pakistan retains more value in each dollar it exports but exports fewer dollars. The pattern is consistent with a tariff structure that penalises exporters and more productive firms that need better technology and higher quality inputs.
If Pakistan is serious about implementing the tariff reforms, the NTP must be followed by the rebinding of tariffs closer to applied rates and by deeper, reciprocal free trade agreements (FTAs) with several of its important trading partners.
THE WRITER IS AN ASSISTANT PROFESSOR OF ECONOMICS AND RESEARCH FELLOW AT CBER, IBA

items.title: Building modern financial infrastructure for gold
items.summary:
Pakistan has always understood gold. Families buy it for weddings, preserve it for emergencies and pass it from one generation to the next. For many households, it performs functions that the formal financial system has failed to provide adequately: savings, protection against currency depreciation and access to money when circumstances change. The opportunity is to build modern financial infrastructure around a familiar asset and make it accessible to people who cannot afford conventional quantities.
The Competition Commission of Pakistan estimates annual gold consumption at 60 to 90 tonnes, with more than 90% of trading outside formal channels. That tells us something important. We do not have to create demand. Demand already exists. What is missing is a convenient, transparent way for ordinary Pakistanis to acquire small amounts, hold them safely and sell them when needed. Digitisation can address each of these requirements, provided the underlying structure is sound.
My experience
items.author: nadeem.hussain
items.content:
Pakistan has always understood gold. Families buy it for weddings, preserve it for emergencies and pass it from one generation to the next. For many households, it performs functions that the formal financial system has failed to provide adequately: savings, protection against currency depreciation and access to money when circumstances change. The opportunity is to build modern financial infrastructure around a familiar asset and make it accessible to people who cannot afford conventional quantities.
The Competition Commission of Pakistan estimates annual gold consumption at 60 to 90 tonnes, with more than 90% of trading outside formal channels. That tells us something important. We do not have to create demand. Demand already exists. What is missing is a convenient, transparent way for ordinary Pakistanis to acquire small amounts, hold them safely and sell them when needed. Digitisation can address each of these requirements, provided the underlying structure is sound.
My experience in financial inclusion has taught me that a product will achieve scale only when it fits the customer's circumstances. For lower-income households, four requirements matter: security, transparency, liquidity and trust. Alongside these, the entry amount must be affordable. Someone who can spare Rs500 should not have to wait until they can purchase a coin or a bar. Equally, someone putting aside money today must know that it can be accessed tomorrow if a household need arises.
Consider how a digital gold savings account could work. A customer buys Rs1,000 of gold through a mobile wallet. The money purchases a fractional holding in physical gold maintained with an independent custodian. The next day, the customer adds Rs500, then another Rs2,000 the following week. Each purchase adds a clearly recorded weight to the account. The customer is accumulating gold according to available cash rather than having to organise cash around the size of a gold product.
The customer then has a choice. Someone saving for a daughter's wedding can continue buying until the balance reaches the quantity required for physical delivery. Someone facing a medical bill can sell part of the holding and retain the rest. Another customer may sell the entire balance. The ability to sell anytime should be central to the proposition, with clear arrangements for execution and settlement. Physical delivery is an option for the saver, rather than a condition for accessing value.
This is where liquidity becomes critical. A low-income customer cannot necessarily predict when money will be needed. School fees, medical expenses and interruptions in earnings do not follow an investment calendar. If buying takes seconds but selling involves unexplained delays, the product has failed an essential test. Customers should see the available sale price, know when proceeds will reach their account and receive them reliably. Providers must arrange the liquidity required to honour this commitment as their customer base grows.
Security begins with the underlying asset. Every gram credited to customers must be supported by an equivalent quantity of physical gold. That gold should be independently held, insured and audited, with customer ownership legally protected and separated from the platform's own assets. Otherwise, we risk creating a digital balance that looks reassuring while leaving the saver exposed to the operating company's financial problems. Technology can record ownership, but it cannot substitute for reserves, custody and enforceable rights.
Transparency requires more than displaying a daily gold rate. The customer should see the weight owned, its rupee value, the purchase price, the sale price and every applicable charge. The difference between buying and selling prices must be visible before a transaction. Physical delivery costs and minimum delivery quantities should also be clear. Gold prices can fall; a secure holding does not guarantee a profit. Customers must understand both the market risk they accept and the service for which they pay.
Trust develops when these arrangements work consistently. An audit helps, but so does a successful sale, a timely payment and a complaint resolved without difficulty. Women deserve particular attention because household ownership does not always mean individual control. An account should establish whose gold it is, who can sell it and where the proceeds go. The convenience of digital access should strengthen the owner's control. It should not introduce another intermediary between a woman and an asset that belongs to her.
There are different ways to build this infrastructure. One model uses certificates recording fractional ownership of vaulted gold. Another represents that ownership through digital tokens. Both require appropriate regulatory approval, clear custody arrangements and protection for customers. Blockchain may support record keeping, but the customer should not need to understand it to save. The practical questions remain straightforward: does my gold exist, what does it cost, can I take delivery, and can I sell it when I need the money?
Distribution should use the accounts and applications people already have. Banks, wallets and fintechs could allow customers to purchase small quantities manually or through regular savings instructions. Gold-backed lending can subsequently provide another option for customers who prefer to borrow against their holdings. However, savings must first work independently: easy purchases, protected ownership and dependable sales. A limited pilot should test these functions, including withdrawals during busy periods, before providers expand to millions of customers across the country.
For providers, the commercial test is equally important. Small balances require low costs, efficient custody and sufficient transaction volumes. An expensive product will exclude precisely the customers it is intended to serve. Scale must improve affordability while preserving these safeguards.
Pakistan's gold opportunity therefore extends beyond lending against jewellery already sitting in a household cupboard. It includes helping people build an asset gradually, in amounts they can afford, while retaining the freedom to change their minds or meet an emergency. Security, transparency, liquidity and trust are the foundations. Small quantities make participation possible. Reliable selling makes participation practical. We have already seen how digital distribution can widen financial access. The next step is to apply that capability to an asset Pakistanis understand and give the customer control over buying, holding, taking delivery or selling.
The writer is the chairman of the Pakistan Fintech Network

items.title: Tax net: time for enforcement
items.summary:
Pakistan's policymakers are saying many of the right things: affordable housing finance, cheaper credit for SMEs and farmers, export promotion, IT development, digital payments and targeted assistance through BISP. Otherwise, concessions create revenue gaps eventually recovered from the same salaried employees, compliant businesses and consumers. items.author: AAH Soomro
items.content:
Pakistan's policymakers are saying many of the right things: affordable housing finance, cheaper credit for SMEs and farmers, export promotion, IT development, digital payments and targeted assistance through BISP. These priorities deserve support. However, subsidies and concessional financing cannot substitute for a sustainable revenue base. Who will finance these ambitions if substantial economic activity continues to escape effective taxation?
Broadening the tax net remains the missing piece. Relief for documented taxpayers must accompany measurable progress in taxing previously undeclared incomes. Otherwise, concessions create revenue gaps eventually recovered from the same salaried employees, compliant businesses and consumers. Pakistan needs a system in which the remaining undocumented carries a credible cost, while compliance offers predictable treatment and protection from harassment.
The Asaan Tax Scheme illustrates this challenge. On November 3, the government acknowledged before a parliamentary committee that participation had disappointed and announced plans for enforcement. Reporting on the proceedings indicated that FBR possesses information on approximately 3.7 million retailers, including identity and utility records for 1.4 million. The challenge is converting available information into verified liabilities and sustained compliance.
The experience follows the disappointing Tajir Dost initiative. Consultations, simplified procedures and concessions have struggled to overcome resistance. Some businesses cite corruption and uncertainty; others fear losing their competitive advantage against undocumented rivals. These concerns require institutional reform, but cannot justify permanent exemption. The state must protect taxpayers from arbitrary treatment while ensuring that deliberate evasion attracts consequences.
Repeated amnesties further weaken compliance. When undeclared wealth periodically enters the system on favourable terms, honest taxpayers receive the wrong message. Similarly, higher withholding taxes on non-filers must not become a permanent substitute for assessing actual income. Paying more on occasional transactions should not purchase indefinite freedom from filing returns, explaining accumulated wealth and meeting continuing obligations.
FBR collected approximately Rs13 trillion in net taxes during FY2025-26. Crucially, the achievement was against a revised target. Record nominal collections deserve recognition, but cannot alone demonstrate successful tax widening. The real test is how much additional revenue comes from previously untaxed incomes rather than existing taxpayers, inflation and transaction-based deductions.
The IMF has reinforced this message. At an SDPI conference, reported on November 6, its Pakistan representative Mahir Binici highlighted untapped agricultural, property and provincial services taxation. He stated: "These reforms can only be durable and deliver dividends if the burden is shared, vulnerable households are protected and the benefits are visible." He also emphasised revenue mobilisation of at least 15% of GDP to support public services.
Without durable revenues, development expenditure remains vulnerable whenever fiscal targets become difficult. Private capital cannot carry every public responsibility. Dams, railways, urban transport, universities, hospitals and climate resilience require reliable funding. Ambitions in artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing depend on education, research, electricity and digital infrastructure. Fiscal weakness ultimately limits both economic opportunity and national resilience.
Agricultural taxation is a decisive test. The IMF's 2026 review identified agriculture as the largest undertaxed sector and highlighted implementation delays following agricultural income tax reforms. Small farmers facing volatile weather and crop prices deserve protection. Large agricultural incomes should nevertheless face taxation comparable to other incomes. Provinces must publish collection results and disclose who benefits from agricultural subsidies. Political influence cannot remain an unwritten exemption from fiscal responsibility.
Enforcement should begin with substantial, demonstrable discrepancies. Property purchases, vehicle registrations, commercial electricity consumption, imports and business receipts can identify declarations inconsistent with economic activity. Retailers, wholesalers, professionals, private schools, hospitals, restaurants, jewellers and estate agents should face consistent scrutiny where taxable income exists. Selection should follow evidence and published criteria, with time-bound appeals and proportionate penalties. Businesses below applicable thresholds must remain protected.
Documentation must also become easier. Expand electronic invoicing, simplify federal and provincial registration, and make digital merchant payments affordable. Offer consumers incentives for verified receipts. Require verifiable compliance for subsidised business credit and government procurement. Publish quarterly dashboards showing additional collections, active taxpayers and resolved appeals. These measures align with the IMF's October mission emphasis on digital invoicing, third-party information and risk-based audits.
I have advocated withdrawing the Rs5,000 banknote and documenting gold transactions. A phased withdrawal deserves examination alongside banking access and safeguards for legitimate cash users. Currency reform alone cannot establish whether wealth has been taxed. High-value gold and property transactions need verified identities, realistic valuations and traceable settlement. The objective must be a durable audit trail backed by effective enforcement.
Other countries have confronted powerful interests. Saudi Arabia detained princes and business leaders at the Ritz-Carlton during its 2017 crackdown. China has removed senior military officials over alleged corruption. Malaysia imprisoned former prime minister Najib Razak following a corruption conviction. South Korea convicted former president Park Geun-hye and Samsung's Lee Jae-yong in a bribery scandal. Vietnam's anti-corruption campaign has reached senior officials and business leaders.
These are accountability examples, not interchangeable models of tax administration. Pakistan should enforce the principle that influence offers no immunity, while preserving due process. Saudi Arabia's phased electronic invoicing programme provides a practical administrative lesson. Lasting reform requires institutions that investigate fairly, collect consistently and spend transparently. A country capable of confronting formidable security challenges must also establish fiscal fairness. Carrots have their place, but voluntary compliance cannot remain voluntary taxation.
The writer is an independent economic analyst

items.title: Tax refunds under Section 7E
items.summary:

items.author: MUZAMMIL HEMANI
items.content:
The constitutional validity of Section 7E of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, has been settled, but the practical issue has entered a new phase. The judgment does not automatically amend an income tax return, remove an amount appearing in IRIS or generate a refund. The present question is therefore no longer whether Section 7E was constitutionally valid. It is how taxpayers can correct their tax records and recover amounts paid under a provision subsequently declared void from its inception.
Section 7E was introduced through the Finance Act, 2022. It treated 5% of the fair market value of specified capital assets held by a resident person as deemed income and imposed tax on that amount at 20%, producing an effective levy of 1%. Although framed in terms of capital assets, it operated, in substance, upon immovable property. Its validity produced conflicting decisions, while certain petitioning taxpayers received interim protection subject to depositing 50% of the disputed liability.
The controversy was resolved in Sher Muhammad Mughari v Federation of Pakistan. On May 7, 2026, the Federal Constitutional Court declared Section 7E ultra vires the Constitution and struck it down as void ab initio. It also annulled the proceedings, actions, assessments, demands and notices initiated under the provision and restrained the authorities from giving effect to it. The expression "void ab initio" is important because the court did not merely discontinue the levy prospectively. Applying the doctrine of pith and substance, it found that the levy was imposed upon the capital value of immovable property rather than income. Following the Eighteenth Amendment, Entry 50 of the Federal Legislative List excludes taxes on immovable property from federal authority over capital value, while Entry 47 authorises taxation of income other than agricultural income. Calling the levy "deemed income" could not alter its essential character or enlarge parliament's legislative competence.
The judgment provides the substantive basis for relief, but taxpayers must still follow the procedure. FBR issued instructions to its field formations on September 23, 2026, directing that requests for revision of returns filed in consequence of the judgment should not be rejected. Where revision results in a refund, the subsequent refund application is to be processed expeditiously in accordance with the applicable law and procedure. Revision therefore establishes the corrected tax position but does not, by itself, constitute an order granting repayment.
The appropriate treatment depends upon how the taxpayer originally dealt with Section 7E. Some taxpayers included and paid the complete liability while filing their returns, while others filed their returns first and subsequently furnished a separate Section 7E computation and payment through IRIS. Petitioners covered by interim judicial directions may have deposited only 50% of the computed liability.
Where the full amount was paid, the entire Section 7E liability should be eliminated and the corresponding payment recognised as excess tax. Where the liability was computed at 100% but only 50% was deposited under an interim order, the entire computation should be removed, but the potential refund is confined to the amount actually paid. The unpaid balance is not refundable; it merely ceases to represent a valid liability. Where payment was made separately after the original return, correction may be required both in the return and in the separately furnished computation or associated payment record. In practice, the first step should be a year-wise reconciliation of the original return, wealth statement, Section 7E computation, computerised payment receipt, any interim order, departmental correspondence and the IRIS ledger. The amount computed must be distinguished from the amount deposited. Unless records are correctly linked, a valid claim may not translate into a refundable balance in IRIS. Where revision is required, an application may be submitted under Section 114(6), identifying the omission or wrong statement requiring correction and explaining its connection with the constitutional judgment. The revision should ordinarily remain confined to the consequences of Section 7E. Once the revised return and related records correctly eliminate the liability and recognise the payment, a separate refund application would ordinarily be required under Section 170.
Section 170 permits a taxpayer who has paid tax exceeding the amount properly chargeable under the ordinance to apply for a refund. Any admitted excess is first applied against other outstanding tax liabilities under Section 170(3), after which the remainder is refunded. Section 170(4) requires the commissioner to issue a written decision within 60 days of receiving the application, after providing an opportunity of being heard. An adverse order, or failure to decide within the stipulated period, may attract the appellate remedy under Section 170(5).
Limitation requires particular care. A refund application must generally be filed within three years of the relevant assessment order or the date on which tax was paid. Older payments may therefore raise questions concerning the applicable starting date and the effect of a subsequently revised return or assessment record. FBR's direction to process applications in accordance with law does not resolve every limitation issue, and taxpayers should not assume that revision necessarily renews the period for claiming a refund. Affected persons should act promptly and address limitation expressly.
FBR can facilitate implementation through a standard electronic workflow, a dedicated revision category, a documentary checklist and automated reconciliation of Section 7E payments. IRIS should display the original liability, amount paid, revised liability and amount potentially refundable. This would protect revenue against unsupported claims while allowing genuine refunds to be processed consistently.
The judgment has settled the constitutional status of Section 7E. The remaining challenge is administrative implementation. Taxpayers must use the statutory route carefully, while the tax administration must ensure that a levy declared void does not continue to survive merely as an unreconciled figure in an electronic record. The wider institutional test is whether a final constitutional judgment can be translated into accurate corrections and timely financial relief without generating another cycle of litigation. A transparent revision-and-refund process would protect taxpayers, provide certainty to field officers and demonstrate that effective tax administration includes not only collecting amounts lawfully due, but also returning amounts that the law no longer permits the state to retain.
The writer is a tax professional with extensive experience in corporate and international taxation in Pakistan

A Karachi police station house officer was suspended after an audio recording allegedly showed him apologising to a drug dealer and trying to settle the matter instead of taking legal action.

items.content:
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz removed Jhelum Deputy Commissioner Mir Raza Ozgen from his post on Sunday after intermediate computer science exams in the district were postponed ahead of her scheduled visit.
The Computer Science papers for the Intermediate Second Annual Examinations 2026 were originally scheduled for November 10. The Rawalpindi Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (BISE) later postponed the morning and evening papers in Jhelum district to November 30, citing the deputy commissioner’s recommendation and administrative arrangements linked to the chief minister’s visit.
Maryam Nawaz Orders Immediate Removal of Jhelum DC
Maryam Nawaz reacted after the exam postponement drew criticism.
She said she had already instructed officials to ensure that her district visits did not inconvenience the public or disrupt normal activities. She called the development a violation of those directions and ordered the deputy commissioner’s removal with immediate effect.
The Punjab government subsequently transferred Ozgen and directed him to report to the Services and General Administration Department for further orders.
Meanwhile, Asma Ijaz, a BS-19 officer of the Pakistan Administrative Service, was posted as the new deputy commissioner of Jhelum.
Exams Restored to Original November 10 Schedule
The chief minister also ordered authorities to hold the affected examinations according to their original schedule on Tuesday, November 10.
She criticised what she described as “foolishness” and “misplaced over-smartness” by the district administration and said students should not face disruption because of arrangements for her visit.
This reversed the earlier BISE decision that had moved the papers in Jhelum to November 30. The postponement had applied only to Jhelum district, while examinations in other districts under BISE Rawalpindi were due to proceed normally.
Maryam Nawaz Issues New Instructions for Official Visits
Following the controversy, Maryam Nawaz issued broader instructions to commissioners, deputy commissioners, regional police officers and district police officers across Punjab.
She directed officials not to close markets, shops, businesses or other establishments because of her visits. She also told authorities not to seal residential streets or restrict residents’ movement in the name of security arrangements.
The chief minister said security measures should remain discreet and should not create unnecessary inconvenience for the public.
She also warned officials that failure to follow the instructions could lead to strict action.

items.author: ProPK Staff
items.content:
A Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh suffered damage on Sunday after an attempted attack targeted the Saudi capital, as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis continued to intensify.
Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said falling debris caused limited damage to an Aramco administrative building. However, authorities reported no deaths or injuries. Witnesses also reported shattered windows and visible damage across several floors of the Aramco Tower in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD).
Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack. The group said it carried out multiple military operations using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones against targets in Saudi Arabia. These included Riyadh’s financial district, King Khalid International Airport, Aramco oil storage facilities and the eastern Saudi city of Abqaiq.
Saudi Air Defences Intercept Missiles
The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences intercepted missiles launched towards Riyadh.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said Saudi forces intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards the capital. Authorities also reported intercepting two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and southern areas of the kingdom.
Residents heard loud explosions across Riyadh during the interceptions. Saudi Civil Defence issued an alert before later announcing that the immediate danger had passed.
A Reuters witness reported blown-out windows across several floors of the Aramco building. Meanwhile, Saudi authorities said the falling debris caused only limited structural damage.
Riyadh’s Financial District Becomes a Target
The King Abdullah Financial District is one of Riyadh’s most prominent business areas and a major part of Saudi Arabia’s economic transformation programme.
The district contains high-rise office towers, luxury retail outlets, residential properties and public spaces. It also hosts major Saudi and international businesses, including Goldman Sachs.
The headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund (PIF), are also located there. The Saudi stock exchange is based in the district as well.
KAFD also contains a major metro station and receives heavy commuter traffic, particularly during morning hours. Therefore, an attack on the area represents a significant escalation compared with previous strikes focused mainly on military or energy infrastructure.
Houthis Step Up Attacks on Saudi Arabia
Aramco facilities have faced repeated attacks in recent months.
The Houthis have targeted Saudi oil refineries, storage sites, tankers, corporate facilities and other energy infrastructure as hostilities between the two sides resumed.
The latest incident came only hours after Saudi Arabia’s Education Ministry announced that schools in Riyadh would return to in-person classes following weeks of remote learning caused by earlier attacks.
Saudi Arabia has also faced repeated attacks on airports and other civilian infrastructure.
An attack on Riyadh’s international airport in October killed 13 people, marking one of the deadliest attacks inside the kingdom since Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen conflict in 2015.
The Houthis have also recently seized large areas along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline from forces aligned with the internationally recognised Yemeni government.
Yemen Conflict Intensifies Again
The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
Saudi Arabia then led a military coalition into Yemen in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
A United Nations-brokered truce introduced in 2022 largely halted major fighting for several years. However, the ceasefire collapsed in July 2026, triggering a renewed cycle of Saudi strikes and Houthi missile and drone attacks.
According to the account cited by Dawn, tensions rose after the Houthis allowed an Iranian aircraft to land in Sanaa despite Saudi control over Yemeni airspace.
The Houthis later announced a maritime blockade against Saudi Arabia and began targeting Saudi vessels, territory and energy infrastructure.
The group subsequently expanded its territorial control along Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and over 300,000 displaced since the latest round of fighting began.
Pakistan Condemns Houthi Attacks
Pakistan has repeatedly condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and described them as violations of the kingdom’s sovereignty.
Islamabad and Riyadh currently have two defence arrangements aimed at strengthening collective deterrence.
These include the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia and the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, which also involves Türkiye.
Under the Makkah Defence Alliance framework, Pakistani, Saudi and Turkish leaders have agreed on mechanisms to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities if required.
Pakistan’s military spokesperson, Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, said in October that Pakistan was providing Saudi Arabia with “whatever support is needed” amid the continuing Houthi attacks.
However, he also stressed that the alliance has a defensive purpose and does not have an offensive mandate.
The latest attack on Riyadh comes as Saudi Arabia seeks greater assistance from its allies while facing sustained missile and drone attacks from Yemen.
Via: Dawn

items.content:
Pakistani tech startup RLabs has won the GOAL Startup Award at the Silicon Valley November Summit, gaining international recognition as it prepares to enter the US market.
RLabs is led by Harris Ahmed, a graduate of the National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST). The startup was incubated at Pakistan’s National Incubation Centre for Aerospace Technologies (NICAT).
The Silicon Valley November Summit was held from November 2 to 5, 2026, and was organised by global innovation platform and venture capital firm Plug and Play.
RLabs was among 18 startups from around the world selected to pitch under Plug and Play’s Global Overseas Acceleration & Learning (GOAL) program.
What Does RLabs Do?
RLabs develops technology involving extended-reality (XR) simulators, synthetic data and machine training.
Ahmed said the company has spent years using XR technology to train people to operate complex machinery. It is now applying the same experience to training artificial intelligence and machines.
According to NICAT, RLabs is also developing a proprietary large language model (LLM) to power a modular, cross-platform simulation engine.
NICAT claims the technology can reduce simulation development time by as much as 75%. The figure is a claim from the incubator and has not been independently verified.
RLabs Preparing to Launch in the US
Following the Silicon Valley recognition, Ahmed said RLabs is preparing to launch in the United States.
The move could give the Pakistani startup access to a larger market for simulation, artificial intelligence and machine-training technologies.
Ahmed said RLabs presented its technology before a gathering of more than 3,000 attendees, including startup founders, venture capital investors, corporate executives, innovation leaders and government representatives.
Government Praises RLabs
Federal Minister for Information Technology and Telecommunication Shaza Fatima Khawaja congratulated the startup on its achievement.
She described the award as a proud moment for Pakistan and said the recognition reflected the potential of Pakistani technology talent and the country’s growing startup ecosystem.

items.author: Carolina Pichardo
items.content:
The challenge is not solely to declare new protected areas, but ensure they have effective management
Originally published on Global Voices
The stunning beauty of the Dominican Republic’s north coast at Los Haitises National Park. Photo by Jason Boldero on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).
When you think of the Dominican Republic, the first thing that might come to mind is paradise where sun, sand, and sea combine to offer unforgettable experiences to Dominican families and global travellers alike — but the country’s deep sea is also of critical importance.
Jonathan Delance, director of conservation of the National 30×30 Program of the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, says that Dominican marine ecosystems are one of the country’s “greatest natural and strategic riches” — diverse, highly connected, and fundamental to national life.
From an ecological standpoint, coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, dunes, beaches, pelagic zones, and deep-sea ecosystems sustain biodiversity. From an economic and social standpoint, they are the foundation of tourism, fishing, and coastal protection.
Despite relevant research being conducted in the country, information remains limited. According to Delance, some of the available studies on Dominican deep waters have had a geophysical, geochemical, or geological focus, rather than an ecological one. This is largely because deep-sea research is expensive, complex, and requires specialised technology, such as remotely operated vehicles, acoustic equipment, deep-sea cameras, and highly specific taxonomic capabilities.
Precisely because of these limitations, for a long time the National System of Protected Areas lacked a clear representation of deep ecosystems and their underwater geomorphologies, a gap that began to close with the inclusion of the Beata Underwater Ridge as a conservation object within the Orlando Jorge Mera Marine Sanctuary, representing a relevant step forward for the country.
As part of the scientific basis for this process, Delance explains that the technical report on deep-sea fauna documented research between 900 and 4,200 metres deep, recording 1,855 biological observations and 3,294 organisms. One of the most interesting finds was 148 morphospecies, defined in the book Marine Biodiversity as a “group of specimens that can be distinguished from others on the basis of morphological characteristics,” including poriferans, cnidarians, echinoderms, chordates, arthropods, annelids, mollusks, and other yet undetermined organisms.
The pelagic fauna expedition conducted in 2024 covered 2,771 kilometres (1,722 miles) and identified six species of cetaceans, 15 species of birds, as well as sharks and turtle routes. Environmental DNA resulted in the identification of species — including more than 400 morphospecies — along the entire food chain, demonstrating the health and complexity of this space.
Despite these advances, Delance notes, important gaps persist: “We need more information on taxonomic identification at the species level, genetic connectivity, oceanographic dynamics, seasonal distribution, cumulative impacts, biogeography of deep species, and the response of these ecosystems to underwater disturbances, climate change, and other pressures.”
What is deep-sea mining?
According to the International Seabed Authority (ISA), deep-sea mining (DSM) refers to the extraction of mineral resources from deposits located on the deep seabed, typically found between 400 metres (1.300 feet) and 6.5 kilometres (4 miles) beneath the ocean’s surface.
There are three primary types of mineral deposits. Polymetallic nodules (PMN) were discovered on March 7, 1873, during the Challenger expedition; scientists described them as “several peculiar black oval bodies which were composed of almost pure manganese oxide.” The ISA states that they are composed of manganese, iron, silicates, and hydroxides, and can be as small as micro-nodules or as large as 20 centimetres. They are commonly found on the west coast of Mexico in the Pacific Ocean (also known as the Clarion-Clipperton Fracture Zone), as well as the Central Indian Ocean Basin, and the Peru Basin. While polymetallic nodules can be found in lakes, the ones with greater economic value are typically located at depths of 4,000–6,000 metres (2.5 miles–3.7 miles), in areas with an extremely low sedimentation rate.
Polymetallic sulphides (PMS), which contain large amounts of copper, zinc, lead, iron, silver and gold, were first discovered in 1948 as part of the Swedish Albatross oceanographic expedition in the Red Sea. Later, in 1963 and 1966, scientists also found metalliferous muds and brines in the Red Sea Rift System.
Finally, cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts (CFC) are found at depths of less than 400 metres (1.300 feet) to more than 5,000 metres (3 miles), mainly in areas with strong volcanic activity. While similar to polymetallic nodules in their composition, these crusts are attracting interest from mining companies because they can contain relatively high amounts of cobalt, as well as platinum, rare earth elements, nickel, and manganese.
The ISA has signed 15-year contracts with 22 contractors for DSM exploration, with most of them covering PMN, eight going to PMS and five to CFC.
The contractors range from national governments — including South Korea, India, Poland and Russia — to research institutes and private companies. A small number, such as South Korea, India and China’s Ocean Mineral Resources Research and Development Association, hold contracts across more than one deposit type, while the majority have a single contract.
The Dominican Republic’s position
The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which opened for signature in Montego Bay, Jamaica, in 1982 and entered into force in 1994, establishes the overarching legal framework governing ocean space, marine scientific research and environmental protection.
A central component of the Convention is the definition of “the Area,” the seabed and ocean floor beyond the limits of national jurisdiction. UNCLOS declares the Area and its resources to be the “common heritage of mankind,” and establishes the ISA to administer these resources and regulate their exploration and eventual exploitation.
Between 2020 and 2025, the Dominican Republic had an active participation in the ISA, which is headquartered in Kingston, Jamaica.
At the ISA Assembly (ISBA28) in July 2023, Edward Pérez Reyes, the Dominican Republic’s then representative to the ISA, who twice served as its vice president, presented the country’s position on deep-sea mining. While he recognised the importance of these minerals for an energy transition, the DR advocated for a moratorium until there was a solid legal framework and sufficient scientific evidence to guarantee the protection of marine ecosystems. He also proposed sustainable alternatives, the circular economy, and recycling, as well as an equitable distribution of benefits and strengthening of the management of marine resources.
“The Dominican Republic was never against the International Seabed Authority or the process outlined by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea,” Pérez Reyes, who is now the DR’s ambassador to Japan, explained. “Quite the opposite. We always understood that the international community’s effort to regulate the exploration and eventual exploitation of the seabed was a legitimate exercise. Before that legal framework existed, the risk was that countries with the technological capacity to do so would act on their own. The Convention came precisely to prevent that, and to establish common rules for everyone. So, the discussion was about something else. The question was whether the international community was already in a position to move from exploration to commercial exploitation. Our impression was that it was not yet.”
The DR’s stance, he said — the result of an inter-institutional process involving the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources, the Ministry of Energy and Mines, the National Authority for Maritime Affairs (ANAMAR), and more — was never intended to halt the process. Rather, it was to allow science to keep advancing and for the ISA to finish building the regulatory framework that the Convention itself had mandated it to develop. “Every time we learned of a new research study,” Pérez Reyes recalled, “we ended up thinking that there was still much more to know. And that led us back to the same reflection: we had to continue researching before deciding such great consequence.”
Even today, the principles that guided that position still seem valid to him, though the information on which decisions are made can always change. “If science provides new elements, a responsible state has to analyse them,” Pérez Reyes added.
For Delance, scientific exploration of the deep sea is necessary to better understand these ecosystems before considering any form of utilisation. In his view, the DR still lacks key information, including biodiversity baselines, bathymetric and geomorphological maps, data on vulnerable species, ecological connectivity, oceanographic processes, environmental risks, and the resilience of ecosystems.
He believes that the Dominican stance in favour of a precautionary pause in deep-sea mining responds to the need to first generate sufficient scientific evidence to properly plan, regulate, and protect these spaces, and warned that if deep-sea ecosystems are not protected, the DR and wider Caribbean could lose still-unknown biodiversity, genetic resources of potential scientific value, migratory corridors, and essential habitats for threatened species. The country must therefore move, Delance believes, toward marine spatial planning in order to balance conservation and the sustainable use of these strategic ecosystems.
Environmental groups raise opposition
The Magua Ecological Foundation, which is committed to environmental conservation, biodiversity protection, and the sustainable use of natural resources, categorically disapproves of deep-sea mining in the DR, cautioning that the impacts could be severe and irreversible.
Its president, Manuel Alejandro Rodríguez, said that deep-sea mining represents a significant threat to marine ecosystems, whose biological richness and ecological value are fundamental to the well-being of present and future generations. DSM could lead to habitat destruction, species loss, pollution, and disruption of ecological processes, and potentially cause irreversible environmental damage due to the release of metals and other polluting substances into the marine environment.
“In an island nation like the Dominican Republic,” he stressed, “whose seas support extraordinary biodiversity and are essential for activities such as fishing, tourism, scientific research, and the protection of coastal communities, the risks associated with deep-sea mining far outweigh any potential economic benefits.”
Reaffirming the precautionary principle as a fundamental pillar of environmental management, he added, “As long as scientific uncertainties persist regarding the consequences of this activity and there are no guarantees that it can be carried out without causing irreparable damage, it is essential to prioritise the conservation of our marine ecosystems.”
The Foundation wants the authorities, the private sector, scientific community, and society in general to strengthen the protection of our oceans, promote public policies based on the best available scientific evidence, and commit to sustainable development models.
Sixto Inchaustegui, president of Grupo Jaragua, another NGO working for the sustainable management of biodiversity, said that the DR does not know where deep-sea mining activities could take place along its coasts, especially since its continental shelf is very narrow and the country relies heavily on marine and coastal ecosystem services, including tourism, fisheries, and protection against hurricanes. Such ecosystems are already highly threatened and degraded due to land-use changes, mangrove loss, erosion, overfishing, coral mortality, pollution, and other pressures, all of which are being exacerbated by climate change.
New representative to the ISA
On July 14, Ambassador Nancy Patricia Franjul Pérez presented her credentials as the DR’s new permanent representative to the ISA, and reaffirmed the country’s commitment to help develop a solid, transparent, and science-based regulatory framework for the exploitation of mineral resources in the Area.
Franjul Pérez also emphasised the critical role of the ISA at a time when the international community seeks to balance resource security, marine environmental protection, technological development, and the equitable distribution of benefits. ISA Secretary-General Leticia Carvalho said she looks forward to continuing the dialogue, “including on the draft exploitation regulations and the wider work of the Authority, in a spirit of transparency, environmental responsibility, and respect” for the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The future of Dominican marine protection
In 2024, the DR became the first Caribbean country to surpass one of the targets of the global 30×30 environmental commitment, protecting 30.8 percent of its waters. As Delance explained, however, the challenge now is not solely to declare new protected areas, but to ensure they have effective management.
Currently, more than 90 percent of the protected marine area has management plans, a fundamental tool to guide conservation, regulate permitted uses, monitor ecosystems, and support decision-making. Looking to the future, efforts must focus on moving toward effective protection by strengthening monitoring and technological surveillance, regulating maritime traffic, developing national scientific capacity, and generating more research on deep ecosystems.
The DR will participate alongside Colombia in a scientific mission belonging to the inaugural programme of the REV Ocean, the world’s largest ocean research vessel, which will conduct the Beata Ridge mission in 2027.
The expedition will allow for the study of the deep ecosystems of the Beata Underwater Ridge, generate information on its biodiversity and ecological connectivity, and assess potential threats to strengthen ocean conservation and management. The country will also initiate a marine spatial planning process covering both protected and unprotected areas, enabling better organisation of ocean uses and supporting evidence-based decision-making.
This story was originally published by Raiz Climatica, with support from the Caribbean Deep-Sea Mining Media Fellowship, a joint venture between Climate Tracker Caribbean, Jamaica Environment Trust, Rise Up for the Ocean, and EcoVybz Environmental Creatives.

items.title: Court overturns $31,054 divorce payout over premarital home's rise in value
items.summary: The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals has overturned a previous decision regarding a premarital home. The court ruled that the husband is not liable for the home's market value increase during marriage. This ruling clarifies how separate property and marital contributions are treated in divorce cases. However, the former wife is entitled to financial interest from mortgage principal payments made during the marriage.

A woman was allegedly tortured and electrocuted to death by her husband, with the help of his sister, brother-in-law and nephew, in Ahmed Nagar within the jurisdiction of Cantt police station.
The suspects allegedly tied the woman, identified as Misbah and a mother of two, to a cot before subjecting her to an electric shock. A woman was allegedly tortured and electrocuted to death by her husband, with the help of his sister, brother-in-law and nephew, in Ahmed Nagar within the jurisdiction of Cantt police station.
The suspects allegedly tied the woman, identified as Misbah and a mother of two, to a cot before subjecting her to an electric shock. Her in-laws reportedly attempted to portray her death as natural, but burn blisters on her feet, noticed while her body was being prepared for burial, raised suspicions about the circumstances of her death.
According to Okara DPO spokesperson Irfan Sandhu Jutt, Cantt police received information that Misbah's sudden death was not natural and that she had allegedly been murdered by her husband, Tanveer, in collusion with his relatives.
Read: Three of a family electrocuted
The victim's mother, Faizun Nisa, alerted the police. When police reached the scene, Tanveer allegedly fled.
Taking notice of the incident, DPO Dr Asad Ijaz Malhi directed the Cantt police to arrest all those involved and ensure that they were brought to justice.
Acting on scientific evidence, police arrested the main suspect, Tanveer, and his brother-in-law, Asghar. Raids are under way to apprehend the remaining suspects.
A case has been registered on the complaint of the victim's mother against four nominated and three unidentified suspects.
Misbah's body was shifted to the District Headquarters Hospital for a post-mortem examination.
Police said the findings of the autopsy would help establish the exact cause and circumstances of her death.

items.title: Türkiye supports Azerbaijan's efforts for lasting peace in South Caucasus: Erdogan
items.summary:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Sunday reaffirmed Türkiye's support for Azerbaijan's efforts to establish lasting peace in the South Caucasus, saying the liberation of Karabakh had opened the door to a new era in the region.
"Just as we have supported Azerbaijan's just struggle, we also support its sincere efforts to establish lasting peace in our region," Erdogan said at a joint news conference with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in Shusha, celebrating the sixth anniversary of the liberation of Karabakh.
Speaking after a bilateral meeting with Aliyev at the Shusha Governor's Office, Erdogan said he was pleased to be in Azerbaijan for the sixth anniversary of the Karabakh victory.
