items.author: Anadolu Agency
items.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Sunday reaffirmed Türkiye's support for Azerbaijan's efforts to establish lasting peace in the South Caucasus, saying the liberation of Karabakh had opened the door to a new era in the region.
"Just as we have supported Azerbaijan's just struggle, we also support its sincere efforts to establish lasting peace in our region," Erdogan said at a joint news conference with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in Shusha, celebrating the sixth anniversary of the liberation of Karabakh.
Speaking after a bilateral meeting with Aliyev at the Shusha Governor's Office, Erdogan said he was pleased to be in Azerbaijan for the sixth anniversary of the Karabakh victory.
🇹🇷 Turkish President Erdogan reaffirms Türkiye’s support for Azerbaijan’s efforts to establish lasting peace in South Caucasus during joint news conference with Azerbaijani counterpart Aliyev in Shusha
🤝 Erdogan says Karabakh’s liberation opened new era in region, praises… pic.twitter.com/z2iesCAYEb
— Anadolu English (@anadoluagency) November 8, 2026
He also recited verses praising Shusha, describing it as a city that warms the heart like a cherished saying and a glowing ember, adorned with fragrant roses.
Erdogan expressed his respect and gratitude to those who lost their lives in the struggle for Karabakh's liberation and thanked veterans for their sacrifices, wishing them health and long lives.
He said the Azerbaijani people, united under Aliyev's leadership, had restored Karabakh's freedom through great heroism, describing the victory as a reflection of Azerbaijan's just cause and a source of pride for the entire Turkic world.
Erdogan said Azerbaijan's liberation of its territories from occupation during the 44-day Second Karabakh War in 2020 had ushered in a new era in the South Caucasus.
"The task before us today is to crown the victory achieved on the battlefield with lasting peace and stability," he said.
Türkiye appreciates Azerbaijan's efforts
He also praised Azerbaijan's ongoing reconstruction efforts in the territories.
"We greatly appreciate Azerbaijan's efforts to rebuild Karabakh and restore the region to its former vitality," he said.
"Every home with a renewed hearth, every structure rising and every piece of historical heritage being restored in Karabakh demonstrate the Azerbaijani people's confidence in the future," Erdogan said, adding that Türkiye would continue sharing its experience and contributing to reconstruction and development efforts.
He highlighted several joint projects as examples of bilateral cooperation, including the Türkiye-Azerbaijan International Forestry Training Center and Nursery Facilities established in Cebrayil with contributions from Türkiye's Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry.
Erdogan said construction had also begun on a 40-classroom school covering 14,500 square meters in Aghdam, adding that he hoped to inaugurate the facility with Aliyev next year.
Referring to infrastructure developments during his journey from Fuzuli International Airport to Shusha, Erdogan noted that the delegation had passed through seven tunnels.
"These seven tunnels demonstrate how successful infrastructure construction in the region has been," he said, expressing his belief that Shusha and Fuzuli would look very different during his next visit. He attributed the progress to the determination and commitment of Azerbaijan's leadership and team.
Türkiye-Azerbaijan ties
Highlighting the deep-rooted ties between the two countries, Erdogan said relations between Türkiye and Azerbaijan had reached their current advanced level after passing through various tests of history.
"Relations between Türkiye and Azerbaijan have reached their current advanced level after passing through various tests of history. This unity of hearts, which we describe with the motto 'one nation, two states,' is an everlasting torch that draws strength from our shared past and illuminates our future," he said.
He emphasized that the bond between the two nations went far beyond their shared language, history and culture.
"This is why we regard Baku's joy as Ankara's joy and Shusha's pride as the pride of our entire nation," Erdogan said.
Erdogan also stressed the significance of the Shusha Declaration, signed on June 15, 2021, which elevated bilateral relations to the level of an alliance.
"Those seeking to weaken our brotherhood, reinforced by the alliance we forged with the declaration signed in Shusha on June 15, 2021, will never achieve their goals, now or in the future, just as they failed in the past," he said.
"With God's permission, our unity will endure forever," he added.
Erdogan said Türkiye and Azerbaijan were also working to promote this vision across the Turkic world, describing the Organization of Turkic States' progress as the most tangible result of their shared determination and efforts.
Read More: Turkish parliament approves Makkah defence pact with Pakistan, Saudi Arabia
He thanked Azerbaijan for its efforts to strengthen unity and solidarity across the Turkic world during its chairmanship of the organization and said Türkiye would work to make the organization more effective and institutionalized during its own chairmanship.
Azerbaijan-Türkiye unity 'eternal and unshakable'
For his part, Aliyev expressed gratitude for Türkiye's support during the 44-day Second Karabakh War, emphasizing that Azerbaijan would never forget the solidarity demonstrated by Erdogan and the Turkish people.
"Throughout the 44 days of the Second Karabakh War, you (President Erdogan) and the brotherly Turkish people stood by our side. This will never be forgotten," Aliyev said.
He described the unity between Azerbaijan and Türkiye as "eternal and unshakable," stressing that attempts to undermine their close relations would fail.
"Our unity and brotherhood with Türkiye are unshakable. Those who seek to drive a wedge between us will never succeed," he said.
Aliyev noted that the Second Karabakh War had once again demonstrated the unity between Türkiye and Azerbaijan, recalling that the Shusha Declaration formally elevated bilateral relations to the level of an alliance.
He stressed, however, that the two countries had always been allies, even before the declaration was signed.
"The peoples of Türkiye and Azerbaijan are brotherly peoples. There are no other peoples and states in the world as closely connected as we are. This is our great wealth," he said.
"The Shusha Declaration merely placed these historical and cultural relations within an official framework. What unites us is our shared history, ethnic roots, language, literature and spiritual values. This is a great wealth. Today, interstate relations are also developing on the basis of this wealth and strong foundation," he added.
'We will not allow anyone to come between us': Aliyev
Aliyev reiterated that neither country would allow outside forces to undermine their solidarity.
"We, as two peoples and, above all, as two leaders, protect this wealth. We will not allow anyone to come between us or cast a shadow over our unity, brotherhood and solidarity for their own personal interests," he said.
Aliyev also praised Türkiye's growing international influence under Erdogan's leadership, saying the country had become a major power with a voice in global affairs.
"Türkiye's strong economy, powerful industrial potential and political weight are realities today. This makes us very happy and also strengthens us," he said.
He noted that Azerbaijan had also undergone significant development in recent years and continued to make steady progress.
"We are much stronger together. Türkiye-Azerbaijan unity is an important factor in a region covering a vast geography. It is a factor of stability, cooperation and security," Aliyev said.
Concluding his remarks, Aliyev said Erdogan's presence in Karabakh on Victory Day, despite his busy schedule, once again demonstrated the strength of bilateral ties to the world.
"I am certain that this unity will be eternal. No one in Türkiye or Azerbaijan has any doubt about this," he said.
"We were together in the past, we were together during the war, we are together today, and we will be together in the future," he added.
Flags waving side by side
At the conclusion of his remarks, Erdogan recited verses by Azerbaijani poet Bakhtiyar Vahabzadeh celebrating the shared identity and solidarity of the two countries.
"May God grant that our red flag with the crescent and star and the glorious flag of Azerbaijan continue to wave side by side in the skies forever," he said.
Erdogan also congratulated the Azerbaijani people on Nov. 9 State Flag Day, sending his greetings and affection to the people of Azerbaijan and thanking Aliyev for his warm hospitality.
Following their speeches, Erdogan and Aliyev shook hands and raised each other's hands together for a photograph.

items.title: PM Shehbaz raises youth loan limit to Rs25m under business, agriculture schemes
items.summary:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif increased the individual loan limit under the Prime Minister’s Youth Business and Agriculture Loan Schemes from Rs7.5 million to Rs25m, with the loans to be provided in easy instalments.
The decision was taken at a meeting chaired by the prime minister to review the disbursement of loans to young people and the implementation of the two schemes.
A total of Rs292 billion has been allocated this year to provide loans to young people under the schemes, according to a briefing at the meeting.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif increased the individual loan limit under the Prime Minister’s Youth Business and Agriculture Loan Schemes from Rs7.5 million to Rs25m, with the loans to be provided in easy instalments.
The decision was taken at a meeting chaired by the prime minister to review the disbursement of loans to young people and the implementation of the two schemes.
A total of Rs292 billion has been allocated this year to provide loans to young people under the schemes, according to a briefing at the meeting.

— Prime Minister's Office (@PakPMO) November 8, 2026
The prime minister directed that 30 per cent of the loans be reserved for women to help them achieve economic independence and encourage their participation in business activities.
He also directed that the minimum age for applicants be reduced from 21 to 18 years to enable young people to start businesses and take part in agricultural activities at an earlier age.
PM Shehbaz appreciated the efforts of Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb and his team in putting in place effective arrangements to provide financial support to young people for business and agricultural activities.
The meeting discussed various measures to empower young people, create business opportunities for them and increase their participation in the agricultural sector.
The prime minister directed the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Authority (SMEDA) to provide all possible assistance to young people under the schemes, including guidance on starting businesses, business consultancy and technical support.
He also instructed the relevant authorities to launch a countrywide awareness campaign to inform young people about the schemes, available opportunities and government initiatives so that more applicants could benefit from the facilities.
According to the briefing, 581,341 young people have received loans since January 2023, a figure 10 times higher than the number of beneficiaries over the preceding 10 years. Loans worth Rs313.9b have been disbursed during this period.
During the 2026-27 financial year, an estimated 266,700 young people are expected to receive loans worth Rs292b under the schemes, the meeting was told.
The prime minister said young people were a valuable asset for Pakistan and that the government was committed to empowering them, harnessing their potential and providing them with decent and productive employment opportunities.
The meeting was attended by the finance minister, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Youth Affairs Rana Mashhood Ahmad Khan and Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Talha Barqi.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan’s services exports recorded a growth of 22.6% during the first quarter of FY 2027, mainly due to higher earnings from information technology (IT) and other business services.
According to data compiled by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS), services exports reached $2.72 billion in July-September FY27, compared to $2.22 billion in the same period last year.
The sector also maintained its growth in September, with exports increasing by 15.35% to $929.87 million against $806.14 million in September last year. Telecommunications, computer and information services remained the main contributors to this growth.
IT Sector Drives Pakistan’s Services Exports to $2.72 Billion in First Quarter of FY27
Data from the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) shows that exports of telecommunications, computer and information services increased by 17.7% during the first quarter of FY27.
These exports reached $1.246 billion in July-September, compared to $1.059 billion in the corresponding period last year.
In September alone, the sector generated $435 million in export earnings, marking an 18.21% increase from $368 million in the same month last year.
Other business services also recorded strong growth. Their exports increased by 27.98% to $622 million during the first quarter, compared to $486 million a year earlier.
Meanwhile, transport services exports grew by 9.66% to $295 million, up from $269 million in the corresponding period last year.
Services Imports Also Increase
While exports continued to grow, Pakistan also recorded a rise in services imports during the first quarter of FY27.
Services imports increased by 16.32% to $3.55 billion in July-September, compared to $3.05 billion in the same period last year.
The monthly figures also showed a significant increase. Services imports reached $1.21 billion in September, up 26.38% from $959.53 million in September 2025.
Transport services accounted for the largest share of services imports during the first quarter, followed by travel services.
Services Trade Deficit Remains Almost Unchanged
Despite the increase in imports, Pakistan’s services trade deficit remained almost stable during the first quarter of FY27.
The deficit stood at $832.16 million, slightly lower than $834.88 million recorded in the same period last year. This represents a decline of 0.33%.
However, the monthly deficit widened by 84% in September to $282.76 million compared to the corresponding month last year.
Services Exports Cross $10 Billion in FY26
Pakistan’s services exports also showed strong performance in the previous fiscal year. Total exports increased by 18.81% to $10.04 billion in FY26, compared to $8.45 billion in FY25.
In rupee terms, services export earnings reached Rs2.815 trillion, marking a 19.33% increase from Rs2.359 trillion in the previous fiscal year.
The latest figures highlight the growing contribution of IT, telecommunications and other business services to Pakistan’s export earnings. Continued growth in these sectors could further strengthen the country’s services exports and support its foreign exchange earnings.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Higher Education Commission (HEC) has opened registration for the fourth cohort of its Digital Learning and Skills Initiative (DLSI) 3.0 in collaboration with Coursera. The programme will provide eligible university students, faculty members and staff with free access to thousands of online courses for six months.
Students and faculty members of HEC-recognised public and private sector universities can apply for a free Coursera licence under this initiative. The programme aims to help participants develop professional skills, gain industry-recognised qualifications and improve their career opportunities.
HEC Opens Registration for Free Coursera Courses Under DLSI 3.0 Cohort 4
Through this six-month licence, participants will get access to more than 25,000 online courses, according to the latest Cohort 4 announcement. Coursera offers courses in various fields, along with professional certificates, career-focused specialisations and digital skills training.
Who Can Apply for HEC DLSI 3.0?
The programme is open to students enrolled in 16-year education programmes or higher at HEC-recognised public and private universities. Faculty members of these universities can also apply.
Applicants must have a valid CNIC or B-Form number to complete the registration process. However, alumni and students or faculty members of affiliated colleges are not eligible for the programme.
How to Apply for Free Coursera Courses
Interested applicants must visit the HEC e-services portal and create an account. Those who already have an account can log in directly.
After signing in, applicants need to select the e-courses option and complete the online application form. Once submitted, the relevant university focal person will review and verify the application.
Applicants should wait for the verification process to finish. After approval, eligible candidates will receive an invitation link from Coursera. HEC advises applicants that receiving the invitation may take at least one month.
Once they receive the invitation, applicants must open the link and create a Coursera account if they do not already have one. They can then access the HEC Coursera portal and enrol in their preferred courses.
Important Conditions for the Free Coursera Licence
HEC has also outlined some conditions that participants must follow to keep their free licences active.
Applicants must accept the Coursera invitation and enrol in at least one course within 15 days of receiving the invitation. They must also complete at least one individual course within 30 days to retain their licence. Failure to meet these requirements may result in the cancellation of access.
Participants can enrol in multiple courses during the six-month period. They can also download their certificates electronically after completing the relevant courses.
How to Register for HEC DLSI 3.0 Cohort 4
Eligible students and faculty members can submit their applications through the following official links:
Online Application: https://eservices.hec.gov.pk/
Registration Guidelines: https://dlsei.hec.gov.pk/site/registrationinfo
The initiative offers university students and faculty members an opportunity to access international learning resources, develop practical digital skills, and earn professional certificates without paying course fees.

items.title: How China’s clean-tech machine is reshaping the global climate fight
items.summary:
China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country.
In fact, the nation’s green-manufacturing juggernaut, built in part through heavy subsidies from Beijing, nearly matches the current total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change, according to a Reuters analysis.
Those loans and grants stemmed ​from a climate-finance program the world’s wealthiest nations agreed to at a 2009 United Nations climate conference on the premise that industrialized nations made outsized contributions to the climate crisis – and had outsized means to help poorer countries pay to clean it up.
A Reuters investigation in ‌2024 found that most global climate finance comes in the form of loans – and sometimes at market interest rates that funnel billions of dollars back to rich countries.
items.author: Reuters
items.content:
China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country.
In fact, the nation’s green-manufacturing juggernaut, built in part through heavy subsidies from Beijing, nearly matches the current total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change, according to a Reuters analysis.
Those loans and grants stemmed ​from a climate-finance program the world’s wealthiest nations agreed to at a 2009 United Nations climate conference on the premise that industrialized nations made outsized contributions to the climate crisis – and had outsized means to help poorer countries pay to clean it up.
A Reuters investigation in ‌2024 found that most global climate finance comes in the form of loans – and sometimes at market interest rates that funnel billions of dollars back to rich countries.
China took a different approach, funneling billions in subsidies into its own green-energy industries, serving its own national interest to dominate next-generation manufacturing domestically and globally.
The result: massive and rapid market-share gains in solar panels, batteries and battery minerals, electric vehicles, wind turbines and other green products.
China remains by far the world’s biggest greenhouse-gas emitter because of its large population, concentration of heavy industry and reliance on coal power. But its huge clean tech exports mean it has also become among the biggest global forces in reducing climate-damaging emissions.
The Reuters analysis used customs data to calculate the value of Chinese exports ​of clean technologies to countries classified by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development as developing nations.
Those exports alone will help the Global South avoid 257 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions (MtCO2) per year once deployed – an amount equal to the annual carbon dioxide emissions of France, according ​to analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. This year’s exports from China, meanwhile, are on track to avoid 337 MtCO2 in the Global South, the analysis shows.
Reuters was unable ⁠to find a reliable single estimate of how much greenhouse gas emissions are avoided as a result of global climate finance from rich to poor countries.
The OECD estimates a fifth of all rich world climate giving in 2024 came from the private sector.
The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the High Ambition Coalition – ​an informal coalition of nations that has advocated for substantial climate finance – did not immediately comment for this story.
The $132 billion figure derived by Reuters for China’s global climate contribution also includes an estimated $40 billion of Chinese foreign direct investment into clean-technology projects in developing countries. The investment data was compiled by Mathias Larsen and Xiaokang ​Xue at the London School of Economics.
That brings China’s contribution to nearly equal to the $137 billion in climate finance that wealthy nations provided to poorer ones in 2024 under their UN climate pledges, according to the most recent figures provided by the OECD.
The figures are not directly comparable. China's total largely reflects commercial transactions focused on clean energy development, while climate finance can also support other types of programs like developing climate-resilient agricultural techniques or cleaning up damage from major storms or floods.
But the comparison illustrates the extraordinary scale at which China's manufacturing economy is now shaping the energy transition in poorer countries.
The findings point to a potential shift in the mechanics of the global energy transition, according to Li Shuo, a veteran observer of China ​at UN climate talks who heads the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
For years, climate talks focused on how much money and technology wealthy countries would provide to poorer ones to help them decarbonize. China's manufacturing boom is creating another pathway: Driving down the price of clean technology through self-interested innovation ​and scale – until developing countries adopt it for economic reasons.

"You can align it to your economic agenda," he said.
Export giant, diplomatic mouse
Beijing has so far shown little interest in translating its commercial might into diplomatic leadership at global climate talks since President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from international climate cooperation in 2025.
China’s diplomatic role likely will take ‌center stage as nations ⁠gather this month for the UN’s COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey.
Bilateral agreements between heavyweights Washington and Beijing have traditionally paved the way for international climate agreements, including the landmark 2015 Paris deal to limit global warming. But Beijing may be unwilling to go on alone without its geopolitical counterweight at the table, according to former climate negotiators.
Beijing may also be worried that taking a bold stance on global carbon reduction would bring unwanted pressure for China to give more climate aid or cut its own fossil-fuel emissions, observers say. China emits about a third of all carbon dioxide emissions and still burns coal for more than half its power.
"How China engages on different levels in the coming years is the most fundamental thing that is going to happen on climate because of both their role in clean-tech deployment… but also because of their emissions profile," said Jennifer Morgan, Germany’s former climate minister.
China’s Ministry of Commerce said the country is an important contributor to the global green transformation, ​and that its wind and solar exports have cumulatively reduced global emissions by ​roughly 4.1 billion tons of CO2 over the past five years - the ⁠equivalent of around 80% of the total emissions of the United States in one year.
"Against the backdrop of a global climate governance 'action deficit,' China will continue to uphold a responsible attitude, working with other countries to address challenges, overcome difficulties, and jointly promote global green and low-carbon transformation and sustainable development," it said.
Forcing out fossil fuels
Meanwhile, China's manufacturing boom has made renewable energy more affordable in the developing world.
When Ethiopia banned combustion engine car imports in 2024, for example, it was the ​first country to take such a dramatic step toward electric vehicles. The decision was less about emissions and more about cutting its fuel import bill, its deputy minister of transport at the time told Reuters.
"No one in Ethiopia is ​asking COP to pay for any of ⁠this; the economics have just switched. It is just the cheapest and best solution," said Larsen, a senior policy fellow at the London School of Economics, who built the database of Chinese green investment used by Reuters in this story.
China has been by far the world’s biggest supplier of electric vehicles over the past few years, as dozens of subsidized automakers have waged a fierce price war in China and dramatically increased exports.
The green transition has been similarly pragmatic in Pakistan, which imported 17GW worth of solar from China last year, according to data from Ember, roughly on par with Germany’s installations that year. Those panels will cut emissions and, more importantly, provide cheap, reliable power in a country that ⁠often has neither.
Nearly two ​thirds of China’s exports of solar panels, and the cells needed to make them, went to the developing world last year, according to Reuters analysis of customs data.
The picture is different in ​wealthy countries like the United States and parts of Europe, which in recent years have imposed tariffs and other restrictions on Chinese clean technology to protect their domestic manufacturers from the surge in shipments.
The United States, for example, imposes tariffs exceeding 100% on Chinese electric vehicles and has taken other measures to effectively block them from the market.
"What is striking is that policies originally designed to address ​climate change are now facing opposition not because of their climate impacts, but because of concerns about trade and competitiveness," said André Corrêa do Lago, a veteran climate negotiator for Brazil, which hosted last year’s climate summit.

items.author: AFP
items.content:
Cooking and bathing became difficult when taps ran dry in Batam, an Indonesian island where residents are protesting as data centres spring up to power the global artificial intelligence boom.
The area had suffered a "long drought" caused by low rainfall, the local water utility operator told AFP, as a strong El Nino cycle exacerbates dry weather.
But, as in other countries, anger has been directed at the data centres, warehouse-like facilities that keep apps and artificial intelligence tools running, with water often used to cool their humming servers.
Frustration is bubbling over in Indonesia and Malaysia -- especially in regions bordering Singapore that are seen as a prime location for new tech facilities.
At first the main reaction was, "thank God industry is coming" to Batam, 54-year-old tradesman Juniardi Adinda Sembiring Gurukinayan told AFP.
But severe recent outages hitting the municipal water service in some Batam communities meant "sometimes I skipped my shower".
"We cannot eat rice without water. We cannot cook vegetables without water," he said.
At the worst point, dozens of angry residents staged spontaneous protests outside Nongsa Digital Park -- a new cluster of data centres and other amenities, designated a special economic zone.
People in the district believe "that the water shortages... are related to the construction of data centres", Juniardi said.
The drought caused the nearby Nongsa Reservoir to run very low, and supply systems were further disrupted by an electrical fault, said Ginda Alamsyah, a spokesman for water utility operator Air Batam Hilir (ABH).
The tech park receives water from a different source, Duriangkang Reservoir, an industry source told AFP.
Authorities in late September told developers they must build plants to desalinate seawater for cooling, to avoid straining local resources.
Companies behind operational or planned data centres at Nongsa Digital Park include the Singapore-headquartered BW Digital, DayOne, and Princeton Digital Group.
Another owner, Hong Kong-based Gaw Capital Partners, said it was "aware of the distress and frustration expressed by local residents in Nongsa and surrounding Batam communities" over water shortages.
To ensure sustainable operations, "our data centre facilities must deploy a combination of advanced engineering, efficient architectural designs, and renewable energy sourcing," it said.
That includes using so-called "closed-loop" water systems that reuse resources and so require less fresh liquid.
As residents demanded a return to normal water supply at one protest last month, AFP saw a police officer filling up buckets they had brought to Nongsa Digital Park.
In nearby coastal village Mata Ikan, people had to use seawater to wash after defecating, said demonstrator Rahmat, 52, who like many Indonesians goes by one name.
"The water crisis has been going on for the past year, but it got worse in the last six months," 38-year-old Sulastri said at her home, where supply was out, so she poured water from a plastic bottle to wash dishes.
"Many of us here run small stalls. We used to make ice cubes, but we can't anymore."
The government has been distributing water from tanks driven around, but Sulastri said it was "smelly" and "yellowish".
AFP contacted the local government BP Batam, and Indonesia's ministry for economic affairs, which regulates Nongsa Digital Park, for comment. Neither responded.
Recent disruption to water distribution "was not caused by data centres or AI or investors entering that sector," Amsakar Achmad, Batam mayor and head of BP Batam said in October, according to local media.
The decline in water supply was instead "due to weather and climate factors", he said.
Data centre capacity in Southeast Asia is projected to triple from 2025 levels by 2030, driven by a tenfold surge in AI use, according to a KPMG report.
This can put pressure on water supplies, but also electricity grids still heavily reliant on planet-warming fossil fuels.
The data centre construction boom in Indonesia and Malaysia began when resource constraints led hyper-connected Singapore to halt new developments between 2019 and 2022.
It has since ramped up, boosting both countries' economies as governments and tech giants pour hundreds of billions of dollars into training and running AI.
Ginda said water provider ABH supports policies to encourage investment and development in Batam, south of Singapore and connected to it by undersea cables.
But he added that water demand must be managed properly, adding that ABH is trying to boost the capacity of Batam's six reservoirs by dredging them, with cloud seeding another option in dry periods.
Read More: Environmental groups embrace AI, even as they warn of data center impacts
North of Singapore, Malaysia's Johor region has become "one of the largest emerging AI infrastructure clusters in the world", according to researcher James Chai of the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute.
Just half a decade ago, Johor hosted 10 megawatts of data centre capacity. That has ballooned by a factor of 200 to 2.1 gigawatts today, Chai said.
The environmental cost could be high.
By 2035, data centres are forecast to swallow up one-third of Malaysia's total energy consumption, the deputy prime minister told parliament in July.
The Nongsa Digital Park area, a hub for AI-based data center and digital infrastructure development, in Batam, Riau Islands, on November 3, 2026 . AFP
The government said at that time it would only approve data centre projects after ensuring sufficient energy and water supply capacity.
Johor residents have protested over dust pollution and flash floods linked to data centre construction, as operators build closer to residential areas.
"Johor is at a critical inflection point," Mohd Fadhil Md Din of Malaysia's University of Technology told AFP.
"It has the potential to become Southeast Asia's leading sustainable data center hub," but only if it manages resources and spatial planning carefully, he said.
Pushback sometimes works
In Kota Damansara on the outskirts of Kuala Lumpur, a plot of land intended for a data centre remains empty after local opposition.
The developer withdrew its planning permission application in August, after its neighbours spoke out online, lobbied their MP and gathered more than 9,000 petition signatures.
Jahaidi Harun, 72, had been concerned that the proposed data centre could be noisy and pressure existing infrastructure.
Data centres "use a lot of water," the retiree told AFP, adding that, as in Batam, "if the rain doesn't come for one month, we all feel it".
Following the withdrawal, Malaysia's human resources minister Ramanan Ramakrishnan told local media he wasn't against "development or investment".
But "for large-scale projects that could affect the residents' lives, the people must have a say".

items.author: Sports Desk
items.content:
Pakistan moved closer to securing a place in the semi-finals after producing a dominant 3-0 victory over Maldives in their second Group B match of the SAFF Cup at National Stadium Dhaka on Sunday.
Pakistan scored all three goals in the first half.
McKeal Abdullah opened the scoring from the penalty spot before Najeebullah Bettani struck twice to put Pakistan firmly in control of the vital encounter.
Bettani doubled Pakistan's advantage with a well-timed finish after Junaid Shah delivered an inviting cross from the left. The forward made a perfectly timed run into the penalty area to get ahead of his marker and poke the ball past the goalkeeper.
He then completed his brace with an impressive individual effort. Collecting a clearance on the right after Pakistan had defended deep in their own half, Bettani brought the ball under control before unleashing a powerful strike beyond the helpless Maldives goalkeeper.
The Maldives enjoyed slightly more possession but struggled to turn it into meaningful attacking opportunities, while Pakistan proved more threatening in the final third.
Pakistan registered 15 shots, five of them on target, compared with the Maldives' seven attempts, of which only one was on target.
Both teams looked for further goals after the interval, but neither managed to find the breakthrough as Pakistan comfortably saw out the contest to claim all three points.
Pakistan must now await the outcome of the remaining Group match between the Maldives and India to confirm their semi-final qualification.
The Maldives need a substantial victory over India on November 11 to overhaul Pakistan and keep their hopes of reaching the last four alive. Otherwise, Pakistan and India will advance to the semi-finals.
In their earlier game Pakistan had lost to India 3-2 after a sensational finish.

items.author: AFP
items.content:
Every 90 seconds, an electric three-wheeler rolls off the production line at an Indian factory, underscoring a transformation that has made the country the largest market for battery-powered auto rickshaws.
At a bustling plant run by Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, workers and robots fit cells into battery packs, attach body panels to metal frames and fix wheels into place, racing to meet demand for vehicles known for navigating the chaotic streets of the world's most populous country.
In September, more than one in two new three-wheelers sold in India was electric, compared with about 8.5 percent of cars and 11.6 percent of two-wheelers, reaffirming its position as the world's largest electric three-wheeler market.
"Our company has grown six times in its EV penetration in the last five years," said Mahindra LMM's chief executive Suman Mishra.
She said adoption accelerated over the past two years as government subsidies, improving vehicle quality and falling operating costs combined to make ownership more attractive.
E-rickshaws first appeared on New Delhi's streets more than a decade ago, often assembled in roadside workshops using Chinese-made batteries fitted to modified pedal-powered tricycles.
But the sector has since eaten into the market for sturdier fossil-fuel-powered three-wheelers, becoming a major industry as manufacturers such as Mahindra expand their share.
The shift has altered the look and sound of Indian cities.
Across northern India, e-rickshaws now queue outside railway stations and bustling markets, replacing the thumping noise of traditional "tuk-tuks".
Mahindra is one of 15 finalists shortlisted for the environmental Earthshot Prize, to be awarded in Mumbai by Prince William on November 17.
For many drivers, however, earnings outweigh environmental benefits.
"Money is coming straight into my pocket," said Afroz Alam, a 31-year-old driver in Hyderabad who switched from a gas-powered model to an EV this year.
The cost of charging his vehicle saves him several hundred rupees a day, helping repay the loan he took out to buy the more expensive electric version.
"It may seem expensive, but then it levels out with the gas money you no longer have to pay," he told AFP.
Analysts agree economics is the key driver of adoption, with falling costs of batteries and rising fuel prices widening the advantage of e-vehicles.
Indian think-tank CEEW estimated in 2025 that petrol three-wheelers cost more than twice as much per kilometre to operate over their lifetime as EVs.
"Rickshaws, which operate continuously throughout the day, accumulate fuel savings rapidly," said Bidisha Bhattacharya of the Delhi-based Chintan Research Foundation.
Read More: Tesla to pull the plug on Cybertruck after years of poor sales
The trend has also been welcomed by policymakers in India, which imports most of its oil and natural gas and has scrambled to manage energy costs, since conflict in the Middle East erupted in February.
Climate think-tank Ember said India consumes less transport fuel per capita than China did at a comparable income level in 2012, helped by the spread of cheap solar power and declining battery costs.
"In the race to curb oil imports, India is already far ahead," Ember said in a recent report.
Yet hurdles remain, with adoption uneven across the country.
E-rickshaws are common in cities such as Lucknow but far less visible in Mumbai, where limited parking and charging infrastructure complicate ownership.
"In Mumbai, there is no parking at all," Mishra said.
"So you can park on the side of the road for a (fuel-run) vehicle, but how do you do it for an EV when you have to charge it?"
Supply chains pose another challenge.
Last year, China restricted exports of rare-earth magnets, an essential component in electric motors, forcing several Indian automakers to cut or suspend production.
New Delhi has responded by promoting domestic manufacturing, including battery cells, most of which are still imported from China and South Korea.
"Two players are very close to commercialisation of their cells in India. We have to be patient," Mishra said.
The bigger question is whether the success of e-rickshaws can be replicated in private cars and, eventually, trucks, which consume far more fuel.
Bhattacharya said commercial fleets could provide the next breakthrough.
When taxis transition to electric power, she said, they would help build the charging networks and consumer confidence.
For drivers already making the switch, the argument remains simple.
"They keep saying the battery will fail," said Mohammad Ali, 26, who bought an e-rickshaw this year.
"Do a trial, take the vehicle and do it for a day. They don't know yet how much money we are saving."

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
A Pakistani technology startup, RLabs, has received international recognition after winning the GOAL Startup Award at the Silicon Valley November Summit in California. RLabs, led by National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST) graduate Harris Ahmed, earned the award for its work in artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced simulation technologies.
The achievement highlights the growing potential of Pakistan’s technology industry and its ability to develop solutions for international markets. RLabs is now preparing to expand its operations into the United States.
Pakistani AI Startup RLabs Wins Startup Award in Silicon Valley
The Silicon Valley November Summit was organised by Plug and Play, a global innovation platform and venture capital firm. The event attracted more than 3,000 participants, including entrepreneurs, investors, technology experts and corporate executives.
RLabs was among 18 startups selected from different countries to present their innovations under Plug and Play’s Global Overseas Acceleration & Learning (GOAL) programme.
What Does RLabs Do?
RLabs specialises in extended reality (XR) simulators, synthetic data and machine training technologies. Its solutions help train people and intelligent machines to operate complex equipment and perform specialised tasks.
Harris Ahmed, who graduated from NUST in 2018, has spent nearly a decade developing XR technologies for training people to operate sophisticated machinery. He is now applying that experience to artificial intelligence and machine training.
Ahmed described the company’s approach as using human training experience to develop machine capabilities. He also announced that RLabs was preparing to enter the US market.
According to his professional profile, Ahmed has a background in computer graphics and virtual reality development. He has also participated in training programmes at Draper University and the University of London.
RLabs Develops AI-Powered Simulation Technology
The startup was incubated at the National Incubation Centre for Aerospace Technologies (NICAT), which supports emerging technology businesses in Pakistan.
According to NICAT, RLabs is developing its own large language model (LLM) to power a modular simulation engine that can operate across different platforms.
The technology aims to reduce simulation development time by up to 75%, potentially making the creation of advanced training environments faster and more efficient.
Such solutions have applications in industries where workers and machines need to perform complex tasks in controlled virtual environments.
Government Congratulates RLabs Team
Pakistan’s Minister for Information Technology and Telecommunication, Shaza Fatima Khawaja, congratulated Harris Ahmed and the RLabs team on their international achievement.
She described the award as a proud moment for Pakistan and said it demonstrated the potential of local technology talent and the country’s growing startup ecosystem.
The minister also appreciated Ignite, the government’s technology innovation organisation, for supporting entrepreneurship and helping emerging businesses access international opportunities.
She said Pakistan wanted its startups to do more than compete in global technology markets and contribute to shaping the future of innovation.
Pakistan’s Startup Industry Gains International Recognition
RLabs’ achievement comes as Pakistan continues its efforts to strengthen its technology sector and create opportunities for local entrepreneurs.
The government has taken several steps to support startups, including the development of technology parks, incubation centres and innovation hubs. The recently inaugurated National Technology Park in Islamabad will also bring startups, established technology companies and research organisations together.
The World Bank is also considering a proposed project that includes a $50 million Fund of Funds to encourage venture capital investment in Pakistan. The proposal is expected to be considered for approval in early 2027.
For RLabs, winning the Silicon Valley award represents an important milestone as it prepares to enter the US market. The recognition also shows how Pakistani startups are developing AI and advanced technology solutions with the potential to compete internationally.

US Approves Nvidia AI Chip Sale
items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Trump administration’s decision to allow Nvidia to sell advanced AI chips to Chinese companies has raised fresh national security concerns in the US. A new investigation by The New York Times found that several companies approved to purchase or handle Nvidia processors have business connections to US-blacklisted firms and Chinese military contractors.
The investigation has raised questions about how effectively US authorities screen Chinese companies before granting them access to advanced American semiconductor technology.
One of the companies approved by the US Commerce Department is New Matrix, a Chinese firm established around 17 months ago. According to the investigation, reporters who visited its registered office in an industrial park outside Beijing found an apparently vacant space. Neither the building directory nor the industrial park management had any record of the company.
US Approves Nvidia AI Chip Sales to Chinese Firms Linked to Military
Chinese corporate records also linked New Matrix’s owners to Wise Road, a private equity fund that the US placed on its trade blacklist in 2024 over allegations that it helped China acquire strategically important semiconductor businesses. Two analysts who reviewed the records suggested that New Matrix could be connected to companies associated with the blacklisted fund.
US Approves Around Two Dozen Chinese Companies
The Trump administration approved Nvidia’s H200 processor sales to China in December 2025, reversing some earlier restrictions designed to prevent Beijing from accessing advanced chips that could strengthen its military capabilities.
Under the arrangement, Nvidia chips manufactured in Taiwan must first pass through the United States before reaching Chinese buyers. The arrangement also allows Washington to collect a 25% tariff on their value.
The US Commerce Department has reportedly approved around two dozen Chinese companies to purchase or handle H200 processors. These include major businesses such as Baidu, BYD and Tesla Shanghai. Alibaba, Tencent, ByteDance and ZTE Kangxun Telecom have also reportedly received approval.
Each approved company can purchase tens of thousands of H200 chips, although none had reached its permitted limit at the time of the investigation.
Liza Tobin, a former China director at the White House National Security Council, questioned whether the US government and Nvidia were conducting sufficient background checks on approved buyers. She expressed concerns about whether companies were properly following the licensing requirements.
However, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security defended its screening process. The agency said it carefully examines applications for potential national security risks. It also reported imposing $324 million in penalties for export violations during 2025 and hiring more than 90 enforcement officers in 2026 to strengthen oversight.
Investigation Finds Links to Chinese Military Contractors
The investigation also identified other approved companies with connections to Chinese military suppliers and businesses facing US restrictions.
One example is Maginfra, a relatively new Chinese company whose registered office also appeared vacant during the newspaper’s visit. Analysts suggested that the company had links to Inspur, a Chinese technology firm previously placed on the US Entity List over its involvement with China’s military.
Corporate records showed that Maginfra and Inspur shared personnel and patents. Both companies also had government ownership connections.
Another approved buyer, Zhejiang Yindun Cloud Technology, had links to Range Intelligent Computing Technology Group. The latter provides cloud computing services to military contractors and supports a satellite programme operated by the defence bureau of China’s Hebei province.
The investigation also identified Shanghai Jiatang, a company originating from state-owned Datang Telecom. The company supplies technology to China’s military and operates under the China Academy of Telecommunications Technology, which is involved in military cryptography development.
However, the investigation did not establish that any of the approved Nvidia processors had reached China’s military. The corporate connections instead raised concerns about whether existing export controls can prevent restricted organisations from accessing advanced chips.
Nvidia Defends Its China Business
Nvidia defended its sales to China, arguing that the Chinese military has little reason to depend on American semiconductor technology.
The company also said Beijing had restricted H200 imports to encourage the use of locally manufactured processors. Nvidia maintained that its limited exports to China continued to support American jobs and manufacturing.
The company’s financial disclosures showed that H200 shipments to China-based customers accounted for less than 1% of its data centre revenue in the quarter ending in July. Nvidia also said in August that its revenue forecast for the following quarter did not include any data centre sales to China.
Meanwhile, Chinese AI companies have increasingly explored access to advanced American processors through overseas data centres, particularly in Southeast Asia. US officials have previously raised concerns that some Chinese firms could use foreign companies and infrastructure to bypass American export restrictions.
The latest investigation has renewed debate in Washington over the risks of allowing advanced AI chip exports to China. In December 2025, a bipartisan group of US senators also proposed legislation to prevent the administration from relaxing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China and other countries for two and a half years.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Democrats are planning to unleash a flood of new legislation targeting artificial intelligence systems and data-center development when they take control of the US Congress in January, lawmakers, congressional aides and advocates said.
The plans would mark ​a sharp shift from the Republican-led Congress, where lawmakers largely focused on promoting AI development and declined to pass legislation restricting aspects of the ‌technology at a time when voters turned against the rapid development of data centers and their extensive power needs.
Democrats plan on introducing bills aimed at shielding consumers from rising electricity costs tied to data centers, requiring independent testing of advanced AI systems and clarifying when AI companies can be held liable for harm caused by their products, they said.
Any legislation would face steep odds while Republican President Donald ​Trump remains in the White House, as he has repeatedly dismissed calls to write mandatory rules for AI technology.
On Friday, Trump said he would work ​with US states that "want to become RICH" by embracing AI, without offering details.
But Democratic lawmakers and outside advocates said control of ⁠congressional committees would give the party a platform to advance proposals, compel testimony from industry leaders and build support for action if AI systems cause real-world harm. Representative ​Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat and chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, already said this week that AI executives should be called to testify under oath.
Read More: How Trump’s broken bargain broke his coalition
Federal government restrictions on ​AI development could hurt the industry's profits if they slow the release of new models or prompt the companies to change how their AI tools perform to address concerns that their products are harming people.r
Technology shares sold off dramatically on Thursday on growing concerns that a new Congress will slow AI development, and also on fears that the massive capital expense on building out AI will ​not yield sufficient returns.
Stocks on Friday extended their slide in both Europe and Asia following the rout, though Wall Street futures pointed to a modest bounce for the Nasdaq later ​on Friday.
Multiple bills likely
Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Thursday at an event in Washington that protecting consumers from higher energy ‌costs linked ⁠to the rapid expansion of data centers would be among his priorities next year.
Representative Lori Trahan of Massachusetts, one of the Democratic Party's leading voices on AI policy, plans to push legislation requiring independent experts to evaluate leading AI models against safety standards, said Francis Grubar, her deputy chief of staff. Trahan will also pursue legislation clarifying that companies can be held responsible when AI systems act in harmful ways, he said.
Representative Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat from California who is seeking to chair the House Science Committee, ​said Democrats would focus on developing "responsible regulations ​for AI while also fostering innovation."
Abdul ⁠El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat who won a Senate seat on Tuesday, called during his campaign for an independent agency to oversee AI regulation with the power to police tech companies developing the technology.
Public concern about AI is already high. Most US voters think ​Trump's administration and Congress are not taking the risks of AI seriously enough and want the government to write new ​regulations for the technology, ⁠according to a Reuters poll published in October. A crisis could build enough support to overcome presidential opposition to AI regulation, said Ed Mills, who manages policy research at Raymond James.
"The probability of legislation is much higher than people anticipate," he said.
Congress can override a presidential veto with the backing of two-thirds of lawmakers in both chambers. Democrats could also try to ⁠insert AI ​regulation into routine bills that must pass Congress each year, Mills said.
Democrats also plan to use their ​new authority to intensify scrutiny of the industry's most powerful companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. Lofgren and other Democratic House committee leaders in October asked OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Alphabet's Google and SpaceX to detail their ​security practices and report instances of their AI tools taking actions that their designers did not intend.

items.author: Onsa Mustafa
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has directed relevant authorities to develop a clear roadmap with specific timelines and targets to establish a digital payment system across Pakistan. The government aims to accelerate the transition towards a cashless economy by improving internet connectivity and making digital payment services accessible to the public.
The prime minister issued these directions while chairing a high-level meeting in Islamabad on November 6 to review progress on the government’s cashless economy initiative. He said promoting digital transactions remained a key government priority and noted that the initiative had already started producing positive results.
Pakistan Moves Towards Cashless Economy as PM Orders Digital Payment Roadmap
According to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Office, Shehbaz Sharif stressed the need to ensure reliable internet connectivity across the country. He also directed authorities to make technology easily accessible so that people from different areas could adopt digital payment services without difficulty.
The prime minister further instructed the relevant departments to address complaints related to digital payment services promptly and improve the overall experience for users.
During the meeting, Shehbaz highlighted the importance of the government’s Raast QR Code initiative in encouraging digital transactions between consumers and merchants. He directed authorities to expand its use and promote QR-based payments for everyday transactions.
He also called for an effective awareness campaign to encourage electricity and gas consumers to pay their utility bills through QR codes printed on their bills. All ministries and government departments must ensure the complete implementation of the cashless economy plan.
The meeting was informed that federal and provincial government departments were making progress in shifting their payment systems to digital platforms. Most government institutions are expected to complete the digitalisation process by December.
The government has also moved towards digital payments under the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP), with all beneficiary payments now being processed through digital wallets.
See Also: Pakistan and Sudan Agree to Cooperate in Combating Cybercrime
Authorities are also developing an advanced digital payment mechanism for areas without internet connectivity. Work on infrastructure improvements is underway to expand internet access nationwide and support the wider adoption of digital financial services.
In another major development, the government will discontinue cheque-based payments into Asaan Assignment Accounts from November 15. Starting November 16, all payments into these accounts across Pakistan will take place through the Raast digital payment system.
The meeting was informed that the relevant drawing and disbursing officers had already received training to implement the new payment arrangement.
The latest directives reflect the government’s efforts to reduce reliance on cash, expand digital transactions, and improve access to financial services across the country.

items.author: AFP
items.content:
Kavem Hodge hit an unbeaten 140 to extend West Indies' lead to 315 on the fourth day of the second Test against Bangladesh in Sylhet on Sunday.
West Indies reached 345-3 in their second innings when bad light halted play, with Hodge hitting 17 fours and a six off 189 balls and Amir Jangoo also unbeaten on 20.
Hodge, who scored his third Test century and passed his previous highest score, was backed by opener Brandon King, who made 61, and debutant Kevin Wickham, who scored 78 for his second half-century of the match.
West Indies resumed the day on 7-0, trailing by 23 runs.
King and Joshua Da Silva put on 85 for the opening wicket, before Taijul Islam trapped Da Silva lbw for 36.
King continued to attack, reaching his half-century off 62 balls.
He was dropped by Towhid Hridoy on 56 off Taijul before Mehidy Hasan Miraz dismissed him for 61 off 84 balls, caught by Najmul Hossain Shanto at first slip.
West Indies went to lunch on 128-2, with Hodge and Wickham at the crease and their lead at 98.
'Chaseable'
Hodge reached his half-century off 78 balls, while Wickham needed 68 deliveries to bring up his second fifty of the match. The pair took West Indies to tea at 259-2, with their lead extended to 229.
Hodge completed his century after the break, reaching the milestone off 142 balls with 11 fours and a six.
Hodge said he was pleased to contribute after failing to convert a start in the first Test in Dhaka, adding that the West Indies would assess conditions before deciding when to declare.
"It's always nice to contribute to the team," he said. "We just have to come tomorrow and assess ... play it by ear and keep going moment by moment."
Taijul broke their 165-run partnership, dismissing Wickham for a career-best 78 off 107 balls after he chipped the ball back to the bowler. West Indies were 284-3 when Wickham departed.
Bangladesh missed another chance to remove Hodge when captain Shanto dropped him off Nayeem Hasan on 117.
Jangoo, who scored a century in the first innings, joined Hodge and helped push the West Indies lead beyond 300.
Hridoy was confident Bangladesh had a strong chance on the final day, saying the pitch remained good for batting.
"If we can get a good start, 350 is chaseable, in my opinion," he said. "But as I said, the start is very important."

items.title: PM Shehbaz briefs Nawaz Sharif on K-P security, economic challenges
items.summary:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) leader Nawaz Sharif in Lahore on Sunday and briefed him on the security situation in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), the country’s economic challenges and the government’s ongoing reform agenda, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said.
According to the PMO, the meeting took place at Jati Umra, where Nawaz was briefed on the government’s ongoing reforms, particularly economic reforms, the challenges facing the country and measures being taken to address them.
The two leaders held detailed consultations on national political matters and steps to improve the economy, according to the PMO.
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz also attended the meeting.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz also attended the meeting.

وزیرِ اعظم نے میاں محمد نواز شریف کو خیبرپختونخوا میں امن و امان کی صورتحال کے…
— Prime Minister's Office (@PakPMO) November 8, 2026
The meeting took place as consumers faced another increase in electricity prices. The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA) notified a Rs2.36 per-unit increase on Saturday under the monthly fuel cost adjustment for September.
The higher electricity costs came amid expensive LNG imports and uncertainty over supplies. Pakistan was expected to spend about $1.29 billion on 22 LNG cargoes between November 2026 and February 2027, including 10 spot-market cargoes estimated to cost $863 million.
The Power Division also warned that fuel price adjustments could rise two to three times between December and February as international LNG and coal prices increased and hydropower generation declined during winter. The department cautioned that consumers could face a further financial burden, alongside increased power load management.
The meeting also followed the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in K-P on October 11, after President Asif Ali Zardari approved the summary on PM Shehbaz’s advice under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution.
The federal government cited a deterioration in the law and order situation and a rise in terrorist attacks as grounds for the decision. Under the proclamation, the provincial chief minister, cabinet members, advisers and advocate general ceased to hold office, while the governor assumed powers assigned to him by the federal government.
Read: PHC strikes off petitions against governor's rule
The measures also included the deployment of the Pakistan Army to assist the civil administration under Article 245 and the appointment of Dr Muhammad Fakhr Alam Irfan as the province’s chief secretary. An 11-member advisory council was formed to assist the governor, while a separate administrative arrangement was announced for 12 districts to be placed directly under the federation.
At a briefing in Peshawar on Saturday, Governor Faisal Karim Kundi said the provincial government had planned Rs70 billion for the police and Rs10.3 billion for the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD) during the current financial year.
Plans also include installing anti-drone systems in Dera Ismail Khan, Lakki Marwat and Bannu, as well as addressing vacant police posts and improving security infrastructure. Officials said the province faced a shortage of about 17,000 police personnel.
Despite continued intelligence-based operations (IBOs) by security forces, terrorist attacks across K-P have persisted, with police and security personnel increasingly coming under fire. Terrorist incidents in the province rose by 195 per cent between March 2024 and September 2026, according to security reports presented to the federal cabinet. The reports also recorded 170 drone attacks against police and security forces in 2026, compared with none in 2024.

items.author: Shraddha Goled
items.content:
Anjali Sardana and Pronto entered India’s domestic services market in 2025 to solve a familiar urban problem: finding reliable house help on demand. The result was a quick commerce-style home services platform, combining technology-led recruitment, standardised training and a hyperlocal network of professionals.
Pronto, which competes with Snabbit and Urban Company, says it has served more than half a million households across 11 cities. But the real story of Pronto is being developed far away from the homes and houses that its professionals visit.
This is being built in Silicon Valley.
Footage recorded by professionals working in thousands of homes every day is helping shape the next generation of robots.
The first signs of this ambition emerged in May 2026, when Pronto was reported to be exploring ways to generate physical AI training data using footage captured during household chores. And since then Sardana and Pronto’s ambitions have solidified.
In July, Pronto formalised the experiment through Verified, an opt-in premium service in which housekeepers and cleaners wear head-mounted or body-mounted cameras during visits.
In October 2026, Sardana set up Provision Labs, a physical AI venture based in San Francisco, which will collect data to train and test AI systems designed to perform real-world tasks using robots and other machines. It will work with developers building physical AI models.
A few days later, Provision Labs announced that it is acquiring Mumbai-based Basilisk Industries, a 2023-founded company focused on perception technologies, which help machines interpret their surroundings.
Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision’s hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models. Watwani and his team are said to have developed a 3D hand-tracking model and built the first version of a lightweight tactile glove to capture touch-related data.
Given this timeline, the fact that Pronto doubled-down on its experiment after the May 2026 introduction does not seem surprising at all.
The relationship between Pronto’s household data collection and Provision Labs’ operations, however, remains unclear. Inc42 asked Pronto how the two businesses work together, if at all, but the company declined to comment.
The unanswered question is significant: could a network originally built to deliver household services become an acquisition channel for the data needed to train global robotics systems?
Why Record Workers?
The first reports around Pronto’s collection of worker data triggered a backlash over surveillance and privacy of house help professionals.
To assuage some of the critics, Pronto said that customers are informed about the terms several times before recording begins, while personally identifiable information is automatically blurred or removed on the device.
“The raw footage is deleted immediately after the work is done, and no one ever accesses it. For 48 hours, an anonymised, end-to-end encrypted recording is available only to the customer, who can watch it in the app to check the work. After that, we use the anonymised footage for AI training, as our terms set out,” the company told Inc42.
Pronto said more than half of the professionals participating in Verified already earn over ₹40,000 a month. The company claims workers feel safer knowing there is a record of their work, but no independent studies have been conducted to validate these claims.
What’s the point of all this?
Unlike chatbots, which can learn from the enormous repositories of text and images available online, physical AI systems need to understand how the real world works. A robot must learn how to pick up objects, fold clothes, navigate a room, and respond when something does not go as expected.
This requires large volumes of real-world, multimodal data capturing movement, spatial information and interactions with objects. Such data is considerably harder and more expensive to collect than internet-sourced text and images. ANI quoted a Goldman Sachs report estimating that general-purpose robots could require around 10 Mn hours of high-quality physical interaction data to reach production-level capabilities.
The Missing Data Layer
One can see the physical AI stack through four layers. The data layer captures real-world interactions, while the model layer uses this information to train vision-language-action models that translate what a robot sees into actions.
The simulation layer through platforms such as NVIDIA’s Isaac Sim allow these models to be tested in virtual environments before deployment. Finally, the edge layer runs them on physical robots, with real-world feedback informing and enhancing the training process.
Global technology companies such as NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, Amazon, OpenAI and Anthropic are building capabilities across the model and simulation layers of physical AI.
India has some representation at the robotics and deployment end, with companies such as Addverb, CynLr and Perceptyne developing robotic systems and automation technologies.
But it is the data layer that is seeing a growing crop of Indian startups, alongside global data companies building collection operations that rely heavily on India’s workforce and physical environments.
Humyn Labs, EgoData, Egolab.ai, Neocambrian AI, Human Archive, and Objectways have deployed people on the ground to collect footage across household chores, but several are also working with manufacturing units and other industrial environments.
Head-mounted or body-mounted cameras and sensor-equipped gloves or even full body suits have become commonplace as the next phase of robotics takes shape.
For India, the opportunity has echoes of its earlier role in the AI supply chain. Over the past decade, India has become a hub for data annotation, with workers labelling images, text and audio used to train AI models.
Physical AI takes that outsourcing model a step further. Indian workers’ movements, workplaces and interactions with objects are becoming the training material.
Abhinav Kukreja, founder of Neocambrian AI, sees India’s large and diverse physical environments as an advantage over markets such as the US, where access to comparable real-world data is more limited.
He believes the next phase of robotics will see an explosion of different embodiments and form factors. For India to participate meaningfully in this transition, it needs to control an important part of the underlying ecosystem. “I strongly felt that this layer would not be compute, architecture or algorithms, but the data layer,” he said.
Y Combinator-backed Human Archive is pursuing a similar opportunity, with a model that involves home service workers, cooks, cleaners and domestic help wearing cameras inside homes and private properties.
Cofounder Rushil Agarwal told Inc42 earlier that the Indian market’s appeal lies in the diversity of industries accessible within the geographical boundary and the large labour pool. This is difficult to replicate in the US.
Notably, Human Archive was evaluated by Snabbit too as it looked to launch a Pronto-like data collection pilot. However, the home services company eventually dropped the proposal.
Human Archive raised $8.2 Mn in a seed round led by Wing Venture Capital and NVP Capital. Pronto’s $45 Mn Series B also saw participation from Lachy Groom, cofounder of robotics model startup Physical Intelligence; Groom has also backed Provision Labs. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs, led by former Nazara CEO Manish Agarwal, has committed $20 Mn towards expanding its data collection network.
The supply side, meanwhile, is becoming more competitive. Data collection rates fell 30% between January and June this year, an industry executive told Inc42 earlier.
More suppliers have since entered the market and synthetic data generation has improved rapidly. But in the long run, the demand for human-captured footage could shrink as physical AI models mature.
The larger question is who captures the value and what happens to the workers. We’ll come to the latter soon, but the current situation does not give us any clarity on what this segment might look like in a few months.
While Pronto says more than half of its Verified professionals earn over ₹40,000 a month, Human Archive has cited compensation in the range of $1-10 per hour for its data collection work. These disparate compensation structures highlight the lack of clarity on the economic model. One cannot draw parallels between the kind of data captured either till the industry further matures.
At this point, companies are throwing a lot more money than they are willing to to attract workers who will readily collect data that can in a few years replace them.
Indian manufacturers and industrial units may recruit workers, deploy cameras and collect footage, while the resulting models and intellectual property are developed and owned elsewhere. This value drain could have serious consequences on the Indian economy and the jobs landscape.
For data suppliers, the challenge will be moving beyond one-off collection contracts to building differentiated datasets that command lasting value. As more and more companies come into the picture, the collection of egocentric data and first-person footage is about to become highly commodified and consumerised.
The Elephant In The Room: What About The Workers?
Like we mentioned, the business opportunity comes with a difficult labour question. The blunt reading of the matter is that Indian workers are training the robots that could eventually replace them.
Videos circulating on social media have raised concerns about whether workers even understand why they are wearing cameras. Some workers have reported discomfort from prolonged use, which may stretch to 5-10 hours a workday, while others believe the devices are intended to monitor their productivity.
Every company maintains that workers are informed about what is being captured and why. However, when collection happens through partner businesses, the responsibility for communicating this information shifts to those partners.
An openDemocracy investigation, meanwhile, found that workers at two Delhi factories were asked to wear cameras supplied by Egolab.ai without being told their purpose.
Such incidents raise questions about informed consent, compensation, the privacy of other people captured in recordings and ownership of the resulting data.
India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose implementation is scheduled for May 2027, adds another layer of regulatory uncertainty. Speculation is that the government may regulate these services, but to what extent can it stop individuals from participating is unclear.
For Sardana and Pronto, the opportunity is significantly larger than just a quick home services platform.
The data from the broad range of everyday human activity by Pronto workers can fuel Provision Labs and Basilisk’s next big plays and turn them into even bigger companies than Pronto.
Whether Pronto and Provision Labs will eventually work together has not been answered. But the value of Pronto’s network may very soon be the footage of what its professionals do, rather than the quality of the service itself.
[Edited by Nikhil Subramaniam]

items.author: News Desk
items.content:
The Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) has not approved Rs1.094 billion for the purchase of a new luxury executive jet for the military leadership, contrary to claims circulating on social media, officials have clarified.
According to ECC sources and Ministry of Defence (MoD) officials, the allocation is exclusively meant for the maintenance, operational overhaul and induction-related logistics of an existing aircraft currently being used by the prime minister.
The clarification comes amid social media claims that the government had sanctioned funds for the procurement of a high-end executive aircraft, such as the Embraer Lineage 1000, for military leadership.
Read: Aviation systems to be upgraded
Officials said the amount had been misrepresented, stressing that the approved grant was linked to the upkeep of an existing government-owned aircraft and did not involve the acquisition of a new one.
The financial figures also contradict claims of a new purchase. An executive jet of the Embraer Lineage 1000 class is estimated to cost between $25 million and $50 million or more, equivalent to approximately Rs7 billion to Rs14 billion. The Rs1.094 billion allocation, estimated at around $3.9 million, is substantially below the aircraft’s purchase price.
Officials explained that the funds would cover essential maintenance requirements, including engine overhauls, avionics upkeep and other operational expenses associated with the state’s existing VIP transport fleet.
Read More: Govt not financing purchase of new PIA aircraft, says finance adviser
They maintained that allocations for the maintenance and operational requirements of government-owned aircraft fall within routine administrative and budgetary procedures.
The officials termed the portrayal of the allocation as funding for a new luxury aircraft for military leadership factually incorrect and misleading.
