items.author: Reuters
items.content:
The rising cost of living will be top of mind for Americans as they head to the polls in Tuesday's midterm elections which will determine control of Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's term.
What follows are results from a Reuters/Ipsos poll of ​1,765 US adults conducted nationwide Thursday through Monday — making the survey distinct from an exit poll which includes voters surveyed ‌as they leave polling stations. The poll had a margin of error of 3 percentage points for registered voters.
The cost of living
Some 48% of registered voters in the poll say the cost of living is the top issue for deciding how they will vote, compared with 26% who say democratic norms and 13% who point to ​immigration. US fuel prices have surged since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February.
Donald Trump
Trump has urged supporters to ​pretend he is on the ballot in an effort to energise his Republican Party. The Reuters/Ipsos poll showed ⁠that 48% of people who planned to vote — or already had done so — said they thought of their ballots as a vote against Trump, ​compared to 25% who said they were voting for him. Some 25% said Trump was not a factor in their vote.
Read More: US voters head to polls to deliver midterm verdict on Trump
Iran
Trump has argued that war ​was necessary to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons. Some 25% of voters think military action has been worth the cost, and 55% say it has not been worth it. Some 18% weren't sure.
Election integrity
Voters overall trust the US electoral process, with 77% saying they are confident their ballots will be counted but 45% saying they think ​voter fraud is a widespread problem. Trump has falsely claimed that massive numbers of non-citizens vote illegally and election officials worry the administration could disrupt ​the election or certification of results it views unfavourably. The White House says its goal is to safeguard election integrity and voting security.
Household finances
Some 49% of Americans think ‌their household ⁠finances have gotten worse since January 2025, when Trump returned to power, compared with 13% who said their finances have gotten better and 37% who say things are about the same. Trump campaigned ahead of the November 2024 presidential election with a promise to turbocharge the economy, but his presidential approval has fallen in recent months to the lowest levels of his political career, including among Hispanic Americans who swung in his direction in ​2024. The latest poll showed 54% ​of Hispanics said their household ⁠finances have suffered, while 10% said they had improved.
Transgender sports
Some 38% of voters ahead of the election said keeping transgender girls and women out of women's sports was a very important issue or the most important issue, ​compared to 25% who said that about protecting the rights of transgender people.
Data centers
Some 42% of registered ​voters in the poll ⁠said limiting the construction of data centres used to power AI was very important or the most important issue.
Mega donors
The ultra-rich face few limits on how much they can spend to influence federal elections. A bipartisan majority of registered voters — including 93% of Democrats and 71% of Republicans — think it is ⁠inappropriate for ​billionaires to contribute tens of millions of dollars to influence elections.
Political options
While poll respondents appeared ​to narrowly favour Democrats over Republicans for this year's congressional elections, they remain divided on which party has good ideas. Some 43% of registered voters in the poll said Democrats ​had at least some good ideas, while 39% said the same of Republicans.

items.content:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he made ​a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Washington would stop $4 billion in funding to Israel after the end of ‌this year.
It was not immediately clear which funding Trump meant or how exactly the funding would be stopped at the end of the year, given that the memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion in US military aid to Israel each year does not expire until 2028. Conversations have been underway on how ​Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
Speaking to Fox News' "Fox & Friends" programme, Trump said Israel no longer needed ​the funding and that some Democrats and left-wing politicians were using the US financial support to Israel as ⁠a talking point to criticise Republicans.
Read: Questioning strategic logic: US military support to Israel
BREAKING: President Trump says the U.S. will end roughly $4 billion in annual aid to Israel by the end of the year, revealing that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed to the decision.
“Because they don’t need it,” Trump said during an exclusive interview on @foxandfriends,… pic.twitter.com/ItBUcMrtuZ
— Fox News (@FoxNews) November 3, 2026
"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 ​billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump said. "We've already agreed that by the end of this year ​we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it," he said.
Neither the White House nor Netanyahu's office responded to Reuters' requests for comment.
US public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters ​and 66% of Democrats believe the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20%, respectively, when the question was first asked ​in 2017.
Criticism of Israel
Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries, and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to ‌challenge decades ⁠of US support for Israel.
Read More: California governor says US military aid to Israel must be conditioned
Abdul El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim US senator if he wins in Michigan in the midterm elections on Tuesday, opposed unconditional military aid to Israel, saying US funding should prioritise US citizens.
Abdul El-Sayed:
I don't know about you, but I don't pay my taxes to buy another country a bomb or a tank.
That's Israel, that's Egypt, that's Saudi Arabia, that's Pakistan.
My interest is making sure that our kids get good schools, that we have functional roads, that we're… pic.twitter.com/ORdKaqIYC0
— Clash Report (@clashreport) November 2, 2026
Trump said the left used the US funding as a "signal of unfairness" and that he could not allow that to happen. He specifically mentioned El-Sayed when explaining why he said Washington was stopping the money.
"Because ​they (Israel) don't need it, and because ​why should we suffer the ⁠slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don't need it? It's a bad, it's a bad talking point," Trump said.
Some members of Trump's Make America Great Again movement have also become increasingly critical ​of Israel, accusing it of having misled Trump — who campaigned in 2024 on a promise to avoid ​foreign military interventions — ⁠into believing Iran could easily be defeated in a war.
Congress passed a law in 2020 authorising the funding for Israel, but the Senate and House of Representatives must still pass appropriations bills every year to distribute and release the funds.
Netanyahu said in an interview with an Israeli television channel in ⁠October: "If you ​think we're going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that's tens of ​billions of dollars in American aid for the defence budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won't happen because America has changed."

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Concerns over the security of Pakistani citizens’ personal data have emerged during a parliamentary committee meeting, with a lawmaker calling for stronger safeguards and suggesting that citizens’ information should remain within the country’s borders.
The issue was raised during a meeting of the National Assembly Standing Committee on Information Technology and Telecommunication, chaired by Syed Aminul Haque, where officials briefed lawmakers on the Pakistan Digital Authority (PDA) and the government’s digital transformation plans.
Committee member Musa Gilani expressed concerns about weaknesses in the country’s existing data protection arrangements, warning that additional measures are needed to ensure the security of citizens’ information.
He said Pakistan’s digital systems still have several shortcomings when it comes to protecting sensitive data and urged the government to pay greater attention to these vulnerabilities. Earlier reporting on Pakistan’s data governance policy and citizens’ rights has also highlighted the importance of safeguards for personal information.
Gilani argued that Pakistani citizens’ data should remain within Pakistan, raising the issue of data localisation as the country expands its digital infrastructure.
However, his remarks reflected a recommendation during the committee proceedings rather than an announcement of a new government policy requiring all citizens’ data to be stored locally.
Federal Minister for Information Technology Shaza Fatima Khawaja, responding to questions about the Pakistan Digital Authority, explained that the authority would issue standards governing aspects of the country’s digital systems and data-related processes.
She also clarified that the role of a regulator is different from operational and policymaking responsibilities.
Pakistan Digital Authority Outlines Digital Infrastructure Plans and Data Protection Challenges
During the meeting, the Director General of the Pakistan Digital Authority briefed the committee on the government’s vision for building a digital nation.
He explained that Pakistan’s transition towards a digital economy involves three key pillars, which formed part of the thinking behind the establishment of the Pakistan Digital Authority.
According to the DG, the authority has been tasked with overseeing standards and regulation relating to digital public infrastructure, an important component of the government’s broader digital transformation agenda.
He also highlighted the economic potential of digital infrastructure, suggesting that improvements in this area could positively influence Pakistan’s economy.
The DG referred to a possible economic impact of up to 2%, although the briefing details available did not clarify the exact economic indicator or timeframe associated with that figure.
At the same time, officials acknowledged that expanding digital infrastructure brings significant data-related risks that must be addressed. The authority’s proposed role in governing government data has previously drawn attention.
Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja said the Pakistan Digital Authority was established as part of the prime minister’s vision for Digital Pakistan.
Committee member Musa Gilani welcomed the establishment of the authority and expressed hope that its initiatives would benefit citizens. However, he maintained that protecting personal data should remain a central priority.
He urged the IT minister to consider additional safeguards, particularly measures aimed at ensuring that sensitive information belonging to Pakistani citizens remains secure. Concerns over the protection of citizens’ information against data breaches have also been raised by cybersecurity authorities.
Committee chairman Syed Aminul Haque acknowledged the suggestion and said it would be considered. He also appreciated the Pakistan Digital Authority’s work since its establishment.
The discussion highlights a challenge for Pakistan’s digital transformation: expanding digital public services while ensuring that the systems handling citizens’ information are adequately protected.
For now, the committee’s deliberations indicate growing parliamentary interest in data security and digital sovereignty, but they do not establish that any new data localization requirement has been formally approved.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan’s expanding 5G network has come under scrutiny after lawmakers raised concerns about the uneven distribution of telecom infrastructure, revealing that Sukkur has only two 5G sites despite being a major city in Sindh.
The issue was raised during a meeting of the National Assembly Standing Committee on Information Technology and Telecommunication, chaired by Syed Aminul Haque.
During the meeting, Aminul Haque pointed out that Sukkur, which he described as Sindh’s third-largest city, currently has only two 5G sites.
Another committee member questioned why the deployment of 5G infrastructure in Sindh appeared to be concentrated primarily in Karachi, leaving other cities with limited access to next-generation mobile connectivity. PhoneWorld previously reported on Karachi’s addition of 189 new 5G sites during the rollout.
The concerns highlight the challenge of extending 5G coverage across Pakistani cities while smaller cities and underserved regions continue to seek better connectivity.
Federal IT Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja also noted that growing data consumption has increased the load on telecom networks, making infrastructure development increasingly important.
USF Deploys 468 Telecom Sites as Committee Calls for Better Regional Connectivity
The committee also discussed the need to improve mobile connectivity in Balochistan and other underserved areas.
Chairman Syed Aminul Haque stressed that Balochistan, being one of the country’s most underdeveloped provinces, must receive greater attention when it comes to improving telecom services.
During a separate briefing, Universal Service Fund (USF) officials informed the committee that 468 telecom sites had been installed across the country over the past two years.
Officials said USF continues to prioritise projects in remote and underserved regions, with several connectivity initiatives already completed and others currently underway.
The briefing reflects the broader work of USF in connecting remote areas, where expanding commercial networks can be difficult. PhoneWorld has also reported on USF’s previous connectivity and fibre-optic deployments.
However, the 468 sites reported by USF should not be confused with 5G installations, as officials did not specify that these were exclusively 5G sites.
The discussion raised broader questions about how Pakistan’s 5G expansion is being distributed across different cities and provinces.
While lawmakers questioned the apparent focus on Karachi, they called for smaller cities such as Sukkur and underserved regions, including Balochistan, to receive adequate attention.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Bengaluru-based D2C jewellery brand GIVA has raised ₹975 Cr (about $103 Mn) in a funding round led by Multiples Alternate Asset Management, with participation from existing investors Epiq Capital and Edelweiss Discovery Fund, as it looks to accelerate its offline expansion, strengthen manufacturing capabilities, and widen its product portfolio.
The transaction comprised a mix of primary and secondary capital, alongside an ESOP buyback, GIVA cofounder and CEO Ishendra Agarwal told Inc42.
Early investors India Quotient and Sixth Sense Ventures will partially exit through the transaction while retaining stakes, Agarwal said. Multiples will also secure a board seat.
GIVA’s seventh ESOP buyback, worth approximately ₹20-25 Cr, will benefit around 50-60 employees.
The latest valuation was not disclosed. Agarwal said it was higher than the approximately ₹4,500-4,600 Cr (about $422 Mn to $474 Mn) valuation of its previous publicly announced funding round.
GIVA reported revenue of ₹865 Cr in FY26 as against ₹505 Cr in FY25, according to Agarwal. Its negative EBITDA margin narrowed to single digits from double digits over the same period.
Agarwal attributed the improvement to its maturing store network. Stores operating for more than a year are profitable, he said, with rising same-store sales helping absorb rent and employee costs. GIVA expects to become profitable on a profit after tax (PAT) basis in FY28.
GIVA To Add 160 Stores, Invest In Manufacturing
GIVA operates around 425 stores across India and plans to add 160 outlets in FY27, with a greater focus on Tier II and III markets.
About 70% of its stores are in metros, with the remainder in smaller cities. It plans to deepen its presence in Lucknow, Dehradun, Kanpur, and Surat, while entering markets such as Agra.
Offline retail contributes approximately 45% of revenue, with its D2C channel accounting for 55%. Agarwal expects offline’s share to reach 75-80% over the next three years.
GIVA will also invest in manufacturing capabilities in Jaipur and Mumbai. It outsources bulk manufacturing but handles plating and finishing entirely in-house, along with customised and made-to-order products.
Greater control over plating and finishing would improve product quality and consistency, Agarwal said.
The startup also plans to expand inventory across silver, gold, and lab-grown diamond jewellery, particularly in the ₹10,000-40,000 price range.
Silver Remains Revenue Mainstay
Founded in 2019 as an online-first silver jewellery brand, GIVA has since expanded into gold and lab-grown diamonds.
Silver contributes around 60% of revenue, while gold and lab-grown diamond jewellery together account for 40%, Agarwal said.
Its average selling price (ASP) is around ₹3,500 for silver jewellery and ₹15,000–18,000 for lab-grown diamond jewellery. Blended average order value stands at approximately ₹5,000, with offline orders typically worth nearly twice as much as online purchases.
Within gold jewellery, 9-carat and 14-carat products are gaining traction. Introduced around four months ago, 9-carat gold jewellery now accounts for approximately 25% of its combined gold and lab-grown diamond business.
GIVA is also expanding its men’s portfolio, which contributes around 20% of its silver jewellery business.
Its recently launched demi-fine jewellery brand Ixia remains at an early stage. Agarwal said its revenue was doubling MoM, albeit on a small base.
Building Towards IPO Readiness
The addition of fine gold and lab-grown diamond jewellery has helped GIVA generate more revenue from existing customers. Agarwal said customer lifetime value has doubled among customers moving from silver to lab-grown diamond jewellery.
GIVA aims to become IPO-ready within two to three years, although an actual listing is at least three years away, he added.
The latest investment follows its ₹530 Cr Series C round in June 2025, led by Creaegis. Before the current transaction, GIVA had raised about $164 Mn from investors including PremjiInvest, Northern Arc, and Alteria Capital.
The transaction comes amid investor interest in India’s organised jewellery market, particularly lab-grown diamonds. According to Redseer, India’s lab-grown diamond market was valued at $300–350 Mn in 2024 and is projected to grow at a 15% CAGR over the following decade.
In July, Bengaluru-based Aukera raised ₹90 Cr in debt funding led by Alteria Capital to expand its stores and omnichannel infrastructure. Jewelbox and True Diamond also raised $3.2 Mn and $3 Mn, respectively, in rounds led by V3 Ventures and India Quotient.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan has faced more than 1,000 cyberattacks so far in 2026, according to National CERT Director General Haider Abbas, who briefed lawmakers on the country’s cybersecurity preparedness and the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in monitoring digital threats.
The figures were shared during a meeting of the National Assembly Standing Committee on Information Technology and Telecommunication, chaired by Syed Aminul Haque.
During the briefing, Haider Abbas informed committee members that National CERT operates a dedicated security monitoring centre to identify and monitor potential cyber threats.
He also revealed that the organisation has a total workforce of 70 personnel and has developed AI-powered agents to assist with cybersecurity monitoring.
According to the DG, approximately 30% of the monitoring process relies on AI, while the remaining 70% is carried out manually.
Committee members questioned the organisation’s reliance on artificial intelligence, asking whether AI-based monitoring could introduce additional security vulnerabilities.
The discussion highlighted the increasing role of automated technologies in protecting Pakistan’s digital infrastructure, alongside the continued need for human supervision.
National CERT Outlines Cybersecurity Framework and Annual Security Audits
During the meeting, Haider Abbas informed lawmakers that Pakistan’s Information Security Framework rules were approved in 2023.
He explained that the framework provides a mechanism to assess the cybersecurity readiness of different institutions and identify potential weaknesses in their security arrangements.
According to the DG, government institutions will undergo annual cybersecurity audits to evaluate their security preparedness and compliance with the framework.
The federal IT secretary also informed the committee that provincial governments had nominated their respective departments to coordinate cybersecurity matters.
Committee chairman Syed Aminul Haque raised concerns about an increase in hacking activities around important national dates, including Independence Day on August 14 and Defence Day on September 6.
He asked National CERT officials what measures were being taken to prevent cyberattacks during such periods.
The DG highlighted the organisation’s security monitoring capabilities and its efforts to strengthen protection against emerging digital threats.
The committee also questioned whether Pakistan had sufficient capabilities to respond effectively if a major cyberattack occurred.
The briefing reflects growing attention towards cybersecurity preparedness as government institutions and public services increasingly depend on digital systems.
However, the figures presented during the meeting did not specify how many of the reported cyberattacks were successfully blocked, how many resulted in security breaches, or which institutions were affected.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
A soldier was martyred while security forces killed 17 militants in two intelligence-based operations in Balochistan’s Kachhi and Kharan districts, the military’s media wing said on Tuesday.
“On November 1, 2026, security forces conducted two intelligence-based operations in Kachhi and Kharan districts of Balochistan on the reported presence of terrorists belonging to Indian proxies, Fitna al-Hindustan and Fitna al-Khawarij, neutralising 17 Indian-sponsored terrorists,” the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said in a statement.
The federal government last year officially designated all militant groups operating in Balochistan as Fitna al-Hindustan, accusing India of sponsoring a proxy war through these outfits. Fitna al-Khawarij is a term used by the state for terrorists affiliated with the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
Read: Nine terrorists killed in two intelligence-based operations in Balochistan: ISPR
The first operation was conducted in the Sanni area of Kachhi district, where security forces foiled an attempt by terrorists to establish a roadblock, killing 10 of them. Weapons and ammunition were also recovered.
In the second operation in Kharan district, security forces busted a terrorist hideout. Following an intense exchange of fire, seven TTP members were killed, the ISPR said, adding that weapons and ammunition were also recovered.
On 1 November 2026, security forces conducted two intelligence based operations in Kachhi and Kharan Districts of Balochistan, on reported presence of terrorists belonging to Indian proxy, Fitna Al Hindustan and Fitna Al Khawarij, neutralising seventeen Indian sponsored… pic.twitter.com/ACEpQDCJdI
— DG ISPR (@OfficialDGISPR) November 3, 2026
“Meanwhile, during the intense fire exchange, Sepoy Hikmatullah, having fought gallantly, paid the ultimate sacrifice and embraced martyrdom,” the statement said.
Sanitisation operations were underway to eliminate any other terrorists found in the area, it added.
The ISPR said the counterterrorism campaign under the vision of Azm-e-Istehkam, approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan, would continue at full pace to eliminate the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country.
President Asif Ali Zardari praised the security forces for killing the 17 terrorists in the two operations.
President Asif Ali Zardari on Tuesday paid tribute to the security forces for killing 17 terrorists in Balochistan's Kachhi and Kharan districts, in operations against Fitna al-Hindustan and Fitna al-Khawarij militants.#AsifAliZardari #SecurityForces #FitnaalHindustan pic.twitter.com/NMQoQnIblV
— APP (@appcsocialmedia) November 3, 2026
In a statement, the president commended security forces for foiling the attempt to block a road in Kachhi district, saying their timely and effective action had thwarted the militants’ designs.
He also lauded the successful operation in Kharan district and expressed grief over the martyrdom of Sepoy Hikmatullah.
Also Read: Terrorist killed in intelligence-based operation in Balochistan's Kech district: state media
Zardari said the soldier’s sacrifice for the defence, peace and security of the country would always be remembered.
The president said operations under Azm-e-Istehkam would continue until terrorism sponsored and supported by foreign elements was eliminated.
He also praised the continued efforts and sacrifices of security forces and law enforcement agencies in the fight against terrorism, describing them as a source of pride.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif paid tribute to the security forces for successful operations against India-backed Fitna al-Hindustan terrorists in Balochistan's Kachhi and Kharan districts.
وزیراعظم محمد شہباز شریف کی صوبہء بلوچستان کے اضلاع، کچھی اور خاران میں بھارتی حمایت یافتہ فتنتہ الہندوستان کے دہشت گردوں کے خلاف سیکیورٹی فورسز کے کامیاب آپریشنز کی پذیرائی#PMShehbazSharif #Balochistan #SecurityForces #CounterTerrorism #Kharan #Kachhi pic.twitter.com/pVnDjj0TDf
— APP (@appcsocialmedia) November 3, 2026
According to a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office, the prime minister commended the security forces for the operations while also paying tribute to Sepoy Hikmatullah, who was martyred during an operation against terrorists in Kharan.
He said the security forces were achieving significant successes against terrorism under the vision of Azm-e-Istehkam and reiterated the government's resolve to eliminate terrorism from the country in all its forms.
Separately, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi paid tribute to security forces for their successful operations against Indian-sponsored militants in Balochistan, commending their professionalism in foiling the militants’ nefarious designs.
وفاقی وزیر داخلہ محسن نقوی کا بلوچستان میں بھارتی سپانسرڈ دہشت گردوں کے خلاف کامیاب آپریشنز پر سکیورٹی فورسز کو خراج تحسین
وفاقی وزیر داخلہ نے دہشت گردوں کے مذموم عزائم ناکام بنانے پر سکیورٹی فورسز کی پیشہ ورانہ صلاحیتوں کو سراہا
— Ministry of Interior GoP (@MOIofficialGoP) November 3, 2026
“I salute the security forces for sending 17 Indian-sponsored terrorists to hell,” he said.
He also paid tribute to Sepoy Hikmatullah, who was martyred during the operations, saying the soldier had set a supreme example by sacrificing his life for the country.
Terrorism is a growing problem for Pakistan, with the number of attacks rising every year since 2022, according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global monitoring organisation. Data from ACLED shows attacks in Pakistan rose nearly fourfold to 2,425 in 2025 from 658 in 2022, and over the same period, TTP attacks increased more than sevenfold to 838 from 118.
Although K-P has borne the brunt of terrorism, Balochistan has also remained a major target of Indian proxies, which often target civilians and military installations in the province.
Over the past few years, Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist attacks, with militants frequently targeting convoys, abducting security personnel and civilians, and attacking security and civilian installations.
However, attacks declined noticeably in October, offering a temporary respite after two consecutive months of rising violence. A sharp increase in kidnappings, particularly in Balochistan, nevertheless continued to pose a serious security challenge.
Also Read: Terror attacks in country drop by 37% in October
According to statistics released by the Islamabad-based Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), Balochistan registered one of the sharpest improvements in its security indicators, with terrorist attacks falling by 46 per cent, from 132 in September to 71 in October.
Overall, 143 terrorist attacks were recorded across the country during October, compared with 226 in September.
The reduction was accompanied by a 57 per cent fall in fatalities and a 71 per cent decline in injuries, while suicide attacks also registered a substantial decrease.
PICSS data showed that the attacks claimed 111 lives in October, compared with 260 in September. The number of people injured dropped from 242 to 69, indicating a 71 per cent reduction.
The number of suicide attacks was jointly the lowest recorded during the same period. However, the 169 terrorists killed also represented the lowest monthly figure in the preceding 12 months, reflecting a decline in terrorist fatalities, the report noted.

At Rs. 1,99,999, the asking price is the biggest obstacle to recommending an otherwise excellent smartphone.

items.title: Nigeria’s LemFi expands beyond remittances with app rebuild, new products
items.summary:
Nigerian cross-border fintech LemFi has rebuilt its app and launched a new global brand as it expands beyond remittances into savings, credit and eSIM services.
Founded in 2021 by Ridwan Olalere and Rian Cochran, LemFi lets more than two million customers send money to more than 30 countries across Africa, Asia, Europe and beyond. It processes around US$2 billion in transactions every month.
The company has now introduced savings and credit services in the UK, with other markets to follow, as well as eSIM connectivity that allows customers to buy mobile data in more than 100 destinations without changing SIM cards or paying roaming charges.
To support the expansion, LemFi has re-architected its app from the ground up so that multiple products across different countries sit within a single account. It has also launched a new brand platform, “Ambition has no passport”, which will roll out across its global markets.
“We started LemFi because sending money home was broken. What we learned
items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Nigerian cross-border fintech LemFi has rebuilt its app and launched a new global brand as it expands beyond remittances into savings, credit and eSIM services.
Founded in 2021 by Ridwan Olalere and Rian Cochran, LemFi lets more than two million customers send money to more than 30 countries across Africa, Asia, Europe and beyond. It processes around US$2 billion in transactions every month.
The company has now introduced savings and credit services in the UK, with other markets to follow, as well as eSIM connectivity that allows customers to buy mobile data in more than 100 destinations without changing SIM cards or paying roaming charges.
To support the expansion, LemFi has re-architected its app from the ground up so that multiple products across different countries sit within a single account. It has also launched a new brand platform, “Ambition has no passport”, which will roll out across its global markets.
“We started LemFi because sending money home was broken. What we learned is that the harder problem starts after the transfer,” said Olalere. “Our customers are building careers and businesses in one country while supporting people in another, and the financial system treats them as if they can only exist in one place at a time. We have rebuilt LemFi to work the way their lives do.”
LemFi has raised more than US$85 million to date from investors including Highland Europe, Left Lane Capital, Palm Drive Capital, Endeavor Catalyst and Y Combinator.

items.summary:

The company also recorded a September quarter high for iPhone upgraders in India, CEO John Ternus said during its earnings call.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Apple reported an all-time revenue record in India in Q4 FY26, with its iPhone business setting a September quarter revenue record and Mac and services revenue reaching new highs.
The company also recorded a September quarter high for iPhone upgraders in India, CEO John Ternus said during its earnings call.
Globally, Apple’s revenue rose 12% YoY to $114.5 Bn in the quarter ended September 26, while consolidated net profit increased 11.8% to $30.7 Bn.
“We also set September quarter revenue records in both developed and emerging markets, in addition to an all-time record in India,” Ternus said.
Apple’s global iPhone revenue rose 17% YoY to $57.6 Bn. Alongside India, the company recorded September quarter highs for iPhone upgraders globally, in the US, and in mainland China.
Citing a recent Worldpanel survey, CFO Kevan Parekh said iPhone was among the top-selling smartphone models in India, the US, urban China, the UK, Germany, Australia, and Japan.
Mac revenue increased 24% YoY to $10.8 Bn globally. The business recorded double-digit growth across developed and emerging markets, with all-time revenue highs in India and Southeast Asia.
“We saw double-digit growth in both developed and emerging markets, with all-time records in markets like India and Southeast Asia,” Parekh said.
Apple also recorded a September quarter high for customers buying a Mac for the first time.
Its services business posted record global revenue of $31.6 Bn, up 10% YoY, with all-time highs across most markets it tracks, including India and Latin America.
Apple Pay’s India Entry
Apple expanded its services offering in India with the launch of Apple Pay on September 30, with Axis Bank as its first banking partner.
The service supports Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards, allowing users to pay through their iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch in apps, online, and at contactless-enabled stores. Mac support is expected to follow, while RuPay cards are not supported at launch.
For in-store payments, users authenticate transactions with Face ID, Touch ID, or their device passcode before holding their iPhone or Apple Watch near a contactless reader.
Apple said actual card numbers are neither stored on devices or its servers nor shared with merchants. It also said it does not retain transaction information that can be linked to users.
The company has partnered with payment infrastructure providers, including Juspay, Cashfree, and PayU, to offer Apple Pay across their merchant networks. Apple said the service is accepted by millions of merchants in India at launch, including Blinkit, Zomato, Croma, ixigo, Tata 1mg, and Chaayos, with more merchants and apps to follow.
“India is home to a dynamic and digitally savvy population that continues to embrace a cashless future while expecting the highest standards of security and privacy, and we’re so excited to bring Apple Pay to users in India today,” Jennifer Bailey, vice president of Apple Pay and Apple Wallet, said at the launch.
Apple Pay is available in more than 90 countries and regions and works with over 11,000 bank and network partners globally.
Overall, Apple’s products business generated quarterly revenue of $82.9 Bn, up 12% YoY. However, iPad revenue declined 10% to $6.2 Bn, while wearables, home, and accessories revenue fell 8% to $8.3 Bn.
For FY26, revenue increased 15% to $478.8 Bn. Apple expects December quarter revenue to grow 7-10% YoY, taking quarterly revenue to a new high.

items.title: India Becomes ChatGPT’s Largest Market Globally, User Base Doubles Since January
items.summary:
India has become ChatGPT’s largest market globally by weekly active users, with its local user base doubling since January 2026, OpenAI India MD Prabhjeet Singh said.
Speaking to ET, Singh attributed the growth to Indian users increasingly integrating ChatGPT into their everyday workflows and finding more uses for the chatbot.
The milestone follows OpenAI cofounder and CEO Sam Altman’s description of India during his visit last year as the company’s fastest-growing market and second-largest globally by users. In February 2026, OpenAI said India had more than 100 Mn weekly ChatGPT users.
To reach more users beyond major cities, OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT’s Indian-language capabilities and focusing on Android-first product development.
While the company expects paid subscriptions to grow as users find more value in its products, Singh said its immediate priority is expanding AI’s impact. OpenAI is also expected to make announcements concerning UPI and payments in the coming weeks.
Expan
items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
India has become ChatGPT’s largest market globally by weekly active users, with its local user base doubling since January 2026, OpenAI India MD Prabhjeet Singh said.
Speaking to ET, Singh attributed the growth to Indian users increasingly integrating ChatGPT into their everyday workflows and finding more uses for the chatbot.
The milestone follows OpenAI cofounder and CEO Sam Altman’s description of India during his visit last year as the company’s fastest-growing market and second-largest globally by users. In February 2026, OpenAI said India had more than 100 Mn weekly ChatGPT users.
To reach more users beyond major cities, OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT’s Indian-language capabilities and focusing on Android-first product development.
While the company expects paid subscriptions to grow as users find more value in its products, Singh said its immediate priority is expanding AI’s impact. OpenAI is also expected to make announcements concerning UPI and payments in the coming weeks.
Expanding India Footprint
OpenAI announced its first India office in Delhi NCR and began local hiring in August 2025. At the India AI Impact Summit in February, it unveiled plans for Mumbai and Bengaluru offices and launched OpenAI for India to expand access, infrastructure, and enterprise adoption.
Its partnership with TCS’ HyperVault data centre business starts with 100 megawatts (MW) of capacity, potentially scaling to 1 gigawatt (GW). Singh said OpenAI would consider more capacity as infrastructure comes online.
The capacity will address enterprise data residency and security requirements, while privacy and returns on investment remain key adoption considerations. OpenAI models are also available through AWS’ Amazon Bedrock for local inference, keeping request processing within India.
Enterprises Move Beyond Pilots
Singh said enterprises, global capability centres (GCCs), and startups are moving beyond pilots to production deployments, citing JioHotstar and Cars24.
India is also among Codex’s largest and fastest-growing markets, with significant developer use emerging from tier-II cities, he added.
OpenAI is engaging with government agencies, banks, and financial institutions to strengthen cybersecurity and protect critical infrastructure against AI agent misuse. Singh also backed clear AI regulation to build confidence among consumers, enterprises, and developers.
OpenAI is also expanding advertising on ChatGPT in India. Singh said ads would help support free and lower-priced access alongside paid subscriptions.
He added that advertisers would not have access to users’ personal information and that advertisements would not influence ChatGPT’s responses.
The company has partnered with Razorpay to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT. Under the partnership, Razorpay’s growth marketing platform Engage helps brands prepare product catalogues, launch and manage campaigns, and measure performance.

items.summary:

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Some of Africa’s best startup ideas never become products because the person who had them can’t write code. A nurse in Kisumu knows exactly why clinic appointments get missed. A market trader in Lagos understands the cash-flow gaps that keep small vendors stuck. A logistics manager in Johannesburg can see the inefficiencies that cost businesses millions.
None of them needs to be a software engineer to spot the opportunity, but turning that insight into a working app is where many stall.
The non-technical founder is a familiar figure in African tech. They bring market knowledge, sales instincts and lived experience of the problems they want to solve. They also face real obstacles that technical founders rarely do. Understanding both sides is the first step to building something that lasts.
The downsides of building without a technical background
First is dependence on others to build the core product. For a software startup, the product is the business. A founder who can’t build it relies on freelancers, agencies or a technical co-founder. That dependence can leave them unable to judge quality, estimate timelines or spot when a project is going wrong.
This also leads to high upfront costs. Hiring developers is expensive, and good engineers are in high demand across the continent and from remote employers abroad. Many founders burn through their savings or early capital on a first version before they have tested whether customers want it.
Many such founders then hunt for a technical co-founder. But finding a skilled engineer willing to join an unproven idea for equity is hard. Many founders spend months searching, and some settle for a mismatched partnership that later breaks down.
You also have to take into account credibility with investors. Early-stage investors often ask who is building the product. A team without in-house technical capability can be seen as a risk, especially for companies pitching themselves as tech-led.
Then there is slower iteration. Startups win by testing, learning and changing fast. When every small change needs a developer’s time and an invoice, founders iterate less often and learn more slowly. And there will be communication gaps – translating a business vision into technical requirements is a skill in itself. Vague briefs lead to products that technically work but miss the point.
Why non-technical founders often have the edge
Never fear, there is an upside, or several. Non-technical founders start with the problem, not the technology. Technical founders sometimes build impressive products nobody needs. Founders who come from the industry they are serving tend to begin with a real pain point and real customers.
In addition, domain expertise is hard to copy. A former pharmacist building a medicine-supply platform, or a farmer building an agri-tech tool, understands regulation, buyer behaviour and informal workarounds that an outsider would take years to learn.
Then there are sales and distribution skills. In many African markets the hardest part is not building the app but getting people to adopt it, often through agents, partnerships and trust built face-to-face. Founders with sales, operations or community backgrounds are often strongest exactly here.
Non-technical founders are also able to just focus on building their businesses. Freed from writing code, a non-technical founder can spend their time on customers, partnerships, fundraising and hiring, which are the jobs that decide whether a startup survives. And in addition, tools like AI coding assistants, no-code platforms and specialist build partners have lowered the barrier to getting a first version live. Disrupt Africa recently covered Exten AI, a South African startup letting founders build full-stack apps in plain language. Being non-technical is less of a barrier than it was even a few years ago, as long as founders have the right support.
How Disrupt Launchpad bridges the gap
Disrupt Africa has teamed up with Kenya-based Touch Inspiration to launch Disrupt Launchpad, an app development accelerator built for founders who have a clear idea but lack the technical skills, team or resources to build it.
The partnership combines two strengths. Touch Inspiration, founded in 2017, develops web and mobile apps, AI-powered tools and business platforms, taking products from defined requirements through to launch. Disrupt Africa, the continent’s leading tech startup news platform since 2014, brings an audience of users, customers and investors.
Here is how the programme answers the challenges above:
No team, no problem. Founders get their app professionally built by an experienced development company, removing the dependence on finding a technical co-founder first.
Lower cost of getting started. Development is offered at startup-friendly rates. Selected ventures may qualify for an equity-based partnership, which reduces the cash needed upfront.
From requirements to launch. Touch Inspiration’s process starts with defining requirements, which helps close the communication gap between a founder’s vision and the finished product.
Visibility after launch. Building an app is only half the battle. Disrupt Africa helps put new products in front of potential users, customers and investors, addressing the distribution challenge many startups underestimate.
Who should apply
Disrupt Launchpad is open to aspiring entrepreneurs and existing startups with a clear app idea. It suits founders who:
understand their market and customer problem well, but can’t build the product themselves;
have been quoted development costs they can’t afford upfront;
want a professional build rather than a patchwork of freelancers;
need help getting their product noticed once it launches;
Applications are open now at launchpad.disruptafrica.com.
Being non-technical has never stopped great founders from building great companies. What has held many back is the gap between idea and product. Programmes like Disrupt Launchpad aim to close it, so founders can spend their energy where their strengths lie – understanding customers, selling and growing the business.

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
Peer-to-peer (P2P) lending startup LenDenClub’s parent Vartis Platforms has launched UdhaarSaathi, a digital loan marketplace for small businesses, expanding its lending service provider (LSP) portfolio.
Speaking to Inc42, Vartis founder Bhavin Patel said the platform caters to kirana stores, pharmacies, street vendors, and other small retailers, facilitating collateral-free business loans ranging from ₹15,000 to ₹2.5 Lakh.
With an average loan ticket size of around ₹1 Lakh, Vartis aims to facilitate ₹1,000 Cr in disbursements through UdhaarSaathi by the end of FY27.
The launch comes amid Vartis’ internal preparations for a potential IPO, including strengthening governance across its platforms. Patel said that the company is targeting readiness over the next 12-18 months rather than a listing within that period.
“There is no timeline as yet. The next 12 to 18 months is what we are targeting to prepare ourselves,” Patel said.
The IPO could comprise an offer for sale (OFS), with Vartis currently seeing no need to raise primary capital. However, it may consider a fresh issue to fund a business opportunity or expansion, he added.
Bringing Credit To Retailers
UdhaarSaathi uses merchants’ banking and business transaction data, shared with their consent, to support credit assessment by its lending partners.
It operates as an LSP and loan marketplace, facilitating credit through multiple NBFCs. Vartis does not take credit risk on loans facilitated through the platform.
The platform’s first version went live in February, followed by the final version a couple of months ago. West India currently accounts for its largest customer share, followed by the South, East, and North, Patel said. The company expects to share a detailed regional breakdown by December.
UdhaarSaathi is Vartis’ second LSP platform after InstaMoney, which launched in 2017 and primarily serves individuals seeking small-ticket emergency loans. UdhaarSaathi extends this business to merchants seeking working capital.
Vartis earns fees when repayments are processed through either platform, Patel said.
Founded in 2015 by Patel and Dipesh Karki, Vartis also operates lending technology platform Vartis One.
On the financial front, Vartis’ net profit rose 183% to ₹96.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹34 Cr in FY25. This marked its second consecutive profitable fiscal following a net loss of ₹10.6 Cr in FY24 after the RBI’s crackdown on the P2P lending sector.
Operating revenue grew 43% to ₹338 Cr from ₹236.4 Cr in FY25. Including interest and other income, total revenue stood at ₹366.6 Cr in FY26.

items.title: The Second Life Of Festive Gift Boxes
items.summary:

items.author: Meha Agarwal
items.content:
Some gifts can be more than just gifts; they can be keepsakes. At least that’s what brands are hoping for this Diwali.
Along with the familiar ritual of exchanging sweets, dry fruits and gifts, D2C brands are hoping that customers sign a covenant of sorts while completing their last-minute festive shopping. Because, once the goodies are gone, most boxes often end up in storerooms or dustbins.
But D2C players are giving the humble gift box a second job.
Think handcrafted wooden mini trunks that double up as jewellery organisers or beautifully illustrated tins that find a place on kitchen shelves, or even intricately designed boxes that become decorative pieces in their own right.
When it comes to the festive season, packaging is no longer just about protecting or presenting a product. It is designed to be treasured, reused and memorable.
Gifting platform IGP has designed a bag that doubles as a rangoli stencil. Meanwhile, Jaipur-based artisanal confectionery Bliss & Bite has taken a more luxurious route, packaging its chocolates in hand-painted Pichwai wooden chests that can later find a second life as jewellery boxes or keepsake organisers.
New-age brands Phool, Nihira Mithai, Nutty Gritties, Petite Pie Shop, The Urban Dori and Parna Varna are among those experimenting with festive gift boxes, reusable tins, keepsake containers and multipurpose hampers designed to have a life beyond the celebrations.
The goal is simple. Get consumers to think about the brand and recall it the rest of the year. In the right home, the packaging becomes a marketing asset. And if the gifting experience proves memorable enough, perhaps they’ll return for another purchase.
But here’s the business reality: Behind these creative experiments are design costs, minimum order quantities, production timelines and the risk of being left with hundreds of festive boxes once the celebrations end.
So, as D2C brands try to make festive packaging sustainable, more memorable and commercially valuable, one question deserves a closer look: Can a gift box that refuses to become waste also become an investment that pays for itself?
Beyond Brand Recall
For D2C brands, the real test of festive packaging begins after the celebrations end. Beyond making a lasting impression, the focus is on acquiring new customers, encouraging repeat purchases and sustaining the festive sales momentum long after the season is over.
RENÉE Cosmetics’ festive campaigns have consistently delivered an uptick in sales during Q3 of the financial year (October to December), which typically includes Diwali, cofounder and CEO Ashutosh Valani told Inc42.
The startup claimed that for three consecutive years, sales in the following quarter (January to March) have matched or exceeded Q3 levels. It did not share specific data about each quarter, so the sales numbers could not be independently verified.
Plus, RENÉE cannot attribute these improvements exclusively to its festive season packaging. If you consider the whole campaign, it includes costs for packaging, storytelling, the product itself and marketing activities.
So what can brands do to measure their campaign success and performance? For IGP, rather than assigning a packaging-specific sales figure, it is about examining customer reactions, reviews and social sharing. The customer success team also collects feedback that shapes the next year’s campaign design.
Tarun Joshi, founder and CEO of IGP, puts it, “We judge a festive packaging campaign by whether it leaves customers delighted and makes the experience memorable. Customer delight is harder to count, so we make the packaging useful and DIY-friendly, and look at how customers react and share it.”
But once again, we must stress none of these measures conclusively isolates packaging’s contribution from festive demand, product quality or the broader marketing efforts. In other words, brands can measure what happens after these festive unboxing, but not how much of it happened because of the box.
So, how much should brands spend in terms of both efforts and money on packaging when its returns are so difficult to quantify?
Untangling The Economics
The cost of festive packaging can be relatively easy for an established brand to absorb. For an early stage startup, however, the same exercise can put considerable pressure on margins, pricing and operations.
Valani told us the additional cost has a marginal 1-2% impact on RENÉE’s gross margins, with growing scale and declining customer acquisition costs making it easier to absorb.
IGP, meanwhile, treats creative packaging as advertising expenditure, sometimes building entire campaigns around it.
But the equation changes for early stage startups such as Farm Didi. The startup begins preparing its festive hampers six to eight months before Diwali, coordinating reusable packaging, handcrafted products and production across rural women’s groups. This makes festive gifting a resource-intensive exercise, leaving little room for aggressive discounts.
“That is why it is very important for us to target the right set of customers. We are not looking to target those customers who are looking for heavy discounts,” added Farm Didi cofounder Manjari Sharma.
For smaller brands, minimum order quantities (MOQs) add another layer of risk. Lifestyle brand Includ cofounder Ashwin Rastogi pointed out that customised packaging often requires brands to commit to minimum production volumes across multiple sizes, making the investment difficult to justify if demand falls short. Unlike established players, early stage brands may not have the sales volumes to absorb these costs.
So, while larger brands have more flexibility to absorb or justify packaging expenditure, newer or smaller players must find ways to make every order commercially viable. But even favourable unit economics cannot solve one problem – what happens when brands invest in festive packaging and the expected orders never arrive?
Unlike a digital campaign that can be paused, unsold gift boxes can remain in inventory long after the festivities end. This brings us to a more fundamental question: Should every brand be investing in festive packaging in the first place?
Taking The Gamble
In conversation with industry leaders and startups, it became evident that not every brand needs a Diwali hamper to outshine its competitors and create strong brand recall. Brands need to remember that they need to sell the hampers too to recover their investment.
Arjun Vaidya, founder of Dr Vaidya’s and now an investor at V3 Ventures, believes that brands need to recognise if they have a qualified sales pipeline in the months and weeks before Diwali.
“We are not a Diwali brand, and if you are in the same place, don’t waste time, effort and energy to buy these boxes and do this packaging because it’s a big cost. Having inventory on hand can quickly become a problem,” Vaidya explained.
The problem is that festive packaging has an expiry date. A Diwali-themed box may be difficult to sell once the festival is over, leaving brands with inventory they cannot easily repurpose.
Yet, avoiding festive gifting altogether isn’t necessarily the answer. Food, fashion and certain premium products naturally lend themselves to gifting. Everyday essentials, however, may struggle to attract buyers simply because they come in a festive box. Channel partnerships may drive sales for such brands.
Even for brands in the right categories, execution matters. Festive hampers must offer something genuinely different and, importantly, be priced for the intended customer. A beautifully designed box alone cannot justify an unrealistic price tag.
Rather than competing during peak festive sales, when marketplace traffic costs are high, Includ founder Rastogi suggested occasions such as Halloween and Christmas, where competition is relatively lower and the opportunity to stand out is higher.
Brands can assess whether the additional demand generated will be large enough to justify the upfront investment, inventory risk and higher cost of competing during the season.
Although brands are increasingly pitching reusable packaging as a greener alternative to conventional gift boxes, the real question is how many of these premium wooden boxes, elaborate hampers and reusable containers actually find a second purpose in customers’ homes?
The challenge is that brands have limited visibility into what happens after unboxing. This creates a distinction between packaging that delivers marketing value and packaging that delivers measurable environmental benefits.
A box worth photographing or keeping may strengthen brand recall, but that alone does not make it a right choice if the product itself is not up to par.
THE STARTUP SPOTLIGHT | HOW HYEGLO BEAUTY IS BRINGING SKINCARE SCIENCE INTO EVERYDAY MAKEUP
Hyeglo Beauty is building a skin-first colour cosmetics brand by combining makeup pigments with clinically tested ingredients and functional skincare activities. It claims that its formulations are designed to deliver makeup coverage while supporting skin hydration and overall skin health.
Its product range includes tinted moisturisers, lip and cheek balms, and lip oil stains, with prices ranging from ₹799 to ₹1,350 on its website.
The startup follows a D2C-led model, selling through its own website. It is looking to build its presence in India’s colour cosmetics market, competing with established and emerging makeup brands.
THE DEEP DIVE
ECOMMERCE BUZZ
Numour’s Fundraise: The D2C skincare startup founded by Divya Jain in 2025, is reportedly in talks to raise $3.1 Mn from Sharrp Ventures. e startup combines skincare formulations with beauty devices and sells products across its website, ecommerce marketplaces and quick commerce platforms.
AI Kitchen Startup’s Fundraise: Smart kitchen appliance startup upliance.ai is in advanced talks to raise $3 Mn–$4 Mn in a Series A round. The startup uses generative AI to automate cooking processes and plans to use the proposed funding for R&D, product improvements and international expansion.
Troovy’s ₹100 Cr Bet: The healthy snacking startup has raised ₹100 Cr in a Series B round led by Fireside Ventures. The startup plans to expand manufacturing and offline distribution while entering new categories, including namkeen, biscuits and cookies.
Bijnis’ B2B Quick Commerce Pivot: Bijnis has rebranded as Zorit and raised ₹27 Cr in a funding round led by Sparrow Capital. The Delhi-based startup has shifted from a manufacturer-retailer marketplace to an inventory-led B2B quick-commerce model, delivering products to neighbourhood retailers from local dark stores.
Edited by Nikhil Subramanium

items.author: Debarghya Sil
items.content:
D2C home appliances brand Nuuk is raising around ₹100 Cr (about $10.5 Mn) in a funding round led by Wipro Consumer Care Ventures and RPSG Capital Ventures at a valuation of about ₹500 Cr (about $53 Mn), sources told Inc42.
The proposed fundraise would be larger than Nuuk’s $6.6 Mn Series A round, which it closed in August 2025 following a $2 Mn extension from existing investors Vertex Ventures SEA and Good Capital.
The final round size and valuation could change depending on how the discussions progress, the sources added.
Questions sent to Nuuk, Wipro Consumer Care Ventures, and RPSG Capital Ventures did not elicit a response till the time of publication.
Founded in 2023 by Gazal Kalra, cofounder of logistics unicorn Rivigo, and Shalabh Gupta, former chief growth officer at Noise, Nuuk sells design-focused home and kitchen appliances.
Its portfolio spans cordless vacuum cleaners, fans, heaters, and garment care products, alongside kitchen appliances such as air fryers, juicers, and mixer grinders.
The startup sells through its own website, ecommerce marketplaces Amazon and Flipkart, and quick commerce platform Blinkit. It has also entered offline retail, including a store in Delhi NCR.
While announcing its Series A extension, Kalra told Inc42 that the capital would support portfolio expansion, product innovation, and a wider business footprint. Part of the funding was also earmarked for expanding its domestic supply chain.
In March 2025, Gupta told Inc42 that Nuuk manufactured around 20% of its products in India and aimed to increase this share to over 50% by the end of FY26. Kalra said the company designed its appliances in-house and worked with third-party manufacturers.
On the financial front, Nuuk’s operating revenue rose to ₹16 Cr in FY25 from ₹31.8 Lakh in FY24, according to its MCA filings. FY25 was its first full year of operations. Its net loss widened to ₹39 Lakh from ₹7 Lakh, while expenses increased to ₹16.4 Cr from ₹38.8 Lakh.
The brand competes with established appliance makers such as Philips and Bajaj, alongside newer players including Atomberg and Lifelong.
Investors Back Appliance Startups
Nuuk’s proposed fundraise follows recent investments in home and kitchen appliance startups, with capital going towards product development, manufacturing, and distribution.
In October, smart kitchen brand Beyond Appliances raised ₹110 Cr in a Series B round led by Fireside Ventures, with participation from Dharana Capital and other investors. The startup said it plans to use the funding to establish a manufacturing facility and expand its portfolio into ovens.
Earlier, home appliance brand Nester raised ₹19 Cr in a pre-Series A round in February 2026. Its portfolio includes steam air fryer ovens, toasters, and juicers.
Meanwhile, Inc42 reported last week that upliance.ai was in advanced talks to raise $3-4 Mn in a Series A round. The proposed funding would support R&D, improvements to its interface, and international expansion, with existing backer Khosla Ventures looking to invest further.
The investments point to investor interest in brands developing differentiated appliances – from connected chimneys to automated cooking devices – and building the manufacturing and distribution networks needed to scale.

Individual investors can also place bids as per the non-competitive scheme through the Retail Direct portal (https://rbiretaildirect.org.in).
Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (E-Kuber) system on November 03, 2026 (Tuesday). In case of technical difficulties, Core Banking Operations Team may be contacted (email; Phone no: 022-69870466, 022-69870415).

Only in the event of system failure, physical bids would be accepted. Such physical bids should be submitted to the Public Debt Office (email; Phone no: 022-22603456, 022-22603457, 022-22603190) in the prescribed form obtainable from RBI website (https://www.rbi.org.in/Scripts/BS_ViewForms.aspx) before the auction timing ends.
The yield per cent per annum or the price as the case may be, expected by the bidder should be expressed up to two decimal points. An investor can submit more than one competitive bid at same/different rates of yield or prices in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (E-Kuber) system. However, the aggregate amount of bids submitted by a bidder should not exceed the notified amount for each State.
The Reserve Bank of India will determine the maximum yield / minimum price at which bids will be accepted. Stock will be issued for a minimum nominal amount of ₹10,000.00 and in multiples of ₹10,000.00 thereafter.
The results of the auction will be announced on November 03, 2026 (Tuesday) and payment by successful bidders will be made during banking hours on November 04, 2026 (Wednesday) at Mumbai and at respective Regional Offices of RBI.
The new State Government Stocks will bear interest at the rates determined by RBI at the auctions. For the new stock, interest will be paid half yearly on May 04 and November 04 of each year till maturity. For the re-issued Government Stock, interest will be paid at the rate as determined on the date of original issue of Government Stock and will be paid on half yearly basis till maturity. The Stocks will be governed by the provisions of the Government Securities Act, 2006 and the Government Securities Regulations, 2007.
The investment in State Government Stocks will be reckoned as an eligible investment in Government Securities by banks for the purpose of Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The stocks will qualify for the ready forward facility.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
If you have ever bought a SIM card from an online seller or a shop that did not ask for your fingerprint, the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) has a warning for you. Foreign SIM cards in Pakistan are illegal to buy and sell, the regulator said in a public awareness message this week.
The PTA says such SIMs can be used for fraud and other unlawful activity. Buyers and users, it warned, may face legal and security problems as a result.
What the advisory says
The message is short. The PTA advises people to avoid buying or selling foreign SIMs and to use only locally registered SIMs issued in their own names. It also urged mobile users to make sure their connections are properly registered.
The advisory does not list penalties or enforcement figures. Earlier PTA notices were more specific. A June 2026 notice described the sale and purchase of foreign SIMs inside Pakistan as illegal and punishable under the law.
Why the PTA keeps repeating itself
This is not a first warning. The PTA issued a similar caution in August 2025. Another followed on January 30, 2026. The June 2026 notice came next, and another alert was reported on August 2, 2026.
Earlier, the PTA and the FIA’s Cyber Crime Wing carried out coordinated raids on sellers of pre-activated international SIMs in February 2025. The repeated advisories suggest the trade survived those raids.
How the trade works
The PTA’s concern is traceability. Calls and messages made through unregistered or foreign SIMs are hard to trace, which opens the door to scams, identity theft and financial fraud. A SIM registered abroad also sits outside local controls. The regulator has said such SIMs bypass them, leaving users open to data misuse and financial exploitation.
The sales channel matters as much as the SIM. Earlier PTA material identified British pre-activated SIMs as among the most commonly used in criminal activity in Pakistan. They were available through online platforms and sold with cash on delivery. A pre-activated SIM works on arrival, with no registration step. That convenience is what makes it attractive to a fraudster.
What it means for ordinary users
Most buyers are not scammers. Some want a cheap data plan, some want a number that looks international, and some simply do not ask where the SIM came from.
The PTA’s point is that users carry some of the risk. People using illegally obtained SIMs could unknowingly be involved in illegal messages, which creates accountability problems and possible legal action against them. If a SIM in your possession is used in a scam, the first question investigators ask is who holds it.
The safe route is the one the PTA keeps repeating. Buy SIMs only from authorised franchises or registered outlets, and make sure the SIM is registered in your own name through biometric verification. The PTA also asks the public to report the sale or use of illegal foreign SIMs through its official complaint channels.
What the advisory leaves out
The notice does not address travellers on international roaming, or eSIMs. Both are lawful uses of foreign networks. As worded, the advisory targets the buying and selling of foreign SIMs inside Pakistan. Anyone unsure whether a particular product falls under it should check with the PTA before buying.
It also does not say who is held responsible. A buyer, a seller and an online platform are all part of the chain, and only the seller is clearly named in earlier crackdowns.
Bottom Line
Repeating a warning does not shut down a trade. The sellers operate online and take payment on delivery, and a public notice does not reach them. The PTA has shown it can raid shops. Closing the online route needs action against listings and delivery channels, and the advisory says nothing on that.
Until then, the safest check is a simple one. Count the SIMs registered against your CNIC and confirm you know each of them.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Karachi police recover stolen mobile phones in batches, and District Central’s latest batch is a large one. Officers arrested 15 suspects and seized 435 devices across four police station jurisdictions, according to SSP Central Dr Imran.
He told a press conference that the phones, a mix of stolen and non-PTA handsets, are worth an estimated Rs20 million to Rs30 million. Some were expensive iPhones.
Where the arrests happened
The suspects were picked up from mobile phone markets in District Central, the SSP said. Several of them ran repair shops in markets around Karachi.
Police also recovered specialised hardware they say was used to change IMEI numbers. The SSP said the investigation into the phones and the suspects’ activities is continuing.
What IMEI tampering does
An IMEI is a 15-digit number unique to each handset. It works like a phone’s fingerprint. Police, mobile networks and the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) use it to identify a device and block it when it is reported stolen.
Change the number and the block no longer applies. A handset with a rewritten IMEI becomes untraceable and can be sold to a new user.
Patching is a related practice. According to police, the suspects patched non-PTA devices so they would work on local networks. Phones not registered with the PTA, usually because import duties were not paid, are typically blocked after a grace period. A patch is meant to get around that block.
Two markets, one workshop
The 435 recovered phones fall into two groups that look different on paper: stolen handsets and non-PTA handsets. The same tools and the same repair counters apparently served both.
That overlap is the part of this case worth watching. A shopper who buys a cheap, patched non-PTA phone has no way of knowing whether the shop also handles stolen stock. Demand for low-priced phones sits right next to the supply of snatched ones.
The police statement does not say how many of the 435 phones were stolen and how many were only non-PTA. It also does not say how many owners have been identified. Those numbers will show whether this was mainly a theft case or a grey-market one.
Not the first raid on this trade
Karachi police have been raiding phone markets for IMEI work for years. In 2017, Sindh Police’s Special Investigation Unit raided Saddar Mobile Market and arrested two shopkeepers accused of changing IMEI numbers on stolen or snatched phones.
Recovery totals have varied. In one case, Garden Police recovered 17 stolen phones. In 2022, police recovered 172 phones from a 17-member gang. At 435, the District Central haul is larger than either.
An April 2024 ARY News report on a separate Karachi case said a suspect charged shopkeepers Rs500 per phone for IMEI changes, and that one IMEI could be placed on five handsets. If that practice is common, a single cloned number can make several phones look legitimate at once.
Why this matters beyond one district
SSP Central acknowledged that street crime is a major challenge in Karachi and said police are taking steps to control it and recover stolen property. Recovery is only half of the job, though.
Snatchers need a buyer who can make a stolen phone usable again. As long as repair counters can erase a phone’s identity for a few hundred rupees, a stolen device keeps its value. That value is what keeps street theft profitable.
So the arrests of repair-shop operators matter more than the headline phone count. If charges hold up in court, they hit the step where stolen goods become sellable. If they do not, the same hardware will be back on shop counters.
What buyers can do
Anyone buying a second-hand phone can dial *#06# to see its IMEI and check it against the PTA’s device verification service before paying. A seller who refuses to let you check is a warning sign. A phone sold well below market price needs an explanation.
The test for this case will be whether police publish how many of the 435 phones have been returned to their owners.
