items.content:
Governor Uba Sani has bagged the Distinguished Human Capital Development Champion Award, in recognition of his outstanding investments in education, skills development, youth empowerment and sustainable development.
The Chartered Institute of Human Capital Development of Nigeria (CIHCDN), which honoured him with the award, noted that it celebrates the Governor’s people-centred policies.
The award which was presented at the Institute’s National Conference held at Merit House, Maitama, Abuja, applauds Governor Uba Sani’s initiatives in expanding access to education, healthcare, vocational skills, economic opportunities and improved living conditions of citizens of Kaduna State.
The Institute stated that the award recognises exceptional leadership in advancing education, healthcare, skills development, rural transformation, financial inclusion, youth empowerment and capacity building.
It described Governor Uba Sani’s initiatives as a model of people-centred governance capable of delivering sustainable development and improved opportunities for Kaduna State citizens.
Speaking after receiving the award, the Commissioner of Information and Culture, Malam Ahmed Maiyaki, expressed the Governor’s appreciation to the Institute, for recognising the commitment of Kaduna State to human capital development.
“This recognition is a testament to Governor Uba Sani’s unwavering commitment to placing people at the centre of governance. His Excellency firmly believes that the greatest investment any government can make is in its people, particularly the young, women and the vulnerable,” Maiyaki stated.
He cited the establishment of three Vocational Training and Skills Development Centres in Rigachikun, Soba and Samarun Kataf, designed to equip approximately 32,000 young people annually with practical, industry-relevant skills across 14 trades.
“These centres represent a deliberate shift towards building a productive, skilled and economically independent generation. Our objective is to transform young people from job seekers into skilled professionals, entrepreneurs and employers of labour,” he explained.
The Commissioner further noted that the administration has made substantial investments in education, including the construction of 736 new classrooms, renovation of over 1,200 classrooms, recruitment of 10,000 teachers and training of more than 33,000 teachers to strengthen quality education and enhance access.
He recalled the reduction of tuition fees in state-owned tertiary institutions by up to 50 per cent, alongside expanded scholarship and bursary interventions, demonstrating the Governor’s determination to remove financial barriers to education.
On agricultural development, Maiyaki disclosed that the administration has distributed 1,400 trucks of free fertiliser to 420,000 smallholder farmers, describing the intervention as a major investment in rural livelihoods, food security and economic empowerment.
“Governor Uba Sani recognises that human capital development goes beyond the classroom. It includes empowering farmers to become more productive, equipping young people with employable skills, strengthening healthcare delivery and creating opportunities for families to achieve economic independence,” he said.
Maiyaki also highlighted the Governor’s investments in healthcare, including the revitalisation of 255 Primary Healthcare Centres, improved welfare for healthcare professionals and initiatives to expand access to quality medical services, particularly in underserved rural communities.
He stressed that the administration’s development agenda is anchored on inclusive governance, by ensuring that opportunities and government interventions reach communities, irrespective of political, religious and ethnic affiliations.
“This award is not merely a recognition of achievements recorded; it is an encouragement to do even more. His Excellency remains resolute in building a Kaduna State where every child has access to quality education, every young person has an opportunity to acquire productive skills, and every citizen has a fair chance to prosper,” Maiyaki added.
The Commissioner assured the Institute that the recognition would further strengthen the Governor’s determination to consolidate ongoing reforms and accelerate investments in human capital development.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Update | October 31, 19:33 IST
A forensic audit by KPMG has found that the €3.04 Mn banking fraud at Capillary Technologies’ subsidiary SessionM Czech Republic was most consistent with an external payment-diversion scam involving impersonation of a senior executive and an external lawyer.
Capillary, in an exchange filing today, said the fraud likely involved a lookalike email domain, social engineering and communications through WhatsApp and personal email accounts.
The investigation found no evidence of malware, unauthorised access, mailbox compromise, account takeover or traditional email spoofing in the systems and records examined. It also did not identify any evidence of employee involvement. However, the audit could neither establish nor rule out the use of deepfake audio or video, as original recordings, mobile-device data and call records were unavailable.
Of the four disputed transactions, three payments went to ZZDJB CO LIMITED at HSBC Hong Kong, while the fourth was transferred to ZHONGXIAN TRADING PTE. LTD at UOB Singapore.
While the investigation established the initial transfers, it did not trace the subsequent movement of funds, identify the ultimate beneficiaries or assess the prospects of recovery. It also could not independently verify the company’s payment approval processes due to missing bank-portal and workflow records.
KPMG concluded that the incident was primarily a social-engineering-led fraud. Capillary said it has strengthened payment controls and is pursuing recovery efforts and legal remedies.
Update| July 31, 15:15 IST
Days after it announced a cyber fraud of €3 Mn (about ₹32.7 Cr) at one of its step-down subsidiaries, SaaS company Capillary Technologies said it has initiated a forensic audit to investigate the suspected fraudulent and unauthorised banking transactions.
The audit, approved by the company’s Audit Committee, will be conducted by KPMG Assurance and Consulting Services LLP and will examine the transactions, banking processes, internal financial controls, identify the root cause and recommend corrective measures.
“The forensic audit has been initiated with a view to independently examine the facts and circumstances relating to the incident, determine the root cause and recommend appropriate corrective measures,” the company said in its exchange filing.
Original | July 6, 17: 41 IST
SaaS company Capillary Technologies announced that one of its “recently acquired step-down subsidiaries” has been hit by a cyber-enabled banking fraud, leading to a loss of €3 Mn (about ₹32.7 Cr).
The funds were fraudulently transferred to an unauthorised third-party bank account using advanced deepfake methods including cloning, signature forging, social engineering to impersonate the company’s senior management, Capillary said in an exchange filing. As per the company, the exploit took place just prior to this weekend (before July 3).
Capillary has taken legal and operational measures to safeguard and recover the transferred funds, including working with law enforcement, cybercrime authorities and concerned banks. It further noted that the step-down subsidiary was insured under a cyber and crime insurance policy and the company is also evaluating the extent of insurance coverage and recoverability.
Upon identifying the attack, the company was able to recover €450K. It has also traced bank accounts suspected to be related to the fraud and asked related banks to put the accounts on hold.
“With the swift action by the Company and advice of the relevant local authorities, additional funds were traced, and those accounts have since been placed on hold by the respective banks, reducing the amount at risk. The exact amount currently on hold is yet to be determined,” the company said.
Despite the cyberfraud, Capillary believes that its customer data and the company’s technology infrastructure remains uncompromised.
The SaaS company’s most recent acquisition was global card network MasterCard’s customer engagement and loyalty platform SessionM, which it snagged in February for $20 Mn (about ₹190.7 Cr) to strengthen presence in the North American and Latin American markets.
Besides, the company also acquired Canada-based martech platform Kognitiv for an undisclosed amount last year.
On the financial front, Capillary’s net profit grew multifold to ₹43.4 Cr in Q4 FY26. Its operating revenue also jumped 25% YoY to ₹191.3 Cr in the March quarter. For the full fiscal FY26, Capillary’s profit skyrocketed 296% to ₹52.4 Cr from ₹13.3 Cr in FY25. The top line rose 23% to ₹734.6 Cr from ₹598.3 Cr in the previous fiscal.
Shares of Capillary ended today’s trading session 0.15% higher at ₹515.85.
The incident underscores the growing cybersecurity risks facing enterprises as AI becomes more advanced, highlighting the need for companies to strengthen their defences against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. Last month, Apple’s supply chain data was reportedly exposed after sensitive supplier lists, component details and alleged images of its upcoming iPhone 18 Pro models surfaced online following a cyberattack on its contract manufacturer, Tata Electronics.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Google has successfully run an AI model on a satellite in space and received its first response back on Earth, marking an important step toward its plans to explore AI data centers beyond the planet.
The achievement is part of Project Suncatcher, Google’s research project investigating whether artificial intelligence systems could eventually operate in space instead of relying entirely on data centers on Earth.
Google announced the successful test on October 30, confirming that its experimental satellite had processed an AI request and sent the result back to Earth.
The satellite launched on October 1 aboard a SpaceX rocket and has spent the past few weeks undergoing tests.
Google AI Sends Its First Message From Space
During the experiment, Google sent a request from Earth to its satellite, asking the onboard Gemma 4 AI model to write a short poem about being in space.
The AI model processed the request using Google’s Tensor Processing Unit (TPU), a specialized chip designed to run AI workloads.
As the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, it successfully transmitted its response back to Earth.
The AI generated the following three-line poem:
Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core.
Google described the successful exchange as its “Hello World” milestone, a term commonly used in computing to describe an initial successful test.
According to the company, this was the first complete AI response generated using a data center-class TPU operating in orbit.
Following the initial demonstration, Google conducted additional tests that involved generating more poems and requesting information about the satellite’s operating conditions.
The results confirmed that the AI hardware could process requests in space and communicate its responses back to Earth.
Why Google Wants to Put AI Data Centers in Space
Google is exploring the possibility of building AI computing infrastructure in space to meet growing demand for artificial intelligence services.
AI data centers require large amounts of electricity to power processors and cooling equipment.
Project Suncatcher aims to investigate whether satellites powered by solar energy could eventually handle some of these computing tasks.
The idea is to use sunlight in space to supply energy for AI systems while reducing reliance on electricity generated on Earth.
However, operating computers in space presents major challenges.
Satellites must withstand extreme temperature changes, radiation, and other conditions that can damage sensitive electronic components.
Google’s current satellite is designed to help researchers understand whether its AI processors can operate reliably under those conditions.
The company has not announced plans to offer commercial AI computing services from space.
Google Plans Two More Connected Satellites in 2027
Google’s next step is to test how its AI chips perform over longer periods while exposed to radiation and changing temperatures.
These tests will help researchers determine whether the processors can remain reliable during extended operations in orbit.
Google plans to reach its next major milestone in 2027 by testing two interconnected satellites.
The experiment will explore how multiple satellites could work together to process AI tasks, an important requirement for developing larger space-based computing systems.
The company is also studying the practical challenges of connecting, powering, and managing computing hardware in space.
For now, Project Suncatcher remains an early research effort rather than a fully operational space-based data center.
Nevertheless, the successful test demonstrates that Google’s AI hardware can run an AI model in orbit, process a request, and send the result back to Earth.

In a statement posted on its offici
items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Pakistan on Saturday rejected the Afghan Taliban spokesperson's latest remarks about resolving bilateral issues, describing them as reflective of a “deeply misguided approach” towards the deteriorating relations between the two countries, and said terrorism emanating from Afghan soil remained a major obstacle to normal ties.
The response came after Afghan Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid accused Islamabad of lacking the readiness to resolve tensions with Kabul through dialogue, saying efforts to ease the dispute had so far failed.
Ministry of Information and Broadcasting
31 October 2026
The Afghan Taliban spokesperson’s latest tweet exposes the regime’s deeply misguided approach and unwillingness to confront the root cause of deteriorating relations with Pakistan. The Taliban leadership continues to blame… pic.twitter.com/gNnBnoAJfI
— Ministry of Information & Broadcasting (@MoIB_Official) October 31, 2026
In a statement posted on its official X account, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting said Mujahid’s latest remarks exposed the Taliban leadership’s unwillingness to confront the main issue straining bilateral ties — its failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil.
“The Taliban leadership continues to blame Islamabad’s policies while conveniently ignoring the single most important issue poisoning bilateral relations: its persistent failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil,” the statement said.
It added that Pakistan’s position was unequivocal, stressing that “terrorism is a red line and the security of its citizens is non-negotiable”.
The statement said Pakistan would not tolerate terrorist sanctuaries across its borders that threatened its security or allow its people to remain targets of attacks originating from Afghanistan, adding that Islamabad reserved the right to take all necessary measures, in accordance with international law, to eliminate threats to its national security, wherever they originated.
“Kabul must recognise that the responsibility for addressing these threats rests squarely with the Afghan Taliban regime,” it said, warning that Pakistan’s resolve to protect its people must never be mistaken for weakness.
Read: Pakistan urges Afghan Taliban to take 'decisive action' against terrorist groups
The ministry said the Taliban regime’s continued refusal to address terrorism remained the principal obstacle to normal relations, adding that shifting blame, making assurances and questioning Pakistan’s policies would neither resolve the crisis nor absolve Kabul of its responsibilities.
“Pakistan’s security will not be held hostage to Afghan Taliban’s inaction, evasions or misplaced priorities,” the statement said.
The statement came after Mujahid told Radio Azadi that Afghanistan had made its final efforts through talks to ease tensions with Pakistan, but these had so far produced no results.
He confirmed that messages had been exchanged between Kabul and Islamabad, adding that efforts by mediating countries and Afghan Taliban officials had also failed to reduce tensions.
A day earlier, Pakistan had urged the Afghan Taliban authorities to take “decisive action” against terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory, questioned their “complicity and support” for groups including the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and reaffirmed its right to self-defence.
Addressing an interactive dialogue with the UN special rapporteur on the human rights situation in Afghanistan in the General Assembly’s Third Committee, Counsellor Muhammad Jawad Ajmal of Pakistan’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations expressed concern over the presence and activities of several militant groups in Afghanistan.
These included the TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army, the Majeed Brigade, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province and the East Turkestan Islamic Movement, along with their affiliates operating from Afghan territory.
Read More: Info ministry calls out Afghan Taliban for deflecting attention from terrorist sanctuaries
Relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been strained due to recurring cross-border terrorism and security concerns. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Afghan Taliban administration to prevent terrorist organisations, particularly the TTP, from using its territory to launch attacks inside Pakistan.
Islamabad has rejected Taliban assurances that Afghan territory would not be used against neighbouring countries, arguing that the ground situation and documented militant activity tell a different story.
Pakistan maintains that the terrorist nexus extended beyond the movement of terrorists across the border to their training, arming and operational support.
Security officials estimate that up to 70 per cent of the Fitna al-Khawarij terrorists infiltrating Pakistan were of Afghan origin. They further claim that the Taliban regime had allowed leftover US and NATO weapons to reach terrorist groups, including Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan.
The security establishment also linked the escalation in attacks to the presence of terrorist infrastructure inside Afghanistan.
In 2026 alone, terrorism emanating from Afghan soil claimed the lives of 1,327 Pakistanis and injured another 2,484, according to figures cited by Pakistani authorities.
Read More: Pakistan warns Afghanistan after Kohat attack, says it can eliminate terror threats ‘wherever they are’
Officials said that whenever Pakistani forces targeted terrorist hideouts, the Taliban regime instead moved to defend the militants and their sanctuaries rather than dismantling the infrastructure. The issue, Pakistan has argued, was not confined to TTP.
UN assessments have continued to document the presence of several other militant organisations in Afghanistan, including al Qaeda, the East Turkestan Islamic Movement and Islamic State-Khorasan, reinforcing concerns about the broader militant ecosystem operating from Afghan territory.
Pakistani officials say the continued presence of these groups, combined with training facilities, cross-border infiltration and access to sophisticated weapons, demonstrates that Afghanistan remains an important base for terrorist activity affecting Pakistan.
Pakistan's position, according to officials, remains that Kabul must take concrete steps to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries, eliminate training infrastructure, prevent cross-border infiltration and ensure that Afghan territory is not used for attacks against Pakistan.
The government has maintained that the issue was fundamentally one of Pakistan's national security and that continued attacks from Afghan soil cannot be addressed through denials alone.
Pakistan says it expected the Taliban regime to fulfil its commitments by taking verifiable action against terrorist groups operating from its territory rather than defending or denying their presence.

Delhi NCR-based B2B manufacturing startup CapGrid has raised ₹50 Cr (about $5.2 Mn) in a Pre-Series B round to develop higher-end precision components and expand into sectors such as drone manufacturing and data centres.
The funding round values CapGrid at ₹430 Cr (about $45.3 Mn), cofounder and CEO Dheeraj Tiwari told Inc42. Led by Hero Enterprise Venture Partners, the investment arm of Sunil Munjal-led Hero Enterprise, it included primary and secondary transactions, with participation from Axilor Ventures, Anicut Capital, Nexus Venture Partners, and angels.
Part of the primary proceeds will fund R&D into higher-end engineered precision components, while the remainder will support business growth, Tiwari said. CapGrid previously raised $5 Mn in an extended Series A round led by Anicut Growth Fund.
Matching Suppliers With Orders
Founded in 2021 by Tiwari and Himanshu Raghuvanshi, CapGrid serves original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and Tier I suppliers across automotive, consumer durables, and heavy industries.
It owns no factories. Instead, its cloud manufacturing platform coordinates component design, development, production, and delivery through third-party manufacturers. CapGrid says it uses AI and ML to match orders with suppliers and track production schedules and quality requirements.
According to the startup, its supplier partners operate at around 60% capacity. CapGrid pools orders from different OEMs to put that spare capacity to use.
Its supply chain control tower tracks sourcing, procurement, production, and deliveries, while 14 fulfilment centres across India’s major OEM clusters manage inventory and component deliveries to assembly lines.
CapGrid also offers new product development, import localisation, and value engineering, helping customers develop parts, replace imports, and improve component designs and sourcing costs.
Moving Beyond Automotive
CapGrid initially focused on automotive, tapping manufacturers’ need to source components and manage suppliers. India’s auto component industry recorded turnover of ₹7.59 Lakh Cr in FY26, up 12.7%, according to ACMA. Supplies to OEMs increased 16.3% to ₹6.52 Lakh Cr.
Having expanded beyond automotive, CapGrid now plans to enter drone manufacturing and data centres.
Tiwari said operating revenue grew around 14% to ₹240 Cr in FY26, with ₹350 Cr targeted for FY27. Its annualised revenue run rate has risen from around ₹300 Cr six months ago to ₹360-370 Cr, with ₹500 Cr the next target.
Inc42 Take: Can CapGrid Move Up The Manufacturing Value Chain?
CapGrid’s next bet is to move beyond consolidating component procurement into higher-end engineered parts. Its existing OEM relationships and supplier network give it a base to build on, but spare factory capacity alone will not establish an advantage in more complex manufacturing. It will depend on the engineering expertise CapGrid brings to component development and production.
The commercial question is whether this shift can improve the economics of its business. Operating revenue grew around 14% in FY26, while its FY27 target implies substantially faster growth. Entering drones and data centres could widen its customer base, but without margin and working-capital disclosures, it remains unclear whether more complex orders will translate into better returns.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Intel suffered one of its biggest stock market crashes on Friday, October 30, as its shares plunged 28.6% following a disappointing financial forecast.
The chipmaker’s stock closed at $65.76, wiping out more than $140 billion in market value in a single trading session.
The decline also reduced the value of the US government’s investment in Intel by approximately $11 billion to $12 billion.
Intel warned that weaker PC demand, rising memory prices, and heavy spending on chip manufacturing would continue to affect its business.
Why Did Intel’s Stock Crash?
Intel reported third-quarter revenue of $16.5 billion, an increase of 21% compared with the same period last year. However, investors were more concerned about the company’s expectations for the final quarter of 2026.
Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below analysts’ expectations of around $17 billion. The company also expects its gross profit margin to fall from 43% in the third quarter to approximately 37% in the fourth quarter.
This means Intel expects to keep a smaller percentage of its revenue after paying the direct costs of producing its products. Intel also warned that heavy spending on manufacturing expansion would put pressure on its cash flow. The disappointing forecast triggered a major sell-off, with investors concerned about the company’s ability to maintain growth.
Rising RAM Prices Are Hurting PC Sales
One of Intel’s biggest problems is the rising cost of computer components, particularly memory.
AI companies are buying large quantities of memory chips and other hardware to build and expand data centers.
This demand has contributed to higher memory prices and made it more expensive for manufacturers to produce computers.
As a result, PC makers are facing weaker demand as customers delay purchases or upgrades.
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said customers had already started warning the company about slowing PC sales because of higher memory prices and limited component availability.
He explained that rising computer prices were putting additional pressure on businesses with limited IT budgets.
Intel expects the slowdown in PC demand to continue at least through the first half of 2027.
US Government Loses Billions on Intel Investment
The stock market crash also affected the US government’s investment in Intel.
In August 2025, the Trump administration acquired a stake of approximately 10% in the company as part of efforts to strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturing.
Following Friday’s decline, the market value of that investment fell by roughly $11 billion to $12 billion.
However, the government has not necessarily suffered an actual financial loss.
Intel shares remain significantly above the price at which the government acquired its stake, meaning the investment is still worth considerably more than its original purchase price.
The decline also affected Nvidia, which invested in Intel in 2025.
Nvidia’s shares fell on Friday as the broader technology and semiconductor sectors experienced heavy selling.
Intel’s Data Center Business Is Still Growing
Despite weaker PC demand, Intel reported strong growth in its data center business.
Revenue from its Data Center and AI division increased 78% compared with the same quarter last year, reaching $7.3 billion.
The growth was driven by demand for server processors used by cloud computing companies and AI infrastructure providers.
However, Intel is struggling to produce enough chips to meet all of that demand.
The company needs to expand its manufacturing capacity while also securing more customers for its chipmaking business.
Intel is working to compete more closely with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), one of the world’s leading contract chip manufacturers.
One of Intel’s new manufacturing facilities in Arizona is already operating, while another is not expected to become operational until 2028.
For now, Intel faces the challenge of managing weaker PC demand while investing heavily in the manufacturing capacity needed to support future growth.

items.content:
The All Progressives Congress (APC) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Sokoto State have exchanged accusations following an alleged attack on the convoy of the ADC governorship candidate, Hon. Manir Muhammad Dan’iya, by personnel of the Sokoto Marshal and Community Guard.
Dan’iya had alleged that personnel of the two state-owned security outfits attacked his convoy around the Sokoto Airport at about 9pm on Friday, October 30, shortly after he escorted former Governor Aminu Waziri Tambuwal to the airport for his return to Abuja.
In a statement issued by his Media Aide, Aminu Abdullahi, the ADC candidate claimed that the security personnel blocked his convoy and prevented it from passing, allegedly claiming they were acting on orders from above to stop ADC members from entering Sokoto.
He alleged that gunshots were fired during the confrontation, his vehicle was damaged and two Department of State Services (DSS) officers attached to his security team were detained.
Sanwo-Olu: Hamzat Stepped Down for Me in 2018 without grudges
INEC: We&#8217;ve completed 9 of 14 electoral milestones for 2027
Dan’iya described the incident as a threat to his life and called on the police, the DSS and other relevant authorities to investigate the matter and establish those responsible.
He also urged the security agencies to ensure the release of the two DSS officers if they remained in custody, while calling on the state government to clarify the alleged instructions given to the security personnel.
The ADC candidate further alleged that earlier in the day, personnel of the security outfits had been deployed at entry points into the state, where vehicles bearing ADC inscriptions were reportedly stopped from entering.
However, the APC dismissed the allegations, describing them as fabricated claims intended to attract public sympathy and divert attention from the ADC’s political challenges.
The state APC Chairman, Alhaji Haruna Adiya, said the allegations were part of what he described as a propaganda campaign against the state government.
Adiya, who spoke in a statement, questioned the credibility of the account, particularly the claim that personnel of the state security outfits detained DSS officers and interfered with their vehicles.
He also faulted what he described as inconsistencies in the ADC’s account of the incident, arguing that while the party’s media aide reportedly claimed that security personnel prevented Dan’iya from entering Sokoto metropolis, the candidate’s statement indicated that he had visited different locations in the city to pay condolence visits and attend to other engagements.
The APC chairman also dismissed claims that security personnel were deployed to restrict ADC members from entering the state, explaining that Sokoto was preparing to host a major traditional title conferment ceremony scheduled for Sunday.
He said the event was expected to attract prominent personalities and visitors from different parts of the country, making adequate security arrangements necessary.
Adiya maintained that the deployment of security personnel was aimed at protecting residents and visitors attending the ceremony and had nothing to do with the political activities of the ADC.
He further urged the opposition party to address its internal challenges rather than blame the APC and the state government for its political difficulties.
The APC chairman also said Governor Ahmed Aliyu remained committed to peace and political tolerance, adding that he had consistently advised party supporters against engaging in activities capable of causing political tension or violence.
According to him, ADC members have continued to conduct political activities in Sokoto without interference or intimidation from APC supporters.
He urged the opposition party to substantiate its allegations and focus on presenting policies and development plans to the electorate rather than engaging in what he described as manufactured controversies.

items.summary:
A baby’s diaper, the interior of a vehicle, a protective agricultural covering and a reusable shopping bag may appear to have very little in common.
Yet each can rely on a material category that often goes unnoticed by consumers: nonwoven fabric.
Unlike conventional woven textiles, nonwoven materials are produced by bonding or entangling fibres into a fabric-like structure. Their characteristics can be adapted to different applications, making them useful across industries with very different manufacturing requirements.

Today, the company operates Italian-engineered production lines with an annual production capacity of 24,000 metric tonnes.
A M
items.author: Publishing Partner
items.content:
A baby’s diaper, the interior of a vehicle, a protective agricultural covering and a reusable shopping bag may appear to have very little in common.
Yet each can rely on a material category that often goes unnoticed by consumers: nonwoven fabric.
Unlike conventional woven textiles, nonwoven materials are produced by bonding or entangling fibres into a fabric-like structure. Their characteristics can be adapted to different applications, making them useful across industries with very different manufacturing requirements.
In Pakistan, Master Nonwoven, part of Master Group of Industries, has been manufacturing these materials since 2002.
What began as an investment in developing local nonwoven production capacity has grown into a manufacturing operation serving businesses across hygiene, neonatal care, automotive, agriculture, bedding, retail and packaging.
Today, the company operates Italian-engineered production lines with an annual production capacity of 24,000 metric tonnes.
A Material With Many Industrial Applications
The versatility of nonwoven materials lies in their ability to serve different functions depending on how they are manufactured and specified.
In personal care and hygiene, nonwovens are used in products such as diapers, where different material layers contribute to the product’s structure and functionality.
Neonatal products represent another application area, with material requirements determined by the intended use and product specifications.
In agriculture, technical nonwovens are used for purposes such as crop protection, supporting farming operations that require specialised covering materials.
Automotive manufacturing presents another set of applications. Nonwoven materials are used in various interior and functional components, where their structure and material properties can be selected according to production needs.
The bedding industry also uses nonwoven materials as part of mattress and sleep-product manufacturing.
Across retail and packaging, they are used in products such as reusable shopping bags and protective material solutions.
Although these applications are different, they share one important requirement: manufacturers need materials that meet the specifications of their finished products.
Why Material Specifications Make a Difference
A nonwoven material suitable for a shopping bag may not be appropriate for an automotive component or a hygiene product.
Each application has its own requirements for material weight, colour, structure and performance.
One of the key specifications is GSM, which stands for grams per square metre. It indicates the weight of a material and helps manufacturers determine whether it is suitable for their intended application.
For example, a lightweight material may be required for one product, while another may need a heavier construction.
Colour options can also be important, particularly for applications where the material is visible in the finished product.
Master Nonwoven offers one of the widest locally available ranges of colours and GSM options, enabling businesses to select materials according to their manufacturing requirements.
This flexibility is especially valuable for companies producing multiple product categories or working with different customer specifications.
The Importance of Consistency
When consumers purchase a finished product, they rarely consider the manufacturing processes behind its individual components.
For the businesses producing those goods, however, material consistency is a daily priority.
A manufacturer placing repeat orders needs confidence that the supplied material will continue to meet the required specifications.
Differences in material weight, structure or other characteristics can create complications during production.
To address this, Master Nonwoven operates an in-house laboratory for quality control and quality assurance.
The company also uses end-to-end quality tracking throughout its manufacturing process, helping monitor materials against defined requirements and maintain consistency between production cycles.
Its OEKO-TEX, ISO and CE certifications further support its focus on recognised quality and manufacturing standards.
These systems are important for industrial customers who depend on predictable material performance across ongoing production requirements.
How Industry Demand Is Changing
The importance of nonwoven materials became particularly visible during the COVID-19 period, when demand for hygiene and protective products increased attention on the sector.
However, their applications extend well beyond healthcare-related products.
Agricultural businesses continue to use technical nonwovens, while automotive and bedding manufacturers require materials for a variety of components.
Retail and packaging are also creating opportunities as businesses explore reusable bags and alternative material formats.
In response to different market requirements, Master Nonwoven offers a range of specifications, including oxo-biodegradable material options for relevant applications.
The company’s ability to supply different industries reflects the adaptability that has made nonwovens an important material category in modern manufacturing.
The Manufacturing Behind Everyday Products
The products people use every day are often the result of contributions from several industries working behind the scenes.
A finished mattress, vehicle interior or personal-care product may depend on specialised materials supplied by manufacturers whose names are not visible on the final product.
Master Nonwoven is part of this industrial network.
With more than two decades of experience, an annual production capacity of 24,000 metric tonnes and manufacturing capabilities developed around diverse material requirements, the company supports businesses producing goods for a wide range of uses.
Its role highlights an important aspect of Pakistan’s industrial landscape: the materials behind everyday products are just as essential to manufacturing as the finished products themselves.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Researchers from Microsoft and the University of California, Berkeley, have introduced a free tool called TokenEconomizer that can reduce the cost of using AI coding assistants by up to 31%.
The tool works with popular AI coding assistants, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Pi.
In tests involving 277 coding tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4% to 30.9% while maintaining similar or better results in most cases.
The researchers have made the tool publicly available, allowing developers to use it without paying for the software itself.
How Does TokenEconomizer Work?
AI coding assistants use tokens to understand instructions, read code, and complete tasks. Developers pay for these tokens when using paid AI services.
However, researchers found that these assistants often waste tokens by repeating work, using unnecessary tools, and trying the same failed solutions multiple times.
For example, an AI assistant might repeatedly search for the same file or instructions even though it found them during an earlier task.
TokenEconomizer helps avoid this problem by remembering useful information from previous sessions.
It uses three methods to reduce unnecessary work.
First, it remembers important details about a project, such as the commands needed to test the code. This prevents the AI assistant from searching for the same information again.
Second, it removes tools that the AI assistant does not need for a particular task. This reduces the amount of information the AI must process.
Third, it detects when the assistant keeps making the same mistakes and encourages it to try a different approach or stop wasting resources.
The tool works alongside existing AI assistants, so developers do not need to change the AI models themselves.
AI Coding Costs Drop by Up to 31%
The researchers tested TokenEconomizer on 277 software development tasks using different AI models.
The results showed that the tool consistently reduced costs.

Claude Code running Opus 4.8 recorded the largest cost reduction at 30.9%, followed by Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol at 26.1%.
The researchers also checked whether spending fewer tokens affected the quality of the AI’s work.
In four of the five tested setups, the AI assistants completed slightly more tasks successfully on their first attempt.
However, Claude Code with Opus 4.8 experienced a small decline in its success rate, dropping from 74% to 73%.
This suggests that developers can reduce AI usage costs without significantly affecting performance, although results may vary.
Tool Gets Better With Continued Use
TokenEconomizer becomes more useful as developers continue working on the same project.
During the first few tasks, it collects information about the project and how the AI assistant works.
It then uses that information to avoid unnecessary steps in future tasks.
The researchers found that some projects initially cost slightly more because the tool needed time to learn.
However, by the sixth task, all six tested projects became cheaper to work on.
Removing unused tools produced the largest individual savings, reducing costs by 13.2% to 17.7%.
Remembering useful project information reduced costs by 11.8% to 14.3%, while preventing repeated failed attempts saved another 5.4% to 7.1% when tested separately.
How Does It Compare With Other AI Cost-Saving Tools?
TokenEconomizer is not the only tool designed to reduce how much AI coding assistants cost.
Other tools, including RTK, Serena, and Aider RepoMap, also try to make coding assistants more efficient.
However, the researchers found that these tools did not consistently reduce costs across every tested project.

TokenEconomizer reduced costs across all 30 tested project and model combinations.
By comparison, RTK increased costs in 12 cases, while Aider RepoMap increased costs in 15 cases.
The researchers found that TokenEconomizer performed better overall because it adjusts its approach based on what it learns from each project instead of applying the same method everywhere.
Free to Use With Popular AI Coding Assistants
TokenEconomizer supports Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, and Pi.
It requires Python 3.10 or newer and can run on a regular computer without a dedicated graphics card.
The tool also does not require a separate API key, although developers may still need paid access to the AI coding assistants they use.
TokenEconomizer stores the information it learns about each project locally on the user’s computer.
Developers can download the software from GitHub, and its open-source license allows them to use and modify it.
The researchers believe the tool could be particularly useful for developers who regularly work on large projects using AI coding assistants.
While the tests showed cost reductions of up to 30.9%, actual savings will depend on the AI assistant, the type of project, and how frequently the tool is used.

items.content:
On July 18, 2026, Skyroot Aerospace achieved a historic milestone when its Vikram-1 rocket successfully placed satellites into orbit, becoming the first privately developed Indian rocket to accomplish an orbital launch.
For a country whose space programme was historically dominated by ISRO, it was a powerful demonstration of what Indian entrepreneurs could achieve in advanced technology.
Three months later, Ashlee Vance — the American journalist best known for his bestselling biography of Elon Musk and reporting on the global space industry — turned his attention to India’s technological ambitions.
His question was less about the capabilities of Indian engineers than the willingness of Indian investors to back them. He asked:
“Why are Indian VCs so afraid to take risk and make money?”
The October 22 post accompanied Vance’s Core Memory feature exploring India’s emerging hardware economy.
After three weeks meeting 15 Indian companies, Vance appeared impressed by the technological ambitions of their founders but far less enthusiastic about the state of the country’s venture capital ecosystem. He subsequently doubled down, claiming he had rarely encountered a market where VCs had a worse reputation among founders.
What followed was an unusually candid debate.
Founders complained about investors demanding commercial traction before technologies had been validated, prolonged diligence processes and excessive dependence on founder pedigree.
Investors pushed back, highlighting India’s growing list of deeptech successes, the increasing availability of specialist capital and the structural challenges of financing scientific innovation.
But the timing makes this debate far more consequential than another disagreement on X.
As AI threatens to automate parts of the software-services industry that helped establish India as a global technology powerhouse, the country’s ability to create and own foundational technologies is becoming increasingly important.
India has demonstrated that its entrepreneurs can build complex technologies. The more difficult question is whether venture capital and private equity can repeatedly back such breakthroughs.
Indian Founders Aren’t Just Questioning Capital, They’re Questioning The VCs
One of the strongest responses came from Akash Kulgod, founder of Dognosis, which is developing canine-assisted cancer detection technology.
In a detailed post, Kulgod compared his experience interacting with approximately 80 investors, around 65% of whom were based in the US. His criticism ran deeper than simply stating that Indian VCs rejected his startup.
He said US investors typically made relatively quick decisions, rejecting the opportunity when they lacked conviction in the technology or founding team.
Some Indian investors, he alleged, extended discussions over repeated meetings and visits, only to demand commercial traction or stop responding. For a company developing medical technology, any delays in the development cycle hurt.
Clinical validation, technical testing and regulatory approvals can require years before meaningful commercial revenue becomes possible.
An investor demanding revenue before the technology is proven may effectively eliminate the opportunity instead of properly evaluating the technology.
Kulgod also questioned whether some investors possessed the technical understanding needed to assess unfamiliar scientific problems.
Other founders raised concerns about investor dependence on IIT or IIM credentials, professional networks and the reputations of existing backers when evaluating early-stage startups.
These are undoubtedly individual accounts, not evidence that such practices are universal across Indian VC firms. But they expose an uncomfortable question.
If investors require commercial traction, institutional validation and another investor’s conviction before writing a cheque, how much technological risk are they actually underwriting?
There is an important difference between financing a technology after it works and financing the experiment that determines whether it can work.
Deeptech needs both. And as the experience of several founders in India shows, the latter remains one of the most difficult investment decisions.
The Numbers Show A Funding Surge, But Are More Founders Benefiting?
According to Inc42 DataLabs, Indian deeptech startups raised approximately $500 Mn across 87 deals in 2025.
The sector emerged as one of the most active by deal count, but its funding remained substantially below fintech’s $2.5 Bn, enterprise tech’s $1.8 Bn and ecommerce’s $1.7 Bn.
The latest quarterly figures, however, suggest that investor preferences are changing.
In Q3 2026, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 funding deals, compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in the year-ago quarter.
Funding surged 176% YoY, dramatically outpacing the broader startup ecosystem’s 5% growth.
Deeptech funding nearly tripled, but the number of funded deals actually declined.
Pixxel’s $100 Mn funding round alone accounted for approximately one-third of the deeptech capital deployed during the quarter.
Bengaluru captured around 65% of the sector’s funding.
At the broader ecosystem level, investors also wrote larger seed cheques to fewer companies. Early stage funding fell 18% YoY to $164 Mn across 93 deals, even as the median cheque size increased 20% to $1.2 Mn.
The contrast with the first half of 2026 is instructive.
According to Inc42’s H1 2026 funding report, advanced hardware and technology startups raised $365 Mn across a record 66 deals, reflecting an 18% rise in funding and a 53% jump in deal volume.
That suggests improving breadth of investment during the first half, followed by greater concentration in the third quarter.
There’s no trend to explore here, but this disparity demonstrates why headline funding growth is an insufficient measure of access to capital. Larger investments are increasingly flowing towards a smaller pool of technically validated companies.
So the deeper question is whether more first-time founders pursuing unproven technologies are securing their first institutional cheques, which strikes at the heart of what Vance was saying.
Are India’s VCs Backing Convenience Over Breakthroughs?
A separate debate over India’s startup funding priorities had already exposed a fundamental divide between founders and investors over where venture capital should flow.
In an October 17 post on X, Neosapien founder Dhananjay Yadav questioned why consumer-service startups burning substantial amounts of capital could attract large investments, while deeptech companies generating higher revenues with lower cash burn struggled to raise even a fraction of that money.
Responding to Yadav, Untitled Ventures’ Anmol Maini made a provocative claim that much of deeptech could eventually prove to be a “grift”, arguing that quick commerce and on-demand services might contribute more to the economy.
Blume Ventures partner Arpit Agarwal offered an explanation rooted in investment economics.
Investment capital, he argued, gravitates towards opportunities offering lower perceived risk or disproportionately higher returns.
The distinction to note here is that the economic importance of a technology and its attractiveness as a venture investment are not necessarily the same thing.
This is consistent with concerns Agarwal had raised in an earlier interview with Inc42, where he explained why capital-intensive original equipment manufacturing (OEM) businesses are often poorly suited to conventional early-stage VC financing.
Pixxel founder Awais Ahmed, however, challenged the notion that consumer internet and deeptech should be competing for relevance and the same pie of venture capital.
In a detailed post, Ahmed argued that they represent different layers of the same technological economy.
A ten-minute grocery delivery depends on decades of breakthroughs in semiconductors, GPS, lithium-ion batteries, cellular networks and computing — technologies developed long before their commercial applications became apparent.
Consumer businesses make technology accessible at scale. Deeptech expands what technology can achieve.
Ahmed acknowledged that successful internet companies create wealth that can eventually be reinvested into deeptech. But foundational technologies cannot simply be treated as investments to pursue once quicker commercial opportunities have been exhausted.
Developing competitive capabilities in semiconductors, aerospace, advanced materials or energy requires years of research, specialised talent, experimentation and industrial infrastructure.
And therein lies India’s venture capital allocation dilemma.
The country has spent the past decade building a thriving consumer internet economy. But its ambition to emerge as a global technology powerhouse will require investing in foundational technologies long before their commercial returns become predictable.
The Criticism Ignores How Far India Has Come
Unacademy cofounder Gaurav Munjal was among the prominent voices challenging Vance. In a response on X, Munjal described the assessment as dated and rage-baiting.
He pointed to Astrobase, Airbound and Sarvam AI as examples of ambitious companies successfully raising capital, while highlighting the outcomes achieved by Groww, Eternal and Meesho.
His broader argument was that India’s VC ecosystem had improved dramatically, and that fintech and digital commerce remained important opportunities given the size of the domestic market.
Ather Energy attracted early support from IIT Madras-linked programmes, the Flipkart founders, Tiger Global and Hero MotoCorp before eventually becoming a listed company.
Skyroot has achieved orbital launch capability. Agnikul has demonstrated indigenous launch technology. Pixxel is developing hyperspectral satellites, while Airbound is attempting to commercialise autonomous aircraft.
Munjal’s point was that these achievements challenge the idea that India lacks investors willing to finance complex technologies.
Nevertheless, several high-profile deeptech startups have relied significantly on overseas capital. Airbound’s $37 Mn Series A, for instance, was led by US-based Greenoaks.
An Indian startup’s ability to attract international investors is a sign of some success for the company, but it does not necessarily establish that domestic investors are equally willing to finance such technologies.
Still, Munjal’s argument gains weight from his own next move.
Along with Unacademy cofounder Roman Saini, he is raising a ₹700 Cr fund called Longshot Capital, targeting AI, manufacturing, robotics, spacetech and defence.
It represents a growing pattern: founders who created wealth and operating expertise through India’s first startup generation are increasingly attempting to finance its next.
Indian VCs Have Avoided Real Venture Risk, But That Is Changing
Antler India partner Nitin Sharma offered one of the more balanced assessments.
In a detailed October 24 post, Sharma acknowledged that India’s venture ecosystem had historically failed to generate consistent venture-scale returns partly because investors avoided genuine venture risk.
But he argued that the situation had begun changing.
Sharma identified two categories of founders increasingly receiving backing: the first being experienced technologists and academics, and the second category covering young, unconventional self-taught entrepreneurs.
Sharma said Antler had acted as the first institutional believer in 10 deeptech ventures since 2022.
He highlighted Antler’s investments in companies such as InspeCity, Aspera Aerospace, Green Aero Propulsion, Meine Electric, Mandrake Bio and Armory Shield.
His argument went beyond showing that VCs were willing to invest before revenue. Historically, he explained, early-stage investors were reluctant to back complex technologies partly because they could not identify who would finance those companies in subsequent rounds.
That problem is beginning to ease as specialist funds and larger deeptech investors emerge.
But Sharma acknowledged that India still needs more investors willing to write larger first cheques for ambitious technological bets.
He also identified another serious challenge: demand.
Indian deeptech startups, he argued, struggle to secure paid pilots and procurement opportunities from domestic corporations, particularly outside defence and space.
If Indian companies refuse to become early customers, startups must finance not only technological development but also the prolonged process of creating a commercial market.
India’s investor appetite may be improving. But the institutional and structural environment around deeptech financing and commercialisation must improve with it.
What Established VCs Have Actually Invested
While newer specialist funds are attracting attention, established Indian VC firms have also been investing in deeptech for years.
TC Meenakshisundaram (TCM), cofounder and vice-chairman of Chiratae Ventures, offered a historical perspective in an X thread responding to Vance.
He acknowledged that until 2020, many Indian VCs — including Indian arms of Silicon Valley funds — were reluctant to back hardware and deeptech startups. Concerns over global competitiveness, licensing and certification requirements, the availability of follow-on capital and long investment holding periods have all contributed to this reluctance.
But he argued that the situation had since changed, highlighting companies such as Quanfluence, TakeMe2Space, Cavli Wireless and Metadome.
Chiratae’s investment record supports that counterargument.
Founded in 2006 by Sudhir Sethi and TCM, the firm reports having deployed more than $300 Mn across over 60 deeptech companies spanning AI, climate technology, healthcare, robotics, spacetech and advanced manufacturing.
In December 2025, it launched its Sonic DeepTech programme to accelerate seed-to-Series A decisions, offering cheques of up to $2 Mn.
By May 2026, Chiratae had announced commitments of up to $10 Mn across five startups selected through the programme.
And Chiratae is hardly alone.
This is a counterpoint to the suggestion that Indian VCs have uniformly avoided advanced technologies. But the criticism is also valid, and therefore it raises the question of how deeptech investment should be measured.
The category includes everything from software-led AI applications to capital-intensive aerospace, advanced manufacturing and medical technologies, each carrying different levels of scientific uncertainty and commercial risk.
The more meaningful measure is not simply how many deeptech companies a fund has backed. It is how early the fund entered, what technical risks it financed and whether it supported those companies through subsequent development cycles.
The Problem Goes Beyond The First Cheque
Founders frequently identify seed funding as their biggest obstacle. Some deeptech investors believe the more serious capital shortage appears later.
Speciale Invest, for instance, outlined plans for a ₹1,400 Cr growth-stage fund targeting companies that have demonstrated technical capabilities but need larger amounts of capital for manufacturing and commercial expansion.
A company like Skyroot, which is making rockets, requires funding for design, testing and initial launches. But technological success is only the beginning of the journey towards reliable commercial operations.
Similarly, a semiconductor company may develop a functioning chip but still need substantial capital for fabrication, qualification and customer adoption.
Deeptech businesses require a continuous financing pipeline.
The problem for India is the insufficient seed capital for highly speculative technologies and inadequate growth capital for technically validated companies. Both gaps exist simultaneously.
When the next investor is missing, even the first investor becomes more reluctant to take the risk.
The Capital Powering India’s VCs
Siana Capital’s Siddharth Shah raised another structural issue in his response to the debate.
He argued that India’s venture capital ecosystem is constrained by the expectations of limited partners — the investors financing venture funds.
Deeptech companies can require 10–15 years to achieve meaningful commercial maturity. Yet VC funds often operate within shorter investment and distribution timelines.
One problem is LPs seeking distributions while portfolio companies were still working towards critical technical or commercial milestones.
He also highlighted weak secondary liquidity, difficult exits and the limited availability of long-duration domestic institutional capital.
US-based investor Anu Hariharan raised related concerns about taxation, currency exposure, operational complexity and limited M&A opportunities.
The H1 2026 Inc42 funding report offers another perspective.
While 64% of surveyed institutional investors said they expected to increase their venture capital allocations, respondents also identified geopolitical uncertainty and constrained global liquidity as major risks.
Investor expectations around exits have also shifted. Strategic acquisitions and secondary transactions are increasingly important alternatives to IPOs, particularly for companies unlikely to reach public-market scale quickly.
The problem is that risk appetite is shaped by the economics of the entire investment value chain.
LPs want returns and liquidity. VCs need successful exits to raise their next funds. Corporate customers want proven products. Founders need financing to prove those products work.
Each participant may be making a rational individual decision. But collectively, those decisions can produce a system in which everyone expects somebody else to absorb the earliest uncertainty.
That does not absolve VCs of responsibility for poor diligence or insufficient conviction.
Changing India’s deeptech investment culture will require more than persuading fund managers to be courageous.
Deeptech Funds Changing The Capital Landscape
There is, however, evidence that the supply of dedicated capital is growing.
In the past year alone, India has seen a wave of new funds and investment vehicles targeting AI, spacetech, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, energy and industrial technologies.
Aakrit Vaish, the former Haptik CEO, and Pratyush Choudhury launched AI-focused VC firm Activate in December 2025.
By September 2026, Activate had closed its investment platform at $105 Mn, comprising an $85 Mn early-stage fund and $20 Mn deployed through growth investment vehicles.
Its portfolio includes investments in Sarvam AI, ElevenLabs and Wispr Flow, alongside early-stage bets that have not been publicly disclosed.
The fund’s investor base includes founders, AI researchers, global VC partners and family offices — a different pool of capital from the institutions that traditionally dominated Indian startup financing.
Meanwhile, Transition VC launched a ₹1,500 Cr second fund in July, targeting energy transition, advanced manufacturing and industrial deeptech businesses.
Unlike many conventional seed funds, Transition VC plans to write $2 Mn-$5 Mn cheques into engineering-led startups demonstrating technical feasibility and early commercial traction.
The investment strategies differ, but the pattern is becoming more visible.
The emergence of these funds suggests that India’s financing ecosystem is becoming more specialised. But their mandates also demonstrate that deeptech capital is not interchangeable.
Longshot and AUM are targeting early-stage opportunities. Piper Serica and Speciale’s proposed growth fund focus on companies further along their development journeys. Transition VC targets engineering-led businesses that have already established technical feasibility.
YourNest’s continuation fund addresses another problem: providing additional time and liquidity for existing portfolio companies rather than financing entirely new startups.
More capital is entering deeptech. The unanswered question is whether these different sources of funding will connect to create an uninterrupted financing pipeline from research to commercial scale.
Government Support Is Influencing Investor Conviction, But Execution Matters
The government is also attempting to address the patient-capital shortage. And government policy is also beginning to shape private investment decisions.
Its ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation scheme is designed to support high-risk, research-intensive technologies.
In October, the government approved 19 second-level fund managers with commitments totalling ₹7,131 Cr.
That is a significant development, although the overall scheme outlay should not be confused with capital already deployed to startups.
According to Inc42’s H1 2026 investor survey, 61% of respondents said the India Semiconductor Mission had influenced their investment thesis for deeptech and hardware, while 66% said the IndiaAI Mission had influenced their AI investment thesis.
But this policy support does not automatically translate into greater appetite for every type of frontier technology.
Inc42’s Q3 2026 survey of more than 85 institutional investors found that 39% expected vertical AI applications to capture the most value over the next five years, compared with 23% favouring AI hardware and semiconductors and 14% backing sovereign foundation models.
Investors are interested in foundational technologies, but their expectations of where AI value will accrue remain weighted towards applications. These are survey preferences, not actual deal allocations, and the reality of the investments of these funds will differ from their responses.
Nevertheless, they suggest that even within a booming technology category, investors remain selective about where value is most likely to accrue.
The RDI programme itself has faced questions over governance.
In our Q3 survey, 52% of respondents considered existing disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate but said transparency remained limited. A quarter of the respondents (25%) called for independent oversight.
The government’s role will therefore need to extend beyond announcing larger financing schemes.
Transparent allocation, research commercialisation, industrial procurement and access to testing infrastructure will influence whether policy support ultimately produces sustainable companies.
India’s spacetech reforms offer one example of what coordinated support can achieve.
Skyroot and Agnikul’s technological progress cannot be separated from the policy changes and institutional infrastructure that enabled private participation in the country’s space economy.
The next challenge is to build similarly effective pathways across semiconductors, advanced materials, medical technologies, energy and industrial automation.
It is no longer whether India can produce another Ather, Skyroot or Pixxel.
It is whether an unknown scientist or engineer with a genuinely ambitious idea can access the capital, research infrastructure, industrial customers and follow-on investment needed to attempt something equally difficult.
Not every rocket will reach orbit. Not every chip will work. Not every scientific breakthrough will become a commercially viable company.
But financing those uncertain attempts is precisely what allows an innovation ecosystem to produce breakthroughs at scale.
India has proved that its founders can build rockets. Now it must prove that its capital ecosystem can finance the next hundred, including the ones that never leave the launchpad.
The post India Can Build Rockets, But Can Its VCs Fund The Next One? appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.author: Akshit Pushkarna
items.content:
For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to an adult. Among the clearest signs of evolution and maturity of this ecosystem is the growing number of startups eyeing a public listing now.
For Indian companies, achieving a public listing has for long symbolised operational progression, transparency, and long-term viability. For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation.
Currently, a handful of startups, including the likes of Razorpay, PRISM, PhonePe, among others, are in various stages of their IPO journey. Meanwhile, over 70 Indian new-age tech companies have already crossed the milestone and are now listed on the bourses.
The list also includes Indian companies like MakeMyTrip and Freshworks, which are listed on Nasdaq in the US.
India’s startup IPO wave reached its peak in 2025, surpassing the previous year’s momentum.
While 18 startups listed in 2025, 17 startups have already reached that milestone in 2026. With companies like Cult.fit, OYO, others, eyeing to tap the public markets this year, the list is only expected to grow further this year.
17 new-age companies — Tonbo Imaging, Zetwerk, AceVector, Moneyview, Rentomojo, ESDS, Purple Style Labs, Turtlemint, Klassroom, Shiprocket, LEAP India, Kissht, Aye Finance, Fractal Analytics, Amagi, Shadowfax and SEDEMAC — have made their public market debut in 2026.
As of now, the total market capitalisation of the listed companies stands at over $167 Bn.
To consolidate all the information about listed startups, Inc42 has launched the Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker. From the movement in the shares of the companies since their listing to the financial performance of these companies, the tracker is your one-stop resource to know everything you need about the listed tech companies.
Table not loading? Open the tracker.
Read our methodology here.
Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride
Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22.
While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges.
While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. Over 60 of the new-age tech companies are currently profitable.
In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively.
It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s purview are about a decade old.
From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra’s IPO materialised within four years of its operations.
Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal.
Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr
Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom
The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem.
The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups.
While fintech and ecommerce house 14 names each, 13 enterprise tech startups have listed on the bourses so far.
The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of Tonbo Imaging, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts.
Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups
While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 27 listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru’s ninetineen and Mumbai’s fifteen.
While fifteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube.
Delhi NCR contributes $96 Bn in the cumulative $178 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies.
Last updated: Oct 23
The Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker will be updated periodically with fresh data.

items.content:
‎Some aggrieved youths have ‎retrieved bribe allegedly collected by policemen at a checkpoint along Auchi-Aviele road in Edo State.
The policemen were at the checkpoint when the youths stormed there, accusing them of extorting motorists and cyclists.
In a video trending online, the civilians led by a man on short and armless shirt, confronted and searched the officers, including those bearing arms.
“Search this one,” the youth leader charged, while an armed policeman replied, “Nothing dey my body,” forcing a smile on his face.
“Hold on! Let them search youth,” a voice at the background said.
The policeman was seen raising up both hands as someone frisked him before giving a sign that nothing was found on the officer.
A policeman suspected to be leader of the team tried handing over his phone to the youth leader to speak with an unidentified person apparently to calm down the situation, but the youth leader objected, shouting, “I no wan talk!”
The officer made another attempt to hand over the phone to the youth leader, who got aggressive and hit his hand.
He later asked the policemen and officials of the Vigilante Group of Nigeria (VGN) to leave the scene before he moved to a location where he addressed the public.
“Good evening my people! We were on Auchi-Aviele road and found vigilantes and policemen mounting roadblock here. We got information that they were extorting people so we decided to chase them from here. We found out that they had already collected N4,200 from bike men and others. I’m taking this money to the Area Commander.”
“To the Commissioner of Police, I want you to call the DPO of Agbede Police Station because his men who extorted passengers said they got order from the DPO. While the Vigilantes said their boss from Aviele sent them. They did not spend up to 30 minutes there before collecting N4,200 from road users. That means they could have raised like 80k or 100k if they spent more hours. Imagine collecting this amount from Nigerians who are suffering,” he said.
Daily Trust subjected several key frames of the video to verification using various open source intelligence tools and found no evidence of digital manipulation.
‎
‎The incident has generated reactions from social media users, many of whom have called for an end to police extortion and the alleged collection of money from motorists at checkpoints.‎

items.author: Muhammad Ilyas
items.content:
A summons from the Public Accounts Committee is meant to bring those responsible for public spending to the table. But when senior bureaucrats are called to explain billions of rupees in audit objections, it is often their subordinates who turn up instead. The practice has raised an uncomfortable question for Punjab’s parliamentary watchdog: can accountability be enforced when those expected to answer are missing from the room?
Senior government officials are increasingly failing to attend meetings of the Punjab Assembly's Public Accounts Committee (PAC), sending junior officers in their place despite being summoned to respond to audit objections. The practice has prompted concern among committee members over the level of senior officials' participation in the parliamentary oversight process.
Instead of department secretaries and other responsible senior officials, Additional Secretaries, Deputy Secretaries and Section Officers are frequently attending meetings to represent their respective departments. The issue has raised questions about whether subordinate officers have the authority and relevant information to provide satisfactory answers to audit objections involving public funds.
Public Accounts Committee Chairman Iftikhar Chachar has also taken notice of the matter, maintaining that an officer specifically summoned for the examination of audit objections is required to attend the meeting. Officials who fail to appear may face reprimands from the committee.
Chachar said the situation had started improving since he began questioning officials about their absence and taking notice of the practice. Departments are now expected to inform the committee before a meeting if a summoned officer is outside the country or city.
Such officials are also required to provide evidence explaining their absence and inform the committee which officer will attend in their place to respond to members' questions.
The committee has expressed concern over the repeated appearance of subordinate officers in place of department heads and senior officials. While Additional Secretaries, Deputy Secretaries and Section Officers may represent their departments, their presence can create difficulties when matters require authoritative explanations, final decisions or access to complete departmental records.
The Public Accounts Committee is an important parliamentary forum responsible for examining government expenditure, audit objections and financial irregularities. The participation of senior departmental officials is considered essential for providing accurate responses, explaining financial discrepancies and ensuring timely decisions on audit matters.
The Punjab Assembly is currently examining audit objections relating to the financial year 2023-24, involving amounts reportedly running into billions of rupees. Officials from various government departments are being summoned to explain the objections and clarify discrepancies identified during the audit process.
The absence of senior officials can delay the examination and settlement of audit objections, particularly when junior officers lack the authority to make decisions or provide final explanations on behalf of their departments.
The committee chairman's emphasis on the personal attendance of summoned officers and the requirement to justify their absence reflects the importance being attached to departmental accountability.
Ensuring the participation of department secretaries and other responsible senior officials in PAC meetings remains important for strengthening parliamentary oversight, improving the resolution of audit objections and ensuring accountability for public expenditure.
