items.author: ZAFAR BHUTTA
items.content:
Pakistan has sought Saudi Arabia's support for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) supplies and invited investment in oil storage facilities and refinery upgrades as it grapples with supply disruptions linked to the Iran-US conflict and instability along key regional shipping routes.
Pakistan has relied heavily on LPG imports from Iran through the land border, and the closure of the crossing has raised concerns about supplies ahead of the winter season, when domestic gas demand typically increases.
Islamabad has approached Riyadh for dedicated LPG shipments to help meet the anticipated rise in demand, as disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and security risks in the Red Sea have added to concerns over regional energy supplies.
The crisis has also highlighted Pakistan's limited strategic petroleum storage capacity. The government is now seeking investment from Middle Eastern countries, including Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, to develop oil storage infrastructure.
The proposals were discussed at a meeting between Federal Minister for Petroleum Ali Pervez Malik and Saudi Arabia's Ambassador to Pakistan Dr Rajeh Tami Albugamy, according to a statement issued by the ministry.
The discussions covered strategic oil storage, refinery upgrades, LPG supplies and commercial cooperation in the mining, petroleum and energy sectors.
Malik told the ambassador that Pakistan had approved a tax-neutral bonded policy modelled on international energy hubs such as Fujairah and Singapore. Under the framework, Saudi companies could establish commercial oil reserves in Pakistan without incurring local tax liabilities.
The minister said the arrangement could help diversify maritime transit risks associated with the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait while providing access to Asian markets.
He said strategic oil storage facilities in Pakistan would give Saudi Arabia greater flexibility in managing supply routes and reaching regional markets.
Malik also outlined plans to develop a large petroleum storage and refining complex at Hub in Balochistan, with guidance from Technip Energies UK. The proposed facility would be capable of accommodating very large crude carriers (VLCCs) and could strengthen Pakistan's role as a regional energy corridor serving Central Asian and Chinese markets, the statement said.
The minister also highlighted investment opportunities under Pakistan's refinery upgrade programme, which aims to modernise domestic refining infrastructure, improve efficiency and transition to Euro 5 fuel standards.
He thanked Saudi authorities at Yanbu port for prioritising crude oil shipments to Pakistan during recent disruptions in global energy markets. He also discussed with the ambassador coordination with Saudi Aramco to increase crude oil procurement and arrange dedicated LPG shipments.
Pakistan is also seeking Saudi investment in the multibillion-dollar Reko Diq copper and gold mining project in Balochistan. Saudi Arabia has previously expressed interest in acquiring a 15% stake in the project.
Malik said Pakistan valued its longstanding strategic relationship with Saudi Arabia and had conveyed its solidarity with the Saudi leadership and people during a recent visit to Riyadh.
Both sides said their defence and strategic partnership provided a foundation for broader economic cooperation and regional stability.
The Saudi ambassador reiterated Riyadh's commitment to its relationship with Islamabad and said the two countries stood together in all circumstances, according to the statement.
He also announced that the Saudi embassy in Islamabad had introduced same-day processing of visa applications for Pakistani citizens to facilitate travel and promote business, cultural and people-to-people exchanges.
Malik invited Saudi Vice Minister of Mining Khalid Al-Mudaifer to attend the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum, scheduled to take place in Islamabad on November 12-13.

Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.

There were still "powerful spoilers and detractors," who believed conflict serves them, he added without naming them.
Speaking in Rawalpindi, Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed or whether the US had backed the trip.
"Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome," he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.
Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries' political leadership.
He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy sites of Mecca and Medina. "We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an intra-Yemen conflict," he added.
"Our counter-terrorism operations are based on what we call IBOs, intelligence-based operations... The tempo of the freedom of action of (those) IBOs will further increase," he said.

items.content:
The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) on Friday intensified its efforts to secure opposition participation in the proposed parliamentary committee on electoral reforms as a party delegation met Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas to urge him to join the initiative.
The outreach came as the National Assembly approved the formation of a 30-member parliamentary committee to oversee electoral reforms.
Senator Sherry Rehman said Abbas had sought time to consult before conveying his response, adding that the party was hopeful of a positive outcome.
The delegation comprised PPP Secretary General Nayyar Bokhari, Senator Waqar Mehdi, Nadeem Afzal Chan and Rehman.
"Every political party should ensure its participation in the committee. We all know that the PTI has boycotted parliamentary committees. So we asked them to join this committee, play an active role in it, express their reservations and suggest reforms," Rehman said in a video statement.
She said parliamentary committees were the "heart of parliamentary work", adding that the PTI should also participate in other parliamentary committees to "strengthen Parliament's role".
Rehman added that Abbas had warmly received the PPP delegation, thanked party Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari for the initiative and said he would respond after consultation.
"He told us that he will respond [to the proposal] after consultation. We are hopeful that their response will be positive," Rehman said.
30-member parliamentary panel approved
Meanwhile, the National Assembly approved the formation of a 30-member parliamentary committee to oversee electoral reforms. The proposed body will comprise 20 members from the lower house and 10 from the Senate.
Speaking to the media, Federal Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said the NA speaker would soon issue a formal notification constituting the committee, while the process of finalising the names of its members was still under way.
He added that the PTI had not opposed the motion when it was presented in the National Assembly.
Seats on the proposed committee will be allocated to parliamentary parties in proportion to their numerical strength in the respective houses, he said.
Chaudhry said the committee was being formed to promote parliamentary consultation and consensus on improving the electoral system, ensuring transparency and introducing reforms.
He said the government would seek to give due consideration to constructive, positive and practical proposals from all parliamentary parties, including those in the opposition, as part of the electoral reform process.
He said the objective was to develop an electoral system that further strengthened transparency, public confidence and democratic values.
The minister stressed that electoral reforms were not the concern of any single political party but a shared national responsibility aimed at strengthening the democratic system.
He said all political parties should play an effective role in the process through mutual consultation, keeping the national interest in mind.

items.author: Kamran Yousaf
items.content:
Singapore's Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan on Friday called for translating its strong political relationship with Pakistan into a much broader economic partnership, acknowledging that trade and investment between the two countries remained well below their potential despite six decades of diplomatic ties.
Balakrishnan pushed for greater economic ties during his visit to Islamabad where he held talks with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and later met Chief of Defence Forces and Army Chief Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir.
The visit, the first by a Singaporean foreign minister since 2005, coincided with the 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries and came months before Singapore assumes the chairmanship of ASEAN in 2027.
Speaking at a joint news conference with Dar after their talks, Balakrishnan was candid about the gap between the two countries' close diplomatic relationship and their limited economic engagement.
"To be very candid, at a diplomatic level, we've got excellent ties," the Singaporean foreign minister said. "In fact, they are so good that it makes it even more obvious that our trade relations - looking at the numbers and the data - ought to be much higher."
He described greater trade and investment flows as the "first order of business", calling for stronger links between businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises, in the two countries.
Dar said the two sides had agreed to encourage business delegations and closer interaction between their chambers of commerce. Pakistan has also reopened its Trade and Investment Office at its High Commission in Singapore to facilitate greater business-to-business engagement.
The two foreign ministers also discussed the possible resumption of direct air links between Pakistan and Singapore to facilitate business travel and people-to-people contacts.
Prime Minister Shehbaz, meanwhile, accepted in principle an invitation from Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong to visit Singapore, providing another potential opening for high-level engagement between the two countries.
During his meeting with Balakrishnan, the prime minister identified the digital economy, fintech, infrastructure development, logistics, SMEs and the services sector among areas where the two countries could expand cooperation.
Balakrishnan said Shehbaz's acceptance of the invitation had injected "an additional sense of urgency" into efforts to identify practical areas of cooperation.
One such area is the carbon market, which the Singaporean minister said could provide a new avenue for attracting investment into Pakistani projects aimed at reducing emissions while supporting sustainable development.
The two countries also exchanged a memorandum of understanding between Pakistan's National Disaster Management Authority and the Singapore Civil Defence Force.
The agreement envisages cooperation in disaster preparedness and response, including early-warning systems, search and rescue capabilities, sharing of best practices and possible joint training and exercises.
Balakrishnan said Singapore could learn from Pakistan's experience in dealing with large-scale natural disasters, particularly floods and extreme weather events.
Education, artificial intelligence and skills development also featured prominently in the discussions. The two sides are exploring stronger links between Nanyang Technological University and the National University of Singapore and Pakistan's National University of Sciences and Technology.
The Singaporean foreign minister also visited the National Center of Artificial Intelligence at NUST during his one-day visit.
Beyond bilateral relations, the two sides discussed the rapidly changing regional security environment, including the crisis in the Gulf and its implications for maritime trade and energy supplies.
In a significant endorsement of Islamabad's recent diplomatic efforts, Balakrishnan praised what he described as Pakistan's "unique, but very constructive and valuable role" in dealing with the Gulf crisis.
He noted that much of the energy passing through the Gulf was destined for South Asia, Southeast Asia and Northeast Asia, making stability in the region important well beyond the Middle East.
"We commend you for, and we wish you every success because if you succeed, it's good for all of us," he told Dar.
Dar said Pakistan remained engaged with key regional and international partners and believed dialogue and diplomacy were the only viable means of addressing outstanding disputes.
He also raised the situations in Palestine and Kashmir, reiterating Pakistan's support for an independent Palestinian state based on the pre-1967 borders with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital and calling for a settlement of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute in accordance with UN Security Council resolutions.
Maritime security was another area where Islamabad and Singapore appeared to find common ground. Balakrishnan stressed the importance of international law and the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, given Singapore's dependence on maritime trade.
The two ministers also discussed closer engagement between Pakistan and ASEAN. Pakistan is one of ASEAN's earliest sectoral dialogue partners, while Singapore is due to take over the grouping's chairmanship next year.
Later, Balakrishnan met Field Marshal Asim Munir at the General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, where discussions focused on evolving regional and global security dynamics, regional peace and stability and avenues for strengthening bilateral cooperation.
According to an official statement, Field Marshal Munir reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to stronger ties with Singapore and stressed greater institutional linkages and constructive engagement.
The Singaporean foreign minister appreciated the professionalism of Pakistan's armed forces and acknowledged Pakistan's contribution to regional peace and stability.
Balakrishnan's visit marked an effort by both sides to give fresh momentum to a relationship that has remained politically cordial but economically modest despite six decades of diplomatic ties.
As the Singaporean foreign minister put it at the end of his visit, "60 years is an important milestone, but what matters more is what we do in the next 60 years."

items.content:
Amid an ongoing challenge regarding the non-implementation of superior courts' orders, the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) has reminded the executive that compliance with a judicial decision is a constitutional requirement, not a matter of courtesy.
"To disregard or to delay in implementation of [a court] verdict amounts to challenging the very framework of the legal system," said 10-page judgement authored by Justice Ali Baqar Najafi.
Justice Najafi was part of a three-member bench led by Chief Justice Amin-Ud-Din Khan which heard a case regarding the implementation of a Supreme Court judgement in a sacked employees' case.
The order stated that non-compliance not only disturbs the delicate equilibrium between the court's prestige and the enforcement of the rights but also sets a dangerous precedent that could lead to an executive overreach.
The court said implementing judicial orders is crucial for maintaining public confidence in the judicial system. If their decisions can be easily ignored or set aside by the individuals or entities, public trust in the efficacy of the judiciary and the entire government is seriously undermined.
"Consequently, the erosion of trust in the judicial system may undermine the democratic system," the order added.
The FCC noted that in a constitutional democracy, the rule of law is not just a principle but the foundation upon which the legitimacy and good governance of any system of government rests.
"The Supreme Court of Pakistan and, after the 27th amendment, this [FCC] being the apex court of the country is entrusted with performing the responsibility of interpreting the law, ensuring justice and upholding the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan."
It said the orders of the Supreme Court, as the then apex court, are not merely recommendations or advisories but a legal mandate that must be followed. Such decisions are the culmination of vigorous legal scrutiny and deliberation intended to reflect the values and laws of the land.
In December 2021, the Supreme Court while exercising suo motu jurisdiction restored thousands of government workers, sacked through its earlier August 17 judgement, which struck down the Sacked Employees (Reinstatement) Ordinance Act 2010.
The FCC asked whether the December 17, 2021 order was implemented in letter and spirit. It also questioned whether the non-implementation of the order amounted to the contempt of court.
The court disposing of the listed cases directed the government authorities to comply with the detailed judgement in the sacked employees' case in letter and spirit and consider the petitioners as unconditionally and regularly appointed beneficiary employees.
The court held that the conditions so imposed by the SC on the beneficiary employees were waived/diluted by the respondent-department due to the passage of time and their lethargy, not due to any fault of the petitioner employees.
"Such conduct cannot be awarded with any sentence of appreciation by this court. In this context the inaction on the pact of the employers is marked with caution, persuading us to show our concern to a sorry state of affair.
"However, at this stage we would exercise a restraint rather than acting pro-actively keeping in view the overall circumstances," stated the order.
Some legal experts believe that after 27th Constitutional Amendment, the biggest challenge for the superior courts is to establish their judicial authority. It is an open secret that the executive has a dominant role now in the appointment of judges.
In May last year, the SC ordered the federal government to carry out legislation for giving right of appeal to the civilians who convicted by the military courts in May 9, 2023 cases. However, the order is yet to implement so far.
Interestingly, both the SC and the FCC are silent on the non-implementation of the judicial order in the military courts case. On the other hand, dozens of PTI activists, convicted by military courts are behind the bar and waiting for a legislation so they can appeal against their convictions.

The warning added to concerns over slowing PC demand and the mounting costs of expanding artificial intelligence infrastructure, triggering a broader selloff across semiconductor stocks, Reuters reported.Intel stock was trading at $64.54, down 29.9%, after having fallen to a low of $64.11 earlier in the day.The weakness extended beyond Intel, with shares of Advanced Micro Devices, Arm Holdings, Qualcomm, Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron falling between 2% and 9% in premarket trading. The selloff also hit companies supplying equipment and infrastructure to the semiconductor industry, reflecting growing investor caution over the AI investment cycle.For live updates on US Markets, click here"The market is in a sell first, ask questions later mood right now, and Intel's warning has given investors an easy excuse to take some money off the table across chip stocks," said Matt Britzman, senior equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, according to Reuters.Intel turnaround faces fresh hurdlesIntel's outlook has raised fresh questions about CEO Lip Bu Tan's efforts to revive the chipmaker, which continues to struggle with a prolonged downturn in the personal computer market while spending heavily on manufacturing expansion and AI related opportunities.The company forecast fourth quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below analysts' average estimate of $17.07 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. Finance chief David Zinsner also said Intel does not expect to generate positive cash flow this year, Reuters reported.Read more: Nasdaq sinks 2.2% as Amazon, Intel fuel fresh fears over AI spendingIntel was on track to lose more than $123 billion in market value.Memory costs add to PC market pressureRising memory prices are creating another challenge for the chipmaker. Suppliers are shifting production capacity towards high bandwidth memory chips used in AI systems, pushing up PC costs and putting further pressure on consumer demand.PC chips contributed roughly half of Intel's third quarter revenue. The company expects sales from the segment to decline more than 20% sequentially in the current quarter, following a 5% drop in the September quarter, Reuters reported."It will be important to see if Intel can expand the highly profitable Xeon product supply to help offset this developing weakness in PC," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management.He added, "Bottom line, weaker sales volumes, higher manufacturing costs, and an out of cycle product mix is a recipe for the stock to decline over the near term as future earnings are under a lot of pressure." items.content:
The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) has released draft Open Banking Regulations for public consultation and is seeking feedback from stakeholders on the proposed framework.
The draft regulations aim to foster innovation, enhance competition, and expand access to efficient, customer-centric digital financial services in Pakistan.
They are designed to give customers greater control over their financial data by enabling secure, consent-based data sharing and the initiation of business payments through authorized Third-Party Providers (TPPs).
What the Regulations Aim to Do
According to SBP, the regulations are expected to facilitate the digitization of business-to-business (B2B) and consumer-to-business (C2B) payments.
They will also enable innovative uses of consent-based financial data sharing, including robust credit assessments, improved access to financing for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and the development of tailored financial products and services.
Built on Sandbox Results
The central bank said the draft is aligned with international best practices and informed by the outcomes of the recently concluded first cohort of its Regulatory Sandbox on Open Banking.
The draft regulations provide safeguards for data protection, privacy, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, and consumer protection. They also support the SBP’s strategic objective of advancing digital financial services through a more connected, inclusive, and efficient financial ecosystem.
Open banking has already started taking shape in the country, with BankIslami’s aik launching a Shariah-compliant open banking platform earlier this year.
How to Submit Feedback
As part of the consultation process, the SBP has invited feedback from all stakeholders, including financial institutions, fintechs, technology providers, consumer groups, academia, and the general public, to help refine the proposed framework.
The draft regulations are available on the SBP’s website.
Comments can be submitted by November 30, 2026, via email with the subject line “Feedback on Draft Open Banking Regulations,” or by post to the Payment Systems Policy & Oversight Department, 4th Floor, SBP Building, I.I. Chundrigar Road, Karachi.

items.author: Chris Donkin
items.content:
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) opened a consultation into a proposed framework on the responsible use of AI in the provision of telecoms services, including within network infrastructure.
Interested parties have until 27 November to provide feedback on the proposal, which places a number of expectations on operators including conducting risk assessments of any AI technology used and reporting critical incidents within a set timeframe.
The regulator noted the move was with a view to ensuring “consistent and responsible implementation” of national AI governance guidelines issued in February.
TRAI explained “while the integration of AI into telecommunications is likely to significantly enhance efficiency, it may also introduce new risks if due diligence is not exercised before deployment of AI systems or if due supervision is not exercised over autonomous learning and systemic interactions.”
Risks flagged by the regulator include inadvertent biases, unintended model behaviour and “adversarial attacks” it asserted could impact the resilience of infrastructure.
TRAI proposes operators and registered network providers define internal policies on use of the technology and appoint a committee led by a senior executive to check they are being implemented.
It wants each company to create an internal document covering areas including risk assessments; defining and registering incidents; ensuring human oversight; data governance; and a consumer protection and grievance redressal mechanism.
TRAI’s guidelines are intended for any company with a telecoms licence or an entity authorised to operate and maintain networks under the Telecommunications Act 2023.
The companies will be deemed “accountable for the outcome of all AI systems used by it, irrespective of whether the AI systems are developed internally, procured/outsourced from third party or a combination thereof”.
TRAI will also require AI-related incidents deemed of critical severity to be reported to it in a set form and timeframe.

items.content:
Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a theft that analysts blamed on North Korea and said could be the largest financial heist of all time.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would use company funds to cover the losses. Stablecoin issuers including El Salvador-based Tether and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial froze about half of the stolen assets.
The exchange said customer funds were safe and it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It said earlier on Friday it expected to resume withdrawal services in the next 48 hours. It did not mention the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, but Binance co-CEO Yi He said in a post on X that $3 billion represented only about 2% of the company's total user assets and public reserves.
Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The company has a $1 billion bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1 billion.
Binance other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post on X that the breach as a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate."
The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said.
"Rest assured that we are working non-stop to resolve this, to make
the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged fellow G20 foreign ministers on Friday to work together for greater geopolitical stability and economic prosperity, warning that a series of crises posed serious threats to the global economic order.
But Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's participation in the two-day gathering in Atlanta has roiled many G20 ministers, aggravating deep rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle Eastthat experts and diplomats say could thwart real progress at the meeting.
Canada's foreign minister, Anita Anand, who has been critical of Lavrov's participation, missed the opening plenary session. Her spokeswoman said she was arriving late from a Canada-EU summit in Montreal.
South Africa's minister was also absent, not invited by the US, which holds this year's rotating presidency.
A traditional G20 family photo was left off Rubio's official schedule after some European officials said they would not be photographed with Lavrov. A third of the participants objected, including Australia and Canada, a Western diplomat said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters that he expected the family photo to be scrapped entirely, adding, "In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr. Lavrov together because, as I said yesterday, there is no normalcy with Russia."
The US has sought to focus its allies on trade imbalances while building a coalition to counter China's control of critical minerals, but the wars and their economic impact remain the top concern for many G20 members.
In his opening remarks, Rubio said the world faced various crises that threatened global energy and food supply, trade, and the freedom of navigation.
"We are tasked, on behalf of the nations that we serve, to work together with one another to coordinate responses to emerging crises and to protect our shared interests," he said. "We can help set the context for expanded geopolitical stability and the broader economic prosperity agenda that our leaders will tackle."
With G20 members Russia, China and middle powers such as Brazil and India trying to navigate US-China strategic competition, you have "much more of a split than we've ever had," said Heidi Crebo-Rediker, who was chief economist at the State Department during the Obama administration.
Over the past decade or so, G7 countries would at least "have agreed a coordinated platform before they came to the G20, but now we don't even really have that," she added.

items.author: Business Desk
items.content:
A delegation of around 30 Pakistani technology leaders, founders, and innovators has taken part in Oslo Innovation Week 2026 in Norway, as the Pakistan Software Houses Association (P@SHA) looks to open new routes for the country’s IT industry into the Nordic market.
The delegates held several high-level business meetings during the visit and are now following up on partnership leads that came out of them.
The delegation was led by Kheezran Khan, Director of Marketing and Outreach at P@SHA. It met investors, startups, enterprise leaders, and policymakers from Norway’s innovation ecosystem to explore business-to-business partnerships, joint ventures, and cross-border collaboration.
Meetings at the Norwegian Parliament
The four-day event featured more than 100 specialized sessions. P@SHA delegates met counterparts in fast-growing sectors such as artificial intelligence, deep tech, clean tech, health tech, and the blue economy.
One of the main events for the delegation was a bilateral business networking session at the Storting, Norway’s Parliament. There, Pakistani tech leaders met Norwegian business executives and policymakers to discuss long-term digital trade between the two countries.
Delegates presented Pakistan’s capabilities in AI, software engineering, enterprise automation, and sustainable technology, and linked them to the Nordic region’s digital needs.
They also discussed venture partnerships, joint research and development, and talent models that would let European scale-ups grow with Pakistani engineering teams.
Part of P@SHA’s Strategy 2031
P@SHA Chairman Dr. Shoab Ahmed Khan said the visit was a deliberate step under the association’s Strategy 2031. The strategy aims to triple the IT sector’s export contribution to $15 billion by FY2031.
He said this goal depends on reaching new markets with a strategy suited to each region. He noted that Nordic countries lead the world in digital transformation, sustainability, and deep technology, and value quality, trust, and long-term partnerships.
“By connecting our software houses directly with Norwegian enterprises and investors, we are moving beyond hourly outsourcing toward high-value partnerships in AI, fintech and green technology,” Dr. Khan said. He added that the response the delegates received in Oslo reflects the strength of Pakistan’s engineering talent.
P@SHA said the mission supports two of its three strategic objectives, Export Expansion and Ecosystem and Talent.
It also builds on Global Market Access, one of the national foundations of the strategy, which calls for diversifying IT exports beyond traditional markets, building a strong Pakistani technology brand, and tailoring outreach to each region.
Pakistan and Norway have expanded cooperation in other areas this year as well. Earlier, Pakistan signed its first carbon trading agreement with Norway.

items.author: Shahbaz Rana
items.content:
The government has informed the Senate that the first phase of the Mainline-I (ML-I) project would cost $2.1 billion, as Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif constituted a new committee to finalise funding plans for the second phase of the much-delayed scheme.
The project faces delay even though 67% of the railways' track is unsafe, causing 300 accidents in just three years, the official response to the upper house of Parliament revealed on Friday.
The 1,872-kilometre ML-I from Karachi to Peshawar faces serious funding constraints, compelling the government to look for sources other than China, pledge land with local banks and seek loans from multilateral creditors.
The Minister for Railways Hanif Abbasi informed the Senate on Friday that the estimated cost of the 480-kilometre Karachi-Rohri section is $2.1 billion. He said the final project cost will be determined upon completion of the detailed engineering design, currently under review for finalisation.
The minister said construction is expected to commence during the current fiscal year, subject to completion of all requisite approvals, financing arrangements and procurement processes, with an estimated implementation period of two and a half years.
Pakistan could not secure $8 billion in funding from China out of a total cost of $10 billion, despite the project having been declared the only strategically important initiative under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).
In response to another question, the minister said accidents faced by Pakistan Railways had risen to 300 over a three-year period. As many as 299 accidents were reported from 2023 to 2025, including 241 incidents of derailment of goods and passenger trains. About 84 accidents were reported in 2023, a maximum of 118 in 2024 and 97 in 2025, including 37 head-on collisions.
The ministry of railways admitted that 67% of the track and 60% of the rolling stock has outlived its life, but said that "despite the fact that 67% of the railway track and 60% of the rolling stock is over-aged, there have not been significant investments in railway infrastructure, as required, for more than seven decades of our history".
Due to funding constraints, the government has not been able to fill vacant posts. There were 22,546 vacant positions in Pakistan Railways against pay scales 1 to 22, of which 12,165 are in Punjab, 7,245 in Sindh, 1,840 in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and 1,296 in Balochistan.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has also constituted a committee under the chairmanship of the governor of the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to formalise a financing plan for the second phase, the Multan-Rohri section. The committee met this week to find ways to securitise Pakistan Railways' land to finance the project's second phase.
"Trillions of rupees of land is lying vacant and the government is now looking for ways to give the land as collateral to domestic commercial banks for raising funds for the second phase," Federal Minister for Planning Ahsan Iqbal told The Express Tribune.
The Frontier Works Organisation (FWO), which was eager to construct the Multan-Rohri section, had estimated the second phase cost at Rs470 billion under a build-and-lease model. However, there were issues over who would repay the debt and the quantum of sovereign guarantees the ministry of finance may have to issue, and Pakistan Railways was reluctant to take full responsibility for debt repayments that FWO would raise from local banks.
Out of the Rs470 billion estimated cost, the debt requirement was around Rs365 billion and the remaining money had been sought from the government as a grant.
Sources said that over a 25-year lease, total payments had been estimated at Rs1.1 trillion, but the ministry of railways showed willingness to pay only Rs29 billion. It had projected operational profits of Rs485 billion over 25 years, and the ministry of finance was of the view that at least this amount should be pledged by the railways.
But the railways ministry was unwilling to provide the entire funds, and the ministry of finance was unwilling to provide guarantees against 25-year repayment obligations.
Under the FWO construction model, FWO will complete the rail link in three years by borrowing a maximum 80% of the cost from local banks and securing at least 20% financing from the federal government as viability gap funding. FWO will then hand over the track to Pakistan Railways on a 25-year lease and transfer the title after expiry of the lease period. The total project cost is Rs470 billion.

items.author: SHAHRAM HAQ
items.content:
As Punjab courts Chinese, Austrian and other foreign investors with long-term land leases and tax breaks, local businessmen are asking a simple question: will they get the same facilitation?
The question arose after Austrian ambassador called for faster action on economic ties. "The time has come to take more effective steps to increase bilateral economic cooperation," Ambassador Wolfgang Oliver Kutschera said in a meeting with Punjab Minister for Industries and Commerce Chaudhry Shafay Hussain on Friday.
He said the Punjab government had done remarkable work on promoting economic activity and Austria would examine the potential of setting up small hydroelectric power projects in the province.
"Austria has expertise in hydropower and we want to benefit from its technology," the provincial minister said, adding that small dams could be completed in two to three years. He told the ambassador that the infrastructure in Punjab's Special Economic Zones (SEZs) had been built according to international standards at a cost of billions of rupees and the new federal industrial policy allowed land to be taken on 30 to 50-year lease. He invited Austrian firms to consider agro-based value addition, seed development, dairy joint ventures and wastewater treatment.
Local industrialists welcome the foreign interest but say the offer should not stop at the border. "We are happy to see Austrian, Chinese and other investors coming, but a local manufacturer who has paid taxes for 20 years should not be forced to run between five offices while the foreign company gets the red carpet treatment," said a Lahore-based industrialist.
He added that facilitation should depend on the project and the jobs it created, not on the passport of the investor. Local and foreign investors should get the same incentives, the same speed in approvals and the same certainty that the policy will not change," he said.
Punjab is not the only province that prefers foreign investors, all other provinces, including Islamabad, also want foreign investment as it brings dollars, transfer of technology and much more. However, the hue and cry is not new. Earlier, in consultative sessions on investment policy at the Lahore Chamber of Commerce and Industry, the chamber office-bearers said foreign investment could not be encouraged without promoting local investment and the confidence of local investors must be restored first. The Board of Investment says the government treats both local and foreign investors equally.
The government has offered investors in Punjab SEZs a 10-year income tax holiday and one-time duty-free import of machinery, and has described these as open to both domestic and international investors. Businessmen say the real test is whether those benefits reach a small or medium-sized local firm as easily as a large foreign company.
The need for fresh capital is clear. UN Comtrade data shows Austria bought about $428.52 million of Pakistani goods in 2025, mostly clothing and textile, a growth of 20%, while Pakistan imported goods worth $115.73 million from Austria. Austrian investment in energy, dairy and agriculture is still small compared with textile trade.
Punjab is not the only province competing for capital. Sindh, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan also have SEZs, with many linked to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. Punjab's advantages include its large domestic market and industrial clusters in Faisalabad, Sialkot, Gujranwala and Gujrat. Businessmen say these advantages will matter more if investors see the same rules for everyone.
The meeting produced agreements in areas of cooperation, including hydroelectric power, technical education, tourism, garments, leather, footwear and livestock. However, it did not announce any specific projects, investment figures or timelines. Whether the talks lead to investment may depend on how Punjab treats investors who are already there.

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) collected Rs4.06 trillion in taxes during the first four months of the current fiscal year, facing a shortfall of Rs124 billion but clinging to hopes that it would receive a few more billions along with tax returns on Saturday.
The July-October collection results have been closely watched that came on the heels of two unusual developments – the government's proposal to establish a new tax agency, which it later shelved, and adverse action against office-bearers of the Inland Revenue Service Officers Association for threatening to observe a pen-down strike.
By the last official working day of the month, Friday, the FBR could bag Rs4.06 trillion for the July-October period of the current fiscal year despite setting a relatively low target, according to provisional figures compiled till late in the evening.
The collection was a mere Rs220 billion, or nearly 6%, higher than the last fiscal year but was far lower than the 17% pace needed to achieve the annual target.
For October, tax receipts remained at Rs974 billion, falling short of the target of Rs1.132 trillion by Rs158 billion. The increase in the monthly collection was only Rs23 billion, or 2.5%, compared to a year ago.
However, the tax authorities were hopeful that they could receive Rs20 billion to Rs25 billion along with income tax returns on October 31, the last day of the twice extended deadline for filing returns. The taxes paid along with returns were not portraying a healthy trend, although the number of returns was higher.
As of October 28, compared to the Rs88.5 billion income tax paid along with returns last year, the tax department received Rs85.2 billion this year. Authorities were hopeful that the figure would cross Rs100 billion by late Saturday evening. This will lower the tax shortfall but will not eliminate it.
A few days ago, the government had discussed the idea of either establishing a new tax agency or outsourcing the functions of the FBR. After coming to know about the government's plans, the IRS Officers Association threatened to stage a pen-down strike. The association withdrew from its threat following assurance from the FBR member operations that no adverse action would be taken against them.
However, the FBR suspended two officers and posted another seven in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan on suspicion that they were behind the pen-down strike move. The association president escaped suspension or being deputed in a province.
Tax collection
The FBR got Rs4.06 trillion in taxes during July-October of the current fiscal year, missing the target by Rs124 billion. There was a slim growth of 6%, or Rs220 billion, over the same period of last fiscal year. The numbers will improve after more payments are received along with tax returns in the next 24 hours, in addition to import taxes.
For the current fiscal year, the government and the IMF have given a Rs15.263 trillion annual tax target to the FBR. This requires a 17.4% growth over last year's collection. Unlike in the past, the IMF has made it binding to meet tax goals and the approval of the sixth loan tranche would be contingent upon achieving the first-half target.
However, sources said that the FBR's internal assessment indicated that it would be able to hit Rs14.3 to Rs14.6 trillion by the end of the current fiscal year in June 2027, thus there would be a shortfall.
According to the provisional figures, the revenue board received Rs1.85 trillion in income tax, missing the four-month target by Rs165 billion. For the fourth consecutive month, sales tax collection remained higher than the target. The FBR got Rs1.515 trillion worth of sales tax, exceeding the target by Rs67 billion. Four-month sales tax receipts were higher by Rs155 billion, or 11.3%.
Federal excise duty collection stood at Rs277 billion, almost equal to the target as it grew only 6.5%. Customs duty payments reached Rs424 billion, which was Rs25 billion lower than the target and almost at last year's level with no growth.

items.author: Business Desk
items.content:
The National Grid Company of Pakistan Limited (NGC) is planning to raise up to Rs. 100 billion through Shariah-compliant Sukuk, with an initial issuance of up to Rs. 20 billion, the Finance Division was informed on Friday.
The proposed program will have a tenor of up to 10 years and will be issued in phases through public offerings listed on the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX), subject to regulatory approvals and market conditions.
The plan was discussed at the fourth meeting of the Capital Market Development Council (CMDC), chaired by Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb at the Finance Division.
The finance minister welcomed the proposed issuance, describing it as an opportunity to demonstrate the potential of listed corporate debt instruments and encourage other companies to raise long-term financing through the capital market.
Corporate Debt Issuance Reaches Rs. 291 Billion
The meeting was informed that corporate debt issuances reached Rs. 291 billion during January-September 2026, following Rs. 326 billion raised throughout 2025.
The amount raised in 2025 was 30 percent higher than in 2024, reflecting growing activity in Pakistan’s corporate debt market.
The market also recorded 12 new listed corporate debt issuances worth Rs. 45.4 billion between February 2025 and September 2026, including Sukuk and other debt instruments.
The council stressed the need to encourage more public offerings and expand access to capital market financing for businesses.
Government Pushes to Expand Debt Market
The Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) and PSX have established dedicated Corporate Debt Market Desks to guide companies interested in raising funds through debt instruments.
A one-window listing mechanism is also operational through SECP and PSX, with simplified procedures and information available online. Work is underway to bring the Central Depository Company (CDC) into the mechanism.
The council also reviewed reforms covering taxation, debt issuance, market infrastructure, investor protection and enforcement.
These measures aim to reduce transaction costs, improve liquidity, simplify listing procedures and encourage financing through instruments such as green and thematic Sukuk.
Daily Debt Trading Crosses Rs10 Billion
Trading activity in Pakistan’s debt market has also increased.
Average daily traded value rose from Rs. 3.93 billion in fiscal year 2025-26 to more than Rs. 10 billion in fiscal year 2026-27 as of October 15, 2026.
Thirteen banks have been onboarded and are actively participating in secondary-market trading arrangements.
The council discussed further measures to facilitate banks’ participation in government Sukuk trading through PSX and improve liquidity in the market.
Government Wants Pension Funds and Insurers to Invest More
SECP informed the council that it had consulted 17 pension fund managers and 44 insurance companies to identify barriers preventing greater investment in corporate debt instruments.
The discussions covered the availability of suitable investment products, secondary-market liquidity, issuer disclosures and the broader investment framework.
The finance minister also directed SECP to work with PSX and other relevant platforms to develop practical solutions for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) seeking capital market financing.
He called for stronger engagement with investment banks, financial advisers and business organisations to encourage more companies to raise long-term funds.
Aurangzeb also urged SECP and PSX to renew engagement with MSCI over Pakistan’s potential future reclassification to Emerging Markets status.
He said the next phase of reforms should translate into higher corporate debt issuance, stronger market liquidity and broader investor participation.

items.author: Business Desk
items.content:
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has put millions of dollars into research on solar geoengineering, a set of ideas for cooling the planet by blocking part of the sunlight that reaches Earth.
This comes over a month after Gates’ expressed interest in entering Pakistan’s agriculture for dedicated projects. Locals strongly rejected the billionaire’s announcement.
The most discussed method would release tiny reflective particles high in the atmosphere.
These particles would bounce some sunlight back into space, which could bring global temperatures down. The effect is similar to what happens after a large volcanic eruption.
How the Research Is Funded
Gates is one of the backers of Harvard University’s Solar Geoengineering Research Program, set up in 2017. Other funders include the Hewlett Foundation and the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Much of Gates’ funding in this area has not been publicly disclosed.
The program supported a small outdoor experiment called SCoPEx, which planned to release a small amount of particles from a high-altitude balloon to study how they behave.
Harvard ended the experiment in March 2024 after delays and public criticism. Research under the wider program continues.
Gates Says Research, Not Deployment
Gates has drawn a line between studying the technology and using it. In an interview with Axios, he said he would support deploying it only if the world hit dangerous climate tipping points.
“No way am I pushing the world in that direction,” he said, adding that knowledge about the technology could be “quite valuable.”
He also named two concerns. Relying on it could slow efforts to cut fossil fuel use, and scientists still don’t fully understand how the particles could affect rainfall or cause droughts in some regions.
Why It Is Controversial
Scientists and researchers warn that trying to dim the sun could damage the ozone layer, increase air pollution, and shift weather patterns across borders. Only a few outdoor tests have been carried out so far.
Gates has also been active in Pakistan, where he has backed projects in agriculture and donated to flood relief. Pakistanis have strongly disapproved his involvement in the country so far.
The post Bill Gates Wants to Dim the Sun appeared first on ProPakistani.

items.author: Vinaykumar Rai
items.content:
Update | Oct 30, 19:55 IST
The Competition Commission of India (CCI) has cleared Prosus’ investment in Navi to acquire a minority interest in the IPO-bound fintech company.
“The Target is the holding company of the Navi Group, which offers financial services accessible through a single consumer-facing mobile app. The Target offers transparent, user-friendly financial products through its subsidiaries, all accessible via mobile devices,” the CCI said.
 
Original | Aug 19, 18:54 IST
Global VC firm Prosus has invested $100 Mn (over ₹955 Cr) in Sachin Bansal-led fintech startup Navi, marking the latter’s first institutional capital raise.
The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals, including clearance from the Competition Commission of India (CCI), Navi said in a statement.
The fintech startup did not disclose the valuation at which Prosus is making the investment, the stake the investor will acquire, or how it plans to deploy the fresh capital.
“My association with Naspers and the Prosus Group dates back more than a decade, making this partnership particularly meaningful. Their investment is a strong endorsement of the institution we’re building at Navi,” cofounder and executive chairman Bansal said.
In a statement, Navi said that it is entering its next phase of growth with strong operating momentum across its businesses.
Ashutosh Sharma, head of Prosus India investments and M&A, said the investor was backing Navi on account of its large user base, multiple business lines, and technology-first approach.
“We believe the team has executed extremely well in the last 12 months despite a tough macro environment, which makes the company well-positioned to capture significant opportunities in the sector in times to come,” Sharma added.
During FY26, Navi UPI claims to have strengthened its position as digital payments platforms, while Navi Finserv continued to scale its lending franchise responsibly with AUM crossing ₹13K Cr.
The company also said the Navi Group achieved consolidated profitability in the fourth quarter of FY26 but did not disclose the financial figures.
NBFC arm Navi Finserv’s standalone net profit increased 32% YoY to ₹292.2 Cr in FY26, while its operating revenue rose 8% to ₹2,461 Cr. However, its consolidated net profit declined 46% to ₹93.3 Cr during the year, even as operating revenue grew 17% to ₹2,691.5 Cr.
Navi’s IPO Plans
The investment comes at a time when Navi is reportedly looking to revive its public listing plans. Recent reports suggested that the fintech startup could refile its draft IPO papers with the SEBI by December this year.
Navi is said to be eyeing a fresh issue of around ₹3,000 Cr and has appointed JM Financial, Kotak Mahindra Capital, Goldman Sachs, and JPMorgan as advisers for the proposed offering.
This would mark Navi’s second attempt to go public. The startup filed its draft papers with SEBI in 2022 for a ₹3,350 Cr IPO but later shelved the plan amid adverse market conditions.
Founded by Bansal and Ankit Agarwal in 2018, Navi offers financial products across lending, insurance, mutual funds, and UPI payments. Bansal stepped down as the startup’s chief executive in February 2025 and took over as its executive chairman.
Navi said its UPI platform retained its position as India’s fourth-largest third-party application provider by transaction volume during FY26. Meanwhile, the assets under management of its lending arm, Navi Finserv, crossed ₹13,000 Cr.
The post [Update] CCI Clears Navi’s $100 Mn Investment From Prosus appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.author: editorial
items.content:
With the Middle East on tenterhooks anticipating a new round of US-Israeli strikes on Iran, President Trump has further compounded the equation through his ambiguous stance on a plausible diplomatic initiative in the region. A battered White House incumbent, apparently staring down a projected defeat in the midterm polls, once again raised the stakes by expressing hope that the war with Iran would end soon - though he did not say how. He did, however, voice optimism that the Islamic Republic would not cross the nuclear threshold, hinting at behind-the-scenes maneuvering as Doha diplomats returned to Tehran with a message from Washington.
The diplomatic push got a shot in the arm as Vice President JD Vance also sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei, in an earnest endeavour to revive stalled negotiations. Though Tehran is yet to respond officially, it issued a diplomatic rejoinder at the UNSC, where its representative, Gholamhossein Darzi, condemned the US and Israel for their military aggression. Darzi blamed the duo for an illegal naval blockade, terming it the root cause of maritime insecurity in the Persian Gulf.
This indicates that Iran is unwilling to climb down from its stated position. It wants the US to respect the salient features of the conditional ceasefire deal attained under the Islamabad MoU, and return to the table in all sincerity. Likewise, undoing sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets remain key leverage for normalising navigational routes across the Strait of Hormuz.
The question is, how can this stalemate be overcome so that the warring sides can begin to see light at the end of the tunnel? That is only possible if both the US and Iran stop playing to the gallery for domestic consumption and respect the hectic mediation efforts led by Pakistan, Türkiye, Egypt and Qatar. The least desired at this critical juncture is a misadventure from Israel, or the Houthis going over the brink. Iran's inability to tame the Yemeni-Shia militia and, likewise, Trump's appeasement of Netanyahu are dangerous signs of brinkmanship.

items.title: Innovation against the odds
items.summary:
Pakistan's commendable position in a recent ranking of innovation outputs is a quiet but telling illustration of the country's potential. Pakistan rose to 95th in the Global Innovation Index 2026, regaining "overperformer" status in the World Intellectual Property Rights Organisation's ranking of 139 economies. items.author: editorial
items.content:
Pakistan's commendable position in a recent ranking of innovation outputs is a quiet but telling illustration of the country's potential. Pakistan rose to 95th in the Global Innovation Index 2026, regaining "overperformer" status in the World Intellectual Property Rights Organisation's ranking of 139 economies. While the number may not seem high, it is a relative grade, illustrating how Pakistan generates far more innovation than its meagre inputs - we were 121st in innovation inputs, but 72nd in outputs.
That gap is a tribute to the talent, hustle and resourcefulness of Pakistani inventors and entrepreneurs. The strengths are also concrete and market-driven. Pakistan ranks 10th globally in mobile-app creation relative to GDP, 15th in ICT services exports and 19th in high-tech imports. Each of these numbers reflects a generation that has managed to do well despite creaky infrastructure, patchy policy and limited state support. At the same time, it also shows why local talent wants to leave - they are too good for what Pakistan has to offer them.
After all, the same Innovation Index also places Pakistan near the bottom on human capital, research and infrastructure. R&D spending is just 0.16% of GDP, patent filings lag badly, and startup funding - which was already miserly by international standards - has crashed. For the government, the "overperformer" label should be seen as an insult, not an achievement. Output strength cannot indefinitely compensate for input neglect. Pakistani innovators deserve more. The state must be willing to meet them halfway, either by directly funding more research or creating the conditions for investors to come in. Investment-related laws also need work to ensure that they are no longer avenues for shady lending, but do encourage honest, calculated risk-taking. Only then will Pakistan's innovators be able to achieve more, while also reflecting well on what their country did for them.

items.author: editorial
items.content:
The revival of the Pakistan-China Friendship Hospital in Islamabad under a public-private partnership is a welcome development, particularly at a time when affordable medical treatment remains beyond the reach of millions of Pakistanis. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's announcement that the government will bear the entire cost of treatment at the 182-bed facility, to be managed by the Indus Hospital and Health Network, offers a much-needed example of how public resources can be utilised for the welfare of ordinary citizens. Yet, while such partnerships deserve appreciation, they also expose the sorry state of Pakistan's healthcare system, which remains in complete disarray.
The reality is that healthcare in Pakistan has increasingly become a privilege rather than a fundamental right. Public hospitals are overwhelmed by patients, understaffed and frequently deprived of essential medicines and functioning equipment. Those who cannot secure timely treatment at government facilities are left at the mercy of private hospitals, where treatment can cost more than an ordinary household earns in several months. For countless families, a serious illness means exhausting their savings or selling whatever assets they possess. Many are compelled to delay treatment until their condition becomes critical, while others simply surrender to illnesses that could have been treated had they possessed the financial means.
The government's partnership with the Indus Hospital and Health Network demonstrates that quality treatment can be provided without charging patients. However, the provision of free healthcare cannot remain confined to a handful of institutions or depend indefinitely on charitable organisations and private management. It must become the guiding principle of national health policy. No individual should be denied treatment because of an inability to pay, nor should a family's financial circumstances determine whether a patient lives or dies.

items.author: Farrukh Khan Pitafi
items.content:
Two revelations have jolted the Indian establishment. Former Supreme Court Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul alleges in his memoir that former Chief Justice DY Chandrachud was too deferential to the Modi government, even withdrawing cases that questioned the executive's delay in judicial appointments. That is a polite way to say he was compromised and in turn compromised the judiciary. An Indian Express report exposed how two Election Commissioners (a majority) were bypassed during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. Why the surprise? For twelve years the Modi-Shah-Doval nexus has left breadcrumbs mapping a creeping, hostile takeover of the republic.
The blueprint was written in the blood and silence of the Judge BH Loya case. In 2014 the judge hearing the Sohrabuddin fake encounter case, which implicated Amit Shah, died in suspicious circumstances. Whistleblowers revealed heavy pressure and bribery attempts from within the higher judiciary. The institutional burial of the case warned every courtroom in the country. It proved the state machinery would now whitewash street thugs, while institutional bigwigs eagerly sold their constitutional mandates for a few creature comforts. Whether a post-retirement Rajya Sabha seat for a compliant Chief Justice (Ranjan Gogoi), or a lucrative corner plot for a former Army Chief (VK Singh) who would practically drive his institution into the ruling party's lap to become a junior minister, the price of subverting a democracy was cheap. These fragile egos sold themselves for pennies on the pound.
Once the judiciary was tamed, the rot spread through the hard power structures. As early as 2015, prosecutor Rohini Salian told NDTV's Sreenivasan Jain of instructions from the National Investigation Agency leadership to go soft on right-wing terrorists in the Malegaon case. When I reminded you of this last year, the website of the channel, since taken over by Adani, which had evaded the ban on Indian news in Pakistan, was quickly banned. In 2016 the government bypassed the hallowed seniority principle to appoint General Bipin Rawat as Army Chief. The man would soon find his twin in Pakistan. Ideological alignment, sycophancy and expedience would henceforth trump institutional norms. The compromise is so absolute that the Army now mines ancient Indian texts for strategy under Project Udbhav, and the Integrated Defence Staff hails a Gita lecture to mid-level officers as inspiring.
The Central Bureau of Investigation was decapitated in a midnight executive coup removing Director Alok Verma and Special Director Rakesh Asthana to shield defence contracts like the Rafale purchase from scrutiny. In 2018 four Supreme Court judges, Justices J Chelameswar, Ranjan Gogoi, Madan B Lokur and Kurian Joseph, held an unprecedented mutiny, warning that democracy was at stake due to selective case assignments. The Reserve Bank of India and the Election Commission were overruled on the opaque Electoral Bonds scheme. When Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa dissented against clean chits for the ruling duo, state financial agencies hunted his family.
Capturing reality means capturing data. In early 2019 two acting members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest as the government buried their verified report showing unemployment at a 45-year high. It was leaked to Business Standard. Border realities were similarly hidden until last week, when Indo-Tibetan Border Police Director General Shatrujeet Kapur confirmed ongoing military face-offs with Chinese troops in the territory India administers as Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as South Tibet (Zangnan), exposing the hollowness of the secure border story. After the 2019 Pulwama tragedy, former Governor Satya Pal Malik claimed the Prime Minister and the National Security Advisor told him to stay quiet about intelligence failures, proving that institutions were forced to guard political optics over soldiers' lives. That optic would lead to Modi's re-election and the abolition of Article 370.
The soft power pipeline was choked as ruthlessly. The first move tested the waters with blatant appointments, packing historical research councils with revisionists. The state then installed RSS enforcers as university vice-chancellors to break student resistance. It weaponised anti-terror laws in the Bhima Koregaon case, inventing the phantom threat of the urban Naxal to criminalise scholars like Anand Teltumbde, Sudha Bharadwaj, Shoma Sen and Hany Babu. Global academics like Romila Thapar met petty bureaucratic humiliation, forced to submit her curriculum vitae to a captured committee to prove her worth. Private sanctuaries fell when billionaires caved to government pressure, forcing critics like Pratap Bhanu Mehta out of Ashoka University. The goal was simple: to ensure the next generation lacked the historical vocabulary to question the Vishwa Guru project.
It is welcome that functionaries are finally speaking openly, even if only from the safety of retirement. It looks as though the deal Narendra Modi cut with the dark one for twenty-five years of unchecked power is drawing to a close, and his soul is ready to be collected. His recent manoeuvres fail to land with their old impact. The cracks are widening, and the leaks will only grow. Buckle up for far more shocking revelations.
This raises a terrifying question. When Modi's detractors finally replace him, how will they undo this staggering damage? The blueprint began years ago with Ajit Doval's pitch at Sastra University, where he argued for a ten-year unbroken term to rewire the Indian state. To decontaminate the system, the opposition must pitch for no less. Five years is not enough to dig out the ideological rot embedded by the lateral entry scheme and the unaccountable super-bureaucracy of the National Security Council Secretariat. By parachuting ideologically aligned individuals into Joint Secretary roles, the RSS has bypassed the rigorous UPSC examination, altering the genetic makeup of the civil service so the machinery stays loyal to the saffron agenda long after governments change.
The incoming leadership must also rethink its tools of restoration. The Congress party traditionally prefers polite diplomats from the Indian Foreign Service for the NSA post. But the intelligence community, the true muscle of the deep state, is largely made up of Indian Police Service officers. A diplomat cannot dismantle a hardened police state. You need a policeman who knows where the bodies are buried and how the truncheon is wielded: an officer unaffected by Ajit Doval's sprawling influence, with the moral clarity, motive and institutional memory to serve as the ultimate wrecking ball.

items.summary:
Nations in transition, such as Bangladesh, face a difficult choice. items.author: Imtiaz Gul
items.content:
Nations in transition, such as Bangladesh, face a difficult choice. Burdened by a bitter past and a turbulent present, they must decide whether to hold everyone accountable while protecting human rights or move on in the interest of political and economic stability. The former risks drawing the country into a cycle of political revenge. The latter runs counter to the aspirations of those who struggled against an oppressive regime. This is a major test for the new government: can Bangladesh move beyond personalised autocracy towards democratic governance that people consider legitimate, in the context of the "student revolution" of summer 2024?
The leaders of this revolution, along with many others across the political and social spectrum, refuse to forget the brutal victimisation and persecution of opposition politicians, media professionals, intellectuals and human rights defenders during Hasina's rule, often with the active support of her loyalists at various levels.
This also raises the question of whether Prime Minister Tarique Rehman and his supporters can reduce the civil-military bureaucracy's hold over the political economy as they pursue their reform agenda. Addressing the deeply rooted interests and legacy of the Awami League is a major challenge in an environment marked by political divisions and polarisation.
Tensions remain high in an environment that often turns hostile. This was reflected in the strong remarks made by Nahid Islam, convener of the National Citizen Party (NCP) and opposition Chief Whip, during a media interaction on October 28.
"If we let this government off the hook, we may have to face another fascism. We do not want to have to overthrow another fascist regime at the cost of 1,400 lives again," warned Nahid Islam. He levelled several allegations against the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), saying that "the judiciary remains under the control of those in power, the (criminal) justice system has not been reformed, violence is rampant and the BNP-backed cadres are killing even their own party members" to settle personal scores.
In a reminder of the situation surrounding Pakistan's ruling elites, Nahid Islam also described Bangladesh as a "mafia state".
"Terrorists are armed, ministers and state ministers are also carrying weapons and this is what is called a mafia state," he said, accusing the authorities of failing to arrest "godfathers of the (drug) trade, members of drug syndicates and political leaders linked to the business."
These allegations may sound like an exaggerated charge sheet from a party that claims to represent the youth. However, their central concerns are difficult to dismiss and are common in countries undergoing political transitions. Islam's remarks reflect growing doubts about whether Bangladesh's post-uprising transition is producing meaningful reforms in law enforcement, the judiciary and democratic governance. The central argument of NCP members is that replacing one government is not enough if political patronage, violence, impunity and institutional weaknesses persist.
These concerns were clearly visible in discussions with Bangladeshi veterans and youth representatives during and on the sidelines of the recent annual Bay of Bengal conference. While geopolitics, interstate conflicts, the Iran-US-Israel war and the weakening of the UN-based global order dominated the proceedings, Bangladesh's domestic political and social situation and its foreign relations also featured prominently in various sessions.
One of the major challenges facing Prime Minister Rehman is navigating the complex relationship between Pakistan and India. While many Bangladeshis, both inside and outside the government, want a fresh chapter in relations with Pakistan, the legacy of Hasina's rule and the Awami League's traditionally pro-India position remain obstacles to these aspirations.
Bangladesh's foreign policy is gradually evolving, with a stated intention to engage with all regional countries. Dhaka is seeking broader engagement with China, Pakistan and the United States while maintaining a workable relationship with India. Its dependence on external trade and water supplies also leaves it vulnerable to sudden changes in US trade and aid policies.
Since the summer of 2024, Pakistan has reached out to Bangladesh to regain some of the diplomatic ground it had lost to India. Several diplomatic, defence and education-related initiatives have marked this effort, and a series of visits at different levels appears to have been well received. However, changing the deeply rooted pro-India mindset within the civil-military bureaucracy and governance structures will not be easy. The current government appears aware of these constraints and is therefore proceeding cautiously in its dealings with Pakistan. India, which surrounds Bangladesh on much of its land border and lies upstream of the country's major rivers, remains a major concern.
That is why the present government is keen to focus on fixing its internal socio-economic problems and moderating the political toxicity (calls for accountability of the Hasina era brutalities) while trying to integrate partnerships with China, India and Pakistan without antagonising any regional power.

items.summary:

items.author: Mansoor Raza
items.content:
For over a decade I have taught in three classrooms that never meet. At NED University, my students are mostly middle class. At SZABIST, they come from the upper-middle and upper strata. On weekends, at the Amna Shamima Foundation in Ghulam Zakariya Goth, I teach survey skills free of charge, to girls from low-income homes. Different fees, different futures, one shrug. Interest is abandoned the moment a subject turns difficult. Assignments arrive late, and when they arrive on time, they arrive hollow. At University after four years, the degree is treated as a receipt: proof that the fee was paid, not that anything changed. Call it laziness and you miss the point. The student who ignores an assignment will happily spend nine hours teaching himself video editing on YouTube. His disinterest is selective, which makes it a judgment, not a defect. Young people have run the numbers, and the classroom lost.
The degree is the entry ticket, but the key is connections, not merit. Studying hard begins to look like paying full fare on a train where everyone else rides free. He has not stopped being intelligent; he has become strategically cynical; the cynics are half right. Pakistan's labour market does reward networks. But a graduate with a connection and no skill is a guest, not a colleague, and the door that opened for him closes as quickly. The cynic is right about the entrance and wrong about the staying. Privilege fails in its own way. In elite institutions, a family business or an inherited network makes effort feel optional, and education becomes a finishing school, a social stage rather than an intellectual one. Where failure costs nothing, commitment has no logic.
In the Goth, the logic inverts. These girls have everything to gain, and the course is free, yet attendance wavers. Look closer and the cause is not attitude but architecture. A family relocates for work, and a girl vanishes from the register. A marriage is arranged, and her stitching machine falls silent. A brother's schedule, a neighbour's gossip, harassment on the road to class: something decides whether she may leave the house, and it is rarely her. Her unfinished assignment is not defiance. It is the visible edge of a life in which she does not own her calendar. Deadlines presume autonomy, and autonomy is exactly what she lacks. One group is excused from effort by privilege, the other excluded from continuity by precarity, and both land in the same statistic: the dropout, the late submission, the half-finished skill.
Inflated grades turned marks into currency rather than evidence. Teachers who overlook plagiarism for the sake of peace taught that rules bend. A generation raised on cheating scandals, leaked papers and self-financed schemes learned early that the system is negotiable. We now demand integrity from students whose institutions never modelled it. Add an economy of thirty-second rewards, and a semester-long project paying off years later seems absurd.
The result is credential inflation without competence. Degrees multiply while capability thins. Employers, distrusting degrees, demand references, which feeds the very connection economy students already believe in. Meanwhile, girls who leave skill programmes early drift back into dependency, and a community loses its most plausible exit from poverty, one stitched seam at a time.
Make merit visible through public portfolios, live projects and employer-evaluated work, so that skill can be seen to beat introduction. Shorten the distance between effort and reward with modular certificates and early wins. Bring flexibility to the Goth: home-based tasks, mobile learning and conversations with fathers and brothers, so that permission becomes partnership. And let teachers become what the system is not: consistent, fair and incorruptible in small things.
If we want students to treat education as transformation, we must first make transformation worth more than the receipt. Until then, our classrooms will keep filling with bodies and emptying of learning.
