items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
Trucking platform BlackBuck reported a 41.8% jump in consolidated net profit to ₹41.4 Cr in the September quarter of FY27 from ₹29.2 Cr in the year-ago period.
Operating revenue climbed 55.7% to ₹235.3 Cr from ₹151.1 Cr.
Sequentially, net profit declined 1.8% from ₹42.2 Cr, while operating revenue increased 15.3% from ₹204.2 Cr.
BlackBuck’s profit growth was supported by a sharp reduction in its tax expense to ₹1.4 Cr from ₹9.7 Cr a year earlier. Profit before tax increased 10% YoY to ₹42.8 Cr from ₹38.9 Cr.
The company recognised a deferred tax credit of ₹1.2 Cr during the quarter as against a deferred tax expense of ₹5.9 Cr in Q2 FY26. Its current tax expense also declined to ₹2.6 Cr from ₹3.9 Cr.
Meanwhile, EBITDA rose 39% YoY to ₹50.6 Cr from ₹36.5 Cr. Adjusted EBITDA, which also excludes employee share-based payment expenses, increased 29% to ₹55 Cr from ₹42.7 Cr.
Other income stood at ₹17.8 Cr, compared with ₹16.1 Cr a year earlier. Including this, total income increased to ₹253.2 Cr from ₹167.2 Cr.
Total expenses rose 64% YoY to ₹210.3 Cr from ₹128.3 Cr, outpacing operating revenue growth.
Growth Businesses Gain Ground
BlackBuck’s core payments and telematics businesses reported a 31% YoY increase in revenue to ₹161.4 Cr from ₹123.4 Cr. Revenue from these businesses grew 11% sequentially.
Its offerings include toll payments through FASTag, fuel payments, vehicle tracking, AIS-GPS devices, and fuel sensors.
The tolling business recorded a 17% YoY increase in gross transaction value (GTV) to ₹7,070 Cr from ₹6,039 Cr. The number of tolling transactions rose 12% to 17.4 Cr.
BlackBuck also reported an increase in FASTag issuances and said its telematics business recorded new highs in device sales.
Meanwhile, revenue from its growth businesses, which include managed freight service Superloads, freight marketplace Loads Classifieds, and vehicle financing, surged 166% YoY to ₹73.9 Cr from ₹27.8 Cr. Revenue increased 25% sequentially.
The company said Superloads’ growth was supported by productivity gains in existing cities and expansion into new markets, while unit economics continued to strengthen.
Its vehicle finance business remained on track to achieve EBITDA break-even, supported by growth in AUM on a steady cost base, it added.
Transacting Customer Base Expands
BlackBuck’s average monthly transacting truck operators increased 13% YoY to 8,95,125 from 7,91,670.
Monthly transacting users using at least two services rose 19% to 4.76 Lakh from 3.99 Lakh. However, average daily time spent on the app by transacting customers declined 3% to 41.8 minutes from 43.2 minutes.
Founded in 2015 by Rajesh Kumar Naidu Yabaji, Chanakya Hridaya, and Ramasubramanian Balasubramaniam, BlackBuck provides digital services to truck operators, spanning payments, vehicle tracking, freight discovery, and vehicle financing. It also operates an online B2B marketplace for intercity full truckload (FTL) transportation.
Shares of BlackBuck ended today’s session 1.59% lower at ₹562.3 on the BSE.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Federal Minister for Information Technology and Telecommunication Shaza Fatima Khawaja has said that Pakistan’s Social Media Regulatory Authority will become operational soon, as the government works to strengthen online safety and protect children from growing cyber threats.
Speaking about cybersecurity challenges, the minister expressed concern over the increasing presence of young children on social media platforms and other digital environments.
She pointed out that children are now spending time in virtual spaces, including the metaverse, where parents may not always know who they are interacting with.
According to Shaza Fatima, children are increasingly exposed to cyberbullying and other online risks, making digital safety an important concern for families and authorities.
The minister stressed that cybersecurity is no longer limited to protecting computer systems or government networks. Instead, it has become an essential part of safeguarding people’s everyday lives.
She also highlighted the need to improve mechanisms for reporting cybersecurity incidents so that online threats can be addressed more effectively.
Government Working to Strengthen Online Safety and Cybersecurity Awareness
Shaza Fatima said the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) has been made operational under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), while the Social Media Regulatory Authority is also expected to become functional soon.
The minister emphasised that stronger regulatory mechanisms are needed to address emerging online threats, particularly those affecting children and young internet users.
She also highlighted Pakistan’s progress in cybersecurity over the past two years, claiming that sustained government efforts have helped the country secure a position among leading nations in cybersecurity.
Expressing confidence in Pakistan’s security institutions, she said there was no doubt about their capabilities. However, she acknowledged that more work is needed to improve cybersecurity awareness among the public.
According to the minister, awareness and effective incident-reporting systems are essential for protecting citizens against cyberbullying, online harassment and other digital threats.
Her remarks highlight the government’s increasing focus on online safety as social media platforms and emerging technologies become a larger part of everyday life.
While Shaza Fatima indicated that the Social Media Regulatory Authority would become operational soon, she did not announce a specific launch date.

Pakistan continues to face cyberattacks around the clock, with fake videos, fraudulent calls, and suspicious messages posing serious risks to citizens, Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) Chairman Major General (R) Hafeez Ur Rehman has warned.
Speaking at the closing ceremony of Cyber Security Awareness Week, the PTA chairman said Pakistan remains a major target for cyber threats, with thousands of fake videos circulating across digital platforms.
He highlighted that citizens frequently receive fraudulent calls and messages requesting one-time passwords (OTPs), making public awareness essential to preventing online scams.
The chairman urged people to avoid sharing suspicious or misleading messages without verification, warning that the spread of false information can create further security risks.
Telecom Sector Also Vulnerable to Cyberattacks
Major General (R) Hafeez Ur Rehman acknowledged that Pakistan’s telecom sector is not completely protected from cyberattacks, despite ongoing efforts to strengthen digital security.
He said institutions including NADRA, PEMRA, and PTA have taken measures to secure their systems against potential threats.
However, he stressed that stronger cybersecurity policies and greater public awareness are needed to address emerging risks.
The PTA chairman also referred to the role of the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) in addressing relevant concerns related to suspicious communications.
He emphasized that protecting Pakistan’s digital infrastructure requires continuous security improvements and responsible online behavior.
According to him, the ultimate objective is to safeguard citizens and secure Pakistan’s digital future.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Pine Labs’ net profit jumped over 6X year-on-year (YoY) to ₹38.6 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹6 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, net profit rose 97% from ₹19.6 Cr in Q1 FY27.
Operating revenue grew 24% YoY and 9% sequentially to ₹806.2 Cr during the quarter. Including other income of ₹25.6 Cr, total income stood at ₹831.7 Cr, up 24% from ₹672.9 Cr in Q2 FY26.
Total expenses rose 16% YoY to ₹770.4 Cr from ₹661.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Tax expenses stood at ₹22.8 Cr.
Pine Labs’ adjusted EBITDA rose 27% YoY to ₹215.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, with a margin of 19.2%. Its operating cash flow doubled to ₹350 Cr, while its contribution margin grew 18% YoY to ₹587 Cr. The company had a net cash balance of ₹2,345 Cr as of September 30, 2026.
“Pine Labs has been EBITDA-positive for a long time. We aim to balance investments in new products, ideas and regions while remaining strongly EBITDA-positive. We aim to strike a balance between EBITDA margins of over 20% and revenue growth of 21-23%,” said CEO Amrish Rau.
Pine Labs Sees Growth Across Payments, International Markets
Pine Labs’ two business verticals — digital infrastructure and transaction platform (DITP) & issuing and acquiring platform (AIP) — registered double digit revenue growths in the quarter. DITP’s revenue jumped 21% YoY to ₹440.1 Cr while AIP grew by 30% to ₹274.6 Cr.
During the quarter, the platform processed around ₹4.45 Lakh Cr ($46.5 Bn) in gross transaction value (GTV) across 229 Cr transactions. Meanwhile, its merchant base grew 13% YoY to 11.6 Lakh, while digital checkout points (DCPs), which include point-of-sale terminals and other merchant payment acceptance solutions, increased 17% to 2.23 Lakh.
More than 29% of Pine Labs’ DITP GTV was monetised through flow-based revenue, affordability and online payments, compared with 15% a year ago. Subscription revenue accounted for 27% of total revenue, while 30% of its DCPs generated flow and affordability GTV.
Pine Labs’ fintech infrastructure business recorded over 33% YoY growth in transactions, with its AI-based credit underwriting platform, SignalIQ, processing more than 1.25 Lakh loans a month.
International markets contributed 15% of Pine Labs’ revenue in Q2 FY27. The company operates in over 22 markets and offers credit processing services in more than 17. Revenue from Southeast Asia grew around 40% YoY, while its DCPs in the region nearly tripled to 1 Lakh. Its UAE business crossed 1 Lakh daily transactions, and the company is expanding in the UAE, the Philippines and Singapore, drawing on its experience in Malaysia.
Pine Labs Sees Meaningful Upside From UPI MDR
Pine Labs is seeing a “meaningful upside” from the proposed UPI merchant discount rate (MDR) framework, which could allow it to earn fees on eligible merchant transactions above ₹2,000. It noted that more than 70% of its DCP transactions are UPI-led, while transactions above ₹2,000 account for over 65% of its UPI GTV.
“Our average UPI ticket size is ₹1,400 as of Q2 FY27 with more than 65% of our UPI GTV driven by transactions above ₹2,000. Combined with our stronghold in enterprise, mid-market, and premium retail segments, where transactions above ₹2,000 are common, we are well positioned. Under NPCI’s proposed framework, a 0.4% MDR cap applies to payments above ₹2,000, and we primarily expect to earn our proportion through our acquiring bank partners—a high-margin revenue stream that scales with volumes,” the company said in its shareholder letter.
Around three out of every four transactions on Pine Labs’ POS terminals are UPI transactions, with volumes growing at a compounded rate of around 68% over the past two years, CEO Rau said during the company’s Q2 FY27 earnings call. Under the proposed framework, the acquiring bank’s share of the 40 basis points (bps) MDR cap is expected to be around 11 bps, Rau said.
To capture a larger share of the potential revenue, Pine Labs plans to deploy an additional 10 Lakh soundboxes at merchant locations where UPI transactions are currently processed through competitors’ devices.
“There is a large merchant which has POS machines from Pine Labs and soundboxes from somebody else. Those are the things which we have been missing. We said we should take that back,” Rau said.
He added that soundbox deployment had not been a priority earlier because UPI transactions did not generate monetisation opportunities for the company. “Now that it is monetisable, you can get the full wallet share,” he said.
However, Pine Labs will need to hold individual commercial discussions with its largest enterprise clients before passing on the MDR. Rau also remained guarded on the implementation timeline, saying, “I have nothing more to add in terms of when UPI MDR will go live. Now it is completely in NPCI’s court.”
Shares of Pine Labs ended today’s trading 1.03% higher at ₹123.05 apiece on the BSE.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Dar Blockchain and The Hashgraph Association have selected 18 startups for a new Web3 incubation programme supporting winners of the Hedera Africa Hackathon.
Run in partnership with Tunisian incubator Wiki Startup and investment firm UGFS North Africa, with Softstack as security partner, the programme runs until January 2027. It aims to graduate at least five seed-ready companies by an investor demo day in the week of January 18.
The Hedera Africa Hackathon, which wrapped up in April, drew more than 13,000 developers and 1,300 project submissions. A portion of the hackathon’s prize pool has been set aside to support winners with product development, technical implementation and market validation during the incubation phase.
“Most hackathons stop when the winners are announced. For us, that’s where the real work begins,” said Jaafar Saied, co-founder of Dar Blockchain.
Selected startups will move through four sprints and five jury-audited gates, with 21 workshops, one-on-one expert support and introductions to investors. Teams will also be supported to deploy production-ready products on the Hedera mainnet. The programme targets more than 60 per cent of ventures securing signed letters of intent or launching active pilots by the third milestone gate.
The African startups selected are Nigeria’s GreenAfrica, Beyond Service Game, Upesa, Afiya and Cryptonia CITY; Egypt’s Carboni; South Africa’s Direla; Madagascar’s Nia; Zimbabwe’s RDZ Health; Morocco’s Hedron; and Côte d’Ivoire’s APIx.
They are joined by Effisend X Africa (Mexico), Silsilat Finance (Malaysia), Tedera (Romania), W.A.T.A (Brazil), CryptoMage (India), and US-based KeyRing and Building a Chain of Trust in the Green Power-to-X Market.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
D2C nutrition and dietary supplements brand Ace Blend has raised $9.9 Mn (about ₹95 Cr) in a Series A2 funding round led by 3one4 Capital, with participation from existing investor Fireside Ventures.
The startup will use the fresh capital for clinical trials, supply chain improvements, R&D, and new nutrition formats.
“The first is clinical trials, which are going to be run by credible CROs (contract research organisations) and are intended to be published in peer-reviewed international journals. The second is cementing our moat as a business, which is our supply chain proficiency. The third is a robust testing mechanism that allows nutritional accuracy, pesticides and heavy metals to be tested batch on batch without any human intervention,” founder and CEO Shivam Hingorani told Inc42.
Ace Blend also plans to conduct shelf-stability studies at launch and six months later, which Hingorani said would help build long-term safety data on its products.
“Trust is not enough” in the nutritional supplements market, he said, stressing the need for scientific evidence to support product claims.
Founded in 2018 by Hingorani, and later joined by Saif Mehkri as cofounder in 2022, Ace Blend offers supplements across heart health, brain health, sleep, recovery, gut health, strength and immunity. Its portfolio comprises around 14 SKUs, including plant-based protein powders, superfood mixes, and functional health supplements.
Besides its website, the startup sells its products through ecommerce and quick commerce platforms, including Amazon, Flipkart, Zepto, and Blinkit. Its website contributes around 50% of revenue, with the remainder coming from marketplaces and other ecommerce channels, Hingorani said.
Ace Blend clocked 300% growth in FY26 and has a repeat purchase rate of nearly 48%, according to Hingorani. It is targeting annual recurring revenue of ₹250-300 Cr over the next 12-18 months, with profitability also in sight, he added.
The startup plans to strengthen its supply chain by sourcing raw materials from multiple countries. Hingorani said its vertically integrated model covers ingredient sourcing, formulation, and manufacturing, while automated testing will assess nutritional accuracy, pesticide residues, and heavy metals in each batch.
Ace Blend is also developing new products, including a formulation created with a gut-health specialist to address leaky gut, a combination of natural nutrients intended to lower inflammation, an eye-health product, and a fibre-based format for gut health, he said.
India’s dietary supplements market is growing as consumers become more aware of preventive healthcare and the role of supplements in managing chronic conditions. Investor interest in the sector is also rising. Earlier this month, D2C brand The Stack raised ₹21.5 Cr to expand its product range and invest in R&D.
According to Grand View Research, India’s dietary supplements market was valued at $5.8 Bn in 2025. It is projected to reach $6.6 Bn in 2026 and $12.4 Bn by 2033, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 9.5% between 2026 and 2033.

items.title: Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026: What’s In Store For Startups At Asia’s Largest Tech Event
items.summary:
India’s startup ecosystem is the fourth most valuable startup ecosystem in the world and spans from fintech and consumer technology to AI and deeptech sectors. As founders look beyond domestic markets to build globally competitive businesses, access to capital, talent and technology infrastructure has become increasingly important.
Bengaluru has long brought these ingredients together. For close to three decades, the Silicon Valley of India has been the yardstick against which India’s tech ambitions are measured. The city now ranks 15th among global startup ecosystems and 12th among the world’s largest tech talent hubs.
Meanwhile, Karnataka accounts for 42% of India’s IT exports and leads the country in software exports, biotech, and aerospace and defence manufacturing.
As AI changes how products are developed and businesses operate, the opportunity is expanding – build from Bengaluru and reach the world.
This ambition will take centre stage at the Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026. Org
items.author: Inc42 BrandLabs
items.content:
India’s startup ecosystem is the fourth most valuable startup ecosystem in the world and spans from fintech and consumer technology to AI and deeptech sectors. As founders look beyond domestic markets to build globally competitive businesses, access to capital, talent and technology infrastructure has become increasingly important.
Bengaluru has long brought these ingredients together. For close to three decades, the Silicon Valley of India has been the yardstick against which India’s tech ambitions are measured. The city now ranks 15th among global startup ecosystems and 12th among the world’s largest tech talent hubs.
Meanwhile, Karnataka accounts for 42% of India’s IT exports and leads the country in software exports, biotech, and aerospace and defence manufacturing.
As AI changes how products are developed and businesses operate, the opportunity is expanding – build from Bengaluru and reach the world.
This ambition will take centre stage at the Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026. Organised by the Karnataka government’s Department of Electronics, Information Technology, Biotechnology and Science & Technology, the Summit returns for its 29th edition from November 17-19 at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre (BIEC), Bengaluru.
Under the theme ‘AI & Beyond’, the three-day event will bring together founders, investors, technology leaders, researchers, and policymakers to explore emerging technologies and the businesses being built around them.
Billed as Asia’s largest integrated technology event, BTS 2026 expects more than 60K business visitors, over 25K delegates, 1,800+ exhibitors and 700+ speakers across 120+ sessions.
Participation is expected from over 75 countries and 30+ Indian states and Union Territories. It will also feature more than 20 country pavilions and over 175 international exhibitors on the floor.
The summit will span 18 thematic tracks, covering IT and deeptech, frontier technologies, electronics and semiconductors, electric mobility, health and biotech, data centres, cybersecurity, global capability centres (GCCs), fintech, and the orange economy, which encompasses creative industries. A dedicated India-USA Tech Conclave will also be part of the programme.
The speaker line-up announced so far includes Sandeep Sahai, chief executive officer, Clear Water Analytics, Vivek Raghavan, cofounder, Sarvam AI, Dr V. Anantha Nageswaran, chief economic advisor (CEA), Govt. of India, Ranjani Mani, director and country head – generative AI, Microsoft, Rangesh Raghavan, corporate vice president and MD, Lam Research, Dr Sowmya Swaminathan, chairperson, M S Swaminathan Research Foundation, and Dr Velislava Petrova-Chamova, minister of foreign affairs of the Republic of Bulgaria.
For founders, the programme extends beyond conference sessions to product showcases, investor meetings, and practical guidance on building and scaling businesses.
A Global Startup Showcase
The Startup Pavilion will host more than 1,000 startups, incubators, and accelerators, with startup participation spanning 100 cities. These will include cohorts from the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission’s (KDEM) ‘Beyond Bengaluru’ initiative and the Software Technology Parks of India’s ‘Sayuj’ programme.
Eighteen thematic pavilions will cover sectors including AI, agritech, D2C, fintech, semiconductors, robotics, and SaaS. By grouping startups within their industry segments, the exhibition aims to help founders connect with relevant buyers, customers, and potential partners.
Two dedicated startup stages will focus on ‘Deeptech For Business’ and ‘Consumer Tech For Billions’. Both stages will host workshops and masterclasses on topics such as go-to-market strategies, investor readiness, product management, cybersecurity and AI.
Connecting Founders With Investors
On the sidelines of BTS 2026, the three-day ‘Investor Connect Programme’ will offer curated, sector-specific matchmaking between startups, investors, and corporates. At the pitching arena, tech founders will get a shot at presenting to global VCs.
The three-day initiative is shaped in a way to bring startups face-to-face with investors, corporates, and key ecosystem stakeholders who can unlock collaborative projects, build investor relationships and connect young businesses with potential customers.
The programme will also host a reverse pitching session that will turn the tables, with investors explaining their investment theses, portfolio focus, and the businesses they want to back. Startups will also have access to one-on-one mentoring sessions with entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers and domain experts.
Celebrating India’s Future Makers
Another addition to the broader BTS 2026 umbrella is the Future Makers Conclave, a platform to celebrate India’s next generation of innovators and entrepreneurs. The conclave will bring together founders, entrepreneurs, investors and thought leaders to exchange ideas, share experiences, and discuss emerging opportunities across the technology and startup ecosystem.
The day will feature the BTS Unicorn Felicitation, where the state government will honour Indian startups that have entered the unicorn club since the previous edition. The conclave will also mark 10 years of the Karnataka government’s Elevate programme, which supports startups in the state.
The Bengaluru Tech Summit will also host key industry players, including Infosys, Biocon, QpiAI, Bosch Global Software Technologies, Clearwater Analytics, Booking Holdings, ZS, SAP, eBay, ACT Enterprise, Applied Materials, Fujitsu Ltd, Cloudflare, Qualcomm, Intel, JetBrains, Antithesis, PLAUD, Kyndle IT and many more as sponsors, alongside international partners like Business Sweden, Italian Trade Agency, Australian Trade & Investment Commission, Poland and more.
Together, the startup exhibition, investor programmes, and the Future Makers Conclave aim to make BTS 2026 a meeting point for ideas, capital, and commercial opportunities – giving founders a platform to take their next step towards global growth.
The post Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026: What’s In Store For Startups At Asia’s Largest Tech Event appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.author: Willem Nolens
items.content:
Pay-As-You-Go (PAYGo) solar has done something remarkable. It brought light and power to millions of rural households that the grid never reached, and it showed that these customers will use the installment payment model to purchase assets that improve their lives. But it’s now confronting a challenge that puts this accomplishment — and the financial health and viability of both PAYGo businesses and their customers — at risk.
I have worked in this sector for most of its history, as an entrepreneur and later as an adviser. I believe PAYGo faces a credit problem that affects customers, and holds back companies and funders. The good news is that the problem has a clear root cause, and that cause can be fixed.
 
What PAYGo achieved, and what went wrong
The idea behind PAYGo is simple. A customer gets a solar home system and pays for it in small installments. If payments stop, the system switches off, like prepaid energy. Off-grid solar has grown fast. According to the 2025 market report from GOGLA, the global association for the off-grid solar energy industry, “GOGLA affiliate companies are now serving over 148 million people with solar energy kits.” Though most of these are small solar lanterns purchased with cash, PAYGo has made larger solar home systems affordable for many rural households.
But a solar home system sold on credit only produces impact when the customer can pay for it and ends up owning it. And on this point, the numbers are sobering.
MAF Lab, an advisory firm focused on PAYGo credit that I co-founded and led until 2025, tracks the performance of PAYGo loans across the sector. According to a paper by MAF Lab and Acumen, customers in sub-Saharan Africa had repaid on average 71% of what they owed at one and a half times the loan term, and only 51% had fully repaid their loan by then. More recent MAF Lab data show that even at twice the loan term, only about two in three customers had become owners.
GOGLA’s own data point the same way: Across 17 country operations of seven major PAYGo companies, customers had repaid on average 72% of the contract at twice the loan term. For comparison, according to the same paper, microfinance institutions (MFIs) making loans of a similar size typically see repayment rates of 95% to 99%.
 
Why it went wrong: one company, two jobs
So what accounts for these lower repayment rates? The problem boils down to a sector-wide misalignment in solar companies’ core business activities, as PAYGo essentially turned every distributor into a lender. That is a lot to ask. A distributor already has to buy stock, run logistics, sell and install solar home systems, and provide after-sales service. Lending well is a different job, requiring different core capabilities. It depends on careful credit checks, clear explanations to customers and patient follow-up.
The two jobs pull in opposite directions. Sales teams have targets for this month. The cost of a bad credit decision shows up months later, somewhere else in the company. Growth also hides problems: New loans dominate the portfolio, while trouble in older loans takes time to appear.
The way the sector was funded made this worse. For years, many funders and donors counted every sale as impact, so the companies that grew fastest raised the most money. And companies that could not raise funding had to sell more, since sales at least brought in cash from down payments and potentially from end-user subsidy schemes. Credit checks became very short. Of the more than 40 distributors MAF Lab supported, most left the credit decision largely to the field agent. A call centre then did a quick Know Your Customer check, usually aiming for five to 10 minutes per customer.
One case from my own experience shows how fast this can happen. Since 2021, I had supported a PAYGo company in East Africa that had greatly improved its credit management. It had built a proper credit team that checked whether customers could repay, to prevent over-financing. Then a results-based financing (RBF) scheme started. Sales grew by more than 250%, while the credit team stayed the same size. The average credit assessment dropped to about six minutes. No one decided to lower credit quality. But sales went through the roof, and repayment looked good at first, because most loans were still new. The thinking was that lower prices had made the product more affordable, so credit checks could be lighter. But as defaults eventually grew, it became clear that in fact, many of these customers should not have been offered credit at all.
In response to this issue, at MAF Lab, we helped these distributors improve their credit management. In a previous NextBillion article, Dan Murphy and I pleaded for the sector to embrace this priority, integrating responsible credit management and cash flow discipline into a financially sustainable model we termed “PAYGo 2.0.” And as our research shows, better credit management can increase repayment rates by around 7 percentage points. But when we came back to those distributors just months after the end of our nine-month long interventions to embed better credit management into their business models, many of those credit improvements had been rolled back. The pressure to sell kept winning.
 
Who pays the price
Meanwhile, the consequences of this ongoing issue are exacting a price from every stakeholder across the sector.
Customers pay first: A customer who cannot pay loses the product, and with it the money already paid. But many customers do not realise they are taking a loan. They see their payments as buying “energy tokens,” like topping up their minutes in a prepaid phone. So when they stop paying, they don’t expect to lose the product, or the money they have already paid for it. And customers who do pay carry the cost of those who don’t: The World Bank’s ESMAP Off-grid Solar Market Trends report 2024 estimates that bad debt makes up around 24% of the retail price of an average PAYGo system.
Companies pay next: A weak portfolio means less cash coming in, constant stock-outs and stalled growth. This is not only a PAYGo problem. In a 2025 MAF Lab survey of 27 last-mile distributors, selling solar systems but also clean cooking, phones, motorbikes and irrigation equipment, two thirds offered credit in-house, with most of them claiming they were doing it because they had no other option. The survey also showed that 78% of distributors agreed that PAYGo companies struggle to assess and manage credit risk effectively, and that 70% agreed that customers often misunderstand their PAYGo contracts. As one of them told us, they were not good at pretending to be a bank.
Funders pay last: Many have lost confidence in PAYGo loan books. Funding is now concentrated in a handful of large companies. The smaller, locally owned distributors, often closest to rural customers, find it hardest to raise money.
 
Why subsidies can make it worse
Results-based financing pays companies a subsidy for each qualifying sale, so they can lower prices for poorer households. The intention is good. But when every new sale brings in extra money, the pressure to sell grows too, and results in more overfinancing of customers.
MAF Lab data from one RBF programme shows how that can happen. In the six months before the programme target, two companies sold about 43,000 loans, roughly five times their usual pace. Those loans did clearly worse than loans sold in the six months before and after:
In the first company, the share of customers who repaid the loan and became owners of their solar home system fell from about 61% to 47%. Repayment dropped from 83% to 76%.
At the second company, defaults rose from 15–21% to 27%. Repayment dropped from 85–88% to 79%.
Neither company used the subsidy to lower the daily payment they required from customers. One used it to cut the deposit by about a third. In other words, the subsidy made it easier to get a product, but not easier to pay for it.
I am not against subsidies. But for the poorest households, a subsidised cash sale is often better than a loan. In contrast, subsidies that reward sales volume, without customer protection standards, can harm the customers and companies they are meant to support.
 
The fix: separate sales from credit
We have seen this challenge before in the development sector. In microfinance, a lot of investor capital chasing growth opportunities led lenders to give customers more debt than they could carry. In 2010, this led to the microfinance crisis in India, where over-indebtedness caused some borrowers to take their own lives. India’s central bank responded with clear rules on how much a borrower may owe and how many lenders they may have. Regulators in many other countries followed with their own customer protection rules. While the sector did not initially want to be regulated, this customer protection regulation in fact helped it to become more stable and sustainable, and attract new funding.
PAYGo needs to adopt the same principle: Whoever lends to low-income households must check that the customer can repay, and must be held accountable for their decision to offer credit. That decision should not depend on good intentions, or on how much time there happens to be for credit checks that month.
This does not mean every distributor has to become a regulated lender. The better solution is to split the two jobs: The distributor sells, installs and services the product, while a specialised, regulated asset finance company assesses the customer, sets the loan terms, finances the loan and manages repayment. This is how it works in most mature markets: The shop sells the refrigerator, and a finance company provides the credit.
Separating these two jobs has four benefits:
Better for customers: Credit decisions are made independently, not affected by sales targets and cash flow needs, and customer protection is covered as the lender is a regulated financial institution.
Better for distributors: They are paid soon after the sale. Their working capital cycle shrinks from 12–24 months to one to three months, so cash goes back into stock instead of loan books.
More efficient: One credit team and system can serve many distributors.
Easier to finance: Funders can back one large, transparent loan portfolio instead of many small ones. Over time, that should lower the cost of capital.
 
Why not leave it to MFIs?
MFIs already know how to lend responsibly, so why not let them do it? Many distributors have tried. But in MAF Lab interviews with 15 banks and MFIs in four African countries, most partnerships between financial institutions and PAYGo distributors turned out to be referral arrangements reaching only a few hundred customers per lender.
The reasons are understandable. Branch networks and field visits are expensive, and for a $150 loan to a farmer far from a branch, the costs exceed the income. That is why most MFIs are focussing on urban customers with higher and more stable incomes, located close to the MFI branches.
So a gap remains. Distributors reach rural customers but struggle to lend well. MFIs lend well but struggle to reach rural customers. What is missing is a lender built for exactly this gap.
 
Putting a new model to the test in Uganda
With a team from MAF Lab, we set up in24 to test this model in practice. in24 is a licensed asset finance company in Uganda, owned by a non-profit foundation that guards its mission. We have signed service level agreements with two Ugandan solar distributors: Brightlife and Greenbay.
The process is simple. The distributor’s sales agent submits the customer’s loan application online. in24’s loan officers check the credit reference bureau, assess the application and decide within 24 hours whether to approve it, without a physical visit. The distributor has no say in the credit decision. Once the loan is approved and the down payment is received, in24 pays the distributor, and then manages repayment directly with the customer. As part of the agreement, the distributor does not switch off systems when customers fall behind. Switching off can hurt the customer’s cash flow, for example when the system powers a small business. It also sends the wrong message: that paying is optional, like buying prepaid energy. Instead, in24 treats PAYGo finance as what it is, a loan. Customers who repay well can get a next loan from in24, often a larger one. in24 also reports to Uganda’s credit reference bureau, so customers build a credit history that other lenders can see. In the end, this is about giving rural customers a fair chance at lasting access to formal credit.
Our two partners use the model in different ways. Brightlife has run PAYGo for years. Handing its credit to in24 means it needs to tie up far less working capital in customer loans. Greenbay, active in Kenya and Uganda, did not offer credit at all in Uganda. Now it can, and it expects to sell much more at the last mile as a result.
The first results are encouraging. With around 400 loans so far, repayment stands at 98%. The portfolio is still young, and the coming months will show how loans perform over their full term. A pilot in Mozambique will test whether the model works in other markets too.
 
What the sector can do now
Separating sales from credit is not a magic fix, and it will not suit every customer or every company. But it tackles the root cause rather than the symptoms. Everyone in the sector can help this solution gain traction across the industry:
Funders can measure impact by how many customers end up owning their product, not by how many products are sold.
RBF designers can link subsidies to repayment and ownership, not to sales.
Regulators can bring PAYGo credit under the same customer protection rules as other lending.
Distributors can ask themselves whether credit really needs to stay in-house.
PAYGo proved that rural customers want clean energy and will pay for it. The next step is to make sure that the credit we give them helps them, and helps the companies that serve them grow in a sustainable way.
 
Willem Nolens is co-founder and MD of in24, which has commercial partnerships with Brightlife and Greenbay. He used to lead MAF Lab till the end of 2025, and in that role co-authored three of the reports cited in this article.

items.content:
The 36th Conference of State Finance Secretaries was held on October 27, 2026 at RBI, Mumbai. The theme of the Conference was ‘Role of Quality of Expenditure, Effective Cash and Prudent Debt Management in Enhancing States’ Fiscal Sustainability’. The Conference was attended by the Finance Secretaries of 27 States and three Union Territories as well as senior officials from the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, Controller General of Accounts and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Governor, Reserve Bank of India inaugurated the Conference.
Addressing the participants, the Governor emphasised the importance of maintaining the quality of expenditure to ensure the long-term fiscal health of the States. He also emphasised on the need for the States to adopt prudent borrowing strategies and efficient cash management practices. The Governor urged the States to onboard onto the Unified Lending Interface (ULI) and utilise Programmable Central Bank Digital Currency (P-CBDC) for Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT). He also advised States to make effective use of the State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC) forum. During the Conference, the Governor released a Booklet titled ‘Compendium on Cash and Debt Management for State Governments’. The Booklet summarises relevant concepts, operational processes and good cash and debt management practices in a concise and accessible format.
The meeting reviewed, inter alia, market borrowings by the States, short-term financial accommodation to the States from Reserve Bank, adoption of Benchmark Issuance Strategy by the States, etc.
(Brij Raj)           
Chief General Manager

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
The question of when India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) will finally be monetised has remained at the centre of the fintech industry’s conversations over the past month.
The debate intensified after the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) deferred the introduction of merchant discount rate (MDR) charges on select UPI person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions.
Earlier reports suggested that the rollout could be pushed to January 2027. However, the framework now appears likely to be introduced after Diwali, with the industry awaiting a final announcement.
Under the proposed framework, eligible P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000 would attract an MDR fee of 0.40%, capped at ₹300 per transaction. The proposal has drawn resistance from retail traders, who argue that the charges would add to their operating costs.
The All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA) and the All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation (AICPDF) also called for a ‘No UPI Day’ protest, but eventually withdrew the proposal following a meeting with finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman. Separately, advocate Anjan Datta filed a public interest litigation (PIL) challenging the policy in the Supreme Court. The apex court, however, declined to stay the proposed MDR charges.
Meanwhile, UPI transaction volumes and values declined month-on-month (MoM) in September. The number of transactions fell nearly 1.8% to 24.07 Bn, while their cumulative value dropped 1.5% to ₹29.37 Lakh Cr.
However, the decline that followed August was met with an all-time high in monthly transaction volumes. Average daily UPI transactions increased to 802 Mn in September from 791 Mn in August, while the average daily transaction value rose to ₹97,913 Cr from ₹96,205 Cr.
For banks, payment companies and third-party application providers (TPAPs), the proposed MDR framework could open up a new revenue stream in a market where monetisation has remained a persistent challenge.
Meanwhile, the uncertainty around the rollout has also weighed on listed fintech companies. Reports of a delay in MDR implementation triggered declines in the stocks of Paytm, Pine Labs and MobiKwik, underlining the potential impact of UPI monetisation on the broader payments ecosystem.
As the industry awaits greater clarity on the future of UPI and the economics of digital payments, we are back with the October edition of Five Fintech Startups To Watch. This monthly series spotlights startups operating in some of the most promising and fast-evolving segments of India’s fintech ecosystem.
With that, here are five interesting ventures that caught our attention this month.
Editor’s Note: The list below is not a ranking of any kind. Startups have been listed alphabetically.
Credfix | Helping Distressed Borrowers
Falling behind on loan repayments can quickly turn into a stressful cycle of recovery calls, mounting worries about credit scores and uncertainty over what to do next. For many borrowers, negotiating with lenders, exploring settlement options and dealing with legal notices can be just as daunting as the debt itself.
In India’s about $200 Mn debt collection software market, Bengaluru-based Credfix is trying to help borrowers deal with debt through an AI-powered platform. Founded in 2025 by Ranjan Agarwal, Neeraj Kulkarni and Ayush Kedia, Credfix helps borrowers understand their financial situation and explore ways to repay or settle their outstanding loans. It also helps lenders recover money from borrowers who are struggling to pay.
The startup currently serves over 2 Lakh borrowers with total outstanding debt of more than ₹4,000 Cr. Around 40% of its users are from tier II and tier III cities.
Credfix combines AI-powered tools with human support to help borrowers at different stages of the debt repayment process. Its Risi AI assistant offers guidance on available settlement options, responding to legal notices and dealing with recovery agents.
The startup also helps borrowers negotiate one-time settlements, where lenders agree to close a loan for less than the total amount owed. In addition, it explains borrowers’ rights and provides step-by-step guidance on rebuilding their CIBIL scores after settling their loans.
FOLO | Bringing Entire Wealth Into One View
A person’s wealth is often spread across multiple bank accounts, investments, insurance policies and other assets. Keeping track of everything can make it difficult to know how much they own, how much they owe and how their overall financial position is changing.
FOLO, short for Family Of Loved Ones, is trying to solve this problem with an app that brings a person’s financial information together in one place. Founded in 2022 by Munmun Desai and Vishal Purohit, the startup operates in India’s $171.2 Bn wealth management market, which is projected to grow at over 10.6% annually over the next eight years. It has raised over $2.9 Mn in funding so far.
FOLO is a SEBI-registered investment adviser that collects financial information from more than 650 sources, including bank accounts, mutual funds, stocks, fixed deposits, property, loans, credit cards and insurance policies. This gives users a consolidated view of their assets and liabilities, without having to manually track everything.
The platform uses the account aggregator framework to access financial information in a read-only mode, with users’ consent. It also allows users to share selected financial details with up to four trusted individuals, such as family members or financial advisers, without revealing their account login details.
Beyond tracking wealth, FOLO offers an offline service, called LYNC, to help users transfer their assets to nominees after their death.
The startup claims to have connected assets worth more than ₹20,000 Cr on its platform and crossed 1 Lakh app downloads.
Spring Street | Making Global Investing Accessible To Indians
India’s investors are increasingly looking beyond domestic markets to diversify their bets. However, investing in foreign stocks and other assets can be complicated, with hurdles around research, money transfers, taxes and regulatory compliance.
Founded in 2026 by Nishant Bansal, Spring Street is building a platform that gives Indian residents and non-resident Indians (NRIs) access to international markets through managed investment portfolios. Backed by Nexus Venture Partners, the startup is targeting a growing appetite for overseas investments. Indian residents remitted around $2.6 Bn (₹22,000 Cr) for overseas investments in FY26, up nearly 56% from $1.69 Bn in FY25.
Its flagship product, Prisma, offers professionally managed portfolios investing in international stocks, bonds and commodities. These portfolios provide exposure to markets across North America, Europe, Asia and Latin America, with options tailored to investors’ risk appetites and financial goals.
Spring Street also handles overseas investing, from onboarding and identity verification to remittance paperwork and investment tracking. To facilitate investments under the Reserve Bank of India’s Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), the startup has partnered with GIFT City-based ViewTrade, which is regulated by the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA). ViewTrade acts as the broker and custodian.
Spring Street charges an annual portfolio management fee of 1.25% to 1.50% of assets managed, depending on the portfolio, with no additional commissions on individual trades. Investors need to start with a minimum investment of $500.
UpTik | Unlocking Invoice Discounting For SMEs
Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) often struggle with cash flow when customers take weeks or months to pay their invoices. This can leave businesses short of money to cover everyday expenses or fund their next order. At the same time, retail investors looking beyond traditional investment products have limited access to opportunities linked to short-term business financing.
Hyderabad-based UpTik is trying to bridge this gap by connecting investors with businesses seeking working capital. Founded in 2025 by Ainampudi Vinod Varma, Mudunuri Dileep Varma, Phanindra Kumar and Uma Mukesh Ponduru, the startup allows businesses to raise funds against unpaid invoices, while investors can earn returns when those invoices are paid.
UpTik claims to have grown its assets under management (AUM) from ₹6.5 Cr in March 2026 to over ₹25 Cr in September 2026. Monthly disbursements also rose from ₹3.6 Cr to ₹13.3 Cr over the same period.
Through its platform, UpTik offers retail investors, HNIs and institutional investors opportunities to finance verified business invoices. The startup lists investment opportunities with defined tenures and provides details about the underlying transactions, expected returns and associated risks.
Investors must complete KYC checks, while each deal undergoes due diligence and legal screening. Users can also track their investments and request withdrawals of returns to an in-app wallet.
UpTik provides additional protection against defaults on select deals. The startup plans to expand beyond invoice discounting into other alternative investments, including corporate bonds and startup investments.
Zomint | Democratising Wealth Management
While wealthy individuals can hire wealth managers to guide their financial decisions, professionals and families with smaller portfolios often have to navigate investment choices on their own.
Chandigarh-based Zomint aims to bridge this gap by helping professionals and families manage their wealth through personalised financial advice. Founded in 2025 by Aman Mittal and Shavir Bansal, the wealthtech startup draws on Bansal’s earlier venture, the personal finance content platform Bekifaayati, which claims a community of over 50 Lakh and more than 80 Lakh monthly views. This audience has also helped Zomint build its customer base.
According to a market assessment published in an NSE-hosted document in November 2025, India’s investment and wealth management sector had an estimated annual addressable market of ₹1.1 Lakh Cr in FY25. The assessment projects this to reach ₹2.2 Lakh Cr to ₹2.6 Lakh Cr by FY30.
The startup assigns each customer a dedicated financial expert who uses AI tools and research to track investments, recommend suitable mutual funds and guide financial decisions over time. Its relationship managers currently serve more than 250 families each.
Zomint lets customers start with a monthly systematic investment plan (SIP) of ₹25,000 or a lump-sum investment of ₹5 Lakh. Its investment options include equity, debt and hybrid mutual funds, gold and silver funds, and global investment products available through GIFT City.
Beyond helping customers choose investments, Zomint actively monitors their portfolios and can recommend changes based on market conditions, developments affecting individual funds or shifts in customers’ financial circumstances. This allows the startup to offer ongoing guidance rather than one-time investment recommendations.
Edited by Shishir Parasher

items.content:
Meesho’s Q2 Snapshot
Meesho inched closer to profitability in Q2 FY27. The quarter saw the ecommerce giant rein in its losses, scale its revenues and improve its contribution margins. Yet macroeconomic volatility and loss-making new bets continued to weigh on its bottom line in Q2.
Here’s a quick look at Meesho’s Q2 FY27 numbers:
Net loss narrowed 68% YoY to ₹132.4 Cr
Operating revenue rose 34% YoY to ₹4,131.6 Cr
Total expenses increased 24% YoY to ₹4,382.3 Cr
The Marketplace Engine: As usual, Meesho’s core marketplace vertical accounted for the biggest chunk of its revenues in Q2, driven by a growing base of active transacting users and higher order frequency. What also came in handy were expanding margins, optimised logistics, strong user retention across Tier II+ markets and AI-driven automation.
Costly New Bets: On the flip side, Meesho’s newer initiatives – hyperlocal logistics, digital financial services and AI services – continued to widen their losses. However, revenues from these emerging businesses also rose sharply. The management sees faster deliveries, logistics efficiencies and AI eventually making these ventures more viable going forward.
In line with this, the listed company has invested an additional ₹75 Cr in Meesho Grocery to support its growth and financial requirements.
The Festive Cheer: Going forward, critics will be closely watching Meesho’s Q3 results as the quarter will capture a bigger portion of the company’s festive sales. This is because its ‘Mega Blockbuster Sale’ shifted from Q2 last fiscal to Q3 this year. The leadership expects Q3 growth to appear stronger, although it will require continued elevated spending during the Diwali period.
As the ecommerce giant continues its march towards profitability, here’s how Meesho fared on the financial front in Q2 FY27…
From The Editor’s Desk
Info Edge CEO Quits After 27 Years
Info Edge founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani will take over as executive vice chairman, MD and group CEO from December 3, 2026, succeeding Hitesh Oberoi, who is stepping down after nearly 27 years in a full-time executive role.
Oberoi will remain on the board as a non-executive, non-independent director. He cited plans to focus more on education, entrepreneurship, investing, philanthropy and family.
Info Edge’s consolidated net profit surged 87% YoY to ₹649.8 Cr in Q2 FY27, while revenue from operations rose 12.2% to ₹903.9 Cr. A 164.8% jump in other income to ₹428.4 Cr also contributed to profit growth.
Cognizant Eyes Sarvam Stake
The AI giant is in talks to raise $300 Mn at a valuation of $3.5 Bn to $4 Bn, more than double its previous valuation of $1.5 Bn just four months ago.
The potential investment will make Cognizant the second IT services major to back Sarvam after HCLTech, as IT firms look to strengthen AI capabilities amid growing automation risks to traditional outsourcing.
Sarvam is expanding its enterprise AI business, with customers including LIC, SBI Life, IDFC First Bank, Tata Capital and CRED. It is also pursuing AI projects in the defence sector through an MoU with the defence ministry’s Headquarters Integrated Defence Staff.
Astrotalk’s Profit Zooms 10X In FY26
The spiritual tech startup’s consolidated net profit jumped nearly 10X to ₹222 Cr in FY26, while operating revenue grew 55% YoY to ₹1,823 Cr. Profit before tax nearly quadrupled to ₹296 Cr.
International revenue surged 2.6X to ₹621 Cr, contributing 34% of operating revenue. Ecommerce revenue more than quadrupled to ₹166 Cr as Astrotalk Store expands beyond astrology consultations into spiritual products.
Cash flow from operations rose 21% to ₹229 Cr, while year-end cash and investments increased 41% to ₹917 Cr. The startup said it funded its expansion through internal cash flows. Astrotalk entered the unicorn club in August at a $1 Bn valuation following an ESOP buyback.
Moms Home’s Quick Commerce Bet
Jaipur-based baby essentials brand grew quick commerce revenue from around ₹1 Cr in FY25 to ₹10 Cr in FY26, accounting for nearly 30% of its ₹35 Cr top line. Monthly sales have since approached ₹5 Cr, with the brand selling around 45,000 kits a month.
Contribution margins have declined from 20-25% initially to 10-15%, amid inventory and replenishment challenges. The babycare brand has adapted by focusing on curated newborn and gifting kits and assembling products based on demand to reduce the risk of unsold inventory.
Moms Home aims to generate ₹30 Cr in quick commerce revenue in FY27 and expects the channel to contribute up to 50% of overall revenue in the next 15-18 months. It is also exploring a $3 Mn fundraise and plans to strengthen direct-to-consumer deliveries as it looks to reduce dependence on third-party platforms.
CarTrade’s Mixed Q2
The automotive classifieds company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹66 Cr in Q2 FY27, up 3% YoY and 16.2% QoQ. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 10.2% YoY to ₹213.1 Cr and 5.9% sequentially.
Including other income of ₹23.1 Cr, total income stood at ₹236.2 Cr. Total expenses increased 6% YoY to ₹150.8 Cr but declined 0.9% QoQ.
The September quarter had no exceptional expenses, unlike the preceding quarter, which included a ₹3.1 Cr charge linked to salary restructuring under the new labour codes.
Inc42 Markets
Inc42 Startup Spotlight
Can Firi Make Beauty Shopping Less Overwhelming?
Beauty shoppers today have thousands of products to choose from. But more choices often mean more time spent researching what actually works. Firi is trying to solve this with its opinionated online store that uses AI to research and stock beauty products and delivers them in minutes.
A Curated Store: Founded in 2026, Firi leverages AI agents to analyse online reviews, Reddit discussions, YouTube content and ingredient lists to decide which beauty products to stock. It claims to have so far analysed 50 Mn+ reviews and shortlisted about 3,000 products from more than 3 Lakh beauty products globally.
Delivered In Minutes: Firi currently sells skincare, haircare and body care offerings through its only Beauty Studio in parts of Delhi NCR, where it offers deliveries in as little as nine minutes. The startup now plans to add more dark stores in the city before expanding to other markets.
The Road Ahead: Backed by 360 ONE Asset and Better Capital, Firi plans to now expand into makeup, fragrances and other categories. It is also focusing on scaling its AI-led discovery and fulfilment model. With the homegrown online beauty and personal care market projected to become a $13 Bn opportunity by FY30, can Firi’s AI-led curation model redefine how India shops for beauty products?

items.content: Shapoorji Pallonji Group is looking to raise $150 million to $200 million, according to people familiar with the matter, as the Indian conglomerate faces mounting debt obligations.SP Group plans to raise the funds through private credit by issuing more rupee bonds initially sold by its Eqyizen Investment Pvt. unit in July, said the people, who asked not be named discussing private information. About half of the proceeds will be used to repay creditors of Porteast Investment Ltd., another SP Group unit, they said. The remainder will go toward other group debt, the people said, adding that talks are at an early stage and the size and terms could change.Also read: Shapoorji Pallonji Group wants Tata Sons to consider Rs 25,000 crore share buybackThe fresh financing would help SP Group cut debt at Porteast and reduce pressure on its loan-to-value ratio, the people said. Representatives for SP Group didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.SP Group has faced increasing strain as more debt comes due and it endures a prolonged wait to monetize its assets, including a large stake in Tata Sons Pvt, where executives are locked in a battle over whether or not to list publicly. The Mistry family, which controls SP Group, is the second-largest shareholder of Tata Sons with a roughly 18.4% share.SP Group’s latest fundraising plan comes after the company borrowed about 44.5 billion rupees ($467 million) in September through Eqyizen and dollar bonds sold by another unit called Mercury Finance Co., the people familiar said. That money was used for amortization payments due at Porteast, they said. The group is seeking to complete its new financing by mid-November, the people said.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi
The African Union (AU) has accredited Nigeria’s National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC), under the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA), as a Regional Centre of Excellence in Counter Terrorism for West Africa and the Sahel.
The accreditation fulfils President Bola Tinubu’s vision, announced at the High-Level African Counter Terrorism Meeting held in Abuja in April 2024, to position the NCTC as a regional hub for intelligence sharing, operational coordination, specialised training and capacity building against terrorism and violent extremism.
A statement issued on Thursday by Abu Michael, Head of Strategic Communication at the NCTC, said the designation marked a significant milestone in Nigeria’s contribution to collective African security.
It said the recognition formally positioned the centre to support AU member states, particularly those in West Africa and the Sahel, through enhanced counter-terrorism cooperation and institutional capacity development.
According to the statement, the accreditation gives the NCTC an expanded regional mandate to provide specialised training, joint threat analysis, research, technical assistance, exchanges of lessons learned and other forms of counter-terrorism support.
The accreditation was announced on October 27, 2026, by the Acting Director of the African Union Counter Terrorism Centre (AUCTC), Dr Idriss Mounir Lallali, on behalf of the AU Commission’s Commissioner for Political Affairs, Peace and Security, at the conclusion of the African Lessons Learned Forum in Abuja.
Lallali said the recognition followed a rigorous assessment of the NCTC’s institutional capacity, governance, training programmes, analytical capabilities, coordination mechanisms and adherence to human rights and the rule of law.
He explained that the accreditation process began with the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between the AU and the NCTC in September 2025.
This was followed by a technical assessment mission conducted by the AUCTC in Abuja in December 2025, which produced an accreditation roadmap outlining the institutional standards required for recognition.
Since then, the NCTC has worked to strengthen its governance structures, develop training curricula and operational procedures, improve its analytical and coordination functions, and reinforce its commitment to human rights and the rule of law.
The statement said the successful completion of the accreditation requirements reflected the centre’s institutional development and the collaborative efforts of ONSA, NCTC leadership and personnel, as well as strategic partners.
Announcing the decision, Lallali said: “It is therefore my pleasure to announce that the African Union is accrediting the NCTC as an African Union Regional Centre of Excellence in Counter Terrorism.
“This decision will be conveyed formally to the Government of the Federal Republic of Nigeria through a Note Verbale. It will come from the Department of Political Affairs, Peace and Security, through the AUCTC.
“That Note will set out the terms of the accreditation: an initial period of three years, renewable, the regional responsibilities the Centre now takes on, and the commitments the African Union makes in return.”
Speaking at the event, the National Security Adviser, Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, represented by the NCTC National Coordinator, Major General Adamu Garba Laka, described the accreditation as both recognition of Nigeria’s progress and a responsibility to contribute more substantially to Africa’s collective security.
Ribadu said the development marked an important moment for Nigeria and the continent, while commending Tinubu for his leadership, political will and sustained investment in the country’s national security architecture.
He said the achievement advanced the administration’s Renewed Hope Agenda and fulfilled the President’s vision of positioning the NCTC to serve Nigeria, West Africa, the Sahel and the wider continent.
The NSA also commended the AU Commission and the AUCTC for their technical support and the rigorous accreditation process, particularly acknowledging Lallali’s role in the mapping, assessment and accreditation stages.
He specifically recognised Laka for his leadership and sustained efforts in driving the process to completion.
Ribadu also praised the centre’s officers and staff, Nigeria’s security and justice institutions, ministries, departments and agencies, civil society organisations, communities and international partners for their contributions.
He said the Federal Government and ONSA would continue to support the NCTC in meeting the demands of its expanded regional mandate through appropriate staffing, sustainable resources, institutional partnerships and continued compliance with accreditation standards.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
Association says charges account for up to 60% of fibre deployment costs
By Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja
The Association of Licensed Telecommunications Operators of Nigeria (ALTON) has urged state governments to abolish right-of-way charges on telecommunications infrastructure, warning that the fees account for up to 60 per cent of fibre-optic deployment costs in some states and discourage network expansion into underserved communities.
The association said scrapping the charges, particularly in rural areas and locations with limited commercial prospects, would lower infrastructure deployment costs, attract investment and help bridge Nigeria’s digital divide.
ALTON Chairman, Engr. Gbenga Adebayo, made the call on Tuesday on the sidelines of a plenary session sponsored by IHS Nigeria at the 2026 Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja.
Right-of-way charges are fees imposed for permission to access and use public or private land, roads and other designated spaces to install fibre-optic cables and related telecommunications infrastructure.
Adebayo said the high cost of obtaining right-of-way approvals had become a major obstacle to fibre deployment, making it difficult for operators to justify investments in communities where anticipated revenue might not cover infrastructure costs.
“Today, the cost of right-of-way amounts to a significant part of the cost of fibre deployment. For every one kilometre of fibre that you deploy, in some of the states, the cost of right-of-way can be as high as 50 to 60 per cent of the cost of deploying the entire infrastructure,” he said.
He called for legislation to make right-of-way access for telecommunications infrastructure free, particularly in rural communities and other areas where expected commercial returns were unlikely to attract private investment.
According to him, removing the charges would make network expansion more affordable and encourage operators to extend services to communities with poor or no connectivity.
The ALTON chairman also urged the government to introduce incentives for telecommunications companies investing in areas where infrastructure deployment costs exceeded the revenue they could reasonably expect to generate.
He said existing government intervention mechanisms, particularly the Universal Service Provision Fund (USPF), could be deployed more strategically to support network expansion in underserved locations.
“There are also intervention funds. We have the Universal Service Provision Fund, which is designed for special intervention in those areas that are lacking coverage,” Adebayo said.
He dismissed suggestions that telecommunications operators were unwilling to invest in rural communities, arguing that the challenge was largely economic and could be addressed through appropriate incentives and targeted government support.
Beyond expanding network coverage, Adebayo stressed the need for increased investment in fibre-optic cables, telecommunications sites and network capacity to improve service quality and prepare Nigeria for emerging technologies.
He said artificial intelligence (AI) depended not only on software and computing power but also on the telecommunications infrastructure needed to support reliable connectivity and the transmission of large volumes of data.
Describing telecommunications infrastructure as fundamental to the digital economy, he called for stronger investor participation to address the sector’s infrastructure needs and support Nigeria’s technological development.
Meanwhile, the Chairman of the Senate Committee on ICT and Cybersecurity, Shuaib Salisu, disclosed that the National Digital Economy and E-Government Bill had reached its third reading, expressing optimism that the National Assembly would pass it before the end of 2026.
Salisu said lawmakers were also working on cybersecurity reforms and reviewing the Data Protection Act to strengthen Nigeria’s digital governance framework.
He said the Federal Government’s planned 90,000-kilometre fibre-optic network would help extend connectivity to underserved communities and complement efforts to improve access to digital services.
The senator also identified the Three Million Technical Talent (3MTT) programme as a key initiative for developing the skilled workforce needed to support Nigeria’s growing digital economy.
He urged businesses and industry stakeholders to engage lawmakers early in the legislative process, saying such engagement would help ensure that proposed laws reflected industry realities and the requirements for attracting investment.
Also speaking at the summit, the Chargé d’Affaires of the United States Mission in Abuja, Jimmy Mauldin, called for stronger investment partnerships between Nigeria and the United States, stressing that cooperation should extend beyond trade to include job creation, technology transfer and support for local businesses.
Mauldin identified digital infrastructure, energy, manufacturing, agriculture, critical minerals and financial services as sectors offering significant opportunities for deeper economic collaboration between the two countries.
He said Nigeria’s large youthful population, growing technology sector and strategic position in West African commerce made it an attractive investment destination.
However, he stressed that predictable government policies, respect for contracts, efficient trade procedures and improved security were essential to sustaining investor confidence and attracting long-term capital.
“Capital is mobile. And it’s also important to remember that capital is very selective,” he said.
Mauldin added that reliable electricity and secure communities were necessary for businesses to establish factories, deploy fibre-optic networks and operate efficient supply chains.
The summit brought together government officials, business leaders, policymakers and development partners to examine investment opportunities, infrastructure development and strategies for accelerating Nigeria’s economic growth.

items.author: Henry Oduah
items.content:
Liverpool beat Chelsea in a dramatic penalty shoot-out to reach the League Cup quarter-finals, while holders Manchester City survived a scare against Brighton on Wednesday.
In a clash between childhood friends Andoni Iraola and Xabi Alonso, it was the Liverpool manager who took the bragging rights in the last-16 tie at Anfield.
A 1-1 draw in normal time set the stage for the shoot-out as Chelsea’s Morgan Rogers netted from the spot, only for Cody Gakpo to equalise with a penalty of his own just before half-time.
Chelsea’s Valentin Barco hit the post in the shoot-out before Liverpool’s Kostas Tsimikas wasted a chance to win it when he blazed over.
Ryan Gravenberch was denied by Chelsea keeper Mike Penders, but Giorgi Mamardashvili saved Emmanuel Emegha’s kick to keep Liverpool alive.
After Joe Gomez scored for Liverpool, Blues defender Wesley Fofana miscued into the Kop as the hosts advanced.
It was former Liverpool midfielder Alonso’s third defeat in his three visits to Anfield as a manager following losses with Bayer Leverkusen in 2024 and Real Madrid in 2025.
In their debut campaigns at Liverpool, Jurgen Klopp and Arne Slot both reached the League Cup final and Iraola is on course to follow in their footsteps with the 10-time winners of the competition.
Alonso made just four changes to the Chelsea side that lost 2-0 at home to Tottenham on Saturday, while Iraola made seven changes from Liverpool’s 2-0 win against Brighton on Sunday.
Rogers put Chelsea in front with a 40th-minute penalty after Gravenberch clattered into Moises Caicedo.
But Liverpool were level three minutes later with a penalty of their own as Gakpo converted from the spot following Fofana’s handball.
At the Etihad Stadium, City were pushed to the brink by Brighton in a 2-2 draw before winning on penalties.
City boss Enzo Maresca made nine changes after Saturday’s loss at Aston Villa — which ended the leaders’ 100 percent start to the Premier League campaign.
– Rulli stars for City –
Erling Haaland, Ruben Dias, Elliot Anderson and Gianluigi Donnarumma were among the City stars rested.
Brighton went in front after 30 minutes when Malick Yalcouye steered Georginio Rutter’s shot past Geronimo Rulli from five yards.
Mateo Kovacic hauled City level 20 minutes later with a fine finish that curled into the far corner from 25 yards.
Rutter restored Brighton’s lead two minutes after half-time, slotting home from Jaouen Hadjam’s cut-back.
Vitor Reis deflected in Rayan Cherki’s 72nd-minute free-kick to equalise for City.
Kovacic’s penalty was saved by Jason Steele in the shoot-out, but Rulli denied Brighton’s Yasin Ayari and Lewis Dunk to send City into the last eight.
The sides meet again in the Premier League at the Etihad on Saturday.
Bournemouth extended their blistering run with a 3-0 win against Aston Villa at the Vitality Stadium.
The Cherries beat AC Milan 3-0 in the Europa League last week and followed that up with a 3-0 win at Manchester United in the Premier League on Sunday.
Marco Rose’s men dispatched Villa in equally emphatic fashion as goals from Amine Adli, Lewis Cook and Alvaro Rodriguez made it five successive wins in all competitions.
Crystal Palace eased the pressure on under-fire boss Pierre Sage with a 1-0 win at Fulham.
Eddie Nketiah struck in the 37th minute to give struggling Palace their first win in five games in all competitions.
Sunderland enjoyed a welcome respite from their Premier League struggles with a 3-2 victory against Brentford at the Stadium of Light.
Sitting bottom of the Premier League, Sunderland swatted aside the Bees with goals from Chemsdine Talbi, Tymur Tutierov and Malick Fofana.
Callum Wilson and Igor Thiago netted too late to save Brentford.
Fourth-tier Fleetwood reached the quarter-finals with a stunning penalty shoot-out victory over Premier League champions Arsenal on Tuesday.
Everton host Newcastle in the last game of the fourth round on Thursday.
AFP

items.author: Henry Oduah
items.content:
Newly-crowned Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane was left on the bench as Bayern Munich sailed to a 6-1 win over second-tier Magdeburg in the German Cup last 32 on Wednesday.
Bayern had no difficulty without their star striker, with Michael Olise grabbing a double and Ismael Saibari, Alphonso Davies, Nathaniel Brown and teenager David Santos Daiber also getting on the scoresheet.
Kane received a guard of honour from his Bayern teammates before kick-off as the 75,000 fans at the Allianz Arena saluted the Ballon d’Or winner, two days after his triumph in London.
Bayern got some more good news pre-match, with coach Vincent Kompany discharged from hospital, five days after collapsing at training on Friday.
“We’re also winning for him of course,” Brown said of Kompany. “It’s really good that he’s back home now. He should get some rest, but hopefully we’ll see him again soon.”
Olise tapped in an excellent Saibari assist from close range after 10 minutes but the unfancied visitors levelled five minutes later through Mateusz Zukowski.
Olise returned the favour by setting up Saibari midway through the opening half and added a third from the spot early in the second half before smiling and pointing to Kane, Bayern’s regular penalty taker, on the bench.
Teenage forward Lennart Karl set up goals for Davies and Brown before Santos Daiber added more gloss to the victory with a stoppage-time goal.
Kane remained on the bench for the entire match, with Saturday’s home Bundesliga clash with Borussia Dortmund in mind.
Bayer Leverkusen came from two goals down to win 5-2 against Nuremberg, with defender Edmond Tapsoba netting twice and Patrik Schick, Jonas Hofmann and Lucas Vazquez scoring goals.
Earlier on Wednesday, Germany forward Deniz Undav’s 90th-minute strike took Stuttgart to a 1-0 win at 10-man Paderborn.
Stuttgart, finalists in 2025, had a one-man advantage after Laurin Curda’s 37th-minute red card but could not break down a stubborn Paderborn.
After striker Ermedin Demirovic had two efforts saved, Undav took matters into his own hands and turned in a Chris Fuehrich cross with extra time looming.
“The win is what matters most,” Undav said. “I honestly don’t care whether I’m the one who scores, and that’s the truth. We won, we’re through to the next round — on we go.”
Japan forward Keisuke Goto scored twice in the final 15 minutes to overturn a 2-1 deficit as Freiburg won 3-2 at home against Wolfsburg.
Goto’s Japan teammate Kento Shiogai also bagged a brace, while Freiburg’s Igor Matanovic opened the scoring.
Elsewhere, second-division sides Dynamo Dresden and Hertha Berlin both won 2-0 against Schalke and Jeddeloh respectively, while Kaiserslautern eliminated Hannover.
AFP
