Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said this month that Egyptian membership in ​the pact remained "under serious consideration".
Read: Egypt's Sisi seeks parliament's backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked
Egypt, the Arab world's most populous state with one of the region's largest ​militaries, joined the Saudi-led coalition in an earlier phase of Yemen's war in March 2015 mainly as a naval partner, sending warships to secure Red Sea shipping lanes while pledging air support. It also deployed around 800 ground troops but ​played only a limited combat role.
Egypt was involved in a costly military intervention in Yemen in the ​1960s and has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.
Saudi Arabia is a major ‌political and ⁠financial partner of Cairo, providing billions of dollars in aid, deposits at the central bank and energy supplies under Sisi.
Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and the Houthi militia, which controls the capital Sanaa, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming a volatile front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The ​Houthis have attacked Riyadh's international ​airport and the state ⁠oil giant Saudi Aramco, disrupting flights and oil exports, while aid agencies have warned of worsening conditions in Yemen, already suffering one of the world's worst humanitarian ​crises.
Abdelatty and Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh on Wednesday ​to deliver a ⁠letter to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman from Sisi, who said Egypt's support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders rather than attacking Yemen. Abdelatty said after that visit that Cairo advocates exploring "every ⁠opportunity" to ​resolve the Yemen conflict diplomatically.
Read More: Egypt's Sisi says Saudi defence role would not include attack on Yemen
The Saudi crown prince visited Sisi in ​Cairo on September 15 to discuss security and navigation in the Red Sea after the fighting in Yemen reignited.

items.title: Vote young yet govern much later: West African youth’s struggle for power
items.summary:
In all of West Africa, te voting age is 18, but presidential eligibility ages vary widely
Originally published on Global Voices
Youth mobilized in Africa. Screenshot from DW Africa's YouTube channel
In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18. In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25. However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50 years old before being eligible to run for the highest office. Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.
Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them. They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves. The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?
Age: A shifting barrier
Across the region, the voting age is 18.
items.author: Laura
items.content:
In all of West Africa, te voting age is 18, but presidential eligibility ages vary widely
Originally published on Global Voices
Youth mobilized in Africa. Screenshot from DW Africa's YouTube channel
In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18. In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25. However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50 years old before being eligible to run for the highest office. Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.
Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them. They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves. The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?
Age: A shifting barrier
Across the region, the voting age is 18. However, presidential eligibility ages vary widely. In Gambia, it’s 30; in Senegal, Nigeria, and Côte d’Ivoire, it’s 35; and in Benin, Ghana, and Guinea, it’s 40. In the legislative assemblies, the bar is even lower. In Togo, Benin, Senegal, and Nigeria’s House of Representatives, it’s 25, while in Ghana it’s 21.
The situation in Togo requires closer inspection. On May 6, 2024, the country legally became a parliamentary republic. Under the 2024 Constitution, the eligibility age for President of the Republic is 50. Parliament also now elects the president, whose powers are limited. Authority now rests with the President of the Council of Ministers, who must be at least 40 and is not elected in public presidential elections. Faure Gnassingbé has held this position since May 3, 2025, the day parliament also elected the country’s oldest-ever incoming president of the Republic, Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, 86.
However, the country’s legal age limit is hardly set in stone. In 2002, the National Assembly lowered it from 45 to 35 — a reform the opposition called tailor-made for Faure Gnassingbé.
More recently, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, on July 30, 2026, the Ghanaian government agreed in principle to lower the minimum presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35, defying the Constitutional Review Committee’s recommendation of 30. This legislation will ultimately go to a referendum, requiring a 40 percent turnout and a 75 percent approval.
In 2018, Nigeria set a regional precedent. Under pressure from the youth-led Not Too Young To Run campaign, the law lowered the presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35 and the House of Representatives’ eligibility age from 30 to 25.
According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union, lowering the minimum presidential age leads to younger parliaments. However, Côte d’Ivoire tells a very different story. In 2016, after removing the maximum age limit of 75 to run for office, incumbent President Alassane Ouattara, 83, ran for another term in 2025. The law rarely protects younger generations.
Youths particularly active in street movements
Even though young people have the right to vote across the continent, that does not mean all young people exercise that right. In August 2025, an Afrobarometer survey found that those aged 18 to 35 were less active than their elders in almost all traditional means of political participation. Overall across the continent, they trailed by 18 percentage points in voting, but by a record 29 points in Senegal. Protests were the only exception.
In Togo’s capital of Lomé, the June 6 Movement, sparked by the rapper Aamron’s arrest, brought thousands of people onto the streets. According to the Media Foundation for West Africa, the subsequent crackdown, for which the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) blamed government-backed militiamen, left seven dead.
Similarly, in Madagascar, the September 2025 protests toppled President Andry Rajoelina’s government, resulting in a military takeover. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the overthrown president himself came to power in 2019 on the back of a protest, at just 34 years old.
Comparably, in Kenya, street protests forced the withdrawal of the 2024 Finance Bill. Meanwhile, in Morocco, youth-led protests prompted the authorities to announce youth candidacy incentives and prosecute specific ringleaders.
Although leaderless movements wrest concessions, they rarely last without political parties or trade unions to sustain them.
The gap between participation and representation
The Inter-Parliamentary Report, published on April 9, 2026, found that elected officials aged 30 and under account for just 2.8 percent of all parliamentarians worldwide. Since 2023, progress has stalled for the first time since 2014. More than a third (37.1 percent) of legislative houses have no parliamentarians in this age group.
The lack of youth representation and participation is a significant challenge considering young people under 35 account for roughly 70 percent of West Africa’s population, according to the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference.
According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), at the start of Ghana’s 2025 parliamentary term, despite the legal minimum age of 21, no parliamentarians were aged 30 or under. What’s more, those aged 31 to 40 held just 46 of the 269 parliamentary seats, or 17.1 percent. After Senegal’s 2024 legislative elections, the National Assembly had only five members under 30, accounting for just 3 percent. Although almost 38 percent of registered voters were aged 18 to 35, the Assembly’s average age was 47. Elected at just 44, the country’s youngest-ever president, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, only became an official candidate after his mentor, Ousmane Sonko, was disqualified.
In Nigeria, International IDEA, an intergovernmental organization that supports sustainable democracy worldwide, reported that in 2015, only three of the 360 members of the House of Representatives were between the ages of 18–25, rising to 14 in 2019 — a positive but modest development.
In Dakar, the head of Yiaga Africa, the organization behind the Not Too Young to Run campaign, summed up the situation, stating that the political arena is more open on paper than in reality.
However, Afrobarometer has identified a paradox. While young people do vote less than their elders, they are also excluded from seats of power and the polls. This representation gap is anything but passive; it breeds disengagement. The IPU warns that young people’s absence from parliamentary assemblies undermines institutional legitimacy and jeopardizes trust in democracy. Senegal, listed in the 2026 IPU report as one of the countries where parliament grew younger in the most recent elections, shows that rejuvenation is possible when a political agenda empowers a generation.
Rewriting the deal: money, parties, obstacles
High age limit proponents demand experience. Across the 34 countries that Afrobarometer surveyed, citizens favor an average leadership age of 39. Those calling for a lower age limit seek proven engagement measures, such as lowering the eligibility age, quotas, and forums for young parliamentarians. However, as Nigeria shows, often, the main obstacle is financial.
Nigeria’s ruling party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), has set the total cost of its 2027 presidential nomination and expression-of-interest forms at NGN 100 million (USD 75,000), NGN 30 million (USD 22,521) for the expression of interest, and NGN 70 million (USD 52,550) for the nomination. The Senate will cost NGN 20 million (USD 15,014) and the House of Representatives NGN 10 million (USD 7,507).
Young people will receive a 50 percent discount only on nomination fees, leaving the presidential bill at NGN 65 million (USD 48,789). A Nigerian civil society group calculated that workers earning the minimum wage, NGN 70,000 (USD 52) per month, would have to work for more than a century to buy some of these forms.
The Electoral Act, 2026, signed on February 18, also doubled the presidential candidate’s campaign spending limit to NGN 10 billion (USD 7.5 million) and tripled that of governorship candidates to NGN 3 billion (USD 2.2 million).
At the initiative of ECOWAS and the youth-led advocacy organization Legis360, delegates from 12 countries gathered in Dakar to bring these obstacles to the forefront. In their communiqué, they launched the West Africa Youth Observer Network (WAYON) and called for youth quotas, reduced candidate fees, and spending limits. ECOWAS later announced it would deploy youth-only election observers for Nigeria’s upcoming presidential election on January 16, 2027.
Other countries exemplify how laws can directly impact nominations. According to the IPU, Ecuador owes much of its progress to a 2022 law, which required 25 percent of its candidates to be young adults. Countries with term limits also have considerably more young parliamentarians than the global average. In 2023, the IPU also noted that limited youth funding and a lack of spending limits contributed to aging parliamentary assemblies.
Elsewhere, the obstacles are political. Take, for example, Benin. After disqualifying the main opposition candidate (Les Démocrates) for failing to meet election requirements, current President Romuald Wadagni faced only one opponent (Paul Hounkpe). On April 12, 2026, Wadagni subsequently won the presidential election with 94.27 percent of the vote. In 2024, a constitutional reform that extended the presidential term from five to seven years also raised the minimum vote threshold for securing seats in the National Assembly from 10 percent of parliamentary election votes to 20 percent. This regulation far outweighs a candidate’s date of birth when they have no party machine behind them.
Another example is Burkina Faso. In January 2026, the military junta dissolved all political parties. Meanwhile, in The Gambia, President Barrow will run for a third term in the December 5 presidential election.
Inclusive voting, but flawed representation
Is a system that gives young people the right to elect their leader but impedes their ability to become one themselves fully inclusive? The findings speak for themselves. Although Nigeria has lowered its age limits and Ghana has committed to doing the same, these limits are more a symptom than a cause. Age is not the sole contributing factor.
Critics argue that lowering age limits without also addressing nomination costs, party regulations, and the openness of the political arena would only be the first step on a seemingly endless staircase. What stands between young people and decision-making positions are exceedingly high costs, restrictive nomination practices, candidate exclusions, and even the lack of parties.
Until street movements have credible institutional representatives, they will continue to wrest temporary concessions or, as seen in Madagascar, give way to powers other than those they had hoped for. The primary challenge of the West African Democratic Pact is making young people not only the promised future of politics, but also an active part of today’s representation.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The National Cyber Emergency Response Team (NCERT) has issued a high-severity WhatsApp Web cyberattack alert, warning of targeted phishing and malware attacks that arrive through WhatsApp Web, the WhatsApp desktop app and email.
Government officials and people who handle sensitive information are the main targets, according to the advisory. NCERT has rated the threat level as high.
How the attack works
The advisory says attackers pose as government officials and departments, then send harmful files to their targets. A file sent under the name of an official document can infect a Windows system when opened.
Phishing means tricking a person into opening a link or file, or giving up information, by pretending to be someone trustworthy. Malware is software designed to harm a device or steal from it.
If a system is compromised, NCERT says the risks include remote control of the device, password theft and data theft.
Why a message from a known number is not proof
The advisory raises a second risk, which is session hijacking. A WhatsApp Web session lets a computer use an account already logged in on a phone. If an attacker takes over that session, they could commit fraud from the victim’s own number.
For that reason, NCERT says an unexpected message or file from a number the recipient knows can itself be a sign of targeting. Another warning sign is an unfamiliar device in the “Linked Devices” list in WhatsApp.
What NCERT recommends
The advisory advises officers who hold sensitive information not to use WhatsApp Web or the desktop app on Windows. It also recommends that WhatsApp files not be moved onto official Windows computers.
For everyone, the recommendations are:
End any suspicious WhatsApp Web sessions immediately.
Do not open unverified links, files or messages. Confirm through a separate channel first.
Never share passwords, one-time passwords (OTPs) or verification codes.
Keep Windows, browsers and other software updated.
Turn on two-factor authentication and WhatsApp’s two-step verification.
If a compromise is suspected, the device should be disconnected from the network and the internet at once. Messages and logs should be saved as evidence and not reopened.
Users can check their own account in WhatsApp under Settings, then Linked Devices. Any device they do not recognise should be removed.
Bottom Line
The advisory’s most notable instruction is also its most restrictive: officers with sensitive information should avoid WhatsApp Web and the desktop app on Windows altogether. That is a stronger step than the usual advice to be careful with links, and it suggests NCERT sees the risk as built into the setup and not just a matter of user mistakes.
WhatsApp is widely used for day-to-day work communication, including in offices. Messaging apps tend to feel informal, which lowers people’s guard, and a message from a familiar name carries a trust that email does not. Attackers who copy official names are using exactly that habit.
The practical test of the advisory will be whether departments turn it into written rules about which channels officials may use for official files. Warnings reach individuals, but only policy changes what a whole office does by default.

items.title: [Update] IRDAI Extends Feedback Deadline For Insurance Distribution Reforms To Oct 31
items.summary:
Update | October 26, 12:52 IST
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has extended the deadline for stakeholders to submit feedback on its proposed insurance distribution reforms to October 31 from October 25, following an “encouraging response” to the consultation paper.
The insurance regulator said it has received more than 650 comments on its consultation paper, titled ‘Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution’, released on September 23. The paper proposes changes to commission structures for insurance distributors and expense limits for insurers.
“In view of the significant interest and to facilitate wider participation, the last date for submission of comments has been extended till 31st October 2026,” IRDAI said.
The extension comes amid opposition from insurance brokers over the proposed changes, with the Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) previously seeking an extension of the feedback deadline until December 31, 2026.
Original |
items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Update | October 26, 12:52 IST
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has extended the deadline for stakeholders to submit feedback on its proposed insurance distribution reforms to October 31 from October 25, following an “encouraging response” to the consultation paper.
The insurance regulator said it has received more than 650 comments on its consultation paper, titled ‘Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution’, released on September 23. The paper proposes changes to commission structures for insurance distributors and expense limits for insurers.
“In view of the significant interest and to facilitate wider participation, the last date for submission of comments has been extended till 31st October 2026,” IRDAI said.
The extension comes amid opposition from insurance brokers over the proposed changes, with the Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) previously seeking an extension of the feedback deadline until December 31, 2026.
Original | October 7, 12:14 IST
The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) has said that the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (IRDAI) recently proposed norms could trigger a 60-70% revenue collapse across the insurance broking sector.
Addressing a press briefing, the industry body representatives also said that the insurance distribution sector, which employs over 83 Lakh people, could see the loss of up to 10 Lakh jobs lost as a result of the economic impact of the proposed policies.
This comes days after IRDAI proposed reintroducing product-wise commission caps for insurance distributors. The regulator also proposed tighter limits on insurers’ overall expenses over concerns related to disproportionate increases in commissions paid to distributors.
The industry body has also sought an extension of the deadline to submit feedback on the proposed norms to December-end from October 25 currently.
While noting that the association supports the regulator’s goal of making insurance more affordable and accessible, the IBAI representatives noted that the proposed sweeping changes threaten small businesses and MSMEs.
The resulting job losses could impact insurance awareness, policy renewals, assistance to policyholders, and penetration of insurance among underserved communities, the representatives added.
The brokers also countered IRDAI’s data that showed that general insurance premiums sourced through brokers had risen 37% whereas commission payouts zoomed 173% between FY23 and FY27. The industry body argued that the rise in commissions since FY23 largely reflected the reclassification of off-book marketing expenses following regularisation, and did not reflect inflationary pressures on insurance consumers.
The IBAI also claimed that the entire general insurance industry’s operating expenses averaged around 26.5% of gross premiums as against the mandated limit of 30%. Making its point, the representatives also claimed that policyholders received back ₹84.4 in non-life insurance claim payouts for every ₹100 of premium paid over a five-year period.
This is more than the global average of 72-75%, demonstrating the efficiency of the market in delivering value, the body’s representatives claimed.
The industry body said it was ready to work with IRDAI to address specific market anomalies, such as misselling or disproportionate remuneration. It has also submitted formal letters to the Prime Minister’s Office and the Finance Ministry on the matter.
Notably, the pushback comes as insurtech platforms continue to be up in arms against the proposed norms. Last week, Sanjib Jha, founder of insurtech startup Coverfox, said that the proposal could impact the viability of distributing insurance to rural and low-income borrowers.
Pune-based insurance broker Quickinsure has also trimmed more than 100 jobs in response to the proposal as its founder Anand Shrikhande projected that the industry would see more than 1 Lakh jobs affected due to the changing economics.
The news has also triggered a major sell-off in listed insurtech majors PB Fintech, which operates Policybazaar, and Turtlemint over fears that the IRDAI’s new policies would dent their core businesses.

items.author: Press Release
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
vivo today officially introduces the vivo Y32 in Pakistan, a highly anticipated smartphone designed for users with long, demanding days. Designed for young professionals, mobile workers, and anyone who needs a device that can keep going, the Y32 debuts with a clear and powerful promise: to deliver all-day power without compromise. By combining a massive 8000 mAh All-Day Battery with an expressive design and practical durability, the newest addition to the Y series is engineered to be a reliable partner for work and life, ready to help users power through their day.
Power that Lasts, Today and for Years to Come
At the heart of the vivo Y32 story is its extraordinary battery endurance, built to eliminate power anxiety from morning until night. For a delivery rider navigating the city, a contractor at a job site, or a professional moving between meetings, a dead battery means a disruption to their work. The vivo Y32 solves this with its massive 8000 mAh All-Day Battery, a power cell designed to support the most demanding schedules with fewer charging interruptions. Users can finally enjoy the freedom to use navigation for hours, stay in constant communication with clients, and still have enough power for entertainment on the commute home. It is truly a ‘’Business Never Stops’’ experience.
To put this capacity into perspective, a single charge can comfortably support an uninterrupted daily routine. Imagine waking up at dawn, running GPS turn-by-turn navigation, handling continuous client correspondence, taking real-time product photos, and streaming music in the background; all these can be done without battery anxiety. In a 12-hour mixed-use scenario, the Y32 finished with 20% battery remaining, leaving power for whatever comes next.
But true power is not just about a single day’s charge; it is about long-term reliability. The Y32 is built for the long run with its 6-Year Battery Health. Under vivo’s laboratory testing, the battery is engineered to retain at least 80% of its health after 1,500 complete charging cycles. Based on a full charge every 1.5 days, this is equivalent to approximately six years of reliable performance, ensuring the phone feels as dependable on day one as it does years later. The powerful battery can deliver stable performance even under extreme temperature conditions. Rigorous lab tests also show that Y32 can stand by for 4 hours at -20°C and can maintain storage function for 24 hours at -40°C, helping users brave through temperature challenges.
This long-term reliability is supported by a Smart Charging Engine that learns user habits to reduce unnecessary battery wear, and Overnight Charging Protection that intelligently completes charging before wake-up time. For those moments when a quick top-up is needed, 44W FlashCharge offers a fast and practical way to recharge during a short break, getting you back to your day without long delays.
A Design that Stands Out and Is Ready for Business
The Y32’s design ensures it remains a sophisticated and highly professional companion for any setting. The device moves beyond mere utility, presenting an expressive and sleek physical identity that serves as an elegant social business card for client meetings and formal occasions alike.
This premium look and feel is anchored by the Premium Metallic Camera Design, which provides a strong, modern visual signature for the rear of the phone. Rather than treating the camera as a purely functional element, vivo has elevated the module with a meticulously crafted metallic grain texture and precise detailing, transforming the camera area into a focal point of refined craftsmanship. This structural sophistication is further enhanced by Dynamic Light, which balances the entire camera design. It not only provides real-time, at-a-glance notifications for calls, messages, and key alerts, but also offers different colored light flashes with dynamic effects, bringing the phone to life and reflecting consumers’ style and mood.
Durability Built for the Unexpected Moments
The vivo Y32 is built to handle the realities of a busy workday. It features IP68 & IP69 Dust and Water Resistance, providing extra protection against demanding environments. Whether you are caught in a sudden downpour on your commute or working in a dusty outdoor environment, you can have confidence that your device is built to brave the elements.
This is reinforced with Anti-Drop Armor Design, which provides another layer of protection against the accidental bumps, knocks, and drops that can happen in real life. Backed by an SGS 5-Star Premium Performance Mark for Overall Unit Drop Resistance, the Y32 is designed to be resilient without the bulky look of a rugged phone. It is a device that looks expressive and fashionable while being better prepared for the small accidents of a demanding day.
Availability
The vivo Y32 will soon be officially available for purchase in Pakistan soon. The device will be offered in three colors: Twilight Red, Sunset Orange and Meteor White. To suit different storage and multitasking needs, the Y32 comes in (6GB+128GB) and (6GB+256GB) memory variants, priced at PKR 82,999 and PKR 99,999, respectively. Reddit user u/leftyhyzer16 on the subreddit r/iPhoneDuo posted a picture of his new iPhone Duo, which had developed a crack on its foldable screen right in the middle of the display, where the crease is. Along with the crack, the display of his unit has seemingly also developed a green line of pixels running vertically and another band running horizontally. iFixit, in his iPhone Duo teardown video and blog post, called Apple’s foldable the most repairable foldable, while highlighting that it has a “huge screen problem”. iFixit writes that the issue could possibly be because the support bar in the middle failed to retract properly in specific cases, which put pressure on the flexible screen of the iPhone Duo, causing the cracks. The second theory says that the curved rails of the hinge could be causing the screen to break.

items.title: What Silicon Valley playbooks get wrong about African markets
items.summary:

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Every few years, the same story plays out. A well-funded company arrives with a playbook that worked in San Francisco, raises a big round on the strength of a market-size slide, and burns through it in 18 months.
Think Uber in Nigeria, except that took a little longer.
The post-mortem usually blames “the market”. The market was fine. The playbook was the problem.
African tech does not need protecting from Silicon Valley thinking. It needs that thinking applied honestly, to the conditions that actually exist, rather than the ones a pitch deck assumes. Here are five places the standard playbook breaks, and what tends to work instead.
There is no “African market”
The most common mistake starts on slide two: one continent, one TAM, one go-to-market plan. Africa has 54 countries, dozens of currencies, multiple legal traditions and some of the most linguistically diverse populations on earth.
Lagos, Nairobi and Cape Town are not three cities in one market. They differ in payment rails, regulators, consumer habits and how business relationships get built. A product that wins in Kenya on mobile money can stall in South Africa, where cards and bank apps dominate.
The Valley instinct is to expand fast and localise later. Here, localisation is the product. Treat each new country as a new launch, with its own team, partners and regulatory work, and budget the time accordingly.
Infrastructure is not someone else’s problem
The Silicon Valley stack assumes a lot: reliable power, cheap broadband, a card in every wallet, a street address on every door, couriers who can find it. Startups there build on top of infrastructure. Startups here often have to build the infrastructure first.
That changes the economics. Logistics companies end up running their own fleets. E-commerce players end up building payments. Fintechs end up building identity and credit data. The “asset-light” model looks great on paper and rarely survives first contact.
The upside is that infrastructure becomes a moat. M-Pesa did not just ride Kenya’s payment gap; it filled it, and every business built on top of it since has paid that compliment. Design for load-shedding, patchy data and expensive bandwidth from day one: offline modes, light apps, USSD and SMS fallbacks. These are not edge cases. They are the main case.
You can’t subsidise your way to trust
Blitzscaling assumes growth can be bought: discount heavily, win the market, raise prices later. In many African markets, that trade does not hold. Customers acquired through subsidies leave when the subsidies do, and a brand that disappears after a funding crunch is remembered for it.
Trust here is earned slowly and through people. It moves through agents, shopkeepers, churches, WhatsApp groups and family networks. Cash on delivery, human agents and local customer support in local languages are not inefficiencies to optimise away. They are how a new product proves it will still be there next month.
The companies that last tend to grow slower in year one and much faster in year three, because their customers stay and bring others with them.
The informal economy is the economy
The playbook’s default user has a salaried job, a bank account, a credit score and a smartphone with plenty of data. That person exists, but they are a minority of the market. Most economic activity across the continent happens informally: in markets, spaza shops, taxi ranks, savings clubs and side hustles.
This is not a gap waiting to be “formalised” by your app. It is a sophisticated system with its own logic. Stokvels and chamas are working savings and lending products, with built-in social accountability most fintechs would envy. Informal traders manage inventory, credit and cash flow without software.
The winning products meet these systems where they are. They digitise what people already do instead of asking them to adopt a new behaviour. Spend time in the market before you write the spec, and you will build something different.
The venture math ignores currency and exits
A startup can triple revenue in local currency and still shrink in dollars. Sharp devaluations in markets like Nigeria, Egypt and Ghana have done exactly that to companies with strong local growth. Raising in dollars while earning in naira or cedi is a structural risk, not a footnote.
Exits are the other blind spot. The Valley model relies on deep IPO markets and a long list of acquirers. Here, the exit paths are fewer and slower, which means the “grow at all costs, sell later” plan carries more risk than the model admits.
This is why profitability, unit economics and local-currency funding deserve far more weight than they get in a typical pitch. A business that pays for itself has options. A business that needs the next round on schedule does not.
What works instead
None of this means abandoning ambition. It means swapping a few assumptions for better ones:
Win one market deeply before entering the next. Depth beats breadth when every country is a new launch.
Own the infrastructure you depend on. If a critical layer is missing or unreliable, building it may be your real competitive advantage.
Measure retention before growth. Customers who stay without subsidies are the only signal worth scaling.
Design for the real user. Low data, shared devices, cash, agents and local languages belong in version one.
Build a business that can survive the next devaluation. Watch unit economics in local currency and plan for slower exits.
Hire and lead locally. The people who understand the market should be making the decisions, not advising from the sidelines.
The advantage goes to those who unlearn.
The most interesting innovation on the continent did not come from copying the Valley. Mobile money, agent networks and USSD banking came from builders who started with the constraints and treated them as design inputs.
The opportunity is real: a young, fast-growing, increasingly connected population, and problems worth solving at scale. But it rewards patience, local knowledge and capital discipline more than speed and spend.
The playbook isn’t wrong everywhere. It’s just not universal. The founders and investors who succeed here are the ones willing to put it down and look at what’s actually in front of them.
The post What Silicon Valley playbooks get wrong about African markets appeared first on Disrupt Africa.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Unacademy cofounders Gaurav Munjal and Roman Saini are raising a ₹700 Cr venture capital fund to back AI and deeptech startups, less than two months after upGrad completed the acquisition of the edtech startup.
Named Longshot Capital, the Category II AIF has secured commitments of around ₹250-300 Cr and is targeting its first close in January 2027, ET reported, citing sources.
Munjal and Saini declined to comment on the development.
The Bengaluru-based fund plans to invest in 25-28 startups at the seed and pre-Series A stages, with initial cheques of $500,000 to $1.5 Mn and a targeted ownership stake of 8-12%.
Saini will run Longshot Capital full-time, while Munjal will be involved part-time alongside his role heading Unacademy. Both founders will serve as general partners of the investment firm.
The fund plans to deploy its capital over three years and will invest in India-based startups as well as companies founded by entrepreneurs of Indian origin. Its investment mandate will span AI-led businesses and deeptech segments such as manufacturing, space, defence and robotics, rather than consumer brands and retail businesses, the report said.
The fund will have a lifespan of 10-11 years, allowing it to back businesses with longer gestation periods, particularly in AI and deeptech, according to the report. Its prospective investors include startup founders, family offices and overseas institutions.
The fund formalises more than a decade of angel investing by Munjal and Saini. The two have collectively invested over ₹25 Cr through more than 200 angel cheques in companies including Pine Labs, Dhan, Seekho, Ultrahuman, Snabbit, Swish, STAGE, and Third Wave Coffee.
In August, the duo also invested in Superleap, an AI-native customer relationship management platform.
The proposed fund comes amid growing investor interest in frontier technologies, with Indian AI startups raising $438 Mn across 28 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 265% YoY. Meanwhile, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals during the same period, up 176% YoY.
Unacademy Founders’ Second Act
The move adds Munjal and Saini to a growing group of startup founders transitioning from personal angel investments to institutional fund management.
Snapdeal cofounders Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal raised ₹333 Cr in external capital for Titan Capital in 2024. Freshworks founder Girish Mathrubootham cofounded the AI-focused Together Fund, while CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti joined Singularity Growth as a general partner after his exit. Myntra founder Mukesh Bansal operates venture studio Meraki Labs.
The latest development comes over a month after upGrad acquired Unacademy in an all-stock transaction valuing it at ₹1,955 Cr, more than 90% below its peak valuation of $3.4 Bn in August 2021.
Founded in 2015 by Munjal, Saini and Hemesh Singh, Unacademy started as a YouTube channel before evolving into an online learning platform focused on competitive exam preparation. It raised around $880 Mn from investors including SoftBank, Peak XV Partners, Elevation Capital, General Atlantic, Temasek, and Tiger Global.
The startup became a unicorn in September 2020 and reached its peak valuation of $3.5 Bn in 2021, amid a pandemic-led boom in edtech investments.
However, the reopening of educational institutions and a slowdown in demand for online learning forced Unacademy to rethink its business strategy. Unacademy undertook multiple rounds of layoffs, cut cash burn and scaled down several verticals as it sought to move towards profitability. It also expanded into offline coaching centres to tap demand for in-person test preparation.
Unacademy subsequently explored acquisition opportunities with multiple players, including Allen Career Institute, K-12 Techno Services and upGrad. Its earlier merger discussions with upGrad fell through over valuation differences before the two companies revived negotiations and signed a term sheet in March. The acquisition was completed in September.
Meanwhile, Munjal, on X yesterday, pushed back on criticism against the risk appetite of Indian deeptech investors, highlighting that startups like Astrobase, Airbound and Sarvam AI have been able to raise large rounds in short time periods. He also noted that consumer tech companies like Groww, Eternal and Meesho, all of whom went public in recent years, have provided “spectacular outcomes”.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Apple’s first foldable iPhone has barely reached customers, but its durability is already becoming a major talking point. The iPhone Duo has suffered a disappointing result in a widely watched durability test, raising questions about how well the expensive device can withstand physical stress and everyday exposure to dust.
The latest findings come from popular YouTube channel JerryRigEverything, where Zack Nelson subjected the iPhone Duo to scratch, dust and bending tests. While the phone performed reasonably well in some areas, its folding mechanism and inner display struggled under more demanding conditions.
The biggest concern is not simply that the device failed the test. It is the potential cost of repairing the damage, particularly for customers paying a premium for Apple’s entry into the foldable smartphone market.
According to Nelson, replacing the iPhone Duo’s inner display could cost approximately $1,000, making screen damage an expensive possibility for owners.
The results have also drawn attention to the challenges Apple faces in making its first foldable smartphone as durable as consumers might expect from a conventional flagship iPhone.
Dust Resistance and Display Durability Come Under Question
The iPhone Duo carries an IP68 dust and water resistance rating, but Nelson’s testing revealed a potential weakness around its folding mechanism.
During the test, sand and dirt entered parts of the hinge assembly, affecting the magnets responsible for keeping the phone closed. As a result, the device could no longer shut completely and remained slightly open.
The findings are particularly notable because the hinge is one of the most important components of any foldable smartphone. Unlike a conventional handset, a foldable relies on moving mechanical parts that must continue working through repeated opening and closing.
The screen tests also produced mixed results. The outer display, protected by Apple’s Ceramic Shield 2, performed relatively well, showing only faint scratches at level 7 on the Mohs hardness scale.
However, the flexible 7.6-inch inner display proved considerably more vulnerable, developing scratches at level 2. Its matte nano-texture coating helped make some of these scratches less noticeable while the display was switched on, but did not prevent the underlying damage.
The most serious failure occurred during the reverse-bending test. When Nelson applied pressure to the unfolded device in the opposite direction, a permanent green line appeared across the inner screen. A second bending attempt caused additional display damage, eventually leaving the inner panel unresponsive to touch.
However, it is important to distinguish these extreme stress tests from normal usage. The findings reveal potential weaknesses under demanding conditions but do not establish that every iPhone Duo will experience the same problems.
Is Apple’s First Foldable Worth the Durability Risk?
For potential buyers, the durability concerns introduce another factor into an already expensive purchasing decision.
Foldable smartphones offer the convenience of a compact phone and a larger display in a single device. However, their flexible screens and complicated hinges also create potential points of failure that conventional smartphones do not have.
The iPhone Duo’s test results suggest that buyers may need to exercise additional care, particularly around dust, debris and pressure on the unfolded display.
There is also a difference between resistance to repeated folding and resistance to accidental damage. The latest durability test highlights how dirt entering the mechanism or pressure applied in the wrong direction can present a challenge.
Repair costs make the issue even more important. With an inner display replacement reportedly costing around $1,000, accidental damage could become a substantial additional expense beyond the phone’s purchase price.
Meanwhile, early software complaints have added to the discussion. Videos shared online show some applications struggling to adjust properly when switching between the smaller outer screen and the larger unfolded display.
These issues suggest that Apple may have more work to do in refining both the hardware experience and software support for its new form factor.
For Pakistani consumers, where premium imported smartphones already command high prices, durability and repair costs could become important considerations before investing in Apple’s first foldable.
The iPhone Duo remains an important addition to the foldable smartphone market, but its early durability results highlight a familiar challenge: delivering an innovative folding design is one thing, ensuring that it remains reliable and economical to maintain is another.
For Apple, the next test will be how the iPhone Duo performs in the hands of everyday users, rather than under the deliberately harsh conditions of a durability test.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) says it has broken up an international child abuse network in which a father allegedly produced and sold explicit videos of his own children.
Speaking at a press conference in Islamabad on Sunday, Additional Director Mohammad Shoaib Khan described the NCCIA child abuse network case as the first of its kind in Pakistan, with a father found involved in such offences against his own minor children. That description is the agency’s claim and has not been independently verified. No court has ruled on any of the allegations.
What the NCCIA alleges
Khan said the children involved were aged between four and five. According to him, the material was traded in closed online groups, with payments made in cryptocurrency.
The alleged ringleader is from Skardu and was arrested with help from international agencies, he said. Evidence and leads were recovered from Islamabad, Multan and South Punjab, and raids were continuing to arrest other people who helped run the network.
The agency has not named any suspect. It also has not said how many people have been arrested in this case, what charges have been filed, or which international agencies took part.
Other cases the agency cited
Khan pointed to a second case in which four members of an alleged gang were arrested after investigators examined about 60 videos recovered from a child’s phone. He said the suspect approached children aged six to 14 on social media and offered them money, and that the material was then sold abroad through messaging groups. He added that two Chinese nationals had been convicted earlier in connection with this crime.
He also described a Karachi case involving a minor girl who attempted suicide after months of harassment. She is receiving hospital treatment. Khan said the agency, working with her family, traced and arrested the main suspect in Islamabad within 13 hours. The suspect had allegedly harassed and blackmailed her for two to three years.
Separately, on October 23, the NCCIA’s Karachi zone said it had arrested suspects from three firms accused of producing and selling sexually explicit animated content, including animated child abuse material, to overseas customers.
Zero-tolerance directive
In a separate statement, NCCIA Director General Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi directed officers to adopt a zero-tolerance policy against people harassing citizens online, especially women and children. A meeting on the subject covered social media monitoring, cyber harassment cases, public awareness and the digital handling of complaints.
The scale of the problem
The cases the NCCIA described are specific, but the wider numbers explain why child protection groups treat them as part of a pattern.
Source
Finding
UNICEF
An estimated 1.5 million children in Pakistan experienced online sexual abuse in one year.
UNICEF
Around 85 per cent of perpetrators were known to the victims.
UNICEF
71 per cent of victims told no one; none surveyed reported through police, helplines or social workers
Sahil
At least 1,914 child abuse cases were reported nationwide in January to June 2026.
Sahil
1,015 child sexual abuse cases, 558 abductions, 101 missing children, 35 child marriages
Sahil
98 cases of pornography following sexual abuse
Sahil
58 per cent of victims were girls; ages 11 to 15 most vulnerable.
Sahil compiles its figures from newspaper reports across all four provinces, Islamabad, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan. That means the true number is likely higher, since cases that never reach the press are not counted.
What families can do
Khan urged social media users to think before uploading intimate material and not to share one-time passwords, bank details or personal information. He also warned about fake numbers and websites used to empty bank accounts.
Victims of cybercrime can call the NCCIA helpline on 1799, which the agency says operates 24 hours a day. Parents who find concerning content involving a child should not delete it, since it may be evidence. They should report it to the helpline and, where needed, to local police or a child protection organisation.
The most important figure in this story may not be the arrest. UNICEF’s finding that most perpetrators are known to the child, combined with the fact that no surveyed child used a formal reporting channel, points to a gap that enforcement alone does not close.
Investigators can trace payments and trace accounts, as they say they did here. But in cases where the person responsible is a family member, a child has almost no way to raise an alarm. Detection then depends on schools, doctors, neighbours and platform monitoring.
If the allegations in this case are proved in court, the test will be whether the response extends past the arrests: prosecutions that hold, protection and counselling for the children, and reporting routes that a child could realistically use. The NCCIA has not said what care the children in this case are receiving.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Sunday launched the PM Youth Chromebook Scheme, a programme to hand 500,000 refurbished Chromebooks and internet devices to students across Pakistan within two years.
At the launch ceremony in Islamabad, he personally distributed laptops and internet devices to high-performing Grade 9 students and students from seminaries. For many of them, it may be the first computer they have owned.
PM Youth Chromebook Scheme registration is handled through an online portal run by the Inter Board Committee of Chairmen (IBCC), and not every student can use it.
The scheme aims to distribute 500,000 refurbished Chromebooks and internet devices over two years. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif launched it in Islamabad on Sunday. For families wondering whether their child qualifies, the eligibility rules matter more than the headline number.
Who qualifies
Selection is based on the results of the 2026 annual examinations. High-performing Class 9 (SSC-I) students in Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan are eligible.
Only students enrolled in public-sector schools can apply, and private school students are excluded under the criteria announced so far.
At the launch ceremony, the prime minister handed devices to high-performing Grade 9 students and to students from seminaries.
How to register, step by step
Eligible students can check their details and register on the official portal at pmychromebooks.ibcc.edu.pk.
The process, as described in the source:
Open the portal and select your educational board.
Enter your B-Form number, CNIC number, roll number or registration number, whichever applies.
Type the number without dashes or special characters.
If the record is wrong or cannot be found, the student should contact the relevant board or school administration.
Keep the exam roll number and B-form handy before starting. Most lookup failures in portals like this come from a mismatched number or a typing error.
Deadlines differ by board
The last date for registration varies by educational board. There is no single national deadline. Students should check the notice from their own board and not rely on messages forwarded in family or school groups.
The scheme is large in number but narrow at the entry point. A target of 500,000 devices over two years sits beside an initial eligibility pool limited to high-performing Grade 9 students in public schools. Those two numbers do not obviously match, which suggests either later phases for other classes or a larger share going through other channels, such as the seminary group shown at the launch.
The government has not said which. Until it does, parents of Grade 8 or Grade 10 students and of private school students have no official answer on whether their children will ever qualify..

The sale will be subject to the terms and conditions specified in the General Notification F.No.4(2)-B(W&M)/2018 dated March 26, 2025, issued by Government of India, as amended from time to time. State Governments, Union Territories with legislature, eligible Provident Funds in India, designated Foreign Central Banks and any person or institution specified by the Bank in this regard can participate on non-competitive basis, the allocation for which will be outside the notified amount. Gabon restored access to social media on Saturday, its media regulator said, after an eight-month suspension that sparked widespread criticism.
The High Communication Authority (HAC) pulled the plug on social networks, including Facebook and TikTok, on February 17, blaming content posted online for stoking conflict and division in society.
The crackdown came as Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema faced a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election.
“The HAC has decided to lift the suspension of social media platforms,” spokesman Jean-Claude Franck Mendome said in a statement read on television.
Facebook and TikTok, the most-used platforms in the central African nation, as well as YouTube and Instagram, were shut down, while WhatsApp was on and off.
Some people still managed to access social networks via a VPN, with provider Proton reporting a 60,000-per cent increase in downloads of its VPN tool the day after the ban came into force.
The HAC said the suspension aimed to “allow the government to adapt its legal framework to better regulate social media”.
The government now requires social media users to provide formal identification, effectively ending online anonymity.
The HAC said it was working with Meta – which owns Facebook and Instagram – as well as TikTok and YouTube to “improve content moderation” on those platforms.
Gabon’s opposition had slammed the social media ban as an abuse of power.
Former prime minister Alain-Claude Bilie-By-Nze, who has been in prison since April over alleged abuse of trust and fraud dating back to 2008, was one of the policy’s most vocal critics.
Critics have cited the social media ban and Bilie-By-Nze’s arrest as examples of a repressive climate in Gabon, shattering hopes that President Nguema’s rise to power would lead to democratic change.
The 2023 coup that brought the military general into office ended 55 years of rule by the Bongo family, sparking scenes of jubilation, and he was elected president in April last year. (AFP)

Speaking at Korea’s National Day reception on October 23, 2026, in Abuja, Korean Ambassador to Nigeria H.E. Jeong Yoan highlighted Korea’s historic transformation from a war-torn nation in 1953 to a global economic power.
He emphasised that mutual support and international solidarity were central to Korea’s survival and remain key to its foreign policy.
“We do not come with all the answers. We come as friends and partners, ready to share, learn, and grow together,” Ambassador Jeong stated, identifying Nigeria’s vibrant youth population as its greatest asset.
Underlining this developmental synergy, the Ambassador pointed to key collaborative milestones, including the recently ground-broken Abuja Centre for Entrepreneurship—a joint project by KOICA, SMEDAN, and UNDP designed to nurture local start-ups.
Additionally, he said Korea’s Smart School initiative alongside UBEC has reached over 8,000 Nigerian children and trained 300 educators, while KOICA-FAO partnerships continue to pioneer green agricultural jobs.
He said major Korean conglomerates including Daewoo E&C, LG, Samsung, Hyundai, and Solpia also continue to deepen their footprint in Nigeria’s energy, manufacturing, and digital technology sectors.
Reflecting on the cultural bridge uniting both nations—from K-pop and Korean dramas to Afrobeats and Nollywood—Ambassador Jeong called for global unity, grounding the bilateral relationship in shared human values: “One Heaven. One Earth. One Humanity.”

items.author: Ibrahim Musa Giginyu
items.content:
The Emir of Katsina, Dr. Abdulmumini Kabir Usman’s address to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s Presidential Campaign Council during its recent visit to the Katsina Emirate has sparked mixed reactions among residents and political observers.
While some have described the monarch’s remarks as a courageous act of patriotism and a demonstration of responsible leadership, others believe he crossed the boundaries of his traditional institution by publicly addressing prominent political figures on sensitive political issues.
The reactions gathered momentum days after an audio recording of the visit went viral on social media.
In the recording, the Emir was heard urging political leaders to prioritise citizens’ welfare, promote peaceful coexistence, and address the challenges facing Nigerians.
The remarks attracted attention because they appeared to depart from the usual formalities associated with such visits, with the monarch delivering a blunt message about the responsibilities of political leaders to the people they seek to govern.
The Emir, who received the delegation led by Governor Dikko Umaru Radda and the Director-General of the campaign council, Senator Abdul’aziz Abubakar Yari, stressed that politics should not be reduced to hostility, confrontation, or personal attacks.
He urged members of Tinubu’s 2027 campaign council to place the interests of citizens above political ambitions, warning that leaders would ultimately be held accountable for how they discharged their responsibilities.
In the audio, the Emir told Yari that political leaders must support the people if they expected divine assistance in their own endeavors.
“DG, you are on board now, and as a community leader, I must say the truth whenever I open my mouth. You have to assist the people for God to assist you, whoever you are. We should know that God will surely ask us someday,” he said.
The monarch also called for unity among political leaders in the North-West, questioning the region’s response to persistent insecurity and the difficulties faced by farmers.
“We should unite ourselves, especially the North-West. North-West, where are we? Different forums here and there, and yet we are denied the opportunity to go to our farms, and we keep quiet. No, we have to talk,” he said.
During the visit, Yari said the delegation was at the palace to pay homage to the Emir and seek the support of the Katsina Emirate and the people of the state for Tinubu’s re-election bid.
Katsina-based political analyst, Dr. Bashir Ibrahim Kurfi, described the Emir’s address as an expression of responsible and responsive leadership, saying it reflected what many Nigerians expected from traditional rulers.
Kurfi said the monarch had identified fundamental issues requiring urgent attention, particularly insecurity, economic hardship, and the need to improve citizens’ living conditions.
He noted that while many residents welcomed the address as a timely reminder that public welfare should remain the priority of elected officials, others interpreted it as a significant intervention in the political conversations surrounding the 2027 general elections.
According to him, the Emir’s emphasis on the welfare of ordinary Nigerians reflected the concerns of people struggling with the rising cost of living and insecurity.
He added that political leaders should devote more attention to delivering on their promises than engaging in struggles for political power.
However, a politician, Ibrahim Ahmad KK, said he did not consider the substance of the Emir’s remarks wrong but disagreed with the manner and timing of their delivery.
KK argued that publicly addressing prominent political figures in such a manner was inappropriate, adding that the Emir could have convened a private meeting to raise the same concerns.
“He has the power to call for a meeting secretly and address all the valid issues he raised that day, but addressing top public figures publicly like that is wrong, and this is my personal belief,” he said.
He added that the incident could reignite discussions about the relationship between traditional rulers and politicians, particularly the limits of public criticism by traditional institutions.
In contrast, Malam Abubakar Ahmed, spokesperson for Senator Ahmad Babba Kaita, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) governorship candidate in Katsina State, said the Emir’s remarks accurately reflected the realities facing the region.
He said the monarch’s position aligned with the ADC’s advocacy for people-centred governance across the North-West.
“ADC is going to run a people-centred government, and that is why all the ADC candidates in the North-West have agreed to run a consecutive government approach to issues simultaneously in order to be able to tackle those pressing issues affecting the people of the region,” he said.
Despite the differing interpretations of the Emir’s address, the debate has drawn attention to the expectations of citizens regarding leadership, accountability, and the role of traditional institutions in public affairs.
For supporters of the monarch’s intervention, his message was a necessary reminder that the welfare and security of the people should take precedence over political interests. For his critics, the controversy centres on how such concerns should be communicated to political leaders.

The sector has been reeling under pressure from elongated project execution cycles as clients take time to assess the impact of new technologies, especially artificial intelligence (AI), on their businesses.Read more: Swiggy may rebound to Rs 190, but charts do not signal a trend reversal: LKP’s Vatsal BhuvaAt the beginning of the results season, analysts had anticipated double-digit aggregate revenue and net profit growth for the companies under their coverage, helped by broad-based momentum. "Expect 13 of 18 sectors to deliver double-digit sales growth, led by automobiles (around 29%), consumer discretionary (over 23%), industrials (over 22%) and nonbanking financial services (over 27%)," said Elara Securities (India).

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round.
The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied all projections to win an unprecedented fourth term at the helm of Latin America’s largest country.
According to official results, he won 51.75 percentof the votes to 48.25 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls.
With Lula’s victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries — such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru — all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump.
After a campaign marred by scandal and mud-slinging, Sunday’s vote plunged into chaos after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extending voting by two hours, at the request of Lula who said buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.
Supporters of Brazil’s President and Workers’ Party (PT) re-election candidate Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva react to the presidential runoff election results in the state of Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 25, 2026. Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on October 25, 2026, as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round. (Photo by NELSON ALMEIDA / AFP)
Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some parts of the country due to heavy rains, but his camp lashed out at the country-wide extension.
“Either we win. Or we win. Consider yourself warned,” pro-Bolsonaro lawmaker Nikolas Ferreira wrote on X as the votes streamed in.
The bitter campaign laid bare the deep divisions in the country of over 200 million people.
“It’s a disgrace. We’ve never had anything like this in Brazil, and now they’ve come up with the idea of extending the election period by two hours,” said Aurelio Junior, 45, a dentist in Brasilia.
Jacqueline Maria Lima de Franca, 34, a business owner in Rio de Janeiro backing Lula said it was “more than fair…everyone should have the right to vote, and that was being neglected.”
– Lula rises from the ashes, again –
Lula, a defining figure in Brazilian politics over four decades, was blindsided after his first-round defeat to Bolsonaro.
The left swung into action with massive rallies declaring “Never Again Bolsonaro,” where protesters recalled the former president’s chaotic handling of the Covid pandemic, devastation of the Amazon rainforest and cuts to public programs.
Lula also revamped his social media strategy, taking video selfies and even bought his first cellphone, while supporters carried out a feverish campaign to change the minds of family, friends and neighbors, and encourage them to vote after high levels of abstention.
His re-election marks another remarkable comeback for the man who grew up dirt poor in the northeast in a family of illiterate farmers.
Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months.
The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.
In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but voters complain about the cost of living and a sense of insecurity.
Lula’s social policies became a point of tension as he expanded welfare programs during the campaign.
“Brazil needs more time with Lula, primarily because the country is on the verge of falling into the clutches of fascism,” Maria Fernanda Elisbao, a 21-year-old editorial assistant, told AFP.
– A tricky term ahead –
Lula heads into a fourth term with a country divided, with almost half of the nation voting against him and desperate for change.
“We’re in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat — buying meat is out of the question,” said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro.
Already one of the world’s oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030.
He will thus have spent 16 years in power, following his first stint as president from 2003 to 2010.
Lula is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right.
His options are also constrained by the economic outlook, with growth expected to slow.
He has also come under renewed pressure to confront rampant insecurity in a country plagued by criminal factions that sow terror in working-class neighborhoods.
The president’s campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump’s United States.
Voters must “choose a country where the flag is respected,” he said, his raspy voice more hoarse than ever after a tireless campaign. He accused his rival of wanting to “govern with the American flag.”

items.content: Mumbai: India's equity valuations are at their lowest levels in six years following the recent market decline sparked by a slew of factors, including foreign selling, a weaker rupee, higher crude prices and rising US bond yields. But that may not be reason enough for overseas investors to reverse their pessimistic view, as stocks here, despite coming off their highs, remain more expensive than their emerging market (EM) peers.The dollar-denominated MSCI India Index trades at around 18.5 times its 12-month forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, the lowest level since May 2020. It hit a record high of 24.54 times in September 2024, when the Sensex and Nifty reached their all-time highs.135200161The valuation measure is down from 22.5 times at the start of the year and below its 10-year average of 19.7 times, but investors do not appear to be in a hurry to pile into battered Indian equities."The Nifty forward PE looks cheap only if you believe the forward EPS," said Vivek Iyer, partner and CIO at Rational Equity Asset Management. "With crude where it is, we think consensus estimates still have cuts ahead, so the true multiple is higher than the headline."In dollar terms, the Sensex and Nifty are down 18%-19% so far in 2026, while MSCI India has fallen 15.4%. Other than MSCI China, which has dropped 20%, most other markets are up.Read more: Swiggy may rebound to Rs 190, but charts do not signal a trend reversal: LKP’s Vatsal BhuvaIyer said the recent equity decline is more of a "large-cap de-rating" as mid- and small-cap stocks are still trading at a 50%-70% premium to their historical medians. "The broader market has not reset at all. The reset is incomplete," he said.Foreign investors tend to compare Indian equities with their regional peers. The MSCI Emerging Markets Index trades at 8.7 times forward earnings, down from 13.3 times at the beginning of the year and below its 10-year average of 12.05 times. India's valuation is roughly double that of EMs.Among other major markets, MSCI US, the most expensive, trades at around 18.8 times one-year forward earnings against its 10-year average of 19.2 times and has gained 12% in dollar terms so far this year. Taiwan and Japan trade at 16.8 times and 15.4 times forward earnings, respectively, versus 10-year averages of 15 times each, with the two markets gaining 57% and 17% this year. China trades at 9.2 times forward earnings versus its 10-year average of 11.5 times.Read more: Nifty bears tighten grip as crude, geopolitical risks, FII outflows mount: 5 factors to decide D-Street’s fate next weekThe argument in favour of India is that Indian equities have always traded at a premium to their peers because of the country's relatively stable corporate earnings outlook and broad-based market."We would avoid prescribing a fixed India-EM premium as fair value," said Saurabh Patwa, head of Equity and Portfolio Manager at Quest Investment Managers."A meaningful premium is justified where businesses deliver superior earnings growth with durability," he said.For now, many investors are not buying that argument, pointing to faster growth in South Korea and Taiwan, where semiconductor and chipmaking industries have emerged as some of the biggest beneficiaries of the global AI boom."In the near term, AI and data-centre investments are creating stronger growth opportunities in markets such as South Korea and Taiwan, competing for global capital," said Patwa.A decline in crude prices will be critical for Indian equities. "The valuation compression has been concentrated in large caps, particularly crude-sensitive and rate-sensitive stocks such as oil marketing companies, paints, autos, aviation, cement, consumer discretionary and lenders," said Iyer."That is where foreign selling has been concentrated because that is where the earnings risk from $100-plus crude is greatest."

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
By ANTHONY OGBEIFUN
As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general election, the country stands again at a familiar crossroads: the choice between narrow, sectional calculation and the broader national demand for justice, fairness and peace. Elections are not merely contests for power. In a plural society such as Nigeria, they are also referendums on whether citizens believe the state belongs to all of them.
Few Nigerian voices expressed this truth more memorably than the late elder statesman and Dan Masanin Kano, Alhaji Yusuf Maitama Sule. In May 2015, Sule led a delegation of the Northern Leaders Forum to congratulate then President-elect Muhammadu Buhari. His counsel on that occasion remains strikingly relevant today.
Sule told Buhari: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.”
It was a simple statement, but one carrying the weight of Nigeria’s history. The country’s recurrent crises—ethnic suspicion, religious tension, electoral violence, insecurity, economic exclusion and the erosion of public trust—are not disconnected accidents. They are symptoms of a deeper disorder: the feeling among many citizens that fairness is selective, opportunity is unequal and power is used to reward loyalty rather than serve the common good.
Sule understood this. “Behind every crisis anywhere in the world is injustice,” he said. And the antidote, he insisted, is “justice.”
That insight should guide every political party, candidate, campaign organisation and voter ahead of 2027. A nation cannot be held together by slogans alone. Neither can it be governed successfully by force, intimidation or the temporary advantage of incumbency. Sule warned: “The world itself can never be governed by force, never by fear, even never by power. In the end, what governs is the mind. What conquers is the spirit and the weapons of governing the mind and conquering the spirit are justice and fair play.”
Nigeria’s 2027 election will therefore test not only the popularity of candidates, but the moral seriousness of the political class.
Justice, in the sense Sule meant it, is broader than court judgments or legal technicalities. It includes fair representation, equitable distribution of public resources, respect for the rule of law, protection of minorities, credible elections and equal treatment before public institutions.
It means that a farmer in Zamfara, a trader in Onitsha, a teacher in Lagos, a fisherman in Bayelsa and a herder in Sokoto should all be able to expect the state to protect their lives, respect their rights and respond to their needs without discrimination.
Sule put it plainly: “If you do justice to all and sundry — and I say all and sundry — because Allah says, ‘If you are going to judge between two people, do justice irrespective of the tribe, religion or even political inclination; justice must be done to whosoever deserves it.’”
That standard is demanding. It rejects the politics of “our turn” when it becomes a cover for exclusion. It also rejects the politics of revenge, where one group’s victory is treated as another group’s defeat. Nigeria needs leaders who can rise above such thinking.
The late Dan Masanin Kano was equally clear that justice must not be selective. “I am not asking you — and I know you will not — to discriminate against any part of Nigeria,” he told Buhari. “But I am asking you to do justice to all parts of Nigeria.”
For political parties preparing for 2027, fairness must begin before the first ballot is cast. It must be visible in candidate selection, zoning arrangements, internal party democracy, campaign financing and the treatment of aspirants.
When parties manipulate primaries, impose candidates, marginalise women and young people, or allow money to determine nomination, they weaken the legitimacy of the eventual winner. A flawed process produces a fragile mandate. And a fragile mandate makes governing harder, especially in a country where citizens are already sceptical of political promises.
Fairness also requires issue-based campaigns. Nigeria’s problems are real: insecurity, unemployment, inflation, poor infrastructure, weak public services, climate pressure on agriculture and widespread poverty. These challenges do not respect ethnicity or religion. Candidates should therefore be judged on their plans to secure communities, create jobs, reform institutions, expand opportunities and restore public confidence.
A campaign built on fear, sectional resentment or religious division may win attention, but it cannot build a nation. Sule’s warning remains urgent: force, fear and power cannot govern the mind or conquer the spirit. Only justice and fair play can.
Sule linked justice directly to peace and development. “Justice will bring about peace,” he said. “Peace and stability are the pre-requisites of development.”
No society develops sustainably in an atmosphere of fear. Investors hesitate where contracts are uncertain and violence is common. Farmers abandon land where insecurity prevails. Young people lose hope where merit is ignored and corruption rewards the connected. Communities retreat into distrust when they believe the state protects some citizens more than others.
Peace is not merely the absence of gunfire. It is the presence of confidence: confidence that elections will count, that courts will be impartial, that public offices will serve the public, and that no region, faith or class will be permanently shut out of opportunity.
The 2027 election offers Nigeria a chance to rebuild that confidence. But it will require more than campaign rhetoric. It will require electoral institutions that are visibly independent, security agencies that act professionally, political actors who accept results peacefully, and citizens who refuse to be used as instruments of violence.
Nigeria does not lack talent, resources or ideas. What it often lacks is the disciplined commitment to justice that turns diversity into strength rather than division. Maitama Sule’s message was not addressed to one president alone. It was addressed to every Nigerian leader, in every generation, and to every citizen who hopes for a better country.
As 2027 approaches, voters should ask hard questions: Which candidate will uphold the rule of law even when it is inconvenient? Which party will distribute opportunity fairly? Which leader will govern for all Nigerians, not merely for those who funded a campaign or share a regional identity?
The answer should not be based on sentiment, ethnicity or fear. It should be based on justice.
Sule’s counsel remains a compass: “With justice, you can rule Nigeria well. Justice is the key.” If Nigeria’s political class embraces that key, the 2027 election can become more than another contest for office. It can become a renewal of the national promise—a step towards a country at peace with itself, fair to all its people, and capable at last of fulfilling its vast potential.
•Ogbeifun wrote in from Lagos.
The post Justice, fairness, peace and Nigeria’s 2027 election appeared first on Vanguard News.
